Love this game. Similar in play style to Everquest and Rift, but those games can't compare. This game has three huge things going for it: the Story, the Boss Mechanics, and the Community!
RE: Story
True it starts off pretty slow, and the trial simply won't get you into the story proper. It's not until you hit 50, the story truely comes alive and keeps you glued to the screen, ready to buy the Heaven's Ward collection asap.
RE: Mechanics
FFXIV: ARR, has perhaps some of the best boss mechanics I've experienced in an MMO. And I'm not talking just raids. Most the MMO's I've tried have good boss mechanics with end-game raids, but this game has them from the first dungeon forward. And not only the dungeons, but also story-related instances, you need to be wise about how you address the enemy or you just may not survive.
RE: Community
I love the fact that when you que up for a dungeon that you'll find yourself playing with characters from other servers. And Final Fantasy fans playing this game seem like some of the nicest people. Granted you'll get a troll now and again, but for the most part people are helpful and polite. The game even promotes mentoring of new players, and achievements for helping strangers, so you'll find a friendly face nearly every step of the game.

The Room is essentially an escape-the-room game with multiple "rooms". Your objective is to figure out this **** puzzle box in this attic. To help, you have your wits and a spectral eyepiece, which can sometimes reveal clues, look through certain surfaces; but mostly make it harder to see the boxes themselves.
Unfortunately, since you're in an attic, there isn't much in terms of ambient light, so it can sometimes be hard to see puzzle elements.
Hints are available for every puzzle element, and the game's nice about it - there are multiple clues available, which you unlock one at a time for your current element after some time has passed since your last clue/since you moved to your current element. Usually the first clue will direct you to the element in question, while the last clue will generally tell you either how the element is manipulated or where the codes are located on the box.
The actual puzzles themselves are (relatively) short; the full game can be finished in about two hours with either judicious use of the hint system or familiarlity with other games of this general type.
Get it if you're a fan of escape-the-room games and are okay with a short game. Avoid if you've got a low brightness screen or if you're not a fan of short games.

Summary:
The Room, not associated with Tommy Wiseau. You have inherited a safe from a recently deseased relative. I think. The plot is pretty vague, but it adds to the atmosphere of "supernatural alchemy". The actualy game is a series of boxes that are unlocked by completing multiple tasks, done either sequentially or simultaneously. Typically finding a key, opening a drawer, picking up a piece of metal, recognizing the shape and placing it on a similarly shaped indentation on the other side of the box, which opens a panel exposes a keypad, and now you have to search for the hidden combination. Trying to connect all the dots can have you playing for hours. And no longer, because that's how long it takes to beat the game.
Thoughts:
Contrary to the uninanimously high approval ratings, I would not count this as a "great" game. What makes a game great is being good at multiple things: world design, mechanics, story, etc. This game is perfect at one and exactly one thing: intuitive design. Meaning it leaves a serious of dots for you to connect but doesn't hold your hand while you search for the next dot. If a game is too helpful then it's boring, not helpful enough and it becomes frustrating. The Room strikes a perfect balnce and that's what makes it a brilliant puzzle game, but it's lack of substance and replay value means it can't be remotely compared to "real" games with deeper stories and time sensitive mechanics. So it's not the best game of all time, but it has it's place on a few niched top 10 lists.

No, it's dead.  But you can enjoy shades of it in Death Star Battle (more on that later) and in some less-subspacey game modes.
Subspace is a game where you start with a gimped, impoverished ship, surrounded by variously-powerful enemy ships (some of which will completely ignore you rather than fight you until you grow large enough to be interesting to them; some of which will target you precisely because you are a small fish), and prizes that you can seek out to become more powerful.  Unless you're ganged up on, or surprised, or if you're still a small fish and don't have the speed and agility and powerups to get away, it's relatively hard to kill you if you don't want to fight.  It's much, much easier to kill you when you're fighting, because you consume your own regenerating health to fire your weapons.  So combat is very much about commitment, and about punishing others for overcommitment, and about reasons to fight (collecting a high bounty, revenge, control over an area, control over flags) rather than to run away.  And also about surprise and numbers and 'vulching' - swooping in to kill an enemy weaked from combat with a third party.
That game, the game I just described, is dead.  It no longer exists.  Of the zones in this game today, the only one with the
to support that game is the Chaos one.  Which still skips the 'small fish' phase, and which doesn't have the required population for the game model to work and be fun.  When you go to Chaos you don't find chaos; you find serial 1v1s with people who have no reason to commit to fighting with you, and bots.
The other zones mostly don't have anything like the classical ruleset.  Take Trench War: almost every ship has a one-shot-one-kill weapon.  If you can always kill an enemy in one hit,
no longer matters, there's no longer such a thing as a 'weakened enemy', it longer matters that you consume your own health when you shoot.  Only positioning and aim matters -- in a game with coarse-grained keyboard movement.  Trench is fun, sure, but it's not Subspace any more than a Tower Defense arcade game is Star Craft 2.
Yes!  It's not always that populated, but DSB can be fun with only four players between the two main teams (and I see those low numbers only because I work at night in the US.  And I still see much larger numbers, f.e. when the Finns come online.)  In spite of what might seem like massive deviations from the classical ruleset, DSB still has the fundamentals of energy management, commitment to fighting and punishing that commitment, reasons to fight, and so on.  The ships also have subtle but important differences, like they did classically, even if they're different differences.  And whereas Trench has ships that are sort of a chore to play, every ship in DSB is satisfying and useful, and every ship should be played somewhat differently, to make the most of it.  At a first glance a Warbird (Tie FIghter) might look like a mirror of the Terrier (A-Wing), but then you note: Tie Fighters can spam bullets while losing a lot less enegy; A-Wings can boost (shift-move) without losing energy, are much more maneuverable, and regenerate faster.  So with Tie Fighters you tend to keep at range and try to control an area so that your teammates can get easier kills, whereas with A-Wings you prefer to move in and dodge around fire to deftly kill enemy ships.
So grab the Star Wars shipsets and sounds and come play DSB.  It's fun, and it's as Subspace as you can get in this fallen world.  When you're frustrated with DSB, or when its population is lower, play Trench Wars.
Newbie tips: cycle through help screens with F1.  When you're done, hit F2 until you can see your teammates as you prefer.  Attach to your teammates (anyone in DSB; Terriers only, in Trench Wars) and then detach to help them, and try to stay alive so that they can attach to you and keep the fight going.

I figured, for review #100, I'd review a chunk of my childhood. I've played this game, on and off, since... fourth or fifth grade?
This game recently came to Steam, free-to-play, and I'm genuinely surprised to see that most of the same servers I used to play years ago are still up and running, and the community is still friendly - Legitimately friendly, not the kind of "friendly" you come to expect nowadays where "friendly" is silence. People will be eager to help you learn the ropes, and more often than not people will encourage you when you're doing bad, cheer you on when you're doing well, and generally be engaging in a meaningful way.
I can't stress enough how pleasant it is to play video games with people who act like mature human beings and not racist, misogynistic, and completely toxic. Hell, upon creating a new account (because I can't remember my information from the late 90's) and joining a server, I received a few PMs asking me if I was new or returning, and if I needed anything. That's a rarity nowadays.
Subspace is a 2D space shooter with a variety of rulesets. Different servers approach the game in varying ways. One popular server, Trench Wars, ends up being relatively slow paced due to how quick you can die. Another server, Death Star Battle, tries to emulate Star Wars, and is incredibly fast paced. Even then, each server has multiple minigames often going on, such as duels, CTF with their individual rulesets, or more. With the wide variety of servers available, you're bound to find something that fits in with your playstyle.
I can't stress enough how wonderful it is to see this game on Steam, and I sincerely hope it gets a population bump from it. It was this game and Sony's Infantry that carried a significant chunk of my childhood.

If you're looking for a game where the sound design makes you feel like your punching a bag of crunchy tortilla chips, with all the gorey, gooey fun of MK. This is the beat-em up you're looking for. Combat is fast and fun, the character designs are good and the levels have a ton of diversity.
The weapons and berserk fatalities make for a grand ol' time. And when they give you an option to be bad♥♥♥♥♥ they really do sell your ungodly ability to end lives as you run through jobbers like a mobile woodchipper with a grudge. (The final mission alone has one the best killing spree segments I've ever experienced.)
The Bosses, albeit shallow, do make you want them dead. Their designs are cool, and they are held in some of the coolest boss rooms I've seen (Cage match with a bear? Bring that♥♥♥♥♥♥on.)
Add on couch MP where 3 others can hop in so long as you have the controllers for it and you got yourself a night of russian action.
There will be some annoying segments, but none that really ruins the gameplay enough to dig on it too hard. The only real gripe I have is that after you learn the majority of the moves you don't really get anything further in terms of new combos.
Cons aside, its a good game, well worth it's price range. The limit to only couch MP doesn't do much to hurt how fun the game is when you do have people to play with. A solid 8/10 through and through.

My best friend introduced me to this game, and it quickly became one of my favorites.
It tackles two odd tropes: being a cop, and being a cop in Hong Kong.
The Asian world is often overlooked as a setting for open-world games, and Sleeping Dogs highlights what a massive mistake it is. Bright neon lights shine overhead as you drive through crowded streets, vendors and tourists plague the sidewalks, and an uncanny mixmatch of colors swirl together to give a strange contrast to the grey and brown of, say, Grand Theft Auto's cities. The game world is, admittedly, a bit too crowded at times, and some textures don't hold up all that well, even in the Definitive Edition, but, when you race along the pavement in the glistening storm, with the life of a city brimming up around you, it's an experience unmatched in its genre.
The gameplay is mostly divided into two branches: Triad and Officer.
Officer gameplay is most centered around protecting civilians, solving cases through side quests, and generally tackling things in a non-violent fashion. Triad gameplay is a martial arts cousin of the Batman Arkham franchise, with an attack button and a counter button taking up most of your combat controls, with some melee weapons and firearms sprinkled in. You're rewarded with EXP for violent acts, such as environmental takedowns, where you shove someone into a doorway and slam the door on their head, or toss them into a fan and watch their brains become a mess of pink textures and glimmering blood. These are *NOT* morality systems. You're not encouraged to choose one or the other, but rather to balance them both, which is a relieving break from the "MAKE YOUR CHOICE" design philosophy that sank the seventh generation.
The story is nothing to write home about, but it is intriguing and well-presented. If nothing else, it does an excellent job of mimicking the stress an undercover position would place on an officer, and the conflict of loyalty and respect that would come with it. Wei Shen is a likable protagonist, and he only grows more endearing throughout the game, just like Winston and several of his Triad compatriots, and Raymond and his fellow police officers. There's a stark duality here that is thankfully ignorant of the player's wishes as a deciding factor. You *do not* choose the ending. The ending is prewritten, and it's well-written, which is more than I can say for several player-determinant stories.
I can't recommend this game enough. If you enjoy other crime-centric open-world titles, such as Grand Theft Auto or Saint's Row, and want to try something new, you'll find it in Sleeping Dogs. It's odd and charming all at once, with a thick layer of polish to keep it running with its heart shining through.
It's clear the people who developed this game cared about making a good game, and I think that's all that really needs to be said.

Summary:
The Room, not associated with Tommy Wiseau. You have inherited a safe from a recently deseased relative. I think. The plot is pretty vague, but it adds to the atmosphere of "supernatural alchemy". The actualy game is a series of boxes that are unlocked by completing multiple tasks, done either sequentially or simultaneously. Typically finding a key, opening a drawer, picking up a piece of metal, recognizing the shape and placing it on a similarly shaped indentation on the other side of the box, which opens a panel exposes a keypad, and now you have to search for the hidden combination. Trying to connect all the dots can have you playing for hours. And no longer, because that's how long it takes to beat the game.
Thoughts:
Contrary to the uninanimously high approval ratings, I would not count this as a "great" game. What makes a game great is being good at multiple things: world design, mechanics, story, etc. This game is perfect at one and exactly one thing: intuitive design. Meaning it leaves a serious of dots for you to connect but doesn't hold your hand while you search for the next dot. If a game is too helpful then it's boring, not helpful enough and it becomes frustrating. The Room strikes a perfect balnce and that's what makes it a brilliant puzzle game, but it's lack of substance and replay value means it can't be remotely compared to "real" games with deeper stories and time sensitive mechanics. So it's not the best game of all time, but it has it's place on a few niched top 10 lists.

Went in hopefully expecting something like Streets of Rage, or Capcom/SNK arcade brawler style gameplay.  Sadly, it's nothing of the sort.  No move-cycle combos, no real specials, no slight pause upon hit contact make the combat feel completely detatched and spammy.  This made all the more choresome as the screen is flooded with enemies, limiting you to jump-kicks and slides as seemingly the only viable offensive strategy, should one not wish to get caught in one blow from the masses and promptly stun-locked to death.
Great pixel visuals, albeit tarnished with animation that leaves much to be desired; the 2-frame walking animations in particular, at 60fps in motion stand out as rather cheap and sorely dated.  Decent music, however the deliberate low-key and sombre tone of the tracks lacks energy, further starving the on-screen action from conveying any real sense of agency.
Overall a painfully bland and somewhat boring beat-em-up, with little seemingly invested  into the actual feel of the game. Sadly far off par from the like of Streets of Rage Remake, or even the original Megadrive games.

A wonderfully simple game focusing on the moral dilemmas seen at the border while a war is going on. You play as an immigration inspector whose job is simple, either deny or accept immigrants to the country based on what documents are presented and what the guidlines are. As the days continue, the rules change, either updating or by being removed, directly influenced by the events happening in the various countries. More and more people are seen who are directly affected (such as one man who has all his documents in order but his wife doesnt and are both at risk of dying in their home country). Do you follow the rules or do you follow your morals?
The game can be difficult as there are daily payments such as rent, heat, and food. You get paid for each correct admittance or denial. People will sometimes offer bribes at the risk of a citation. The first two citation have no real penalty, serving as warning. Every citation after costs credits. As more rules are presented, the process can take longer, leading to fewer credits being rewarded. The player has to find discrepancies between the documents presented and the applicant (such as height, weight, different looks, expiration dates, etc.). These descrpencies become more difficult later on (such as passport expiring during their stay in the country). The game has a max of 31 days if you get one of the final endings as well as an endless mode (unlocked after getting a code for getting a certain ending)
Music is there, just in the main menu and the endings. There are 20 endings, based on what you do during the days and who you let in and out as well as certain spoiler events later on.
Graphics are simple and get the job done. Nothing special, small amount of nudity once the body scans are unlocked to detect weapons and drugs.

The Game is fun. Decent Graphics, Simple Controls, Great mechanics, and a not-too-shabby 'tutorial'.
There are a few drawbacks, though. Replayability is a bit on the low side, as progression is a bit slow and you end up doing very similar missions over and over until you have a ship capable of actually fighting Pirates, which can take a while to get.
There is an occaisional bug here and there, but other than that the game runs smoothly.
Aside from the progression issues, I see potential in this game. I love how you can run out of fuel in an uninhabited sector and have to call a nearby merchant for help. I like the money system, how you can ferry goods from one place to another to earn a profit. I like how the gameplay feels, and I would love to see a Multiplayer function.
Overall, great game. Definitely worth the money... oh wait, this game is free. also a plus.

From the old Minecraft mods, to various Zachtronics games, and now Factorio, it's been one failure after another to try and play this type of game.  They usually feel too shallow, too vague on directions, too alien in UI elements, and so on.
Yet, something about Factorio is different from the rest.  It turns the process of learning these machines and how to make them into a gradual and more engaging process.  It does an excellent job of slowly introducing new mechanics, and has plenty of depth to keep you engaged beyond the basic idea.  Don't get me wrong, it's not perfect; the UI bindings by default are a bit strange and occasionally you'll run into a mechanic that just doesn't seem to be controlled properly (for example, being unable to filter inserter functions by resource means you can't separate the coal from the iron, adding some extra challenge as you sort out a way to make your system work).
Aside from what's mentioned here, if Rimworld's tutorial were half as good as this one it would have been purchased by 50% of Steam's userbase overnight.
Still, if you're like me and enjoy basic management games while
never quite being able to "get into" other management games of the genre, give Factorio a spin and you may be as surprised as I was.
Darksiders got a proper PC rerelease for free, Resident Evil/Biohazard 7 is actually good (and not just a crappy PT clone), Rimworld is progressing rapidly, XCOM 2 has controller support, and I found an automatic management game I don't hate.  Why is 2016 suddenly so great?

[GLORY TO ARSTOZKA]
(actual review)
You work as the only customs officer in Arstozka, trying to process as many people as possible. Everyone you process successfully gets you money. But the rules get more complicated as the game goes, and too many screw-ups will get you fired. You have to feed your family (who have the worst immune systems in the world), keep them warm, and get them medicine if they get sick (which is every other day). I like the setting, and because it's pixelated and has nothing fancy to process, it will run on pretty much anything. It's not for everyone, but I really liked it.

A good game can create a unique environment that the player takes part in. Papers Please is one of those games. Although Papers Please barely ever leaves your small inspection desk in the corrupt communist country of Arstotzka (glory!) Lucas Pope is able to create an expansive universe where you feel fully involved. The game itself doesn't have much to it; it is beautifully simple and at some times annoyingly challenging. The overall goal is to make enough money inspecting travel papers to feed your family. You can do this by following every regulation, taking bribes, catching criminals, letting criminals through, or secretly leading a revolution. It doesn't matter, play the way you want to play. What really makes the game great is the setting. From East Grestin to the United Fed, the politics and controversy in the world surrounding your low-paying job is what makes Papers Please feel different from most games. Although it takes place in a large, complicated world with 7 giant countries, you hardly ever see the game outside of your work station. Instead, you get word of what is going on through immigrants and emmigrants coming and going through your inspection booth. Terrorists and secret societies demonstarte conficts outside and inside countries. You may not directly see the universe Lucas Pope creates, but you definitely feel like you're living in it.
TL;DR - Papers Please may be a simple game, but it creates a vast universe that you feel like you're taking part in, even if you don't see it first hand.
Side note: Many people seem to dislike this game because it wasn't what they expected it to be. You have to know that Papers Please is a PUZZLE GAME. It has a good storyline and a unique playstyle, but when it gets down to the basics, it is essentially a "spot the difference" sort-of thing.

My best friend introduced me to this game, and it quickly became one of my favorites.
It tackles two odd tropes: being a cop, and being a cop in Hong Kong.
The Asian world is often overlooked as a setting for open-world games, and Sleeping Dogs highlights what a massive mistake it is. Bright neon lights shine overhead as you drive through crowded streets, vendors and tourists plague the sidewalks, and an uncanny mixmatch of colors swirl together to give a strange contrast to the grey and brown of, say, Grand Theft Auto's cities. The game world is, admittedly, a bit too crowded at times, and some textures don't hold up all that well, even in the Definitive Edition, but, when you race along the pavement in the glistening storm, with the life of a city brimming up around you, it's an experience unmatched in its genre.
The gameplay is mostly divided into two branches: Triad and Officer.
Officer gameplay is most centered around protecting civilians, solving cases through side quests, and generally tackling things in a non-violent fashion. Triad gameplay is a martial arts cousin of the Batman Arkham franchise, with an attack button and a counter button taking up most of your combat controls, with some melee weapons and firearms sprinkled in. You're rewarded with EXP for violent acts, such as environmental takedowns, where you shove someone into a doorway and slam the door on their head, or toss them into a fan and watch their brains become a mess of pink textures and glimmering blood. These are *NOT* morality systems. You're not encouraged to choose one or the other, but rather to balance them both, which is a relieving break from the "MAKE YOUR CHOICE" design philosophy that sank the seventh generation.
The story is nothing to write home about, but it is intriguing and well-presented. If nothing else, it does an excellent job of mimicking the stress an undercover position would place on an officer, and the conflict of loyalty and respect that would come with it. Wei Shen is a likable protagonist, and he only grows more endearing throughout the game, just like Winston and several of his Triad compatriots, and Raymond and his fellow police officers. There's a stark duality here that is thankfully ignorant of the player's wishes as a deciding factor. You *do not* choose the ending. The ending is prewritten, and it's well-written, which is more than I can say for several player-determinant stories.
I can't recommend this game enough. If you enjoy other crime-centric open-world titles, such as Grand Theft Auto or Saint's Row, and want to try something new, you'll find it in Sleeping Dogs. It's odd and charming all at once, with a thick layer of polish to keep it running with its heart shining through.
It's clear the people who developed this game cared about making a good game, and I think that's all that really needs to be said.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I purchased this game about 3 days ago, and have a total of 42 hours of playing time. So to put it simply, I absolutely cannot stop playing this game (which rarely happens).
Overall Impression: Factorio feels like a strategy game, but may not be for everyone. You basically wonder around gathering resources (which is and understatement, because the point of the game is to automate the resource gathering and managing). To me, it's like re-living the days of playing Age of Empires against a few bots, but MUCH more satisfying. Factorio is addicting, and I have yet to remember a game that has kept me playing until 7:00 AM. Overall for the price, it's worth it.
PROS:
-Lightweight, no issues with game crashing, or bugs, or anything else that negative that is outside of gameplay
-A Great game if you like thinking about managing and automating resources. Tis an odd thing to enjoy, but it's 10/10 in giving you the ability to basically do whatever you want when it comes to building your factories.
-A Great game if you are patient. I've had to rebuild my overall factory/city like 3 times. Enjoyed planning it out again too.
-You get the complete factory experience without having to work a factory job (wouldn't recommend working a factory job).
-Lots of fun, the game is challenging in a lot of ways that doesn't make the user want to immediately quit. It's very rewarding.
CONS
-I think the music could be a bit better. I could not really stand to listen to the music past the 20 hour mark, just because it had some odd tracks. I imagine there could be a bit of improvement with that so the vanilla music is at least tolerable, if not catchy.
-Visuals could perhaps look a bit better (better close-ups, some icons are not distinct enough, better effects). Overall these are minor things that could be fixed easily, or ignored altogether (as they did not really impact how much I liked this game overall).
Overall, it's a great game if you like strategy. Bonus points for being actually pretty dang good for being Early Access.

If you ever wondered what Streets of Rage might look like as a grindhouse action movie, this is the game for you!
Mother Russia Bleeds is a side-on style brawler, cut from a similar cloth of many late 80's to early 90's arcade classics including the Streets of Rage trilogy, Final Fight trilogy, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989 version), Renegade (Nekketsu Kouha Kunio-Kun), and their countless knock-offs, spin-offs, and tributes.
However, Mother Russia Bleeds is set apart by featuring an overwhelming amount of over-the-top violence, gore, drug references, and even some nudity and crude humor. Kind of like a Saturday morning cartoon version of a 1970's Sonny Chiba movie.
The character handling is very sharp, well-designed and straightforward to learn. There's basically one or two attacks appropriate to each common situation, so settling into a comfortable pattern of dispatching each new crowd of enemies feels challenging and skillful without being overcomplicated.
There's a great impact to nearly all of the various attacks, whether straddling a mobster and slugging on him in a shower of blood and broken teeth or cracking a skinhead across the side of the skull with a baseball bat. It's a game that unabashedly revels in the crazed excess of over-the-top splatter violence. And in that respect, it's certainly fun.
That brings me to probably the biggest fault of Mother Russia Bleeds; it accomplishes said goal a little too well. It doesn't so much "cross the line of good taste" as it does completely and unambiguously blow past it. This is a game featuring frequent, almost constant drug use, references to prison♥♥♥♥♥♥ BDSM nightclubs, suicide, mass murder, and what I can only describe as torture porn.
I'm vehemently anti-censorship, and the game still gets a big reccomendation from me. However, I'd also reccomend that you brace yourself before playing, because things are going to get weird before all's said and done.
Oh! And they totally missed the perfect opportunity for a "Winners Don't Do Drugs!" reference in here somewhere. Somebody dropped the ball, what the hell, guys!?

EDIT:
The game got an update and the developer is warning people that old reviews may not be accurate, so I decided to update my review as well. The gameplay is unchanged, but they added a few new blocks. All but one of them behave the same, but one block they added was TNT. Although Minecraft already has this, it is cool to see in this game as well. Overall, the game is improving. However, I still don't believe it is complete enough to be on Steam and I stand by my negative opinion of the game.

Many reviews talk about this game as if it revolves around one box in one room. I don't know what game they were playing. There are five different boxes in five different rooms. This was a great little puzzle game.
It takes place in (like the title suggests) one single room, but that room contains a very, very, very, very complex, mysterious box that you have to open throughout the game's 5 Chapters. There have to be hundreds of different mechanisms inside that thing.
The solutions are easy enough to not be frustrating, but some require a good bit of thinking and are rewarding to figure out. And if you ever get stuck, a hint will be available after some time of no progression.
The graphics show great detail in the boxes and have a repeated theme of neat astral symbols (especially later on), and the shapes and colors of the mechanisms blend in but still give sufficient information on what you can click on and move to solve puzzles. The music is minimal and fits the mystical atmosphere, and the sound effects are extremely satisfying when you solve something.
The only problem I had here was that in Chapter 2 I had a graphical bug that hid the puzzle solution.
If your graphics setting is at "low" in Chapter 2 an area around some gears may be pitch black without textures, and since I didn't know this I couldn't see the switch that was supposed to be there. After switching to "medium" I could see everything and continue, though with a lot of lag, but after turning settings back to "low" the texture fixed itself and there was no problem for the rest of the game.
Definitely play this for a great puzzle game. It's short, but I got it on summer sale (going on now) for $1.24 and I'll be getting The Room 2 next for sure.

This game comes as a pleasant surprise to me.  As a general statement, many management games that focus on automation and machinery completely fail to hold my attention for long.  From the old Minecraft mods, to various Zachtronics games, and now Factorio, it's been one failure after another to try and play this type of game.  They usually feel too shallow, too vague on directions, too alien in UI elements, and so on.
Yet, something about Factorio is different from the rest.  It turns the process of learning these machines and how to make them into a gradual and more engaging process.  It does an excellent job of slowly introducing new mechanics, and has plenty of depth to keep you engaged beyond the basic idea.  Don't get me wrong, it's not perfect; the UI bindings by default are a bit strange and occasionally you'll run into a mechanic that just doesn't seem to be controlled properly (for example, being unable to filter inserter functions by resource means you can't separate the coal from the iron, adding some extra challenge as you sort out a way to make your system work).
Aside from what's mentioned here, if Rimworld's tutorial were half as good as this one it would have been purchased by 50% of Steam's userbase overnight.
Still, if you're like me and enjoy basic management games while
never quite being able to "get into" other management games of the genre, give Factorio a spin and you may be as surprised as I was.
Darksiders got a proper PC rerelease for free, Resident Evil/Biohazard 7 is actually good (and not just a crappy PT clone), Rimworld is progressing rapidly, XCOM 2 has controller support, and I found an automatic management game I don't hate.  Why is 2016 suddenly so great?

is a creep-em-up low-res walking simulator in a fairly small area.  It's the sort of horror game where nothing horrible happens; something horrible has
happened, and the game is a merely a framework to draw out the experience of finding out the backstory, doling it out in little dribs, drabs, and cryptic fragments.  There's no battles with eldritch beings, no desperate flight from predatory monsters, no jack-in-the-box jump scares.  It's more like hearing a campfire ghost story told by a skillful storyteller, who deliberately keeps the pace slow to draw you in before dropping each fresh abhorrent detail.
Like many of the "walking simulator" genre, the case could be made that this really isn't a game at all; just a horror story in the guise of a game.  Here, though, I find that forgivable for three reasons:

This is the type of game where it irritates me that I *have* to say "yes" or "no" to recommending a game.  I finished this game with an overall response of "...meh."  I wouldn't recommend it to *me*, but I see that many other players have enjoyed it, and the graphics were quite nice, the game ran smoothly, and it was a fairly simple game that didn't take long to play through.  I'm going with "no" by a very *small* margin, and mosly because the game has such a lot of praise already and sometimes I find differing opinions can help me make up my mind about a game I'm torn on (though for the moment, the game is free, so there's that to consider as well.)
I think the biggest problem for me is that the game description, between the first paragraph and the "facts about fingerbones" section, just gives too much away.  I suppose the author was trying to avoid negative reviews by keeping people from playing it who might be looking for what the game "isn't", but I think one has to risk that, and based on the general positivity of the reviews I think the author *could* have risked that.  For myself, because I knew what *wasn't* coming, and I had a good idea of what was, a lot of the suspense was lost.
The second issue as far as suspense building went was the music.  I found it somewhat irritating rather than moody: if you stand in one place too long trying to figure out what you're supposed to do - which, since you're given very little lead, is going to happen - I found it would just stay on one note, and the irritation that caused would pull me out of the puzzle I was working on, and therefore the atmosphere that the author was trying to build around me.
Thirdly, I also think that one more setting should be added - because there are several back-and-forth runs, movement speed should really be something else you can increase.  I grew frustrated at the slow speed every time I was going through areas I'd already passed and knew - again, breaking that aura of suspense that this type of game needs in order to succeed.

Overall a charming game but not one I can recommend.
Positives:
* The art style is gorgeous, everything is so visually appealing and the art style is quite unique. I'm infatuated with the backgrounds, for example, the complex hammer and sickle sign on the road/bridge level.
* Nice, simple moveset. When a fighting game gives me a light/medium/hard punch and kick I get annoyed and typically default to medium (cause I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥. This game has punch, kick, grab. And honestly, when there's an enemy or two left and you dash-grab one and pummel 'em- SO satisfying!
* Well executed "checkpoints." Many a frustrating level made me saying "more checkpoints!" Looking back, (on the standard difficulty), there were just enough. It was a nice amount of difficulty, no spoon-fed do-overs, no brtual lack of checkpoints.
* Effective use of weapons. Never did I have a weapon and feel invincible, but I would NEVER avoid grabbing one. With limited uses you cannot spam them, and they deal enough damage you'll be scrambling to pick it up before the enemy.
Negatives:
* Difficulty != More enemies. Seriously, every SINGLE level is just a grind. I'd rather fight a handful of enemies that are varied and tough to beat- fighting 10,000 on ascreen forces you to use ♥♥♥♥♥♥, cheesy moves over and over and over..
* Controls can totally♥♥♥♥♥♥the bed sometimes. There were moments when trying to attack a group of enemies, instead of just punching a few dudes, you autolock onto a grounded enemy and then you're punished for it. Ludicrous. Trying to grab projectiles requires precise timing which you can't afford because, see above, there's too many enemies to deal with to take the time to do so.
* The writing/plot is practically nonexistant, or poor. A lot of the dialogue was just bad- anything Vlad says sounds moronic. Especially his closing remarks at the end. Or, right before the pool boss fight, that James Bonde-esque "Let me just give you a huge plot point because... I'm the baddy!" Or anytime Mikhail explains himself in this psuedo-profound way it just falls short.
So while I may not recommend it, I still enjoyed it-for the most part. I'd honestly love to see these folks make more games, but maybe of a different genre/play-style. (Fingers crossed they keep their art team)!

A really fun and absolutely brutal beat em up with some rough edges.
You play as a character of your choice from four. You're a Russian Gypsy who is kidnapped by the government and exerimented on with a drug called Nekro, which can restore life or be used to go into a frenzy that increases your attack power. Then there's something about a revolution. Honestly, this game defines the phrase under written. It feels like entire scenes of exposition are missing. What's more, the character you choose has zero effect on the dialogue, which feels like a missed opportunity.
While the story is underwritten, the presentation is absolutely top notch. Using pixel graphics that look like they belong on the SNES but with the brutality of Hotline Miami, this game mixes old school beat em up gameplay with a shocking level of violence. Punches land hard, letting you feel every blow. Faces crunch, heads explode when shot, and a whole lot more. The soundtrack is wonderful as well, making up for where the story is lacking by making an absolutely disturbing and grimy atmosphere, particularly in my favorite level in the game that takes place in a sexually perverse night club, which honestly feels a lot like the recently released Turkish horror movie Baskin. Which is nothing but a compliment, because that's a great horror movie.
As I understand it, this game has pretty standard beat em up gameplay. Use four buttons to string together combos to defeat wave after wave of enemies. I myself don't have a ton of experience with the genre outside some general knowledge of the big titles, but I found the gameplay to be really challenging in a good way... most of the time. Checkpoints are very generous in this game, so dying rarely feels too catastrophic, save for the penultimate and last boss fight, which requires you to go through multiple stages a piece before you can fight the boss. This is where the other rough edge comes in. For the most part, the game feels great, and most of the time if you die it's your fault. But there are times where the game feels extremely cheap. several times in the last level I would make the mistake of getting hit then getting my entire health bar depleted because I was stun locked by six different guys. Situations like this are rare, thankfully, but they can be quite infuriating for those with little patience.
Special mention goes to the boss fights. They're a mixed bag in terms of quality, with them generally leaning towards good, and each one has its own special gimmick, with the highlight being a dude in nightvision glasses you have to stun on a train track so he gets run over. The penultimate fight is honestly a bit disappointing in terms of gameplay (I won't spoil what the fight itself is since conceptually it's almost hilariously badass) but for the most part the bosses provide a good break form the standard beat em up gameplay.
There isn't too much more to say about Mother Russia bleeds, aside from the fact that the title would make a great punk band name. It's a fairly standard beat em up whose main selling point is its horrific violence and sleazy atmosphere. Definitely not for everyone due to the difficulty spikes, but worth a look for fans of games like Hotline Miami or the beat em up genre. Just bring a strong stomach.

The world's most enjoyable Anti-Drug PSA.
--------------------------------------------------------------
is a side scrolling beat-em-up in which you play as one of four gypsies, arrested and taken away to a research facility hidden away beneath a prison and forcibly experimented on with a new superdrug known as Nekro. Nekro, aside from being highly addictive, both empowers its user and can keep them going. With its power, you break out of prison with one goal: revenge for those who did this to you. Along the way, you get wrapped up in a prison riot, a gay fetish dungeon, and a revolution that could shake all of Russia.
As for gameplay itself,
offers a simple yet satisfying combat experience that can only be described as brutal. You can pound enemies' faces with your bare hands, slash their ribcages open with chainsaws, violently extract any Nekro within their spasming corpses with your syringe, or just beat the absolute crap out of them. It's satisfying and violent. Oh so incredibly violent. There's plenty of weapons to pick up akin to
, meaning combat options evolve beyond just "beat the dudes," if only by a little.
The game's unique selling point is the beforementioned Nekro drug. During the game, you can inject the drug into your character to either heal them for about 1/3rd of their life, or to enter a steroid filled state, in which you knock enemies aside with the greatest of ease, attack faster and harder, and can even instantly pound enemies' skulls into mush. In order to get more of the drug, though, you have to extract Nekro from spasming bodies, which can slow the game down as well as be a near fatal decision during combat.
is difficult. Part of it is due to genuine challenge, and part of it is due to poor gaming design. In particular, enemies with guns deal an absurd amount of damage if they hit you, especially shotgun wielding enemies in later levels. They're very difficult to dodge in the fray of combat. A lot of people have problems with the walkie-talkie segment on the train level, but personally I didn't mind it too much. The game does offer some interesting level design, however, beyond just scrolling right; there's doors to pound open, motorcycles to avoid, train tracks to swerve out of the way of, helicopter fire to dodge, and more stuff I'm probably forgetting. It's nothing spectacular, but it's better than "just go right."
Asthetically,
is gorgeous. The pixel art fits well with the
levels of graphic violence, and the game is not afraid to show some horrific stuff. The soundtrack, while good, I could hardly remember while I was beating the crap out of guards. The narrative is somewhat simple, but it did a good job of drawing me in.
Probably the biggest tragedy of this game is that it is both short and does not offer online co-op. While it being short is acceptable, the lack of a way to play with friends aside from local is a puzzling inclusion in 2016. It really bogs the game experience down, as smashing people's face against the pavement is way more fun with friends.

Okay, so after playing this for a few hours, and then trying out the PTS server. This game is impressive. It is nice to see an early access game with Dev's who give regular updates on what their working on and keeping us informed on what their next major movements are going to be. I've bought alot of early access games all with high hopes, and to my dismay have been disapointed more often than not by the Dev's suddenly loosing interest in their own project and disapearing off the face of the planet.
Now even though this game is a Very early Alpha Game, the game play is quite enjoyable and it looks like it's only going to get better as the game progresses towards it's end goal. Now the Enviorment of the world outside the tutorial zone and Main base area in the PTS is completly different than what you'll see if you buy this game right now and load it up. the PTS server shows the enviorment that you see in their video's. thing is, the PTS has nothing to do, no quests, no mobs after the tutorial zone(no tutorial for the tutorial zone) It's just enviorment and Animation right now, and it looks amazing, even on medium settings.
Now here's the downsides right now that i'm hoping will get fixed with their next major update.
1. The game has A LOT of quests, and the tracker doesent work on half of them, and for the ones it does, usually the map will show you a wrong location (you'll easily find yourself loking for something where the map tells you to, but the object/NPC is usually 50 meters away from that spot)
2. Enemy AI are single minded and have Zero ability to do anything other than rush at you, in alot of situations they won't even attack and you can easily stand ontop of a rock to make quite a few just stand there, so the combat can be a bit stale against certain enemies. (This is of course something their working on according to their newsletters and i look forward to seeing the improvements.)
3. No Party system. Really this is the only thing right now that truely bother's me. the inability to party up with friends or other players means you can't really play together. but again, it's an early Alpha, and this is one of those things their working on.
These are really the only things i've personally had any real issue with. theres some collision bugs that are weird, and certain mobs can be difficult to hit because their small and will easily invade your personal space where you can't easily aim at. but these are pretty typical issues of an early access game so to complain about them would be to serve no real purpose. (reporting them as bugs serves a purpsoe though and i do plan to do so)
In the end i'd recommend this, and like me, hope the game continues to get better and better. Cause i've been keeping an eye on this game since it first came to steam. And finally bought it because unlike most early access games, it hasent faded away after it's first year. It's only gained more momentum.

Transistor is the second game by Supergiant Games, developers of Bastion. I really enjoyed Bastion, but I definitely think it was flawed. Transistor builds upon everything in the best way possible, and is absolutely fanastic as a result.
First thing is the art. Oh man it's amazing. There is so much diversity in colour and style for some of the setpieces, and all of the enemies are really unique. Without spoiling anything, I will also say the shift and direction of the artwork towards the ending of the game is really fitting and very well done. It's a really wonderful sight to take in while playing, and it's all backed by an amazing soundtrack. Supergiant actually just released the soundtrack on vinyl on their store and I grabbed a copy - it's a great pressing!
Next thing; the story. One of my dislikes of Bastion was the cohesiveness of the story. I understand that they were trying something different with the narration, and that itself was very cool, but it was still too much for me to wrap my head around. When I finished the game for the first time, I barely had any understanding of what transpired. Transistor is a massive improvement. The presentation of the story and world have much more clarity, yet the storytelling itself is still very artistic and unique. The pacing is also much better than in Bastion, which I found dragged on a bit. While things did move a little fast in the beginning, I found I was able to piece together the setting by myself pretty accurately. However, I didn't like that tidbits of information on characters (which are the only way to really understand the setting of the narrative) are withheld until the player uses that character's function during an enemy encounter. This sucks because there are a limited amount of encounters throughout the game. Yes, there are more than enough encounters to reveal all information, however some encounters are obviously more difficult than others, so using an unfamiliar function may not be the best choice. I personally didn't encounter any problems, but this is still limiting to players who may not find the combat as easy.
And that brings me to the combat. It took me a little over an hour to get used to it and understand it, (there's a very minimal tutorial on it) but once I got the hang of things, I really enjoyed it. It's a nice blend of real-time and turn-based elements. However, the whole home area system isn't well done. I think it would have been better if you could go to the beach area (an area where you can practice the combat) at any point in time. Also, it would have been nice if you were able to look up any function whenever you wanted to see how it worked instead of waiting to find one of those access points. Otherwise, the combat itself is very fluid and unique, and proves a challenge when limiters (options that increase difficulty by say, spawning more enemies, or limiting your powers etc.) are in use.
I would give Transistor a final score of 8.9/10. This is a really great game and I highly recommend everyone experience it. It has an amazing soundtrack, beautiful artwork, fun combat and a fantastic story.

Not being much of an Indie game player before this, I have to say I am BLOWN AWAY by what's on offer in this genre. The music was utterly beautiful and the graphics made me gasp with sheer delight at times. Beautiful colour use and overall aesthetic. Thanks so much to the devs for putting this together.

So recently thanks to a friend I was able to re-play this classic game, it'd not faired all that well gien it's a 27 year old game but it was still playable and as much fun, and annoying (lol) as it ever was. When I saw Wings! Remastered on the store I had to buy it, mostly for nostalgia reason's, and taking me back to being that 17 year old spending most of my nights playing this on my Amiga.
There are one or two minor things such as the text in the journal between missions will sometimes when it runs to two pages display much larger than it should and thereare one or two minor control issues I have experienced using the XBox Controller which are irritating but not all that much of an issue.

As for the gameplay itself, well it's not going to win game of the year it is a solid game which is as fun to play as it was in the 1990's, and it is evident that Cinemaware have ensured this is a loving recreation of that original game which was at the time one of the better Amiga games available and today still stands the test of time as being a fun game.

Wings! Remastered fails due to laziness. And this is infinitely more disappointing because Cinemaware produced this remake, a group well known for immersive detail.
Cinemaware games produced some of the most legendary computer games -- Defender of The Crown, It Came From The Desert, Sinbad and the Throne of the Falcoln, and many others. The idea behind a Cinemaware game was that it was a movie... starring YOU!
But that's where this one REALLY misses the mark. To be a character in the movie, you need to make choices. You make no choices in this game. It's just a linear path of one of three arcade sequences.
Not only that, these sequences don't even look good. Cinemaware wanted 350k for the remake, and I was an enthusiastic backer. But looking at this product, I'm glad it didn't make it. This is more like a college student's final project than a computer game worth more than five bucks. The chief arcade sequence -- the dogfights -- are clunky and the enemies always start in the same position. There's no throttle, there's no jamming, there's nothing that makes Red Baron (from 1990!!) superior even to this day.
As someone who never played the original there is nothing here to enjoy. Far too simple and repetitve.

PROS:
- Simple gameplay, get into the action fast with easy-to-pick-up controls (mouse, beyboard or controller support)
- Journal-style storytelling is captivating and well-done, keeping up with major events of the wartime period
- Varied mission styles (3D flying, 2D bombing runs, isometric strafing missions)
- Missions are quick allowing you to rattle off several before needing to leave the house
- Classic, original soundtrack brings some of us back to a more original era of PC gaming
CONS:
- Arcade-style physics for your biplane fighter in the 3D flying world
- Generous hitboxes for your targets in the 3D flying world
- Game play is easy for veteran gamers on medium difficulty
- Mission repetition, after a while you've seen it all
- Limited presentation value, not much going on inbetween missions as you just click to the next chapter
- Ground terrain in the 3D missions showcase a scarce landscape below making it feel like a mobile game

I just punched through a wall, why can't I just smash the walkie talkie if it's so important that I lose when the enemies grab it? I couldn't even throw it off screen like every other item. I wish there were more explicit combos or a better move variety. I got pretty bored with the fighting after the first 20 minutes. It felt like enemy health was inflated just to make the combat last longer. There were some enemies that felt like they required 20+ hits to take out which is just too many.
The hitboxes were pretty frustrating. It felt like if I whiffed if I was even a pixel above/below an enemy. I understand that the developers want positioning to be important but it made it hard to move quickly between enemies and keep the combat flowing.

I couldn't even kill a single enemy with it, even after letting it get stuck on enemies for a few seconds (what I felt should have been more than enough to kill them). A real shame because the story seemed kind of interesting and I really like how this game looks. I just hate the way it plays.

What a very, very strange game... As the title suggests, official documents have quite a large part in the gameplay. In fact it's a solid 95% of it. Another couple aspects come into play later on, but I'll try to keep this little review spoiler free. Essentially, though it's based in a fictional country, it blatantly states that it's set in 1982, and there's two nations that have East Grestin and West Grestin, so it's obviously hinting at East and West Germany, or more specifically perhaps East and West Berlin. Who knew that checking people's documents to allow, deny, or even detain them, could be so much fun! The style, though simple, is very appealing. The theme song, though so simple, seems quite powerful. There's also multiple endings, and I think you'll be just as surprised as I was when you find out just how many there are!
Though it's so simple, there IS some character development here and there, you'll get to know some recurring characters, and your decisions sometimes have real weight to them. You're afting people's lives when you allow, deny, or detain them. Sometimes you get some extra snippits of information from people going through your booth that makes you want to pass them when their paperwork isn't right, or make you want to deny them even though they're good to go. This game truly is evidence that just like movies, music, and paintings, videogames can produce works of art as well. If all you want in a game is fast paced shooting or super complex puzzles that will have you scratching your head for days trying to figure it out, this isn't for you, but if you're keen on details and have the patience and focus to basically go through multiple small puzzles in order (checking things like names, birthdays, pictures, genders, serial numbers type things on documents, possibly even  official stamps and the like), then this is right up your alley.
Don't worry though, it doesn't drop all this on you at once, it eases you into it day after day. You'll get better at it with each playthrough. I'm on my 3rd now, and I think I have it pretty well mastered in terms of knowing what to look for, but I still occasionally mess up and miss little things. By the 4th playthrough, I bet I'll get barely any mistakes at all. As you can see, there's quite a lot of replay value. It all depends on if you get get into the gameplay style or not. Try watching some vids on Youtube. Personally, I love FPS games, survival horror, Civilization, and stuff like that. I didn't expect to much like this passport and document checking simulator, which it KIND of is I guess, but I very much do enjoy it. The style, music, and character development is fantastic. Anyways I think I've sid all that's worth saying without spoiling much about the game. Highly recommended for those who see videogames as a potential art form like 'This War of Mine'!

Papers, Please is a survival horror game detailing the human trafficking trade in soviet russia in the 1750s.
And now on to the review!
Papers, please is very intuitive and provides a proper moral choice system for a game, if they should even exist at all. (they should. at least in this context where it's the main element of the game versus a small act that you do every once in awhile that determines your next action.) Regardless there are a few points that really highlight the urgency and instilled fear from a dystopian society. The people of Papers, Please are what I imagine most North Korean citizens to be like, so afraid that they think they have nothing to fear.
The gameplay elements are somewhat limited, as there are no upgrades. the money system is somewhat flawed as well, my first time playing my entire family died and I couldn't pay the rent, so everything ended there. Second time around, I accrued so much money I finished the game easily and without any discrepancies against me with $400 in my pocket and nothing to spend it on. Another thing is, with the lack of things to actually do, each day only gets more difficult without any real features added, and while it was fun for the ~8 hours I played it, I realized there were 20 endings, all from differences in actions and moral choices. Wait, I went through one ending when I died after I couldn't pay the rent and THAT'S considered an ending? Oh good, exactly what all games with moral choices do, inserting paths and choices so you have to play it for LONGER just to see all the content. I digress, is that really the worst thing, though? Not like all our choices should just lead up to one ending where the game says "good job racking your brain trying to choose what's right in a grey world of good vs evil, you are rewarded a blank trophy. Your identity is not relevant."
Of course not, that's humbling and well-defined and too truthful for it to be entertaining! Papers, Please disregards all of that and you can make your choices however you see fit: compassion, action or blind faith. The great thing is, you can go all three ways at different times and the truth behind the better idea is left to your best judgement. It really all depends on what you do and how interesting it comes out to be, but the fact that Lucas Pope can make what I do at work all day actually fun, I applaud the man. My only problem with the entire game is that it doesn't have any increase in stimulation, it's the same game from the beginning to end just with more difficulty.
It's a good game.

Wings does something no other recent war game has done (in my experience). It tells the story of war with a genuine sense of charm, depth and chivalry.
This game makes me smile! I played the original through many times in my childhood. This is a lovingly crafted remake that even plays like the original. All of the original dialogue, music, flight mechanics, and graphics have been carefully remastered.
The new voiceovers for the journal entries are a surprisingly welcome addition. All of the original music is preserved and the melodies I fell in love with years ago are even more enchanting now with excellent orchestrations and live instruments (or really excellent samples).
I have recently been playing the original using an emulator and I can say that seeing the two side-by-side is nothing short of impressive, not only because of the vast graphical and audio improvements, but primarily because of how little it has changed in every other way--which is exactly how I hoped this remake would be.
Thanks to the team for bringing back a bit of my childhood. Now my son and I are enjoying Wings! Remastered together.
Note: I saw mentioned in one review that you cannot land in this edition if you have ben shot down. I can confirm that just like in the original, you can land your plane safely after being shot down, it just depends on how your plane is damaged. whats the word of the day with mother russia bleeds? Span, spam enemies, spam screen diarrhea, spam attack, spam stunlocks, spam dogs, spam spam spam and more spam. When i wasn't losing my character in the sea of enemies that were repeatedly stunning my a**, I was spamming the dodge and kick button.
The simple bit is that this game is bad. Its got a lovely art style, and i am crazy for that hotline miame theme, but it is ruined by terrible gameplay. Hitbox and enemies being the biggest issues.
In the beginning it is good, great even, but it feels like the developers got bored or were duped by how to raise the stakes. So later on you get alot more of reskinned enemies with more health. As a veteran of Golden Axe II, i can get behind that, but this game is something else, nearing the end levels, it is just hordes upon hordes of enemies. Sounds fun at first but you need to know what the enemies are.
Fat dudes- big crap ton of health, stuns you on hit, stops slide kicks.
Swat/Spetsnaz- staggers on hit (basically a very brief stun), usually tons of these dudes, lots of health
Shield- invulnerable on one side, can shield bash, if you get caught you can expect to fly across the map. lots of health
Female Swat/Spetsnaz- usually attack you out of swinging range, main attack is slide kick that sends you flying and stuns you.
Soldier- gun wearing buttlords, don't usually drop guns unless scripted, lots of damage, trying to hit them is a pain, as guns appear to be able to hit your hitbox after a 90 degree midflight turn WANTED style.
Anyone with a gun- better hope he walks to you, otherwise you are screwed. 2 hits can kill you, a swat with a pistol fires very quickly, and the shotguns can cover the entire field in fire. Good luck getting to them fast enough to side kick them otherwise it is pretty much an instant kill. Ive lost count of the amount of times a single swat came in and one shotted myself and my ai counterparts, in under 3 seconds with a pistol.
Something rather annoying is that it will switch very rapidly to a shoot out during skirmishes, so your entire team will be finishing off the last group of rustled ruskies when a single enemy will walk out on the opposite end of the field and singlehandedly end everyone.
The worst thing by far is the dogs. Those m************ dogs. Their main form of attack is a pounce, grapple, and stranglehold. Once they begin their pounce animation you are screwed. Are you in the middle of dodge? Too bad. Are you in the middle of a slide kick? Too Bad. Are you mid air in a jump? Too Bad. And they have more health than most of the mob enemies! Do you have something pressing that you need to do? Too Bad. Enjoy the sight of your character disappearing under a dog and the surronding area swarmed with burly swat and mafia, Because it will be common.
All too often, would be in the middle of a slide kick, catch the very first frames of a pounce and get grappled for 2 seconds, and as soon as the mutt is off my shredded carcass it would be blasted by the mob of mobs. dog! grounded! Female Swat! moved and grounded! Swat! punch stunned! Swat with pistol! murdered. OR since the game loves flooding a level with large quantities of the same enemies, Dog! grounded! Dog! grounded! Dog! grounded! Dog! grounded! DEAD DEAD and DEAD.
F*** Dogs, Furry A*******.
Back to Spam, there are boss fights, where the basic thing to do is just find the thing to spam. Spam dodging, spam punch, spam grab.
Spam Dodge to avoid the spam mobs that flood the level, a single hit is a dreadful precursor to a stunlocked death.
Spam punch to reduce the huge health pool of a misc to continue the plot
spam grab to toss away the spam mobs that flood the level.
feels like a bleeding monty python flying circus sketch with the amount of spam involved in this.
The best things are the Art, the music, the eastereggs, and the characters on a small level. They all have their little backstories and nothing else, I would love to see more about them, rather than swearing at them for getting mauled by a dog, or beaten to death by 9 mafia members who are just throwing regular punches.
Before anyone gets on my A** about gitgud, I did finish the game, didn't get the good ending, went through the last level again to see if I could get it, but apparently when ai uses the nekro it blocks that off. And i couldn't be buggered to punish myself by running through that a third time.
In conclusion, looks cool, plays terrible. Get it cheap or, straight up don't get it at all.

For a MOBA, its a good take on the genre. However it cannot overcome the typical down falls of the toxic player pool, unbalanced characters, and senseless ELO. I have had countless hours on the standalone but recently went to Steam. The Season 4 meta is completely trash, and Hi-Rez is a questionable company, but things are looking promising for Season 5. Finally, after years of nonsense and no "real" map changes for conquest, the development team is taking a complete approach to what they should have done all along. In reality, the game is well done, but Hi-Rez caters too much on pushing new Gods (Heroes) that make no sense. Gods that bridge too many gaps like burst damage Guardians, burst damage Warriors (solo lane/top lane), and niche gods that players will fight over to play because of balancing issues. As I write this review, Ullr who was well balanced has become completely broken because Hi-Rez was pushing a Tier 5 skin for the God which you have to pay a considerable amount of money to unlock. This is what Smite has become, a general faceroll money grab. Unfortunately I cannot say I truely recommend this game, however it is a good supplement to LoL or Dota if you want to try out a different feeling MOBA. Lets hope Hi-Rez can pull their head out and start pushing a game that actually makes sense to play, and not one that just keeps producing content becuase they feel they have to, quality over quantity. I as a dedicated high ranking player from Season 2 have gone from playing 4+ hours a day to one that plays maybe 4 hours per week because of the misguided approach the development team has taken.
Massive character selection allows for an incredible amount of game variation.
SMITE is extremely fun, even though you may need to pay a bit of money to have lots of fun, it's still very fun especially for a free to play game.

Free to play game and not pay to win! I grinded to unlock all gods without spending money. If you want to test out a god's abilities, you can try any god in jungle practice. You can normally play any god you want even as a new player through renting with favor, a currency earned simply by playing the game. You can rent a god for 24 hours with 300 favor, which really is not much. The only thing you can really pay for other than gods is cosmetics. I find the game very enjoyable most of the time, but there are several issues with it.
Matchmaking is bad. The ranked divisions are Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Diamond, Master, and Grandmaster. I am a Grandmaster 1v1 player (top 25) and it is not uncommon to face players in the Platinum division, which is 3 divisions below me. On top of this, for some reason the game will reward me more Tribute Points (earning TP increases your rank) for beating lower ranked players than higher ranked players. I also lose less TP for losing to lower ranked players, and more for losing to higher ranked players. This is the opposite of what it is supposed to happen.
Playerbase seems very toxic. Every 1v1 match I play, I enter Do Not Disturb and mute my opponent so they cannot interact with me in any way. The amount of toxic people playing the game is hard to believe and kind of upsetting. It does not matter if you are playing the lowest level or the highest level. Even most streamers BM their teammates. In casual matches it is not uncommon for me to mute 2-3 teammates, while I almost always have to mute at least 1. Chances are if someone is not BMing, they aren't saying much of anything or you are winning and they are not dying. Just remember there is a mute button, and if you find someone that seems cool, try to add them and play with them. If they turn out to be toxic, don't feel like you can't delete them.
Balance is okayish. Gods are often overpowered on release or, with Ullr recently, buffed far too much when they have a big expensive skin coming out. I think the balance team often makes questionable decisions but nothing that makes the game unplayable to me.
These are the main issues I can think of with the game, but it is not nearly enough to stop me from playing it. I've met some great people playing Smite, including my SO, The gameplay is very enjoyable, especially some of the challenges I face in 1v1s. I don't think bugs are as big of an issue or as common as some people may make them out to be. Give it a try! We need more players. Just remember the mute button and don't get discouraged if bad MM puts you against someone with 1000+ hours lol.

8/10
+ stunning visuals
+ good music
+ nice gameplay, not too difficult but challenging enough
+ amazing graphic/UI design and worldbuilding
- poor use of a female protagonist
- disappointing ending
This is a beautifully-crafted game - stunning hand-painted visuals with good music. (I know that everyone has been raving about the music but it's personally just not to my tastes. I still think it's mostly good, though.)
There's an interesting and engaging story and the battles are a lot of fun and not too difficult. World-building is amazing - Cloudbank is a world that will stay with you and find its way into your dreams. And the graphic / UI design on this game is probably some of the best I've ever seen.
I do have issues with the game, mostly with the ending, which I found personally to be incredibly disappointing. I expected a lot more from a game with a female heroine. I expected it to adhere less to patriarchal norms and conventions, but ultimately Transistor didn't do that for me.
Still I think it's definitely worth picking up on a sale. Some people might find it worthwhile at full price - it didn't have enough story for it to warrant full price for me personally.
*Nick Wooster seal of approval*

During my 5 minutes or so with this game, my assessment is this:
Voxelized is an early access title where you click on blocks, causing the blocks to disappear. That's it.
On the launcher you can customize your resolution, change graphics, and bind keys. Keep in mind that there is only one option: Ultra High. At the main menu you have 6 buttons: Play, Multiplayer, Options, Credits, Quit and Languages. Multiplayer and Play are both inaccessable at the moment, though. You would think that at the least you would be able to access an options menu where you would be able to change something like resolution or audio settings, but the game doesn't even have that. One it does have, though, is a slider for music on the main menu. That doesn't work. But it plays music anyway.
When you click "Play," it changes to a screen with 4 world options: A normal world, a flat world, a hardcore world, and a "bonus world". The last two don't work, so I went with the normal world. Now that I was in the actual game, I clicked Escape, hoping I would be able to access some sort of settings or inventory. What I got was a list of controls, some audio sliders and a "climb up blocks" slider. You heard me right, a slider to toggle between two options. If there's any praise I have for this game, it's about the audio sliders for different things like music, building sounds, and birds chirping, which can't be said for lots of modern triple A games.
What I didn't notice however, was an inventory. The game has none. From my understanding, you can only place the last block that you left clicked on, and you have an infinite number of that block. Weird.
Obviously since this game literally has no content, I started to dig down. But once I got to some red tiles underground, I fell through the bottom of the world and found myself falling from the sky onto the surface of the world again. Trippy.
This uninspired, incomplete game has absolutely no future or potential at all. It's not fun, and never will be. It's not even worth buying for a profit off the trading cards, you have better things to do with your time than play this.

It's also a tad more lax than LoL or Dota, but those coming from MOBAs like the aforementioned ones should find that the mechanics are a bit similar.
As with all online games that have a relatively large playerbase, the toxicity is---and may always be---a problem within the community, especially towards new players who have seen their friends or favorite streamers play this game and decided that they wanted to dip their toe in to experience the fun. I understand that it's not an uncommon thing to bash new players who come in fresh and wide-eyed, eager to learn, when they're doing terribly. And it's also understandable that not every new player will be receptive to constructive criticism when they're tilted, couple with the salt of their teammates' BM adding insult to injury, but I still am taken aback every time I see a teammate or someone from the enemy team either BM me or others. (And by no means am I excluding myself since I can admit that I've fallen privy to making rude comments while tilted. I'm a bit of a hot-head so it's taken a considerable effort over time on my part not to be "that person".)
Anyway, I still regularly play it on a daily basis and continue to have fun (although these recent changes have made me uneasy and aprrehensive as to what Season 5 will bring... only good things, I hope). I will say that there are... issues surrounding matchmaking and, well, the game is still "new" so everything's kind of... Chaotic. And "unbalanced". But nevertheless, I'm optimistic that my favorite MOBA will fix these issues over time.
If you find that it's not your cup of tea or were discouraged by those you've encountered, I apologize. I would like for those that were discouraged to try and reach out to others and maybe discuss, or perhaps try again with a safe group of acquaintances, about any qualms you may have. I wish you luck and hope that you may enjoy Smite as much as I have.
VVGL (Good luck!) and VVGF (Have fun!).
