This game is like Monopoly: a game usually played in large groups with friends and family, takes some time to learn the rules, requires a lot of compromise with others, and -- a big point --- is known to destroy the bonds between others. This "Monopoly" has a few different flavors, though Official Rules [Conquest] is the main rule set that you have to go by, since the game's balancing is solely based upon it. This way of playing takes the longest on average: 3 lanes, 5v5, jungle, in typical MOBA fashion. Notoriously has been avoided due to the seriousness/salt associated with the mode, but with the evergrowing playerbase being introduced to the game via ads or the SPL, this game mode follows the "stomp or be stomped" motto.
Every other mode is off of the vanilla version, and the best mode of them all, in my opinion, is either Quick Play [Siege, a two-lane, 4v4 mode, with a "ticket" counter which releases a big bad boy after you get 100 tickets... or until the big bad spawns in the center jungle; pub-stompy as hell, but a ton of fun when the teams are of equal skill; full party, or two-man queue, required] or Family Rules [Assault, an all-random, all-mid, 5v5 mode, but with no "passing go", no backing; you kill until you die, then you get to collect your rent].
Arena, a 5v5 free-for-all with a ticket system, has two goals: bait the enemy team so they can foolishly have a wave of minions go into their portal [and deduct tickets en masse], or sit in front of your portal as the only tank and clear minions for 5 minutes as your carries aggressively 1v3+ despite the fact that you knowingly recalled. This is the mode that you're supposed to start off on. This is basically Monopoly Empires, or Minions Monopoly: it has a simple ruleset, so it's good for newcomers. Definitely not my favorite mode due to the amount of cheese comps flourish. Literally a mode built for one-combo wonders.
Joust, a 3v3, one lane, game mode, used to be my favorite, as it felt fairly balanced in comparison to the other modes. By balanced, I meant the perfect amounts of salt and mechanics. In the former half of Season 4, the only safe Joust was a Ranked Joust; in the latter half, the only safe Joust is a Bots Joust. Clash, a 5v5, two lane, game mode, has always been my least favorite, because, in Season 3, there were too many objectives to keep tabs on [literally had two Conquest objectives slapped inside the mode with no care], and in the beginning of Season 4 [some claim that it still exists, others do not], the snowball was so catastrophic that people died from the resulting avalanche.
The game's itemization, balancing due to items, and overtuned god releases has left me --and many others-- tired and on-edge. It took one and a half years to say goodbye to this game, though 4+ months of that time was a hiatus. I knew it was time to stop playing so frequently when I resorted to spamming the Voice-Guided System [VGS] during a match where my ADC was needlessly aggressive early game against an early game-oriented team... and I actually resorted to taunt-spam near the mid/late game despite knowing the enemy team suffers in the late game. That happened months ago, when I was solo-queueing a game and went against a full party with two other solo-queuers.
I'm typically a pacifist, a humble person when it comes to video games -- not opting to play overly-aggressive unless I know that it'll lead to a kill, making sure my team knows the game plan, warding when necessary, etc. I mained the Support role, despite starting off in the game playing Mages and high-skillfloor Hunters. I swapped around roles after a while, testing out every character there is to play, and it was legitimately fun. I'm sitting at 90 Mastered Deities [out of 92, as of this post] and three Diamonds [Khepri, Sobek, and Skadi]; my distaste for the game started to settle in while I was in the late 70s, if not earlier. Near the end of my "reign", I played more aggressive, with limited callouts, no warding, etc., because it didn't feel as though I needed to, since my team "wouldn't listen to me" regardless.
This game will keep you preoccupied for a while, and you will have fun playing it, so long as you play the characters the meta heavily favors, stay in bot matches, or play in premades [full parties for the gamemode] and hope MMR bones the enemy team. Playing a spicy character that is unfavorable in the meta, like a Zhonger Donger or a Kuzenbro, is basically death, either to BM or to your own self-loathing. I would probably wait out on the game for another few months, because the game's current state is why I've given up on the game entirely, and I'm 95% sure that my leave will be permanent.
Season 5 is coming, and the team at Hi-Rez Studios is trying its hardest to get the game back to a healthy state. Unfortunately, those promises fall to my deaf ears; many chances were given, and it was the last straw. I await the day where they release a premium-priced game that isn't strictly-online, because the amount of love and attention the design team puts into the game is probably what kept me playing for as long as I had.

I heard Plague Inc was moving from iOS to PC and sharpened my pitchfork. So tired of Steam being so cluttered with expensive mobile ports that make it hard to find actual games among them. Then I read the positive reviews, here. Put it in the back of my mind. Fine, maybe it's decent -- but I'm not paying full price for this. Maybe when it drops to five bucks for awhile, I'll try.
Something spurred me to make the impulsive move to eventually buy the game, anyway. And I played it. And . . . it was good. It was really good. Not perfect and lots of room for more compelling and complex additions, but . . . a really solid improvement over the old flash game or the iOS game. This is the way you need to think about making a port to PC. This is the attention and consideration that should be paid.
If you haven't played this type of game before, go check out the mobile version. If you like that, you're likely to enjoy this a lot, too. If you couldn't stand that, the PC version might not be for you. In other words, if you liked the original, this is more of that - and better.
Overall, $15 might still be a little pricey for this type of game. I think $10 would be ideal. It shouldn't be a deal breaker, though; if nothing else, put this on your list and come back to it when it's a little cheaper, if you are hesitant.

This game... is absolutely amazing.
Only game where I was hyped to the max for, and it STILL exceeds my expectations.  Not only did It sing to my ears, it stuffed my eyes with scenery porn and filled my ears with its sad, yet thrilling music.  My fingers were never bored and nor was my imagination.  I constantly had to improvise my abilities and strategy to create a deadly artform that showed my expression of love for the game, all from a dgital USB sword that did all the talking for me.
-The music is part of the story, The art is part of the gameplay, and the gameplay is part of the immersion.
-The sword talks for you, and is customizable to fit your playstyle in any way you want (ESPECIALLY) end game
-The entire game you will be in awe of the scenery your first playthrough.  And your fifth playthrough, if you get that far.
--Things you need to know as well:--
-The hidden areas (break room) are ALL worth checking out.
-Red can hum to the music!
-Using the "Limitors" make the game waay more interesting once you get the hang of it
-Challenge yourself to not use the same setup the second game as you had in the first.
-Explore your surroundings, you'll learn even more about the world of transistor as well as find a few artistic cutscenes that are "hidden" in the game!
-The game is just short enough to be satisfying, like a good anime.
--Now, I can't be fair without a few cons, can I?--
-Enemies will stop moving off screen (use to your advantage)
-The second Playthrough's easter egg does not last through the entire rerun like it should (however it's still worth playing through because of the difficulty increase!)
-The break room's enemy wave thing needs an endless mode.
-The game is short.  I want it to last forever!! *cries*
-Users with low-end graphics cards will not see the full beauty of this game.  It might even run slowly no matter what.
-Users with crappy audio speakers / drivers will NOT see the full beauty of this game.
-Users who do not buy the soundtrack will not be able to get the music out of their heads until they do.
-Users may feel like they're part of a system.  Ignore this feeling.
-Users may experience side effects like slowly turning into a proccess.  This is just your imagination, ignore it.
-Users may experience crying from the sheer beauty of the game.  Do not be alarmed, this is normal.
-Users may experience deja vu.  This is normal, ignore the nagging feeling that the system has reset and that you're actually there a second/third/thousandth time.

8/10
+ stunning visuals
+ good music
+ nice gameplay, not too difficult but challenging enough
+ amazing graphic/UI design and worldbuilding
- poor use of a female protagonist
- disappointing ending
This is a beautifully-crafted game - stunning hand-painted visuals with good music. (I know that everyone has been raving about the music but it's personally just not to my tastes. I still think it's mostly good, though.)
There's an interesting and engaging story and the battles are a lot of fun and not too difficult. World-building is amazing - Cloudbank is a world that will stay with you and find its way into your dreams. And the graphic / UI design on this game is probably some of the best I've ever seen.
I do have issues with the game, mostly with the ending, which I found personally to be incredibly disappointing. I expected a lot more from a game with a female heroine. I expected it to adhere less to patriarchal norms and conventions, but ultimately Transistor didn't do that for me.
Still I think it's definitely worth picking up on a sale. Some people might find it worthwhile at full price - it didn't have enough story for it to warrant full price for me personally.
*Nick Wooster seal of approval*

Exploration is kind of neat for a few minutes until you notice the repetitive nature of it, with randomly generated platforms almost identical to yours with the amount of turrets seemingly scaled to the number you have. Not only is this game very flawed on a gameplay level, it is also just downright broken on a technical level. So there's a few minor bugs like the game starting in Russian by default for whatever reason, and the final upgrade for turrets not displaying the amount of money it costs, but then there's the game-breaking ones like the armory not functioning as intended, and occassionally getting stuck "in combat" forever, unable to jump to other platforms or do anything. -Supported Languages. Supposedly it supports nine languages.

-Badge. Steam trading cards/badge are available.
-Achievements. It only has one achievement. Great for people who like perfect game achieves.
-Development. As said before, the game is in early alpha but the developer seems to be fairly active in making it better.
CONS:
-Birds. I like the idea of being able to turn down their noise but it doesn't allow me to.
-Sensitivity. The mouse sensitivity is WAY too high. Please allow us to change this.
-Doors. The sound and texture are both bugged.
-"Inventory". I know he said he was adding one but I feel as though some explaination should be added for the current.... thing.... that exists.
-Flying. I wanted to fly around the world and observe. Nope. No fly mode that I could find.
-Trees. Only one kind of tree? Odd.
I would say 3/10 with potential and worth a try for the badge alone. Might add more if I play more.

This is, by far, the greatest MMORPG out there today.  I had beta tested the initial attempt at the game (FFXIV 1.0), but didn't bother to purchase/play it after the testing because it was far from good and us testers let Square Enix know this.  Instead of completely trashing the attempt, they took the project and rebuilt it into FFXIV: ARR.  I beta tested that as well, and played it for about a year straight without any breaks to get distracted from any other games.  I came back to it and again was stuck on it.  Even went as far to purchase it again on Steam, even though I already had an active account.
The main storyline is absolutely amazing, and there hasn't been any other MMORPG out there that comes even remotely close to how great this story is, and that's saying a lot when SWTOR is out there.
The constant attention to the game from the developers and continuing to make the game grow with new content and an extension on the main story every 3 months is unheard of.
Old timers like myself who remember the good ol' days of challenging raids in Vanilla World of Warcraft will get sucked in by the challenging dungeons, trials, and raids, and their more difficult varients as well.
Crafting lovers will get lost in joy over the way the crafting and gathering in this game is their own class and have their own skills.  Unlike other games where you just have the materials, click a button and it's crafted.  You actually have to use skills and kind of combat the item into making it and/or make it of better quality.  Oh and your gear matters as a crafter as well.  Item levels for crafting and gathering? *mind blown*
Site seeing, some well known areas found in other Final Fantasy games can be found here as well, as well as the graphics in this game is pretty damn good.  If you have a good PC and a FF fan, you are in for a major treat.
All classes/jobs in the game can be done on a single character, so you do not need to have alts to be able to experience and enjoy other roles in the game.
Tons to do with side activities, working with beast tribes, house decorating, squad leading, Arena style pvp, Triple Triad card gaming, Chocobo Racing, Free Company (what guilds are called in FFXIV) Airship exploration, and so much more.
Yes, there is a subscription, but it's worth it and honestly, the best MMORPGs are always going to be the ones that have subscriptions only (a dying breed as the world of entitled brats take over gaming.)  Thank you Square Enix for flat out stating that you will NEVER go free to play and would rather shut the game down before you go free to play on either FF11 or FF14, that's why they are 2 of the 3 strongest MMORPGs out there.

The concept is terrific, and the scenarios are awesome, however there should be a few changes that would make the game immessurably better:
1. Plague types mimic eachother. The Neurax Worm, Simian Flu, and Necroa Virus are from my experience the only unique plagues, which makes them very fun.
Why, you may ask? The answer is because they're not a literal copy-paste of the symptoms and transmissions the way all the other plagues are. (Bacteria, Virus, Parasite, etc)
This can be fixed by tailoring the symptoms and transmissions to each plague type.
For example, the Parasite should have more effective Symptoms along the lines of Insomnia and Diarrhea.
How the heck would a worm give the host Anaemia?
How would the worm have airborne transmission? It wouldn't. It's a worm.
It could be transmitted through feces, because it's a worm. But since a virus doesn't/can't/whatever get transmitted through feces, the parasite can't because it's a copy-paste.
This is the game's biggest issue in my opinion.
2. Discovery.
What tends to happen when the plague is discovered is that nobody cares for a couple months (seconds), then everybody focuses all their efforts on curing it. EVEN IF ALL IT DOES IS MAKE PEOPLE COUGH.
What should happen:
The plague is much easier to discover, however the way the cure gets researched should be changed drastically: Focusing instead on the severity and lethality, location, and wealth.
For example, if it's discovered and has no symptoms, and is isolated to Europe, nobody should really care. Especially not America. Why would they?
If it's isolated to cold regions, people should recognize that. People in hot countries wouldn't care, and people in cold countries would care.
If it just causes diarrhea, which isn't lethal, and is isolated to poor countries, then the rich countries wouldn't care until it gets to them. Because that's what would happen in real life.
Making infected people sneeze shouldn't have the whole world focus on curing it. We don't even have a cure for the Common Cold.
There should also be a very low, but still existing chance that the cure never gets found, the plague is uncurable.
We have many plagues that don't have any cures, even though we've had years and years to find them.
3. More possible strategies past "Hide, Infect, Kill".
That is ALSO the strategy behind Viruses, even though the way they work is supposed to discourage that.
A big way to help with this:
Multiple strains of the plague. You start with one strain which can be mutated into a new strain for each body catagory: Disgestive tract, brain, bloodstream, organs, etc.
Each mutation adds a new strain, and you can chose which strain to mutate.
Mutated strains do NOT get removed or replaced, they retain their original transmission and symptoms, and comtinue on thier merry way as before, allowing them to get cured or eliminated.
You have one strain that makes people cough, and another that makes them fart for example.
You can mutate one of them, which combines the pre-existing mutation with the new one, making the host cough/fart AND sneeze/diarrhea, but you still have the previous strains that only cause coughing or farting. This would happen with every single mutation, and each strain would have a different "Symptoms Tree". As such, your digestive tract strain cannot get blood stream traits such as Anaemia.
You'd need a new strain to do that, which you would mutate out of your default, symptom-less strain.
This would also make the cure develop differently and people react differently, because they have to cure multiple strains, and different countries would focus on different strains based on what is affecting them, that are constantly mutating. (for example, the USA has a strain that is very drug resitant and causes lesions.
Sudan has a different strain that causes Comae, but is very succeptible to drugs and is easy to research. Who researches which one, and when?)
This would make for a VERY dynamic, unique and interesting cure procedure.
That, plus what I mentioned back in Num. 2 should make the game significantly less repetitive, and by consequence, more fun.
Also, a way to get to islands after they've closed their ports would be welcome. Either add airports to all countries, add "private" airplanes and ships that can spread infection, or let birds migrate and bring the infection with them outside the "Bird Migration" event. And letting advanced waterborne diseases just "wash up" on shore. Prefferably all of those.
Currently, if you don't infect Madgascar/Greenland/Whatever before they close their ports, you're screwed. Because there's literally no way to get to them.
Really, I guess this is more of a suggestions block, but the verdict:
At the moment, the game is NOT worth 15$. 5 would be good, but not 15$.

Basically a deviantArt sci fi album realized into a videogame, for better or worse.
Pros and cons, from most to least importance:
Pros:
Excellent grasp of the third person shooter controls (good camera) and surprisingly good player character movement animations (cribs off fluid weapon animations from games like Max Payne 3???).
Weapons are super satisfying to use. Time/effort budget clearly went into weapon handling - great feel of recoil, screen shake, and very nice sound effects. Core combat feels satisfying, probably the most polished element of the game - which is a good thing, since that's the thing the player does the most.
Nicely detailed environments, especially interiors (exteriors do suffer a bit from the MMO symptom of having huge, blank spaces)
I like that interacting with context-sensitive objects doesn't require me to aim my cursor at something like almost every other MMO, takes some of the tedium out of it.
Cons:
Main issue right now would be tutorials. Translation issues aside, navigating most of the game's systems like questing, buying/selling things, and levelling up/using the skill tree is really, really unclear, and the interface doesn't help.
The game being a translation in progress probably doesn't help things, but UI definitely needs a revamp. Half the time I don't know whether or not I'm buying an object at a vendor, dropping it out of inventory, accepting quests or quest rewards. Even little things, like putting in descriptors next to the icons that appear when you right-click interact with an inventory object, would help.
Audio overall is pretty cool, but BGM always seems to be playing directionally from an environmental source, which is kind of weird (it's pretty funny imagining a sci-fi space station thing playing nothing but generic MMO music like an inoffensive shopping mall)
Player characters probably need better voice actors later on
There's a level 15 mob of enemies camped outside the entrance to the first major exterior environment in the game that's just going to chew up all the starting players in 2-3 hits, what's up with that.
Overall it's not a bad MMO, just a pretty incomplete one.

A remake of the classic game for the Commodore Amiga, it brings back all the old memories.
The game is a flight sim/arcade flight shooter that plays out in WW1. You play as a pilot and go on patrols (regular flight sim), strafing runs (arcade action of shooting targets on ground) and bombing runs (same as strafing, but with bombs only and limited shooting of attacking planes).

Like a lot of people surely did, I bought this game for nostalgia's sake. I remember enjoying it immensely when I was (a lot) younger and the remastered version seemed lovingly crafted, maintaining the feel of the original with just the right amount of graphical polish applied. And most certainly, the nostalgia carried me blissfully through the first ten or so missions. If I had stopped playing at that point, the game would have received a thumbs up. However, things began to go down hill quickly after that...
1. The game is crushingly repetitive. There are only three basic mission types (dogfight, strafe and bomb), which with the simplification of the dogfight missions (see point 2), makes the 250 odd missions that take you through to the end of the war a terrible grind.
2. The original game attempted to mix up the dogfights a little, with enemy planes sometimes appearing on your tail or off to the side of your formation. As I recall, there was even a mini-game in which you had to shake Jerry off your tail at the beginning of the mission! In the remastered version, no matter what the text states at the beginning of the mission, the enemy is always in a clump directly ahead of you. Add to this the fact that the enemy AI is disturbingly single minded and entirely predictable, while your wingmen are lucky to score a single kill in any given mission and every dogfight essentially plays out the same.
3. There are a number of irritating bugs... These are just the ones that I ran into, but there are more reported in the forums.
In summary, the game is a more-or-less faithful recreation of a classic game, let down by sloppiness, irritating bugs and a staggering level of repetition that frankly cannot stand the test of time.
A 2 year old kid could have done better.

I find this a pleasant attempt to bring to date a great Amiga classic. What you have to remember is this is a floppy disc epic. So translated to today it may not fair very well in being well varied. Yes the missions are practically identical to each other. But you have to remember the era this came from. Often games worked by changing the program and not the visuals.
So what does that mean well you will like its Amiga counterpart only take part in 3 different scenes:
Dogfighting – Territory is generally a field and a sky jazzed up so its not simply a plain colour like the Amiga days. But it typically involves you blowing up a number of enemies that vary in number and type.
Strafing – Flying down a road at a simulated 45 degree angle in a vertical scrolling scenario. Sprites do get moved around to add variety but essentially its shooting anything that is useful to the Axis. (Never liked this the guns are tricky to get aimed properly before the screen scrolls over the targets)
Bombing – Traditional vertical scrolling style with a set of bombs and a designated target that needs to be blown up. Again sprites are moved to add variety. Targets change but again very repeated as with the rest of the game.
Now in today’s standards this ain’t going to impress people as a game to play all day like it could achieve back when it came out on the Amiga. My advice is treat it in short bursts. Do say 5 missions a day it will keep you engaged rather easily from start to finish. This is something that many of the negative reviews seem to make the mistake of. It is a hollow game but as I keep pointing out in this review take it in the context which it was made originally. It is after all a remake not a reiteration.
One negative point that is well made by other negative reviews though is the friendly AI sucks they are very linear natured and will often shoot you if you are between them and the enemy. And they are not very likely to actually kill anything at all. And the enemy AI can seem a little dormant too. I really want to say that this is simply maybe the developers do not feel the modern gamer is up to the hardcore play to frustration days of the Amiga. However I think it was just poor programming. I tend therefore just to treat the friendly AI as my tag-a-long rock star friends while I play the machine gun rock.

The Room is the first in a series of three games (two of which have been released on PC, the third is still only on Android and iOS).  It is a 3D puzzle game where you must manipulate ornate wooden boxes, highly detailed mechanisms, locks and gears, light puzzles and secret panels to unlock the secrets of the 'null' element.  Each part of the puzzle you unlock unfolds another room with more of the puzzle to unlock.  The whole game is point and click, with fluid and responsive movements all controlled by mouse.
It is exceptional, but then the store page reviews have probably already given you a clue to that.  The game conveys perfectly the textures you are manipulating which, along with the atmospheric audio, creates an incredibly tactile feel to every moving part.  The puzzles are taxing without being impossible, and each solved part provides a level of satisfaction that ensures you can't wait to unlock the next part!
Anyone who is familiar with the Myst series of games, Obduction or the incredible puzzles of the once-great
by Kheops Studios (not to be confused with other games of the same name) will definitely enjoy this one!  As far as difficulty goes, the pitch seems perfect (easier than some of the Myst games, but still sufficiently challenging).
There is a small glitch that affects anyone playing on monitors with anything greater than 60Hz refresh rates, where the marble in the final maze puzzle can get stuck, making the puzzle impossible to complete.  However, this can be remedied in one of two ways: either switch to the beta version of the game in your Steam library (because the developers released a fix for it in this version), or simply lock your referesh rate to 60Hz for that puzzle.  Personally, I play the beta version, but I've also tried locking my refresh rate and both solutions work just fine.
The only other small disappointment is that the developers don't seem overly fond of porting their work to PC and so it is possible that the third game might never find its way to Steam at all (which is a shame because ALL the games are equally brilliant).
The Room is an incredibly tactile and involving puzzle game that will appeal to anyone who'd appreciate unlocking a complex series of wooden boxes to access what is inside.  The intricate puzzles are both highly detailed and a lot of fun to solve, and are original and varied, making The Room an exceptional game.  A word of warning: this game will absolutely make all other puzzle-based games feel decidedly 'meh' when you see what can be achieved by the developers of this series!
Highly recommended!

The concept is terrific, and the scenarios are awesome, however there should be a few changes that would make the game immessurably better:
1. Plague types mimic eachother. The Neurax Worm, Simian Flu, and Necroa Virus are from my experience the only unique plagues, which makes them very fun.
Why, you may ask? The answer is because they're not a literal copy-paste of the symptoms and transmissions the way all the other plagues are. (Bacteria, Virus, Parasite, etc)
This can be fixed by tailoring the symptoms and transmissions to each plague type.
For example, the Parasite should have more effective Symptoms along the lines of Insomnia and Diarrhea.
How the heck would a worm give the host Anaemia?
How would the worm have airborne transmission? It wouldn't. It's a worm.
It could be transmitted through feces, because it's a worm. But since a virus doesn't/can't/whatever get transmitted through feces, the parasite can't because it's a copy-paste.
This is the game's biggest issue in my opinion.
2. Discovery.
What tends to happen when the plague is discovered is that nobody cares for a couple months (seconds), then everybody focuses all their efforts on curing it. EVEN IF ALL IT DOES IS MAKE PEOPLE COUGH.
What should happen:
The plague is much easier to discover, however the way the cure gets researched should be changed drastically: Focusing instead on the severity and lethality, location, and wealth.
For example, if it's discovered and has no symptoms, and is isolated to Europe, nobody should really care. Especially not America. Why would they?
If it's isolated to cold regions, people should recognize that. People in hot countries wouldn't care, and people in cold countries would care.
If it just causes diarrhea, which isn't lethal, and is isolated to poor countries, then the rich countries wouldn't care until it gets to them. Because that's what would happen in real life.
Making infected people sneeze shouldn't have the whole world focus on curing it. We don't even have a cure for the Common Cold.
There should also be a very low, but still existing chance that the cure never gets found, the plague is uncurable.
We have many plagues that don't have any cures, even though we've had years and years to find them.
3. More possible strategies past "Hide, Infect, Kill".
That is ALSO the strategy behind Viruses, even though the way they work is supposed to discourage that.
A big way to help with this:
Multiple strains of the plague. You start with one strain which can be mutated into a new strain for each body catagory: Disgestive tract, brain, bloodstream, organs, etc.
Each mutation adds a new strain, and you can chose which strain to mutate.
Mutated strains do NOT get removed or replaced, they retain their original transmission and symptoms, and comtinue on thier merry way as before, allowing them to get cured or eliminated.
You have one strain that makes people cough, and another that makes them fart for example.
You can mutate one of them, which combines the pre-existing mutation with the new one, making the host cough/fart AND sneeze/diarrhea, but you still have the previous strains that only cause coughing or farting. This would happen with every single mutation, and each strain would have a different "Symptoms Tree". As such, your digestive tract strain cannot get blood stream traits such as Anaemia.
You'd need a new strain to do that, which you would mutate out of your default, symptom-less strain.
This would also make the cure develop differently and people react differently, because they have to cure multiple strains, and different countries would focus on different strains based on what is affecting them, that are constantly mutating. (for example, the USA has a strain that is very drug resitant and causes lesions.
Sudan has a different strain that causes Comae, but is very succeptible to drugs and is easy to research. Who researches which one, and when?)
This would make for a VERY dynamic, unique and interesting cure procedure.
That, plus what I mentioned back in Num. 2 should make the game significantly less repetitive, and by consequence, more fun.
Also, a way to get to islands after they've closed their ports would be welcome. Either add airports to all countries, add "private" airplanes and ships that can spread infection, or let birds migrate and bring the infection with them outside the "Bird Migration" event. And letting advanced waterborne diseases just "wash up" on shore. Prefferably all of those.
Currently, if you don't infect Madgascar/Greenland/Whatever before they close their ports, you're screwed. Because there's literally no way to get to them.
Really, I guess this is more of a suggestions block, but the verdict:
At the moment, the game is NOT worth 15$. 5 would be good, but not 15$.

First off, please ignore my listed "play time", as I have thousands of hours logged in Subspace, and thousands more in Continuum, the version now available on steam.
I'm in my 30's now, when I was 13 I was introduced to this game by a friend. I poured every free minute of my time after school into this game, 99% of the time playing the Death Star Battle server. This game is a major part of my childhood, and a major part of my interest in gaming today.
I cannot recommend it enough, even now, over a full decade after I stopped spending most of my time online chatting with friends, or tunnel bombing for kill ratio, I still find myself occasionally dipping in for some casual fun. The biggest challenge to that, for quite some time, has been the shrinking community. Now that it finds its way to steam, I am hoping it will once again get an active community.
At its prime, this game had over a dozen active community servers, active leagues will weekly matches, squads, and annual playoffs... over the years as the community has shrank the efforts it took to maintain activity eventually overtook what was available from players. I hope so badly, that just as Continuum was born from the passing of Subspace, that now on Steam Continuum can thrive once again.
This game has an incredible history! It was made by a big game company but abandoned after they couldn't convince people to keep paying for it. Then it went free on community ran servers, and eventually, a few dedicated community members re-created the game as Continuum to keep it going for the fans. It's an amazing example of what is possible with dedicated gamers. I had so much fun, it was the first game I ever modded, and the first game I ever created custom servers, and gameplay modes. I made a silly little racing game within this game by creating a custom map and ship skins. There is a lot possible here. Give it a try, its free, no microtransactions, no BS, just lots and lots of fun.
Goodluck Continuum! I hope you never fully die.

Now I first played this game in April 2000. So I've pretty much done everything that can be done in this game, but my favourite zone is SSCU DeathStarBattle. A great public, a good community and lots of people willing to answer questions and help out new players. The following advice applies to SSCU DeathStarBattle.
THINGS YOU MUST DO TO ENJOY THE GAME:
1. Settings
--a. Change the resolution to the highest your monitor can handle, it's crucial. It affects visibility and thus survivability.
2. Advice
--a. LEAVE the default help and newbie chats - they are not monitored and infested with vile racist trolls. Type this to leave them:    ?Chat=
If playing SSCU DeathStarBattle, type ?chat=dsb to get help from the community. Use the ; (semi-colon) key to initiate chat here.
--b. Be prepared to die, a lot. It will seem other people can kill you and no matter how much you shoot them you can't kill them. This is all down to the fact the game has a steep learning curve, people will shoot and shoot until they are within 1 bullet of death and from playing this game long enough will know exactly how many of each ships' bullets they can eat before they'll pop. It'll literally take u a week to get used to shooting and flying and then being able to kill people.
--c. In SSCU DeathStarBattle, you have a few Specials which differ from ship to ship. Learn to use these to maximise your kills per death.
--d. Press F1 and cycle through all of the menus to find the default commands for the controls. Try everything.
--e. Fight OUTSIDE as much as you can in ship 1 and ship 5. you will gain a much quicker understanding of ship flight, aim and so forth. For every shot you get hit by, you can shoot about 10 bullets. So try to dodge and counter in short bursts.
Basic Keybinds
Press F2 to cycle the score box. Press Page up and down to move the little red arrow next to other players. Use F7 to 'attach' to one of these players as a turret. Stay on, or hop off again with F7 as a means of fast travel to the action. You can make the box bigger and smaller by pressing escape to bring up the main menu, then pressing page up and down again.
Shift+Insert lays a portal that you can return to within 1 minute. You return instantly and there is no energy requirement to return, useful for escaping certain death. Insert again to return to the location you laid the portal.
So I hope this helps, my ingame name is Kassius so drop me a message by typing :Kassius:message and I'll help you out.
Peace.

The game:
You enlist during WW1 as a british combat pilot and start your career strafing, bombing and dogfighting Fokker Eindeckers and Balloons with your Sopwith Camel. The rest of the game you will be strafing bombing and dogfighting Krauts in Doppeldeckers and Dreideckers and Balloons with your Sopwith Camel. Sounds boring? It isn't. Because the game tells your story like a diary and you quickly identify with your ego, your squadron mates and try to get more kills than your fellow pilots. Even if there are more or less always the same missions the game (for me) never gets boring. After or before every mission, you can read another page of the squadron's journal, telling, what is happening at the moment. Historically army movements, plans for the squadron, own feelings, the actual mission, all can be read there and really tells a story to deepen into. The action sequences and missions are good, but it is mostly all about the atmosphere the game tries to convey.
Everybody not knowing Wings or Cinemaware or who is looking for a realistic WW1 plane simulator might be disappointed. This is more story-telling and kind of pure nostalgia for old-school gamers.
08/10 would crash into squad leader again.
PS: Where's the "It Came From The Desert"-Remake? And "Antheads"?

This was a fun, short, yet fun brawler. Reminding me more of the Streets of Rage series if anything. Its been a while since we had a good classic like brawler, while there was Charlie Murder and Castle Crashers, they had RPG elements, and wasn't a true brawler of itself. Which, thankfully, this game delivers on.
The controls are simple and easy. Grab, kick, punch, and jump. Along with a quick step as a sort dash and dodge. The short dash makes it easier to pull of moves on the fly like lunges or grapples. Its nice and fluid to me, as well as satisfying from the crunches and smashes that come from beating heads in with weapons or just your plain bare fists. All 'n all, a system that works.
The story is very interesting to me, how it ties the drug, Nekro, over to the actual gameplay. Everything about the story ties into the nekro. Chaos, rampage, riots, civil war, and death itself. Towards the end of the game,
I love this because it shows that no matter what, the nekro is the reason for this or that. Its everywhere like a plague, and how people use it affect them and them alone.
Enemies and allies A.I. is an iffy matter. It gets more iffy when the ally A.I. affects the outcome of the game. So if you're at the end of the game, its best it'd be done with real people, or by yourself, if you are going for a specific outcome. The enemies make it a hard game to talk about having fun with, as playing on Normal on your own will have your own posterior handed in to you on a platter made of you. Towards the last 2 stages, it became almost insane, and forced me to use A.I. teammates. To me, this makes it hard to replay this game often, as because of the lack of online multiplayer, it limits options quite a bit. Yes though there may be couch multiplayer, if there is going to be a multiplayer option it should include both online, and couch multiplayer options. If it worked for Charlie Murder... But as for enemies, its hard on normal. Not kidding. They gank you a lot and if you aren't playing carefully, they can knock you down real quick. So if playing alone, please please please play on easy. Its more fun. Promise.
Music is fantastic. It sets the mood for each and every stage, and I love how it gets more and more intense or faded when you're away from the boss, or getting closer. It really does give the game a tone that it keeps consistant it itself, the stage, and the story throughout the game.
Overall, fun game. Would definitely recommend to play with some chums as it cuts the nitty gritty for those that just want a fun bloody brawler. For playing alone though, you might wanna give it a pass, as there isn't a lot to replay for save for the arena. Heck I'm even finding it hard to get back into it right now. Maybe later they'll include online multiplayer for fun with other buds, which is what I hope for as I do not have a lot of gaming friends in my vicinity.
TL;DR     I only recommend this game for those with gaming chums that you can reach out to. Solo's beware.

This game is rife with issues...
Gimmick boss fights. All of them. Most of which involve some kind of extremely high damage attack or instant kill the player can recieve for making a minor mistake.
Cheap deaths and damage. Lots of them/it. To be honest, the game that comes to mind off the top of my head is Mighty No. 9. Especially, again, the boss fights.
Extremely rough mechanics. It's trying *so hard* to be Streets of Rage, but it just doesn't seem to know how to get there properly. There's issues with this on both sides, on one hand attacks are too fast and feel weak despite doing decent damage, but on the other hand things like grab and punch or throws (during the actual throw animation) don't do damage around the animation. meaning you can throw an enemy and immediately get punched by another one before it recovers, even with how fast the animations are.
And it's a shame too, because the game does try super hard to let you know what it's trying to be. There's a stage where you fight on top of a moving train. There's a fight with a wall you have to punch through while fighting off enemies. They even have the shaking railroad tracks, and a boss fight with a moving steamroller that reminds of the bulldozer from SoR3 (though you can't punch it). It knows what it wants to be, it's just the whole thing is so poorly implemented.
Where I gave up was the last boss. It has three phases, the first is an extremely frustrating slog designed to wear you down, and the last is incredibly RNG and can spend long amounts of time completely invulnerable if you get even slightly unlucky. The real kicker? No mid boss checkpoint. The rest of the game throws checkpoints at you excessively during stages with minimal penalty for death (no wonder why, with all the unneccessary cheap damage), and the one place where a bit of forgiveness would have made sense, there is none.
Frankly, I gave up trying to beat it. I could turn the difficulty down, and do the stage over... But nah, this game just isn't worth it. Kinda asking myself why I played as far as I did.
Luckily I got this in a Humble Bundle, but if you're looking for a beat-em-up steer clear and buy River City Ransom: Underground instead. Or even better, go grab the Streets of Rage Remake, it's free and completely excellent. Wish there were more quality beat-em-ups, guess I'll just have to keep watching and waiting to see what Arcsys does in the future.

For all that though they've worked in a surprising amount of story and a funky sort of creepy atmosphere.
I've heard this was a port from a tablet game, but unlike a lot of cross-platform ports this has worked really well - no glitches that I could find as a result of the transfer.
Hints are helpful in a way - it means you don't get stuck just because you missed a tiny detail right back at the start of the level, because at times it's not very intuitive where you need to go next. I fully understand what "Early Access" is intended for and the reasons to have it. I have supported many titles while in this phase of development. That being said, "games" like this are why people hate the Early Access platform on Steam so much.
I have 20m of playtime and ran into several core issues with this project that reveal not only general lack of experience in game development, but complete waste of resources within the company on this project.
Issue 1. The game settings have no English translations. You can set the language to English, all the game HUD, menus, and dialogues correctly show in English, all the game settings however do not...
Issue 2. Long load time on Unreal Engines splash screen. I don't mind seeing Unity/Unreal splash screens what so ever. What I do mind is a 3m load time watching the splash screen just repeat itself over and over during this 3m leaving NO indication that the solution is loading properly.
Issue 3. You cannot access game settings until you have made a character and are in-game. Settings should ALWAYS be available to the player regardless of what point in the game they are. Video options need to be made available before ANY gameplay. Not only to ensure the player starts off the game the best chance of immersion but because most enjoys chunk when changing core video settings (if you even can at the point of gameplay).
Issue 4. The UI is pretty god awful. I feel like I have to spam E all over the place to "investigate" stuff and the result is usually something like "uh, this is a thing. eww". Popup help menus cannot be closed or minimized in ANY way and often block the items they are instructing you to use. Not all menus use the same key to close said menu. Other actions that should not be allowed to happen when menus are up still occur. If I am reading a book in game and have a menu with buttons, clicking should not shoot my firearm....
Issue 5. Voice Acting. I believe the studio is Russian (which is no issue) but the "English" voice acting is spoken by a Russian with pretty heavy accent. I don't mind if the character is intended to be Russian but there was nothing defining the setting I was playing in so it broke immersion pretty hard. That all is ignoring the fact that the sound quality wasn't great, and the fact they are wasting money on voice acting when they havent even taken time to fully localize the project and this early in the games development MANY dialogue options WILL CHANGE, voice acting this early in the project is a waste of resources.
Issue 6. The first quest of the game is looking for small screws on the ground. Small little items a few pixels big that are black against a dark grey background... I get this is a MMO and there will be mundane quests but come the ^$%^ on....
Issue 7. Development group didn't/doesn't have any of the legal work required to release a game complete. They lost the programmer AND the code which is why they haven't update in so damn long. They have to rebuild what they had as far as codebase from scratch. No game on Steam should be released in a state where the development team and Steam may have to riup down the game from the storefront because the devs can't fill out the basic legalities required to release a product....
To call this a "game" at this point is pretty generous. This may be a solid proof of concept but definately not worth buying into at this point.

The following review is from an enormous fan of the original Wings on the Amiga (it's my favourite game of all time!):
I was initailly quite excited to hear of the kickstarter for Wings, but then I started to have severe doubts - how could the original ever be bettered and what if they made a ♥♥♥♥♥♥up' of it!
After playing a demo of the kickstarter project last year, my doubts became even more pronounced; it retained very little of the original's charm and atmosphere.  So I pretty much ignored all further interest in the project until recently..
After watching a recent youtube video of Wings Remastered, my interest began to grow again.  I paid a 'few quid' for it and I was pleasently surprised:  Wings Remastered Edition is very faithful to the original and improves upon it in many aspects.
The strafing min-game is massively improved upon from the original and is much more visceral and enormously fun to play!
The main cockpit flying game is also much more realistic and visceral, but I simply don't find the AI as intuitive as in the original Wings.  There are still some incredible battles to be fought, but the fights seem to feel quite generic in comparison to the Amiga version.
The 3D cockpit fights were the main magical element, that made the Amiga version feel so good; whether by design or fluke.  It was always going to be a difficult act to live up to and the remastered version almost nailed it...but not quite.
Still worth a buy (especailly as it's currently so cheap) and I'm certainly glad that I eventually decided to do so!

It's a graphical update of an Amiga game by Cinemaware, indeed the first Amiga game I ever owned; and the thing you need to know about Cinemaware games is they attempted to tell a story, like old fashioned movies. Whether you enjoy the game then depends upon your ability to engage with narrative; one of the criticisms you'll see of the game is that some missions are too hard, putting you up against impossible odds. This is deliberate, your pilot is expected to die at some point, that's why you have a Memorial Wall for them, and a squadron you can keep adding new pilots into, who then also might die. In Bloody April life expectency for RFC pilots was down to two weeks, and this happens in game too; it's telling the story of the First World War, and you are only a part of that.
Here things get tricky. The central narrative remains charming and, if you forgive it certain liberties (it's written from an American perspective, when American volunteers were not that common pre-US entry: The Allies are always flying SE-5as long before they became available) tells an interesting, if occasionally movie cliche story.
There are vertical scrolling and faux 3d shooting sections, and these have been faithfully implemented and are very short doses of fun, as they were in the original. However the core of the game is the 3d dogfighting and it is, sad to say, very shoddy. Your AI wingmen will shoot through you to try and hit targets, and the enemy NPCs will do the same, often flying into each other, and you out of target fixation.
Pilots who have survived your mission with you, been credited with doing so on the post mission report, can actually die on the squadron update all the same. And whilst it is possible to save-scum a single pilot surviving the entire war (and in the Amiga original too, I've done it both on Hard here and there too) your chances of doing so are largely random because of the above AI issues. I've had my own wingmen ram me before trying to get at a target I was shooting at.
Dogfighting, being a simplistic affair which you could perhaps understand back in the olden days, is here ruined by the spawning of the enemy directly in front of you every time. There is no other tactic than moving to one side, letting them charge your wingmen, and then sniping them off from behind.
There is no volume levelling or clear three dimensions on the sounds either, so it's often hard to tell who is hitting what; is that noise coming from your shots landing, someone behind you hitting a different aeroplane, or...?
Missions often contradict the charming writing, both on plane type, plane numbers or even the actual mission type; and can be won or lost because the actual conditions are met before you realise what you should have been doing. I've seen "Shoot down fighters" actually appear as both defend and intercept bombers, and if you don't notice the bomber in the scene (the friendly one will spawn behind you, so that's easy to do) and someone else shoots it first...
The dogfight is also visually repetitive, only having a single scene that differs depending on light conditions and weather overlays.
And some Achievements don't seem to work at all; so far completing the game, completing it without roll back and even bombing a simple truck don't work.
However, I adored the original Wings. So I had some fun with the game all the same, and not just because of nostalgia. It's current price amount of fun though? Not at all. In all honesty it should be a £1-£5 purchase, at most. But...
Strangely, I have to say... No. There's some really weird, or just hamfisted issues with the game even compared to the original.
The introductory movie is the most obvious one; the original was perfectly timed, to contrast the purr of the Wright Flyer's engine, the pacifist seeming quote from Orville Wright scrolls up to building crescendo, then ... another engine noise starts immediately, the dogfighting planes come from screen left machine gunning away. In this remake, it completely ruins the cinematic effect; the quote scrolls up slowly long after the crescendo has completely stopped,
and then the intro continues. Dramatic moment completely ruined!
Also they've not used the same length of character string for your pilot as in the original, so if you did own that game and had a long name, you have to truncate it now.
As mentioned the AI just spawns in front of you now; originally they'd at least set up interesting starting positions. Those are gone now. Also gone are certain missions types, like being intercepted yourself and having to shake someone off your tail.
I personally find the voice over added to the plot distracting, but that's personal taste. The original soundtrack is there if you want it however. But then so too is the original
; if you still own an Amiga and the original it actually costs less to buy both it and a licensed Amiga emulator than Wings Remastered! And if you are somewhat shady, ahem... it's completely free. As is the modern Rise of Flight for the basic F2P game, if you want far, far better graphics and a much better round experience.
I'm somewhat glad I bought WR! all the same; but then as I say, I adored the original so it's revisiting an old dear friend for me. But I wouldn't recommend it to most of you, especially not at it's current price.

In the mid-90's there was a game called Escape Velocity released by Ambrosia Software, where you flew around in spaceships in a 2d universe, completing economic or combat based missions. I recieved a copy free copy of this game on a MacWorld Magazine disk and was immmediately hooked. I spent endless hours of my youth exploring the the Escape Velocity univerise. It's an open world, where you follow quests and decide which faction you were going to join and others that you were going to become enemies with. You could join the Confederates, Rebels, Pirates, or just remain an independent trader.
Endless Sky is clearly modelled after the Escape Velocity series (Escape Velocity, Escape Velocity Override, and Escape Velocity Nova) and anyone who was a fan of those games should be playing this.
That being said, for me personally, Endless Sky brought back a lot of nostalgia from my gaming days in the 90's. Growing up I had a Macintosh computer, which really limited my computer gaming choices. There were the early Bungie games (Pathways Into Darkness, Marathon, and Myth 2) as well as Blizzard's Warcraft and Starcraft games. Bungie, Bllizzard, and Ambrosia Software were my three go to gaming companies and they all sparked my passion for gaming.
Enough nostalgia, let's talk about the game. You start off with a trading ship and have to complete several trading missions in order to pay off the morgage you got for your first space ship. As the game goes on, you begin to explore the galaxy, earn more credits, learn more about the main plot, and eventually build and upgrade your ship. There appears to be one main storyline to this game (as opposed to the EV series where you followed a certain faction's story line) but you can go about it at your own pace. Some side missions pop up which also add an element of intrigue. All the missions require you to either take people/cargo somewhere, to fight other ships, or analzye something. At both the beginning and end of the mission there are no cutscenes but instead you read and sometimes make decisions on what was said.
The combat is a bit difficult to get used to at first and you'll need to buy another ship and upgrade a bit before taking anyone on. The first few hours playing this, not unlike my high school days, I always got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked. If you keep grinding out the trade missions, you'll soon have a ship to be reckoned with and can go face to face with everyone who wronged you. Also you can hire a fleet of ships to help fight along side you although you'll have to pay them x amount of credits to retain their services.
I've played this game for several hours and it has kept me entertained and curious on how the story line will unfold. It's not ground-breaking at all, sometimes I got lost trying to figure out where the story picked up at, and the game is outdated graphics-wise but I'm recommending it.
I'm also looking forward to the user created mods. Escape Velocity had a similar editor where there were a lot of great user created mods released for free and kept the game new and exciting after you exhausted the original game.
If your curious, give it a shot. You got nothing to lose but time - it's free.

In a room, there is a box, if you prod the box in the correct way, another box will be revealed. Prod this box in the correct way, another box is revealed and so on and so forth.
Sounds a bit drab, but its actually a very slick, albeit short, puzzle game. Hardened puzzle gamers will not find it too much of a challenge and for those that do, the hint system will hold your hand. But it sucks you in and does not feel like a chore to play, audio and visuals are lovely, the story, for what it is, is a tad predictable, but you're not playing it for the shallow plot. You're playing it to prod, poke and move around all the beautifully rendered components to see what wonderous contraptions are revealed next.
A thumbs up from me, just don't expect many hours worth of puzzling..

I found the interface a bit meddlesome at some points, but over all it flowed smoothly and the interactive design made it much more immersive.
Pros:
* Great puzzles, and lots of them. They build on each other.
* Good Story to investigate and uncover
* Music accompanies the game well
* Controls were very immersive in feel
Cons:
* A bit short overall
* Interface was sometimes hard to maneuver, especially with the turning screen vs. turning keys dynamic
* No actual end to the story line
Overall, worth your five bucks for a few hours of brain stimulating fun and suspense.

Factorio looks like old times Command & Comquer, has a tech tree deeper than that of any Civ game, and gives you freedom of choice like hardly any other game!
You are the engineer of your factory, and your goal is to use resources to advance your research and launch a rocket to win.
You start out with nothing, and you will end up with miles and miles of conveyor belts of multiple speeds, railroads, flying robots and factories making all the stuff autonomously that you could mostly also make yourself, but in smaller quantities. Your assembly lines are always too small, so you reiterate constantly. Hunting for efficiency or perfection? You can always redo everything, and yet it is never enough to satisfy you when you shut off the computer after a surprisingly quick round of 4 hours.
Although it's not finished, this game takes my mind on a grand tour out of everyday life, into a world of production lines and optimization!
Highly recommended!

Party-trick: watch MACHIN3 leave negative comments on this review, oblivious as to what Early Access means.
This is a very early alpha. Buy this if you want to support the dev, and support their vision. Do NOT expect a fully developed experience, because that is NOT what early access means. The game has about a day's worth of content at this point, but the devs post development updates regularly.
This game's strongpoints so far are the combat, design, and the scope of things.
The combat is highly satisfying, especially for an MMO. Think Mass Effect, but with more solid shooting. It's brisk, quick, Shots register as if it were an FPS, and I hope that's something they keep throughout the development. Right now, there are only a handful of weapon types, but more types will be added later on.
The design is a dash of cyberpunk and general sci-fi. The armors in the game so far, about 10 sets per class totalling in 30 sets or so, all look really nice and varied. The insectoid looking ones are my favorites.
I bought this game wanting to ensure it gets a full release. I am under no illusion as to what I bought, and you shouldn't be either. It's an alpha, don't expect this to be a full game yet.
A legitimate complaint is the scarcity of actual content releases, but communication from the devs is ample, and the regular news updates are good to see. There is good reason for the lack of content updates; I suggest you read the latest news on that before making the decision whether to back this project or not.
TL;DR
Fun alpha, promising ideas, but infrequent updates. Buy if aware what alpha means, Cue ridiculous comments from our personal Messiah

In the state that the game is right now, it's not finished. Clearly, since it says "Early Access", this is a work in progress. Don't expect anything else. The game hasn't been updated in ages, and the devs had a previous project that failed which turned into this game instead. If you find yourself full of distrust due to years of abuse, you'll find lots to whine about regarding this game. If you're a healthy and happy individual, you'll find fun players and at least 20 hrs of gameplay, and if the update comes out at some point, even more gameplay at a later date!
However, what is in the game right now, is very enjoyable! There's quite a bit to do, at least 20 hrs of gameplay if you rush like a madman, and know how to make money fast. If you're slow, and take your time to ensure you complete everything, there's even more time to spend.
The environments are varied. The graphics are nice. There's a single vehicle (As far as I saw), which is a shame, but it does help. There's a decent amount of guns and armors, and the skill-trees are at the very most half-finished. Still gives you variation in gameplay, what's there is good!
Right now, there's some new bandwagon some angry guy has started, where he's trying to create a second "No Man's Sky" incident, but he's not provided any sources or reliable information regarding the alleged "Paid reviews" that the "developer has put up"..
All in all, I'd give this game a 6/10 for what it's like right now.
The studio's had a rough time the last 4 - 6 months, and they're finally recovering from the effects of what happened.
I'm more than happy to support these guys. Their game is good, and they could make it even better. Of course, I say could, because at this pace, if the "gamer" rage culture gains a foothold, we could lose a potentially very good game.
Now, I'm not biased. Which is why I'm not raging blindly like an entitled manchild. The game is buggy. Sometimes reloads get messed up and you end up reloading twice. There are areas where you simply get stuck in some hole and can't get out without chat commands. The AI for the enemies like to jitter side to side, making them a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to fight.
The game isn't perfect. It's a work in progress. If you're not ready to embrace a game that isn't finished yet, and that needs a bit of polish - this isn't the game for you. Not yet. Save your money for now, and come back to check the progress in a few months. But don't start shouting "SCAM! SCAM!" if you do buy it. The team has been transparent from the start. They said they ran into issues. They said they don't know when they can release a new patch. They are showing lots of content updates in the newsletters.
Patience is a virtue.

Subspace is one of the greatest online games of all time, but it's also one of the first, released almost 18 years ago. It is absolutely devoid of modern conveniences and chock full of features long since forgotten. The control scheme is straight out of 1980s arcade games, and there is no handicap system of any kind.
This is a very, very difficult game to learn.
It is also a game you might never get good at no matter how hard you try. With over a thousand hours played during its early years, I never got good, at least not by many people's standards. What I did manage to do was find a role and fill it well. One thing this game excels at profoundly is allowing players freedom and individual initiative, and this includes the freedom to tag along or be a cog in a group effort. Depending where you play you might find yourself running with a flag or swarming with a huge team. Your goal might be to win the flag game, your goal might be to to ruin it. You may excel in open-air duels or thrive in twisty mazes. This isn't a game for everyone, but there's something special here for everyone who takes to it.
So when you test this game out, do it with an even temper and preferably a drink. Start in spectator mode, hit F1 to get a look at the commands, and for heaven's sake ask questions. At this late date we are REALLY good at answering questions. Most importantly, if you find the server you joined to be too fast, too slow, too cramped, too difficult? Try a different server. These game variants have survived long years of competition, and they did it by being unique. To be frank, I cannot stand most of the servers that are popular in this game. They're just not for me or my playstyle. Chances are you'll feel the same way about the servers I like most. That's the beauty of this game: It's a finely honed cross-section of the best and weirdest ideas dreamed up by the millions who've played it since 1996.
But all this is easily lost on the player who approaches it carelessly and without patience. Get yourself nice and relaxed, put on your Dwarf Fortress hat and get out your old Urban Dead notebook. This is going to hurt, but you'll thank yourself for it.

I put around 100 hours into the original Sleeping Dogs several years back on my old PC; on my new, much more powerful machine, I was thrilled to play the definitive edition. It's not merely a re-release - it's a reworking of the graphics and a slight improvement on the already fluid and fun combat system, and it contains additions to the campaign (extended narrative, extra cop side missions) that are worthy of the repurchase cost for fans who already have the original (specifically those who liked it and want to play it again). Because I had already finished the campaign as well as played through the DLC episodes, I was hesitant to buy the same game twice, but when it went on sale for $7.50, I struck and was very happy I did. This is not only an extended and much more immersive experience; it works better on newer software and hardware architecture. It manages to pack Hong Kong more densely with NPCs and greatly improve environmental textures and weather while demanding much less of my GPU than the original release. They both hit some of the same framerates, but with settings cranked, my video card chugs along very loudly to the original release while it's capable of rendering more with less power in the definitive edition. Truly an optimal redesign for the PC.
For the many who've already played Sleeping Dogs and loved it, I 100% recommend picking up the definitive edition IF you want to play through the campaign again or if you haven't played the DLC episodes (and I'd wait for a sale). You may find the experience enjoyable as I did or you may feel like you're wading through the same water (albeit much more detailed and highly rendered water). If you've never played the game, this is the edition to get - it's a very fun open world game in the vein of Grand Theft Auto with tons of collectibles, a martial arts beat 'em up combat system, great driving mechanics, fun missions and side-objectives, and, most importantly of all, a good story fronted by a compelling protagonist who leads a double life as both an undercover cop & triad member and a Chinese-American immigrant & Chinese national. As another Asian-American who's faced confusion stemming from a bi-cultural background, I find Wei Shen to be a well written, sympathetic and multi-faceted hero/anti-hero. In addition, the ties the campaign and DLC episodes share with HK Crime and Kung Fu films (references, atmosphere, setting, style) alone are enough to draw me in to its highly detailed vision of modern Hong Kong and keep me playing in it time and time again.

I thought I'd write a short review of the game based on the fact that I've played and completed the original several times since it came out in 1990. I've now played this version to mission 100 as I write this, on Medium difficulty, so if your experience differs, it maybe because I haven't found all of the features available at different missions or difficulty levels!
Introduction/Menus - 8/10 - These are ok, although the behaviour of the trees in the introduction is daft (who's ever seen a thick tree trunk blowing in the breeze), but I wrote these off to the fact that the Cinemaware products were always a bit tongue-in-cheek. The rest of the GUI and menus are fine, easily navigatable and quick to respond and a few more options than the original also (difficulty level etc.)  The save option is a nice addition now too.
Graphics - 7/10 - Pretty good overall, better explosions and polished looks, and I really like the weather effects.  Sadly, some of the graphical capabilities aren't used when they are needed most, such as during the winter missions (where's the snow/ice??), and this makes every mission feel the same graphically.  The plane and balloon models are nice but some graphical features prove worthless, like the dials in the aircraft which don't animate.  The scrolling missions are probably where the game most resembles the original in looks, feel and sound.  The framerate is nice and smooth
Sound - 6/10 - The sound quality is fine, and the sound effects are not quite right.  The engine sound is nowehere near as variable as the original Amiga release; you really used to get a feel for your engine gathering speed during a dive, slowing to a stall during a prop-hanging session whilst pointing at the sun, and it really used to add to the atmosphere that at any point, you could fall to your death in this rickety "death crate". Sadly, this is no longer the case, it's a static sound. Steep diving is accompanied by an irritating "overlaid" sound effect of a plane nose-diving, which goes away immediately at a trigger-point. Stalling the enginer no longer seems to take place (unless this is only a feature of the harder difficulty level perhaps??), which is a shame, as this was accompanied by a lovely sound of impending doom as you hoped the engine would splutter into life again. The original sound of the guns jamming has gone too, and replaced with a short sample to imitate what the original did.  They would have done better just using the original samples from the Amiga version to be honest in this case.  It was the variety that made it what it was - fun.
There's no empathy in the voiceover reading and because the spoken words are nearly always incorrect compared to the written journal (which does appear accurate to the original Amiga version), then the effect becomes far from feeling that you are a first world war pilot, fearing to go into the skies again and cherishing every moment of life; instead it just makes you feel like you are sat in the RFC canteen, reading someone elses journal, whilst some irritating british guy is reading the journal over your shoulder out loud and deliberatly getting it wrong to put you off enjoying it.  Also, where you really want the voice-over is in the discussions with Col. Farrah and at various special points in the game, like receiving a medal.  But no, sadly they spent far too much time letting the british guy improvise whilst reading the journal to bother with 2 seconds of audio in the right place.
Gameplay - 6/10 - I feel a bit mean here, but the reality is the gameplay just isn't as good as the original Amiga Wings.  Yes it's fairly polished, yes it's 25 years old as a game concept, but the original was really, really fun to play, which is all that mattered. First the good points.  The gameplay is smooth, it's got the original feel to a degree, it's got some nice new features such as being able to see over your left/right wings and rear tail.  The controls work well and the loading times are nice and fast so there's no waiting around, which is nice.  But ... where have all the nice features gone from the original??  Why can't I loop the loop anymore, or climb hard and stall the engine?  Why am I stuck going at a single pace now, whereas in the original I could climb and fly slow, or dive and gain loads of speed to launch into a loop or simply race along the ground at speed?  Why is it that every single time I shoot an enemy plane down, the tail always come off?
The AI of your fellow pilots is atrocious.  They fly far to close and I've had 4 mid-air collisions now where they have run into me whilst I'm flying straight ahead before the dogfighting has even begun.  Although you would get the odd air collision in the original version, they didn't just stupidly fly into you, it only used to happen when they were flying to avoid getting shot, or whilst we were both turning, which is then acceptable risk.  Also, the enemy plane dogfights always start in front of you which is moronic especially when half the time the journal says that you "surprised" the enemy, or they "surprised" you, from above, below, behind, etc.  On the original Amiga version, this then translated into you actually starting the mission knowing they were above, behind, below etc., and sometimes it would mean starting a mission with an enemy already on your tail (which I add, also appears to be missing from this new version - where the camera would go to "tail-cam" showing you with an enemy on your tail that you had to shake-off).  All of this is gone from this version as far as I can see. You no longer have the luxury seeing your pilot slam into the ground after an air-struggle, this is cut short and replaced with the same spinning shot of your plane, nicely parked but destroyed, no matter how you hit the ground, even upside-down.
Lastly, the mission objectives themselves.  The game basically cuts short in your mission whilst enemy aircraft are still in the sky.   Whilst the original game did cut short if you failed in your mission whilst there were enemy planes in the sky (such as on the enemy bombing missions - where you had to shoot the bomber down within a certain time), the rest of the missions were open-ended, and they let you try to get more kills from the enemy aircraft.  In this incarnation, apparently everyone goes home once the baloon is burst and chalks it up to experience with no hard feelings at all.  If only the real aerial war had been like this, they could have all gone home for tea and cucumber sandwiches by noon.
Pros:
Nice updated graphics
Controller Support (I use a PS3 pad which works nicely), with a nice response/feel to the controls
Kept the original theme music and overall feel
Cons:
The variation, freedom and features of flying/dogfighting is not as good as the original Amiga release
Some of the missions are inaccurately marked on the aerial photography leading to mision failures
The voice-over is inaccurate and irritating
Some journal pages and photos are the wrong way around to the original, detracting from the enjoyment of the journal
Summary:
Is it worth buying?  Yes, if you can get it on the sale for a few quid and you want to relive the old game and don't have access to an Amiga or emulator, then get it; it's a decent little game.
However, if you are playing this because you really enjoyed the old version, I mean, really enjoyed it.... don't aim for the skies with your expectations.  It's a real shame they have cut corners to provide an up to date experience of this classic.

EDIT: recent update/patch changed AI behavior. Enemy planes are much easier to shoot down even on hard difficulty, having less HP. On the other hand, your plane also seems to be more fragile, and you get slightly stunned with a bright flash every time the baddies score a major hit. They are also much more likely to ram your plane, and your AI wingmen seem more effective. Nothing to change the basic opinion on the game, though.
Only recommended for those who played the Cinemaware original back in 1990. In that context, this is more than a remaster, it's complete recreation with simple modern graphics and sound. You're a pilot that's experiencing WWI, and there's a lot of story as the war progresses. In the original this was all text but was still very captivating. Here it's fully narrated by a very competent actor, but the voice often doesn't match the well written text. Minor issue.
Missions include dogfights, balloon busting, bombing runs, and strafing. Each is a mini game basically and they are very repetitive, as they were in the original. Almost nothing ever changes, which is why someone with no fondness for the original is very likely to get bored quick. Otherwise a nice re-telling of what was an excellent game a quarter of century ago. Can't believe I just said that. If you didn't play the original, no need to get this, and it's not worth more than $10 honestly. 6/10.
