If you're a fan of the original WINGS game, you'll love this. This is the game I bought an Amiga to play, and seeing that it had been released on Steam in a remastered format meant I had to buy it.
If you're *not* familiar with the original game, you may have some concerns.
Firstly, the game plays well, is graphically good, and seems to be very stable.
The audio is adequate, and the controls are fine. I've been using a logitech gamepad. The game does let you play with keyboard, but... yuck.
The three mission types - dogfight (3D), strafing (isometric) and bombing (top view) are all well realised updates to the original cinemaware versions. I have absolulely no qualms with the last two, but the dogfighting is where most people might get a bit irritated - especially if they're not familiar with the original Amiga release.
1. It's easy.  The first thing you should do is crank this game up to hard.
Seriously, this puzzled me. Playing this on the 'normal' setting felt stupidly easy. Perhaps it's harder when you're using the keyboard, but if you're not and you know that you're supposed to push 'forward' to point your plane 'down', then you really need to crank this up.
2. The mission descriptions don't really match the missions.
eg: You always start facing the enemy, even if it says you surprised them.  I honestly can't remember whether this was true in the orignal or not, but it's something that I would think should have been an easy fix, and it would have added to the game considerably.  For me, this is the only *real* flaw with the game.
3. No rudder.
Yeah, the original didn't have it either, but having played a lot of flight games since, I found myself missing it. This is a remastered version of the original, so I'm not complaining about it myself, but it's something that prospective new players should consider.
4. Quite samey missions.
As above. The original game was effectively the same mission played out in a few different ways... but it's a bit of an issue if you're used to more modern games... but WINGS fans will probably not mind too much.  Fixing #2 would probably fix #4, to be honest, as you'd be starting with a variety of conditions.
5. No free look, padlock, etc.
Yeah, this game was originally written back when nobody really knew what a padlock was. You'll just have to get used to that.  Your guy looks in the direction of the enemy, mostly, and the addition of the helpful arrows (which I would prefer to be able to turn off, to be honest) makes finding the enemy easy enough.
I hope they're continuing to develop. I'd love to see a fix to Point #2, which really is the only thing that is bugging me about the game as it stands.
Is it worth full price?  I bought it on 25% special at around $12 USD, and I'd have to say that was pushing it in the modern market. Nostalgia will only get you so much dollar value, and while I think this is a GREAT remaster of a truly classic game, there are plenty of arcade plane shooters out there which will hit the spot for many gamers.
In short - if you remember playing this game when younger on the Amiga, you'll probably still love it.  If you don't remember it, then it probably doesn't hold up as well compared to more modern games... but I'd definitely recommend it if it was on a decent special.

Before you read this review, please consider that I have NOT played the original game. Therefore, I can't give it any credit for nostalgia.
Allright, let's get this show on the road:
Wings! Remastered Edition is (as the name implies) a remastered version of the original game form 1990. The game offers three types of missions, isometric strafing runs, top down bombing runs and 3D dogfighting.
Bombing- and strafing runs are somewhat fun, since the enemy's actually trying to shoot you down. The dogfighting?
Hooooo boy. Now let it be said that I've played and liked many repetitive games, but this one takes the cake.
The dogfighting missions are ALWAYS the same: you'll start in the same area, with the enemies right in front of you, even though the mission briefing said something completely different.
I've played this game for over and hour, and I'm still fighting the same bloody enemies; if you hate the Fokker E.III, this is the game for you.
To make matters worse, some of these mission are utterly pointless, since they'll pit you and your wingmen against unarmed balloons without escorts, or a single enemy. And that single enemy isn't an ace and/or flying some superplane, mind you. Just some regular single sod who's about to have a really s@#*!ty day.
The controls are dumbed down, even for an arcade game: you can't do loopings or control the speed of your plane. There's only one playable plane and it turns painfully slow (aren't biplanes known for their agility?), and the camera's stuck in that weird position right behind the pilots head. There is a first person mode, but you'll have to hold down a button to use it.
Like many other games, your machine gun can overheat if you're too triggerhappy. When that happens, the game will pause to show you a text card telling you about your overheated gun. Who in their right mind thought that this was a good idea?!
Ugh. Last but not least, there seems to be but one campaign, which means we're once more stuck with shooting evil germans. I really wish they'd leave that cliché to WW2 games.
Pitch perfect remake and great nostalgia - controls are slightly clunky but then that just adds authenticity as the Amiga controls were a bit ropey as well :)

A FLAWED REMASTERING
I fondly remember playing Wings on my old Amiga some 20 years ago, spending MANY hours playing it over and over again. It was probably my favorite Amiga game ever. Although this remastering looks great graphically, it's incredibly flawed and not an exact copy of the original. It's still fun to play, but if you've ever played the original, you may be disappointed as I am.
GAME MECHANCS AND PRE-MISSION TEXT
My biggest problem with the game is that it totally ignores all the mission text you see right before you jump in to dogfight. I'm talking about the white narration text on a black background just before the mission starts. Numerous times it will read "We surprised them and came up on their tails" or "We spotted the enemy down below", but EVERY SINGLE TIME you start and the enemy are STRAIGHT ahead of you. Ever. Single. Time. Nothing changes. VERY lazy developers!
The original game actually followed this text and sometimes missions threw you in really bad starting positions where the enemy is on your tail or coming up from the side or something. With this version, EVERY mission starts out the same and it gets really boring after a while. My dogfight tactic of choice always is to point up to the sky, get as high as I can, then dive the enemy as they pass under me to attack the AI planes. It never fails and is just as predictable as the missions are.
YOU CAN NO LONGER LAND YOUR PLANE SAFELY
In the original game, sometimes your plane would take so much damage and you would have to force a landing. Sometimes you would crash into another plane and have to force a landing. Sometimes you walked away, other times you didn't. In this version everything is considered instant death, so when you crash that's it, no walking away.
THE REASON IT WAS CALLED "CINEMA"WARE
One of the things that was great about the original game was that if an enemy got on your tail, it would enter this "cinema mode" where all of a sudden it's like you're watching an old film and you're in 3rd person view behind the enemy plane chasing yours, allowing you to try to shake it off (which then put you back in 1st person view if you succeeded.) In this game that is totally gone, so if a plane does get behind you, you have to work a little harder to find where it is.
BOMBING RUNS
I am only half way through the game, so this may come up later, but in the original, if you were bombing an aerodrome and enemy planes managed to take off, you actually had to fight them as they flew down from the top of the screen. I have yet to see this happen in this version.
OVERALL
It is still fun, but the fact each dogfight mission starts out exactly the same is what kills this game for me. I miss the original version!

games back on the Amiga had a certain magic about them. When you clicked the disk into the drive and started to load you instantly knew you were in for something special.
was one of the real standouts, at the time, it was one-of-a-kind and interestingly I can still say the same 25 years later! WWI games continue to be rare.
A valid argument against Wings is that the gameplay is too simple, and yes, by modern gaming standards, the gameplay is rather basic more akin to a casual game. It is also rather easy so hardcore gamers might find limited enjoyment. The introduction of saving your progress every 5 missions could have been excluded in my view considering the overall difficulty.
That being said, it still has something many modern games often lack, and that is atmosphere & immersion. In
, this is created primarily by the ongoing story shared in the form of a
diary, vividly putting you into the mind of a British WWI fighter pilot from snot-nosed rookie to seasoned ace. You get a strong sense of their fears & ongoing personal challenges as they patrol the front, and when you realise that the average life expectancy of a new pilot in WWI was only 11 days it really drives home the emotions those pilots must have had going up in fragile wooden bi-planes day in and day out on what must have seemed a never ending war.
Along with the 'humanising' components of the story, there is also a good dose of historical context
. Wings taught me more about the First World War & those pioneering fighter pilot days than any teacher did back in school!
The gameplay itself is split into three distinct modes; Dogfighting, Strafing & Bombing. Strafing & Bombing levels are top down/isometric views of your plane giving you a specific target to destroy
. These add some variety, although the real fun is in the dogfighting mode.
In Dogfighting, it is more a simulator cockpit view
. All of these modes feel very authentic to the original, although AI could have been improved for dogfighting. The real risk I have found, is not so much being shot down, but rather running into your wingmen or German pilots.
Again, this comes back to my earlier point about the game being too easy as once you learn how to avoid collisions survival
is almost guaranteed. Destroying the Balloons missions particularly offer no challenge. I always remembered there being a good chance of being shot down by AA fire in the original, yet I can head directly to a balloon in the remake and always get the win.
I am a bit torn in my view in one respect. While I really like the authentic re-creation, I would have also liked to seen more enhancements/improvements to counter the simplicity. To offer a harder challenge, keeping the soul of
but offer more variety. More work on different mission scenarios, improved plane controls
, different starting positions or altitudes
, better AI, even more randomness in plane destruction model or longer missions would have been welcome.
Despite the repetitive nature of the game, and the relative ease,
continues to be so much fun to play. My first session I couldn't put this down for over 6 hours! It is perhaps the best & most authentic Amiga remake I have played to date. The musical score is top notch
, voice acting is exceptional & graphical improvements
honour the original feel while adding more visual detail.
Whether you are a fan of the original or never played
before, this is truly a classic game. It has good replayability
& accessible to casual gamers while also teaching you a bit about the horrific years of the First World War.

Subspace isn't the perfect 2D action MMO... but it's damn close.
Its graphics are dated and some aspects of the game aren't as well-explained as they could be. The small community that have stuck with the game since its first release in 1997 can be a little hardnosed towards newbies. Those are the bad points.
The good points? Regular player-run events. Highly competitive league matches. Many different ways to play the game even within the same "zone" (game server). Crisp, responsive controls. Easy to learn but with a high skill ceiling. The chance to meet people from all over the world... and kill them!
Ultimately, Subspace is just a 2D spaceship game, but it's the first and finest of its type - a game that has yet to be bettered even after all these years. It has the magic to keep you coming back time after time if you can just stick with it, see past the graphics, and not pay too much heed to the sometimes irksome chat banter. The game is without doubt a timeless classic and any fan of MMOs owes it to themself to at least give it a try.

One of the very first MMOs, and still one of the most fun and accessible. SubSpace excels as a 2D combatitive time sink with community and personality, letting you play a few casual games of Hockey or Football, or a fast pace rampage in Trench Warfare, or the old solo or team Death Matches. The simple mechanics are easy to learn but difficult to master, and you can always find a place to hone your skills against fairly equally matched opponents.
SubSpace is nearly 20 years old, which is important to remember because it shows how incredibly well made this game was for its time that it's still a genuinely amazingly fun game to play to this day. It was developed by Virgin Interactive Entertainment, who were notable for titles like Dune II, Earthworm Jim, Resident Evil and Devil May Cry, and the excellent design shines through. The Continuum client was launched in the face of hacking and the downfall of VIE, and has become host to one of the most awesome long running gaming communities of all time.
The nature of gameplay means there's always something new to learn or a new style of play to try, and it's honestly a delight to play on and off for several years and then discover a new server or a new method of playing or a new control or ship that you weren't aware of. The variety is an integral part of what makes SubSpace so fun.
* Customization is a powerful component of SubSpace. Way before TF2, profiles provided the concept of Loadouts, and can be mixed and matched with other functions. There are a heap of little extra features which you might never use, but which are great for players who have been around a while
* The community deserves special mention. Nearly two decades of server birth, death and evolution offer some great history which you can check out. There are tons of content, history and even things like player lore/stories to explore outside of the Client, and they're all easy to get involved with
Games with big gameplay or game design mistakes don't survive for very long, and after 20 years of honing and adaptation, SubSpace is at its peak. While there are gameplay modes that people just aren't going to like, there are a handful more that they will, and it honestly becomes quite difficult to find something to dislike about this game. One could argue that the graphics are passed their prime, and that's true, but it's insignificant in terms of gameplay and is only worth holding back on if you can't bare to have fun under lower resolution 2D graphics.
One thing that many have issues with is familiarization with the game client. There's a steep learning curve and it's often difficult to get started playing a game without knowing the ins and outs. Fortunately there are some fantastic getting started guides, and I've referenced a few below. If you're looking for immediate play without learning some controls and nuances, this game might not be for you.
Subspace Continuum is available for free and has a tiny filesize. It takes a few minutes to see if it's your thing, but be sure to try a few different server types and ship types until you find something you enjoy.

I'm not a big fan of beat 'em ups and I also rarely go into games with big expectations, but for some reason they were moderately high for Mother Russia Bleeds and it did not deliver.
First of all, the game looks great, there are a lot of different backgrounds, a lot of differently looking enemies and allies and some alright bosses. But that's pretty much all the good things it has the offer.

any decent
also surprised me a lot, as I can't force myself to accept a game about 4 gypsy street fighters taking on the whole Russian army with their bare fists as a serious one. I expected jokes. Any. Fun ones. And the game was actually dark and grim but not to the point of actually making you feel for the characters.

are poorly developed and you barely learn anything about them, except for the short texts during loading screens.
Aaand we get to the most important parts of a beat 'em up - combat mechanics and gameplay. And this is exactly where Mother Russia Bleeds fails the hardest. Calling the
simple would be a compliment - there are literally no combos to do, so chaining different types of punches/kicks does nothing and you will most likely spend at least half of the game doing the very same move that knocks enemies around.The fighting, in general, is not very exciting, except for the times when a bunch of gun wielding enemies are appearing and you have to sacrifice a virgin every time you try to slidekick them in order not to slide inbetween their legs, because of the
. Last, but not least, this is hands down a game made to be played in Co-op (Yay!) by up to 4 people (YAY!), but does not support online Co-op (Boo!). I haven't tried Local Co-op just yet (I'm willing to, because the game might actually be fun), but I have my fear of setting up multiple controllers on one PC. So, on my solo playthrough, I decided to go with a full squad of AI, because I thought bots would be quite useful (probably due to my recent playthroughs of L4D2 and Vermintide without full squads of people) and I'm not afraid to say that this is the worst ally AI I have seen in a game so far in my life. Bots will never prioritize more dangerous/more important targets (stronger enemies, gunners), they'll never help you ("Oh, you're getting swarmed and are knocked down? Well, the 3 of us better keep bashing this single dog over here!") and I'm yet to see them effectively damage a more complex boss. In the middle of a huge fight they will just ditch  you to extract a dose of Necro, although they have 2/3 and are full health even when you're fighting everything on the screen with 0 Necro and 20% health and they will NEVER heal you with their Necro (L4D2 bots healing you when they're at 1hp, anyone?). But the worst part is that, when ANYONE dies, they'll just swarm up on his body and get 100%-to-0'd getting knocked around with the intention to revive the person. Because of that, you will often see 1 bot get swarmed and killed and the other 2 dying for no reason because of bad AI, leaving you alone with a number of enemies spawned for 4 players. They can serve as decent distraction at times, especially in boss fights, but I can't say if playing with 0, 1, 2 or 3 bots is best, because I've tried 0 and 3 so far and 0 felt a tiny bit better.
If you've read through my review and still want to give the game a shot - get a copy on a discount and grab a friend or 3 for a Local Co-op of the game with a few beers and some pizza. It's bound to be fun.

Voxelized is at this point a garden variety sandbox game that might cost more money than it's worth. It's extremely early access and is still in the early, early, early stages of development, meaning that it has a ton of issues and there's not much to do. If you're looking for a cheap game that's lots of fun or an indie alternative to Minecraft, I honestly wouldn't recommend this.
There are so many issues with this game right now. The movement is choppy, the design is generic, the blocks differentiate themselves very little from already existing sandbox games, there's a jumping glitch, there's no inventory, no way to see which block you're using, no way to interact with doors, and the only achievement in game is not only a secret achievement- but it's broken.
With all of those complaints, you're probably wondering why I recommended this game - and here's why: It's a work in progress. This is one of the earliest versions of a game I've ever seen released on Steam, and the awesome part is that the developer is listening to people's feedback on the game and using that feedback to help improve it. Think about that. If you buy this game now, you can literally help shape what it becomes. How awesome is that?
Right now, this is something that you have to accept at face value. It's getting worked on, and there are a lot of issues that you're going to need to put up with if you intend to play it at this stage, but it's only going to get better from here. If you really like sandbox games, if you really like taking chances, creating, seeing games evolve, or having your opinion matter, this is probably something that you should look into.

Voxelized is one of the earliest of Early Access games I've ever played. It is, frankly, amazing that they are accepting money for it at this stage of development. Luckily I didn't have to pay money for what looks to be a tech demo as I got my key from a Greenlight promotion run by the dev, but you should not by any means pay money for this until some actual game arrives.
The first thing I do when I start a game is try to go to the options menu. This game doesn't even have one (it has a button, but it's grayed out, along with several other features). Once you get into the game things only go downhill. In a block building game, the first thing you're going to want to do is mess around and build some blocks, right? The inventory is apparently still a work in progress too because it's just a list of buttons on the left side of the screen that can only be accessed while the game is paused; not to mention they're all default Unity buttons, something I haven't seen Air Control. Air Control! After figuring out how to get a block in my hand (figuratively, because of course there's no block nor hand) my first mission was to build a tower and see how high I could get. This simple task proved impossible. In games like Minecraft you can jump while facing down, place a block, land, and repeat to gain height quickly. In this game, trying this tactic is a fool's errand. The game will randomly decide to bounce you into the stratosphere, usually straight up but not always, and after falling from a fairly significant height (and many other smaller ones along the way) I decided I didn't want to go through the struggle of trying to get back up and gave up, shut down the game, and came to write this review.
There are other technical details I could pick on like the awful music (at least they do provide separate volume sliders for everything, which is a positive) or that it's uglier than Minecraft, but really what it comes down to is that there's precious little game there right now, and what is there doesn't work very well. You've got a handful of block types with an inventory that is as slow and tedious as the molasses-like movement system, and...well, that's it really. The state of development is similar to Minecraft's indev, or even earlier. If you absolutely must get your Minecraft fix on Steam and think Voxelized is the ticket, maybe it'll eventually be worth your money, but for now it's safely a pass.
Just get a free minecraft clone.

This rather pathetic tech demo/test program passing greenlight and being for sale in the actual Steam store clearly exemplifies just how broken Steam is at the moment.
The price, without discounts, of this... thing is €3.99 in the EU1 store, but there is nothing here. Sure, you can move around in the world and you can remove and add some blocks, but that is pretty much it. We can go all metaphysical and ask "what is a game?", but I'm afraid that just about any way you ask that question, the answer is "something that isn't Voxelized".
Now, the developer seems to be saying that he wants the community around his... creation to shape it, and let him know in what direction to take it, but that is disingenuous, at best. To me, that is him basically saying that he's completely devoid of any ideas or ambitions of his own, and he wants the "community" to design his game for him, and that would be... you know... pretty bad. I wish I could come up with some other explanation, but seeing as how he's provided no framework and presented no design or plan of his own for what Voxelized is supposed to become, it becomes clear that this really is something considerably less than just a very early alpha of a game.
It truly is no more than a simple test program, that, through the massive faults of the Steam Greenlight process and Steam vetting of what is offered up for sale in the store, has been elevated to a for-sale product. And no amount of labeling as "Early Access" can change the fact that this... thing, has no business whatsoever being for sale to unsuspecting customers.
Hell, if he wanted feedback, then perhaps a Greenlight page would have been a good place to get it, but instead, this developer has broken new ground - instead of letting your paying customers just be your QA, he's asking them to also be the design team. I strongly suspect that the only reason he's not making them also be the development team, is that he lacks the programming chops to build the scaffolding needed around his... product to allow it to be modded.

This game is somewhat easy to pick up, but hard to master. People have been playing this game for a while and spent crazy amounts of time in it, why? we don't have p2p, or some other BS. it's all skill.
There are different kinds of zones, some are T v T, FFA,  Flagging (static flags (point domination) and movable ones) and events. Hell, I've even seen someone modify a server so much with bots they built an RPG (Mystic kingdom).
You have 8 ships to choose from, each with it's own playing style.
You can have squads (clans), chats, banners(small images next to your ship), and the best thing of all LEAGUES!
This game is international, you can meet people from Europe, Asia, South America, etc, since game is somewhat simple, you don't really need to segment a zone (server), it works great!
I would say this is the Quake 3 arena of shooters,
Extreme games in particular has superior settings to any other zone.
Zones are player run, there's no corporate entity pulling strings for some profit or appeasing a board of stake holders, there's no profit here, it's all for the game.
Development tools are free, forever. If you don't like a zone, shut up and make your own. Make your own maps, and make your own bots. Shape a zone just the way you like it. Bots are availble in a number of programming languages, I've seen frameworks built on C++ (Mervbot), Java (TwCore), Python (Pythoncore) and modules for an alternative server written in C and Python (I think) (ASSS).
As a personal note, I no longer play as much as I used to, family, friends etc come in the way, I like the community, it feels like you can speak your mind without fear of censorship, I've made some friends and I still chat with them from time to time. I was also able to do some software development, helped build and maintain a zone (honing online community skills), designed websites and banners and was part of very fun leagues for a while.
If you like, communities, arcade style, 0 BS, games, you might want to give this game a try.
If you're all for the graphics, or storylines, context or hand holding, this is probably not for you.

Hey all,
I used to love this game on the Amiga, actually I still have the gae on Amiga witht the box and everything. And I was really anticipating the release of this version. For first , they almost kept the entire story from the Amiga so if you played it as often as I did you should remember the story and notice that only a few things have changed. They have introduced a few bonus missions for you to fly instead of your pilot going for leave to london and sutch. Also the journal is now read to you in english so you can have the game running in a differnet language but the audio is still english.
For those that never played the original here the basics. The game leads you as a/manny pilots through a flight journal of a British WW1 fighter Squadron. You will have to do different types of missions sutch as strafing ground targets, bombing differnet types of enemy positions from Airfields to trainstations to submarines and so on. And last of course the dogfights. This is as it was in the original the only combat were your pilot can die. you might get shot down in other missions but you will not die there. Exept if you loose to manny aircraft your pilot will get kicked from the squadron.
They got some things right and some not, as it will be with any game played. I like the better graphics but the game in bombing mode or strafe mode feels to fast, considering your aircraft of that time only flew about 140Kp/h. Next thing is yes they did a nice 3d version of the dogfights but it still looks a bit outdated , and i am missing the trenches on the ground aswell as planes that you shot down actually being down there and not blowing up leaving no trace they ever existed. Also a dislike is the way planes go down now, it seems you only have to hit them with 10 bullets and the plane is history, AND it dropslike a rock. They indeed did put in some interresting stuff like wings ripping off and sutch but it doesn't feel the way the old wings gave you.
Overall I say yes this game is worth it, and helps Cinemaware get back on their feet. Support them because it is thatnks to companny's like these that made gameing as big as it today. Without these pinoeers there might not be a gaming industry.

Totally worth the $20 it cost to get in right now, and I can't wait to see where they go with this.

First things first, this game is very clearly in Alpha! Do NOT expect a complete game! That being said, this game is at a much better point than most others are at in Alpha. Visually, the game is all there, it looks good, animations are decent, proper shading and lighting is all done, the art style bares a heavy resemblance to Mass Effect and XCOM, but still stands well enough on its own.  Progression is very limited right now, with only two weapons and three armor types, no melee or abilities yet. the free-aim combat is very welcome and works well, but theres nothing to really use on it yet, as enemies are relatively slow, predictable, and can mostly be defeated by just walking backwards while firing to stay out of their melee range. The map and quest markers are horrible and will have you tearing your hair out over the most basic objectives which would be child's play with any other game's map (collect x number of objects, take object to npc, visit all the locations, etc).  There is no crafting yet either. However, the reason I still recommend this game is because the devs are actually working on things. the game has improved significantly already, and they do well to keep the community informed on progress behind the scenes. Its not there yet, but I think this game may actually live up to its potential, a very rare thing among early access titles.

For an Alpha this is not too bad. However I must say before I continue that if you are looking for anything that resembles a completed game that this is not it. That being said with what we currently have the groundwork for something amazing is here. The Devs are a 10 man independent group working on this title. And they have posted a lot of information on the website and other places on there hopes and progress of the game.

Set in the beautiful city of Hong Kong officer Wei Shen is tasked to bring down the local Triad gang Sun On Yee as an uncercover cop. He gets introduced into the mafia by his old friend Jackie Ma from where he starts working his way up to the top of the criminal circuit. Wei Shen is a loyal person, that loyalty brings him into trouble in both sides of the law because trying to do good takes it toll and possibly his sanity.
The story is well written and ensures that the protagonist doesn't climb up in the ranks too fast in an unrealistic manner. Obviously you shouldn't expect the drama, character relations and humor known from the GTA franchises in this game. Simply because this game depicts how it feels like to survive in a triad gang, not how to save your marriage or how to setup your own drug empire in the middle of a desert.
With the Definitive Edition this game received a graphical update and boy does it show. If you ever want to visit Hong Kong, play this game first. Not that it will be a perfect tour guide, but it really captivates the atmosphere of this asian city with its many districts. Clean and modern looking in 'downtown' area, flashy neon signs and dense ugly looking high-rises in the poorer parts of the city and the many houseboats docked at the docking area. While playing this game I often felt like I was playing in a living, breathing world. That's something I didn't always have while playing a GTA game. Sure I've never been in Hong Kong or any asian city, but after playing this game it kinda feels like I did.
The graphical update also shows during cutscenes where it looks like this game is actually just two years old instead of the original four. There can be some graphical glitches here and there, i.e. npc's popping in/out of screen in front of your face and certain visual effects not always appearing while driving vehicles. But nothing too troublesome.
I only played this game with a controller so I can't give any input on how it feels with mouse and keyboard. In general I'm very positive about it although there are some points which did annoy me. First off the driving mechanics could be better, even while playing with a controller I have to tab my stick constantly while making larger turns instead of one fluid movement. Bikes have a larger turning radius than cars and driving a car backwards is like driving on ice. But you'll get used to it eventually and thus won't be as big of a problem than in the beginning.
The combat in this game is clearly pointed towards melee combat. Reason being that in the triad culture most fights are fought with bare hands and less with fire arms like we're used to in the west. There are a lot of fighting moves to learn and they all transition perfectly with each other when fighting. The downside to this is that the weapon combat not as refined as in other games.

Awesome story, great music, beautiful art and a lovely and very novel RPG experience.  I would honestly say this is one of the best RPG video games I've played.
And it gets even better once you complete the story and play it in recursion mode.  There's some truly fun stuff unlocked by leveling up even further.
I love the idea that all of the character's attacks are named like programming functions.  You tie them together to produce a more complicated attack.  Finding effective combinations can be difficult at first, but it's worth the effort, because some of them are truly amazing!  (Spark() enhanced with Spark(), once you get a second copy of it, for example, but you'll likely have to finish the story before you can do that!)
The game lets you discover details about people the functions are derived from by using them in three different ways, eventually giving you a complete dossier/biographical summary on them, each of which gives insight on the background events leading up to the game.  The first is to use the function directly, producing some kind of effect.  The second is to apply them to another function, modifying how it works.  The last way is to apply them to a passive slot, enhancing the main character in some automated fashion.
The best way I found to discover good uses of functions that suit my play style was to try them each way, using the descriptions of what they do as a guide.
The only downside is how short the story is.  However, a short game can often be far more polished and higher quality than a longer game.  This is an example of an amazingly well-made short game.  Worth every penny, even at full price.

If you're looking for a new MMO made within the last few years, this is easily one of the best. Unlike most MMO's on the market, FF14 is actually story driven. While the writing isn't always the most amazing, and the voice acting can be hit or miss on some characters, the overall end product is quite well presented. And the story itself is overall quite good, and does a great job at making you feel heroic and important at appropriate times. There are innumerable non-main storyline quests available if you care to do them. Every class has their own unique story to follow. And some side quests that are hidden away for you to find are true gems. There are hundreds upon hundreds, if not thousands of hours, of content to do in quests alone, depending on your pace and weather you're the kind to read everything offered. (Which I suggest, particularly in regards to speaking with nearby characters during main story quests to get an abundance of bonus dialogue that can often be amusing, insightful, and interesting.)
Many of the areas within the game are quite beautiful, making exploration quite enjoyable for new players, and older players who have long since seen everything will find many 'favorite spots' dotted about the game that they can always return to if they feel like it. Some scenes are truely a sight to behold when seen at just the right time.
As for the gameplay, for anyone who has played Square's previous MMO, FF11, you might find the grind to be somewhat familiar. Or, some might find it to be conciderably easier. Your milage may very based on personal perspective and experience. In terms of leveling, it's far from as mindnumbing as many other games, as Square included several systems to lessen the time sink involved in leveling, in addition to offering items that can increase exp gain. Casual play could see you through to cap with your first class, mostly by following the main quest, within a few weeks provided you read and watch everything. Rushing hard and skipping everything you could cap within a week, maybe two depending on your free time. Combat, contrary to many shallow complaints by people who likely never saw a job past 30, is not extremely slow. A global CD of 2 seconds is not the end of the world, and becomes largely irrelevant rather quickly as classes accumulate off gdc abilities you can use between them. Without even reaching the original~ level cap, you will find most every class has something you should be doing at all times provided you aren't being deliberately lazy and coasting through combat on one or two buttons whie your party does the work. That's a player problem, not a game problem.
While there is mountains more that could be said about any number of things, if anything should be mentioned, it's the flaws within the game. It's not perfect. The game's dungeons and raids can range in difficulty from childishly easy, to eye gougingly, aggrevating, difficult. Especially if you have poor party members. Square's idea to lock some content behind a pre-made party wall makes playing all the end game content difficult without a dedicated group to play with. And depending on what server you join, there may not be much, or any, end game playerbase, while others might consist of nothing but end gamers standing around waiting for queues. As amazing as the game looks, many areas are devoid of relavant content past certain levels. As a result, many places will appear entirely dead because there's no reason for anyone to return after a certain point outside of leveling or rare events like hunt mob spawns. Again, this is largely server dependant, but is~ a problem none-the-less. It causes players to concentrate in select few places over time and leaves the world feeling empty, even when a server is completely full. Playing with Free Company members, or joining newbies that you see and taking the opportunity to level something new can do wonders to avoid this problem. Or be a loner that doesn't care about other players being around. That also works, but is kinda boring to me. Perferences. Once you've spent an inordinant amount of time in the game, you might find that the selection of dungeons, while large, grows increasingly repetative after you've leveled multiple classes and have seen the same boss for the 200th time. It's annoying. While not a problem for new players, or even for most players within the first several months or more of playing. For long, long time players. It's aggrevating. The game needs more dungeons, especially of the lower end leveling kind. The biggest flaw in the game, and the quickest to grow tiresome, are the FATES. Randomly spawning overworld combat events. Square overuses FATES for literally everything they can shoehorn them into. Seasonal/special events? Go do FATES. Grinding end game relic gear? Go do FATES. Grinding levels? FATES. FATES get old, and they don't age well. In a few, rare instances they're done well. While it might occationally be lackluster now, with low player turnouts due to the new expansions and higher lvl cap making the fight easier, coupled with fewer people actually needing the rewards. Keep your eyes open for Odin in the black shroud if you do play. That~ is a fate that was done right, and is still exciting to stumble upon even to this day, where I have long since passed any need to participate in it. And if it's on a good day, you might experience something rather impressive to behold, as others in the past have when finding him for the first time.
In summery, the game isn't perfect. It's got problems. At least a few more than are listed here. And some common complaints are often blown far out of proportion by people who haven't, or refused, to get invested in the game or give it a fair chance. But it's got an abundance of good points as well. A great story. Great presentation. Solid gameplay. Ongoing support which will someday amount to an even larger game than it already is. Possibly far larger (hopefully). A growing class/job list that provides plenty of variety, all at your fingertips on a single character, and much more.
Of all the recent MMOs that I've played, and I've played more than a fair few. FF14 is head and shoulders above the rest, with a potentially strong future to boot. I'd easily give it 9/10. The flaws it has aren't enough to hold it back from being great, and only really~ impacted me after thousands~ of hours of playtime, and I'll keep playing whenever the opportunities arrise in the future.

I have wasted at least half a year's worth of hours on this game during my life. It's one of the games I point to when someone asks me about PC gaming, and why I'm a PC gamer (along with: Wing Commander series, Baldur's Gate series, Age of Empires series (♥♥♥♥ 3 IMO), most of the Sid Meier's games, among others).
This game epitomizes what I consider to be PC gaming. I figure other people can explain it better than me, so I'm gonna just give some examples:
My favorite server (from the past, I think it's gone now?): 17th Parallel. It was Soccer with Subspace Continuum mechanics. The main game was fun, but they'd also host events (separate from the main pub). Some would be completely different from the main game, like a huge mothership (controlled by one player) with X amount of turrets (other players) trying to find a new planet with an enemy fleet (other players) attack.♥♥♥♥♥♥could get intense, and was always fun for the amount of time spent hosting. There would be bots set up in different "pubs" (or maps within the specific server) which you could use to help challenge other players to duels. Or they'd automatically host other kinds of events.
Desert Storm server. Dude, this server was the most fun I've had in any game ever... Every ship was turned into a different kind of infantry unit (machine guns, bazooka, sniper, etc). Several control points ("buildings", key strategic spots, etc) with an assortment of spawn areas dotted across the map that unlocked/locked depending on which control points were held. And the body count would rise to a righteous degree, the killing, the war, the blooooood... We'd spend hours having the most epic battles ever. You'd acquire coins and XP for getting kills (more with killing sprees) and helping capture control points. XP unlocked soldier types (sniper, bazooka, etc), and other things like Rank, new catagories to purchase from, etc. But the real thing was the coins. Spend those and you could have a tank. Or nuke the enemy team. Or whatever else. All this could turn the tide in the endless war. Instead of losing, your team would go to victory.
And that's just two servers. Subspace Continuum is definitely worth your time. It's on another level entirely. Some servers have steep learning curves. Others simple to learn, kinda hard (but not really) to master. Once you get into it, it'll be your new addiction.
All of this, and more, for free.

If you're still pondering downloading this game, go ahead and give it a click. It takes all of about 10 seconds to download (80 seconds @256kb/sec) plus some other, short download times in game. It's taken me longer to write this review than it takes to jump in and start playing.
Now if you're looking for more helpful information, here's a brief summary of the most populous zone (and my personal favorite, SSCU Trench Wars.
Trench Wars gameplay consists of all 8 ships in a coordinated basing match, with the goal to capture and hold a flag located at the top of the base (North of where you spawn) for 3 minute blocks. This public arena alone can capture your fascination for hundreds of hours.
The ships are also based on different units one might find in trench warfare. After entering the game, press one of the following key combos to play:
Esc + 1 : enter as Warbird, the sniper ship. Warbirds strong bullet kills every other ship with a single shot. It's fluid movement also makes it the most popular ship in the game.
Esc + 2 : enter as Javelin, the grenade ship. Javelins (javs) have a bouncing bomb, making them one of the most fun and dangerous ships in a basing match.
Esc + 3 : enter as Spider, the Machine gunner. With the ability to spray many bullets very quickly, spiders are most effective in pairs, where they can quickly take apart an entire team.
Esc + 4 : enter as Leviathan, the tank. Leviathans (levis) have a single ultra powerful bomb, which decimates everything in the explosion radius. But they're so slow, you have to be exceptionally talented to make it to base!
Esc  + 5 : enter as Terrier, the supply truck. Terriers are the fastest ship in the game, responsible for supplying fresh troops to the battle. Players can attach by having the terrier's name ticked in the F2 menu, and pressing F7.
Esc + 6 : enter as Weasel, the spy. Weasels can fully cloak, sneak into the enemy's base, and surprise attack!
Esc + 7 : enter as Lancaster, the shotgun infantry. Lancasters can multifire, making their shots almost impossible to dodge!
Esc + 8 : enter as Shark, the minesweeper. Sharps can repel enemy bullets and bombs away, as well as leave mines for careless enemies to slip into. But be careful, they have no bullets!
Beyond pub, there are literally hundreds of additional events, and several unique, thriving competition leagues. But you've done enough reading for now, get in and play!
Also, my in game name is WillBy, if you see me, be sure to say hello!

Seriously couldn't stop for the first 11 hours.  A fantastic game in its very beginning, and I cannot wait for more developments. The simple story in it self is incredibly compelling given its minimalist nature.  It even brings something to life something that I think many people who fantasize about space travel have considered.  Essentially, would you be able to recover from a crash landing given the adequate resources and technology?  What could you really do even with minimal supplies, and what ever technology survived the crash? Would the right stuff even survive? What challenges do we face? If you play with someone more experienced, vastly, at the game they might just deploy a fortress of a base without much explanation due to their knowledge - but the real joy in this game is figuring out how things work for yourself.
The pacing is great, the enemies are still a threat and you could possibly still stalemate in multiplayer if you can't get your resources. It really is a sandbox that you make as challenging as you want for yourself, with tons of options to skew the difficulty up or down.
It runs flawlessly, looks great, and doesn't explain much to you. That is the fun in this game - there is a lot of upgrades, a lot of content and possibly endless ways to approach the end of the game - which I am absolutely nowhere near. Probably the best building/management game I've ever played because it really is just simply fun and almost like a complex puzzle - but one YOU built.

Winds of Trades is a trading game that is accessible enough and streamlined for newcomers but has enough features and personality to hold the attention of fans of the niche.
Positives
+ The political and stock market mechanics are well-implemented and offers multiple approaches to the game.
+ Developter solicits feedbacks and regularly updates game with said feedback.
+ Smuggling illegal goods is a great feature.
+ World events that can affect the game add a lot of charm and keep things from being too predictable.
+ Fairly large selection of ships and upgrades.
Neutral
o The game's dynamic simulatoin of an economy is both its greastest strength and obstacle; there is a fair amount of menus to help you understand overall prices of all colonies in one screen, but the player seems to be forced to look up each town to understand consumption and plan their strategy accordingly.
o Can be hard to predict the level of demand and drop of prices when selling goods, but maybe that's a fault against me rather than the game.
o Combat is rather plain, but is fairly balanced.
Negatives
- Have to manually select each ship when they are in a fleet to trade goods, they are not "consolidated" all at once.
- I'm probably being picky here but when selling a good it would be nice to have the tool tip pop up showing lowest/highest price like it does when you buy goods.
- I may be wrong here but other than establishing colonies later on you can't build up existing colonies industries like you can Patirician.
Overall it offers a good value for the price,  looking forward to how this game evolves and what the developer has to offer in the future.

Here is a list of glitches that forced me to refund the game:
1.- The game has unplayably low FPS on Linux using the open source Nvidia driver (GeForce 640M) so I tried lowering the game's resolution.
2.- Lowering the game's resolution is useless, the whole UI shrinks with the game view, so at sizes small enough to be playable, you cannot even see the text in the screen. The game has a "Scale UI" feature, but it doesn't help. You can only scale the text a little bit, and at High quality graphics there's a lot of aliasing that renders part of the text invisible and therefore unreadable.
3.- This compares very badly to other 3D Unity games that I can still play in my PC with the open source driver (admittedly not at a great speed, but they can be played).
I couldn't experience the gameplay due to those issues, so I do not recomment this game unless you are using the proprietary NVidia driver or a modern ATI card. Also, if you have a low resolution screen, I don't recommend this game, you won't be able to read the text.

A unique multiplayer game that is heavily influenced by your ability to manage your ship's turn rate and momentum, which will be inherited by your weapon projectiles. As a predecessor to Infantry Online, Subspace Continuum is a bit more limited in scope, but still offers more than enough challenge and depth to keep you hooked for years trying to hone your skills as a pilot. Unlike many multiplayer games, Subspace truly achieves the feeling of "massive" multiplayer combat, with chaotic team battles commonly involving over 30-40 players at a time.
Similar to the custom maps in Warcraft 3, Subspace Continuum offers the added variety of multiple zones each with their own set of game rules and objectives, allowing you to change up how you play based on your personal taste or current level of stress.

Sleeping Dogs features Wei Shen, an undercover cop struggling to balance his Triad loyalty and police responsibilities on the streets of Hong Kong.
The game features a well-crafted martial arts combat system, blending combos, counters, light and heavy attacks, and grabs/throws to create freeform fights that emphasize flow and diversity over efficiency. Environmental attacks and upgradeable special moves round out the variety.
The real selling point is the map design - Hong Kong is lovingly rendered with beautiful levels of detail, from crowded market streets to curved highways overlooking endless rows of shipping docks. It's a delight to simply drive along the coastal highways and listen to the rippling shoreline or zip around the market districts. It's downright breathtaking, and stands head and shoulders above GTA's cities in terms of sheer visual interest.
The story is solid, albeit a bit standard. Gunplay, driving, and some side activities like gambling or drug busts provide a solid variety of activities for the entire map. Music, sound and voice acting are top-notch.
This is a a polished and cinematic take on the GTA sandbox formula, I thoroughly recommend it.

I spent over 100 hours on the original Sleeping Dogs several years ago on my old PC; on my new, much more powerful machine, I was thrilled to play the definitive edition. It's not merely a re-release - it's a reworking of the graphics and an improvement on the already fun, fluid combat and driving mechanics, and it contains additions to the campaign (extended narrative, extra side missions) that are worthy of the repurchase cost for fans who already have the original (specifically those who liked it and want to play it again). Because I had already finished the campaign as well as the DLC episodes, I was hesitant to buy the same game twice, but when it went on sale for $7.50, I struck and was very happy I did. This is not only an extended and much more immersive experience; it works better on newer software and hardware architecture. It manages to pack Hong Kong more densely with NPCs and greatly improve environmental textures and weather while demanding much less of my GPU than the original release. They both hit some of the same framerates, but with settings cranked, my video card runs much harder & hotter in the original release while it's capable of rendering much more with less power in the definitive edition. Truly an optimal redesign for the PC.
For the many who've already played Sleeping Dogs and loved it, I recommend picking up the definitive edition IF you want to play through the campaign again or if you haven't played the DLC episodes (and I'd wait for a sale). You may find the experience enjoyable as I did or you may feel like you're wading through the same water (albeit much more detailed, highly rendered water). If you've never played this modern classic, this is the edition to get - it's a very fun open world action/adventure game in the vein of Grand Theft Auto with tons of collectibles, a martial arts beat 'em up combat system, great driving mechanics, fun missions and side-objectives, and, most importantly of all, a captivating story fronted by a compelling protagonist who leads a double life as both an undercover cop & triad member and a Chinese-American immigrant & Chinese national. As another Asian-American who's faced confusion stemming from a bi-cultural background, I find Wei Shen to be a well written, sympathetic and multi-faceted hero/anti-hero. In addition, the ties the game shares with HK Crime and Kung Fu films (references, atmosphere, setting, style) alone are enough to draw me in to its highly detailed vision of modern Hong Kong and keep me playing in it time and time again.
(9/10)

Pros: Its a classic WWI game, Great vocals and a more story oriented experience rather than simulation.
Cons: It's historically innacurate, It's still a classic game, It's not Red Baron. Performance is so-so for a game as simple as it is.
This is not worth the asking price to be honest. It isn't a bad game and will bring nostalgia to some I'm sure, but its also not really that great of a title. It is simply a classic game with a new coat of paint. The flight dynamics can be easily handled with keyboard or mouse.
When you compare it with Red Baron and other WWI flight sims, this comes up very short in all areas except the story. The better games pride themselves more on simulation and less on personality or characters. Wings! gets the personality right, but totally falls short in everything else.
Historical accuracy is visibly lacking. While there have been games like Wings of War which were less historical and more arcade, yet remained fun, this title really needs work if it is going for more story based immersion. But then, this was made years ago before people started to care a lot about that.
Really what this title needs is fresh investment and a full update to modern times. Fix all the glaring errors with the historical accuracy and it would be the benchmark in WWI flight games.
When it is all said and done, the intro price, even with a small sale, is a bit much. If this game is $5-$10 then you might find something.  If you are a nostalgia nut then you'll enjoy it. Otherwise, I'd wait for a sale and don't bother with this.

This game reminds me a great deal of Pandemic on Kongregate (and other sites, I suspect) - in many ways, it plays almost identically. But it's a far, far more polished version. It feels like the Blizzard take on Pandemic - polished up to an addictive shine. There's a lot more items to 'research' with your DNA points, more countries to infect, and a variety of different kinds of diseases to choose from. And then it adds additional features that make it far more interesting - combos of different symptoms with special effects, the ability to choose your starting country, cross-country animal-based infection, random events that can help or hinder your progress... The game's not done yet (this review written during Early Access) and it's already completely and totally supplanted Pandemic in my mind.
And this time, you have options in case someone sneezes in New York and Madagascar CLOSES EVERYTHING. :D

I really wanted to like this game. But this game doesn't have a learning curve. It has a learning cliff. One hundred stories of jagged broken glass that slams you in the face the moment you install it and enter the first menu. You'll enjoy it from the moment you install and see the pretty graphics until you actually try to play it. At that point it's all downhill until you find the only other enjoyable part, uninstalling it.
If you like reading more than playing, getting stomped by heckling high ranking opponents. Being one shotted by characters that mark you from across the map and then one-shot-kill you. Then this game is for you.
.
.
.
The good: graphics. It's free. You can unlock all of the in-game content that affects the gameplay for free.
The bad: Long wait times to play. No one using voice. No in-game explanation of the vast number character abilities, items, relics, and set up options. Several encyclopedias worth of information to read before you can play any character and actually win.
Every character has access to a hundred items, each with multiple stats, passives, and auras. But if you want to know what works for one character and not another you have to sift through pages and pages of guides made by the community.
Oh and by the way, there are three or four game modes and no one build works for all so be prepared to do that for every character, class, and game mode you want to play. Five classes. Almost 100 gods. Three primary game modes. A different build for each god in each game mode. You do the math.
And to top that off - Plenty of high ranking players that like to build premades and pub stomp. Along with trolls who will drag out a conguest game forever and never actually attempt to finish it.

So, I'm going to give this a positive recomendation, though I'm not super excited about the game and it is understandable if you pass it up. I'll explain why.
The short is: It's well put together for the most part; combat is little awkward but mostly avoidable. It is free, but seems to lack an end-game goal.
Oh, and if you do start, get the Cargo ship first. Consider the others once you're out of debt. In the Trading screen, hold Shift, Ctrl, or Alt to buy/sell multiple items at once.
The long is:
First the good stuff:
Price: I don't know their intent with the game, but it is free. I've not found any kind of microtransaction BS, so it is completely free. Hard to argue with that.
Few bugs: I shouldn't have to count this as a good point, but with the market as it is...
Autosave: VERY frequent. Should the game crash or you get killed, it will send you back maybe a minute or two of playtime.
You can build a fleet of ships, rather than just having to upgrade one giant ship. There is some control in the orders you give. I still recommend only having a fleet of very big ships, and sticking to one ship until then.
It isn't hard to build up money after the early game.
Everything has a 100% sell value. So if you buy stuff by mistake, it just costs you a second to correct it. Goods change value by planet, but equipment and ships don't, so buy and sell those wherever.
The bad stuff:
Mouse control for direction and shooting is unavailable, but would have been nice (I'm thinking like SPAZ).
Your fleet isn't good at staying near you if they are freighters. So don't buy small ships for your fleet, they are pirate bait. Big ships can at least survive long enough to resolve the situation (regroup and kill, run away, land on planet, etc).
It is very easy to miss the storyline (I did) when trying to make a quick buck early on.
The economy doesn't evolve. Values in each system stay exactly the same. While this does make things easier, it also removes any incentive to find new trade routes when you have a good one. This also means the jobs don't really evolve, so the stuff you see early on is all that will be there.
Each solar system feels tiny. You warp in next to the planet, and... that's pretty much it. Everything happens within sight range of a planet, so each system feels tiny, and all systems feel identical when you're flying around.
You start in debt. I realize this is part of the point of the game, but it feels weird having that weight hanging over our head for so long when jobs pay very little.
You can't switch between piloting different ships in your fleet.
The game doesn't seem to have an end goal, so you kind of have to set them for yourself. "Ok, I'm in debt. Let's get out of debt", "Ok, I'm no longer in debt, let's get a ship that doesn't suck". "I've got a decent ship, let's get the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the Galaxy". After that, uh, I don't know, keep going? Get a fleet I guess?
Getting money is also a grind. You start off in debt, which means your #1 goal is to make as much money as possible in as little time as possible, because if you don't you'll run out. Running goods from system to system is probably the easiest and most boring way to do this. Once you get out of debt, it's all profit though. I mainly stuck to cargo runs, which does appear to be the fastest way to get cash, once you have some decent capacity.
The pirates are just random enough to be annoying but not consistent enough to be a threat to plan for until very late in the game. With your first ship it really is just a crapshoot if there is enough friendly ships to kill the pirates before they get you. Even with mid-size ships it is far better to run away than try to fight. Big ships can stay and fight, but it is still usually easier to just run away. If you're making money cargo-hauling, don't even bother with weapons until you have a super freighter or a Behemoth, and even then I'd say wait until you have two of them, because you can still just run away.
Verdict: Above average

Poitives:
+Free
+Will run extremely well on a toaster.
+Expansive universe with a lot of detail for each world.
+Well written and thought out descriptions for everything planet, ship, and object in the game.
+Interesting quests that you will come naturally if you always check out the space ports.
+Simply but (mostly) relaxing trading mechanics.
+EXTREMELY immersive dispite it's simplicity.
Negatives
-No music, although you can easily fix that by setting your own music (say the soundtrack FTL) in the background.
-The game is bad at explaining things. There is a fine difference between having your hand held as your lead down a completely linear experience (ala Call of Duty) and not actually telling the player how to use even basic controls. For example, the game told how to open up your star map by hitting M to select a star system and that you jump to that system by hittingJ. What the game didn't tell me was that you had to actually EXIT your star map, THEN hit J to jump to the system.
As I said, you will randomly (and rarely) find quests if you visit the space port in each system, but nothing in the game even alludes to this fact, I found that out by accident. Also, you have to hold the space bar to quick buy a large amount of things in the trading area, which again I learned by accident (before that I was clicking for each and every piece of metal I was buying up).
-Combat is random, not all that interesting, and is always one sided one way or another. Pirates will randomly appear in a sector. If your a fighter, you turn your ship and fire your weapons at the enemy and hope they die before you do. If you are in a freighter, your guns turn so you don't have to (although freighters really suck at turning anyway) and again, you have to hope they die before you do. Either a single pirate ship will jump into a system teaming with a dozen friendly ships and die immediately, or six pirates will jump on you as your leaving a planet and blast you to bits without you being able to do anything. Death just makes you reload back to whatever planet you were last landed on, but that only highlights what a nusance combat in this game is.
Still, on the whole the game is one of the most immersive games I have played in years, and it is VERY easy to lose an embaressingly large amount of time to this game.

The Room is a puzzle game about opening a box, which continues to grow in complexity and difficulty.
There isn't much plot, the set up is simple: A relative has gifted you with the house and this box in the attic, and you try to solve it for some reason. Throughout the game you'll find notes left behind for you, which add a little flavour to the overall experience, but there isn't any depth to it really. The best comparison i can give to this is a cthulhu-esque plot, an investigator goes down a rabbit hole and finds things which are beyond his ken.
The gameplay is pretty simple, but its execution elevates it beyond most puzzle games. You manipulate bits and pieces on the box to solve the various puzzles on it, and you sometimes get an item for solving one of the puzzles in order to solve another puzzle on its surface, These can be pretty easy, while others can tax your brain a little if you aren't a logically minded person. What makes this game so fantastic though is the view point, everything is directly in front of you. Its really easy to rotate the box and look over the thing from a wide perspective, or zoom in to examine various aspects of it as you please, nothing is obscured, its just a matter of figuring out the correct order to solve each puzzle, in order to solve the greater puzzle of that section of the game before moving on. There is only one box, and its carefully designed for a fantastic experience. Unlike other puzzle games of a similar nature, your not going back and forth between different rooms or stations, wondering which station needs to be done next or if you missed something in a room five corridors back. It keeps everything focused, and this makes it far more enjoyable.
Graphically speaking its not mind blowing, but for what its worth they took their time crafting a very intricate puzzle box. It looks very nice, and there were no bugs or glitches to speak of which i encountered that caused any issues.
Overall, The Room is one of my favourite puzzle games of all time because of how well focused it is. I'd recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a quick, highly enjoyable puzzle game to just sit back and unwind with.

A good chunk of Transistor owners will already have played through Bastion - if you liked that, chances are good you'll like this. I'll be talking from the perspective of somebody who played through Bastion as a whole twice, and finished my first Transistor run a good 5 minutes before writing this. Transistor plays quite similarly on the whole, imo. Game mechanics have an overall similar feel, but some elements have been evolved. Discounting the story, it's about as much of a sequel to Bastion as Mass Effect 2 was a sequel to Mass Effect 1.
Weapon choices and strategy are dialled up, with a large mix of both active and passive slots (compared to 2 active + 1 special) - and any single weapon can be put into either slot, with differing effects. Weapons can also be layered on top of another in a slot, with another different effect depending on which weapon is on the bottom and what you put over it.
Although real time movement and combat are still available, you need to make use of what is basically a ~5s time-freeze button on a ~10s cooldown against all but the most trivial enemies. This particular element is almost like a very toned down version of Frozen Synapse's turn based combat. You press the button, plan out your ~5s worth of moves carefully, press the button again and watch yourself execute those commands while everything around you moves in ultra-slowmo. After the commands are finished, everything goes back to normal and your beepity boopity magic time fridge goes on cooldown. The extra twist is that while this is on cooldown, you lose the ability to use pretty much all weapons, meaning you have to make good use of combat bonuses like backstab (hit from behind for extra damage on some weapons), combo (use your basic melee and then something else for a fixed "combo" damage bonus), as well as actual weapon combos (such as damage amplifying abilities before your hard hitters).
Overall, I found this mechanic made the combat a superior experience, although my satisfaction did not actually increase compared to Bastion when completing combat. Successfully fighting off superior foes while outnumbered wasn't exhilerating - it was expected. Even after trialling loadouts to find the best ones and then pulling off the "correct" ordering for these rarely resulted in more than a "cool, I can continue with the story now" feeling. It never felt like a grind, it just wasn't as enjoyable to me as the mechanic suggested it might be. I am technically a competitive PvP player in LoL though, so my PvE opinion is probably a little harsh.
New weapon stategies and fancy new magic fridge mechanic - anything else I should know related to combat? As a matter of fact, yes. The third major combat change is actually the dying mechanic. Instead of having regular extra chances on death, your weapons double as lives. If you "die" you lose your most valuable weapon for the remainder of this fight and the fight after, but regain all of your health. This makes combat very forgiving, and most of the highest value weapons are not your basic damage sources in combat, so finishing a fight never funnels into "oh crap I have nothing but utility weapons" unless you do really, really poorly in a fight (at which point it'll be faster to reload the fight anyway).
Optional auto-targetting for weapons was removed, although with the magic fridge mechanic I didn't miss it at all. I actually thought combat in Transistor was far less frustrating in its "bad" moments. Some of Bastion's later fights were a little unpleasant, and some weapons did not work intuitively with the commando roll (which was also removed in Transistor, RIP) but I virtually never got frustrated with combat in Transistor.
Graphics, audio, and story depth are about par compared to Bastion. There's ironically even fewer characters that you meaningfully care about, although there are quite a few extras that have a minimal, passing importance.
Bastion's skill test areas told backstories for characters, and weapon drops were only forced to be used very briefly, with no ill-effect of any kind for swapping back to your old standbys. Transistor forces you to play around with every single unlock in every single slot to get all of that same backstory. I understand the decision for doing so (most people would be missing out on fun/good weapon combinations without it), but it wasn't my preference to have to knowingly choose a worse weapon combination if I wanted to read more backstory.
There's a few other minor annoying details, but nothing I can't look past - certainly nothing that made me outright stop playing.
One of my favorite parts of Transistor (at least over Bastion) is actually the ability to easily save progress and/or swap loadout. There are access points to do so after every fight or two, making it easy to take breaks as you progress through the game.
It's basically another Bastion, but with a game's worth of experience for Supergiant Games to take on board, and I enjoyed it about as much as I did Bastion. And that amount is quite a lot.
Second playthrough update: unlike Bastion, Transistor's combat actually continues to change over the course of the second run as new unlocks become available. Combos with close to full unlocks are more satisfying to pull off against tougher enemies as well.

Transistor is a game that I wouldn't hesitate to define "incomplete". It has a very nice setting, an extremely beautiful atmosphere and artistic direction as well as an interesting and deep gameplay, but the story is too short and rushed to be fully appreciated. Many aspects of the plot remain completely obscure to the player even after completing the game and having fully decrypted all the profiles of the side characters, giving just an hint of what's actually happened and leaving most of the details to suppositions. As I stated the gameplay is very deep, as the Function system offers an extremely wide variety of possibilities and combinations to be used on the field, but since the game is so short the huge potential of this system is lost for the large part and even revisiting the story (which is necessary to complete the game at 100%) will rarely give the player the chance to use a complex strategy to win a battle.
Don't get me wrong, I liked this game and I think it's really beautiful (I'm giving it a positive review after all) but I also think that if the developers gave more depth to the narration and invested more time in planning different battle situations it could have been a small masterpiece. As it is, Transistor is a flawed gem that surely deserves to be played but ultimately leaves a feeling of something missing. Which, considering the artistic and technical level, is a real pity.

This game... Where to begin? I cannot help but recommend SMITE due to the hours of fun that I have had playing this game. I want to note that I have over 100 hours played, about half of that time was on Xbox, where I first found this game. I saw it on the Market and remembered hearing a lot of amazing reviews.
The Pros:
- Reliable Servers: Usually you will have a match, win or lose, then leave and join a new match with little time between matches. Usually, you wait a minute or less before you are in the match.
- Variety of Gods: You can play a Mage for a game, but decide that you like Assassin better, so you change next round
- Bountiful Items: Your builds will be extremely interchangeable. Do you like Devourer's Gauntlet? Transendence is a good replacement
- Gameplay: The gameplay is amazing, if you are new to MOBAs, then don't worry. If you are a veteran, you will have fun.
The Cons:
- The Balancing of Gods: More often then not, Gods will be unbalanced at release. This is usually oversight on how abilities can be used, and how your abilities combo together. These are usually fixed within the next patch, or next few patches. Ex. Skadi: Used to be broken, through having an amazing skillset, no jump, but an Ice Patch to skate on, and would just crush people in a good player's hands. Now, she is reasonable and balanced.
- Countering: Another problem is Countering good builds. Most of the time, if your team loses two or three slugfests with a Scylla using a good build, you have a level 20 God who can demolish everyone, who is around level 14 or level 15.
- Buying Gods: Buying Gods is more of an inconvience rather then a huge issue. The bigger problem is chosing who you want to buy. If you haven't played with Amaterasu, and you want to try here, you shouldn't waste your time trying to learn a character that you do not like.
Conclusion:
SMITE is a Free to Play game that will entertain most of the MOBA fan base, and keep people intrigued in the game. Hi-Rez did an amazing job, and the only problem you will have if you are a completionist is the fact that you cannot achieve some skins, as they were a limited time event, or they no longer are obtainable because the items were related to a dead service (Looking at you, Curse....)
