Let me just go ahead and say that I'm not the biggest fan of the game. That being said, I really appreciate when a developer listens to feedback and tries to implement it into their game. The developer is really passionate about this game, and I commend them for that. Let me break down what I thought of the game.
Presentation
Presentation leaves a lot to be desired. The texture quality is very low. The game is made in Unity, and it kind of just looks like default textures for all of the environments. Also, all of the cities are just copy and pasted throughout the world so it doesn't really feel like you are traveling between cities. The water is actually quite nice, and it has really good reflections as well. Easily the best looking part of this game. The UI is just okay. Not super consistent. They seem to go for a old paper kind of look for some of the UI, and the rest is just a clean modern looking one. Again it doesn't look bad, but it's just okay.  The music is very good, I kind of get a Pirates of the Carribean vibe, mixed with some Runescape. It does a lot to add to the experience.
Content
This game is pretty deep and does have a pretty good amount of content. It has 4 different game modes, which are just different versions of the same campaign. There's Millionare, where the first company to 1 million dollars wins, Marathon, where the company with the most money at the end of 10 years win, Conquest, where the game ends when all of the over companies go bankrupt, and Sandbox. The worlds are procedularly genereted, but they are pretty small so it is kind of hard to tell. There are 4 or 5 different ships which all have different storage capabilities, sailing speeds, and number of canons. Each attribute will help you out in various parts of the game like battles or delivering goods. This is a single-player only game, and while there is a good bit of content, most of it ends up feeling very similar to one another.
Gameplay
To me this is the best part about this game, and even this is still pretty flawed. This game a very good management simulator. It is somewhat deep in it's mechanics, but when the game first launched there wasn't a tutorial at all. It just threw you in there with you knowing absolutely nothing about it. Fortunately the developer listened to the feedback and has implemented a tutorial now, so that's very good. The game is all about buying low, and selling high. If you can do that enough you can buy more ships, sell to more ports, and eventually unlock contracts to make even more money. Contracts typically have you deliver goods to a certain place in a certain amount of time. They pay out bigger, but also come with the possibility of losing out on a lof of money. I do like everything I've mentioned thus far about the gameplay, but it will get a little repetitive in not that much time. The things I don't like about the gameplay are the battles and the difficulty. Let's start with the battles. They are a turn-based civilization kind of combat. That wouldn't be bad, but I just don't like that kind of gameplay. So I'll say objectively, not a bad part of the game, but subjectively, I don't like it. Fortunately it doesn't come up too often depending on your difficulty. Now about difficulty, this is isn't overly hard or complicated. What I'm talking about is when you get low on money there is no way out of it. You are basically screwed. Sometimes one bad deal can ruin you. There is no loan option of anything like that. You might be able to sell a ship, but if you only have one that obviously won't work, plus you don't get very much from selling the ships, certainly not enough to buy another one.
Overall
This game is pretty rough around the edges, with some glaring flaws. The developer is very passionate about this game, and seemingly wants to put out a good game as well, plus this is their first attempt at a full-release game.

Winds of Trade is an interesting game with a lot of potential to be the big trade game of 2017. That said, around launch (mid February 2017) the game is a little rough around the edges, and has room for improvement. In the first nine days after launch there have been four patches that added quality of life improvements and bug fixes, as well as a tutorial to explain the basics of the game. So far, the developers have been very receptive to feedback from the community and seem very committed to work with the community to turn this into the great game it can be.
Winds of Trade probably could have launched in early access for a month or two, but what's done is done. The developers are actively improving the game post-launch, so for me that's fine too. If you want to experience a richer, more fully featured game, add the game to your wishlist and "Follow" to get updates for patches, then check back in a few weeks.
Current features:
- Randomly generated world with 20 cities, spread across a few islands with multiple countries.
- 20 different goods, with production trees that require input materials to produce their output.
- Prices that fluctuate based on supply, demand and availability. It's not as immediate as in Patrician, which causes some balance/exploit problems right now. The devs are looking into this.
- Industries in cities level over time, and new ones might appear once a city grows larger due to being supplied with goods.
- Some goods are illegal in certain countries, but smuggling is a real possibility (with risks).
- Different ships have different trade-offs, as well as an upgrade system to customize each ship with different types of sails or cannons. Different cities have different upgrades!
- Automated trade route system, which unlocks once you have 3 ships.
- Contract system with different assignments/quests to transport specific packages between cities, or to supply a city with a type of good.
- Option to start the game with all "unlockable" features unlocked. This is great for a second play through (or a third, or a fourth...)
- Stock market for non-player companies (think Industries in Railroad Tycoon), that works based on actual performance. This unlocks once you have 9 trade licenses.
- Turn-based combat with pirates, though your faster ships have a good chance of getting away from them, and not risking themselves to be sunk.
- Colonies, which unlock once you are friendly with a city/country (haven't used this feature yet).
- Events that change the circumstances in the game. Two countries might go to war, and they start issuing assignments to transport troops or arms to the front lines. Demand for arms goes up, and by proxy the demand for iron and coal. A country might have a bad harvest, and it will produce less food for a while, affecting prices.
This is pretty long list of features, but there are a number of rough edges on using them, or at least some room for improvement. Some of the unlockable features are not visible until you meet the criteria for them, possibly leading you to believe the features don't exist early on. Price tables were not sortable at launch, but they are now thanks for a patch. A lot of places now have useful popups with price information, and cities show how much resources they consume.
There are unfortunately no fleets in the game, yet, but you can copy orders from one ship to another if you want to have multiple ships work the same route. You can add ships to control groups, similar to how that works in strategy games, but that is only useful if you are manually trading. Fleets might stand a better chance against larger pirate fleets.
The map size can not be changed, which is something quite some people asked about. This might get addressed, but the devs stated they chose this size to balance world size with keeping it small enough so you can know and remember all the cities in the world. In my game so far (4-5 hours of gameplay) I have Trade Offices in 9 cities across two countries, and I don't find myself wishing for more cities yet. Easier management of trade routes and a better insight into trade opportunities between cities is something I find myself thinking about more... because larger cities tend to both produce and consume a lot of different goods and thus you find yourself studying the cities and making notes about what each city needs and what they produce in excess. The second patch added a tooltip to prices in the "for sale" list of a city, so you can put the city's price in context with the lowest/highest price, as well as the average. The fourth patch added insight into a city's domestic consumption of resources, which makes it clear that they consume a *lot* of resources.
TL;DR: this game has a lot of interesting systems in it. A game of this complexity is difficult to get right in one go. Luckily the devs are producing patches every few days to address smaller and larger concerns. Check out the discussions, and the patch notes, and use that to judge whether you want to buy the game for its current features and future potential, or whether you want to wait until more of the potential has been realised.

I've played trading games for many years, and was looking for something new.  Before I played this game, I followed it a long time on Twitter, watching development, getting more excited as the game progressed.
When final release came, I was not disappointed!  The first thing that strikes you when you start the game is the gorgeous music!  The soundtrack is absolutely AMAZING, and sets the stage for the game perfectly.
The graphics are clean and neat and bright -- very cheerful and pleasant to look at.
At first the game seems very simple -- take goods from point A to B and try to make a profit.  However, as you progress and reach milestones, (owning three ships, for example), you unlock more and opportunities -- creating automatic trade routes, the ability to found your own plantations & mines, buying stocks in production facilities and more!
Fail contracts with the wrong people and there are more consequences than a simple penalty fee...
The world is dynamic, prices changing based on supply and demand.  Each world is unique!  You can play as a pirate or a merchant fleet, running a clean ship or smuggling things into port.
A vast array of ships each have different specialties and upgrades.  Captain experience determines special skills that can be tailored to each ship's mission.
Contracts allow you to make some easy money if you can get to the destination by the time limit.  They can also help you improve relations with each of the different countries... or hurt them.  Taking sides in a war can have definite benefits!
I feel like I have just scratched the surface of gameplay in Winds of Trade!  So far, a very VERY enjoyable experience that is also quite addictive!  Highly Recommended!

A game about corruption and choices that made me sit back in my chair with my head between my hands as I reflected on what I had done.  Emotional and poetic with simple gameplay that remains challenging and intense.

In Papers, Please, you play the role of a customs worker at the Arztotzkan border. You examine the paperwork of travelers, and determine whether to accept them into Arztotzka, deny them, or in some cases, detain them. The amount of people you correctly stamp determine your paycheck, which you must use to support your family.
While doing your job, you'll come across many people with many different stories. You'll have to choose between doing your duty (and by corollary, supporting your family), or helping complete strangers. Although most of these choices don't have an impact on the final ending, it still makes an impact on you (arguably even more so than whatever ending you got), and the various story arcs combined with unique gameplay make this definitely worth buying.
The game has pixel graphics, but it's more SNES than NES, and the graphics are good enough to play the game. There is basically one song in the soundtrack of the game, which plays during menus and intermissions. Whether those are good or bad is up to you.
A lot of people don't like the fact that most of your choices don't change the ending, but I think that's good. These are random people who are in a bad spot. Whether you accept or deny them, you go through their mini-story and you never see them again. It's not really which ending you got or if you were overall good or bad, it's the experience and interactions with people that make this game good. The protagonist's personality is never openly revealed, regardless of what choices you make. You can make your character whatever you want them to be.
If it's on sale, easy pick. If not, I'd take a look at gameplay videos to see if it's your cup of tea.

I'm already a huge fan of the first game, and absolutely love the idea "What can we do in 30 seconds".... so how does the sequel stand up?
Honestly, I think the Sequel is a significant improvement in every way.  They cut much of what made me hate replaying the first game a second time, and gave me more content.  The game is rather excellent in gameplay, but it still has a few issues.
The biggest change with this game is that while they cut out the "alternative" games (the different centuries with different gameplay that just wasn't that enjoyable) they did implement a full story and adventure where the player runs around between quests.  It allows a more coherent story and world, and is an interesting change.
The only real problem I have with the game is the game sticks to the two line dialog screens, which would be fine, if they weren't filled with the dullest story ever, and it tries to stretch it out for 77 levels.   It's not that it's bad but I've put in 16 hours into the game so far, I'll probably have to put in double that to fully get everything and the fact is the story is long and not very good.   Time goddess is greedy, main characters are doofs, enemies are funny.  I wish there was more focus on the enemies or the "Theme" of each level, than trying to character build characters that have been built up well for 30-40 levels already.
It's not bad, but it's just there's a lot of story and it's not as engaging as I think it wants to be.
On the other hand, the gameplay itself is better than ever.  Enemies appear on the map so there's no feeling of randomness while running around the overworld or dungeons.  There's maps for some of the larger dungeons.  The ability to use Goddess statues on maps (if they are placed), free heals (if placed), new features, a rather enjoyable plot line (even if the story is weak), and great new mechanics.
Each stage is similar for the most part.  A 30 second count down with a way to reset it, usually paying the goddess statue money to give you a brand new 30 seconds.  Two titles on each stage (you no longer have to beat the stage to save them, thank god), they added in "medals" for the player to find while walking around between levels (mostly just investigate anything that's unique or out of place, I've found almost every one without a guide)
But I really like when the game breaks these rules.  I've seen a 99 second count down with no way to reset, I've seen timers based on something other than the typical "Spell of destruction being cast" and each of these stages are a breath of fresh air.   The other levels though are great and unique as well.  There's a good variety of targets and mechanics that you will need to use to beat the stage rather than always running to the end of the stage getting levels and beating the boss.
To me it feels like the first game was constrained by the engine and rules they made, they rules remain in the sequel but are able to be broken that it's a lot of fun to see what's coming next.
So I easily recommend this game.  I am having a ton of fun and at 10 bucks that's a great price, plus you get the original game as well.  I recommend playing the original game first, because it is enjoyable, but if you enjoy the Hero 30 storyline in the original game, I can't stress enough that you should play the sequel.  It honestly feels like they did the original game and then did it correctly this time.  It's not a remake, but it feels like it's a improved version of what they wanted to do in the first game.

You begin with 1 ship to your name in a procedurally generated island cluster filled with 5 different factions and 3 trading opponents.  It's all about buying cheap, sailing to a nearby city, and selling high.  Making enough money to expand your fleet and even build your own colonies.
A tutorial is definitely needed, and I want more depth to the combat (or the ability to be a pirate myself!) but overall, I had a lot of fun with the game and for the price I would certainly recommend it.

I applaud the developer for his efforts and the ideas behind this project but unfortunately the result has come out very flat.

You had ships going from the East Indies to America, and from Europe to South America, and EVERYTHING in between. What a WONDERFUL era to have a trading game, in this style, where you can create a company, and make a trading empire that spans the globe.
The only thing is, NO YOU CAN'T. The game uses procedurally generated maps?!?! Not only that, but they are TINY procedurally generate maps! You get some fake countries, fake cities, on some fake islandds that make you feel claustrophobic. The map is so small, you do not ever feel like you are in charge of an Ocean Trading Company. It is more like a large lake trading company. At MOST it is a small sea trading company, with the amount of cities in the game from the generated maps, no way in hell you can consider that an ocean trading company.
STAY AWAY from this game, if you thought you were getting a game that had expansive possibilities. This game is very limited in scope, which ruins all the fun in my opinion.
This game is ONLY worthwhile if the dev realizes that creating Earth, with the hundreds of port cities that were bustling centers of business during the 18th and 19th centuries OR barring that, you add the option to alter the size of the generated maps, to be MUCH larger than what is currently available.. YES, this would be very labor intensive, I am sure of that, but it would mean you are creating something that no other game as done since Uncharted Waters: New Horizons for the SNES. Kalypso doesn't do anything more than small sections of the world in each of their games, which limits those in scope too. If someone could take the time to create the entire world, then that would be something worth spending money on. This though. . .well this is similar to windwar, except turn based battles, and inferior graphics.
This game is not expensive, and at it's current price point, it is definitely possible to be a decent purchase, but not with what is available in game at this time. The trading system is very basic, and the maps are so small, most people will most likely be disappointed. You will have to make your own judgement, but I expect many people will refund this game shortly after buying it, because of the things I listed, not to mention other things like not being able to put ships into fleets, not being able to attack other ships, or the fact that pirates are invisible and just attack out of nowhere. That last one actually is ok to me, but the fact that there seems to be no recourse for dealing with pirates, such as finding and raiding their base, does make you feel too powerless.
In closing, don't burn your money on this game at this time, but if you really like the idea of this game, just WAIT for the dev to get wise and add some basic features that should have been available on release. I don't think this game is early access, though some say it is. It seems like it should be though, and needs lots of work to be worth more than $3-$5.
It's okay, has some potential. I could write more but I'm not getting paid.

This is a good game, however not really sure it's worth a fifteen dollar mark up.
The game has great art style and graphical design, great soundtrack and sound effects, and easy to learn controls.
However, there are a few things that frustrait the crap out of me with my time with the game. The controls of the game aren't bad by design, however, they can feel clunky and somewhat unreliable at times. Hit boxes on enemies can prove to be a bit out of proportion, and it can be found difficult to keep steady fighting. While being easy, they are also very limited, and can get bland really quickly.
The other thing that is frustraiting is the checkpoint system. Not anywhere near as noticably bad until you get to the final two stages. They feature a final multistage fight with a boss fight. Lose anywhere inbetwen, and you have to restart the entire fight over again. This made me quit the game several times, simply because it takes tedious work to get back to the actual boss fight, and then your paranoid about loseing the fight because of having to waste time again.
Which brings me to my next gripe. In my furvor of quiting to settle the frustration, I come to find there is no friggin continue from last checkpoint option. So, this means, when I needed to take a break from the final level, I HAD TO DO IT ALL OVER AGAIN. It takes quit a considerable amount of time to get to the end too. So I have to wonder why they didn't implement a continue option. It's not like it would've been hard to do so.
But, these are smallish complains, and I'm sure the whole checkpoint thing won't bother many, I just hate being forced through tedious work over and over again.
I still recommend the game, just get it on a sale price, doesn't take long to experience everything the game has to offer.

This is a copy of the review I've written on GOG:
JourneyQuest Season 2 is one of my most favorite pieces of media of all time. It's funny, heartfelt, and clever. It's a wonderful mix of fantasy, comedy, drama and romance. The second season continues the story of the heroic party consisting of Perf, the (as he himself admits) worst wizard in the world, Nara, a serious Elven archer and Carrow, a zombie with a soul. Wren, a bard who chronicles the adventures of the party, Rilk, a surprisingly smart orc, and the assassin also return. And new characters are introduced, such as Karn, a progressive Barbarian King, and the Wicked Kings, the evil rulers of the world. This season broadens the scope of the story. While the plot of JQ Season 1 seemed to take place in a 1 kilometer radius, the world of JQ 2 feels much more expansive. Every single returning character becomes more 3-dimensional here. Nara gets to do more, Perf becomes far more than a copy of Rincewind, Carrow falls into a deep struggle with his faith, Glorion shows a side of himself that's everything but funny and we learn that Rilk and Wren are deeply in love with each other, but are seperated by the language barrier between them. Among the new characters, Silver Tom, a silver-tongued, but mean bard, (played brilliantly by Fran Kranz) stands out the most - he is ambitious, manipulative and a joy to watch. Yeah, there is some stuff that doesn't quite work (for me). While Season 1 was entertaining from start to finnish, some scenes in here feel not as interesting. Season 2 has lower lows than Season 1, but the highs far outshine anything that can be found in the first season. By the end of the show you'll be in love with all of the characters and sad that your time with them is already over. The production value, btw, is surprisingly high for an indie production with a budget that is dwarved by Hollywood standards.
If you thought the first season was entertaining, definitively check this one out. Because part 2 surpasses part 1 in nearly every capacity.

Very good game exploring the concept of a chinese boxes riddled with contraptions, trinkets, secret trays and drawers. Everything is pre-animated, but it feels and looks so
that the mechanical whirrings or the folding surfaces appear to be powered by a real physics engine.
The story is obviously bare-bones but helps drive you forward, as well as being well integrated with the machines you interact with.
You'll have to find your way through the "boxes" contained in this room one at a time; each will have several hidden buttons and missing bits, and you're required to uncover its mysteries by interacting with them and solving the puzzles. Pushing this button will make a secret panel slide somewhere... inside you'll fine a weird tile, where could it fit? Aha!
You'll rotate around and above said boxes/contraptions as if you were physically there, but interact just with your mouse (or touch surface). Rotating and zooming is needed to find puzzles and get a new perspective on things. There are a few unfair bits but they're really sparse, nothing you'll have to worry about.
Very important: there's no stamina bar, no punishment for clicking too much, no "find the item" section... this is pure machinery pleasure. Fiddle with their wooned smoothness all you want.
It's a relatively short game (5 levels for 3-5 hours of gameplay) but it looks extremely pretty and polished. It's a joy for the eyes and wonderfully animated.
Definitely get it if you like eye candy and mechanical puzzles, especially at such a low price point.

Well what can I say that hasn't been said yet. ALOT is good about this game. Just a few things are bad.
FFXIV has got quite a fun endgame after you finish the main story line. I keep returning to it. I'm level 60 for ages now, but there is so much to do. Mainly gear progression for me. Which is grindy but not to much.
There are different endgame options for different kind of people too. For example you can get 'relic/anima weapons' which are end tier weapons. These can be gained purely by grinding-like mechanics. But there are gear and weapons you get by doing dungeons and making sure you get your weekly cap of 'X-currency' (tomestones). There is also hardcore raid gear to be gotten, for the peeps who are more serious in doing the hardest raids. I'm not much of a hardcore 'savage difficulty' raider. Not doing them isn't handicapping me in a huge way either.
Just a few cons about the game for me:
Story quests are dreadfully boring at some times. Storyline quests shouldn't involve 'fetch this or that' or 'talk 10x times to citizens around town' quests.. This get's WAY better after 3.0 though and I truly hope, for new players, they remove/alter some earlier quests. Because otherwise you will get a habit of skipping thru half of the stuff you have to read.
I miss an immersive feeling with this world. This is because the whole 'world map' consists of multiple 'instanced' area's. Which do have loading screens in between. It's something that will probably never change. I accept it now but it took me a while. Most area's are very beautiful though!
And I really miss oldschool FF prerendered absolutly astonishing cutscenes! There are a few, but I want more! :P
All in all, the game feels very relaxed and has a good balance between difficulty levels. It's a game for everyone, but will take a lot of your time :)

MInimum is a graphicly minimalistic, yet somehow beautiful, third person MOBA styled shooter that is full of creativity, fun and good times.
Whilst it doesn't have huge detail for it's textures, MInimum is a good looking game, and runs superbly, even when recording. I would compare it's FPS performance as similar to that of TF2 or CS:GO, which are both made by the huge company Valve.
You can collect materials in game which allow you to make Weapon and Item Schematics, which allow you to buy weapons and make your own custom loadouts. There are shotguns, assault rifles, burst fire rifles, sniper rifles, laser guns and more.
Your character can also be either male or female.
There are three gamemodes, though you'll probably only play two: Team Dethmatch and Titan mode.
TDM is quite self-explanatory as I'm sure everyone knows how THAT gamemode works.
Titan mode however, is interesting: You fight enemies as usual, and kill creeps to collect powerups. Then, a giant computer controlled robot/monster forms for each team, and the one with the most powerups wins. Then, the winning titan destroys walls in a path to the other teams base, which it will then proceed to destroy. This takes time, though, and often the other team will kill the opposing titan, and the battle continues.
There is quite a lot of depth to Minimum, and it is a very enjoyable game that I didn't really play until the last week, despite having it quite a long time before the Summer Sale happened.
My rating for minimum: 8.5/10, could use some more maps, weaponry and gamemodes.

Minimum is great. Even though the graphics are designed to be as simple as possible, the game is extremely pretty. I have yet to have any connection issues, and everything is fast and responsive.
The main game mode is really the only thing I've played as of yet (since the other option is Team Deathmatch, and, gross) - if you're familiar with Soul Wars from RuneScape, it's close to the same style as that. The objective is to kill the other teams' titan, so that yours can walk up and destroy their base.
Overall, it seems that all of the weapons are generally balanced. There are a lot of reviews that claim otherwise, but that is because of the 'snowball' effect that's potent in this game - the more kills you get, the more you power up your weapons. It's an interesting idea, and seems to effect all weapons equally (except maybe sniper rifles, because it's hard to retrieve your loot, but they're decent even without a power-up.) Melee does do a TON of damage, but the only real way to make it viable is to sneak up on your opponent or to stack up as much speed from your armor that's physically possible - because if you're paying attention, there are multiple movement abilities put on weapons throughout the game and you can walk backwards at the same rate as walking forward (which I personally like) - and force them to switch weapons in order to hit you.
There are a few glitches that forces me to lower my rating - but none of it really affects gameplay. There a few (3-5) instances of objects existing where they really don't, and the interface can accidentally cover your tutorial and there's no way to close it, and sometimes your bullets DO get confused and look like they're flying the wrong way, but hey, whose don't?
This is a fresh new version of a fps - it's faced-paced and interesting. I'd recommend to my friends 8/10

One of the best multiplayer games I've played in a LONG time. I'm incredibly picky about my multiplayer shooters and I tend to dislike the typical war-shooter copy paste that's going around nowadays. Minimum is a barebones shooter where your skill is determined by how fast you can maneuver and how well you can aim.
Minimum is a fast-paced, strategic twitch shooter with solid, simplistic gameplay and so much more to come. There
a community playing this game right now,  and people do keep up with it. It only takes about 4 seconds to connect to a match with all 10 people. The developers
release updates fairly often, and they're high quality and expansive. I bought the game when it came out and even before the content they've added the game was good.
Things to like:
- The art style fits the game very well. The game doesn't have any sort of premise, so it doesn't try to fit any strict stylistic rules. The result: Firemen astronauts with Barney heads being attacked by raptors.
- At the same time, the environments look very good. The map design is fluid and clean while having tremendous asthetic appeal. Maps have a well-organized balance of long range and close quarters areas.
- Gameplay is very solid and clean. No frills, just skills. There are guns, giant grenade launchers and flaming swords to fit any playstyle. The better you are at aiming in two dimensions (something most modern shooters don't train you for) the better you'll be at this game.
- Developers talk with the community! There's a thread on steam regarding weapon balancing and ideas, there's a website with forums for users to talk with developers, and the devs listen!
- Matches have incredibly good back and forth. I've played matches where my team was seconds from losing only to take the next ten minutes making a coordinated effort pushing back and winning the match.
- Movement is fast and smooth, akin to playing scout in Team Fortress 2. Except now you can play as a scout with flaming swords and a sniper rifle.
- If you don't like multiplayer (or just need a break), there's a really fun horde mode where you face off against ninjas, raptors and knights.
- It isn't free to play! This means you can actually have fun! Players can't buy weapons to have an advantage over you. There are skins for sale in game, but they're actually easy enough to get without spending any money. Because of Minimum's integration with steam's inventory system, you can trade and sell items you get by playing for skins you might want. I traded a few weapons for a pretty kickass shinobi armor set that I use all the time.
Things to be aware of:
- Balancing is a little tricky at the moment. It's easy to get frustrated at players that have the game figured out a little better than you might.
- Getting kills buffs you, dying detriments you. This sounds frustrating, but with the way the game is balanced it isn't too much of a challenge. If you take time to practice and figure out what works best for you, it won't matter that you were killed and lost your level five weapon because you'll know how to earn it back.
- Obviously still some bugs and lag issues, as this game is still being developed. Getting rubberbanded every few matches is a little annoying but I'm sure it will be resolved eventually. However, the servers are generally very good. I usually have a ping of 20ms or less.
So I hope me writing this enourmous review will convince a few people to pick up this game while it's on sale. It's only $4 right now, and we could always use more players.

I read that a lot of people compare it to GTA. Since I don't play GTA, this review will try to cover and talk about aspects that maybe GTA has too. Therefore, sorry if some of the points may look, from your point of view, like something to be expected from a 2014 game and shouldn't be seen as selling points.
The plot is truly interesting, and although is widely known that you take the role of an undercover cop, things are not as plain as it may seem. You're not an average undercover cop, you're a person suited to fill that role, with a particular psychological profile. You'll infiltrate in a main branch of the Triad, in Hong Kong, and things won't go as smooth as you'd like. That profile won't help and you'll get caught in something a bit more deep, a bit more scary, a bit more of your own.
It won't be about choosing sides, it will be more about merging in both, without leaving any trace, nor any part of you.
It will be more about swimming inside a stream, while trying not to follow its flow.
Gameplay - Wise, I didn't feel disappointed at all. The environment is gorgeus, accurate, colourful yet gray. Turns, hills, alleys, signs.
Driving is fun but steering is a must, and makes things more exciting. Shame there aren't many car models.
You can't steal a car and make it yours by driving it into your parking lot, but you'll own many cars, obtained by buying them or by doing main missions and / or side missions. Same applies for motorcycles.
While cars can't be customized, noone says that you can't steal them and drive them through all Hong Kong, shooting at other cars' tires or directly at their front window. Aim well for a clean headshot, will you? Or if you feel like you need a new car, keep putting the pedal to the metal, jump from your seat to the roof of your new love interest or hit them until they'll stop driving.
And there will be lot of pursuits. Relentless pursuits. Be it in North Point or in the highway, drive wherever you want, just get rid of the pursuers. This is one of the things I liked most from the game, as it's one of the few cases where you'll hold a firearm and you'll see cars exploding.
Because what has been seen by many as a flaw, my eyes and my racing heart tells me otherwise.
Firearms are rare, very rare so that you won't feel overpowered and start a killing spree. You'll treasure them and hide them. You won't waste bullets and you'll scavenge a lot. And you'll enjoy the moment when you'll use your gun to set a car on fire, or while taking cover behind a counter, against a volley of bullets.
Gunfires will make you remind that you're made of flesh, so don't try to run against your enemies. Take cover and plan the right time to shoot.
This scarce source of guns makes hand-to-hand combat the way to clean the path ahead of you. Keep countering, break their arms, thair legs, their teeth. Use everything at your disposal: a fan, a swordfish, a boiler, a railing, or take them hostages and use their bodies as shields, or put them inside the boot; they may change their minds.
There's still more, but I don't think I should spoil everything.
Secondary missions are interesting, they add layers to an already thick background, encouraging you to live this game more deeply, on both sides of the same coin.
They will encourage you to explore to the fullest the map, uncovering favors, races, secrets and so on.
Buy it, because I didn't tell you everything, and because it deserves more sunlight than shades.

In Papers, Please, you play the role of a customs worker at the Arztotzkan border. You examine the paperwork of travelers, and determine whether to accept them into Arztotzka, deny them, or in some cases, detain them. The amount of people you correctly stamp determine your paycheck, which you must use to support your family.
While doing your job, you'll come across many people with many different stories. You'll have to choose between doing your duty (and by corollary, supporting your family), or helping complete strangers. Although most of these choices don't have an impact on the final ending, it still makes an impact on you (arguably even more so than whatever ending you got), and the various story arcs combined with unique gameplay make this definitely worth buying.
The game has pixel graphics, but it's more SNES than NES, and the graphics are good enough to play the game. There is basically one song in the soundtrack of the game, which plays during menus and intermissions. Whether those are good or bad is up to you.
A lot of people don't like the fact that most of your choices don't change the ending, but I think that's good. These are random people who are in a bad spot. Whether you accept or deny them, you go through their mini-story and you never see them again. It's not really which ending you got or if you were overall good or bad, it's the experience and interactions with people that make this game good. The protagonist's personality is never openly revealed, regardless of what choices you make. You can make your character whatever you want them to be.
If it's on sale, easy pick. If not, I'd take a look at gameplay videos to see if it's your cup of tea.

So, you land on an alien planet. Steal the resources, pollute the air, kill the natives, burn their villages to the ground, plunder their cultural artifacts and grind them up to make chemicals for your military/industrial labs. And humans call this 'entertainment'.
11/10

This isn't your typical "craft stuff" game. Oh, you can manually mine your basic elements at first: stone, coal, iron, and copper. Then you can smelt iron and copper plates. But then, why not create coal-powered miners to work for you? And then a pump, boilers, and steam engines to get electricity going. Then some conveyor belts to get products moving around. And robot arms ("inserters") to move things on and off those belts.
Later on, trains. And train signals as well, so you can automate your trains.
At some point, you'll have so many conveyor belts that you'll despair of having more room to build. Enter the roboport, which hosts flying robots that can fly around fulfilling requests, so you can get a more flexible system. Oh, and it hosts construction robots as well, to build plans you lay and to do repairs for you.
Oh, did I mention that all the while, the planet's native buglike species is trying to kill you? So you'll need to develop weapons too, from automated gun turrets to lasers to a tank with explosive shells.
But aside from all that, what really makes this game is the intelligence with which it was written. Opening a stone furnace to retrieve newly-forged iron plates is tedious? No problem; just control-click to grab the plates as you run by. Laid all your conveyor belts in the wrong direction? No need to tear them up; just lay new belts over them in the correct direction and they'll replace the originals (which will go back into your inventory). Replacing an early robot-arm inserter with a more advanced model, or a slower furnace with a faster one? Just stick the new one right on top of the old one and it seamlessly replaces it. Find yourself building the same set of things over and over? Make a blueprint out of them and have your robots build it for you!
This is a great game. A glorious sandbox for people who like to use their brain.
This GAME is awesome those who love problem solving and want to be an engineer this game is for you.

Everything that is mentioned about what this game is, is going to be the case, although as it is in EA/Alpha, some are currently not in game yet......BUT.......
So far, the game state is in fact better than other games I have tested in even Beta stage or even on release, and even with the lack of current content, there is enough to do to keep you occupied, and to get a feel for what the game is and will be. There are of course a few bugs, but actually not that many that I have found, and none of them gamebreaking in any way.
The game IMO plays like the trailer, but without some of those features added in, which is understandable, those who say it is nothing like the game, I cannot comment why - but I understand that a game in Alpha/EA will not have all features, and the game will be like it is in the trailers (and the game is EXACTLY like the 2nd gameplay video, those that comment only on watching the 1st one, will of course be disappointed, but the gameplay one is accurate)
If you think you will enjoy this game, and like to help mold/shape it then you should definitely give it a go - quests are not just go kill x amount, and you are not hand held for most of them, you have to go search and discover, and this may not work for all kinds of people, but it does go to show the true atmosphere of the game that is already apparant.
Although there is no character customization or classes yet, you still dont feel the same as everyone else, as armour currently looks good, and different enough to not notice, and you can still enjoy the combat/questing without those defining skills, and again IMO I enjoy the game without so many key features, I know am going to love it when all the features are in.
TLDR: It is EA/Alpha, there are lots of things not in, but the game itself is polished enough for EA/Alpha to get an atmosphere and feel for the game, and enough content to keep you happy if you want it, and if the game seems like the game you might enjoy when all the features mentioned are in - then no harm in getting now to try.

After sinking a lot of time into this game I say it's time I give my opinion on it. Smite is a game that CAN be easy to get into if you have friends to help guide you, or you take it slow and use outside sources to learn the game (HIGHLY RECOMMEND READING GUIDES AND WATCHING TIP VIDEOS.) The game is actually FAR more balanced than a lot of the reviews say. People don't understand that there are items in the game to counter every single character. A big culprit of people whining is Loki. Build some protections then, stop trying to burn your way through his HP bar before he gets through his. Survive his burst and he's easy to take down.
The COMMUNITY- Smite doesn't exactly have a good rep with a good or bad commonutiy. You'll find both types or players in every single game, though my experience has been a lot of people willing to help. You don't have to kiss♥♥♥♥♥or anything, just be nice and people will show you that same respect.
The SUPPORT- People playing the game fail to realize that if you send in support tickets whining about a God and comparing the numbers that the support team can't really do anything based off of your ONE request. If you send something in mentioning a literal bug or error, maybe an animation not matching a voice line then it gets fixed. The game gets balanced heavily based on the Smite Pro League. Seeing what Gods are performing well and which aren't. Smites devs recently made it public they've been keeping track of the stats of every God to check performance rating
Conquest..- The entire game is balanced around the most popular mode Conquest. This does make sense, it's the most popular mode and it's used in the pro league similarly to Dota 2 but with this can make some Gods feel unfair in other modes. Gods like Zeus can be game changing in things like Arena or Joust solely because he wasn't designed for that mode, but as mentioned earlier you can still counter everything if you know how to properly play.
Pay to Win?- NO. Smite never has, and never will be pay to win. Unlike other game having features that paying real money gives you in game advantages, spending $$$ on Smite will ONLY ever reward you with cosmetic items. This being said though, starting out I could see how one could feel limited with the amount of Gods the game has to offer. It's tough to earn the main currency in the game 'renown' without it feeling like a grind. To that I say, do research before hand and save up to purchase a beginer friendly God that you can learn the games mechanics on. A great god to learn on is Neith, she shows flexibility, escape, strength and once you get better suited with this god can quickly become one of the scariest enemies to be seen. (Not that you have to, but I would recommend unlocking the Ultimate God pack, it unlocks all current and future gods and is a great way to test out characters without grinding.)
IMPORTANT NOTE: Starting Smite, I didn't know this so I difure new people would like to know.  You don't have to outright buy Gods, it's very possible to play the game to it's fullest purely by renting Gods. For about 2 games worth, you can rent any God for 1 day.
Final Thoughts- This game is great for anyone into the style, though it can be tough to get into and learn even the basics. Do some more research to see if this is the game for you!

This game flew under my radar and I only got it as a result of the December 2016 Humble Bundle. I'm glad I did because this game is great.
At first it looks very style over substance but in reality the underlying mechanics make this a well designed Beat Em Up. You have Punch, Kick, Grab, and Jump as well as an incredibly important dash move that can be used to quickly get in on enemies as well as dodge attacks. The Health Management system is utterly brilliant, instead of healing with Chicken dinners your character will syphon energy out a dying enemies. It's utterly ghoulish but adds a lot of strategy, do I want to grab some health and leave myself open to the enemies? It's smart and adds decision making to a game genre that at times can be rather mindless.
Basically imagine if the Streets of Rage developers were told to out EXTREME the Mortal Kombat series, and they hired Garth Ennis to write it. That's Mother Russia Bleeds. If you love Side-scrolling beat em ups you gotta try this.

I've only played for a little bit but I can already tell this is a fun game.  There are three multiplayer modes and I've only played Team Deathmatch so far, but it's very addictive.  The pace is very fast, like Quake, Unreal Tournament, etc.  One nice thing I like about it is that you  get your 'upgrades' from drops from killed enemies.  One of the frustrating things of Quake, UT and similar games is that there are power ups at specific places, and it's possible to steam roll once your team sets up in certain places.  Since killed enemies(and allies) drop goodies in Minimum, that's not a problem.  You keep fighting, you keep moving, and you keep upgrading.  Armor upgrades are persistent for the round, and weapons upgrade automatically when picking up power ups(one drops per dead body).
Titan looks like a fun mode.  Haven't played it, but the concept is straight forward.  The titan map I did see is really small(smaller than the TDM maps I saw!) so I imagine it's a blood bath.
There's a crafting system, which, like everything else, is straightforward and minimalistic.  There's a variety of options for weapons, armors, and weapon skins.  You slowly but surely accumulate materials as you play rounds and the cost to craft new things isn't absurd(as is true with games like Warframe, where you spend *tons* of  time getting the crap needed to craft even one thing of value)
Small learning curve, but tons of fun.  The 'Minimum' theme is all throughout the game, from menus to the gameplay, and I definitely think it's done right.  It makes everything feel sleek and responsive.  I much rather prefer games like this than made-for-console games that are sluggish in almost every way imaginable.
I bought this on sale, but I would recommend it even at full price.  This is a great throwback to old FPS games with fast-paced arena-style action and a novel aesthetic.

My thoughts on FFXIV are that it is a diamond in the rough:
Pros:
-Fun gameplay at max level and well designed fights
-Being able to level all classes on a single character
-Wonderful soundtrack
-Very nice graphics
-Good levels of character customisation and variety of gear so your character can stand out in a world of cat-girls
Neutral:
-Content patches are fairly regular ~3.5 months per patch, but the content in them can often feel like it only really lasts a few days to a week other than daily stuff
-Very Casual friendly, everything but extreme primals (1 fight per patch) and savage raids (4 fights every other patch) is incredibly easy and accesible to everyone.
-The story: if you are a fan of jrpgs there is a good chance you will love it, if not there is a good chance you will find it fairly mundane, cliché and at times cringey.
Cons:
-The first 30 levels are absolutely agonising to play through to be honest, poor design is rampant here, you will only have a few skills, your hand will be held massively and fetch quests are everywhere, the story also can be overwhelming here because they provide you with massive walls of (mostly) unvoiced text
-the early areas are mostly empty with the playerbase mainly being at max level so this can be off-putting to new players, dungeon queues still wont be that terrible for the most part though.
-PVP: the pvp content for the most part is pretty good fun, the problem is that the community likes to tell everyone it's terrible and therefore the queues are always dead.
-The platform locking: buy the game on steam and you have to buy all future expansions on steam when its possible to get them cheaper elsewhere, the steam version of the game is treated as entirely seperate to the PC version.
Note: the issue of levelling being slow and the main story quest often feeling long winded to players who dont thouroughly enjoy it will largely be fixed with the next expansion: 'Stormblood' as it is likely the developers will insert a purchasable potion to skip straight to the end of the current expansion 'Heavensward'
In summary: I really love FFXIV as you can probably tell by my playtime, but there is times where it is absolutely frustrating to play this game, the developers sometimes release content that makes up a big chunk of a new patch that is dead on arrival or within a week, but if you want to try a MMO try it out for yourself.
Continous updates with new content and events. Community is lovable and the story is, by my preferences, the best I've seen in mmorpg.

Updated/Actual Review:
I "reviewed" this game about 2 years ago and it's come so far that I realized that this game deserves an actual review. I had been hearing about the original Plague Inc game for years when I got this and for the price I was genuinely afraid that it was going to become repetitive and not worth it. Well ladies and gentlemen, I am here to say that I was gladly wrong(ish). Was the game worth it's price in early access, well that is up to the person who was reviewing it. It WAS repetitive and it DID get boring after a while back then (even though I still loved it) but I have no doubt in my mind that if you enjoy games like this you should absolutly buy this. Let's go through the list.
Notice: DID and WAS (the game has since been updated and these comments are no longer relevant)
Gameplay: When I first began playing I joked about how this was like flash games where you just click whatever you can to advance your goals but I was wrong. This is a strategy game based on how you direct your pathogen, when you reveal yourself and how you keep yourself from being revealed. You could also argue resource management (I've seen friends without DNA points just after being found) but this personally isn't a problem I've had. With the many different pathogens which all change up gameplay entirely, your job is to simply destroy the world...easy right? There are only two real stages to the game right? Infect everybody without being found out/ Panic and be found immediatly (or hate the world on nanobots and panic on necroa virus) and then kill everybody. It can easily be summed down in words but as I've said, you can't just click everything to win. You have to move your virus in just the right way (I prefer boats, easier to get at Madagascar and Greenland but mostly because I like boats) and make sure that it can spread in the countries it moves to. You can easily be found out in your first country (if you're a first timer) and dead before you even know it. This gameplay allows players to have a basic strategy game without the extreme amount of time and thought process required for games such as Civilization or Europa. It also allows for fast games so you can easily sit down and play a game of Plague Inc while you're waiting for something (just remember, any computer is a laptop if you're brave enough). Of course, saying this I need to say that it can be difficult for people to pick up at first. I don't mean it's difficult to understand the controls I just mean newcomers should start on easy and work their way up. I could easily continue but I do need space for the rest of the review, sorry. (9/10)
Sound: The music is pretty good, kind of ominous but you kind of need that for a game about killing everyone. I think they got the music design right for a game like this, but this is a strategy game, while music is nice to listen to it isn't really that important. It is the kind of music that keeps your head in the game and that's all that really matters. The sound design is excellent, there's no lag on the sound design, the bubble popping noise makes me want to pop more bubbles, I almost feel sad when I play with cheats on and I don't pop any bubbles. (9.5/10)
Graphics: The graphics are good, I don't really see what they could do better. The world feels alive, that's all I can say. You really do begin to feel like you're killing the world and as you slowly watch as the world stops moving it really does feel empty (the world you've just destroyed you monster, not the graphics quality). There are real pictures for some of the countries (I wanted to say most but in truth I'm not sure) thanks to help the devs asked for from the community and the work had payed off tremendously. While some of the map of the world could be looked at to be made more realistic, for a 15/16 dollar game (sorry, don't know the U.S price) they hit the mark. (8/10)
Workshop: This is important, I seriously felt the need to add this. The Steam workshop adds a whole new dynamic to this game. There's no longer just a set number of deceases, there's new ones being made all the time and while many games are starting to embrace the workshop, this one's been doing it for a while now and I must say, the community is just excellent.
Multiplayer: (WILL REVIEW AT A LATE DATE MAYBE. #foreveralone)
Overall: This game is just absolutly excellent and while I don't play it as much as I used to it has earned a place in my Steam Library and is definitely worth its base price. Mind you of course that you are paying extra in this version for better graphics, better sound and workshop support but it is so worth it that I would even recommend getting this if you have Plague Inc on your phone.

This game is fantastic, with incredible replay value.  Easy to play but hard to master, you may find it useful watching a few demos on YouTube to figure out different methods others use to win but, in the end the most fun is finding your own way after a lot of experimentation. Ever played Oregon Trail?  Where things happen a little differently every time and you're not sure what's the best decision, but try anyway?  Replace a wagon with a shuttle and dysentery with space pirates and you get a vague idea of how things can be in space.
Game 1 - Chose fighter because it's the coolest.  Decide to take on a few wimpy looking pirates; die immediately.
Game 2 - Chose fighter again for same reason.  Gradually swamped in debt as I fail to make money, credit score is pathetic, prospects not good.  Pick up "Pookie" and go to deliver.  Death by pirates.
Game 3 - Choose a freighter.  Ship running shoes and metals, food and electronics.  Buy a better freighter.  Ship more things.  Make more money.  Buy second freighter.  Repeat.  Buy hauler.  Missions and trading.  Buy 'nother hauler.  Repeat, etc.  Trade in 3 haulers for Behemoth.  Take on pirate planet in massive ship named "Bada**motherf**er".  Die spectacularly.
It's kinda what you make it to be.  Some people will think it's boring, others will love it.  Hey, it's free, so either way no real loss.
Graphics - Well it's no tech demo...
Audio - Felt this was pretty lacking.  No soundtrack, but there's Pandora.
Gameplay - Good overall, no real complaints.
User friendliness - A little off-putting at first, but you figure it out.
Creativity - Updates for more variety would be nice, I'd say I played about 12 hours and I'm getting bored with it.  Of course, there could be a lot more coming up, but it's a little slow-paced at the moment.
Overall if you like space games, FTL, building your way up from nothing, etc, give it a shot, it's not bad for a free space sandbox.

Just gonna copy and paste my review of the first game since it is essentially the same thing with an expansion of the story and some mechanics:
Probably one of the most intriguing games I have ever played merely because before I played it, I had gone a tirade on how grinding mechanics in single player, story driven RPGs is a sign of bad pacing and should be removed from them. Naturally of course this is a single player, story driven RPG where grinding is THE ENTIRE POINT of the game and makes it of the best paced RPGs I have ever played. I mean, it's genius. Just take a story of a JRPG, have the combat system be the most optimal move auto-spammed endlessly (like a usual turned based RPG for grinding), and have the combat speed multiplied by 60. Then BAM! You take what would have been an half hour grinding in a dungeon in a regular RPG is turned into a half minute race against the clock to beat the boss. I suppose on that point it is less of an RPG and more of a puzzle game, where you attempt to find the most optimal way to grind and beat the boss in 30 seconds. Probably one of the best examples of good pacing in an RPG, with strangely enough the most grinding in any RPG ever (since time is relative).

Games with a lot of dialogue can be enjoyable if the content are well written and enjoyable.

They don't even make fun of the characters archetype or the story itself. The story is something that is commonly seen that doesn't have a unique twist and the way they portray the revenge story was poorly written and the messages it conveys is terrible and the story lack a cohesive direction.
Overall, half minute hero 1 had more variety of activities and deconstructs jrpg better.

I read that a lot of people compare it to GTA. Since I don't play GTA, this review will try to cover and talk about aspects that maybe GTA has too. Therefore, sorry if some of the points may look, from your point of view, like something to be expected from a 2014 game and shouldn't be seen as selling points.
The plot is truly interesting, and although is widely known that you take the role of an undercover cop, things are not as plain as it may seem. You're not an average undercover cop, you're a person suited to fill that role, with a particular psychological profile. You'll infiltrate in a main branch of the Triad, in Hong Kong, and things won't go as smooth as you'd like. That profile won't help and you'll get caught in something a bit more deep, a bit more scary, a bit more of your own.
It won't be about choosing sides, it will be more about merging in both, without leaving any trace, nor any part of you.
It will be more about swimming inside a stream, while trying not to follow its flow.
Gameplay - Wise, I didn't feel disappointed at all. The environment is gorgeus, accurate, colourful yet gray. Turns, hills, alleys, signs.
Driving is fun but steering is a must, and makes things more exciting. Shame there aren't many car models.
You can't steal a car and make it yours by driving it into your parking lot, but you'll own many cars, obtained by buying them or by doing main missions and / or side missions. Same applies for motorcycles.
While cars can't be customized, noone says that you can't steal them and drive them through all Hong Kong, shooting at other cars' tires or directly at their front window. Aim well for a clean headshot, will you? Or if you feel like you need a new car, keep putting the pedal to the metal, jump from your seat to the roof of your new love interest or hit them until they'll stop driving.
And there will be lot of pursuits. Relentless pursuits. Be it in North Point or in the highway, drive wherever you want, just get rid of the pursuers. This is one of the things I liked most from the game, as it's one of the few cases where you'll hold a firearm and you'll see cars exploding.
Because what has been seen by many as a flaw, my eyes and my racing heart tells me otherwise.
Firearms are rare, very rare so that you won't feel overpowered and start a killing spree. You'll treasure them and hide them. You won't waste bullets and you'll scavenge a lot. And you'll enjoy the moment when you'll use your gun to set a car on fire, or while taking cover behind a counter, against a volley of bullets.
Gunfires will make you remind that you're made of flesh, so don't try to run against your enemies. Take cover and plan the right time to shoot.
This scarce source of guns makes hand-to-hand combat the way to clean the path ahead of you. Keep countering, break their arms, thair legs, their teeth. Use everything at your disposal: a fan, a swordfish, a boiler, a railing, or take them hostages and use their bodies as shields, or put them inside the boot; they may change their minds.
There's still more, but I don't think I should spoil everything.
Secondary missions are interesting, they add layers to an already thick background, encouraging you to live this game more deeply, on both sides of the same coin.

The true genius of this game is that it's actually a masterclass in logistics programming that tricks you into wanting to eradicate aliens for their resources. It's the agony of always being one part short to complete your fancy new subsystem that's connected to a main line of cargo that you've already spent hours carefully connecting only to realize that you could move something just 2 tiles and add one more inserter here or there to improve it by only 0.25%. That's a huge number in the world of this many moving parts and most players of this game would likely agree.
The sense of progression is something akin to Civilization where the start of the game provides you with 2 sticks that you can rub together to make your first furnace glow that will have to be powered by fuel you hand gather. By the end you'll be in charge of a giant series of machines that spans across a literally infinite map that just simply wants more and more. Your robot army will help put fuel in your tank so that you can drive to site, destroy all of the aliens around it, design a new system on top of it, add it to a blueprint and plop it down with one mouse click right next to your new train depot that's piping ore into smelters 10 minutes (in train speed) away in the other direction.
If you get lost, there's a lot... and I mean a lot of information out there from other players that also realize this game is as much of a theory and programming language as it is a game. I personally think experimenting until everything on fire is the best kind of science so I've spent quite a few hours now just hooking things up to things and trying to figure out exactly just how far I can take the programming circuits. Sure I could have played the game and won several times over, but this very much the hybrid between real-time strategy base building and Transport Tycoon I didn't know I really wanted until I just blew almost a whole week of free time playing it.
Of course YOU can play this game exactly how you want, because after all it's multiple games at once. It's a formidble tower defense game and turtling is a viable strategy. You can turn the aliens off and just build a fancy factory that hordes resource, or you can play the game the "right" way and work towards building a rocket to get off of this alien infested rock. A very supportive mod community makes a ton of completely optional enhancements that do very minor things like improve quality of life, or add complete overhauls that seemingly have created expansions for the base game. I just experimented with a mod that overhauled how the game generates resources, which drastically changed my entire strategy. Again, I say option because the base game already offers 100's of hours of enjoyment if you find what it is that I personally enjoy:
Destroying an entire planet..

This game has no jump scares, which is excellent, has some interesting atmosphere, which is nice, and as many have said, it deals interestingly with dark subject matter, but...
It's sort of trite? And I don't just mean in the sense that it's short enough to play through in 35 minutes or less. I just mean that, even with all the endless back-and-forth wandering it entails (and yes, you'll be walking the same routes over and over throughout play) and the creepy lighting and soundscape, it's just - short and simple, with not a real shock to be had. The ending, which I won't spoil here, becomes fairly obvious as soon as you're a couple of notes in, or if you have any basic sense of how these sorts of "deep, dark, horrid secret" games almost always work.
The character whose jottings guide you around, whom you are probably supposed to be, is of the instantly-repulsive, pretentious sort, even before you learn the full extent of his misdeeds. I'm sure the point must have been to make you dislike this person from the moment you read what they wrote, or else things would have been far more subtle.
Basically, while this game is creepy and has nice atmosphere, it does nothing new with the sort of person who is revealed to you through the pages you read. It's the same sort of see-the-end-a-mile-away, "AND THEN YOU WAS SKELETON!" writing that we've come to expect from atmospheric little horror games which can rightly boast no jump scares, but which then at the same time do nothing to shock that you couldn't just as easily see on the evening news or any article about very bad people doing very awful things to those around them.
Maybe, as a survivor of CSA, I'm sort of jaded, but frankly, this game is almost less horror, and more simply pointing out "See, look! People are bad and do awful things to those they're expected to protect and care for!" with some "horror" accoutrements in the form of creepy sounds and cobweb riddled, darkened rooms, and frankly, if you don't already realise in this day and age that there are plenty of horrific people in the world who already flourish doing the sorts of things that come up over the course of Fingerbones, and don't find the thought distasteful without needing indie horror games to remind you, then I don't know what to tell you.

Amazing Game, a parody on RPGs that is really underrated and a great sequel to the first game. The story is funny, and when it gets serious out of nowhere it is, most of the time, really done well.
Compared to the first game, the tone is really different and the game itself stops being a complete parody around the end of the first "chapter" (Overture).
The gameplay keeps the core mechanic of the first game and greatly expands it, being basically Hero 30 with classes, a new revamped Allies system and skills. It kinda slows down compared to the first one thanks to the skills but there is a way to turn their effects off to get the feeling of rush from the first game.
While I do recommend playing its prequel first, especially because the story has some important ties to the first one, it is not required at all and most of the jokes and characters won't really stop being interesting.
The crafting and cassino system are not really well done, but they are not required at all and are clearly there to keep the game going after it ended, though are not executed really well.
On the other hand, the Time Attack, Map Creation are really cool and can keep people who really liked the game interested. The game has some really cool quests, but that can be kind of "grindy" if people didn't really like the Global System, which is a system that tranforms the game into a more traditional RPG outside of the main quests.
Finally, the game has loads of content, and if people liked the core gameplay, they really won't be running out of time anytime soon, as long as they have the coins needed to keep going.

Updated/Actual Review:
I "reviewed" this game about 2 years ago and it's come so far that I realized that this game deserves an actual review. I had been hearing about the original Plague Inc game for years when I got this and for the price I was genuinely afraid that it was going to become repetitive and not worth it. Well ladies and gentlemen, I am here to say that I was gladly wrong(ish). Was the game worth it's price in early access, well that is up to the person who was reviewing it. It WAS repetitive and it DID get boring after a while back then (even though I still loved it) but I have no doubt in my mind that if you enjoy games like this you should absolutly buy this. Let's go through the list.
Notice: DID and WAS (the game has since been updated and these comments are no longer relevant)
Gameplay: When I first began playing I joked about how this was like flash games where you just click whatever you can to advance your goals but I was wrong. This is a strategy game based on how you direct your pathogen, when you reveal yourself and how you keep yourself from being revealed. You could also argue resource management (I've seen friends without DNA points just after being found) but this personally isn't a problem I've had. With the many different pathogens which all change up gameplay entirely, your job is to simply destroy the world...easy right? There are only two real stages to the game right? Infect everybody without being found out/ Panic and be found immediatly (or hate the world on nanobots and panic on necroa virus) and then kill everybody. It can easily be summed down in words but as I've said, you can't just click everything to win. You have to move your virus in just the right way (I prefer boats, easier to get at Madagascar and Greenland but mostly because I like boats) and make sure that it can spread in the countries it moves to. You can easily be found out in your first country (if you're a first timer) and dead before you even know it. This gameplay allows players to have a basic strategy game without the extreme amount of time and thought process required for games such as Civilization or Europa. It also allows for fast games so you can easily sit down and play a game of Plague Inc while you're waiting for something (just remember, any computer is a laptop if you're brave enough). Of course, saying this I need to say that it can be difficult for people to pick up at first. I don't mean it's difficult to understand the controls I just mean newcomers should start on easy and work their way up. I could easily continue but I do need space for the rest of the review, sorry. (9/10)
Sound: The music is pretty good, kind of ominous but you kind of need that for a game about killing everyone. I think they got the music design right for a game like this, but this is a strategy game, while music is nice to listen to it isn't really that important. It is the kind of music that keeps your head in the game and that's all that really matters. The sound design is excellent, there's no lag on the sound design, the bubble popping noise makes me want to pop more bubbles, I almost feel sad when I play with cheats on and I don't pop any bubbles. (9.5/10)
Graphics: The graphics are good, I don't really see what they could do better. The world feels alive, that's all I can say. You really do begin to feel like you're killing the world and as you slowly watch as the world stops moving it really does feel empty (the world you've just destroyed you monster, not the graphics quality). There are real pictures for some of the countries (I wanted to say most but in truth I'm not sure) thanks to help the devs asked for from the community and the work had payed off tremendously. While some of the map of the world could be looked at to be made more realistic, for a 15/16 dollar game (sorry, don't know the U.S price) they hit the mark. (8/10)
Workshop: This is important, I seriously felt the need to add this. The Steam workshop adds a whole new dynamic to this game. There's no longer just a set number of deceases, there's new ones being made all the time and while many games are starting to embrace the workshop, this one's been doing it for a while now and I must say, the community is just excellent.
Multiplayer: (WILL REVIEW AT A LATE DATE MAYBE. #foreveralone)
Overall: This game is just absolutly excellent and while I don't play it as much as I used to it has earned a place in my Steam Library and is definitely worth its base price. Mind you of course that you are paying extra in this version for better graphics, better sound and workshop support but it is so worth it that I would even recommend getting this if you have Plague Inc on your phone.

Take Castle Crashers, ok?
Take Castle Crashers, drench it in actual realism, with an immediate, and very pressing plot. Soak it in thuggery and blood, put it in the oven for about 400 until it burns to a crisp. Inject it with this here green stuff; and the result, is awful.
I mean, the result; is a pixelated beat em up about what I am guessing is Russia, and some sort of tyranical mob sponsered by a black colored t-shirt.
You beat people up in teams of two and the AI is 100% better than you. Sergei and Boris for life.
This game also suffers the same 'Psi-qualms'; which is to say; the air in front of me is very dead, but nothing else is. I myself am included in the list of 'things that are very dead'. Fortunately for me, I picked a dude who would rather me live. Shove some green stuff inside of me, whatever it is; and we're good to go again until it happens again.
Its likely just me, after all, this happened in Castle Crashers too, where I never actually knew where everyone was, so I was just punching near the dude in front of me, when in all actuality; he was basically diagonal from me.
Similarly to Castle Crashers again, it does group combat well. If you can stay on your feet, you can reduce four or five dudes into a pile of bodies in a few moves. Each punch and kick has its own weight and timing to it, and it all feels about as nice as get blasted with cool water on a hot summers day.
The art style is lazy.
But, if you're looking for more Castle Crashers but harder; can't go wrong, really.
