Minimum is a 3rd person multiplayer shooter that uses a minimilistic aesthetic with blocky shapes and solid colors. My friends and I picked it up over the steam summer sale while looking for some simple games we could play together. We found the matchmaking to be buggy, but still fun.
The main mechanic of the game involves you picking up powerups that drop from killed enemy's that upgrade your weapons up to 3 times, giving them more damage/new mechanics, as well as collecting materials to craft/upgrade armor sets. Powerups are lost on death but armor remains.
It has 3 game modes: Team Deathmatch, Horde mode, and a mode called Titan, where both teams try to escort a giant robot into the enemy base to destroy a power core. We mostly just played Titan mode, and had a fun time.
There are some pretty cool weapons like mine launchers and laser rifles, though some of them are imbalanced*Cough*Bouncechaingun*Cough*, meaning someone like me (Completely average at best) can stomp even people who are much higher skill level. Some, like the Cryo Sniper, are so weak/Hard to use that it makes it difficult to complete quests that require kills with that weapon.
There was an issue with rubberbanding, sometimes the servers lag out a little bit and makes everyone jump around, but it only happened maybe once a match, if that. The matchmaking as a group is a mess. Sometimes the group leader gets into a game while everyone else is stuck in a lobby, sometimes invites would not bring you into the group, and it seems the game won't put you on the same team if you have more than 3 players in your group.
TLDR: Fun, but buggy. Play it, if you don't mind dealing with bugs

The game is very promising and very well thought out. The visual style the developers went for is appealling as well. Gameplay is intuitive and rewards players who do what they need to to win. Team killing, as I have learned through experience, will penalize you. However, those are the only reasons I am recommending the game and not refunding it immediately. The game seems to suffer from a lack of optimization. I am running a modern gaming rig, 32gigs of ram, over a terabyte of free space, nvidia drivers (all up to date and snuff), the full package, and I suffer EXTREMELY from what I can only guess is lag. Rubberbanding all over the place, misfiring grenades (which ultimately lead to a lower score, and frustrated team mates), all the while with all settings to the lowest possibly (which pretty much would ultimately leave the game looking like a turd that came from a pre-alpha build's♥♥♥♥♥hole, if it weren't for the fact that would be pretty close to the truth.) It is almost pathetic to think that games I can play (I.E Warframe, Skyrim, LoL) that are cranked up to the max, some with graphic mods, and this game, which has no textures to speak of, no real graphics, somehow undoes the very fabric of the computer itself.
Communication ingame seems rather limited. Players don't seem to communicate, if at all. Text-chat was barren first 3 games I played, and I have no idea if there is even a Voice chat, team chat, etc.
The game's tutorial guides you through one type of game mode, titan battle, which is pretty much the main attraction to the game, as it was featured in it's title. Despite being, you know, giant behemoths of polygons, these things are pretty brainless to the players in general. To an extent, I feel like it is a glorified version of payload from TF2, which is weird because of the many differences between the two, but the end goals are almost the same. Object A goes to point B where you win. However, the way to reach that objective is much different and certainly interesting and fun. (Probably the worst analogy ever, so just go play through the tutorial or watch a video of it on youtube, and you'll kind of get what I mean, eh?)
there are two other modes, team death match (Self-explanatory) and horde mode. It would have been really nice if horde-mode had a tutorial, so I know what I am doing and how it goes, but once you die the first time in it, you pretty much know what is going on. BUT for those who want salvation from that frustrating surprise, its you and 4 others against enemy Ai cosplaying as if it were halloween. Also dinosaurs are in it. Basically, "how long can you last?".
Gameplay wise, the game is great. Unfortunately, there are some issues. One design flaw I noticed was that when you kill enemy players, they drop parts and pieces to make you more bad♥♥♥♥♥then before. Sadly, anyone can pick up these pieces. I wouldn't mind this, but there are a few issues here, such as players who are utterly useless (LIKE ME) following other players who are decent and can somehow run the game killing enemies, and stealing their hard-earned buffs. Obviously, jokes aside, this is a problem. One idiotic leech can turn the tide of an entire game from winning to losing in a couple of seconds just by dying. However, the beauty of this, which I am guessing the devs were going for (right?) was that ENEMIES can pick up the fallen bits and become buffed themselves. This is a good strategy, as it means you will always be moving, and it does allow planning by both sides during the game.
There is item purchasing in this game, though it is done through in-game currency. From what I can tell, no pay2win scrublords (Although I could be grossly mistaken. I only got to play 3 games total after all.) Guns are pretty much run of the mill, though they make a difference, and using them properly is crucial (Protip, grenade launchers hurt you and your allies. I found that out by killing a friendly turret and player by rubberband accident.)
The game is good, but I feel like it needs more to it for it to thrive. It's great fun now, but play a few matches over a couple of days, and that steam will run out. With only three game modes total, the game could definitely use a bit more diversity to it, even if it was something like Capture the flag (Which would be fun as hell in this game). Deathmatch (Battle free royale, not team deathmatch) would also be cool, to see who is the most minimal in that lobby. Private matches are possible, which is nice touch, but again, with only so many modes possible, it's tough to say how long this game will last.
The game is great, the art style so simplistic it'll ♥♥♥♥ your computer right up it's cooling unit so it can't even play the game, audio and announcer are great (They are frequent, but not enough for you to pull out your hair like in other games), and playing it just feels right. Until your computer offs and screws you with bad framerate. The game has been out for almost a year now and this game feels unpolished in certain regards, though, which leaves me tough to review positively or negatively. Also, there's a reason why it's 10$ I'm sure. Not that I am complaining. (4$ summer sale)
I think that if you are in the mood for a shooter, this
be a game for you. But like I said, if those laggy-framerate issues on your bad♥♥♥♥♥rig can't be contained, you might just want to steer clear from this, or request a refund. The fruit on top is titan mode, and it's definitely good fun if you can run it smoothly.
If you have the time and cash, give the game a shot and if you like it keep it, and if not, then refund it.
TL;DR : Game seems unoptimized, has been out for a year, only 3 game modes, one short tutorial for one mode, cool art style, greephix are good. framerate issues rubberbanding fun times to lag. GG WP NO RE. Katana users automatically win with rubberbanding assissting them.

This game, like a lot of beat-'em-ups, is very fast paced and can get very gruelling.  What sets Mother Russia Bleeds apart, however, is much more than I expected when first going into this game.  The first few minutes of the story immediately grabbed my attention and what followed up held my attention.  The art style, the attention to detail, the variety of enemies, the brutal gore, all of it was masterfully created.  The controls are smooth and seem to just blend with everything so well that the game can't be blamed for your 20+ deaths, (which will happen, I can almost guarantee,) and it feels satisfying to land a held punch attack or perform an awesome combo.
Something else, too that shocked me was the storyline.  This game is surprisingly well fleshed out and deep for being the standard style of 2D fighting games.  The story makes you feel for these characters and when they say or do something badass, you can't help but to get hyped up for what's coming next.  Ivan, the biggest and strongest is my personal favorite to play as but there are three more characters that shift up the gameplay to some level, from being a big, hulking tank to being a fast, fragile fighter, to being a well-balanced and easy-to-comprehend murdering machine.  The enemies are formidible opponents, though, so don't be shocked when you easily feel overwhelmed even with bots and a friend on your side.
All in all, it's a very fun game to play to kill a little, (or a whole lot,) of time with a buddy or just going solo for a challenge.  (P.S., the power-ups are cool, too.)

I have quite a few hours logged in Project Genom since it became available on Steam Early Access, and I have seen most of the flaws with the game - the in-game graphics do not match the trailer; only 2 of 6 weapon types, and 3 of 6 armor types are implemented; quite a few of the quests have incorrect location markers, or none at all; there is no crafting to speak of yet; there is only one vehicle, which comes quite late in the game; there is lag (moderately bad at peak times, other times it is more inconvenient than bad; not all of the content has been translated to English yet (some is still in the developers' native Russian); weapons occasionally disappear when logging out/logging back in; players get stuck in the environment; not all skills/abilities have been implemented in the game yet; no character customisation (yet); player guilds and groups are in-game but have no real function or benefit; and the chat system is pretty basic but still functional. That is what I can come up with off the top of my head...
Some of those issues are things that will be resolved during Alpha testing and beta, while "the rest" are content that will be added over the remaining Alpha time.
The in-game graphics not matching the trailer? The graphics have been hard-set in the most recent builds to be lower than the max-level possible, for performance reasons. With the code optimization work and tweaks happening at the moment, improvements will be seen there, and those same improvements should eradicate or vastly reduce the lag issues.
The mission location indicators being incorrect or missing? Some of them are, indeed, misplaced (this is still an alpha, after all), but some of them are an attempt by the design team to encourage players to explore and discover for themselves. The balance and wording of quest instructions and the type of mission location markers you get will be tweaked by the dev team over the course of the alpha, in line with comments from the testers. It does mean a bit more thought is required than for the average MMO, so if you are looking for an easy thought-free title to relax to and avoid engaging brain cells, this is probably not the game you are looking for.
The reason that the late arrival of the vehicle is a problem is largely because of the size of the game world. We are certainly not looking at something the size of Guild Wars Nightfall, LotRO or Minecraft, but it is still pretty large given the current stage of development.
But with all of that, the biggest thing that makes me optimistic for the game is the team behind it - the developers, designers and artists have all shown considerable talent for such a small team to produce something that, to me, seems very polished for the stage they are at in the development process. Most of the team are active enough on the game forums that I sometimes wonder when they find the time to actually do any real work. Members of the team can be seen in-game quite regularly, if you know which names to look for, and there is a very active group of GMs and community helpers both in-game and on the forums looking to deal with as many problems as possible.
In short, I have seen quite a few Early Access games, including some from major publishing houses, and not many had the potential and foundation that Project Genom has. The task for them now is to build on that foundation, and fulfill that potential. Will they achieve that? Honestly I do not know, but the signs are looking good.

If you've played Half-Minute Hero (the first game), The Second Coming is a true sequel that certainly builds upon its origins but on a much larger scale. You control a small, useless "hero" in an RPG world, set to save that very world from certain destruction. Not much different from most other classic RPGs, I know. The one caveat is that you only have 30 seconds to do so, and therein lies the series' unique gameplay and quirky humour.
Rush through the intro, the world is about to end. Battle monsters to level up, do side quests to unlock alternate routes or equipment, become better than the Evil Lords and destroy them, all in less than half a minute. Just as you've completed the credits, a new threat appears, and you have to do it all over again! While it is possible to beat many of the quests (levels) within this time limit, you actually get to rewind time to make it all more digestible. Though, the Goddess of Time is not a fan of the greater good, as she takes an increasingly larger fee each time you make use of her ability.
The Second Coming contains several new campaigns to a tried and loved concept without changing the formulae too much. While the first game was a nice little distraction from daily chores, you'll have to take a week off to complete all of the content in this game. And you should complete it all, as that is where a lot of this game's quirkyness and gameplay challenge actually lies. In addition to a plethora of new quests, there's also a map editor and a multiplayer segment added, so the fun can continue endlessly if you so wish! And if the map editor is not enough, there is literally an endless mode as well, which is comparable to a boss rush.
It's definitely a title that hands you a unique experience along with a lot to do compared to what you paid for it. Did your download finish yet?

It may seem unassuming from the screenshots, but make no mistake, this is one of my top 10 games of all time. And it almost didn't come to the West at all. It was a Japan only PSP game for years before getting ported on the fly due to the success of the first game on Steam.
Half Minute Hero 2 is a direct sequel to the first Half Minute Hero, and it contains similar gameplay to the Hero mode from the original. You play as a series of powerful heroes in different time periods and must embark on a mission to save the world from whatever threat exists at that point in time. The twist? It's only 30 seconds till the world is destroyed and only the Time Goddess can turn back time and let you survive - but only if you pay her.
This sets the stage for one of the most crazy fast-paced RPGs ever made, and while it felt somewhat repetitive in the original game, The Second Coming turns it up to 11 with a huge cast of characters, eargasmic music from the greatest video game composers to ever grace the planet, and even a giant mecha-slash-castle that serves as a home base AND a robotic monster slaying machne.
Very few games have used many heroes across time before, but when they do, they seem to pull it off very well. Just look at Live A Live. This game is no exception and the story keeps on getting better as the game progresses.
That's not to say this game isn't flawed, far from it. The missions can still be a little repetitious as the game goes on, and the story, while fun, won't win any awards for best writing (though it may hit you in the feels). But as a sum of its parts, it's a glorious homage to old school RPGs while not getting bogged down with old school gameplay and being original enough to do its own thing.

For one Normal mode plays more like something closer to expert in most cases, the randomizing of events are interesting but often erratic and timing on DNA "points" for evolving your pathogen is often too infrequent or nonexistent at the worst possible times in game. For example, I've been trying to win with the Necroa Virus (Zombie Plague Virus) for quite some time now. In my latest attempt I had the entire planet infected, yet I was one point away from making the virus lethal and waited five or so minutes for that last little point I needed while research started spiking all over despite my having put points into delaying/slowing down research, so, as I finally got that one point, the cure research miraculously got distributed, the anti-zombie miltiants showed up and I literally lost in mere moments all because of that. In short, I'd wait until this game was on sale if you are interested, otherwise, it will in my book be considered a borderline "troll" or "rage" game with the faults I have witnessed so far in the program logic and timing. In short, it is one thing to be a challenge, a whole different thing to be so erratic that progressing is nigh on, or completely impossible, on a normal challenge setting.

This game, like a lot of beat-'em-ups, is very fast paced and can get very gruelling.  What sets Mother Russia Bleeds apart, however, is much more than I expected when first going into this game.  The first few minutes of the story immediately grabbed my attention and what followed up held my attention.  The art style, the attention to detail, the variety of enemies, the brutal gore, all of it was masterfully created.  The controls are smooth and seem to just blend with everything so well that the game can't be blamed for your 20+ deaths, (which will happen, I can almost guarantee,) and it feels satisfying to land a held punch attack or perform an awesome combo.
Something else, too that shocked me was the storyline.  This game is surprisingly well fleshed out and deep for being the standard style of 2D fighting games.  The story makes you feel for these characters and when they say or do something badass, you can't help but to get hyped up for what's coming next.  Ivan, the biggest and strongest is my personal favorite to play as but there are three more characters that shift up the gameplay to some level, from being a big, hulking tank to being a fast, fragile fighter, to being a well-balanced and easy-to-comprehend murdering machine.  The enemies are formidible opponents, though, so don't be shocked when you easily feel overwhelmed even with bots and a friend on your side.
All in all, it's a very fun game to play to kill a little, (or a whole lot,) of time with a buddy or just going solo for a challenge.  (P.S., the power-ups are cool, too.)

- A unique sci fi atmosphere
- Badass looking space suits!
- An opportunity to constantly meet exotic and interesting species- then kill them
- A few nice looking visual effects that are oddly satisfying
- A very helpful and polite player community
It's definitely one of THE games to keep an eye on as it develops, but heavy grinding into the game right now is something you wanna do at your own risk. First Impressions:
Okay, I'm still not sure what to make of this game, yet.  It's..  It's the video game version of Tommy Wisaeu's "The Room" (the voice acting!  Oh God!  Soon as my character started speaking, the first thing I blurted out was "I DEED NAT HEET HUR!  I DEED NAAT..")  It's SO BAD that you just can't take your eyes off it.
Here's the good thing, though.  Everything that's wrong with it is all par for the course in an Alpha!
Now, here's the narcissism.  I've played a lot of Alphas.  Not much get changes after that.  An Alpha is a playtest of a WORKING. GAME.  Some developers have gotten the wrong idea behind what an Alpha is supposed to be and Early Access is NOT a replacement for the term Alpha.  Early Access is exactly what it means.  Early Access to a COMPLETE. GAME.
I've heard there's quite a few promises to update the graphics textures, etc etc etc and I'm not going to hold my breath for it.  What I've seen so far in the few hours I've had in it (less than 5 at the time of this review) is ... a positive outlook.  There's quite a bit here for an Alpha and there's SO MUCH refining that needs to be done, but the basics are SOLID.
I'm not quite sure what the devs have planned yet and I'm not about to tell them how to do their jobs, but they bit off way more than they could chew.  They made a huge area with metric crap-ton of quests where the majority of the difficulty in the quest is figuring out where the♥♥♥♥♥♥to go next.  It's a lot of running around hoping something pops up over an object you can interact with.  They put WAY too much effort into making the first portion of the game BIG that they have SO MUCH that needs to be fixed that if they just focused on a smaller area, the rest would've been a lot easier and faster to impliment.  I'm assuming they ran out of money and the Alpha/Early Access/Avalon Packs scheme is an effort to try to restock the warchest in order to carry on.  I got my Gold Pack.  Sadly I didn't know about this game until after Foundership was over.
Avalon Packs are available to buy, but not available in the game yet.  However, if you've played some of the game and you feel like it's worth it to you to see where the game can go, then I encourage you to buy into one of the packs and stock that warchest.  With what I've seen in the Alpha, the Devs are very serious about seeing this game through.  A lot of effort went into what's there, but they definitely bit off a big chunk that I don't think they were prepared to deal with.  Throwing money at the problem, in this instance, is probably the best thing they can do.  Hire more people, get what's here FLESHED OUT and polished before moving on to more content.
The best thing I can advise the Devs to do right now, if they even have the time to read this:
Ignore the naysaying.  You're doing fine.  Knuckle down.  Polish what you have right now.  Worry about expansion later.  Make YOUR vision, not some angry harpy in the comments vision.  And for the love of GOD please DO NOT change the terribly-accented voice cast or, at the very least, keep them on and provide an option to switch to a native english speaker.  I know that's expensive to pay 2 voice actors to read the same script, but this is a novelty that's likely to keep people talking about this game and you WANT THAT.

I really wish this review had a sideways or 'maybe' option. Don't get me wrong, it's a fun game but there are a few things that really start to drag it down after awhile.
Pros:
-Who doesn't like the chance to destroy the world?
-The idea is engaging and fairly original for a video game although there are alot of movies based on it.
-Lots of options, the mutation choices alone will give you lots of action and challenge.
-The developer has added extra info pieces for people who like lore or get tired of the 'start and go here' style of play.
-Love the movie based pathogens, they added a bit of extra fun and also more options than mutate or die.
Cons:
-The tutorial option is still under development. I can understand that they wanted to get this out and start making money but not adding the basic beginner's guide is lazy in my opinion.
-Constant overhead view of the world. You can zoom in on single countries but not down into the actual streets to see what's happening.
-The countries need more info in their tabs! It would have been helpful especially at the beginning to figure out why my pathogen wouldn't spread in certain countries.
-Show the whole list of mutations from the start-not after you mutate the item before it. Would help with choosing a path and style of play.
-Change up the pathogens a bit, several of them have the same or very similiar options. Change some of them and add more content similiar to the movie based pathogens.
To wrap it all up, I had a great time playing this game. It was fun and intriguing for quite awhile but once you beat it that's it. There really isn't much more to do after beating the main game/scenarios. Nothing really changes past the way you mutate your pathogen. If I could do this all over again I'd probably wait for a sale when it's at or under 5 dollars unless they come out with more content/finish the game.

A cautious recommendation here. Mother Russia Bleeds is certainly a very enjoyable game, and a brilliant one to pick up for those fans of old school brawlers and beat 'em ups akin to Streets of Rage or Final Fight, but Mother Russia Bleeds is certainly not without it's problems.
First, the positives. Combat in MRB is extremely responsive and satisfying (if a little repetitive) with a great degree of challenge (though unlike the games it clearly takes influence from, this challenge is legitimate and not just the type arcade games used to get more money out of their players). Honestly, that difficulty is the best bit of MRB. Whether playing through the relatively short campaign or any of the quite entertaining arenas, a legitimate challenge is presented to the player, something few Beat 'em ups can really claim to do, not to mention the story mode is fantastic. While only 8 chapters long (9 if you include the tutorial), which is roughly 3-4 hours of gameplay for a first sitting, the weird journey and weird bossfights contained within the campaign of MRB are absolutely fantastic and brilliant fun to play through and/or beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of.
This is not to say that Mother Russia Bleeds is without problems, though. One or two sections in the campaign can seem a little cheap, and the necessity of playing the Arena mode to unlock new "nekro" strains can be a tad annoying, as the difficulty in arena is much more cheap than that of the campaign. The length also is a downside. Yes, the game is very short (but a hell of a ride), and that could very easily put people off.
Mother Russia Bleeds is a superbly gory, entertaining beat 'em up that's completely and utterly insane. Absolutely recommended for fans of beat 'em ups, but less so to those not as familiar with the genre.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is Square Enix's way of showing that they care about our experience and is the reason why I love the Final Fantasy series.
There is no reason why you shouldn't try this MMO. There is a 14 day free demo (with some chat and levelling restrictions but still enjoyable), and if you like what you play, then you can get the game along with 30 more days of free (non-sub) game time! That's a whooping 44 subscription free days!
Now let's get into the pros and the cons.
Pros:
- Fantastic soundtrack (as expected from a final fantasy game) composed by Nobuo Uematsu.
- Polite and helpful player base. (Don't know what to do? Ask a bypassing player and they'll usually answer and provide even more help than you would initially expect.)
- Role Playing is an option and you can create custom macros!
- Enjoyable story to share with your friends
- You can play and level all classes with just ONE character!
- Frequent patches
- Not pay to win
- A plethora of side and main content
- Controller support (you can also change button layouts from Xbox to Playstation)
- CROSS PLATFORM!
- New player friendly (story mode is basically a tutorial that teaches you new things slowly as you progress)
- Seasonal events such as Halloween and Christmas
- The pleasure of making new friends and joining a guild for the first time.
Cons:
- Small instanced zones (though it shouldn't be a problem after the Stormblood expansion comes out with the end of PS3 support)
- There are a lot of kill and collect quests that may become repetitive (but to be expected of in MMOs)
- The story almost seems nonexistent somewhere in the mid-game
- Non-story quest dialogue is somewhat uninteresting to read most of the time.
I am enjoying A Realm Reborn as a fan of the Final Fantasy series and have barely scratched the surface (yet) and there's not much else to say, go try this game out for yourself.

Wanna get a hidden gem? Here is your chance
The first Half Minute Hero was ingenious puzzle game where the goal was to complete different kind of areas under 30 second. If the 30 second goal was failed, then time could be rewinded for ever increasing pay. The first game also featured some jrpg elements like new equipment (which couldn't be brought to earlier levels).
Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming takes the mechanics of the first game and jrpgfies them and adds some completely new mechanics. Some of the changes are global level ups and removal of equipment restrictions. This results the game being considerably easier than the first game and time of the levels doesn't really matter anymore. There is time attack mode, but unfortunately it suffers also from the same global character syndrome.
However, what is achieved with those changes is that the Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming is a genuine rpg and a very good one. Admitted, the script is written without much thought, but half asessed parody of more popular rpg branches goes well with this game. Half Minute Hero SC knows what it is capable and doesn't try to be anything else than light-jrpg...
Well that is besides the music, for some reason the soundtrack of the game is really over the top and features songs/compositions from 24 different artists. This includes multiple Final Fantasy composers and Chrono Trigger composer. And if you think those were the only ones worth mentioning, you are very wrong (the list just would be too long). Soundtrack of the Half Minute Hero SC doesn't pale in comparison to any other game-soundtrack. It isn't long, but it is compact and packs a huge punch and enhances the game massively! What is best about the soundtrack is how it is used. There are moments in the game where the soundtrack is utilized near utmost perfection. For example final mission of Ragnarok story arc and its vocal track was something from which those big and old franchises could learn. I think have have never stared battle result screen as long as I did after that mission, for it featured instrumental version of that same song (a thing, nothing short of brilliant).

I really wish this review had a sideways or 'maybe' option. Don't get me wrong, it's a fun game but there are a few things that really start to drag it down after awhile.
Pros:
-Who doesn't like the chance to destroy the world?
-The idea is engaging and fairly original for a video game although there are alot of movies based on it.
-Lots of options, the mutation choices alone will give you lots of action and challenge.
-The developer has added extra info pieces for people who like lore or get tired of the 'start and go here' style of play.
-Love the movie based pathogens, they added a bit of extra fun and also more options than mutate or die.
Cons:
-The tutorial option is still under development. I can understand that they wanted to get this out and start making money but not adding the basic beginner's guide is lazy in my opinion.
-Constant overhead view of the world. You can zoom in on single countries but not down into the actual streets to see what's happening.
-The countries need more info in their tabs! It would have been helpful especially at the beginning to figure out why my pathogen wouldn't spread in certain countries.
-Show the whole list of mutations from the start-not after you mutate the item before it. Would help with choosing a path and style of play.
-Change up the pathogens a bit, several of them have the same or very similiar options. Change some of them and add more content similiar to the movie based pathogens.
To wrap it all up, I had a great time playing this game. It was fun and intriguing for quite awhile but once you beat it that's it. There really isn't much more to do after beating the main game/scenarios. Nothing really changes past the way you mutate your pathogen. If I could do this all over again I'd probably wait for a sale when it's at or under 5 dollars unless they come out with more content/finish the game.

A very interesting point and click puzzle game!
The Room is about solving puzzles. Mostly it's about solving very mechanically focused, intriguing contraptions that were a marvel to watch unfold. They get bigger and more complicated as you solve more and more of the various mechanisms built into them.
The gameplay involves a lot of rotating and twisting things, such as keys and dials, which can mean a lot of mouse movement. It also features an excellent hint system, which points you in the right direction without being too obvious if you haven't made progress in a little while.
There's a small storyline that accompanies your journey, involving your relative and their research into something called the "Null" element. Though not the strongest narrative, it was enough to keep me pushing forward and make me want to jump right into the second game!
The Room is fairly short, so I would recommend picking up the second one along with the first. Despite it's length, it stands out as a unique take on the puzzle genre that I definitely want more of.

First of all, Factorio runs smooth as silk. It's incredibly well optimized and receives consistently excellent updates from an incredibly competent dev team. I haven't seen any other devs who put so much effort into optimizing and tweaking the game so it runs better, faster, and more stable. They rewrote the entire multiplayer system when they saw that their original design was unworkable once you got past a few players. Now you can easily have a hundred players or more without too many issues!
The modding support is insanely good, it's rare to see a game support so many different things with modding. There are more things that I'd like to see, but overall it's an excellent system with a lot of flexibility.
And of course, the game itself is excellent. It's one of those games that'll have you working on one part of your factory for hours on end trying to perfect it. Then you realize that your production lines are in top shape, but now your raw material isn't keeping up... Everything grows and grows. At some point you realize that your current factory has a fatal flaw, and you need to start over with what you've learned. It's insanely addictive and always has your attention. There's a reason some call it "Cracktorio".
For things that still need to improve, there isn't really a proper ending. Personally I'm not too bothered by it, since I know I want to go for launching as many rockets as I can as fast as I can, but a lot of people aren't satisfied with that.
There are also a few slightly clunky things in the base game. For example, the Chemical Plant has a crafting speed of 1.25, making calculating ratios kind of a pain, and it doesn't line up with the Oil Refinery which is at 1. It does line up with the Assembling Machine 3, but the only thing that you use for that is Processing Units, which use so little Sulfuric Acid and take so long to make that the ratio is irrelevant.
But the biggest thing for me, at the moment, is the combat. It's far too easy, especially once you know how to quickly build up without over-polluting the area. Because of that, the biters are just an annoying nuisance rather than dangerous. The combat is also far too fast-paced, a single large worm can nearly instantly kill you if you're not wearing several shields. Harder enemies simply get more health and damage, leading to a situation where the only good weapon is the flamethrower and you simply have to carry around at least 3 shields at all times. I'd rather have more variety in what we can use, more varied enemies and bases, different ways that I'm attacked and that I can use to defend.
That being said, at the moment they are planning to address the combat in the next update (0.15), so hopefully these complaints will be reduced or eliminated.
Of course overall I would very strongly recommend Factorio. If you enjoy crafting and building complex machinery, you'll enjoy it. If you enjoyed SpaceChem, you may like this. If you played a lot of modded Minecraft, such as Feed the Beast, and enjoyed the tech mods, it's almost guaranteed that you'll like this.

I've had this game sitting in my library collecting dust. I meant to play it earlier, but I never really found time to do it, so while stalling for writing my story, I loaded it up randomly. And to be honest, I am impressed.
What's impressive about this game that warrants no more than forty minutes of gameplay? First of all, the game itself. It's a primitive operating system with a primitive chat system that allows Protagonist-kun to chat with all of their buddies from high school. You can view your list of friends and their profiles, allowing you to peek into their lives over the years. Very subtle details that teach you small things about unimportant characters, and even foreshadowing of our main character, Emily. You can even change the color of your text and your profile icon. The only person you chat with, however, is Emily. Every chapter in this game is one chat session with Emily-
The setting of this game is very simple and very basic. The screen of Protagonist-kun's Windows 1 computer. It adds the sense of style, flair, charm to the game. If the game were to be a modern, twenty-first century chatroom, it would feel very different.
Now onwards, what makes this game worth spending about 30 minutes? If you are the type of person who can appreciate text-based interaction and (in some cases) a relatable plot, you will be riveted to this game for the duration of its time. The story of Emily is Away is focused almost completely around the relationship between Protagonist-kun and Emily. You get glimpses into her life at different times, you get to hear about how she's been doing, tell her about how you've been doing, and eventually things will change.
The gameplay itself is basic. Chat with Emily; you're presented with three options every turn. Choose one, and then hit keys on your keyboard to "type" a response. Some dialogue choices affect your actions or relationship. Some, Emily will remember. Put yourself in the protagonist's shoes, and enjoy the story or cry, whichever will work.
This is a story-based game. Everything revolves around the characters, or mainly
character. Don't expect to have an omnipresent knowledge of everything; you only know what you're told, or what you notice. That being said, this game is full of little details and references to culture- the things that Protagonist-kun types and then deletes and types again, the profile information, the bands and symbols.
One important thing before I cut my rant short is that
. You don't
anything for them. You
what to say. Protagonist-kun will not listen to you word for word. You are simply a puppet master's apprentice whose puppet has its own thoughts and feelings.
To end my rant, I recommend this game for its easy to pickup story and its potential. One thing that could be improved on is the actual story interactivity, which is linear and limited and more of a flavor detail than an ending changer. Some good things about this game are its attention to detail, subtle things you may not pick up, along with references to recent culture and excellent use of character. If you liked Emily is Away, also check out Digital: A Love Story. It also tells a short story, but with a much more interesting user interface (think ASCII messaging systems) and tons more characters and interaction and story and heart-break. I can guarantee you, no offense to developer of Emily is Away, Kyle Seeler, but Digital is by far one of the best short-story games I have played.

Buggy, poorly designed crap. Even a straight-up clone of Lunar Lander would have been far superior. Ignore my play time - I only played this game for about 30 minutes before giving up, and idled the rest of it for the card drops. I'm embarrassed to have left the game running that long.
I guarantee you won't make it even 5 minutes before running into a bug that causes multiple landing pads to spawn, with at least one of them buried inside the terrain you're supposed to avoid crashing into. I know this because in a half-dozen attempts I ran into that bug every single time by the second or third stage. That means the developer didn't even bother with the bare minimum amount of playtesting to see if their game worked before selling it.
All of the other problems mentioned in Karuil's review also apply: Poor physics. Broken scoring. Dull levels. I'll also add a terrible camera system as well. There's no minimap, and as you drift down towards the terrain, the camera won't start scrolling until you've reached the bottom third of the screen. So by the time you see how close you are to crashing, it's probably too late to do anything about it.
It's not worth a dollar, or any amount of money at all. There are far better options on Steam if you're looking for a Lunar Lander-style game. Hardcore players can go for

Disclaimer – this game was received as part of a challenge among friends.
To say that this title is "heavily inspired by" Lunar Lander is putting it mildly.  This is a buggy clone with additional "features" that don't add to the experience.
The physics are just far enough off to feel wrong.  Thrust mostly seems to work, but acceleration trails off far faster than it should.  The maps themselves did seem random to a degree, but every one was “fly to the right for half the map and then start looking for a landing zone”.  The landing areas themselves were usually visible, but buggy.  I had multiple instances where I “landed” on the right patch of ground, only to keep falling through the terrain and blow up.  I also had at least one level where I fell through a landing zone and still managed to beat the stage by drifting into a second landing zone inside the terrain I had just fallen through.
You can select from multiple ships at the beginning, but the only noticeable change was in the amount of fuel each ship started with.  The random events after beating a level all gave the same options of more points, more fuel, or an extra life.  Even the scoring function bugged out in at least one run.  Score seems to be calculated as remaining fuel (more or less), but I had one instance where I only completed the first stage and suddenly had over 19000 points.  The average score would probably be more like 200.
On the plus side, the game ran without issues, and is small enough that you only have to regret a tiny amount of wasted disk space.

Awesome MMA and story. Awesome game in general. Driving cars etc is terrible but that don't matter cuz you're about to kick some serious Hong Kong criminal dynasty♥♥♥♥♥as a undercover police officer named Wei Shen. But you don't have to follow the rules though..

Solid open world game, great variety
Premise: Creators couldn't choose between a criminal and a cop, so they made you an undercover cop. So you can do whatever the hell you want, but  you're still a cop
Gameplay: Involves martial arts, and requires actual skill to master, like the Batman Arkham series. Also has guns, but they're few and far between. You'll get far too lost in the martial arts to even mind.
Main Story: You'll grow to like a lot of the characters, but no you're really not going care about any of them. It's modelled after an over the top, cheesy Hong Kong action movie, so I guess it's intentional. Without spoiling anything, Wei has to infiltrate the triads on behalf of the police. The progression is solid and doesn't feel rushed.
Length: I run into my first issues right here, there aren't enough REAL side missions to keep you interested. Mostly just races and favors, which is a shame because the map is huge and full of small chores instead of actual missions. I would've preferred 10-15 hrs of main story and 15 more of QUALITY side missions. Don't get me wrong, the small quests are fun and have their place, but you need actual side missions ALONGSIDE small missions to build interest and replayability.
Replayability: The only thing replayable here is the main story, which is pretty good. The side quests are pretty lackluster outside a few good ones. But, you burn through those quickly. If you like the game a lot, you'll beat the game once, finish the side missions, then go back for the main story only.
DLC: The only thing worth noting here is Nightmare at North Point, don't even bother with Year of the Snake... And I'm really disapointed they didn't just integrate into the main game, that would've been a lot smarter. The DLC is solid, but you start out with a fully upgraded health bar, and the game just takes away all your cars, clothes, etc. It takes the personality and customization out of the game and makes everything feel detached.
Overall: 8.5/10 Took points off for lack of real side quests and unintegrated DLC. Really solid game, would love to give it a 9.5/10, but I'm just gonna look at its flaws objectively...

Should you play this game? Yes, and here's why:
-The story is badass and at times very brutal.
-The setting is a busy, gang-ridden urban Hong Kong with lots of bad Chinese English. You can almost smell the dim sum.
-You feel like you're in a Hong Kong crime action film
-The fighting is satisfying enough without being too sensitive.
-Some challenges actually very challenging (beware poison knives challenge)
Some things to be warned:
-At times doing the many side missions can become very reptitive and boring. I have done so many drug busts from the comfort of my home in this game that it felt like checking the mail.
-The models of NPCs don't vary much, especially the street gang members. It really took away from the big city feel beating up the same guys wearing the same clothes everywhere.
-Though it took me 40 hours to go through this game at a leisurely gaming pace (doing side missions as I pleased, not investing too much into beating the game), I felt like the middle lacked depth. The bread on the sandwich was good, but the meat was old and dry.
TLDR; Good Story. Repetitive. Get it on sale only.

I'm not big on reviewing games. I tend to think that games speak for themselves and their developers.
If a game is bad, the majority of the community will think it's bad, and it will make no money. Furthermore this will tarnish the developers' name and discourage people from supporting them in the future. The community thusly weeds out the bad apples from the vast crop that is Steam.
If a game is good, the majority of the community will think it's good, and support the developers by buying the game, making in-game purchases, and encouraging their friends to play the game as well. The developer flourishes, the community grows. Everyone benefits.
Early access is not so cut and dry. You've got games with promise that start poorly but rise to the top through sheer determination and overwhelming support from a small core group that not only support the developers financially but doggedly provide testing and feedback as they grind through a buggy mess, hour after hour. Likewise you've got games that, from the first moment you boot them up, are an irredeemable mess. You've got games supported by AAA developers that are just in the Early Access scene to rake in extra cash. You've got games that were only intended to fail from day one of development.
Project Genom is of the first camp. This Steam release was a gutted product, made obvious by the lack of content present in earlier independent alpha-stage testing periods, poor netcode, and lack of servers that can support even five hundred concurrent players.
However, 50+ hours can't lie. This game does have content: a fairly large map to explore, plenty of quests to keep you busy, stylish and unique weapons and armor that you can feel good about grinding credits for... and we haven't even seen everything that the developers are almost ready to roll out, yet.
Now, if you've got discerning tastes, then you already know Early Access titles are more or less not for you - and I'm not the kind of person who will be able to convince you otherwise. You can read the other reviews, you can look on the developers' website and comb through the forums, you can even play the game yourself and clearly see what I'm talking about, then refund the game and go on about your day like you probably have done with so many other Early Access games. As is your right.
However, this is a game worth keeping your eye on. Even if it isn't quite up to snuff right now, it will be. The guys at NeuronHaze work their asses off, and it shows. Every day there are Mods ingame not only helping players, along with the dedicated nonpaid Helper players, but also providing updates direct from the dev team themselves so that we know what to expect currently and in the future. The community is incredibly helpful and understanding, with players like myself who are farther along in the game regularly taking the time to explain convoluted questlines and unclear mechanics to newcomers.
NeuronHaze themselves are a development team I feel very comfortable endorsing as well. They don't keep their playerbase in the dark. They are upfront about other projects their team is working on. They are reaching out to network professionals for assistance with their netcode when other developers I have personally interacted with would scoff at the very idea. They have a clear roadmap laid out and are actively working to accomplish their goals.
So if you like the ideas this game brings to the table but are put off by the usual Early Access complaints I strongly urge you to at least check in on this project once in a while. While it would of course help to support Project Genom any way you can, it would be stupid to ask anyone to support something they don't believe in. Wait it out, keep an eye on it, and when the time comes that all the bugs are worked out you can make your decision.

A 'practically endless' sci-fi -inspired sandbox with a distinctively classical gameplay... It kinda saddens me that this kind of game concepts are pretty much ignored by the AAA studios and publishers, because I'd love to see a game where I could do all of this in first person. (Star Citizen, maybe?)
Teh arbitrary list of pros and cons goes here:
Pros:
- An original sci-fi world with its own lore, locales, races, thingmagajigs etc. Lots of descriptions, random events and tiny detail you could admire for hours and hours...
- The game leaves the exploration and discovery to you and there's direct benefits as well as risks to it. I know its hard to achieve with the level of writing shown here, but I kinda wish there was a random map generator and/or more rogue-like elements for additional replay value.
-The learning/grinding curve feels rough and tedious at times, but it's never unfair other than in the way you'd expect it
to be. (You're a lone, debt-ridden pilot in space, anyone could be your enemy if you decide to make them one...)
-You can be a transporter or a merchant and moreover, it's profitable and compelling enough on its own, you never feel like the story or the gameplay is forcing any of the combat and conflict on you. (This is what practically every other sci-fi -themed, or rather, every other videogame is guilty of...)
-It's not like they forgot about conflict either, sure you can become a space pirate or a bounty hunter, even a scout if you will, but it's way more risky than being a merchant, and rightly so.
Cons:
- Combat is clunky, you feel like inertia is your main enemy, as you and your opponent spin around in awkward circles  briefly barraging each other with your weapons before flying off in separate directions... (Most of of the time is easier to avoid fighting all together, and true enough, transporters and freighters are not even designed for combat, but having it in there, I'd love if it was a bit more accessible to a new player, since I don't feel any sort of motivation to try and learn about combat in its current form.)
- "Everything is ready for you.." This is kind of hard to pin down and sure, a lot of it is convenient and makes sense from the 'viewpoint of a game' but it's still kind of iffy how you never have trouble finding wares to sell off in other systems, or nice, paying passengers that won't mind even if you take a detour here or there, missions for a lone hauler with no-one to protect their freight and so on. (I'd say there's lots of room for additional writing and game design here, maybe a 'hardcore mode' of sorts too if some of the features prove too harsh for the casual player.)
- This one is probably the hardest one to explain, but in writer's terms it goes like: 'Does your story tell about the most interesting time of your protagonist's life and if not, why?' At the era presented in the game, a lot of space is already discovered, and although space pirates still roam about, the age of corporate warfare has largely passed, and overall, space is a lot more of a peaceful and prosperous of a place that what it used to be. Sure, it makes for an easier livelihood if you're a lawful merchant, but let's say for an example, wouldn't it have been more interesting to be a pilot at the time of discovery or a smuggler at the 'end times', scraping against the law and corporations to make meets end in a rat race for scarsening resources... (Okay, not that I should try and pretend being a sci-fi writer or anything, but just saying that additional eras to play in could also be a nice addition. Or an easily accessible 'lore/map editor' perhaps? My bad if there already is one... Yup, there already is one. Maybe I'll have to get writing and see what I can do about that 'end times' era.)

I've had this game sitting in my library collecting dust. I meant to play it earlier, but I never really found time to do it, so while stalling for writing my story, I loaded it up randomly. And to be honest, I am impressed.
What's impressive about this game that warrants no more than forty minutes of gameplay? First of all, the game itself. It's a primitive operating system with a primitive chat system that allows Protagonist-kun to chat with all of their buddies from high school. You can view your list of friends and their profiles, allowing you to peek into their lives over the years. Very subtle details that teach you small things about unimportant characters, and even foreshadowing of our main character, Emily. You can even change the color of your text and your profile icon. The only person you chat with, however, is Emily. Every chapter in this game is one chat session with Emily-
The setting of this game is very simple and very basic. The screen of Protagonist-kun's Windows 1 computer. It adds the sense of style, flair, charm to the game. If the game were to be a modern, twenty-first century chatroom, it would feel very different.
Now onwards, what makes this game worth spending about 30 minutes? If you are the type of person who can appreciate text-based interaction and (in some cases) a relatable plot, you will be riveted to this game for the duration of its time. The story of Emily is Away is focused almost completely around the relationship between Protagonist-kun and Emily. You get glimpses into her life at different times, you get to hear about how she's been doing, tell her about how you've been doing, and eventually things will change.
The gameplay itself is basic. Chat with Emily; you're presented with three options every turn. Choose one, and then hit keys on your keyboard to "type" a response. Some dialogue choices affect your actions or relationship. Some, Emily will remember. Put yourself in the protagonist's shoes, and enjoy the story or cry, whichever will work.
This is a story-based game. Everything revolves around the characters, or mainly
character. Don't expect to have an omnipresent knowledge of everything; you only know what you're told, or what you notice. That being said, this game is full of little details and references to culture- the things that Protagonist-kun types and then deletes and types again, the profile information, the bands and symbols.
One important thing before I cut my rant short is that
. You don't
anything for them. You
what to say. Protagonist-kun will not listen to you word for word. You are simply a puppet master's apprentice whose puppet has its own thoughts and feelings.
To end my rant, I recommend this game for its easy to pickup story and its potential. One thing that could be improved on is the actual story interactivity, which is linear and limited and more of a flavor detail than an ending changer. Some good things about this game are its attention to detail, subtle things you may not pick up, along with references to recent culture and excellent use of character. If you liked Emily is Away, also check out Digital: A Love Story. It also tells a short story, but with a much more interesting user interface (think ASCII messaging systems) and tons more characters and interaction and story and heart-break. I can guarantee you, no offense to developer of Emily is Away, Kyle Seeler, but Digital is by far one of the best short-story games I have played.

We were all stupid teens, or, will be. We will all, or already have, made mistakes. We all lost our friends, or will. We lost our prince or our princess or will. Emily is Away is a big old trip down a bumpy road of memories, bad decisions, good decisions,  trials of friendship, burned bridges, and old faces. It makes you physically connect and immerses you with Emily, and Emma, and even Brad, Mike, and Travis; you lose yourself as you scramble to save everything and hopefully try to do things right.
And just like last time, you can't.
But that's not really a bad thing. We're here; or will be here, we grew, we learned, we adapted, we expanded. Emily is Away hits you in the gut the same way life did, and for some that punch is too much. For others, it's a good escape back to old days, what could had been, to let the mind wonder - and then it pulls you back to reality even though it's 10 years ago and nothing has changed. To some, that's sadism, to other's, it's wisdom and growth.
I guess - I guess my grasp of the English language isn't well enough to express what I feel. Longing, sadness, yet...thankfulness? Sad joy? Or maybe deep down this game relates to us so much that we can't but help to feel a mixed bag of feelings. And that's not really a bad thing, unless you HAVE to absolutely win, you HAVE to absolutely change the past...then I can't recommend this game to you. You won't get the point. You won't enjoy it.
The point isn't about winning.
The point of this game is about living.

I originally played
on mobile a couple of years ago. The PC version updates the textures, but keeps everything else the same. This includes the control scheme, so you will end up doing a lot more clicking and dragging than you ever wanted to. Other than that, my original review holds up:
Out of all the mobile games I have played so far,
is by far the one that feels the most like a premium experience. If there is a AAA category on mobile, this is a prime example of how to do it right. Ironically an independent studio made it, which just shows you how nontraditional this space is.
From the title you might expect
to be a game where you are stuck in a room that you have to escape from. In fact it turns out to be the opposite. You are in a room with a safe that you have to figure out how to get into. Being a puzzle game, you find everything you need to get in somewhere on the safe itself. The game is divided into chapters: each time you open the container you find another inside that you must open. You start each chapter by inspecting the container to identify the points that you can interact with it. Many of these points will do nothing until you obtain some object (a key, a cog, a crank, etc) from another part of the container. All your interactions are intentionally tactile, making good use of the touch screen.
The puzzles tend to do a good job of walking the fine line between being too hard and too easy. I was concerned at the beginning when it insisted on continuously giving me hints. It soon stopped and I realized that I was sorely unprepared for what I had gotten myself into. Most of the levels were quite enjoyable, giving just enough challenge to result in a satisfying “Aha!” moment. Even when if you get completely stuck, the game gives optional hints. There are usually a set of hints for a particular puzzle. They start general and vague and progress to being so specific that I never had to look online for an answer.
The story is told through a series of notes left by the previous owner of the safe. They had been researching what they call the Null element, and the game soon takes on a creepy old-world mysticism vibe. In a lot of ways it reminds me of
, though of course it is not a horror game. The story tropes, the tactile interactions with the world, and even the visuals all contribute to this feeling. The game was lauded when it came out for its visuals, and they still hold up for the most part. There were a few textures that I would have liked to be higher resolution, and a couple of times I was distracted by jagged edges on objects, but it wasn’t a chronic problem. Also if you get the PC edition this should be less of a problem as they touched up many of the textures.
One of the important things in a mobile game is being able to pick it up for quick sessions and put it down at will.
manages this by saving after every action, so you are free to leave and come back as often as you need to. I did not find it difficult to remember what I was in the middle of doing when returning to the game.
If you have a choice of different devices to play on, go with the one with the largest screen. I played on my Nexus 5, and there were a few times I felt cramped and had to lean in close to inspect objects. The game is also quite dark, so you will have a hard time playing anywhere near sunlight.
There are five chapters in the game (four at launch and an epilogue that was added to lead into the sequel). It was not an especially long game (took me a weekend of moderate playtime) but it was not nearly as short as
.

A beautifully designed puzzle game with amazing graphics and effective atmosphere.
I solved this game on my iPad a few years ago and decided I needed it in my Steam collection as well, because it really is that good.  There are definite graphical improvements here in the PC version, and I thoroughly enjoyed getting to play this game again on a bigger screen.  The soundtrack is atmospheric and brilliantly sets the mood throughout the entire game.  It is sometimes eerie but never overdone.  The game retains a calm feel and pulls you in from the start.  It is deeply immersive and easily one of the best puzzle games I have ever played.
Gameplay is fun and immensely satisfying, with an interface that is intuitive and never frustrating.  The puzzles themselves are not only gorgeous but thoughtfully designed with just the right amount of challenge.  You can expect to complete the game in one sitting with the full playthrough lasting only a few hours.  With this in mind, I feel that the $4.99 price point is more than fair especially if you consider quality over quantity.  Nothing in this game was added for the sake of just making the game longer.
I highly recommend this game for anyone and especially fans of the puzzle genre as this is easily one of the best titles available.

Play both ‘The Room’ and its sequel ‘The Room Two’ back to back for maximum calm and relaxation; a zen 3D puzzle experience not unlike the original of the ‘Myst’ series but in a much tighter space. Delicious bite sized progression throughout the long sequences in both ‘The Room’ and ‘The Room Two’ provide warm sensations of  accomplishment.
Tackling these games in the morning with a cup of java in hand allowed me to optimally apply my powers of observation; 3D puzzles requiring movement around complex objects with multiple buttons, hidden spaces, concealed switches, and deviously coded patterns kept me intrigued for hours at a time. The art is pretty, the models are well researched and historically accurate, the audio is gentle and all together create an immersive and consistent experience that one can only describe as professional.
Attention Achievo hunters:
Each game is about 5 hours with 100% each,
(5 and 7 achievements respectively).
Pick up both ‘The Room’ and its sequel ‘The Room Two’ either at full price or on sale.... you will be happy.

I'm not going to go light on this game just because it's free. It's on Steam so it's  open to criticism.
Basically, this game suffers the same weaknesses as almost all other Github games. It was developed in an echochamber by entitled coder(s) with apparently little playtesting or outside player input, and the end result is a bunch of code that doesn't interact well. Lots of mechanics work against each other, and the game is barely playable as a result.
The problem with Github is that the average Github coder is a self-proclaimed creator who neither plays the game he helps create or listens to player input. The command structure is basic and not even the person who approves code merges bothers to playtest what he approves. As a result, Github games are always going to be barely playable messes. There are not many games that live up to the word "sequel". "Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming" is definitely not one such game. This sequel of "Half Minute Hero" expands on the simple game-play by adding more items, skills, and developing the already amazing storyline. "Second Coming" has a more traditional RPG feel but still has a distinguishable style that fans have come to love from the first game. One new feature allows the player to level up the base level of the hero. This allows a player to start at a higher level when they begin a new quest. Another new feature is the ability to create and share custom maps with other players. A core mechanic from “Half Minute Hero” is the ability to find new armor and weapons as you play the game. You are able to go back and play the same map again so that you can earn weapons that you may have missed. You may also find a different path that may lead to a secret. These new features, combined with the story, make this game worth buying.
The “Hero 30” series is known to have a great story that spans across the different game modes. The story is filled with great characters to fight by your side, tongue and cheek comedy, and the every so greedy Time Goddess. It takes place hundreds of years after the first game where the Hero has saved the world from destruction. I won't spoil the story for you as it is very well done and is worth experiencing for yourself. All in all, if you are looking for a fast paced game brimming with personality and content then “Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming” is worth your TIME and money but remember....
You only have 30 SECONDS to save the world.

Mother Russia Bleeds is a great game that offers you a great soundtrack, challenging bosses, and fun, somewhat satisfying gameplay.
Pros:
-Soundtrack: The soundtrack is fast paced and is quite memorable at times.
-fighting: Although not the best, (due to enemy hitboxes being pretty small) it does feel quite satisfying to grab someone mid air and slamming them in the ground, or punching someone with a charged punch. Fixing the hitboxes on enemies would make the fighting fantastic.
Cons:
-Characters: The characters could use a splash of personality. You have 4 main characters to choose from and all of them have the same dialogue during converstions. Giving the characters unique dialogue could make them more memorable and likeable but as it stands, they're all pretty bland.
-Story: The story is nothing to write about (ha ha) but the one thing il'll say is that it focuses too much on the whole "this country is falling apart" story rather than the story about how you ended up in a lab and what exactly this "necro" drug is.
Overall, it's a pretty good game. 7/10

This game is awesome. Brings back the glory days of the beat-em-up with some over the top violence thrown in. The music and sound effects are top notch and the visuals have that nostalgic style that brings to mind the glory of the late 80s, early 90s arcades. The controls are easy to learn and combos easy to achieve. The fact you can pick up guns and blow people away is pretty cool to. Drugs are good to children.
The one criticsim that has to be made is the lack of online co-op. Sure it's cool to get a few people around the same PC old school style but to play a 4 player co-op game you really need the online support. That being said if you know someone else with a gamepad who wants to sit in your presence for a few hours there is not many more enjoyable ways to spend a few hours. Get some beers and start pummelling some Soviets.

Mother Russia Bleeds is one of those games that grabs you by the genitals and screams at you to go kill more people in the most brutal way possible. It's painful but you do it all for the sake of that sweet satisfying sound of a spine smacking against the ground.

About most important - the gameplay in the game is excellent, with good difficulty level balance. If you want to play a single-player beat’em’up with such a nice and friendly appearance I can highly recommend it to you. Otherwise think twice before buying copy of this game.

This is a puzzle - or more accurately a series of puzzle boxes.  They are beautifully detailed and I want to own real, tactile versions of them! "Transistor" is a combination of exquisite art and engaging turn-based combat. The world this game takes place in, the city of Cloudbank, is stunning to look at. The motif of the environment is an oddly utopian sort of cyberpunk, or that's at least the best way I can describe it. The point is that this game's look and world-building are its strongest assets.
The protagonist, Red, has lost her voice after narrowly evading an assassination attempt. She fights an A.I. hivemind known as the Process, a rapidly spreading scourge that is destroying Cloudbank. However, Red has the power of the Transistor, a sort of giant sword/paddle that talks and is largely the only voice the player hears throughout the game. You have to guide Red through the city to uncover who tried to kill her, the truth behind the Process, and how to stop it.
The combat in the game is above average, but it's not gonna knock your socks off. You enter a designated area and fight enemies in groups. After you've eliminated the last enemy you'll get experience and will be able to continue through the map. The key to combat is using the Turn() function to freeze time and map out you plan of attack. You're limited in how much you can move and attack during Turn() though, so you have to strategize and make sure not to die between usages as you're unable to attack until Turn() recharges.
You can acquire loads of different abilities, known as Functions, in "Transistor" and each function can be used in three different ways depending on how you equip them. This makes for a very flexible and customizable combat experience. There is also a challenge mode are built into the main game where the player can run through different tests involving speed, strategy, and endurance. Successfully completing each test grants additional experience.
I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the music in this game. Simply put, it's absolutely stunning and probably the best game soundtrack I've hear since "Fez." Lots of lilting, sleepy jazz tracks accompany you as you stroll the empty streets of Cloudbank. The music tends to be somber in most places and suits the environment and narrative well.
"Transistor" is a game that sucks you right into its world and make you fall in love with it. The audio and visual presentation is unforgettable. The game also manages a great world-building experience without any exposition, which I love because I personally can't stand exposition. The combat takes some getting used to and the fact that Red only moves at the same slow speed will frustrate some. However the high customizability of the different Functions means you can find your ideal way to fight.

As a poorfag, I often browse the free tag, looking for that something to peak my interest. So, on occasion, I came across "Fingerbones", which was my first horror game experience, and, to just tell you right now, I'm glad it was.
When I booted up Fingerbones, I was immediatly put off by the piexalted, minecraft-style grafics, though after 5 minutes realized, that they didn't matter at all. The great atmosphere was created simply by the content of the memos, which you need to find as the games objective, pretty much, and by the very eerie background music.
The one thing that bothers me looking back, was the constant going back and forth to progress the short story. This, in my opinion, took away too much of the suspense as you progress.
As for the story, giving away anything would be too much of a spoiler and fun-ruiner, so just let me tell you: It's creepy and I hated it in the way a horror story should be hated (sounds weird I know): It made me feel very uneasy yet intrigued so that I wanted to get quickly to the conclusion while at the same time, I wanted to explore everything so that I could pick up as much information as possible.
I liked Fingerbones because it is, in a way, the exact opposite to i.e. FNAF, in that it does not use any jumpscares and solely relies on text and music for the horror experience which was nice. Also it being very short (easily doable in half an hour) makes it easy to swallow for non-horror people like me.
Rating 7,5-8/10

Back during the PS2 generation, there was a sireis of games known as True Crime in which tou play as a martial arts cop trying to bring down a crime organization. After some time the license eventually landed with Square and Sleeping Dogs was  born. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover detective back in Hong Kong after living in America. His mission is to infiltrate the sun-on-yee triad and reach the highest levels using his numerous skills.
Gameplay-wise it's a bit of a GTA clone with the action ramped up to 11. While having the standard driving and shooting segments, the addition of a Arkham series like martial arts mechanic adds some freshness to the experience. This adds up to a Jon Woo-like playing evperience. Some of the most fun I had in this game was laying fisticuffs on whomever stood before me.
The definitive edition adds all the DLC including some outfits that alter your martial arts fighting  style.
As far as gripes go, some of the dlc doesn't integrate into the main story easily enough. There's an enter-the dragon like fightin tournament DLC that is activated from the main map, but you'll be near the end of the game before you're able to take it in which decreases the utility of the rewards, and the other story DLCs are handled in their own campaigns meaning your rewards dont cross over. Plus the story seems a bit by-the-numbers but is passable to tie the action together.
All in all I found the game to be a fun experience as it added some high action elements to the sandbox crime simulation genre.

This is my first hunting game. As of writing, I only have about 22 hours of gameplay and owned the game for four days. Here's what I've learned and recommend you doing.
theHunter is a game where it's free to play to an extent. After making an account and verifying the e-mail, you will be given a .243 rifle with a standard scope, and a 12GA shotgun with buckshot, birdshot, and slug shells. For the first three days, you get a free pass to hunt anything you want without a license and you can explore and hunt at every reserve.
After the first three days are up where your membership is free, your account turns into "guest." What's that mean? It means you can only hunt certain animals for free based on a weekly rotation. You can earn in-game currency (known as gm$) to buy anything but certain ammo and deployables like animal urine or bait.
At first, I was upset that this game has a pay wall, but not long before I met the community in different multiplayer maps. I let people know I was new and I asked to learn as long as I didn't interrupt their hunt. Everybody said "Sure, just follow my lead." every time.
For five hours, a good guy had me take turns shooting deer and claiming trophies. I wanted a better experience with this game to hunt with other players, so I dropped $54 into the game for a 3 month membership and a Whitetale Isle Bundle, with a pet scent hound (along with other call items).
The game does "nickel and dime" you, but once you are happy with your equipment, you need not to buy more unless you want to switch your hunts up. The ongoing renewal of your membership makes your ammo refill for free, gives you a hunt-all license, and a pass to every reserve.
I'm happy with the game and the money I've spent.
Also, this game requires patience and hearing. I do not recommend playing the game with distractions around you. You will usually be able to hunt 3 to 4 animals per hour. To newer players, I recommend doing the tutorials first and hunting on Whitetale Isle until you are comfortable with your shots and tracking, and see if you like the game before spending real money. Your patience in hunting will often reward you with great trophy kills. Big 14-point bucks, giant moose, elk, grizzlies, you name it.
June 13th, 2017 UPDATE: Well worth the money I put into the game. It was more entertaining than some of the modern single player triple A titles. The entertainment value has been superb, yet with all things, repetition can get tedious. Time absolutely flies by when you're stalking and hunting in this game.

The graphics are nice just by virtue of the game being in Unreal Engine 4.
