Behind this platformer game, you find a serious content: 2+2, 30:5, 8x6,10-3, etc.. In other words, to finish a level you have to answer 10 questions right. Answer wrong and an enemy will appear. You should know that there is 20 questions lying around, with secret areas, with dangers like pits or sharks or simply to get out of lids (which is representing your file). If you run out of lids or fall into a pit, you're taken back to the beginning of the level, loosing all the progress you've made.
That's why the game can become a little harder if you want the bonus.... For example, answering in order from 0 to 9 will give a bonus point. Or answering the question that's shown at the bottom of the screen by hitting the right truck (else you'll loose a lid) is also a nice add. Gathering all the items (books, ships, ice creams, smileys, etc..) will also improve your score.
Math Rescue adds challenge in that way and it's a nice incentive for children to train their knowledge in maths. Even for an adult, it should do the trick. The best option that the game offers is the customization: choose the difficulty according to the children's age, choose if you want to mix the operations or not (Episode 2 and 3 have all of them, contrary to Episode 1) and choose if you want problems with words for all questions or half of them or none at all. And that option alone is interesting for anyone that would have an hard time in English. The game isn't translated and so, if you're not an English native speaker or your kid isn't, the problems will not be solved easily.
Math Rescue is an old game. It's been developed a long time ago (requiring dosbox is showing you that it has some age). So the graphics are also from that age. They're colorful without so much nuances, the font used is characteristic from that age. The soundtrack is cheerful.
The commands are also easy to use, albeit if you have an azerty keyboard, the game isn't adapted for it. The only time I needed to think in qwerty was to close the game (asking to press Q to quit - however, with azerty, you have to press a).
I can recommend easily this game to anyone wanting a math game for the children. While it's not the one I've played when I was a kid, I would have probably enjoyed this one. By the way, the game comes with the three episodes set in different worlds (in space, in candy land and under the sea), so, it's a nice change of scenery. True, you can find the original files for free around (and manage by yourself installation, dos-box and anything else, like I did when Colonization could be found as an abandonware) - I even found a site where you can play it in your browser. You can choose the version you want after all, it does not change anything for the game in itself: a good gem.
PS: Yeah, I got the key to the 3D Realms Anthology in a bundle, enabling the possibility to play Math Rescue. And I would do it again, because I needed that game to test it because of my work in digital education.

"Transistor" is a combination of exquisite art and engaging turn-based combat. The world this game takes place in, the city of Cloudbank, is stunning to look at. The motif of the environment is an oddly utopian sort of cyberpunk, or that's at least the best way I can describe it. The point is that this game's look and world-building are its strongest assets.
The protagonist, Red, has lost her voice after narrowly evading an assassination attempt. She fights an A.I. hivemind known as the Process, a rapidly spreading scourge that is destroying Cloudbank. However, Red has the power of the Transistor, a sort of giant sword/paddle that talks and is largely the only voice the player hears throughout the game. You have to guide Red through the city to uncover who tried to kill her, the truth behind the Process, and how to stop it.
The combat in the game is above average, but it's not gonna knock your socks off. You enter a designated area and fight enemies in groups. After you've eliminated the last enemy you'll get experience and will be able to continue through the map. The key to combat is using the Turn() function to freeze time and map out you plan of attack. You're limited in how much you can move and attack during Turn() though, so you have to strategize and make sure not to die between usages as you're unable to attack until Turn() recharges.
You can acquire loads of different abilities, known as Functions, in "Transistor" and each function can be used in three different ways depending on how you equip them. This makes for a very flexible and customizable combat experience. There is also a challenge mode are built into the main game where the player can run through different tests involving speed, strategy, and endurance. Successfully completing each test grants additional experience.
I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the music in this game. Simply put, it's absolutely stunning and probably the best game soundtrack I've hear since "Fez." Lots of lilting, sleepy jazz tracks accompany you as you stroll the empty streets of Cloudbank. The music tends to be somber in most places and suits the environment and narrative well.
"Transistor" is a game that sucks you right into its world and make you fall in love with it. The audio and visual presentation is unforgettable. The game also manages a great world-building experience without any exposition, which I love because I personally can't stand exposition. The combat takes some getting used to and the fact that Red only moves at the same slow speed will frustrate some. However the high customizability of the different Functions means you can find your ideal way to fight.

I have more than 2k hours into Smite, been playing since the Beta. I wish I could say this game is amazing, but it isn't... at least not anymore.
Please read these articles, they are quite interesting to read and will explain much of my opinion:
Greed.
Back in beta, they seemed to not care so much about money. The purchasable items were only cosmetic. They still are only cosmetic, but there is a trick. Now, instead of having purchasable skins on the holidays or random sales, they have offered purchasable items for almost anything you can think of. Loading frames, skins, emotes, etc. If you have thought about it, Hi-Rez has too. Every free game needs support, and I won't bash Hi-Rez for wanting money, but they are SO greedy! They make skins that are only purchasable from chests for example- You have to pay money to MAYBE get a skin you want. Most of the time it is a useless item that you get from chests.
Balance.
The game was only balanced back in beta. Nowadays, with 80+ gods, Hi-Rez flat out ignores some gods, and they don't get updated for months or even years. Hi-Rez gives all the love to some gods, while others they simply don't exist. Some items are OP, and most are completely useless. Hi-Rez has failed the community as whole by ignoring major balance issues.
HiRez Themselves.
Hi-Rez treats their employees horribly. Erez, the owner, is said to be very harsh to his staff. He play tests the game with his staff, and if they beat him he will make them nerf those gods just so he can win. It's "do what Erez says and don't disagree with him." I am pretty sure almost all the past staff (from the beta days) have left Hi-Rez because of how they run themselves.
The Community gets Ignored, always. They don't care what the community says, only what will make them more money.
TO SUM IT UP
Hirez doesn't care about the game and only cares about money. They'll ignore Gods for years in terms of balancing leaving many either underpowered or overpowered. They constantly ignore the community and will cut corners on EVERYTHING to get your money. They also treat their staff horribly and the owner is a selfish prick. PLEASE DON'T SPEND YOUR MONEY. They don't deserve it from you.
As a player who has loved this game, and has been there from the start, I hate to be writing such a hateful review. I see smite becoming obsolete in the next year or two. If Hi-Rez listened to the community, they would be much more successful. This game had great potential, but the selfishness of the devs killed that. This is a money pit at it's finest.

I would like to congratulate the creator, David Szymanksi, for his little hidden gem of a game that gave me a bit of a panic attack. Heh.
First of all, the subject is quite taboo, but I am glad that someone had the courage to tackle it. And has done so in a very subtle, but highly disturbing way. I have a longstanding love affair with horror in general, but I have only played a few horror games. I am glad this one is among those few games.
The mechanics are incredibly simple, you just explore the environment and interact with some of the objects. But I believe that it works in the advantage of the game as it leaves room for immersion and tension buildup. And oh boy, does it build it sooooo fast. I played about 23 minutes of those 27 with my heart lodged in my throat. And the last 2 with a panic attack. For me, this is a mark of good horror. No cheap jump scares here. Just a disturbing mental image that kept on building itself over and over.
The soundtrack is fantastic and it makes the story even more compelling.
A few final thoughts and impressions: I dreaded going back in the bunker every single time. I dreaded opening that hatch. And what I heard in the cellar completely tore me apart.
Loved this game.
10/10

I'm basically going to be writing a book so i'll put the really important stuff right here.  As of 10/17/16 this IS an early alpha game, that means if you buy it you are paying to test it, you are not paying for a finished product. It is even more unfinished than a beta and you WILL experience a lot of bugs, server lag, and random crap thats going to make you say wtf.  If you can't handle any of that stuff and don't want to support the developers by purchasing the game then this isn't for you right now.
If you're still here i'll asume that means you know what an alpha is and are at least kind of interested in helping the developers test the game.  The absolute best part about this game currently is the great community of testers it has.  I have played many mmos and this game has one of the best communities I have ever seen.  The people are friendly and helpful with no trolls so far, good thing too because there currently isn't an ignore funciton added yet, and for those who enjoy sci-fi movies/games the people are completely on top of their reference game.  As it is there the game does have a lot of potential, and the combat is a lot of fun, but you do have to get used to the server lag.  The developers are working on this issue now.  Until they have things worked out expect fairly frequent desyncs that are easily fixed by logging out to the character select screen and then back in maybe once or twice per hour.  The starting zone after exiting the brief training section has been experiencing a large amount of serve lag so picking up objects and questing inside of the building can be frustrating.  This zone is pretty small and shouldn't take too long even with the server lag and it becomes much more bearable, but still not perfect once going outside.
As of now there are only weapon and armor skill trees added to the game with a test crafting skill that doesn't really have much use yet.  The only weapons are rifles and pistols added with more weapons coming later (blades, shotgunes, snipers, glaives).  As far as gameplay and leveling go most people including myself have been grinding mobs and exploring as the combat and enviornments are pretty enjoyable.  There are a lot of quests added, but some of the objectives are a bit unclear still so expect to ask for help from the community or do some exploration on some of them as the developers work on improving the questing as well.  The combat is done as a 3rd person shooter, with 1st person possibly planned for the future (no eta on its release).  The animations make the combat feel similar to Mass Effect and Starship Troopers mixed into an mmo.  Although they aren't completely finished, even the low level armors look really nice which is a welcome change from most mmos where all of the armor is just an eyesore until you get to endgame gear.   The gear does need some balancing work done as to be expected from an alpha.  So far I have encountered a decent amount of enemy varieties and environmental biomes.  The developers have stated that they don't plan on doing any more character resets for the foreeable future unless they really need to because they understand that it is an unpleasant experience.  The developers also have a fantastic sense of humor, and put that into every aspect of the game that they can while still keeping a serious tone to it.
There are clearly environmental objects and animations missing or unfinished which are serving as placeholders, but despite this there is still a TON of interesting stuff to explore.  The current character customization is limited to male or female at the moment with no actual customization features, although they are planned for later.  As far as graphics go the game looks good especially from such a small team of developers, however there is some fuzziness that will likely be fixed before release.  The option menues to control things like sound and keybindings hasn't been added yet.  I enjoy listening to the game soundtrack, but if you prefer turning it off that can't be done from in game yet.  The keybindings are pretty standard and easy to use, but if you want to change them the only way I know to do that for now is through the .ini file until the options are added to the game.  Most of the non-player dialogue hasn't been translated to English yet, but all except for one case of written words that I have encountered has been translated.  The Syndicate (guild) system is in development, but they are in a usable state already, there is also a grouping system to play with others, but as stated earlier there is no ignore function or friends list yet.
This is easily one of my favorite games of 2016, and I really do think that this game is going places as long as the developers keep doing what they're doing, and  the steam community doesn't tear it apart by not understanding what an alpha is.  There aren't many sci-fi mmos out there, and this game has the potential to be a really good one when it is finished.  For those who enjoy sci-fi, helping developers test their games, and can endure all the silly, and not so silly bugs, then I would highly recommend this game.  It is in a state where there is already a lot of content, but I can't stress enough that it is only in a state that will be enjoyable to those who don't mind lag and bugs that can sometimes make some players lose some of their progress.  If you are looking for a more finished game and have no desire to support the developers by purchasing the game then; I would recommend waiting until the full version is released.

This game is really fantastic. Everything, the mechanics, the gameplay, even the graphics are great (for what it is). There's no substantial complaints about gameplay or bugs.
The first thing I would love to be added to this game is the ability to join more factions. Currently there is only one faction that has a story line you can play, and from what I understand, the developer is working on making more factions playable.
The second thing is multiplayer. Right now the game is turn-based (landing or going into hyperspace counts as a "day"), but I would absolutely *love* to see a multiplayer mode become available. The dev has already spoken about how he will NOT add multiplayer, but I think it would add a much higher level of replayability to this game if, in addition to the single-player campaign mode, there were a player-driven multiplayer mode as well.
The last thing (and this is a bit of a stretch) I would love to see would be a mobile port of this game. It runs fantastically on any (and I mean *any*) sort of hardware, given its simple graphical nature. A mobile port (to iOS, Android, AND Windows mobile) would infinitely increase this game's success and exposure, and I would adore playing this on my phone.
Oh, and don't forget Steam Workshop support. The dev has also spoken about this explaining the modding on Endless Sky uses a different system than Steam Workshop's but this would also make the game much more fantastic.
Overall this game is a simple space sim that has SO much potential in it, and I'm excited to see where the developer takes it.

Papers, Please is simply one of my favorite games ever. It puts you in the place of a border guard of a fictional east-block-ish country, and the gameplay consists of checking the documents of people coming through. It is engaging as all hell and is a steal at 9 euro.
The most important thing, however, is that this game shows how videogame art is done. It is not about text-blocks or voiceovers of highminded ideas or even interesting character arcs, but instead making you experience and feel something you wouldn't have otherwise, in this case, to give you a sense of what an unnamed bureaucrat in this position must feel like.
The mounting day-to-day pressure as a paranoid political climate lead to ever-tightening paperwork requirements. That feeling of annoyance over people that delay you, because you have to process at least 3 more people to just break even today. The rare moments of sympathy or regret, when you have to turn someone away over a technicality because you CANNOT afford any more mistakes today. But above all else, the stress and OCD-triggering of meticulously going over every detail to look for descrepancies. It is my favorite illustration of the difference between fun and engagement and its success is a milestone in the histroy of game development.

When I think of games that push the envelope of what's possible, I often think of
. Although it has been a few months since I've played this game, I often think about dealing with EZIC, a group of rebels trying to subvert political plays. Do I ignore them as a good citizen under authoritarian rule, or do I play along because they say they have the countries best interests at heart? What about the station guard who tells me that for every citizen I detain, I will get a cut of his bonus? Do I detain perfectly innocent people just because I have to buy medicine for my son at the end of the day?
This is a game full of mysteries, intrigue, and decision making - all built on the foundation of game mechanics that boil down to administrative duties and paper shuffling. The fact that designer Lucas Pope was able to succeed on creating such an engaging - and yes, fun! - game is kind of perplexing. It also shows that the interactive medium still has so many avenues of gameplay and storytelling to explore.

If you LOVED the first title you'll...
...feel torn on this one.
It's not a bad game. Like all sequels it does everything its predecessor did with bells and whistles added. Unlike the previous title, you get an art gallery, unlockable costumes for the Time Goddess, and  a more cohesive plotline with cutscenes and character development.
But that's what's off-putting for some. The first title had miniature 30 second quests selected from a world map where the boss, area, and quest were all self-contained. The bosses were made to be humorous and you'd get a small 4 sentence 'epilogue' to the quest that had a joke or two in it. The plot-line was backdrop: it merely explained why you were traveling the world.
The Second Coming places the plot in center-row and heavily emphasizes it. You get cut-scenes pre and post quest, flashbacks while you travel the world map, and character exposition and development. Bosses are no longer humorous with ridiculous motivations for their actions: they are taken much more seriously. Granted, we aren't dealing with Final Fantasy levels of writing and exposition, but the humor is considerably toned down. You'll either appreciate the expansion or hate it vehemently.
There were some casualties in transitioning to a story-driven game. Whereas you were timed in the previous title and graded on it after a quest, this game merely continues on with the storyline after a quest is finished. They've done away with the quest completion screen, which details your time and objectives completed, so the game places less emphasis on speed-running. Ironically, time is less emphasized in the series than ever before.
The sequel DOES fu*k up in two indisputable ways: the ability to go back to completed quests in a time trial mode and the ability to level up in the over-world map. When you level up outside of a quest, your level carries over to the next quest. Which means the element of grinding is introduced in a series where a 30 second quest's challenges include getting strong enough to defeat a boss. You can realistically grind outside of a quest so that when you enter it you're already set to beat the boss, which is beyond ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in this series. Secondly, while you can go back to completed quests to beat the clock, you keep all of your current equipment and levels, which is doubly insane and defeats the point of the 30 second timer and a time trial challenge.
Granted, you don't NEED to grind, ever. But the fact that it's even an option is just as bad as auto-aim in a PC FPS.
Two ♥♥♥♥-ups aside I'm really split on this game. The previous title had a more arcade-like feel and you could pick up and play it whenever and put it down a minute later. This title has a more continuous feel to it, and in transitioning to a serious RPG some of the humor of the last title is lost. I miss bosses that wanted to blow up the world because others confused their species for a similar looking species. But it's still an enjoyable title that tries something new with the base 'Half-Minute Hero' experience still lying underneath.
If you like defeating op monsters in a super-fast battle,this game is for you.

Transistor is probably the most visually stunning game I've ever played. I like its art style so much, that ever since the game was released (maybe even a little before that) 99% of my wallpapers have been Transistor themed.
Both the graphics and the soundtrack are amazing, but thankfully the gameplay is also fantastic! The mix of real time combat and turn() planning not only make the game feel fresh and serve to set it apart from Bastion, but also give the player the chance to experiment with two very different styles of play.
Personally, I prefer to freeze time, plan carefully and then hit all my enemies with a devastating attack, so I try to use turn() as much as I can. But no matter which style you prefer, I'd recommend to everyone to play Transistor with a gamepad, the controls are super simple and feel very good.
Another great thing about this game is how even though there are relatively few functions (abilities/attacks) available, all of them can be combined with each other to create improved variations of a base ability, or used on a special passive slot to gain completely different effects, which gives the game a lot more depth than you'd think.
The story is beautiful and sad at the same time, and serves as a perfect backdrop for the gameplay. As it's usually the case with any good book, film or game, the only bad part is that feeling of emptiness after you finish it and realize that it's over. Time to play it again, drool over how beautiful everything is and try new combinations of functions!

The 58th year of Shouwa, early summer.
It’s June, and the summer heat has arrived earlier than it does most years.
By day there are crickets, and by night there are cicadas.
We’re in Hinamizawa, a small village in the countryside.
There are fewer than two thousand people here. But every year, there is an event.
This event is a mysterious death.
On a certain day in June, someone dies, and someone else goes missing.
The series of deaths is connected to the upheaval surrounding the dam construction project.
A murder case that was covered up is being reenacted.
Is it a conspiracy? A coincidence? Or perhaps a curse?
Someone who was supposed to be there isn’t.
Someone who wasn’t supposed to be there is.
Someone who was alive last night is dead now.
And someone who is here right now isn’t alive.
So, there is no way to avert tragedy. There is no choice but to give up.
But don’t give up.
Only you can stand up to this.

While I have an unpopular opinion, kind of, I thoroughly enjoyed this chapter of Higurashi and would call it my second favorite thus far presented {only losing to the excellence of theme, topic, and structure of Ch.3}
So why do it like it better than most of the others? Well there are a couple of key reasons; namely if Ch.3 is the most perfected cycle of the similar structure in the previous 3 chapters, then Ch.4 is the most coolest way in conveying Higurashi's mystery right before it starts becoming solved in Ch.5.
With this chapter, you're a undercover cop investigating a kidnapping case that is filled with political tension surrounding a Japanese government official. Just know that this story really helps you get an idea of what the answer to the mystery is and gives great context to what will occur in the future of these tales. Without heading into spoiler territory, it brushes on certain aspects of the village that are impossible to understand from an inside perspective- Namely, the uncanniness of a village like Hinamizawa.
I absolutely love this one, no questions asked, and I think it really gives certain characters deserved spotlight. Finally rounding out the cast into individual favorites.
My only complaint is the price doesn't coinside with the length. 5 dollars for 4 hours is a bit much- in comparison to the other chapters 10+ hours and 7 dollars.

So, I've been playing SMITE for almost 5 years, with FAR more hours (out of Steam) than my profile suggests. So obviously, I love the game. But here's why I recommend it.
First of all, it's free-to-play, and it's FAIR free to play. Meaning you can try it free for as long as you like, with the only limit being limited God (or Champion) selection. But the free gods are GOOD, meaning you're not disadvantaged for using them, and you're not forced to buy new ones. And if a particular god is on your wishlist, it doesn't take too long to earn individual new gods of your choice for free either. Then, if you like the game and want all the gods, now or ever, RIGHT NOW, it's a decent price to get all the gods in one simple purchase. Which is the only thing that makes this "pay to win" - and a one shot charge, for half or third of the price of a AAA game, is perfectly fair. Think of it more as an unlimited free trial with a reasonable full-game purchase, rather than free-to-play, or free-to-pay. Not to say there aren't constant opportunities and incentives to throw ridiculous amounts of more money at the game, but everything else you buy is merely cosmetic - nothing realistically helps you win or gives you any competitive advantage.
So primarily, I recommend the game because it costs nothing to try, and doesn't extort gross amounts of free-to-pay money from you if you do decide to invest. And, of course, it is INSANELY FUN if you like competitive games, especially if you have friends to play with and/or against - and I've actually met and made close friends playing this.
The gameplay itself has lots of modes, meaning there's variety in game play and if there's a mode you don't like, you don't have to play it.
The only real downsides are a) you play with and against other humans, who sometimes act like unevolved monkeys and anonymous internet asshats and b) the game is regularly being patched and upgraded, so it can be a difficult game to play casually, as items and abilities can change without anything overt telling you that in-game.

Higurashi When They Cry Hou-Ch. 4 Himatsubushi is a kinetic visual novel, the fourth one in the Higurashi series and the last one in the Question Arcs series.  Unlike the previous chapters, this time, the main character is a rookie investigator from Tokyo named Mamoro Akatsuka.  This time, the main focus is on Rika Furude.  Although Mion, another character from the previous Higurashi chapters, does make a couple of brief appearances, the other main characters-even Keiichi-do not make any appearances this time.  The only other character we get to see is Ooishi and he's quite important in helping Akatsuka.  Also, the setting takes place in June 1978, 5 years before the Hinamizawa Disaster.  (For those who don't know what it is, you should play Higurashi Ch. 3 before playing this one, as I won't reveal spoilers.)  Akatsuka is sent to investigate the kidnapping of the Minister of Construction's grandson but as the details are confidential, Akatsuka must do so quietly.  He encounters Ooishi during the course of his investigation and enlists his help.  Also, he meets Rika, who, at first, appears to be the typical, innocent girl, but then he notices certain behaviors in her, particularly her talent of foreseeing future events, that puts him on alert but he doesn't think far enough to realize (until it's too late) that he should have...Ok, that's bordering on spoiler territory so I'll stop right there.  ;)
Moving on as to what I thought of this chapter.  It's the shortest one in the Question Arcs series but I enjoyed it.  It was a refreshing change of pace to have a different main character this time and to see how Himamizawa was during the time of the Himamizawa dam protest (as we know that in the previous chapters, Keiichi learns about the protest as a past event since he wasn't present at the time it occurred).  Also, out of the four main female characters, Rika is definitely my favorite so I was happy to see that she got a chapter focused around her this time.  The story was well-written and although there were definitely horror elements (as per usual in the Higurashi chapters), there was also more sadness (although, to be fair, there was sadness at the end of Higurashi ch. 3).  The art, music, etc., were like in the other chapters so there's nothing different to comment on those aspects.
Overall, I would say that if you liked the previous Higurashi chapters, this one is worth picking up as well.  It's a great one to tie up the Question Arcs series.  I'm totally excited for Higurashi When They Cry Hou-Ch. 5 Meakashi, as it'll start off the Answer Arcs series.  I'm glad I finished this chapter before the next chapter is to be released.  ^^

David Szymanski does it again with what's almost a formula, for having walking simulators (there has got to be a better word for that) tell short, compact, horror stories that raise some very interesting questions. From a storytelling perspective, there's not much that can be said about Fingerbones that can be said about The Moon Sliver, where you are playing a mysterious protagonist in an abandoned, low-res, lo-fi setting, trying to answer questions about why it's abandoned, and who you are. This one answers the second pretty easily, but the "why you're there" part is what drives it - or the need to answer some other disturbing parts of the environment. It uses maybe two or three paragraphs of text the entire game, which just goes to show you that dialogue in unison with razor sharp level choices is a way to say thousands of words.
Maybe the very best, and funniest line here reveals the narrator's short-sightedness and blind hypocrisy in the name of an arrogant ideal, but one that's not too far removed from the reasoning of many people, who may not consider the logical extreme of their thoughts. Okay, I don't want to spoil it, but I thought this was a little better than The Moon Sliver, despite being maybe a third or fourth of the length - it was harder to get lost, and I thought its topic about evolution and scientism was more interesting and relevant, and more worth revisiting, if just to reflect on without any "answers." (I'll give The Moon Sliver this: it is longer and more chilling, with an imaginitive fantasy environment.) Even if this game is short, AAA deveoplers would be wise to look at it to launch more costly walking sim parts in the future. Endless Sky is a clone of an old Mac shareware game, Escape Velocity. Escape Velocity was known for its simple but addicting gameplay, in which you start off as a captain of a shuttlecraft and dropped into a massive galaxy to explore and make a living as a trader, a pirate, or join in the war between the Confederacy and the Rebellion. It was an incredibly non-linear experience for its time, and later iterations of the game added more factions and alien races with their own unique ships, weapons, and hidden missions.
Endless Sky plays and controls almost exactly like Escape Velocity, though with some added menu functionality. Your map for instance will track prices of commodities on different planets, so that you can plan effective trade routes without having to consult a FAQ.
I have only put about 75 minutes into the game so far, and thus I have not fully explored the galaxy to see the full variety of factions and races at work, but I am getting that same old feeling from this game. The tone of the writing so far doesn't seem nearly as campy as that of Escape Velocity, and a lot of the planet art looks pretty mundane (the lone programmer isn't an artist, thus necessitating pulling a lot of resources from the public domain), but as this game develops and if it ever gets Steam Workshop support I have a feeling that there will be a great deal of new and improved content on the way. You could either spend another hour trying in vain to tweak Arkham Knight to run worth a♥♥♥♥♥♥ or you could take a chance on this free game. Make the wiser choice.

You can switch classes as you please either by building up a large, controllable fleet or you can keep yourself independent and mobile buy selling your current ship and buying another.  then you are free to explore the galaxy (as long as you pay off debts) as you please and uncover a set of suprisingly deep and well thought out storylines by working with different factions and alien races. Transistor is probably the most visually stunning game I've ever played. I like its art style so much, that ever since the game was released (maybe even a little before that) 99% of my wallpapers have been Transistor themed.
Both the graphics and the soundtrack are amazing, but thankfully the gameplay is also fantastic! The mix of real time combat and turn() planning not only make the game feel fresh and serve to set it apart from Bastion, but also give the player the chance to experiment with two very different styles of play.
Personally, I prefer to freeze time, plan carefully and then hit all my enemies with a devastating attack, so I try to use turn() as much as I can. But no matter which style you prefer, I'd recommend to everyone to play Transistor with a gamepad, the controls are super simple and feel very good.
Another great thing about this game is how even though there are relatively few functions (abilities/attacks) available, all of them can be combined with each other to create improved variations of a base ability, or used on a special passive slot to gain completely different effects, which gives the game a lot more depth than you'd think.
The story is beautiful and sad at the same time, and serves as a perfect backdrop for the gameplay. As it's usually the case with any good book, film or game, the only bad part is that feeling of emptiness after you finish it and realize that it's over. Time to play it again, drool over how beautiful everything is and try new combinations of functions!

Uhh... Sh*t, i'm speechless. How can i put this down? Let's see... Take the character development, the RPG style and the feels of the Final Fantasy golden era, and a ground-breaking game concept such as the 1st Half Minute Hero game. Give them some wine, some private space, you know what i'm talking about. Wait for 30 seconds and you get this game. This game just feels like it knows what it is, and does what it should do amazingly. The first game did it nicely, but... there was something missing. The RPG feel was kinda lacking, the character development was not done to maximum potential, and the gameplay just felt a bit too linear. It was basically a concept with an insane amount of potential. Now, don't take me wrong. i played the game, i liked it. But this game managed to squeeze every ounce of potential off of the concept, and did it in the best way possible. The sheer amounts of content in this game are impressive. Multiplayer, Level Editor, Steam Workshop support, infinite mode, time attack And almost 30 hours of main storyline. The soundtrack is possibly one of the most well composed ones out there, boosting the game feel by a lot. None of the characters in this game are stand-off or flat in any way, but the game doesn't slap your face with their attitudes, and are just dang fun to play with. The storyline's fairly simple to understand, but complex enough to keep you interested into what's going to happen. As i already said, this game knows what it wants to be, and does it in the best way possible. The feeling of the game is silly in an enjoyable way, but this can change to best fit certain parts of the game (such as when Coo dies in the 4th chapter, so sad ;_;). In my opinion, though, the best improvement from the previous game is how they handled the Overworld outside of quests. In the first one, the overworld was almost not there. It was a level select, pretty much. But in this one, you could walk around, raid Dungeons outside of quests, visit villages without the 30 seconds limit, buy gear that you couldn't afford during quests, and just generally have a good time. Then again, this game's 10€ (11, including the DLC containing perhaps the best DLC section ever made, check some of my screenshots out for more information).  AND by paying 10€, you even get the first game! That's even more content for such a low price! In total, the first and the second are gonna be roughly 50-55 hours of Gameplay. So yeah, if you have some spare money on your wallet and still don't have this game, this is definitely the way to go if you like RPGs and fun games.

I don't review many games but I have to say this game is by far one of the most intresting games I have played so far!

This game is a worthy successor to the first game, which you get for free when buying this, so that's a hell of a deal right there. While the first game felt a bit more of a parody of the whole JRPG genre, this one feels more like they're playing it straight, while at the same time keeping their very unique and quirky style. While this game doesn't seem to feature extra modes like Evil Lord 30, Princess 30, or Knight 30, it does expand greatly upon the Hero 30; play an entire JRPG adventure in 30 seconds style, adding things like weapon crafting, global dungeons, a traversable map, collectibles and a pretty sweet castle. This game isn't quite as out there as the first, but it also feels better from a gameplay perspective, now when you go back to get certain titles or equipment, you may do so with your full party and equipment from where you are in the currently, not being restricted to items that you had on your first pass of the level.
These games have always felt more like puzzle games to me rather than JRPGs, you have to figure out how to level up, manage your money, and do it all within a certain time limit. The game gets very intense in later levels, and has an absolutely fantastic soundtrack that makes the best parts of this game shine even brighter. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of JRPGs or anime, or anyone who like speed-running games. There are other modes to speak of, but I haven't played the Multiplayer yet, though the Infinite Hero mode was really fun, you basically just keep leveling up and fighting one Evil Lord after another, trying to set a high score, changing levels every 10 bosses you defeat.
Honestly this game is a really fun game to just pick up and play, its levels take probably 1-5 minutes, with the longer ones being probably at least 10-15 minutes, but there are a lot of levels, and it feels good to binge play or to just do 3-4 levels at a time. The levels consist of you sprinting around a map, fighting enemies, helping people, leveling up, and trying to defeat some sort of enemy in 30 seconds, on the normal setting, time is paused in towns, and you can reset time by paying a certain amount of money to a goddess statue in town, the fee gets greater and greater each time. The story can be a bit bland/jrpg-ish when it's not being funny or having completely badass moments. The characters are likable, even if Yusha is kind of that emo jrpg protag, he's still cool, and he's only really bad if you choose to make him be bad. I highly recommend playing the first game before you play this one, there are lots and lots of references to the first game, and you would probably be missing something if you just jumped right into the second one, which should kind of be obvious, but don't worry, as I said, you get the first game free with the purchase of this one. I'm just gonna stop my disjointed ramblings now and say: It's a good game, full of good humor, fun characters, and a great OST, which also comes bundled with the game.

Definitely one of my favorite RPGs that I have played recently. I saw this ages ago and did not get it. I did play the first one but the first game had plenty of problems in it (Such as quests being nearly identical to each other and not much variety in them). That was a stupid decision. This game fixes all the problems in the first game and makes it a almost perfect game. Here's how.
Story:
There are 4 (5? I'm on Ragnarok at the minute and I don't really know if there is more.) eras to play in this game. They all have different stories. The eras are Overture, Judgement, Revolution and Ragnarock. Judgement is a kind of part 2 to Overture so it does not have a different protagonist unlike the others. I will only explain the Overture story because 1. I don't want to spoil much. 2. I don't want to waste time on a review. So overture follows the story of Yusha. A royal commando sent on a mission to destroy the Evil Lords alongside a group that contains Yashu and Guy. The Evil Lords get their hands on the Spell of Destruction. This spell makes the world end in 30 seconds. Thus the 30 second gimmick. Wow. I thought Overture had a bit more to the story that I could say without spoiling anything. Anyway over to the gameplay.
Gameplay:
This really is the highlight of the game. So basically you are hunting Evil Lords and♥♥♥♥♥♥ They use their Spell of Destruction to make the world end in 30 seconds. This means you only have 30 seconds to teach the Evil Lord a lesson. Each quest (level) starts off with the Godess telling you things that may help you  defeat the Evil Lord. Each Evil Lord has their own quirk. For example. The Light boss blinds the player with light every few seconds and can be defeated using some kind of dark energy. Anyway the actual gameplay. After the godess tells you♥♥♥♥♥♥ you need to scurry around the map and take out monsters to level up and talk to villagers. You're basically trying to level up as fast as you can and take down the evil lord before 30 seconds is up. However you can pray to the Time Godess to reset your time however it costs money to do so. There is more to the gameplay but I gotta type this quick so whoop.
Music:
Oh my god. Oh my actual god. This music. This is SO good. I have been listening to this all week. It really is a pleasure to listen to. It's basically chiptune mixed with normal stuff. It is such a good blend. There is not much I can say about the music apart from its amazing.
Graphics:
It's pixel art. Nuff said. OH WAIT! I almost forgot about the animation parts. Okay so there are small parts of this game that are animated. These are pretty cool i guess. I mean they dont really show it off that much and the animation does not have a lot going on in it so yeah.
Overall Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming is a great game and I highly reccommend the game. It is fun, addicting and...fun. So what are you waiting for? Buy it now! Heck, You get the first Half Minute hero with it.

Pros:
-Easy to learn, even without a tutorial.
-Clean and clear menu and UI.
-Works while you are AFK or OFFLINE.
Cons:
-Everything requires PC (refresh very limited stocked shops, most high tier items in shops, pvp).
-It takes forever to progress without spending any money.
-Feels like it was ported from mobile.
-Free to start, meaning that if you want to get anywhere in this game you will have to shell out more money then every AAA title.
-Costs energy to do jobs, which make you money, to buy things, to do more jobs, which costs energy, that you need to pay with PC to refresh.
All in all, I do recommend playing the game for free. It is a great game, but you need to be careful with spending money on this game. Its a slippery slope considering it uses the pay to progress faster method. If you really enjoy it then go for it, but if you just want to progress faster, theres better choices for games that dont cost you an arm and a leg just to play more then the very limited time the energy system allows you to.

The final chapter in the Question Arc arrives. And the aproach that this chapter is going to take is one very original. Changing the assets from the previous ones and introducing new crucial factors that will help you understand and get a grasp of the answers that everyone is looking for.
Great "bonus" chapter and really interesting.

If you've come this far - there is no turning back. Himatsubushi is a "Bonus" chapter of the Question Arc. Centered upon my personal favorite character, Furude Rika, the reader is taken back to a time before the previous three chapters. Knowledge is gained (or perhaps just confusion) regarding the Three Families of Hinamizawa by a young public official sent from Tokyo to investigate an incident. Ooishi-san is very present as well as he assists (and laughs along) with the green detective.
Absolutely play through this if you enjoyed the previous chapters of Higurashi: When They Cry. Support 07th Expansion. Seriously. We need more chapters!
Yes, my only 'con' here is that it was short. This can be forgiven as it was a 'bonus' and I don't believe the length detracts from the overall added content it provides to the series. Now, let's all make our charms and hang them up in an attempt for an expedient release of the next chapter. Nipah! ^-^

The unfortunately shortest chapter so far, with a different point of view and all the creepy goodness of the series. There is a non-insignificant number of typos in this version, hopefully patched in the future. All-around recommended and necessary next step in the story as the last of the "Question Arcs".

So this is by far the shortest chapter and takes its place BEFORE the Question Arc (ch.1-3).
It solves questions u had after reading ch.1-3 and kinda prepares for the folowing Answer Arc. Which probably correspond to the second season of the anime.
For those who are just starting with this serie, theoretically u could start with this one and turn back to ch. 1 afterwards
This time u experience the story through a police man who just got into Hinamizawa for work. It is the time before Keichi moved to this village, meaning it's the time when there was the so-called ''Hinamizawa Dam-war'' which had important influences on the future (ch.1-3.)
In fact u don't exactly HAVE to read this one bc it isn't exactly a part of the Question Arc, but I would totally recommend it. Otherwise u'll miss very very important aspects of the story and u won't be able to classify when what where happend.
It's more than worth it for everyone who adores higurashi or likes creepy stuff - like always.

By far the best-paced of the first four chapters, since it doesn't take several hours of gameplay for it to, y'know, actually get to the point.  If you're unfamiliar with visual novels or with the series, you may actually want to start here and then go back to Chapter 1.
Everyone else, well, buckle in.  At its heart it's just as batshit insane (in a good way) as the first three, but this is told slightly differently and with a much more realistic tone.  Right up until the major groin-kick at the end, of course.  You might think this is a recommendation or not.  In any case, if you liked the last three, it's more of the same.

Himatsubushi is the shortest of the Higurashi arcs, and yet has some pretty important details in it for figuring out what's really going on. It is also the last of the "Question arcs", so with this and the previous 3 Arcs, you have all the "clues". You also get a taste of things to come since you have an entirely different protagonist and setting for this Arc, which becomes the norm from this point onwards. While this story may be fairly short, it is filled with stuff you should keep in mind as you get into the later arcs as the mystery unravels.
And... that's really all I can say. This is probably my least favorite arc, but I still like it. Besides, it being on Steam serves as a reminder that my favorite storyline, Meakashi-hen, is right around the corner. Can't wait. :D

Working at a job that deals with people's well being can be incredibly taxing. Your decision determines whether their lives continue in bliss or go up in flames. It's hard to stare someone in the face and tell them they are wrong, despite their best efforts. Papers, Please gives you the task of being a border checkpoint agent.
With that comes tasks such as checking passport information and following the rules set out by your company. Should you disregard those rules, you will be penalized and may end up losing your job, family or life. It's a very serious game of give and take with people who are honestly trying their best and others that want to game the system.
Most people will never experience such a scenario in their own lives, but this game truly hits home for those that work in public services. Being a doctor, nurse, clinician, phychologist or any kind of care giver can put an incredible strain on your mind. Maybe you gave the wrong advice, or your administration of medicine was done too early; hell, maybe you just looked at someone wrong.
It's never easy to hear a sob story and then deny someone a basic human right that you take for granted. Denying passports and reading that the person is upset can be stomach turning. You feel desperately bad, even if they should have just followed the rules.
Mixed in with all these moral quandaries is a plot about a corrupt government and a rebel group attempting a coup. You can safely ignore them and still have a satisfying experience, but delving into the complexities of the plot in Papers, Please reveals something interesting; maybe you don't agree with everything.
It's easy to be a dutiful citizen and get nothing in return, accepting that life is♥♥♥♥♥♥and clocking out for the day. It's difficult to stand up to oppression and change the face of the world. Papers, Please gives you an opportunity to see what that change can do and how you can be the catalyst for a revolution.
Or you can simply do your 9 - 5 job and get a decent paycheck and a nice apartment. The choice is yours, but no choice is easy. Thankfully, your save file can be split into branching paths, allowing you to experience every possible scenario.
The graphical style and music bring home the entire package. It feels oppressive and familiar. It looks like an SNES game, but it feels unique. It sounds like the USA lost the Cold War, but it also shows a country in disarray. It's bleak, but beautiful.
The only flaw would be that the game is a bit short. Also, that branching path system doesn't make all of your choices concrete. Having a system by which one mistake ruins your game would be more in line with the self-reflection the game is pushing on you, but I can understand that it would make the game feel incredibly daunting.
Regardless, Papers, Please is worth a play by anyone interested in a more realistic look at humanity. A job that most people never thought of and will probably never see first-hand. It's truly a modern masterpiece and well worth the $10 asking price.

I have a hard time expressing what I feel about this game. I gave it a lot of time to try and enjoy it, but at a certain point I realized I was putting more effort into trying to enjoy it than I was actually enjoying it.
It isn't that it's bad necessarily, it's that it lacks all the charm that made HMH1 such an amazing experience. I don't think the designers even know what made HMH1 so good, because even as someone who played the original for over a hundred hours while aiming for top scores on the leaderboards, I can't even tell you what made it so good. It came out of nowhere, it was an amazing game, and I couldn't get enough of it. It's like a lightning strike. It was so randomly amazing that it can't even be properly dissected. It had that "X-Factor" that so many products claim to have, but is only ever obtained by complete accident.
HMH2 plays like Marvelous AQL was trying to hit all the notes HMH1 delivered, but that's the problem. HMH1 didn't feel forced or practiced. It's like they had the right people at the right time working on the same thing, and something amazing happened. HMH2 feels forced. Everything about it just feels tedious in comparison to HMH1.
It happens in every industry. Led Zeppelin had plenty of songs, but only one "Stairway to Heaven", and how do you top something like that? How did they even make that? I bet they don't even know. And that's what I think HMH1 is. It's the video-game equivalent of "Stairway to Heaven". It's amazing and epic in every regard, the reasons that make it such a legendary experience will never be able to be fully explained, and as a result nothing that follows it will ever live up to the same experience.
It isn't that HMH2 is bad, it only suffered the misfortune of following HMH1. On its own, this game might've been a 7 or 8/10 derivative JRPG, but as a follow-up, it made me feel physically depressed to play. I know that sounds extreme, but I was so in love with HMH1, to see this happen... it's like Hangover 1 to Hangover 2, or Mass Effect 1 to Mass Effect 2. Sequels to something mind blowing rarely ever work. The game developers accidentally created something amazing with the first release, and they're going to continue to rehash it as many times as they can because life is long and they want to keep themselves employed, but this franchise will never be as good as it was when it first started.
If you didn't like HMH1, you might like HMH2 because it plays more like every other JRPG on the market than the odd whatever-the-hell-that-was that HMH1 was, but if you loved HMH1 as much as I did, this game is probably going to be a brutal reminder of why good things can't last. They rarely occur, and they're always so amazing that they can't be recreated or relived. Just have to hold out for that next moment when it feels like lightning strikes, and enjoy the hell out of it for knowing how fleeting that feeling is.
I have yet to beat this game, but go back every now and then just because I do eventually want to finish it.  I never get more than a mission or two done at a time though - it definitely feels like a slog.

Not as funny or challenging as the first game.
The parody aspect is excellent when it's present, but sometimes the game forgets it's supposed to be a parody and tries to be serious and emotional, resulting in many awkward cliche moments that just aren't funny or interesting. It's worth sitting through those for those brilliant silly Half-Minute Hero moments though, and there are more than enough of them to justify sitting through the boring overall story.
This has a lot more features than the original game, which I've got mixed feelings about.
Classes don't do much, but they're a nice idea. Battle formations are awesome. Searching for medals on the overworld? Eh, why not. I'm indifferent about skills and Hero Castle stuff, though I think a lot of people would probably like those. I don't know.
Since you can now grind on the overworld for permanent level ups, and are allowed to keep the gear you've obtained in later quests even when redoing quests, there's never any point in strategizing as to which gear and path will let you earn the best time, as you can just come back later in the game with max levels and the best equipment, and redo the quest with no challenge. Maybe I'm being too harsh as there's a separate Time Attack mode that plays more like the original, but I just don't see the appeal of redoing story quests in a different mode.
This game is much more friendly to newcomers and casual players than the original was, and so it is the best place to pick up the series, though veterans of the original may be disappointed that it's nowhere near as challenging.
Still a great game though, and I had a ton of fun with it despite all the things I've nitpicked about it. I definitely recommend both Half-Minute Hero titles to anyone who's a fan of retro console JRPGs, and since you get the first game for free with this one, my complaints are pretty much null!
TLDR; Very funny and good, rant about it being easier than the first game, and new features being meh, still worth your time, buy it!

This is clearly a work of passion. The amount of time, thought, and work the dev must have put into this is just fantastic. Though I'm sure it started as a hobby project, it's clearly grown into something more. I never write reviews, but this is a game that truly deserves it.
It's a much more realistic trading/space sim than most others, and this is a good thing, as it gets rid of several annoying problems that often plague such games. For one, exploration isn't a blind dive into potentially troublesome situations since local maps can be cheaply bought to reveal the surrounding area. In addition, you can track prices on other planets without manually visiting them, thereby allowing you to plot trade routes quite easily. The story and lore is done through text. You can read as much or as little as you'd like, but the dialogue is natural and very well-done. The tutorial mission is fantastic, optional, and teaches you the basic controls. The synopsis for each planet gives each character and really does make each feel unique. Banter between ships is rather repetitive, but you're going to get that no matter how many unique lines are written.
The game aims to be flexible, and it does that extremely well. The risk/reward of piracy vs. trading is quite balanced. Losing a ship to pirates early during a risky job can feel devastating (as it should), but it's usually only a temporary setback. Conversely, taking a risk and trying to capture that ship that outguns you can be both a disaster or an enormous bolster to your ranks. The number of times I've said, "Oh man, almost!" have been too numerous to count, but most importantly, they've been accompanied by a feeling of excitement rather than frustration.
The dev has crafted the game in a way that pretty much anyone can add content or create plug-ins. I'm sure the content of the game will expand by leaps and bounds in the coming weeks. There are occasional bugs, but you can merely check the dev's github to realize he's still working on them. The fact that this is open-source will mean that these are crushed more quickly than usual as other users can fix them as well. Over 600 commits to git since March 2015 show how frequently the game is tweaked, bugs fixed, and content added. Perhaps the biggest drawback to the game currently is that the sounds are rather basic and there's no music. However, I'd expect both of those issues to be addressed soon enough. I can only hope the dev continues to develop more games, as this is the sort of endeavor that shows the true brilliance that indie games can yield.
Lastly, to address most of the negative reviews: if you can't figure out how to play this game, you are legitimately brain-dead, likely incapable of tying your own shoes. Sure, the game doesn't hold your hand, but the commands are pretty basic and the intro tutorial teaches you everything you need to know. "pirates op they kill so fast" - Well, no♥♥♥♥♥♥ flying into a known pirate haven with a starter ship probably isn't going to go well. Use your brain. So yes, if you're a potato with insufficient energy to power a lightbulb, you probably won't like this game. And I don't think that's a bad thing.

Working at a job that deals with people's well being can be incredibly taxing. Your decision determines whether their lives continue in bliss or go up in flames. It's hard to stare someone in the face and tell them they are wrong, despite their best efforts. Papers, Please gives you the task of being a border checkpoint agent.
With that comes tasks such as checking passport information and following the rules set out by your company. Should you disregard those rules, you will be penalized and may end up losing your job, family or life. It's a very serious game of give and take with people who are honestly trying their best and others that want to game the system.
Most people will never experience such a scenario in their own lives, but this game truly hits home for those that work in public services. Being a doctor, nurse, clinician, phychologist or any kind of care giver can put an incredible strain on your mind. Maybe you gave the wrong advice, or your administration of medicine was done too early; hell, maybe you just looked at someone wrong.
It's never easy to hear a sob story and then deny someone a basic human right that you take for granted. Denying passports and reading that the person is upset can be stomach turning. You feel desperately bad, even if they should have just followed the rules.
Mixed in with all these moral quandaries is a plot about a corrupt government and a rebel group attempting a coup. You can safely ignore them and still have a satisfying experience, but delving into the complexities of the plot in Papers, Please reveals something interesting; maybe you don't agree with everything.
It's easy to be a dutiful citizen and get nothing in return, accepting that life is♥♥♥♥♥♥and clocking out for the day. It's difficult to stand up to oppression and change the face of the world. Papers, Please gives you an opportunity to see what that change can do and how you can be the catalyst for a revolution.
Or you can simply do your 9 - 5 job and get a decent paycheck and a nice apartment. The choice is yours, but no choice is easy. Thankfully, your save file can be split into branching paths, allowing you to experience every possible scenario.
The graphical style and music bring home the entire package. It feels oppressive and familiar. It looks like an SNES game, but it feels unique. It sounds like the USA lost the Cold War, but it also shows a country in disarray. It's bleak, but beautiful.
The only flaw would be that the game is a bit short. Also, that branching path system doesn't make all of your choices concrete. Having a system by which one mistake ruins your game would be more in line with the self-reflection the game is pushing on you, but I can understand that it would make the game feel incredibly daunting.
Regardless, Papers, Please is worth a play by anyone interested in a more realistic look at humanity. A job that most people never thought of and will probably never see first-hand. It's truly a modern masterpiece and well worth the $10 asking price.

First of all, Factorio runs smooth as silk. It's incredibly well optimized and receives consistently excellent updates from an incredibly competent dev team. I haven't seen any other devs who put so much effort into optimizing and tweaking the game so it runs better, faster, and more stable. They rewrote the entire multiplayer system when they saw that their original design was unworkable once you got past a few players. Now you can easily have a hundred players or more without too many issues!
The modding support is insanely good, it's rare to see a game support so many different things with modding. There are more things that I'd like to see, but overall it's an excellent system with a lot of flexibility.
And of course, the game itself is excellent. It's one of those games that'll have you working on one part of your factory for hours on end trying to perfect it. Then you realize that your production lines are in top shape, but now your raw material isn't keeping up... Everything grows and grows. At some point you realize that your current factory has a fatal flaw, and you need to start over with what you've learned. It's insanely addictive and always has your attention. There's a reason some call it "Cracktorio".
For things that still need to improve, there isn't really a proper ending. Personally I'm not too bothered by it, since I know I want to go for launching as many rockets as I can as fast as I can, but a lot of people aren't satisfied with that.
There are also a few slightly clunky things in the base game. For example, the Chemical Plant has a crafting speed of 1.25, making calculating ratios kind of a pain, and it doesn't line up with the Oil Refinery which is at 1. It does line up with the Assembling Machine 3, but the only thing that you use for that is Processing Units, which use so little Sulfuric Acid and take so long to make that the ratio is irrelevant.
But the biggest thing for me, at the moment, is the combat. It's far too easy, especially once you know how to quickly build up without over-polluting the area. Because of that, the biters are just an annoying nuisance rather than dangerous. The combat is also far too fast-paced, a single large worm can nearly instantly kill you if you're not wearing several shields. Harder enemies simply get more health and damage, leading to a situation where the only good weapon is the flamethrower and you simply have to carry around at least 3 shields at all times. I'd rather have more variety in what we can use, more varied enemies and bases, different ways that I'm attacked and that I can use to defend.
That being said, at the moment they are planning to address the combat in the next update (0.15), so hopefully these complaints will be reduced or eliminated.
Of course overall I would very strongly recommend Factorio. If you enjoy crafting and building complex machinery, you'll enjoy it. If you enjoyed SpaceChem, you may like this. If you played a lot of modded Minecraft, such as Feed the Beast, and enjoyed the tech mods, it's almost guaranteed that you'll like this.
And it even has a demo! Try it out!

I saw this game was free and didn't expect much of anything from it, after all it's only a small game, totally free to use (no adverts, malware or anything bad that i've found), and 2D. But the reviews were mostly positive so i gave it a go. And i'm glad i did, really didn't expect anything so simple to be so addictive and well made!
Controls are a little tricky, but you can change that easily and besides, you're flying a spaceship - i kinda think things like that shouldn't be easy. But once you've got you're head around what you're doing (flying from solar system to solar system, trying to make some money and not get shot out of the sky), you want to go further and further and explore more and more. Be warned though, you'll be killed in no time if you pick a fight with the wrong ship in the wrong system. Take time and build your ship up to something decent before picking a fight, or seeing as the code is openly changeable, just change the ship you have in your saved game! Suprisingly doing this still doesn't take the fun out of flying around and exploring, and picking fights with fleets of ships in pirate sytems.
But even if you play the game properly, there's plenty to do and a multitude of ships to choose with a large variety of things to add-on to your ship. My one and probably only problem with the game is that there's not enough space on most ships to add anything much in the way of extras. This isn't always a bad thing as spaceships could easily become over powered, but as i mentioned, it's easy to change your ship manually with a text editor and an over powered ship is still great fun and very capable of being killed.
Picking fights is far from all there is to do though, you can make small amounts of money trading goods, but it's far easier to make a few quids by completing jobs on the missions board. They vary from transporting tourists or goods, rushing deliveries, to escorting ships or even hunting them down.
For those that are inclined it's very easy to add your own artwork to the game, add your own ships, or expand on the game in your own ways; there's really no limit to what a creative mind could do with it. I've got just over 20 hours on the game so far and haven't found any bugs yet. How many paid games can say that?
Best thing about the game for me though is how quick it is to switch on. Most games i play these days seem to take about 10 mins, but i can play this one if i've got just 5 mins here or there, it even saves automatically on switch off. It's just that i'd rather just fly to that next system and blast one more pirate before i do.
It's like Sid Meier's Pirates but grander in scale but more modest in terms of production. Great game.
Incredibly addicting. I feel guilty getting this much enjoyment for free. It should cost a few bucks at least.

Fun & simple fps if you can find a server with anyone on it. I have a limited amount of time with the game so take it with a grain of salt, but I could really see this as being fun with friends.
It has three modes: 1-TDM, 2-Horde, 3-Titan
1-TDM is what you'd expect from fps.
2-Horde is also what you'd expect from a fps. It's playable without other people, but I don't think the horde mode will interest you for more than an hour while solo.
3-Titan is about protecting your teams giant robot while it takes out the other teams power core. The two teams titans will fight it out to get to the next stage, bashing down a path, and then smashing the power core. Fairly simple.
The combat mechanics are simple shoot or smash the enemy and run/jump.You have a primary and backup weapon.  Each weapon has two modes: shoot and special ability. Not all weapons can aim down sights, that's a special ability. You also have a tertiary equipment slot for grenades or turrets. There's an interesting mechanic of leveling your weapons through kills, as long as you can stay alive, upon death your weapons reset. There's a metagame of collecting resources during play to build match-permanent armor, and building weapon blueprints between matches. If you're thinking about trying it out do it. I've seen it on sale semi-regularly. Make sure you pick up the 5-pack for you and your friends.

Final Fantasy XIV is a good game. Visually it looks amazing and the gameplay is really fun.
However there are a couple things that take it away from being at the top spots for MMO's i've played. Firstly the world size, although there are plenty of zones to explore they are all instanced. This means to go between each zone requires a loading screen which doesn't seem that bad but there also 2 areas in each major city meaning you have to load every time between them. Also unlike other MMO's the zones feel rather restricting. By that I mean that there's a set area you can walk in and there's a lot of predetermined areas you can't walk over where its just an invisible wall all the way around the object instead of letting you freely explore over it. This is minor really but it makes the world feel smaller.
Secondly questing. Before you can move on in the game at all you must complete the Main Story Quests with over 180 between level 1 and 50. Once at 50 you have to play through exactly 100 more quests before you can even enter or use anything heavenward related. The quests still continue after that currently going post 60. This quest system isn't bad but after getting to 50 you have to spend way to much time going through pointless quests unless your interested in the storyline.
Now that aside it is a really fun game. It has a fun class system which allows you to have 1 of every class on one character allowing you to switch between them when your not busy. Each of them requiring its own leveling. This system means that your not tied to one class and allows ou to play what's needed at the time. The boss fights are really fun with the Sync system meaning even people higher level than the boss will be synced with gear and level to help you so you get a more rea experience as to what it was like to do it when it was first released. I feel a little background info on gaming history is always helpful when choosing games so a brief intro.  The majority of my time spent PC gaming over my life has been dominated by Counter-Strike.  I could, and in my younger years did, play that game for 12+ hours a day when possible.  Minimum has many of the same qualities for longevity of interest that Counter-Strike does but in an entirely different package.
This is one of the most fun multiplayer games I have played, ever.  It's up there with UT99/UT3, Quake 2/3 and it's offshoots, Painkiller, HL2:DM, and while it has many CoD-like qualities it absolutely bests any of the non-WW2 games.  I know I'm having fun when time seems like it's flying; that only happens for me when playing the aforementioned games, running in the forest or cooking in a restaurant kitchen.
The netcode seems good but I have yet to play with above 80 ping so I can't comment on how it does above that threshold.  The game runs very well and looks good on systems ranging from new-5 years old.  A decent netcode and scalability are things that make or break these games so check that off as approved.  You don't need to change 6 or more settings with console commands to fix the game, it works fine out of the box.  Also, unlike CSGO, the bots in multiplayer are just adept enough to kill an above average player every once in a while and gives lower skilled players a decent challenge while waiting for a server to fill up.  Which, thanks to the matchmaking system, happens pretty quickly.
All of the maps are enjoyable to play and have resources scattered in heavily traveled areas to encourage engagement on a regular basis.  There have been a few games where the server was full and the majority of the players in the server were camping the far reaches of the map, action was hard to come by then.  For the most part games are near constant engagement followed by either a death or a short recovery/relocation so it's hard to get bored of playing.
There is a medley of guns and armor to choose from, all with their own intricacies to suit different playstyles.  If you like to run around and just wreck faces you will probably like a combination of Mini Launcher/Beam Rifle/Bullet Hell/Speedy Shotgun/Dash Shotgun with the Ninja chest and leg armor with a Berseker helmet.  All of the sniper rifles are useful in their own way, some are much better after getting powerups.
As a sniper you're not always in the best spot to pick up the resources before a teammate or enemy gets them so I would suggest avoiding the Rail Sniper unless you plan on being very mobile with it because all you will likely do with it is rack up assists, the Dash Shotgun or Beam Rifle is a good second weapon with it.  All of the other snipers are good for short-term long-distance engagement once you learn how to use each of them to their potential.  You still need to be more mobile than you would be in most modern FPS (CoD) games with a scoped weapon to keep gathering resources to at least give yourself a full armor stack before mid-point in a match.
The katanas are fun to play with but unless I'm in a server of low-skilled players/half of them are bots I don't rack up near as many kills or have a good K/D ratio had I decided to just use guns.  That said, I haven't messed around with them enough to give a competent recommendation on them.
Maximized guns are a HUGE thing in this game.  10% more damage is no joke, do the math.  You can roll the dice on your 20% chance in crafting or you can just buy them on the marketplace.  A couple bucks will get you every Maximized gun you'll likely want to use and is well worth the price of admission.  I have $60 in CSGO skins/keys and they didn't make me any better at CSGO so this was a no-brainer once I saw them on the Market.
I'm not the biggest fan of some of the in-game menu elements.  I often double click on the images only to realize I didn't actually craft the armor.  The symbols for accessing the gun loadout/crafting/store buttons confused me for the first few weeks I played the game, maybe I'm alone here.
This game is awesome and would only get better with a larger playerbase and more content.  I implore the gaming community to jump on this train.  At $35 for 5 copies you've made 5 people, up to 10 if you count significant others(!!!), happy they didn't spend $60 on a game that has a once-through storyline and about 30-40 hours of multiplayer before you move on to the next half-baked shooter.  Real joy in life comes from accomplishing personal goals and making others happy.  Knock out 2 birds with 1 stone, buy the 5 pack and gift the other 4 to your buds.

An excellent game for those seeking a more thoughtful experience.  There's a thread of story glue linking the puzzles together but ultimately the main focus is on the puzzle boxes themselves -- nested one within the other and with a certain physicality to them, especially in the earlier boxes.
This would be amazing to play in VR (if it supported such a thing, or if I had a VR setup, but sadly neither is the case at present).
Some of the later puzzles sacrifice some of the realism, with more liberal use of your "invisible ink" eyepiece and parts of the boxes emerging from hammerspace or doing other physically impossible things (often also involving the eyepiece), but ultimately I don't think this detracts from the experience at all -- rather it adds to the atmosphere.
Pixel hunts aren't entirely eliminated; most puzzles rely on you finding keys or other artifacts or clues hidden on or within the puzzle box itself; but nothing ever felt unfairly hidden, there were always clues for the observant.  Nothing really requires out-of-game knowledge, although there are certain themes that you would probably appreciate more with that knowledge.  (These are both good things, in my view.)
Sadly it's fairly short, although it's also priced to match; one sequel is already out, and it sounds like more will be following, so there should be enough to scratch that puzzle-solving itch.
