The battles are automatic and fast, in contrast to the slow paced and repetitive traditional JRPG. And yet it is compelling since you have to watch your health and take care of having the right level when you go against each enemy (leveling is very fast during the matches, though).
The matches involve small puzzles (some of them optional) where you have to visit certain points in the right order during 30 seconds bursts of time. You can reset the 30 seconds timer every time you visit a goddess statue but each time you need to spend more money on it, thus you have to use your time wisely and try to find out what's the best way to do it. The matches are sometimes quite tense, you can only relax between matches or when you visit a town.
The custom maps, multiplayer and other goodies (various sets that will warrant you extra hours if you are a completionist) give it some replayability, also way more than your average RPG.

Having 100%'d this game after 40+ hours and found myself wanting more, it's safe to say I thoroughly enjoyed this game.
Whereas the first game's RPG mode was only one of several different modes with unique gameplay, Half-Minute Hero: The Second Coming scraps those secondary modes and focuses solely on the high-speed RPG. You spend most of the game doing quests that usually give you a 30 second time limit to complete them. It's hard to impossible to actually complete any quest in that amount of time however, so there are almost always Goddess Statues to reset the timer for a small amount of gold. Each of the 80 or so quests pretty much boils down to going to a town to find out how to solve the gimmick blocking access to the boss, solving the gimmick, then going to beat the boss... resetting the timer whenever necessary. Thankfully, a surprisingly engaging hilarious story and the occasional quest that mixes things up keeps the formula from becoming too grating.
The biggest difference between this game and the first is the world map. Instead of simply picking a quest, you actually explore with your team in true RPG fashion. You can even level up, collect gold to spend on items you may have missed during quests, and go into some dungeons free of a time limit. Best of all, your level will carry over to the quests you play, lessening the amount of grinding necessary to complete each one. Another great thing is that you can use any gear in any quest after you obtain it. The first game locked gear away making it all feel kind of pointless, but in this one, if you want to take your ultimate gear to the first quest and wreck the boss in one hit, feel free!
There's really not much more to say. This baby is well worth the asking price, especially since it comes with the first game AND the entire soundtrack (which has some damn great tunes in it).

Not a terrible game by any means, just uninspired and not very engaging one.
The extremely low resolution (which isn't even adopted consistently, as some elements of the interface are pixellated differently than the main area while the lighting effects are high-res, leading to some stylistic dissonances) was a very poor choice for this particular game. Since the whole point-and-click mechanism depends on the player's ability to locate particular objects within the environment, rendering these objects as indistinguishable blocky blobs can only lead to tedious and annoying experience. The narrative ambitions of the storyline are also severely curtailed by the limited graphics: all of the "creepy" or "dramatic" moments come off as quaint at best. Pixelation of this magnitude causes a powerful alienation effect which seems out of place in a game attempting to tell a captivating story.
Speaking of story, I'm sorry to say that it consists mostly of tired clichés seemingly pulled together from bad 1980s Call of Cthulhu scenarios. The few interesting and original ideas are left underdeveloped; the characters (including the PC) are paper-thin. Since there is very little to look at, one would expect the writing to be the main driving force behind the narrative; unfortunately, it is merely adequate, with some irritating anachronistic word choices and lines of dialogue reminiscent of school plays.
Gameplay-wise, The Last Door offers no innovation at all and does little to alleviate problems present in the adventure genre since its inception. There is way too much walking around at an unhurried pace and trying random combinations of objects in hope to guess the developers' intentions. None of the puzzles felt particularly clever and some depended on the kind of nonsensical (or at best extremely non-intuitive) object interactions that point-and-click games are notorious for.
While playing through all the four episodes was a mildly entertaining distraction, at times the game made me feel bored and miserable and there wasn't a single aspect of it which in my eyes would make it stand above the average. I'm afraid I can't recommend it with any enthusiasm.
I should also note that the game crashed twice upon entering new locations; fortunately, the auto-save feature worked as expected and no progress was lost.

And the conversation of her being upset plays out the exact same every time, with the same options you can choose from, the same options that all won't change anything at all.
Maybe it's fun for one playthrough, to just see how the story plays out, but there's no replay value, the "branching narrative" is a lie. If you do decide to replay, you'll only get disappointed.

Mother Russia Bleeds is a 2D beat 'em up game where you take on the role of one of four underground fighters. Each are insignificantly different and say the same dialogue so it comes down to your preference as to who to choose. There are two modes to play, arena where you fight until you drop and Story. There is nothing to drastically different to this title that you wouldn't be able to hold your own if your familiar with the genre but you'll want to start with Story nonetheless. You'll start off in a grim looking camp and are taught the basics of combat as you fight some hobos for money.
Things quickly go bad for you as the fight is raided and you are detained & used as a lab rat for a new experimental drug the Soviets are making. This drug will be the main theme of the title and your greatest ally. With it you'll be able to heal or enter in enraged, drug fueled mode where you can devastate your enemies and pull off Mortal Kombat like fatalities. To refill your needle, you simply jam it into any wounded enemy twitching on the floor and you can inject yourself with that, no problems. As you can likely tell by this point, Mother Russia Bleeds is full of extreme violence and tons of drugs.
Like any good beat 'em up there are weapons laying around at times to turn the tides on your enemies or be on the receiving end if you let your guard down and focus on the other unarmed foes. We have our usual weapons such as batons, tasers and even chainsaws but unexpectedly guns do play a rather big roll on later levels. Guns are extremely dangerous in this title; one shot is usually enough to do you in so disarming them takes priority in most situations. Some enemies do not drop their rifles upon death but occasionally someone will drop a pistol, shotgun or Ak47 that gives you the ability to effortlessly mow down tons of enemies. There is no way to tell how much ammo is left so it's be wise not to get too confident and let yourself get surrounded.
With how gory and violent this game is, it lends the combat an impactful feel to it. You and enemies will start to look horribly wounded as you take damage, their deaths & innards look pretty detailed considering the retro look of it and corpses do not simply disappear, leaving you to witness the aftermath of the battle. As you get further into the game and the drug you repeatedly use starts to take its toll on you it becomes more and more twisted. While you may start off in a shanty town pretty soon you'll be fighting fat gimps in the middle of a party with your new found “dog”. It helps to keep things interesting and unpredictable throughout even though most of your time will be punching someone’s face in.
Alongside punching you'll have a button to kick, one to jump and another to dash. There is no blocking so the dash will be all you get in the form of defense. One minor feature that I love and many others of this genre lack is the ability to move when you charge your attack. There is nothing more awkward than to wind up your punch and have to take it out on thin air in order to be able to move again. Positioning is important as well, it can be easy to be a bit far into the background and miss your 2D opponent completely. If you are feeling particularly brave you can catch weapons thrown at you out of the air, considering you have good timing and don't take a used needle to the eye trying to show off.
Unless you have friends nearby you will sadly be unable to show off to anybody due to Mother Russia Bleeds only having local coop. It is a blast with others and there is an option to turn off friendly fire for when you just want to quite literally stab your friend in the back. This can be replicated to an extent if you have no one to play with due to being able to add bots though they are not that great at staying alive. It's a nice addition nonetheless. To spice things up the game may throw you a few curve balls like needing to protect an NPC, dodging sniper fire or leading a group of rebels against the military with mixed results but are rare enough to not be annoying.
What I do find tedious is the method in which you unlock new drugs. Having to survive to round 10 on an arena may be a good way to get people continually try the Arena mode but gets old fast. It takes quite a long time to get that far into the waves and by the time that you unlock a few you'll be so worn out on the combat that you no longer care to try them. There are some interesting effects such as jamming an enemy with a needle to turn him into an ally so it's a shame they are tedious to get. Each stage does have unique enemies so isn't all bad and the ever growing stack of corpses as you fight on is awesome to witness.
There is little story to be found and what is there isn't particularly interesting though serviceable. With none of the 4 characters having unique dialogue there is no reason to read it twice, luckily you can skip all the talking scenes by just pressing Start. At the end of the game you'll have one final encounter and depending on how you handle it will get one of two endings. The sprite-work and gritty atmosphere are simply fantastic. From fighting a bunch of junkies in an empty pool to fighting zombie pigs in the sewer they are all a sight to behold. Music is pretty good as well and blends nicely with the mayhem of the combat. That's what it really comes down to, do you love mayhem and are you fine with punching a dogs face in? If so, even with its few quirks, Mother Russia Bleeds is one of the best beat 'em ups to be released in quite some time.

I started playing Papers Please for the third time and I am still impressed about how well it is put together.  The graphics are only on par with NES but they take advantage of the lack of polish to make a very bleak and oppressve world.
On one hand the game feels like working a day job (complete with an unhappy boss if you screw something up), but I like this becuase it forces you to pay more attention to what you are doing.  You have to read and understand everything going on in the world or you might slip up, and the more mistakes you have against you the less money you make.
That's another thing - you really get the feeling that you are struggling to make ends meet, and you feel it at the end of every day.  It motivates you to want to do better so you can keep food on the table and heat your home.  I'm sure it sounds like a cliche to everyone who had working parents, but the game really drives home how important it is and how difficult it can be to live day to day.
The story is very compelling too.  The interesting events are notable but at the same time understated compared to most games.  Everything just feels like another day even though every one of your actions have definite consequences.
Excellent game, I'm sure I will be playing this for years to come.

The reason for giving PG a negative vote is based on nearly 15 hours of play. Coming into PG with a mindset that it is currently labeled that as 'Alpha' stage of development, my current feelings are more based on the overall design and approach of the development team and not the early and very rough stage of development. Before the details I will say the initial idea of the game has appeal and could be good if exercuted as promised.
The overall idea behind PG seems good on the surface but as you progress it becomes clear that PG drifts from the impression given by the developers and turns it into just another indie effort by an in-experienced group of people to use a game engine and make yet another game that does not stand out out in any way.
It looks like the player models and the components of the initial starter zone are purchased quality assets and the other zones are leagues apart in quality which seems to indicate they were slapped together with limited experience in such design or the use of the Unreal engine. Having explored what must be around 80% of what is available I was left with that impression.
Clearly unrealistic terrain design, numerous invisible walls where there should be none. Unable to even walk over a little rock. Falling through the surface many times and getting stuck in the terrain. Considering this is only a small part of the promised zones in the final game I find it hard to believe that they can expand into many quality zones based on current work. I suspect PG will be in long-term development to ever reach the promised game.
The sample of quests available are too cryptic and only because of their design. Many have no logic, little useful information and it felt more like playing a badly made pixel-hunting adventure game and getting frustrated. Just from chat it was clear many struggled with the questing.
The same can be said about the partially implemented character building system because what was implemented was confusing to the new player.
There are other issues such as server/network performance but that is understandable considering it's stage of development.
Wikipedia: 'Alpha is the stage when key gameplay functionality is implemented, and assets are partially finished. A game in alpha is feature complete, that is, game is playable and contains all the major features. PG, as it is, does not fit that definition and therefore came to EA too soon.
Therefore, I cannot recommend it currently.

An absolutely amazing game, there are tons of good things to say about Transistor, as well as a few bad.
Good:
1. It has an incredible art style, both for the animated cutscenes and for the in-game battles.
2. Fantastic soundtrack, bringing the main character's story into the atmosphere.
3. Smooth battle system, allowing time to stop as you build up your next action.
4. Intriging storyline in a near-dystopian society
5. All of the computer references. If it's technology, it's probably in here.
Bad:
1. It's relatively short. A lot shorter than I had hoped.
2. As you near the end, the battles get almost obnoxious to sit through, especially the final boss, which has 4 lives.
But is it a bad game? Far from it. While it may not be my favorite, Transistor definitely caught my attention in all the good ways, and for that, i'd completely recommend it to anyone interested.

Transistor might just be one of my favourite games these past 10 years. I can't remember the last time a game kept me playing for 10-12 hours straight. As soon as the game started, the shivers ran down my spine. The narrator, the soundtrack, the graphics and all the questions surrounding what's going on in Cloudbank and soon the battle system - everything is just perfectly executed.
The way you get answers to questions in the game is also quite interesting. You can't just rush through the game and think you'll understand what's going on in Cloudbank, you need to spend time to read about characters and the city itself on boards spread around town. It's an interesting way to indulge the player in the life of the city.
You might say that I'm not one to talk about a game, "20 hours isn't that much", but that's how long it took me to play through the game twice and get all achievements. It's not a long game in comparison to other new titles but if Transistor was stretched out to give more hours, I feel like it would lose what makes it so amazing.
Transistor is an experience that I recommend everyone to have, it'll make you feel all kinda amazing feelings.

I'm a huge fan of EV. This does several things better than EV, and there are things that EV does much better.
ES's strengths:
I really like the finance system in ES much more than just simple credits. I personally wish that the loan system was more complex than it is currently, but I know that this wouldn't be as accessible for everybody. I was very delighted to see how the finances worked.
I also really like how the trade system works. Every planet has a "Trade Center," which isn't available in EV. This allows a TON of flexibility when it comes to trade routes. This functionality works great in conjunction with the features of the Map.
The Map has MUCH more features than EV's. For one, in addition to the great trade options listed above, the map will display prices for each commodity in each system, and compare it with the prices of your current system! This is an AMAZING feature!!!! It also color-codes each system in regards to the actual prices of each commodity. This will let you supercharge trade routes with only a few clicks. It also lets you search for planets and systems that sell specific outfits and ships. Want a Laser Turret? Find a system that's guaranteed to sell Laser Turrets easily!
And, it's free.
EV's Strengths:
Most noticibly, EV's presentation and gameplay are smoother, especially when talking about EV Nova. The art and assets really stand out. Details within the ships' and planets' design give the world a ton of personality that you can really feel. The quick, tight controls of the fighters and the sluggish, aching turn of the heavy freighters are felt as much as seen. Each world has much more personality and diversity than ES's worlds. The planets aren't just described through the text, but their consistency is maintained through the art on the planet and the profile of the world from space. It's all consistent, and that makes you feel like you're actually traveling the stars. It's something Ambrosia is really good at creating. EV also has several government types, each with their own quirks. The political territories feel completely different from one another. Being in Federal space is obvious, and being in Rebel space is obvious. In any EV game, you can immediately tell which faction's space you're in instantaniously.
EV is definitely a more hands-on game, which I perfer. ES is basically an autopilot flier. You can take manual control if you'd like - such as for combat purposes - but you don't need to. EV's controls require you to stay engaged with the world, and therein makes you immersed in the story. If I'm doing cargo runs in ES, I can set up my route, hit "J" and walk away for a full minute while I wait for the series of jumps to complete. That wait time breaks the immersion of the game. And speaking of story, EV Nova actually has stories; several stories are strung throughout the galaxy - each one unique. You can travel through these stories to pick up a ton of great gear, ships, modifications, etc. to become really powerful! As ar as I can tell, ES doesn't have any of those.
The weapons in ES don't feel like their as varied as EV. I couldn't tell the difference between a blaster shot and a modified blaster shot if I saw them both in combat.
Finally, ES's galaxy is extremely small. I explored every corner of the galaxy in about 3 hours.
Now all the above being said, this is a really good tribute, and definitely worth your time. I'm really impressed with how it was all put together. This gets my thumbs-up, and I plan on recommending this to my friends.

Season 1 is great on its own, but Season 2 is the real reason you should play it. There's not much to be said about the story without getting into spoilers, but the first part of Season 1 reminds me of some of the classic haunted house horror games. The gameplay overall reminds of some of the best parts of the oldschool Sierra adventure games. Strongly recommend, especially if you like cosmic horror, Lovecraft, and stories that require some thought.

The Last Door is a retro adventure game that tells a very interesting lovecraftian story.
The story is really mysterious and intriguing, and it is the main reason to keep you hooked to the game. The second best aspect of the game is the sound and music. It made me feel tension and fear at important points of the game, where it gets intense or creepy thanks to the sound effects and the soundtrack.
The puzzle side of the game is pretty simple. Most of the puzzles are the "pick objects around --> maybe combine --> use elsewhere", aside from a few that doesnt follow this mechanic. They are not brilliant, but anyway they are good and are logic (no impossible and crazy combinations). They dont slow down the game so they are ok.
If you dont mind the retro-pixel graphics of the game (that are lovely in some scenarios) and you like Lovecraft or surreal horror this is definitely your game. If you enjoy an interesting story with some bits of puzzling, you will sure like it.

The game pretends that choices matter, but in reality they don't. Just try it. Reset a few times, try other options, see if anything changes. It doesn't. When I chose not to go to the party, Emily ended up with Trevor instead of Brad. Guess what? They're the exact same person. She said the exact same things about him that she did about Brad.
When she wanted to meet me in the weekend, I said okay. She got upset because it seemed like I was abusing her vulnerability to try to hook up with her. I said that it had to be just as friends. She got upset because this time she had romantic feelings for me that I didn't return instead of the other way around. I said no. She got upset because I wasn't there for her. And the conversation of her being upset plays out the exact same every time, with the same options you can choose from, the same options that all won't change anything at all.
Maybe it's fun for one playthrough, to just see how the story plays out, but there's no replay value, the "branching narrative" is a lie. If you do decide to replay, you'll only get disappointed.
It could have been a great game, but your choices should have changed more. There should have been more different endings. There should have been different conversations you can have, instead of different versions of the same conversation. Then it could be interesting.

This is one of the few games in my library that is labelled by Steam as a "perfect game," meaning I've played it to 100% completion. I've played through the regular version a few times as well, so I think at the end of the day I can give this game a decently fair review.
Sleeping Dogs is one of the best "GTA-inspired-but-not-really-GTA" games I've ever played. It lacks a certain degree of polish compared to some of the other GTA-like games out there with it's stiff-feeling gunplay, repetitive animations, less than stellar voice acting from the game's minor characters, and other niggling little details. Despite these things, Sleeping Dogs shines with it's unique focus on hand to hand combat over gunplay unlike other GTA-like games, it's believable and immersive atmosphere, and it's engrossing story that actually makes you care about the characters and the things that happen to them. It is
that a game really immerses me in an effective way, and Sleeping Dogs' lack of polish certainly prevent immersion for a lot of people, but I loved it from start to finish. You play as detective Wei Shen, an undercover Hong Kong police officer tasked with infiltrating the Sun On Yee triad crime ring and dismantling it from the inside. Without spoiling anything, things start to get deep and Wei finds himself trapped between staying loyal to the badge and staying loyal to the criminal code of honor at the same time. The solid story is backed up with satisfying martial arts combat and Sleeping Dogs ultimately rises above all of it's shortcomings.
+Well-written plot with good pacing and believable main characters
+Satisfyingly brutal combat; similar to the Batman Arkham series, but with more depth to it
+Incredibly realistic and believable atmosphere makes the game's world truly look and feel like Hong Kong
+Good soundtrack compliments punchy, impactful sound design
+Did I mention you're a ♥♥♥♥in rad kung fu badass?
+Game somehow remains tasteful in it's extreme violence
+Satisfying twists and climax
-Voice acting for minor characters ranges from "meh" to "pure unadulterated side-splitting engrish"
-Driving mechanics feel oddly slow and weird
-Gunplay is very stiff and generic, and feels almost tacked on at some times
-Game is guilty of several frustrating QTE sections
-Graphics are a little lackluster compared to other titles from the same year
-Lack of overall polish is very distracting at some times
-Some glitches are bad enough to cause mission failures
-Wei Shen cannot sing jesus christ
-A man who never eats pork bun is never a whole man
The positives outweigh the negatives. Trust me. Where other games have polish and flashiness, Sleeping Dogs has soul and character. It's rough around the edges but well worth it. If you're a fan of beat em ups, third person shooters, and good storylines, then Sleeping Dogs is an essential addition to your library. We can only hope to see a sequel someday.

Minimum is fun, lighthearted yet competitive, and inexpensive! The weapons are balanced despite the claims about OP swords; all you really have to do when someone charges you with a sword is back up, jump continously, and shoot. Obviously they'll kill you in seconds if you let them close in on you, otherwise it'd be a pretty useless weapon. With that aside, the 3 game modes are varied; Horde, being the least fun in my opinion, is your basic how-many-waves-of-creeps-can-you-survive mode; Team Deathmatch is just that with the first team to 50 kills winning; Titan, being my favorite mode, is engaging, fun, and strategic for a game with such simple mechanics.
What attracts me most in this game is the reward system: in-game, you have 6 loadouts with two primary weapons available with each, and with every kill you get with either weapon, the weapon upgrades in damage and effect up to 5 levels. However, you lose the level ups upon death. This keeps the game interesting by implementing a tide-like match, swaying back and forth if you aren't careful to stay alive with your upgrades. You collect Fragments and Shards from people, creatures, turrets, and structures that you destroy, which you use to craft and upgrade the armor that stays with you throughout each match; there are many different armor types for you to unlock, encouraging all types of gameplay from Samurai and Ninja armor, meant for hit-and-run playstyle, to Tactical and Olympian armor, meant for a tankier, frontline playstyle, to Disaster armor, for explosives and heavy weapon use if I remember correctly, to several others. Additionally, Minimum is very visually pleasing with all of its vivid colors, especially the increasingly molten glow of your enemies as you damage them. Out of match rewards stem from blueprints and schematics, a system that allows you to unlock all the goodies you want: new weapons, gadgets, and armor for your in-game loadout.
The only downside I see is in the relatively scant amount of people who play this game (though when a match isn't full/somebody leaves, semi-challenging bots with pretty funny names will take empty spots), which is why I recommend you buy this with some friends you'd like to play with in mind.
All in all, this is a very fun game to play and it's inexpensive enough that you could convince your friends to buy it and play with you, which makes for a much better experience. My only hope is that this game will pick up speed so that more updates, maps, weapons, and mechanics can come its way!

I'm an old school gamer; I had an original Nintendo, I had a SNES, I had a Genesis.  As a kid, I used to love beat 'em ups: Double Dragon, Final Fight, Streets of Rage, all the random Capcom ones, etc.  Unfortunately, the genre kind of fell off - for good reason, there's not really a lot you can do with "Walk right, punch people, find boss, punch boss."  Mother Russia Bleeds doesn't entirely escape from the formula, but it does add some significantly interesting twists in the form of guns, grotesque set pieces, and some antics that might be questionable in any other game.  In addition, the fights are brutal, with enemies often having multiple stages of looking "beat down" before they finally drop.  Long story short, this is old school beat 'em up fun that is a little short, but feels incredibly fresh and worth playing through - if only they made an actual old school arcade game of it!  Recommended for fans of the genre.

I started playing Papers Please for the third time and I am still impressed about how well it is put together.  The graphics are only on par with NES but they take advantage of the lack of polish to make a very bleak and oppressve world.
On one hand the game feels like working a day job (complete with an unhappy boss if you screw something up), but I like this becuase it forces you to pay more attention to what you are doing.  You have to read and understand everything going on in the world or you might slip up, and the more mistakes you have against you the less money you make.
That's another thing - you really get the feeling that you are struggling to make ends meet, and you feel it at the end of every day.  It motivates you to want to do better so you can keep food on the table and heat your home.  I'm sure it sounds like a cliche to everyone who had working parents, but the game really drives home how important it is and how difficult it can be to live day to day.
The story is very compelling too.  The interesting events are notable but at the same time understated compared to most games.  Everything just feels like another day even though every one of your actions have definite consequences.
Excellent game, I'm sure I will be playing this for years to come.

What a disappointing sequel !
Half-Minute Hero was a very clever game. At first glance, it seemed to be just a parody : it mocked grindy RPG with cliche story. But once you delved into it you found a very original gameplay system, with lots of cool ideas. The maps were full of secrets and branching paths, and the combat system had some clever mechanics for people that wanted a challenge or wanted to find all secrets.
The Second Coming, by trying to add more stuff is now...a grindy RPG with cliche story. The super cliche plots are force fed to you through endless and pointless dialogs. The "metagame" added is a grindy RPG (not sped up) with linear plot, repetitive gameplay, forced backtracking to unlock all items, etc. Exactly the kind of games the first game was mocking.
The new combat features (Skills, formations, party, classes, etc...) are also completely broken. All attempts to use theses features will be constantly thwarted by the game, which reset your formations, party, equipment everytime a story event requires a single change (which is...almost always). "Luckily" you actually you do not have to use theses features most of the time, as brute forcing is often the way to go.
Unfortunately, brute forcing can be applied to everything in the Second Coming. Most of the cleverness of the combat is gone : there are tons of items, but they don't have special attributes anymore like you could find in the first game. So you just get whatever give you the biggest stats bonus and rush. No need to be clever anymore, just go through the motions, endure the repetitive combats and you will win all missions. Even the secret titles, which used to be a challenge in the first game, are now rather straightforward and super easy to get.
On the bright side, for people who are looking for a challenge, there is a very challenging "endless" mode, but i doubt you will come back to it once you've finished it, since the maps are always the same.
Multiplayer has also been upgraded, but since there are very few players, I've been unable to try it, which will be the case for you too if you don't have friends who own the game.
On the whole, I don't see enough good stuff in this game to alievate the bad, and I can only advise you to stick to the first game. I completed the game, but it wasnt because i enjoyed it, it was only for completion sake and to be sure i wasn't missing something....

An absolutely amazing game, there are tons of good things to say about Transistor, as well as a few bad.
Good:
1. It has an incredible art style, both for the animated cutscenes and for the in-game battles.
2. Fantastic soundtrack, bringing the main character's story into the atmosphere.
3. Smooth battle system, allowing time to stop as you build up your next action.
4. Intriging storyline in a near-dystopian society
5. All of the computer references. If it's technology, it's probably in here.
Bad:
1. It's relatively short. A lot shorter than I had hoped.
2. As you near the end, the battles get almost obnoxious to sit through, especially the final boss, which has 4 lives.
But is it a bad game? Far from it. While it may not be my favorite, Transistor definitely caught my attention in all the good ways, and for that, i'd completely recommend it to anyone interested.

I'll admit, I'm a sucker for crime dramas. I love GTA Vice City, San Andreas, and The Darkness. But as far as story goes, Sleeping Dogs tops them all. It helps that the game itself is fun to play, with melee combat reminiscent of Arkham Asylum-meets-Bruce Lee. I'd be hesitant to call this game a GTA clone, it stands on its own with ease.

PROS: Fun and entertaining with lots of interesting little elements, excellent storyline and side-missions that are more interesting and varied compared to GTA 4 or 5.
CONS: Unfortunately, it is let down by clunky controls, poor camera angles and at times frustrating gameplay caused by slight issues that show a game lacking only that final polish.
Initially, I was quite frustrated by the game; more so than I was enjoying the storyline, excellent side missions and captivating, engrossing environment. But the more I played, the more I enjoyed. I have flip-flopped on the rating so much but finally landed on positive because of the aforementioned pros.
Overall: 8/10 - recommended for 5-10$

Overview in short: A mystery/horror adventure that relies less on shock and scare tactics but on smart storytelling.
The Last Door is an adventure game, that is made in the style of classic point and click adventures, the graphic is retro style, very pixelated - yet you can clearly recognize the stuff you need to see. The story of the game is very well written and reminds a bit on old horror-stories. The author and devs have tried to use the atmosphere of the setting to it's fullest, and this is even more underlined by a magnificient Soundtrack that accompanies this game.
You can solve this game in one go, but you are bound to miss out a lot of stuff, either notes or secrets that are hidden somewhere. So you might have to repeat some of the game, only to find the hidden stuff. As I already said in the short, the game relies on heavy storytelling, there are dozens of books, diaries and notes to be found - they all give hints and help to solve the game, and unfolding the story.
The game is fun to play, although if you know the story, the replayability is bound to the time, you play it again, after some years or months a revitalisation of the game might come in handy. But playing it directly after the first time again is a bit too much. There is only a limited replayability, as with many adventure games, but that doesn't do the game any harm.
The game itself is short, you can well beat the game in less time that I played it, around six to seven hours would be the normal time frame, but you would leave a lot of things unrecognized.

The Room, a port of an iOS title released in 2012 that has no relation to the cult film of the same name, is a puzzle game that sets the player through five stages with the goal of opening a box on each stage. With the aid of a lens that allows for the discovery of secrets, the player solves three-dimentional puzzles in an attempt to discover the truth behind the mysterious box.
The Room is a game that presents it puzzle solving with atmosphere, simulating the sound, visual, and mental state of various escape rooms requiring actual people to escape a room with hints and clues. There is alot of critical thinking that requires observation and memory in order to solve each puzzle. If by any chance a player is stuck or lost, the hint system will gradually point the player towards the next step without giving away the solution.
It is worth noting that the game is only going to be played through once or on occasion, as the game will be compleated in roughly two hours with no replay value after the end.  It is also worth noting that as a result of being an iOS port, the game and actions are designed for touch controls, making the mouse support feel at times stiff. The stiff controls at times is not critical, but only requires the player to adapt.
The Room is a great puzzle game that is worth playing if you are curious about what the puzzle genre or escape rooms feel as an experiance. If you see it on sale, it is worth checking out and playing through for a day.

Outstanding game. Perfect for novices and expert alike.
Visual Novel format where the choices determine your future. It has elements of RPG style games such as Knights of the Republic where you have a 3d view of your attackers have attack / defend type missions that while easy at first, do become quite challenging. From there it takes elements of 2D/3D  type fighting games such as Street Fighter/ Injustice albeit with a very easy control method of only hi/low attack or hi/low block.  Different combinations such as up/up/down/down/up provide power moves such as "Thunder Fist" which deal more damage. After a series of successful attacks you build to a power move where you become stronger and more difficult to block for a short period of time.  While it is simplistic, it is effective and fun.
The artwork and Soundtrack, are first rate and fit the mood of the game.  The 3D animation is simplistic cell shading, but it gives you  a Japanese Manga, detailed understanding of the mood and type of enemy you are facing, While simplistic, it has allowed the adaptation of a very detailed motion capture system  of highly difficult kung-fu moves to be authentically incorporated into the game; Overall a very new novel approach.  Highly Recommend.

Fingerbones is the first horror game by David Szymanski, the creative mind that brought us such gems as The Moon Sliver and The Music Machine. Originally published in 2013, the game wound up on Steam around a year later. This title is a short exploratory horror mixed with narration in the way of journal pages scattered about. It's up to you to unravel the dark story within, by solving a simple series of puzzles.
I would be lying if I said that Fingerbones didn't keep me looking over my in-game shoulder, amidst the eerie crying of a child and dense fog. I was almost certain that I would see some demon-spawn in kid form awaiting me around the next corner, or behind a door. Needless to say, the thick and immersive atmosphere, however simplistic it may be, really sucks you in during the short timeframe of this narrative story. From the stand-alone mechanical howling of the generator in a well lit top level, to the forlorn cries of a child and creepy silence of the basement, every moment is suspenseful in some way.
The game uses Minecraft-like textures, in that everything is heavily and purposefully pixelated. Usually this distracts from any horror element that a game may have, turning them into child friendly PG-13 types. Thankfully, that is not the case here; however brief it may be, the chilling story is enough to send a shiver down the spine of any adult. The game only lasts 15-30 minutes at best, and there are only a handful of journal pages scattered about; it would've been nice if there was more story to this narrative-centric experience.
For a short and free horror title, Fingerbones is one of the best that you'll come across. Prepare to white-knuckle your mouse for the next half hour of entertainment, while anxiously waiting for what may be around the next bend. Take your time, don't rush, and read the pages carefully to fully understand what unimaginable horrors that this poor excuse of a father put his child through. Then, if you enjoyed yourself, go ahead and take a look at the other games from this fantastic developer.

So I bought this game on sale, and it looked really good, but I couldnt play it because my computor was a♥♥♥♥♥♥ but now, on my new computor, It works fine. This game is really fun, Like, REALLY FUN. I'd say that it's a lot more fun than even Space marine was for me, and as an avid fan of warhammer 40k, That means something.
There are a few balance issues though. For starters, jumping backwards is the same speed as running forwards, so you know, Melee is really easy to counter. Speaking of that, Almost everything you come across is a counter for melee.
Shotguns, Miniguns, Sniper rifles, Launchers, EVEN SOME GRENADES WHIPE THE FLOOR WITH YOU. Now, I'm not saying melee is impossible, quite the opposite, It's really fun. Personally i'm a fan of the Heal katana, but i dont see it often. It's just kind of annoying when you get someone with a freeze gun so that you cant move, a fire grenade so you cant heal, and a shotgun to sit right infront of you, but just out of range. Speaking of that, I cant figure out which one, But one of the shotguns seems really freaking broken. In three games, this same guy was wielding it, and it ended up deciding the fate of all three games. I mean what the ♥♥♥♥? It has a set spread and high damage and fire rate. Who thought that was a good idea? It doesnt even have a slow reload speed or anything. Once it starts rolling, it doesnt stop, unless you snipe him down, which you cant do because there's freaking terrain literally everywhere.
Other than that, the gameplay really is quite fun. The main gamemode is titan mode, where, when the game starts, you have enough for one peice of armor, and both teams have a titan. Both titans are invulnerable untill they start to fight.
Pretty much at this point you have two choices, Help destroy theirs, or use excessive force to stop them from destroying yours. After either dies, the other goes on to try break two walls, There are turrets that assist you at this point, but the enemies can destroy those. After either has destroyed both walls, they have to break the enemies power core with four hits. When both die, a new phase begins called the creep round, in which you go around killing some creeps for recources for armor and to power up your titan. There are also golden ones, which are really fast and hard to kill with melee (Rip), Which, as you can guess, gives better recourses and boosts your titan even more. As you kill enemies, your currently equipped weapon levels up up to 5 times. When you die, it resets. I'm not sure how the reset is calculated, but i often end up with level 2-3 out of spawning, which is wierd. So armor has three levels and doesnt reset. Armor has really nice bonuses, For instance, i use a centurian armor set, which gives bonuses to yourself and nearby teammates, like movementspeed damage and healing bonuses. it also raises your health by a bunch. All in all, I reccomend this game. it's really fun, but not without it's kinks. I'd say about a 7.5/10.

First the good:
The game oozes style. Very dark story and environment. The art is great. Gameplay is fast-paced and fun.
Others have complained about the game's difficulty. If you are experienced at beat em ups and/or fighting games like Street Fighter, you will probably not find this game very difficult.
Now the bad:
There are four characters, but there may as well be one. They all have the same story and essentially the same moves. Devs could have made this a deeper game by giving characters different combos/juggles, different stories/personalities, etc. The dialogue is lengthy, poorly written and seems like an afterthought.
Overall the game is worth the price I paid for it ($8), and is good for at least one play-through. However, it could have been an awesome game if the fighting system was deeper, more attention was paid to the dialogue, and characters varied meaningfully in terms of gameplay and story. The game feels incomplete and could have used some more time in development.

A surprisingly good beat 'em up. Beat 'em up's are a fading genre at this point (sadly), mostly occupied by games that don't really have much weight to the fighting mechanics (Code of Princess comes to mind). When I saw a sprite based beat 'em up  set in a grim dark dystopia version of Russia, I was intrigued. Mother Russia Bleeds is a violence tour de force set against the backdrop of sci-fi-ish forced drug usage and social revolution. You play as one of a series of Roma pit fighters beating the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everyone in their way during a quest of unadulterated revenge. You fight huge amounts of enemies at one time and must balance kicking their asses with not getting overwhelmed. Each stage leads up to a boss who you usually have to fight with more creative means, such as blinding them with flashbangs so they stumble into oncoming trains or forcing their weapon to get stuck on some nearby peons so they can't counterattack.
As a beat 'em up goes, MRB is on the difficult side. The amount of enemies is at times staggering and you can't knock out anyone in a mere three hits, short of using an adrenal burst- but using that also saps your ability to heal. There's no roasted turkeys sitting in a garbage can this time around- you have to balance your fighting with harvesting a select few enemies who carry the Nekro drug in their veins, which takes precious time. Similarly, healing yourself leaves you vulnerable. You can play with an AI on your side and he's pretty good usually, although he can be a complete liability in some boss fights due to not being able to react as dynamically.
Excellent action and challenge aside, the game has an issue with hit detection I'm finding. Lining up with enemies can be oddly hit or miss with the attacks, while ranged weapons seem to attack like area effects. This also applies to healing your ally... the healing button is the same as the harvesting one, and the detection of trying to get the one you want, particularly during a chaotic fight seems inconsistent. Further, I feel you also need a controller for this game. It's a bit too frantic and at time a bit unresponsive for a keyboard.
Some fights are also a bit too cheesy. In the clutter of around fifteen enemies, you have to spot who is carrying what weapon, because if someone has a gun, you can get chain hit around 3 times, resulting in death before you could do anything. It's already difficult to figure out where your own character is in these crowded fights! You can repeat them from checkpoints, but when you can be slain over and over because you were knocked down and never allowed to get back up, the sense of skill and tactics fades pretty fast, as well as the fun. Fighting multiple enemies and environmental auto attacks which pulverize you on the ground might be realistic, but it's pretty frustrating to have to keep restarting for that reason. It's also possible to be attacked off screen, especially by gun wielders you can't hit or know are there... expect the AI to be extremely useless in these fights.
There are some bugs I'm noticing. Sometimes enemies become invincible and wander off the screen, preventing any further progress on your part since you can't go backwards. I've also seen Natasha lose her ability to make attacks at random. No idea why- haven't seen it on the other characters. You have to spaz out on the controls to make her punch again.
Graphically, the game has some very distinctive sprites. The demonstrations of horror and gore come off well and some of the enemies really have that mutant look shine via sprites. Items can get lost in the fallen bodies, however. There should be a flash or something for those. It can be very hard to tell garbage from weapons sometimes, let alone your own character from enemies.
All in all, I do very much like this game, some lack-of-polish flaws and questionable gameplay design choices aside. I hope the developers continue to make more, cause Russia's gotta bleed and vomiting from adrenal drug hallucinations has never been so strangely atmospheric.

Sleeping Dogs satisfies the need for a fast paced, action packed crime thriller with a gripping story line. Competing with the ever popular Grand Theft Auto franchise, Square Enix has delivered a masterpiece of dramatic, story-telling adventure. And the story is where Sleeping Dogs surpasses the competition.
SD strikes a neat balance between action and cutscenes -- which are beautifully directed. I never found myself waiting for the scene to end, perhaps due to their brevity, but definitely because they're fun to watch! The plot is gripping, the characters are authentic, and their journeys are moving.
There are a couple of parts where the plot progression seems rushed, but character development still feels genuine. About half-way through the game, I started to feel like Jackie was my best friend too! And did I mention how great the animation in the cutscenes looks?
At least as important as the story telling is the gameplay. Like other games in it's genre, it has a tendency to throw control mechanics at you that are overly simple, yet obnoxiously difficult to execute. Combat and driving controls come with a steep learning curve, but are manageable... but only just. Despite the difficulty, fist fighting a bunch of thugs, or shooting it out while slow mo flying over obstacles is a blast! This all does get easier as you level up with the build ssytem learning new kung fu techniques and street criminal tactics, Add in parkour and some fun mini games to break up the monotony and it's a really fun experience. This game isn't as bad as others in terms of doing several missions that feel exactly the same. You'll still end up chasing down a lot of people, but it's... better some how.
There are some kinks to work out, like running the game in compatability mode was the only way to keep it from looping on the loading screen between missions. The skinny: like every other game in this genre, Sleeping Dogs is plagued with some issues, but for me, it pulls ahead of the pack and is a great game. If you like GTA-type games, you're going to love Sleeping Dogs.

The Last Door starts off really strong. The first chapter has the player exploring a creepy, dark house. The best scene in the game is in this first chapter when the player puts a record into a phonograph. It was bizarre, distressing, and excellent horror. Unfortunately, the rest of the chapters in the game are standard locations that don't do anything interesting. The story itself is very Lovecraftian in its nature revolving around a group of people trying to cross over into another dimension of existence. I found the details of the plot to be somewhat confusing and ultimately uninteresting. It was difficult to keep track of who all the characters were in the game, their motivations, and what their role was. The story is laid out from very early in the game and the details are filled in gradually over the course both seasons of The Last Door. The graphics were really low quality. This is a really low budget, crowd-funded game, so the poor graphics can be forgiven. Pixel art can look really good, and thankfully the sequel does some fantastic work with pixel art. In this game, expect very poor resolution and ugly animations. This game is on the easier side of point-and-click adventures. I didn't need to look up any solutions. It took around 6 hours to finish. The Last Door starts off strong, but unfortunately runs out steam before the end of the game and I do not recommend it.

Transistor, developed by Supergiant Games & Released on  May 20, 2014. According to Metacritic
, it's ranked:
#30 Best PC Game of 2014
#49 Most Discussed PC Game of 2014
#97 Most Shared PC Game of 2014
It's not often that you get to hear about indie game's making it into the spotlight or having set a particular standard@benchmark for it's genre/for a particular gaming market. Transistor is one of the many indie games which deserves recognition. A testiment to it's genre of what indie games are capable of. and more to come.
I've never completed Bastion but the game is still fresh in my memory because of it's unique gaming experience. The narrator. The story. With the same formula, now comes Transistor. It is a RPG, set in the distant future where you play as a female character known as Red. You're wielding a mysterious swordlike object which happens to be the narrator for your entire journey. You will uncover the truth/secrets on what's happening around you and to the town.
The controls are easy to master. The visuals are okay to me. What stands out the most is it's art syle. I am not sure how to describe it, plain, odd and yet pretty. From monster design to each character/ability profile.
Lore
The game offers lore on the abilities you pick up from certain characters. In order to unlock the character's background information, you will be forced to use these abilities differently; active skill, secondary skill or as a passive skill - and this will change your style of play.
Other than that, you will also have to choose limiters. Limiters are another set of passive skills which comes with a trade off. You get additional exp for a handicap in battle throughout the game. For example; You gain 4% more exp but The enemies will strike with twice as much power. User will overload more Functions at once and recover only one per Access Point for an additional 4% exp. This will certainly make the game even more challenging. The good news is that, you are able to disable the limiters.
The Mechanics
At a glance, it looks like diablo/neverwinter nights type of gameplay. You have a hero with 4 active skill. That's on the surface, the fast action side on the battle. Transistor introduces turn - a mode where you will are able to enter and plan out your moves within the given bar? This is a unique mode which requires strategic planning; to maximize the moves with the allocated bar. or just for plain escape.
In transistor, once you lose all 4 active skill, you die@lose that particular level of the game. You have to replay that part of level. If you survived a battle with remaining 2 active skill, you're stuck with them until you come across the next panel. There is no such thing as health potion therefore making each battle more RTS like. You can't go blazing around like in diablo. Most of the time, you will be required to use turn to plan and execute your moves.
Enemy AI
Each enemy was designed differently and they are smart. A mixture of different enemy types is enough to kill you -without proper planning. It can feel punisable at certain point of the game but that's just because we are not equiping the right skill for that combat. If it's too hard, just swtich off the limiters and plan your attacks using turn. Bringing in big guns@skills with takes up a lot of points, doesn't guarantee your success rate.
The Story
Transistor uses the narrator to motivate you to go through the game. On theory, this should work however I find that the pacing is off due to it's design. That was what put me off from Bastion. After a battle, you suddenly find a hidden backdoor, after a battle you suddely let red rest/take shower. The pacing was off for me but I pushed on because I wanted to know Red's relationship with the man in the transistor. When the answer was obvious, I wanted to know how this would end. What happens to the Town and it's people?
My Summary:
Transistor is a creative product. Despite having a linear story and with little replay value, the combat system is fun where it allows users to mix & match their skills and work things out. The journey was worthit.
I went through numeruous battles & deaths, took the puzzles and had a major annoying boss fight. What I got was a poweful, worthwhile & bittersweet ending. So far, only 2 games have left me with such strong impression & none of them are from AAA game titles. On the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Transistor is a 8/10.

Really?  This is the great Transistor that I've heard so much about?
Tranisitor certainly hits many of boxes for the hipster indie gamer you never knew you had in you, such as its thoughful sci-fi noir setting, dazzlingly well-done 2D graphics and, just like Bastion, a great musical score which ties in well with its narrative themes. But the game that it is all wrapped around?  Meh, what a boring game it is.  Run down this corridor into this square and fight something.  Rinse and repeat (might as well be playing Final Fantasy 13 -ooooooooooooooooooooooooh I went there!).  Yes it tries to pull the same narration effect that Bastion did, but even that couldn't temp me to spend more time running down corridors and fighting in so so combat.
Ah, yes, the much talked about comabt system in transitor.  Fighting  is really quite innovative, with a sort of hybrid system of realtime and turn-based RPG mechanics.  Its cool for half an hour, but its gets old really quickly as the same winning tactic (dodge-smash-smash-dodge into cover) works for every fight, and it doesn't present much of a challange. This low level of challange yet having damage-sponge enemies and the fact that every boss seems to come back to life at least twice before it finally dies doesn't entice me to play further.  All in all Transitor is probably the most overrated game i've played in many years.
This was a big shock, esp with Bastion being one of my favourite 2d games ever, but Transistor seems to me like a classic case of style over substance.

Shuyan Saga is a kind of motion comic with choices and fight scenes. My first reaction after seeing it was to be reminded a bit of Avatar, as not long ago I went on a marathon of
and I have to admit that the start of the game gave me some of those vibes.
The art for the comic book/story part is pretty great while the 3D characters and stages are less detailed while still managing to be charming in their own way.
The fighting mechanics are rather simple, requiring the player to click with the mouse on the upper or lower part of the enemy figure to do high and low attacks which can also be chained to make combo attacks. Progressing in the game unlocks some upgrades, like evasion moves or special attacks which help fights remain entertaining as the enemies start to be a bit more aggressive, having more hit points and doing stronger attacks.
I've only completed the first book and started the second, so my comment about the story is from an incomplete point of view, yet I'm finding it quite intriguing. Nothing revolutionary or too original, still everything feels written well, managing to make me sympathize and accept even a character like Jian as the story progresses.
The music is another positive aspect of the game. It never feels out of place, highlighting the various moments of the story sapiently. The Voice Acting is nice too. Shuyan is obviously the star, but I also enjoyed the performance of the rest of the cast.
I really appreciated the choices offered as the story unfolds. While not all choices offer story changing outcomes that I could see, they do shape up a different kind of Shuyan for the reader/player and I find that plenty cool.
The game might feel a little bit high in price but I found it worth every € thanks to an interesting story, good art and great music. The atmosphere of the game feels really charming and Shuyan is a nice protagonist who also makes me wish for a Korra game made in this style.

Shuyan Saga is a great fun interactive comic book game set in the ancient far east.
The narrative portions of the game take the form of a slide show of (I believe hand drawn) comic book panels with a small amount of movement and animation to bring it to life without being over the top or distracting the viewer from the story, this is all acompanied by a full voice cast led by Kristin Kreuk (Smallville, Beauty and the Beast, Chuck, Burden of Truth) in the title role.
The story itself concerns the title character of Shuyan, (voiced by Kreuk)  a carefree princess who loves to study Kung Foo. The player takes the roll of Shuyan as she is drawn into a web of mystery, intrigue and deception as an invading army try to conquer her homeland. Shuyan ends up leading a rag tag band of unlikely friends in a fight to free her country from tyranical rule, and restore freedom and justice to her home.
The fighting elements of the game switch effortlessly between top down arcade style beat 'em up and over the shoulder 1 on 1 martial arts kick 'em up, as Shuyan prooves you don't have to be a large man to be an action hero or to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥
The game is really a piece of interactive fiction in the tradition of Telltale Games, with the combat existing to further the story, not as an end unto itself, and therefore isn't so hardcore that it could put off casual gamers or non fighting game fans.
All in all, if you like to be immersed in a well told story with superb voice acting (especially from Kreuk, who knocks it out of the park in her first attempt at this style of work) which genuinely makes you care about the characters, and you like the comic style art work, there is absolutely nothing here you won't love.
All in all, highly recomended. 10/10.

A surprisingly good beat 'em up. Beat 'em up's are a fading genre at this point (sadly), mostly occupied by games that don't really have much weight to the fighting mechanics (Code of Princess comes to mind). When I saw a sprite based beat 'em up  set in a grim dark dystopia version of Russia, I was intrigued. Mother Russia Bleeds is a violence tour de force set against the backdrop of sci-fi-ish forced drug usage and social revolution. You play as one of a series of Roma pit fighters beating the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everyone in their way during a quest of unadulterated revenge. You fight huge amounts of enemies at one time and must balance kicking their asses with not getting overwhelmed. Each stage leads up to a boss who you usually have to fight with more creative means, such as blinding them with flashbangs so they stumble into oncoming trains or forcing their weapon to get stuck on some nearby peons so they can't counterattack.
As a beat 'em up goes, MRB is on the difficult side. The amount of enemies is at times staggering and you can't knock out anyone in a mere three hits, short of using an adrenal burst- but using that also saps your ability to heal. There's no roasted turkeys sitting in a garbage can this time around- you have to balance your fighting with harvesting a select few enemies who carry the Nekro drug in their veins, which takes precious time. Similarly, healing yourself leaves you vulnerable. You can play with an AI on your side and he's pretty good usually, although he can be a complete liability in some boss fights due to not being able to react as dynamically.
Excellent action and challenge aside, the game has an issue with hit detection I'm finding. Lining up with enemies can be oddly hit or miss with the attacks, while ranged weapons seem to attack like area effects. This also applies to healing your ally... the healing button is the same as the harvesting one, and the detection of trying to get the one you want, particularly during a chaotic fight seems inconsistent. Further, I feel you also need a controller for this game. It's a bit too frantic and at time a bit unresponsive for a keyboard.
Some fights are also a bit too cheesy. In the clutter of around fifteen enemies, you have to spot who is carrying what weapon, because if someone has a gun, you can get chain hit around 3 times, resulting in death before you could do anything. It's already difficult to figure out where your own character is in these crowded fights! You can repeat them from checkpoints, but when you can be slain over and over because you were knocked down and never allowed to get back up, the sense of skill and tactics fades pretty fast, as well as the fun. Fighting multiple enemies and environmental auto attacks which pulverize you on the ground might be realistic, but it's pretty frustrating to have to keep restarting for that reason. It's also possible to be attacked off screen, especially by gun wielders you can't hit or know are there... expect the AI to be extremely useless in these fights.
There are some bugs I'm noticing. Sometimes enemies become invincible and wander off the screen, preventing any further progress on your part since you can't go backwards. I've also seen Natasha lose her ability to make attacks at random. No idea why- haven't seen it on the other characters. You have to spaz out on the controls to make her punch again.

The Last Door - Collector's Edition is a point and click horror game about a man who tries to find out more about his childhood and what happened to his old friends after receiving a mysteriously vague letter from his friend. You have to make your way through an unsettling and dark 1890s London as you piece together a mystery full of well written characters, disturbing secrets and a haunting past filled to the top with the occult.
The game follows your classic point and click formula of walking around, clicking on small objects to pick them up and use later, and solving a whole bunch of puzzles. Personally, I thought many of the puzzles were very clever and interesting to try and understand, even though I couldn't make it through without using guides. This game is actually called "Collector's Edition" because it is the first of two seasons in the story, that consists of the first four episodes. All of the episodes are available to play for free online and I'm well aware of this, but I bought this game for 2 reasons, first one being my wish to support this developer, and also playing them all seperately with months between made it impossible to follow the story because I kept forgetting a lot of important details. This also comes with a few interesting shorts that tie up some looser ends of the story.
The story is definitely my favourite part of the game. You play as Jeremiah Devitt, a lonely philosophy teacher. One day, he receives a letter from his childhood friend Anthony, and the letter consists of a single line, the motto of a student group they formed together to discuss philosphy, science and art, who called themselves the four witnesses. As he tries to find out what happened to Anthony and the rest, as well as his own mysterious past, he starts to get haunted, and soon enough, there's no turning back.
The mystery in the story is presented in a way that you keep getting answers to your questions in each episode, but new questions keep arising all the time, having you constantly curious, but it is still possible to follow what's going on. The characters are also all very well made. The main character, Jeremiah Devitt is silent, polite and classy. This makes him somewhat easy to understand and relate with. My favourite character that plays a huge role in this game is probably Alexandre - he is intelligent, calm and, somehow, very sane and very insane at the same time. With the exception of doctor Wakefield, not a single character felt boring to me, and everyone had some mystery surrounding them.
Can't talk about a horror game without talking about the horror aspect, and this game manages to deliver very well. This game is based more on psychological horror than jump scares. Sure, there will be moments when dead silence is interrupted by someone slamming the piano, but there are plenty of very, very clever scares, with my favourite being the carnival disk from the first episode. The whole idea of something changing in a weird way when not looking is one that scares me a lot, and this game does that very well.
The one thing that seemingly many people like complaining about are the minimalistic pixel graphics. To me, the graphics were the second best thing in the game, right behind the story. Sure, the pixels are big and you're getting a sense of deja vu when introduced to a new character but his face is made of 10 pixels, like everyone else's, so telling them apart can be a real puzzle in itself, but other than that, the art is done really well. Each episode has its own colour palette, the lightning is used really well (and helps enhance the scares), and there's quite a lot of detail even if it's pixelated - take the intro for example. Sure, the game might seem lazy when a human doesn't have many details when looking from a distance, but the bigger objects are incredible - the close-ups of things (like in the intro), the buildings and backgrounds are done extremely well. The atmosphere is also incredible, being just what you would picture 1890s London like.
I also think this game's sound design is worth mentioning - not just because of the very chilling and fitting soundtrack (the intro music is by far my favourite and delivers just the right amount of unsettling feelings), but also because this is one of the only games I've played where I notice how well the sound effects are used. The jumpscares, for example - the carnival disk one does this perfectly. I once tried to listen to that song for as long as I could, but after a while it started sounding too devilish for me to go on. And the jumpscare part was reinforced by a nice slam on the piano. The game also uses suspenseful sounds on loop that get closer and closer as you approach something (meowing, pipes dripping, laughter etc.), and there's also my favourite - clever use of audio channels.
For completionists, the game's achievements are for finding secrets and reading notes - it won't take too long and won't be hard, but it did feel just a bit boring and the length was too short for me, but this is the type of game you should pick up if you only care about the percentage.
Overall, this game does mostly everything pretty well, but if you think the price is too much for a 5 hour game that you can play online, you should play it online or get it on sale because the bonus content is not too good.

I got this for the Lovecraftian tag that brought me face to face with this game. But the true essence of this game owes a deeper debt to the man whom Lovecraft called his "god of fiction": Edgar Allan Poe. You play a young man come to seek out a boyhood friend living in a remote estate out in the country (House of Usher, anyone?). Thanks to an interactive prologue that has to be seen to be believed, you already know what state your friend is going to be in when you find him. But that's just a clever feint. By the end of the episode, you find out that there is a lot more going on than you expected.
The amazing thing about this game to me is how it is able to accomplish so much with so little. It utilizes graphics that I would have expected from a 1980s Sierra adventure game that roughly approximate the look of the objects they represent. But then it combines it with a lush score that evokes its Gothic setting and fairly stellar sound effects that conjure up the required horror better than any graphics ever could. It's a trick that the developers borrowed from old time radio dramas (more recently utilized by the H.P. Lovecraft Historical Society for THEIR new-time radio adaptations): what you hear is always more horrible than what you see.
Puzzles are about as difficult as Sierra's classic run of Quest adventure games, albeit with a click UI. It involves a lot of pixel hunting, logic application and a willingness to use anything and everything on every possible location. You either love this or you don't.
The first episode is a little too overt in its Poe love. If you sat through a high school English lit class, you'll get most to all of the references. But subsequent episodes begin charting their own story course with plotting that recalls William Hope Hodgson's "House on the Borderland", Robert Chambers' "The King In Yellow" collection and the more uncanny stories of Ambrose Bierce. Yes, it also recalls Lovecraft himself but it's worth remembering that the authors I just mentioned influenced HPL in his own storytelling. At this point, I know I'm going to have to finish this game to figure out what's going on.
Oh and there is a special treat in the Extras menu. The Extras consist of vignettes that take place between chapters, driven by characters outside the main narrative. To avoid spoilers, I would recommend skipping these until you finish the game however.
All in all, it was well worth the slight cost involved to buy this game. If you're an old school adventure fan, highly recommended!

Transistor, developed by Supergiant Games & Released on  May 20, 2014. According to Metacritic
, it's ranked:
#30 Best PC Game of 2014
#49 Most Discussed PC Game of 2014
#97 Most Shared PC Game of 2014
It's not often that you get to hear about indie game's making it into the spotlight or having set a particular standard@benchmark for it's genre/for a particular gaming market. Transistor is one of the many indie games which deserves recognition. A testiment to it's genre of what indie games are capable of. and more to come.
I've never completed Bastion but the game is still fresh in my memory because of it's unique gaming experience. The narrator. The story. With the same formula, now comes Transistor. It is a RPG, set in the distant future where you play as a female character known as Red. You're wielding a mysterious swordlike object which happens to be the narrator for your entire journey. You will uncover the truth/secrets on what's happening around you and to the town.
The controls are easy to master. The visuals are okay to me. What stands out the most is it's art syle. I am not sure how to describe it, plain, odd and yet pretty. From monster design to each character/ability profile.
Lore
The game offers lore on the abilities you pick up from certain characters. In order to unlock the character's background information, you will be forced to use these abilities differently; active skill, secondary skill or as a passive skill - and this will change your style of play.
Other than that, you will also have to choose limiters. Limiters are another set of passive skills which comes with a trade off. You get additional exp for a handicap in battle throughout the game. For example; You gain 4% more exp but The enemies will strike with twice as much power. User will overload more Functions at once and recover only one per Access Point for an additional 4% exp. This will certainly make the game even more challenging. The good news is that, you are able to disable the limiters.
The Mechanics
At a glance, it looks like diablo/neverwinter nights type of gameplay. You have a hero with 4 active skill. That's on the surface, the fast action side on the battle. Transistor introduces turn - a mode where you will are able to enter and plan out your moves within the given bar? This is a unique mode which requires strategic planning; to maximize the moves with the allocated bar. or just for plain escape.
In transistor, once you lose all 4 active skill, you die@lose that particular level of the game. You have to replay that part of level. If you survived a battle with remaining 2 active skill, you're stuck with them until you come across the next panel. There is no such thing as health potion therefore making each battle more RTS like. You can't go blazing around like in diablo. Most of the time, you will be required to use turn to plan and execute your moves.
Enemy AI
Each enemy was designed differently and they are smart. A mixture of different enemy types is enough to kill you -without proper planning. It can feel punisable at certain point of the game but that's just because we are not equiping the right skill for that combat. If it's too hard, just swtich off the limiters and plan your attacks using turn. Bringing in big guns@skills with takes up a lot of points, doesn't guarantee your success rate.
The Story
Transistor uses the narrator to motivate you to go through the game. On theory, this should work however I find that the pacing is off due to it's design. That was what put me off from Bastion. After a battle, you suddenly find a hidden backdoor, after a battle you suddely let red rest/take shower. The pacing was off for me but I pushed on because I wanted to know Red's relationship with the man in the transistor. When the answer was obvious, I wanted to know how this would end. What happens to the Town and it's people?
My Summary:
Transistor is a creative product. Despite having a linear story and with little replay value, the combat system is fun where it allows users to mix & match their skills and work things out. The journey was worthit.
I went through numeruous battles & deaths, took the puzzles and had a major annoying boss fight. What I got was a poweful, worthwhile & bittersweet ending. So far, only 2 games have left me with such strong impression & none of them are from AAA game titles. On the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Transistor is a 8/10.

is a beautiful game. Although nothing happens that is ostensibly groundbreaking, you'll still want to have a decent rig in order to appreciate the silky machinations of the ever-changing puzzles. A smooth framerate
goes a long way in suspending your disbelief. There is some pretty spiffy virtual engineering going on; experiencing these reconfigurations smoothly is much of the fun.
The puzzles aren't incredibly difficult, but you may find yourself stuck simply because the textures are well made; you might not realize certain aspects of some puzzles can be manipulated. I'll be honest: at certain points my jaw dropped at what I was witnessing just after sliding something into place. This game is nothing if not labyrinthine.
The story is extremely light yet it is very imperative to the experience. I was engaged enough to worry about the wellbeing of my character. Thankfully, there is a sequel available now. The next time it's on sale I'm certainly picking it up.
Will I replay it now that I powered through it so quickly? Probably not. But the sale price made
worth ignoring how short the ride actually was. I imagine concocting the puzzles was just as much fun for the developer as playing was for me.
