I feel like a lot of reviews of this game are not fair, so I'm going to write as balanced of a review as I can.  Items addressed:
1.  Is it really free?
2.  How does it play?  And, what about those people that say they can't find anything?
3.  Is it fun?
4.  Do you recommend it?
At the time of writing, I have 40 hours in game.  Also,  I am not a hunter in real life.  I have done some target shooting, and some fishing, but that's about as outdoorsy as I get.  I chose this game because I enjoy learning about new things, like hunting, and find that often games can convey interesting nuance that doesn't come through other forms of study.
1.  Is the game really free?  It depends.  Yes, you can play the game for free, and potentially enjoy yourself.  However, your options are grossly limited.  I believe you can hunt everything with the 2 weapons you initially receive, as the shotgun can be used on pretty much anything, but, it is a shotgun....
I chose to approach it as a game with a monthly fee.  I chose to buy a 6 month license.  Along with that license, I got a lot of goodies, including more firearms, a composite bow, some other equipment like scent eliminator, and a tent.  Also, I got a few clothing items.
I also purchased some "EM$" which is the in-game money equivalent (there's also GM$ which you earn in game, but can't be used for very much).  In total, I decided to put in $50, which includes the 6-month license.
With the additional EM$, I've bought a .303 caliber rifle (for hunting larger game), a Hog Feeder, and a couple of odds and ends (better jacket, etc.) tha taylor to my play style a bit.
I have not tried the multiplayer aspect yet.
The rest of this review will be specific to playing with a membership that allows you to hunt all animals, in all reserves.
2.  The game plays like a FPS where you identify animals, and hunt them.  You receive scores (based on real-life scoring practices) for your kills.  I have currently played on 3 of the reserves.  I believe there are 8 or 9 reserves--some are "winter," some "summer," etc.  Any particular reserve always has the same weather, is what I've learned.  Each reserve has specific animals, based on the actual fauna that was the inspiration for the reserve.  Logger's Point, for example, is based on Washington State.  Redtail something is based on British Columbia, etc.  You won't find bears in Logger's point.  You don't find Phesant in the winter reserves.
Your character can be injured in the game.  Apparently some animals may attack.  I have not experienced that, but I did fall once.  It seems, if you've purchased a first aid kit you can heal yourself.  Otherwise, you're returned to a spawn-in point.  I did not see any particular penalties for falling and "dying" (I did not lose weapons, kills, etc.).
As you go around, you see "clues" on the ground.  You may also hear clues.  You use your GPS device (I think it is called HunterMate, or something like that), and it helps you track your location, and what the clue tells you (direction, rough distance, etc.)  Clues may be from the same animal, or you may see several from different animals.  Interestingly, the HunterMate knows the difference (I'm not a hunter, as I stated, so I don't know if this is realistic--seems a bit difficult without lots of training, I'd think, to tell one deer print from another).
I've seen a ton of reviews by people saying they ran around for an hour and never saw an animal, or that they can't find anything, etc.
I have no idea how this is remotely possible.  I suppose if you "run" everywhere and are colorblind (I am colorblind, and I had to change the color of the clues to something I could see better), you could miss clues, and scare all the animals before you see them.  Short of that, I don't know how someone can claim inability to see any clues, or find any animals at all.  The game even provides tips, like, (paraphrased) "hey, you're running--you may scare stuff.  Think about walking or even crouching."   Those typically pop up after you scare something off.
There is a scripted tutorial that walks you through using the HunterMate.  After those, you can go on a hunt on your own.  When you start, you select your starting time of day.  I generally select 7:00 or 8:00 am to start.  10:00 - 2:00pm are "quiet times" for most animals, is my understanding, so I avoid those times.
On my first hunt, out of the first reserve (Logger's Point), I bagged 2 WhiteTail does, and a coyote, in about 20 minutes.  I saw several other animals, but wasn't experienced enough to know how to keep them from running away on me.
3.  Is it fun?  I do enjoy it.  It can be frustrating, too.  I have chased after a Feral Hog for 30 minutes, only to have it flee and not be able to find it again.  I shot a few things with the wrong type of ammo (some creatures cannot be "ethically" shot with certain kinds of ammo--for example, a moose can't be shot with .22 ammo--I guess the idea is that it isn't powerful enough to kill the animal, and thus there's the dilema of causing undue suffering...)  I spawned in at my tent once, and a coyote was right outside the tent, and just by crouching I spooked it.
Oh, they have contests.  Those contests offer GM$ prizes and trophies (virtual trophies).  That keeps it interesting.  I was able to score 8th in a contest (133 people were entered) for largest feral hog.  That was a nice brag to have, even if no one else knew about it. :)
4.  Do I recommend it?  For the most part, yes.  If you expect to enjoy the game and never pay a penny, then probably not.  If you can afford to look at it as a membership type MMO game (though, it is not MMO), then sure, if you are intersted in a game that rewards stealth and patience.  If you're expecting to run around the countryside firing pistols in the air like Yosemite Sam, then perhaps this isn't what you're looking for.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Let me start by saying that the music and art are top-notch. The gore and effects are phenomenally illustrated. The attacks/moves and combos, while very limited in variety all look smooth and clean. However, past the shock factor of the first few heads you smash or the first chest cavity you nonconsensually relieve of organs, there isn't much on offer here that you can't get for free or a comparable price elsewhere - and with online multiplayer, to boot.
In the beat 'em up genre, there are a few things that are very important and can make or break your game. Chief among these are your hitboxes. If I have to guess why an attack did not connect despite all appearances suggesting it should, that's bad. If attacks that appear as if they should hit consistently whiff, something is wrong. And no, I'm not new to these kinds of games nor am I bad; I still own and play my Sega Genesis cartridge of Streets of Rage 2 that I got in 1993. (Yeah, I'm old.) Now, before you point out that those games have some of the flaws I am criticizing here, remember the relevant release dates: 1992 vs. 2016.
In this day and age, while couch co-op is awesome, it should be in support of online offerings, not in lieu of. My friends and family live spread across the continental United States and Europe, like many if not most of the people my age we don't live next door anymore. Online multiplayer being left out of this game is a questionable choice, especially when the community has already shown the online multiplayer is possible by building a mod for it.
Smaller, but still very questiinable as a design choice is that there is only one moveset for all playable characters. No unique characters or moves means less replayability, since all characters play the same it isn't like you want to jump right back in and learn a new moveset like you might have with other games. When you consider that this game is regularly sold for $15, but only has about 4 or 5 hours of story and an arena mode that frankly does more to showcase the games issues than provide enticement to play... this becomes hard to recommend.
I had high hopes going in, and I know I'm the in the minority with this game and fully expect to see that reflected in this review's rating, but this is a no-go.

First off, let me say I have been waiting for this game to become playable for almost a year now.  The concept art, premise, all of it had me hooked from the beginning.  It caught me as a sort of Mass Effect MMO.  And really, there aren't really any "good" (IMO) sci-fi MMOs out there.  They exist, but none of them really stood out as being something that I really wanted to play.  So I am VERY excited for this game.
So far, this game is in pretty rough shape.  It is VERY basic at the moment.
For characters, at this point in time you have a choice between a male and female.  That's it.  It says customization is coming so I'm waiting to see what they do with that.  The models look pretty good, not AAA (it's not coming out of an AAA studio), but still very good.
The gameplay so far is OK. I've spent half of my time running around smashing the "E" key trying to find things.  The early quests are basically fetch quests with very little in the way of combat, which is a shame as I could see it turning people off from the game. Half or more of the quests do not mark anything on the map leaving the player to wander around the starting area over and over and over again, ad nauseum.  This can be very frustrating and I can see players simply leaving these quests unfinished.
There is no tutorial on equipment or leveling up (in fact the tutorial is VERY bare bones).  Or for that matter, there is no indication that you have leveled up or are able to upgrade your abilities at all... you basically just have to periodically check once you figure it out.
Essentially this game needs some direction on what to do and where to go.  It needs a path of progression that is clear to the player.  Also, the "pop-up" style of tutorials need to go.  You are in a small area and these things take up a HUGE chunk of screen blocking your view of the area.  A more classic style of tutorial menus here would be awesome.  It pops up, tells you what you need to know, and if you ever want to look at them you can get to them in a menu.  The current system just HAS TO GO.
The combat is pretty good so far, it is a 3rd person shooter with RPG elements.  The cool thing I like is the Skyrim system of doing things to level up your skills.  It's a bit confusing at first, but it basically works like this:  You gain XP from completing quests to up the overall level of your character.  Then, for example weapons, you level your weapons skills by using a weapon.  You get general purpose weapon "points" that you can spend on upgrading your weapon mastery for different types of weapons that allows you to use higher levels of weapons.  You also accrue specific points for the type of weapon you use as well that grant you upgrades for that type of weapon (e.g. increased damage, crit chance, etc.).  This applies to all other aspects of character progression. Weapons, armor, crafting, vehicles, etc.
The problem with this system is armor. You literally have to take damage to upgrade your armor. I have basically relegated my self to aggroing enemies and just letting them damage me without fighting back.  This armor upgrade path does NOT work well with this game system as you can quickly upgrade things you use like weapons, but are left with armor that lags behind your other skills.
The really "fun" (read: confusing) part comes when you try to equip gear as they tend to require both a specific character level as well as mastery level of that type of wepon.  The only downside I can see to this is if you decide that you want to try a new weapon or piece of armor halfway through the game.
You CAN spend your weapon mastery points in other weapon types.  So, if you are aware of this, you can upgrade the level of shotgun you can carry by using another weapon, for example.  It does not seem like there is a real cap on this, so you can technically spread your points around to all types of weapons, however why would you do that?
The character progression has barely been implemented.  You basically have weapon and armor upgrades right now.  That's it.  No skills, crafting, vehicles, etc.  At this point it is basically a very basic 3rd person shooter. In combat, you basically run around and left click to shoot things. I have not even seen melee weapons as of yet.
The layout of the map is confusing as hell. I do not see a progression in the outside world like there is with most MMORPG games.  You don't start in a zone level 1-5 with quests that walk you through and then take you to the next area.  You simply walk around and if you happen to run into something 2x or more your level, you either run away or die.
Also, to get to some of the lower level quests you have to move through a swarm of higher level enemies.  One lvl6 quest takes you though either an area with level 13-15 enemies, or an area with 15-17 enemies.  This makes no sense.
Another thing to note is that this is coming out of a Russian company.  If you're playing the game in english, not everything has been translated... several things are in russian, including labels for things, dialogue, etc.  Also, the translation can at times be hilarious as Russian phrases sound very wierd in english.  The voice acting is also hilarious... it's like a low budget made-for-TV movie level of bad.  I would say that if you can't afford proper voice acting, stick to text.
The art for this game is pretty damn good overall.  There are obvious things that aren't final including menu art, models, and areas of the map.  There are some areas of the map that look tossed together with placeholder elements.
My biggest gripe is the LAAAAAAAAAAG.  They recently put out a patch to address this.  This has not at all addressed the issue.  When the population is high, the game slogs.  BAD.  There are still issues with what seems like the server timing out.  All of a sudden, everything in the map stops and you will need to either force a reload or log out and back in.  This is seemingly random with no real connection to anything I am doing.
Also, the menu system is kind of poorly thought out.  You have VERY large and confusing trees to upgrade your skills.  You have slots for different types of inventory items (e.g. 8 slots for weapons, 8 slots for armor, 10 slots for crafting items, etc) which makes both using vendors and managing your inventory confusing.  There are really no settings to speak of yet.
So... the big question is would I recommend it?  I've been mulling that over since I've starting writing this.  Overall, at this time, I cannot.  It looks *promising* which is a dangerous word.  Yes, it is still alpha and yes, there is the expectation of bugs and incomplete gameplay.
On the plus, there is a pretty good portion of content in a Early Access Game, which measured by Steam precident, is great (although honestly, this isn't saying much).  It honestly looks like this isn't some trashy cash grab by a developer who doesn't care about their game.  These developers care.  They are trying to put together a good product.  If they keep progressing, yes I can see this being something awesome.
However, at this point in time, the negatives make this a VERY hard sell. Most of the systems aren't in place, there are still server issues, and you are basically playing a point and shoot game. This game is VERY bare bones.
At the end of the day, I can't say that you should pick it up if you want to even be a hardcore tester.  It looks like it can be an amazing game, BUT the drawbacks at this time are preventing me from recommending this title.

chocolate Chip Cookie Dough Brownies
Ingredients:
BROWNIE LAYER:
3/4 cup (1 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter
1 1/2 cups bittersweet chocolate chips
1 cup granulated white sugar
1/2 cup packed light brown sugar
4 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 cup all-purpose flour
COOKIE DOUGH:
3/4 cup (1 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature or almost melted
3/4 cup granulated white sugar
3/4 cup packed light brown sugar
1/4 teaspoon salt
2 tablespoons milk or cream
1 1/2 teaspoons vanilla extract or vanilla bean paste
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 cup miniature chocolate chips
additional miniature chocolate chips, if desired (to garnish the top)
Directions:
Prepare the brownie layer-
1. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Spray a 9x9-inch pan with nonstick spray, then line with a strip of parchment paper so that it covers the bottom and comes up two sides of the pan. Spray the parchment with nonstick spray too.
2. In a microwave safe bowl (or in the top of a double boiler or pan set on top of a pan of simmering water), microwave in 30 second bursts to melt butter and chocolate chips together until all is melted and smooth. Whisk in the sugars, then whisk in the eggs, vanilla and salt. Sift flour into the bowl and stir that in too. Scrape the brownie batter into the prepared pan. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, or until the brownie layer is cooked through (toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean). Place the pan of brownies in the refrigerator to speed up the cooling process (or cool at room temperature and add the cookie dough layer later).
Prepare the cookie dough layer:
3. In a large bowl, use an electric mixer to combine the butter, sugars and salt until soft and creamy (1 to 2 minutes). Mix in the milk and vanilla. Sprinkle in the flour and mix in until combined. Stir in the 1 cup of chocolate chips. Scoop the cookie dough onto the top of the brownies and spread onto the brownie layer. I find that it's easiest to do this if the brownie layer is chilled and firm. Wet your hands or spray them with nonstick spray and pat the cookie dough on top in a even layer. Sprinkle additional chocolate chips on top to create a nicer, visual appearance. For easy, clean cutting, chill the brownies (wrap the brownies with plastic wrap and chill until firm- 1 to 2 hours or up to 2 days).
4. Cut the brownies: Run a knife along the sides of the brownie pan and then use the parchment paper to lift the brownies from the pan and onto a cutting board. Slice the brownies with a sharp knife, wiping the knife with a paper towel between cuts. If you'd like all of your slices of brownies to look clean-cut without edges, use the knife to cut the sides of the brownies off before cutting pieces. Keep brownies slices covered and chilled until ready to serve.

Damn Good!
I played 22 hours over three days... that said, I already finished the game before. But seeing the Definitive Edition on Steam, which includes absolutely all the DLCs made me buy it again... And I definitely don't regret it!
Indeed, this "Definitive Edition" is more hungry in ressources, you gonna need a pretty good computer if you want to enjoy the game really smoothly.
In my case, I played it on a laptop (Ultrabook, Core i7, 10Gb ram, GeForce 620M 1Gb from Asus)... Not the best for this game, but still able to play in 720p with all settings set to minimum and "Low resolution buffering" turned on. It looks more pixelated than GTA IV and goes bellow 15fps quite often but turning it to 800x600 makes the subtitles unreadable. I wonder what the dev had in mind when they set the subtitles that small (even in 1080p, the text is just way too small!)
Gameplay-wise, it's like you never seen in any GTA-Like games: Dynamic combats like you could see in the Batman Series (you gonna master Kung-Fu!), a real Parkour gameplay (not as good as Mirror's Edge or Dying Light, but it still make a "plus" in the game), plus some really cool addition in driving. You can jump from your car while driving to reach another car (really "action movie-like" during pursuits!) or dash enemies with your car by hitting a bouton. It's not a crazy addition, but I find it really smart.
After that you got the now usual character customization (clothes, many shops around the town and some you get as a reward), cars to by, and bit of RPG-like customization.
The main story is blockbuster-like: extremely dynamic, damn immersive and pretty well driven. There's many side-missions (some are interesting to play), races (I find them a lot alike some old school Need For Speed Underground)...
The only thing I kinda regret, is that you hang out with many girls, but there's actually no romance around them, you just call them one time and then they're gone (get the reward from them straigh away, and they vanish from your phone), I think the dev didn't spend time working on this side of the game. While I found it kinda useless in GTA, I feel I miss this possibility in this game.
DLCs wise, the Halloween one if really fun to play and add few more hours of gameplay (yeah we can mee "Not Ping" again! Finally). The whole city went rogue in this never-ending night, people are possessed and we get to meet again some dead guys from the main story (as ghosts)
Year of the Snake puts you more in the cop side of the game, I loved the joke about the uniform, but the DLC in itself is quite repetitive... It kinda sucks to be an every day cop! But there's a story within it which is worth to be played.
I regret they're not totally integrated to the main game though, some combos are missing, we cannot change our clothes... Our cars disappeared... But everything you unlock within the DLCs is unlocked in the main game! So it's not that bad.
To make it short: I put this game in my "Favorite" list, and there's not so much game in there (I'm really picky).
So go ahead and by this game if you like modern open-world games like GTA! You won't regret it, there's a lot of fun playing this one!

This game is a true gem. It's horrendous start seems to keep this game under appreciated in most mainstream circles and I honestly didn't know about it until a certain youtuber started talking about/would never shut up about his bird squad and next thing I knew I was knee deep in this game and am loving every minute of it.
PROS:
-1Char=Any class. 1 Character can aquire and play as every class, no need to make one character for each class and this allows a player to "hotswap" classes as opposed to logging out, changing chars, logging back in
-Recruit a friend. While this is only noticed if you dragged a buddy into your addiction, this feature is great because it truly rewards you for getting other players and the rewards greatly help the sherpas out there (2 person chocobos bro)
-Environment. I haven't reached 50 and touched Heavenward yet but just the starting areas are truly beautiful. I run the game on max and there are SO many little details they put in to this game that make it feel more open world RPG than MMO. Whether it be the realtime weather (w/ physics (ftw)), The godrays and dynamic shadows, the very subtle character physics (it took me getting a 4k monitor to even notice the boob physics, needless to say, I was disapointed with myself), The amazing foliage (it's not Witcher 3 levels but its pretty close to modded skyrim), the cities/towns and NPCs in them... I could go on but you get my point
-Armors and weapons. I'm much more of an armor guy myself (whats the point of doing it if you dont look good doing it), but both the weapons and armor are really stunning. they base stuff is typical medieval platemail and leather but then you get into some scifi sh!t, I saw a bow that, when drawn, deploys a shield because why not. Some weapons are just light, so whatever your kink, they got you covered
-mounts. if you want a plain ol' horse you came to the wrong game, but, if you wanted a giant 2 story tall mecha chocobo or a flying eyeball with wings, then boy your in for a treat. (side note: each mount (for the most part) has their own music and thats just a really nice subtle addition that they didn't need to add)
CONS:
-Mounts (or lack there of). You have to get a permit to ride a mount, but you have to join a grand company to get the permit, but you have to be alteast 25-30 to join a Grand company... I hope you like cardio. I had 5 mounts by the time I could actually ride one, to be fair, most of them were from events, game time "veteran" rewards, and recruit a friend rewards but still... I WANNA RIDE THE CHOCOBO
-1st Person. This game has a 1st person option, and that's cool, but its obvious they intended for people to play in 3rd. There is nothing when in 1st, you don't have a body, theres no head bob, you dont see your weapon or the visual effects/cues from your attacks. Overall just disapointing, especially with the rise of VR and my desire for a SAO-esq future
-Spam bots. I know every game has them and that there are MMOs out there that are WAY worse but it is hard to read pub chats when totally obvious "get tons of mooney for free" ads pop up in the chat box. but thats honestly just a minor preference issue
Well I hope this "totally" not biased review helps some of you that are on the fence about this game. I know subscritions are a turn off but the quality I've gotten was more than worth it, assuming you're going to play the game more than not at all.

Great point & click adventure with an enjoyable Victorian horror story in the style of Poe.  Puzzles are fun, and fit the story well. The puzzles aren't very difficult, however- the entire game is a 3-4 hour investment.

Great game for fans of the cosmic horror / Lovecraft genres. I haven't had this much fun playing a game in this setting since Shadow of the Comet back in the early 90s. It's original, but makes the appropriate nods and references to Lovecraft, while keeping you completely unaware of what is going to happen next.

It's ...not great. The writing, inspired in equal parts by early HPL and his model, Poe, is predictable, formulaic, stiff, and at times some awkwardness emerges, making it clear this is a translation. The art-style, and its pixel count in particular, are a little too sparse, looking both too plain and not expressive enough (what am I looking at, exactly? the artistry in low-res pixel art is to make it pretty and immediately clear, without the benefit of detail - broad strokes!), there's UI/UX roughness as well. Starting with Episode 2, puzzles drift towards the obtuse (use a stone eagle, a net and a shower, plus a mirror, to make a statue cry and fool an otherwise down to earth, harsh nun into mystical rapture - oookay). Sound design is hit and miss, sometimes screaming
at the top of its lungs, not in a good way, I mean.
All in all, it's a tough recommendation: the adventure bits are too contrived, and the story (and its telling) aren't compelling enough. Granted, nobody expects anything groundbreaking from homage, but homage itself cannot be
hamfisted.
Unless any of this sounds exactly like something you would enjoy playing, steer away.

An excellent trading/exploration game, reminiscent of Sid Meier's Pirates.  Feels very well fleshed out for a free game.  At the moment the game feels more concentrated on completing missions than on establishing trade routes (mission cargo is DRAMATICALLY more profitable per ton than regular trade goods).  However, it is entirely viable to play as a cruise ship and carry exclusively tourists, or to play as a cargo vessel trying to make deliveries on time.  Be you a privateer or tradesman, Endless Sky absolutely delivers.
To new players:
1.  Read the player manual.  The tutorial is loose and allows you to be the Captain you want to be, but as far introducing    game mechanics, is a little sparse.
2.  Avoid combat early if you aren't a pirate. Combat is unforgiving.
3.  Use the save snapshot feature.  It is possible to accidentally ruin a game due to autosave in a bad situation.
Areas that could be improved:
1.  Aesthetically, this game is unpolished.
2.  Autosave could be a multiple slot rotation, to avoid the dreaded die-load-die loop.
I would recommend this to anyone who enjoyed titles like Sid Meier's Pirates, or to anyone who likes free stuff!

This game is similar to those IRL puzzle rooms where you and a bunch of friends are locked in a room with one our to escape, where there are tons of puzzles to solve, doors to unlock, secret compartments to find. You are given a mysterious box by a friend, and you have to open it. That's it. But, your friend has, to paraphrase Emperor's New Groove, "put that box in a box, then put that box in another box" and so on. With each new box you unlock, you start from scratch with no idea what to do, and you get to rediscover it all again. It is also similar to those "Escape the..." flash games you see on Kongregate and other game sites where the puzzles really don't have to do with each other, but the graphics are way better than those.
Pros:
+ TONS of puzzles. The puzzles tend to fall on the side of "find a key, which opens a thing, which you need to solve a puzzle to unravel another key", but they are fun and diverse. Sure, there are lots of keys, but there are also lots of keyholes, so finding out where stuff goes is interesting.
+ Art. It had a photorealistic feel, and then there was a kind of steampunk/fantastical element that was really cool. These boxes defy the laws of physics, but it really works with the story.
Neutral:
~ Somewhat linear. There are times when you can have items for multiple puzzles at any one time, but frequently you're railroaded into a correct order.
~ Story is weak, but do you really need one for a game like this? You get snippets of this experiment your friend was running that has apparently gone wrong, but for me, it's all about the puzzles, finding out how far the rabbit hole goes, seeing your work pay off. I'm calling it a neutral because it might bother some people, but I didn't mind it.
- Kind of a minor one, but some of the puzzles make very little sense. I often caught myself wondering why I was doing a certain task, what the purpose was. Like, there's the obligatory "Play back this tune you just heard" puzzle, a lightbending puzzle with mirrors, etc. but there's no real reason any of the puzzles are there apart from because they needed puzzles for a puzzle game. There are a few that require abstract thinking, which keeps it interesting. I guess it mostly works because you don't know how a puzzle's going to work because there are no clues from previous puzzles, and that's the point: to figure it out.
Cons:
-Short. My playthrough was 2 hours, max.
- Controls are a little clunky at times. You have to zoom in to use an item from your inventory on a certain spot, then zoom back out when it doesn't fit, click and drag to move the camera, double click to zoom into a different spot. I like that you (mostly) get control of the camera, because it's pretty to look at and helps with the sleuthing, but all that zooming in/zooming out gets a tad annoying at times. Good thing it's a short game.
8/10. It may or may not be worth the $5 list price depending on your opinion of these kinds of puzzle games, but it is certainly worth it on sale (mine was just over a dollar, and money well spent!)

The Last Door is an exemplary adventure game. The story is engrossing, and the puzzles never fall into that "I have 40 items in my inventory and have no idea what to do next" trap that a lot of older adventure games do. I think there was only one time I felt the solution to the puzzle was a bit obtuse, which is a big deal for me when playing a point-and-click game. I don't want to spoil the story, so I'll only say that the further down the rabbit hole you go, the more demented things become. Where this game really shines, though, is in its atmosphere. I didn't think a game with such simple graphics could create such a rich and foreboding atmosphere, but they way they combine it with incredible sound design creates a level of dread I hadn't felt while playing an adventure game. Do yourself a favor and play this with headphones on and let the game take you on a ride.

The Last Door held my interest the entire way through, which is something I haven't found in most modern point-and-click games. The game isn't held back by its pixel graphics, but succeeds in creating a dark and foreboding atmosphere. The mysteries of the story are intriguing and I am interested to see where the story goes in season 2.

A friend bought me this game as a joke, due to my username. At first, I thought it looked like a rather bad game, and I was not mistaken. However, the several bugs and glitches provide a rather interesting gaming experience. If you want a well-working game, this is not for you. But if you want a game that is going to stay the same no matter how many times you play, this is a perfect game. It will not provide you with an intense gaming experience, and it's also not a game that you'd play for hours in a row. But this is a game that you can always fall back on for a slow and predictable gaming session. The game advertises that it has both mice and rats for you to chase in the game, this is, however, a lie. The only rodents to be found in this game are rats. That is the only lie to be found in the description of the game though. One of the key features is that you can be a cat. And although nothing in the game indicates that you are one, if you just put yourself in the mindset of a cat, then you can be a cat. Another key feature is all of the BUGS! And worry not, this is not put among the key features by mistake. You'll spend a majority of your time experience all the different kinds of bugs. There is more than one way to fall out of the one, singular, and small map that this game has to offer. Finding more and more ways to break the map is certainly one of the more exciting parts of the game. Another fun part is that instead of you pushing things off tables and counters, the THINGS will push YOU off. In this game, the table most certainly has turned. It's a great game that really isn't worth what it costs. I would recommend that you do try to play the game if you get the chance. But if you ever feel like actually buying the game, trust me, do not do it. This is a horrible game that really isn’t worth spending any money on at all. I, on the other hand, still love it though. It has most certainly been a 10/10 gaming experience.

This game is a true gem. It's horrendous start seems to keep this game under appreciated in most mainstream circles and I honestly didn't know about it until a certain youtuber started talking about/would never shut up about his bird squad and next thing I knew I was knee deep in this game and am loving every minute of it.
PROS:
-1Char=Any class. 1 Character can aquire and play as every class, no need to make one character for each class and this allows a player to "hotswap" classes as opposed to logging out, changing chars, logging back in
-Recruit a friend. While this is only noticed if you dragged a buddy into your addiction, this feature is great because it truly rewards you for getting other players and the rewards greatly help the sherpas out there (2 person chocobos bro)
-Environment. I haven't reached 50 and touched Heavenward yet but just the starting areas are truly beautiful. I run the game on max and there are SO many little details they put in to this game that make it feel more open world RPG than MMO. Whether it be the realtime weather (w/ physics (ftw)), The godrays and dynamic shadows, the very subtle character physics (it took me getting a 4k monitor to even notice the boob physics, needless to say, I was disapointed with myself), The amazing foliage (it's not Witcher 3 levels but its pretty close to modded skyrim), the cities/towns and NPCs in them... I could go on but you get my point
-Armors and weapons. I'm much more of an armor guy myself (whats the point of doing it if you dont look good doing it), but both the weapons and armor are really stunning. they base stuff is typical medieval platemail and leather but then you get into some scifi sh!t, I saw a bow that, when drawn, deploys a shield because why not. Some weapons are just light, so whatever your kink, they got you covered
-mounts. if you want a plain ol' horse you came to the wrong game, but, if you wanted a giant 2 story tall mecha chocobo or a flying eyeball with wings, then boy your in for a treat. (side note: each mount (for the most part) has their own music and thats just a really nice subtle addition that they didn't need to add)
CONS:
-Mounts (or lack there of). You have to get a permit to ride a mount, but you have to join a grand company to get the permit, but you have to be alteast 25-30 to join a Grand company... I hope you like cardio. I had 5 mounts by the time I could actually ride one, to be fair, most of them were from events, game time "veteran" rewards, and recruit a friend rewards but still... I WANNA RIDE THE CHOCOBO
-1st Person. This game has a 1st person option, and that's cool, but its obvious they intended for people to play in 3rd. The city of Cloudbank is under attack by an organisation known as the Camerata. The protagonist, Red, a contemporary artist with a golden voice, gets caught up in the mess and is forced to figure out what is going on with the help of the newly acquired Transistor. A sword used by the Camerata that falls into the hands of our classy heroine. Red is guided through her journey by the voices of those who dwell inside the Transistor on an adventure that will leave you perplexed and wanting answers.
The story in Transistor is quite convoluted, requiring you to pay pretty close attention to what is being said by the voices who dwell inside the sword appropriated by Red.
In short Transistor is a science fiction action RPG where you will fight your way through the futuristic city of Cloudbank. Wielding the Transistor (a powerful sword of unknown origin), Red will piece together the mysteries of the Transistor by pursuing it’s former owners.
During an attack by the Process (a robotic force controlled by an organisation known as the Camerata), Red loses her voice to the great-sword known as the Transistor. You come to find Red kneeling next to an unknown man who lies motionless beside her. This man’s consciousness has been absorbed into the sword which, while Red wields the weapon, can speak to her acting as the narrator of the story and Red’s guide.
Red is now being hunted by the Camerata who want to track her down and retrieve the Transistor by using the Process to attack and kill her. Why they want the sword however, is still a mystery.
Transistor logically combines strategy with a fast-paced action experience, resulting in a combination of reactive gameplay and rich, deep storytelling.
I must say, the combat in Transistor is incredibly enjoyable. You have the option to battle in real-time just like any action game, or freeze time to plan out a number of moves to take place during your turn, however each turn has a cost and you can only afford so many moves.
Real-time combat allows you to use your abilities (or functions) on the go but they have a use-time and a cooldown.
Turn-based combat gives you a gauge that is filled up depending on how much the functions you use cost. After your turn is executed you will be placed on a global cooldown of varying time depending on how much of your gauge you filled up. The more moves you use, the longer the global cooldown and vice versa, allowing for true strategic combat.
You gain access to new functions by increasing Red’s level. You can only have four functions on your hot bar at a time but you can combine different functions to grant extra effects such as pulling your enemy right up close to you or switching the allegiance of your foe for a time. However, only a certain amount of functions can be equipped depending on how much memory Red has.
Battles can sometimes be quite unforgiving and if your health bar completely empties you will lose access to a function until it is repaired by visiting functions terminals. If you have no functions left to sacrifice, you will die and restart from the last checkpoint.
For all you completionists out there, you will be pleasantly surprised by how long you get to play Transistor for. Everyone else though, will only get around six to seven hours of play out of Transistor.
There really is a lot to see and do in the city of Cloudbank and beyond, so if you really want to stick to it and unlock/read everything you can, expect to be sitting pretty for at least fourteen hours.
I managed to snag Transistor during a sale on Steam for around $10AUD so in my opinion that is great value for money. And don’t forget all of the Steam achievements/PS Trophies that go along with it.
Immediately upon launching Transistor will you be impressed by the graphics and smooth animations. Personally I was surprisingly awed just by the way Red moves around the screen. The animation of her running with the Transistor dragging along the ground behind her looks really great. Incredibly simple but at the same time quite intricate.
Enemies are fun to watch and discover. I especially like the Jerks which pummel the ground with their piston-flattening arms and the way they persistently pursue Red.
Once again Darren Korb has composed the soundtrack for Supergiant, accompanied by the beautiful vocals of Ashley Barrett. Every song in this soundtrack is amazing to listen to and I must admit, I was hooked on the soundtrack before I even played Transistor. Each piece of music plays it’s role really well throughout the game, and if you’re also a bit of a Darren Korb fan, you can listen to the pieces of music in a place called the Sandbox which is accessed via ‘Backdoors’ that you gain access to once Red reaches level four.
The Sandbox also acts almost like a home base where you can hone your battle strategies in mock battles or practice your planning in timed challenges. Very similar to the challenge levels found in Bastion.
Transistor is a visually and aurally stunning piece of gaming that draws you into Red’s mysterious world. The voice of Logan Cunningham is thankfully quite pleasant to listen to which is quite a relief as you will be hearing his narration for what feels like the entire game.
The story itself is fairly hard to get into which I find to be quite a let down, but once you start to weave your way around the intricacies of what happened and what is happening, you will find yourself wanting to keep going in the hopes of unraveling even more of the enigma that is the city of Cloudbank.
If you love an engaging storyline with lots of questions to be answered, Transistor is right up your alley. But if you want a game that has a different type of strategic combat you haven’t experienced before, you will also be greatly impressed.

If you like challenging beat'em ups, you'll love Mother Russia Bleeds. I never felt that the game was too easy and enemies were just thrown out there. Overall, the game took about 4 hours to beat as Ivan, and I haven't played as any of the other characters or gotten many of the unlockables. A rage-inducing, hyperviolent sensory overload with a brilliant soundtrack. Streets of Rage shot up with a pulsing armful of Hotline Miami. Heads smashed over pavement and undulating veins coursing over the walls.
There are a couple technical nitpicks- when a game is as difficult as this, things like hitboxes are really important, and when you're trying to slide-kick beneath a jump-kicking enemy and somehow get hit it can be really frustrating- but I had an absolute blast with Mother Russia Bleeds. It's not particularly punishing despite its brutal difficulty- checkpoints are pretty frequent and if you die you get a full syringe of health- and Devil-Trigger-Style-Badass-Mode-inducing Ecto Cooler and a full health bar to help you along. Toughest part was getting the alternate ending- though the last boss was fun enough that I didn't really mind that!
Oh, and the soundtrack is fantastic. My one major issue with the game is the lack of online co-op- if that gets patched in later I would be really grateful!

Let me just start out by saying, if you're gonna play this on the "Hardcore" difficulty, prepare to have your balls rocked. This game is unforgivingly difficult. That said, I still enjoy the game very much and I definitely think it's worth buying. I'm about midway through the story mode, and so far, I like the story and gameplay. My favorite character is Boris. I personally think he's the best character, simply because I think he's perfectly balanced (for me, at least).
And of course, I'm assuming the reason why you're looking at this game is because it's a classic-style beat 'em up. Well, rest easy, because there's a lot of that.
There's so much violence and gore, it'll satisfy even the most sadistic. I've seen reviews where people complain about a simplistic combat system, which is arguably true, but that's generally how beat 'em ups go. Moreover on the complaints, they generally whine about having to spam a single move in order to clear out waves of enemies, which you don't have to do. That's like complaining about Mortal Kombat because you can spam a single move in order to beat your opponent. There's actually a lot more combos you can perform than I've ever seen in any beat 'em up style game, you just need to learn them.
I've been playing on a keyboard for the duration of my gameplay, which I will argue is quite harder than playing on a controller. I'm about to connect my DualShock 3 controller, because some moves like rushing or trying to differentiate between "rage boost" and "health boost" can sometimes get a bit tedious. This, by no means, takes away from the experience of the game, but I do believe that if you're gonna play this, do yourself a favor, and hook up your favorite controller. You'll be glad you did (especially on hardcore).
Here's my few problems with the game, though. The story seems to be a bit short, however, I have not completed the game. Each chapter will take you about 30 minutes, and there are eight of these. Of course, there's a boss at the end of each chapter, but some can be
unfair. I won't spoil which ones, but you'll know when you get there. Also, it doesn't save checkpoints. This is what makes the game a headache. If you start a chapter, you better be prepared to finish it, because if you quit, and think you can pick up where you left off, think again. You will have to start all over. It's very aggravating.  My last issue, is that the story is really lack-luster. It's not bad, it's intriguing for sure, but there could definitely be improvement.
In conclusion, this is a very solid game. I haven't experienced any bugs or glitches, and if I did, they were very minor and I didn't notice them. It's frustrating, fun, and ferocious, and I do not regret spending $14.99 on this game, and I don't think you will either.
Gameplay is difficult, but fun. Definitely a wonderful addition to the Beat 'Em Up genre. Combat is simple, as beat 'em ups go, but it doesn't detract from the experience, I believe.

You and your IRL friends obliterate the streets of Russia in the throes of Revolution. Shoot yourself up with drugs to refill hp OR engage frenzy mode (pills vs adrenaline in l4d2). Refill your drugs by draining it from twitching dead bodies.
Good luck getting any though. By the time you walk over to the corpse there's two more mooks standing on top of him ready to interrupt you. The drug supply quickly dissapates, so you either fight the mooks and get no drugs, or absorb them immediately and take a fist to the face. Annoying.
When your party dies you're sent back to the last checkpoint with full hp and maxed drugs. WHAT'S THE POINT OF MAKING SELF-HEALING SUCH AN IMPOSSIBLE CHALLENGE IF DYING GIVES YOU EVERYTHING BACK.
Watch out, checkpoints in the last two levels are so sparse that you could easily end up redoing upwards of 20 minutes because you couldn't figure out how to kill the steroid bear.
Gameplay challenges aside, there's plenty of trouble to stir up. Violent explosions of bloody pixels fire out from your hands as you crush an enemy's head in your palm, or literally bisect him across your knee ala Zangeif. A variety of weapons (including firearms) keeps the gameplay fresh for the 4 hours it takes, and there's a healty dose of competitiveness in co-op prompting you to outperform your friends. The music rules and there's just enough variety in the stages to keep me invested throughout.
This is definitely the sort of mindless headsmashing I'd recommend if you have someone to help play it with you.

The Time Goddess has given me more than 30 seconds to review this game, so I will make use of her charitable nature.
Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming is the second (obviously) Half Minute Hero game. With a good mix of RPG, puzzle, and action all packed into one hilarious RPG which lampoons pretty much everything in those games. You have several stories to go through which span an impressive plot which is told in a series of (technically) 30 second levels. The characters are colorful and the gameplay is amazingly fun. Keeping in touch with true frantic action, you must make all your choices quickly, lest those 30 seconds you have be wasted, or you could always pay the stingy Time Goddess.
The game is extremely fun, with the game keeping the pedal to the metal at all times. The story and dialogue gloriously pokes and prods fun at many tropes present in video games, from forcing you to pick a specific choice to giant robots (who doesn't love giant robots?)! This game, like its predecessor, has an overarching story that encompasses several campaigns following different heroes of different eras, all helped by the Time Goddess.
The gameplay is simple, but fun. You'll find yourself smiling as you plow through fields or Global Dungeons looking for EXP, gold, and items. During missions, you have to balance time and money, adding a strategic / tactical aspect to each and every mission. Do you plow through to the boss and risk being too weak or grind your levels until you're strong enough? Not only there, there's plenty of secrets in the game that'll keep you engaged for awhile as well.
There's also a map creation system where you can create your own maps to play and download creations of other players, to further add to the content of this game!
It also has a multiplayer function, though I've yet to try that out.
Overall, it's an amazing game that is definitely worth the price tag that it has.
Unfortunately for me, the Time Goddess noticed I called her stingy and has taken all my money, my shoes, and my shirt.
Thankfully, I still have my pants. Wait, no. She took those too.

I'd say this game is a weird commentary on the nature of JRPGs. The half minute hero format is interesting, though! You have 30 seconds to defeat whatever evil force is threatening to destroy the world/continent/whatever. Point is, you have 30 seconds! Oh no! That's not NEARLY enough time! Well luckily you have "The power of the goddess" on your side! Essentially you grind for 29 seconds, run to town, and pay N*100 gold to reset the clock, where N=1. This means the first reset is 100g, the 2nd 200 and so on. The challenge shifts from simply grinding until you're sufficiently leveled (the game literally tells you "You>Evil!" to say you're leveled enough) to managing your resets efficiently.
I remember a mission, mission 3 or 4, where all of the good grinding mobs were a good deal further in the level. You will not always succeed the first time through, you need to know all the parameters to the challenge before you can farm and grind effectively.
After you defeat a boss, you usually get put back in the open world, where your level and gold revert to a sort of macro profile. You had 10000 gold and 30 levels in the challenge? Tough, you're back to your global level and gold. The good news is the next time you start a new mission, you start at your global level, so a little in-between mission grinding goes a long way. Also in between missions is my preferred time to buy gear, because there are serious penalties if you can't afford a reset during a mission.
I just got explained some sort of skill system. It sounds like it boils down to grinding a certain weapon to unlock sweet super moves. None of which you can pick, combat is entirely automated all the time. Hell, if you're too overpowered, you dont even get a battle screen, you just run over the enemy and it flies off the map, team rocket style.
The writing is bleh, thank goodness you can skip it with a simple press of the start button. The goddess is this annoying money-♥♥♥♥♥ who loves getting gold, so while she's essential to saving the world, she's also a stupidly annoying character. Your hero is some generic angsty dude, I dont really know what his deal is. It's not very engaging.
Overall, I suggest this game to anyone who likes JRPGs and something new. I'd pay 10, maybe 15 bucks for this game.

Thirty seconds to save the world once again. Half-minute hero second coming plays pretty much the same as it’s predecessor. For those unfamiliar with the series, it basically takes the main elements of JRPGS, like grinding, buying better equipment , doing side quests and beating the boss of the area and gives you 30 seconds to accomplish it. You can reset the clock by praying to the time goddess statues you’ll find in towns(where the counter stops), but each time you do will cost more money than the last one.
So the game is basically a fast-paced puzzle where you must decide what to do first. While the first game had 4 types of game modes, this one only has the RPG one, that is divided in 5 main Arcs. The are various additions to the game though, like a walking castle that serves not only as a base but also as a giant robot you’ll use to fight overly big bosses, an overworld that you can explore for secrets without having to worry about the time and a class and skill system.
The plot is still charmingly silly, parodying classic rpgs clichés and story patterns, packed with charismatic characters and some more serious heartfelt moments now and then. This time around there’s more space for character development and a bigger emphasis on story, all while maintaining  the game’s humorous mood most of the times. For those who don’t want to be bothered with lengthy story though, a simple click on the action button will skip all the text.
Half-minute Hero: The second coming is a worthy successor and an upgrade in almost every way from the original, fans of the first one and newcomers to the series alike should definitively give it a try. It’s well worth your money, and your time.

I have been waiting for a long time to play this game, waiting for a good sale, and even if I only found a 50% one on this Summer Sale, oh man, if it was worth it.
Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming is, as you might have know, the sequel of "Half Minute Hero; Super Mega Neo Climax Ultimate Boy" (the hell is going on with the names, man?), and it does fell true to the first one, while being original on his own.
The story picks up on the year 200, 100 years after the first one, and as the original one, has multiple stories (5 in total, the first one being a bit short as the introduction and tutorial, while the last one is pretty much the ending and final battles), most of them with their own characters, like in the original (the Hero Mode, Princess mode, Evil Lord mode, and Knight mode on the original).
The main thing that has changed here is the seriousness. This game is more serious than the last one, where half the stages where filled with parodies, jokes, easter eggs and references. There are still some quite hillarious stages, but nowhere near before. Instead, you can find parodies and references in the story, maps, and even the items (really? The bike and Buster Sword from Cloud? I rather wear Vivi's outfit...).
The soundtrack is f#cking boss. I'm not even kidding. Not only it sounds way better while having the same style, but each episode of the game has multiple themes for each battle and map. And I can tell you, the music just gets better the further you go into the game.
One main problem is the difficulty...It might be that I'm a Badass, or something, but I found it a bit easy. Specially with the "Global Level system", and the "Global Dungeons". The idea is that you can level up out of the stages, so when you start your next battle, you will start at level 5 or so, instead of level 1. The Global dungeons are a good adition, but it's way TOO easy to level up in them, while searching for the loot on them.
Another trouble I find on this game, is that the story doesn't have multiple routes like the original. Further more, while in the original there where multiple ways to finish a stage, here there are not much of those. There are, though, some secret companions that are not easy to find, and usually need some backtracking to get (like Cozain, who you will need a guide to find, like me).
Something that has also been done well, are the cameos. A good amount of characters from the original can be found in here: Allied characters, the other heroes of the game, some Evil Lords...Even the main character itself! Most of them will join you in some way, and only a few of them will serve of any way on the story (like Geezer, who I'm not gonna spoil who he is, since it's quite obvious, but appears in all the chapters, helping the heroes). The new Formation system also makes the allies feel a bit more usefull than before, and now both you, allies and enemies have skills...Even though they appear out of chance, making them pretty luck-based.
Something great, and that I wanted really bad on the game, is the Map Editor. I mean, IT'S PERFECT! Now you can make your own maps, or download the maps from others, play them alone, or with friends! It makes the game last much more, and it's something that A LOT of games should have by default.
While it took me about 14 hours to unlock most of the original Half Minute Hero, I have played this one for 20 hours, and I'm nowhere near getting everything (Dude, the Demon Maze is a nightmare...). I would totally recommend this game, SPECIALLY if you played the first one. 20€ is a bit too much, though, so wait for a sale like I did. 10€ or less is a good price, and you should buy it from that point. There are probably DLC's for this game, I haven't checked them yet, but you could also buy them to extend the game, if you want.

I enjoyed The Last Door quite a bit.  I didn't ever feel scared, but there was a little dread that creeped up on me.  Despite it's retro graphical style, the game manages to create an eldritch atmosphere of dark mystery, in no small part to it's amazing soundtrack by Carlos Viola.  I found myself wrapped up in the events, and questioning what was really going on, and what would happen next.  The main characters were fairly interesting, but I'll admit, because of the simpleness of the sprites, it can be easy to mistake who is who.  The notes hidden throughout the game are interesting and well written.  Upon completion of the game, I recommend going back with a guide and finding all the secrets, however, some are a little annoying to find.
The soundtrack is excellent, and is provided in the game's local files.  These tracks are used exceptionally well to set the mood, and you will frequently hear new songs throughout your playthrough, even the first episode had a surprising number of song changes.  That being said, sometimes you would step outside, or into a new room, and the song that had just started would end abruptly.  It was a little jarring.
Mechanically the game is pretty standard point and click.  The inventory and interactions are all up to par with modern games (something not all games with "classical" styles bless us with).  Most puzzles are easy, although you may pass some of the objects you need to interact with, seeing as two pixels could represent shading, a book, a note, a cup, etc.  The walking speed is also somewhat tedious, which could have been used to build tension, but I usually just felt bored while backtracking.  Speaking of which, for a game that only takes about four hours to complete, you certainly need to walk from on side of the map and back again an awful lot.  This is, thankfully subverted somewhat with the ability to instantly travel through certain doors you've previously been though via double clicking, and many of the locations have multiple paths which keep things a bit fresh.
I'd like to note that while the pacing of the game was good, and the narrative was engaging, the short length left me without a feeling of closure, and not in an "I can't wait to see what happens next" sort of way, but in an "oh, we're ending it there hm?" sort of way.  I'm not really a fan of the episodic format to begin with, and I may have felt disapointed if I hadn't purchased this game on sale.  I will give the game credit for using the episodes well, I can remember each one distinctly, and it never really felt like I spent to long in one location.  Each episode felt unique, which I'm all for.
Deserves a consistent "overwhelmingly positive" rating, a real gem!

SOO overpriced!  I just spent a whole day playing this and I couldn't put it down - such a huge time investment!  :)
Anyways - this game might have sold me on 2D game development being superior to 3D (focus on gameplay rather than 3D spacial arrangement).
There's a really good learning curve.   I felt great satisfaction when the lights come on how some part of the game works.
Then there's the "futzing".  Futz futz futz.  I can stare at a ship build and go back and forth and back and forth "1 of these or 2 of those or 3 of the other?" trying to tune the ship to work *just right*!  Its comparable to Star Ruler's ship building screen, only here you have to fly the thing and it feels that much closer to the metal.
You start play with a bank loan which will sap all the money you make.  There are ways to "hide" the money and miss loan payments but then your loan size increases due to interest.  Anyways you come right out of the chute with your hair on fire, so to speak, and it is really satisfying to get the loan paid off.  It felt "grindy" during that phase of the game, because you know the starter ship is crap - but the mechanism is believable and compelling  (i.e. rewards aren't too high for doing tasks).
Later in the game other elements come into play that provide really good tension, like capturing ships.  Especially when figuring out some ideal ship-build or fleet-build strategy.  I lost my whole crew trying to capture an enemy ship, and I thought we were well armed.
Replayability is also very high, since once I figured out how some components worked, I wanted to start the whole game over again and try to play a better opening!  Also the concept of compounding interest may come into play, depending on whether this strategy is used...
Lastly - the game is remarkably polished.  It's like it is setting the standard for paid-for games, and it's a high bar indeed.

It's Mother bloody Russia fkin Bleeds. Game itself fun and well made, action great, the controls good, music sounds awesome. But only 8 stages, and actually boring arenas. New unlocking drugs it's kinda pointles, but some of them can add new challenge to game.

Mother Russia Bleeds world was set up in a fictional USSR, where the gonverment tried to experiment their citizen with a drug called Nekro. The player play as a street thug that was given Nekro, and the story is about vegeance for whoever given them Nekro. The game can be played solo with or without ai. You can also play 4 player local coop (with controller) or 2 player local coop with one keyboard.
The game world embraces the weirdness of a fictional USSR, with variety enemies and scenario. There was a scene where you are fighting inside a weird animal fetish club with a gimp as your pet or fighting a prison where some of the enemies are naked. I like these type of scene because it's memorable, it somehow  make this game different from many side scrolling beat em up games. The game background is detailed and very beautiful. With animation like dying people, moving grass, and a brutal riot.
The gameplay is fun and responsive, enemies stagger when you hit them with light or heavy attack. You can pile up some combo with the move set that you can see on the control. From grabbing your enemy and punching them to slamming them from the air. They all feel fun and if used properly move like that can take down more than one enemy. One of the mechanic that I notice was inspired by hotline miami is the finishing downed enemies. Enemies that fall can be finished by punching them while they are downed to kill them once and for all. Be careful though, enemies around you can still attack you. Sadly all character have the same moveset and the move variety is not that big. Making you use the same combo from start to finish.
In addition with fighting player get hold of Nekro. Nekro can be used to heal yourself or can be used to make yourself into a berserk mode. Berserk mode increases your speed and power of your attack or even do some fatality to your enemies. Nekro can only be aquired from fallen enemies that convulse. Some enemies that have their body intact (head is not removed from their body) sometime convulse, and you can get nekro by sampling it from them. Sampling nekro leave you vurnerable to enemies around you making a tought decision to either sample or fight. Nekro itself have different variety like faster sampling, exploding enemies, controlling enemies and many more.
Enemies in this have many variety like dog, zombie, mutant, gang member, gonverment official, and many more. Some of the enemies are a nuisance if not taken quickly like shield, dog that stun lock, and armed official. Gun are very powerful if you get a hold of it, enemies with gun can kill you with two shot. Enemies sometime is too hard that sometime you must use cheap move like sliding or power punch. Good thing the game balance over time to fix some of the enemies.
The boss on this game is what I enjoy except the final boss. The bosses require you to find it pattern and weakness. The final boss difficulty spike that it have 3 phase and if you die in one of the phase you need to restart it from the first phase. It's frustating, especially if you aim for the good ending where you don't use nekro on the boss fight.
Somehow the game felt pretty short for me, about 4 hour of gameplay and then an arena mode. Arena mode is an endless mode that can grant you different type of Nekro. The game right now don't have online coop at this moment, but is planned on the future. I really like if the game will have more future dlc like more mode, costume, music, and many more. The development of this game is pretty slow, since only 4 dev that worked on this game. It's going to be a while before the coop update. If you like brutal fun beat em up and you have 4 spare controller, than this game is for you.

Well, I'll try to be brief about this. So I began playing 3 days ago and have played 52 hours since, so that says something. It's a pretty good game, very immersive and realistic and with a great number of things to do. A lot of animals to hunt, each of them with different and unique ways to do it, whether by tracking or trapping or occasionally accidentally fortunatelly stumbling across them. Fine graphics, easy to run with high graphs in not-too-great computers such as mine, beautiful scenarios and very detailed and realistic animals.
Having that said, I'd just make a very serious complaint about the ingame purchasing system, that depends on earning em$ or buying them with real money. I understand it's not a full-f2p game and that it's already a big huge pro that you get to play it for free regardless of being a member, but the f2p's get so litttle to none "advantage" whatsoever. You can play as a f2p and get a few em$ through competitions if you're good enough, but even so it's pretty tough and rewards so little. You can also try and get some em$ with the "earn em$" system, through sponsors. But it's so very much annoying and works very little. The sponsors redirect you to 30 minutes long surveys with repeated questions and when you're done with it you don't even get the em$, most times. I even tried answering different things several times, and still didn't receive almost no em$. Some of the links are even broken and one of the sponsors doesn't even have stuff in it. To be fair, I did get to receive 33 em$ from a single sponsor after two long repetitive surveys that actually seemed to be the very same one to me. But with 33 em$ i can't even buy ammo. The game devs and whatnots simply exempt themselves from any responsibility regarding the sponsors and these methods (ok, they warn about it before you try), and that to me sounds a little bit of carelessness for their costumers. The other way to buy stuff is with gm$, but it can only be used to buy consumables and ammo, and the ways to earn it are limited to the finite number of missions you can accomplish. To be fair again, there are a lot of missions, so I expect it takes quite a bit of time to complete them all, mainly because f2p's can only hunt 3 fixed species and 2 weekly rotation species, and the missions are species-based mostly.
Anyway, it's a VERY good game, really. Even for a very limited f2p, it's still a very good game. Though I'd suggest anyone to NOT remain f2p for too long, or you'll end up tired and bored of it and will end up disliking the game. The membership values are not expensive at all, and some of the bundles give some very good perks, such as equipments. The em$ packages are not expensive either, and you can get very good discounts for larger amouts. As for myself, as soon as I get a grab on a few bucks, I'm surely gonna purchase my own membership and a buckload of em$ so I can hunt those bucks the way I see fit.

Well after 35 hours I thought I would give this game an honest review.
h1] FREE TO PLAY	[/h1]
Now before you click download, the free to play element of this game is more like a demo. You are given 2 guns, with free reloads, and can only hunt 3 types of animal, with an extra 2 that rotate each week. Upon creating you're account and VARIFYING your email, you will be given 3 days of premium membership which allows you to hunt any animal for the duration.
Unfortunately most of the negative reviews are based on the dislike for this play model. It should be noted however this game is updated regularily and it is now 8 years old.
h1] MY GAME EXPERIENCES	[/h1]
Firstly I was thrown into the tutorial... I nearly didn't last past it. I did 2 parts of the tutorial before I left to the main game. During the tutorial i was unable to change my graphics settings and it looked horrible. Thankfully as I left the tutorial I was given options to adjust it. And I must say for an 8 year old game, the graphics are very nice.
After about 5 hours playing the game, I already felt this was a game I was going to play for some time. I decided to check out the membership costs.. Actually this was a shock. All licenses and islands for just £6.99 for 3 months. Well that was a bargain in my eyes. I normally rate games on quality of play. If you can get £1 for every hour, then its pretty good. I had already played 5 hours so in 3 months I would easily get my moneys worth.
This left me with the issue of guns. You're given one rifle which can only hunt certain game. Thankfully you're also given a shotgun which has 3 types of ammo which covers everything else. I didn't want to spend money on guns, and lures and crap, so I checked out the bundles. This is where I was rather shocked. The Trailrunner starter pack, seems expensive, but it has around £22 worth of equipment in the package, and also has 12 months membership.
That was me sorted!
If you like to hunt, and can ignore the hate from those who feel burned by the FTP model, then I say give the game a go. One of the most brutal, rewarding beatemups out there. And I'm not only talking about the aesthetic, which is brutally beautiful in its own right.
First, to get it out of the way: Mother Russia Bleeds is not a particularly well-balanced game. It's a hard game on its normal difficulty, sometimes approaching the point of cheapness with the amount of enemies they can throw at you. This is especially hard when you're playing by yourself - the game can often turn into a game of managing space so you don't get annihilated - but this issue is mostly alleviated if you have a co-op partner. If you're new or casual to beatemups, go for Easy for your first run.
But make no mistake: co-op partner or not, if you put the time into this game you'll get the systems and it's incredibly satisfying to play. This is a beatemup with eight functional buttons, not including the d-pad/stick movement and taunt button. Each player character shares the same hit/grapple combos, but character stats, hitboxes sizes, and unique moves vary for each of the four characters. Enemy goons may require to be hit to death like you would think, but almost every enemy type will require a specific strategy to dispatch them without getting punished by their special ability. Some mooks prefer opening with slide kicks, others will automatically block punch combos, some will dash-grab into you, and some will divekick you. These enemy abilities may seem really annoying and cheap at first, but as you put time in the game and the challenge arenas, you learn how to deal with every single type with your tools of violence.
Let's talk about one of these tools, the dodge. Unlike a game like Double Dragon Neon, which has a dodge roll/duck maneuever that has invulnerability frames (i-frames), Mother Russia Bleeds has a dash-dodge that works vertically and horizontally. This dash-dodge has no i-frames, which means you can't use it to cheese through most attacks thrown at you, with the exception of grabs. However, it can be used to escape enemy punch-combos, vertically avoid projectiles, create/close horizontal space instantly as opposed to initiating a double-tap run command. Jumps, kicks, punches, and grapples can all be done off a run, and the dash adds a run-property to any move you do during it, essentially allowing you, say, slide-kick on command.
To the game's fault, they don't teach you these sorts of systems from the get-go. The tutorial honestly needs a lot of work and without a guide, you don't learn the pretty neat systems this game has to offer unless you pound your head and thumbs into pulp repeatedly like I did. But once you do...you keep coming back.
Gameplay aside, the other thing that this game really excels with is its presentation and sound. The game is almost entirely pixel-art from top to bottom, with evocative environments setting the stage and grotesque characters punching, taunting, and bloodying up as fights rage on. There is such a sheer quantity of different pixel art for mook types that it's pretty clear why this was in development for so long. The animations, however, are about Capcom beatemup standard at best, and don't expect anything like an SNK fighting game.
The sound design is another real treat here, which was all done by a single composer, Fixions. Hits are meaty and responsive, and audio cues for danger and opportunities are distinctive so they help serve the gameplay. While gameplay sound is relatively crisp and staccato, the music feels usually feels like a low-fi take on Pertubator, which fits in nicely with the grimy and brutal artistic design. The music also tends to use samples such as hearbeats, sirens, and chants to improve the atmosphere.
For $15 you get a campaign that lasts about 2-4 hours depending on the difficulty and your skill. It's a varied romp between different stages including a sewer, city streets, nightclub, and a really fun fight inside and on top of a moving train. Each level has a final boss that is never copy-pasted from previous bosses, and have their own unique moves, stage hazards, and openings to take advantage of. The campaign has a suprising emphasis on the writing for character dialogue between fights, even if the plot/character development is pretty shallow and serves to set up fight after fight. The arena mode is probably where you'll spend a lot of the time if you enjoyed the campaign, serving up 10 stages with their own sets of mooks and stage hazards you'll have to deal with. It's honestly in the arena modes where you can learn the meat and potatoes of the game and you can also unlock alternate types of drugs that have different properties. Some drugs enhance your rage mode, others heal more for less charges, and some cause your enemies to explode like a grenade. Good times.
There's two more things I want to say about this game. First, it lacks online co-op, which can be a problem. Friends in the flesh are hard to come by these days. However, I will say this is a beatemup styled after games of yore, where it was a couch or arcade machine affair with an emphasis on difficulty and score; so, I'm more willing to forgive them for it. Second, this game actually gets support from the devs. One of the huge problems of ported beatemups like Double Dragon Neon or Shadows over Mystara is that post-launch support is poop. DDN is a great game but still really unstable to this day, and Shadows over Mystara only supports x-input, period. Le Cartel have actually taken the time to patch their game for bugs, controller support, and some minor balance improvements and I really appreciate this.
Congrats for making it to the end of my stupid long review of a $15 game. It isn't perfect, but it is a well-made game and I really enjoyed it for the reasons above. I hope you found this review useful in your decision to buy or not buy this game!
