Lets get to what went wrong with the Multiplayer in this game.
1.) No community dedicated servers. They removed the community server browser for some dumb reason. There's no more finding good communities to play the game with. You can either join a lobby full of random people or find real life friends to play with. (Good luck finding real friends to play this with. They probably moved on to other games by now.)
2.) The game takes no skill. With all the usual rants about Killstreaks, grenade launchers, stun grenades, and campers aside, this game at it's core involves no skill outside of your ability to spot out enemies and point and click. This is why I couldn't help but to giggle a little bit whenever I read someone in game chat boast about their KDA to some "scrubs" or "plebs". If you want a true competitve FPS game, get CS:GO.
3.) It doesn't excel at anything. Battlefield 3/4 are much more immersive than Modern Warfare and Counter Strike easily makes competitive cod look like a joke. It tries to be a jack of all trades, but ends up as a master of none.
4) The weapon unlock system is trash. Not much to say about it except you have to be really insecure about your game to force players to grind out a game to unlock a weapon of their choice.

Let's get the most pressing issue out of the way first.
The art style is stupid and gimmicky. There is nothing retro about it, even the Sierra AGI adventure games from the 80s had higher resolution than this garbage. And don't even get me started with mixing different pixel sizes. Nothing ever lines up pixel-perfectly, fonts, inventory and the game use all different pixel resolutions. It looks horrible and the developers should feel bad for doing so. I love pixel art, but this game completely fails to deliver on that end. Just make a text adventure next time.
Gameplaywise, it's a great adventure game with a solid and chilling story, especially if you like Chzo Mythos games or Lovecraftian horror in general. The puzzles leave a bit to be desired, but I didn't really expect hard puzzles from this game in the first place. Music and sound effects bring much life to this game and are easily the most memorable aspect of it.
I feel that The Last Door could've been much more and now it remains a forgettable curiosity and a small one evening distraction. Sane art direction and a more complex and captivating puzzle system would've made this a modern adventure game classic.
Ultimately a bit disappointing, but I suppose I'd still recommend it for the exemplary audio design and atmosphere.

This game is nothing short of a masterpiece, where every bit and piece put into the game is beautiful on it's own merits and comes together as a whole to be this amazing and profound experience.
This is a game where the story and the emotions evoked by it are so powerful that they resonate long after exiting the game. And the soundtrack is a beautiful counterpoint to everything going on and even on its own is worthy of praise, because it is truly one of my favorite soundtracks ever from any form of media.
It's not a particularly long game, but it doesn't have to be. The story tells what it needs to without overstaying its welcome or on the flipside feeling rushed, or overly-simple. And it's written so well that it grips you in so quickly and easily, plops you in with so many questions and the game provides enough hints at answers that it makes you think about everything. There's not much in the way of explaining or straight-up answers, but it doesn't feel detracting from the story or game. It means it doesn't spoon feed you detailed explination to every piece of information and instead leaves it up to you to fill in the gaps it provided, which I personally appreciate a lot.
And the ending, lord, the ending. It's beautiful and sad and I cried the first time through, I cried the second time through, I cried just EXPLAINING the ending to someone...
I bought this game while it was on sale and I regret that because this is a game that I love and appreciate so much that I wish I had bought it full price.

THE GOOD:
Strategist
-The game implores you to make intelligent combat decisions. The strategic planning mode gives you limited free will to lay out an assault to destroy your enemies. It's exciting and invigorating to watch your destruction successfully unfold.
Skills That Kills
-You have a wide set of skills you can obtain called functions. Functions offer a variety of attacks and/or defense to obliterate your enemies. You can combine these functions a ton of ways in creative depth which offers different results each time. So make sure to take the time to experiment.
Watercolor My World
-The world of Transistor is beautiful. Drawn and painted by hand giving you a dark and somber ambience. The atmosphere feels weighted, I swear you'll really feel the state and condition of the world Red is in.
Voice Of The Voiceless
-The story is brilliant and that's all I have to say about that as I don't believe in reviewing the story. It's how you tell it that matters. The dialogue is intricately written. It creates intrigue and immerses you in its rich and deep story.
THE BAD:
The only bad thing I can say about this game is there's an end. I never wanted this game to end. It's replayable but one experience is enough to make this my 2014 game of the year. I don't know, I just can't seem to play it again. I might play it again someday, but nevertheless, Transistor is one of the best games ever created.

The game's shining feature is its artwork of course -- as usually what I feel gets Supergiant Games' awards 90% of the time.  You can delve into the game's "deep" story by Inspecting the abilities you gain at certain points of the game -- as the abilities you gain are from dead citizens of the city you're trying to save, which are absorbed into the Transistor.  This player kinda glossed over the story, because as usual I play games for the gameplay.  As I did enjoy the gameplay itself, I feel it has a few problems.
The combat and core gameplay definitely has its merits, and can be quite enjoyable.  It touts the whole "player's choice gimmick" of either going for more Turn-based gameplay or real-time.   Unfortunately, the game can push you into one or the other, and it's a lot of trial-and-error to figure out which situation suits which playstyle -- and which techniques you should have equipped.  Then of course, you can be punished harshly by having to wait for your Turn meter to build back up in order to use any abilities (Jaunt discluded), getting Tech uninstalled (by getting your life drained all the way) or by dying and having to restart from the last Access (Save) point.  And pending on what you have after you've lost a certain ability in battle,  you might as well restore your save point anyway.
I've found a lot of times towards the ending, and more challenging parts like some of the Tests you can do, there's really no point to do real-time combat, because the game can get very spammy, and almost every ability you have has a stop-wind-up, and cool-down animation which can really get you hurt.   And SPOILERS -- the final boss uses Turn, so pretty much forces you to do the same.
Developers like Supergiant get super praised for a lot of their gameplay designs from Bastion and this very game, but I feel they give an ILLUSION of strategy and thought that a lot of players get fooled over.  This game barely has any strategy.  Yes, you have a wide variety of abilities to learn and tune to your liking, but in the end, there's really only 2 or 3 most effective set ups you'll find to use.
It's worth a playthrough, and I'll even say worth the $20. It's more fine-tuned than the cluster♥♥♥♥ that was Bastion -- though that one was fun too in certain ways.  Bastion had a lot of enemy hell spam, and this game can get to that point towards the end of the game.

This is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. The attention to detail is astonishing, as anyone who plays this game through the ending will find obvious. The level of immersion in this game is also incredible, with the developers having gone above and beyond to make you feel involved, with everything from the speed of the vehicle or even the weather itself; even your smallest choices seem to affect the narration, and in turn the story. There's subtle foreshadowing to the ending, which I found fitting, and wouldn't want to change even if I could. Simply everything here is perfect. And the gameplay offers so much diversity in options, that alone enhances the replayability in addition to the achievements. Play this game.

Transistor is an amazingly fantastic game. It keeps you fully engaged with a fresh, original story and unforgettable characters. It doesn't waste any time, immediately throwing you into the shoes of a young woman standing over a dead man's body. As if that wasn't disorienting enough, the sword that has been driven through the man's body starts talking. And it seems to be talking to
.
You progress through one of the most beautiful worlds I have ever seen in a video game. It strays from the typical monotone, corporate indifference of most technologically futuristic worlds by imbuing every building and streetlamp with color and personailty. The intoxicating setting combined with the incredible soundtrack make for an invigorating experience. You can even take a break from fighting to allow Red, the main character, to hum along with the music.
As you fight your way through the multitudes of unique enemies, you are given access to new attacks and methods of defense. But rather than just choosing your top four favorite attacks and sticking with them throughout the game, you get the opportunity to mix and match each attack to create your own original loadout. For example, you could mix a simple stun attack with a leeching effect in order to continuously deal damage to a stunned enemy, or you could use that same stun attack in combination with with an explosive effect, so that you could stun multiple enemies at a time. Your decisions will deeply effect your entire method of gameplay. But don't worry, no mixture is permanent. You can always go back and switch out certain attacks and create all new ones.
If you plan on getting this game, keep your mind open. Transistor will force you to rethink your definition of a soul and what it means to be fully integrated into a society defined by technology. And remember, as you find yourself growing emotionally attached to a fictional sword, you're not alone. Though some people won't admit it, we've all been there.

10/24/2016 - Your Mass Effect fix
First and foremost, heavy emphasis on incomplete. Hi res textures aren't implemented yet! Game looks great BUT it isn't what you see in the trailer. There's a sweetFX mod placed in the forums of the game with screenshots. If you're heavy on graphics and not already in a relationship with Mass Effect, look before you buy, because it's the Mass Effect feel that hooked me to this game.
But nevertheless, if anybody's looking for a Mass Effect-esque MMO, this is it. The controls, the atmosphere, combat, it all feels like ME. Graphics aren't AAA, but still visually appealing and make use of the Unreal 4 engine. I absolutely love the game so far.
The game shows great promise at the moment, and it gets love from the developer. Today's update implemented bug fixes and animation reworks. And yes, there are a bunch of bugs (non-game breaking). Have fun with it. It's still in Alpha and messing up your first character isn't a big deal, since you get three character slots, all of which you can build as you like.
Gameplay is smooth, but map load times take a couple minutes so I usually alt-tab for that time.  Lag has been improved significantly with the addition of servers, so it hasn't been a problem recently although the occasional desync does happen, which just requires you to go back to the main menu and log back in to your character, which causes the 1-2 minute load time. It has only occured a couple times to me, and it's not a game breaking issue.
It has a unique progression system. Classless, point based, invest your points here, there, etc. So far all that's really needed to be invested into is armors and weapons, but you'll see ingame how many categories there are that haven't been implemented. Skills don't work at the moment. I'm currently investing into a full Assault armor and Assault Rifle character. My next build I'm thinking of choosing either the Tactical or Commando Armor with Pistol build.
The quests promote a LOT of exploration. A lot of it. You'll be sprinting literally everywhere, running to different NPCs, collecting different objects. It can be tedious, but I enjoyed getting to know every nook and cranny of the ship and map, and reading the quest dialogue. One downside (or upside?) is that for some quests, markers havent been put in or even slightly misleading, so you'll likely be asking people or running around everywhere looking for certain NPCs/items, and it helps that the community is extremely helpful and welcoming. Don't be shy. I have seen zero toxicity in this wonderful world chat. For some quests that require you to find certain items, there are steam guides up showing the locations of items. There are enough quests to level you up, but they aren't overwhelming, and you'll complete 99% of the level 1-15 quests by the time you hit the next wave of quests at level 15.
Combat is fun. At the moment, you can utilize the pistol and an assault rifles, which you can swap in and out of. Shots are somewhat laggy and can end up causing you slight trouble when trying to shoot smaller agile monsters, but I still had great fun with it. Mass Effect-feel third person shooter. You level up your weapon skills by killing monsters (allowing you to equip higher tier weapons), and you level up your armor skills by getting hit.
Be careful not to die, because you'll end up having to run from the start of the map. Thankfully, no items or exp is lost. You don't get an ATV until level 25 or so, I've heard, with the completion of quests.
It says I put on 24.5 hours in the past two weeks, the most gaming I've done in the past year or two with nursing school, work, and a girlfriend. That says something. I dabble in a million games, f2p, b2p, subs, and the only games that have hooked me like this one is Mass Effect 1-2-3 (well, and Starcraft 2, but that's a different story).

This game is an interactive (very) short story exploring the dangers of runaway intellectualism in a vaccum of solitude. The player collates the ramblings of a divorced, delusional and deppressed survivalist in notes found as they explore the singular location. As the player progresses they must return to a fixed point to progress, giving the feeling of returnig to the ominously lit surface for a gulp of stale air before delving deeper into the disturbing depths and history of the place. Audio reinforces said historry with chilling inmediacy and the simple geometry and lattice-like, almost fractal pixelated textures keep the imagination engaged, so that the narrative feels more like a memory: a cunning trick given the perspective shift present at the climax.
A simple, yet succesful experiment in interactive narrative that, with little time invesment required and no cost, is very easy to recommend. Please keep in mind some may find the themes on display disturbing.

The Room (note: not based on the films The Room or Room!) is a point and click puzzle game that will be familiar to anyone who has played a room escape video game or done a live action room escape. You are in the haunted attic of a mansion and you find an elaborate and ornate box. By flipping levers and dials, pressing buttons, putting keys in locks, and generally fiddling you slowly open more and more of the box and learn about the secret of the room. The plot is mostly flavour and mood rather than a concrete narrative. Puzzles are fun and generally fair. The game looks gorgeous. At 2-3 hours, I think the game is priced appropriately.
I want to emphasize two things for people considering the game:
First, the built-in hint system is excellent. Automatically after fiddling around for a while, if you're not making progress, the game will help you by giving you a hint prompt. Click on it and you'll progressively get more information. In this way you never feel stuck or under pressure. If you're getting frustrated, take a hint. If not, that's okay too.
Second, while the visuals on the PC version are excellent, the controls remain optimized for touch platforms. The game is very tactile, lots of dragging and rotating and moving things. Although this is replicated here via mouse controls, I think it's probably a little more playable on a tablet for that reason. I beat the game on iPad a few years ago and replayed here. I believe the game is generally cheaper on tablets as well. So if you're a big Steam collector, prefer playing everything on PC, or just want to support the devs, by all means buy this, but if you're considering both the tablet version and this version. I'd go iPad first.

Yes, there are a few a-holes here and there, but for the most part people are willing to help you out. Don't know the mechs? Ask and usually someone will explain it to you. I have had random people just come up and raise me and heal me when I was out leveling. People I had just met and had just joined the same FC and me would give me high level gear just because they made it and they saw I didn't have it. Also, they are pretty easy going and funny. Can't count the number of times I have come across a random dance party or mount war in game. Makes for some very times.
-You can do pretty much whatever you want with your character. Sick of being an archer and want to try out healing? Go do it! All you need to do is go to the guild to start your quest and get your weapon. After that, all you have to do is switch your weapon and armor to whatever you want to be. You don't loose anything from doing this either. If you are a level 15 archor, you stay a level 15 archer until you decide to level it up again. You just equip your bow and the armor for it and you are ready to go.
-Even at end game it doesn't feel like I have to search for something to do. There is still plenty to do even after you finish main quest. There are tons of side quests that have interesting stories and even tie in with main plot. You can get some pretty cool things from doing them as well. There is also an amusment park, housing you can save up to buy (yes, you can own your own house), pony farming, and beast quests, and just so much more.
-You can get married in game. It is actually a really interesting feature. I married someone in my FC and we go matching rings that allowed us to teleport to the other person's side. We also got a mount and the people we invited to our wedding got minions. There are 3 different wedding options to choose from. There is a free option (you get the matching rings and I believe a wedding dress/suit). The 2nd option (the one I chose) includes what I have just told you, plus an emote, and you can customize the wedding. The 3rd one I believe you can choose different outfits and a bit more customization. Over all, it is a very cool feature that I absolutely loved using and loved going to them (someone bought me a bridesmaid dress to wear to their wedding).
The cons
-There is a monthly subscriptions fee. It is cheaper to do the month by month if you only plan on making one character on a server. However, if you plan to do standard, buying more at once is cheaper. (good to note though that they do give you stuff the longer you play the game)
-People who like to immediately do things with friends will find the game a little slow until they hit level 20 main story quest. You get your first dungeon when you get to the level 15 main story quest, and you don't get your first mount until you hit level 20 in main story quest. I believe level 15 story quest is also when you finally get to travel outside of your home region.
-It is more expensive to buy through steam than it is from their website from what I understand. Keep in mind that the one on steam comes with 1 month free subscription. I do not know if the same applys to the one on their website. Best to do your own research.
Overall, it is fun and entertaining game that I would recommend to beginner and upward players.

This game is nothing short of a masterpiece, where every bit and piece put into the game is beautiful on it's own merits and comes together as a whole to be this amazing and profound experience.
This is a game where the story and the emotions evoked by it are so powerful that they resonate long after exiting the game. And the soundtrack is a beautiful counterpoint to everything going on and even on its own is worthy of praise, because it is truly one of my favorite soundtracks ever from any form of media.
It's not a particularly long game, but it doesn't have to be. The story tells what it needs to without overstaying its welcome or on the flipside feeling rushed, or overly-simple. And it's written so well that it grips you in so quickly and easily, plops you in with so many questions and the game provides enough hints at answers that it makes you think about everything. There's not much in the way of explaining or straight-up answers, but it doesn't feel detracting from the story or game. It means it doesn't spoon feed you detailed explination to every piece of information and instead leaves it up to you to fill in the gaps it provided, which I personally appreciate a lot.
And the ending, lord, the ending. It's beautiful and sad and I cried the first time through, I cried the second time through, I cried just EXPLAINING the ending to someone...
I bought this game while it was on sale and I regret that because this is a game that I love and appreciate so much that I wish I had bought it full price.

Had this for a while, didn't get to finishing it until now.
The game's shining feature is its artwork of course -- as usually what I feel gets Supergiant Games' awards 90% of the time.  You can delve into the game's "deep" story by Inspecting the abilities you gain at certain points of the game -- as the abilities you gain are from dead citizens of the city you're trying to save, which are absorbed into the Transistor.  This player kinda glossed over the story, because as usual I play games for the gameplay.  As I did enjoy the gameplay itself, I feel it has a few problems.
The combat and core gameplay definitely has its merits, and can be quite enjoyable.  It touts the whole "player's choice gimmick" of either going for more Turn-based gameplay or real-time.   Unfortunately, the game can push you into one or the other, and it's a lot of trial-and-error to figure out which situation suits which playstyle -- and which techniques you should have equipped.  Then of course, you can be punished harshly by having to wait for your Turn meter to build back up in order to use any abilities (Jaunt discluded), getting Tech uninstalled (by getting your life drained all the way) or by dying and having to restart from the last Access (Save) point.  And pending on what you have after you've lost a certain ability in battle,  you might as well restore your save point anyway.
I've found a lot of times towards the ending, and more challenging parts like some of the Tests you can do, there's really no point to do real-time combat, because the game can get very spammy, and almost every ability you have has a stop-wind-up, and cool-down animation which can really get you hurt.   And SPOILERS -- the final boss uses Turn, so pretty much forces you to do the same.
Developers like Supergiant get super praised for a lot of their gameplay designs from Bastion and this very game, but I feel they give an ILLUSION of strategy and thought that a lot of players get fooled over.  This game barely has any strategy.  Yes, you have a wide variety of abilities to learn and tune to your liking, but in the end, there's really only 2 or 3 most effective set ups you'll find to use.
It's worth a playthrough, and I'll even say worth the $20. It's more fine-tuned than the cluster♥♥♥♥ that was Bastion -- though that one was fun too in certain ways.  Bastion had a lot of enemy hell spam, and this game can get to that point towards the end of the game.

Transistor is an amazingly fantastic game. It keeps you fully engaged with a fresh, original story and unforgettable characters. It doesn't waste any time, immediately throwing you into the shoes of a young woman standing over a dead man's body. As if that wasn't disorienting enough, the sword that has been driven through the man's body starts talking. And it seems to be talking to
.
You progress through one of the most beautiful worlds I have ever seen in a video game. It strays from the typical monotone, corporate indifference of most technologically futuristic worlds by imbuing every building and streetlamp with color and personailty. The intoxicating setting combined with the incredible soundtrack make for an invigorating experience. You can even take a break from fighting to allow Red, the main character, to hum along with the music.
As you fight your way through the multitudes of unique enemies, you are given access to new attacks and methods of defense. But rather than just choosing your top four favorite attacks and sticking with them throughout the game, you get the opportunity to mix and match each attack to create your own original loadout. For example, you could mix a simple stun attack with a leeching effect in order to continuously deal damage to a stunned enemy, or you could use that same stun attack in combination with with an explosive effect, so that you could stun multiple enemies at a time. Your decisions will deeply effect your entire method of gameplay. But don't worry, no mixture is permanent. You can always go back and switch out certain attacks and create all new ones.
If you plan on getting this game, keep your mind open. Transistor will force you to rethink your definition of a soul and what it means to be fully integrated into a society defined by technology. And remember, as you find yourself growing emotionally attached to a fictional sword, you're not alone. Though some people won't admit it, we've all been there.

Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming is carefully orchestrated chaos. It is, at its core, frantic slices of old-school RPG action bookended by massive lumps of old-school RPG text dump. It’s kind of satirical of the grind-fests at old, but it’s that special kind of satire we don’t see enough of that manages to stand strong on its own merits while poking fun at its foundations. It’s inventive and clever and, thankfully, has a skip key for when all that text starts to crush you in sheer weight. It’s also crazy long thanks to an embarrassment of options, which would make its very title an oxymoron if it wasn’t also completely accurate.

Sleeping Dogs takes place in the lively and exotic city of Hong Kong. The players takes the role of Wei Shen who is an undercover cop that came back to Hong Kong from the United States. The game is open world and there are plenty of things to do. The player can go on dates with different women, go to a karaoke bar, street race, drug busts, fight rings amongst other things. The main story does well enough to be engaging.
The combat is where Sleeping Dogs shines. In Sleeping Dogs you can murderise the enemies in all sorts of creative ways. You can break their legs or use the environment to execute the enemies. These environment kills are bloody and harsh. For example, Wei Shen can grab an enemy and then use a table saw to kill them. The blood and the screams of agony only fuel Wei Shen's bloodlust. There are melee wepons and guns available, but it is more fun to fight hand to hand.
There are also costumes Wei Shen can wear. The DLC are provide more adventures for Wei Shen. Also there's a skill progession system as well as new combos Wei can learn. The game also has plenty of Cantonese slang and dialogue that immerses the player well. You can learn some Cantonese whilst bashing enemies heads in.
A great game that any fans of open world RPGs ought to try. It has something for everyone, action, adventure, romance, hookers, karaoke and RPG elements.

The Room (note: not based on the films The Room or Room!) is a point and click puzzle game that will be familiar to anyone who has played a room escape video game or done a live action room escape. You are in the haunted attic of a mansion and you find an elaborate and ornate box. By flipping levers and dials, pressing buttons, putting keys in locks, and generally fiddling you slowly open more and more of the box and learn about the secret of the room. The plot is mostly flavour and mood rather than a concrete narrative. Puzzles are fun and generally fair. The game looks gorgeous. At 2-3 hours, I think the game is priced appropriately.
I want to emphasize two things for people considering the game:
First, the built-in hint system is excellent. Automatically after fiddling around for a while, if you're not making progress, the game will help you by giving you a hint prompt. Click on it and you'll progressively get more information. In this way you never feel stuck or under pressure. If you're getting frustrated, take a hint. If not, that's okay too.
Second, while the visuals on the PC version are excellent, the controls remain optimized for touch platforms. The game is very tactile, lots of dragging and rotating and moving things. Although this is replicated here via mouse controls, I think it's probably a little more playable on a tablet for that reason. I beat the game on iPad a few years ago and replayed here. I believe the game is generally cheaper on tablets as well. So if you're a big Steam collector, prefer playing everything on PC, or just want to support the devs, by all means buy this, but if you're considering both the tablet version and this version. I'd go iPad first.
Looking forward to the third installment being released on Steam.

Before reviewing the game itself, I want to note that the soundtrack with this is amazing. I liked it enough, in fact, that I went to bandcamp and bought the remastered version for both the first and second seasons. It is one of those listens you can enjoy without having it connected to a game, and that accentuates your game-related experience. Even if the game were mediocre, I would get it for that.
Thankfully, the game is great as well.
If you have never played a point-and-click game, the objective is simple. Explore your surroundings by clicking to tell whoever/whatever you are controlling where to go/what to pick up/what to sample, figure out puzzles, and enjoy the ride. It is something that a gaming novice can get into, and that any skill level can enjoy. This is actually a great medium for this type of horror, because it helps establish a sense of dread while luring you deeper into whatever puzzle awaits.
The graphics also work for this, which honestly surprised me, although there are places when a little clarity would assist with puzzles. For example, finding a path in a heap of blocks is sometimes more difficult than it sounds and I managed to get lost a couple of times because of this. This does not harm the game, however, and some things are actually pretty cool to see displayed along a "less is more" approach. There are some solid combinations of sound and visuals presented, too, and they are somewhat frightening. You can see that in the first chapter, and it develops from there.
You can try out the first portions of this for free on the creator's sites, so try it out if you are wondering. Give the medium a chance, too, even if you are torn on it or have played it before and had mixed or negative results, because there is a lot here. Also, you can find other games that use this format and that also add to the horror/comic terror format.

This game is absolutely amazing!! I am not a huge fan of MMORPGs, but this one definately won me over.
-For one thing, the story and lore is pretty deep and engaging. For me, that is a big thing in any game. It is the one thing that I am finding stands out from other MMOs. I have played multiple ones growing up and even recently (Elder scrolls, neverwinter, WoW, City of Heroes, Everquest, Lineage, etc), and I keep coming back to this one.
-Second off, the game is just visually stunning. There have been times where I have just logged on and sat my character down somewhere in the forests surrounding Gridania while I talked to people in my Free Company (guild).
-I love the fact that while I can play with people, I never feel like I am forced to interact with people except for the mandatory story dungeons. Even then, I feel you don't get left behind in these dungeons as much as you do in other games.
-The community is very nice. I played games where you would go and do a dungeon and just get left behind. I don't have the same problem with this game. Yes, there are a few a-holes here and there, but for the most part people are willing to help you out. Don't know the mechs? Ask and usually someone will explain it to you. I have had random people just come up and raise me and heal me when I was out leveling. People I had just met and had just joined the same FC and me would give me high level gear just because they made it and they saw I didn't have it. Also, they are pretty easy going and funny. Can't count the number of times I have come across a random dance party or mount war in game. Makes for some very times.
-You can do pretty much whatever you want with your character. Sick of being an archer and want to try out healing? Go do it! All you need to do is go to the guild to start your quest and get your weapon. After that, all you have to do is switch your weapon and armor to whatever you want to be. You don't loose anything from doing this either. If you are a level 15 archor, you stay a level 15 archer until you decide to level it up again. You just equip your bow and the armor for it and you are ready to go.
-Even at end game it doesn't feel like I have to search for something to do. There is still plenty to do even after you finish main quest. There are tons of side quests that have interesting stories and even tie in with main plot. You can get some pretty cool things from doing them as well. There is also an amusment park, housing you can save up to buy (yes, you can own your own house), pony farming, and beast quests, and just so much more.
-You can get married in game. It is actually a really interesting feature. I married someone in my FC and we go matching rings that allowed us to teleport to the other person's side. We also got a mount and the people we invited to our wedding got minions. There are 3 different wedding options to choose from. There is a free option (you get the matching rings and I believe a wedding dress/suit). The 2nd option (the one I chose) includes what I have just told you, plus an emote, and you can customize the wedding. The 3rd one I believe you can choose different outfits and a bit more customization. Over all, it is a very cool feature that I absolutely loved using and loved going to them (someone bought me a bridesmaid dress to wear to their wedding).
The cons
-There is a monthly subscriptions fee. It is cheaper to do the month by month if you only plan on making one character on a server. However, if you plan to do standard, buying more at once is cheaper. (good to note though that they do give you stuff the longer you play the game)
-People who like to immediately do things with friends will find the game a little slow until they hit level 20 main story quest. You get your first dungeon when you get to the level 15 main story quest, and you don't get your first mount until you hit level 20 in main story quest. I believe level 15 story quest is also when you finally get to travel outside of your home region.
-It is more expensive to buy through steam than it is from their website from what I understand. Keep in mind that the one on steam comes with 1 month free subscription. I do not know if the same applys to the one on their website. Best to do your own research.
Overall, it is fun and entertaining game that I would recommend to beginner and upward players.

Background: Huge Final Fantasy Fan, Bought a PS4 just for FF7 Remake. Anyways!
Replayability: Now this is a weird one. You can swap out the class of your character by merely going into the menus, and putting the correct equipment on. You then get to experience that class story. It is actually 100% recommended and I would go as far as to say it is required as you need at least 2 classes to obtain the Advanced Classes. But this is true for most Final Fantasy Games.
Combat Options: Final Fantasy XIV is the 2nd attempt at a FF Themed MMORPG. For those of you with vast FF backgrounds the Combat type is FFXII with more control of your character placement and equipment slots. For those not familiar with FFXII it is an Active Time battle played out in the general vicinity of enemy spawn points, meaning you can run by just physically running away but you can also attract more enemies as well.
Social Options: The game has been around enough to have many guilds on every instance Server. Experience is shared between those who participate, not just the initial aggressor which means you can't 100% kill steal something, which is a problem in other games.
Final Thoughts: I have since retired from this game after 628 hours due to Burnout...I have great respect for those who continue the good fight, but I just can't continue.
This has consumed my life, yet still no regrets.

Ok, so it's Alpha and a little rough around the edges, but that's to be expected. The Basics are there, but if you're wanting a more "finished" experience, now is not the time to play this game.
But moving into a little more detail, here are my thoughts on some of the areas from my (so far, so brief) playthrough:
Gameplay: so far, so MMO.  Walk here, click this, walk there, interact with that, shoot 10 of them.  More will no doubt come and with more variety, but right now it's straight out of MMO Design 101.
Sounds:  Music is fine - it's not a grand orchestral score, but it's also not dubstep, so that's a win in my book. The WEAPONS need work though.  At they moment they may look *BOOM**BOOM**BOOM* but feel very *pew* *pew* *pew*
Graphics:  An odd one.  They style is very good (imagine if TOR, Wildstar and Mass Effect had a drunken threesome), but the detail settings are way off.  From a distance, objects look little better than an early 00's MMO (looking at you WoW and TOR), but upclose, the detail pops in and you can see the UE4 beauty.
Customisation:  For chracters, there's literally none beyond "Generic Male" or "Generic Female".  However, it's clearly labelled as simply disabled in the Alpha, so that's not a mark down in my book.  As for in-game, the armour/customisation system *appears* to be very promising, with lots of slots (Head, mask/neck chest, arms, vambraces and more), allowing you to have a unique look.  The skill/specialising levels also appear to be tied in with this, although I havent had much of a look into that yet.
As a good review also needs some areas for improvement, here goes:
Movement/aiming is a little off at the moment, frustrating when enemies get up close and/or are quick.  Aiming needs to sped up, or a melee/knockback mechanic implemented to get them away from you.
Sound/graphics need work, but that almost doesnt need mentioning since it's an Alpha release and I'm sure is already planned for.
The main thing this game has going for it at the moment is Promise.  There's a good engine in UE4 and with time the devs can implement some great features to make a good MMO - it just needs time and support.
With the current (discounted at 13/10/16) price of £12, I't say it's a bit of a no-brainer to jump in and give it some support.

This game is breathtaking. The setting and ambience are awe-inspiring and the gameplay is fun and challenging without feeling too frustrating. This isn't quite the same beast as Bastion, but players of that will like Transistor's familiar feel.
The biggest criticism of the Transistor is the story, which quite frankly I don't understand. It is a little ambiguous but it is riveting nonetheless.
The music, the art, the story, the gameplay---its all pretty amazing. Do yourself a favor and experience Transistor for yourself.

Fluid motion, seamless transition into combat segments and humming parts, a well developed soundtrack, a definitive art style, a decent story but fantastic narritive, a lot of attention to seemingly insignificant details.
A lot of good parts can make a good game. But the way Transistor makes them all come together is near perfection. The fluid movement in and out of combat, enhanced by the striking art style and locations, being able to stopp and take in the surroundings while having the beautifuly haunting voice of the PC humming along with the background music.
The story imo is good enough, but it is the way it's being told that makes it compelling. You see and feel the effects of the progressing storyline, it's happening to you, and your limited interaction with the other characters is really well handled, and the interaction is near heartbreaking at times.
I can't go into the combat system to much, while it is quite unique, and very customizable in how you approch it, rarely did I feel I was in trouble. Even with several added limiters, I felt it just took longer, not became harder. Transistor has a surprising amount of depth to its combat system too, and I have heard from friends that the true depth becomes really apparent in the New Game+ mode, but I have not touched it as of yet.
A whole hearted recomendation.

Her companion (some have called him a narrator, comparing it to the narrator in Bastion) I rather liked. He's not really a narrator, but an integral part of the story. While he can't affect the world around him directly, he is using (and I don't mean that in a bad way, I do think he cares about her) Red to do so. and I think that's an important distinction.
The game is a cyberpunk type game, with all the 90's "VR is just as real of a world at the real world" hokom that brings with it. But if you can live with that (or better, revel in it), I think it's a good, if short, artistic game.

Minimum would be a great multi-player game (and note, it is multi-player only), if not for one maximum problem: LAG SPIKES. I don't know what's causing the problem, whether it's un-optimized networking code or a game engine that simply cannot handle Minimum's special physics and effects. Or maybe it's a combination of both, or something else entirely.
It certainly isn't my system specs, which are well above the recommended. At first when I start playing, the game runs smoothly at 60 fps. It runs even faster when I have vertical synch disabled, which I've tried. In fact, I've tried everything to get this game to continuously run smoothly, but nothing works.
When it does run smoothly (and *sometimes* it does), it's a fun and novel take on a 3rd person, multi-player team-based shooter. I love the Lego-like theme of the game, and the many different ways you can modify your equipment and customize your loadouts, using the building blocks-gibs that drop from things you shoot and destroy (which are mainly enemy players). I also love the game's "Titan" mode, and the titans themselves (King Kong, Godzilla, giant mechs, samurai-colossus) are awesome. But oftentimes, as a match progresses - as the players start running and jumping and gunning, and the ballistics start zig-zagging, and the particles start flying everywhere - the game engine/networking starts choking, the framerates start dropping, and severe lag spikes start spoiling the fun.

Alright, gotta be honest here, I've considered this one of the better games I've played, but it's got its own problems just like any other game..
It's got fantastic graphics despite being presented to you in only blocks. The hit animations, procs lighting, ambiance simply all fit too well together into one image. The map designs and the UI are extremely clean, very fitting to the modern style of 2 dementional shapes devoid of depth and complication.
The unique ingame level-ups are also very innovative and revolutionary, it brings tactics into play, thus promoting a whole new level of metagaming. Along with the flashy good looks. Your gameplay also changes as you progress through leveling your weapons, instead of the monotony presented in just about all other games, minimum presents fluidity. The game also offers you 6 loadouts you can customize right off the bat, and then swap around freely in battle, giving the players an incredible amount of flexibility.
Yes, competitive play is viable in minimum. Nothing's significantly better than any other thing, And kills arn't awarded to the best camper in town, but rather to who can control their character to their heart desires, and outplays their foes on an extensive level.
However... Its grasp extends beyond its reach, the game is simply too awesome to have such a fatal flaw. Which is quite a shame, but nonetheless fun. It simply can't hold a playerbase because the progression system is so poor to the point of none existent.  Level has no meanings other than a badge of dedication. All the items in you've so diligently worked for are worth nothing, as anynoob just starting off the game can easily purchase'em off the market for less than $5 in total. Nor is there an ELO rating or dedicated competitive games, which completely shuts off the competitive scene that should be but thriving as we speak. Because the skill spectrum in a typical match is so diverse, an experienced player would quickly get bored as he mows down the wave of charging newbies, whereas on the other hand, the new players would feel bashed upon. Leaving no fun for both parties.
New players would leave so quickly because they have to put up with the monotony upon reaching level 5, as there's probably acquired all the guns they found cool when starting off the game as the point of interest deminishes, the incent to keep playing lingers...
The game may appeal to retro gamers from quake back in the ol'days, where being skillful is all they need to have fun.. But however, times have changed. In our times, it's all about having and preserving a uniqueness that solely belongs to each individual player. In which case, you developers reading this should base your business model off of. A typical example would be CS:GO, or Blaclklight : Retribution (my favorite game). Because the quantity of their items (or skin) hast became astronomical, and the price range of them vary drastically from a few cents to maybe even over $1000. It keeps people attracted because we always want to work for something better than what they have, and the fact that there's almost always something better than what they have. If you make 10 different skins for each weapon, and each of them being 10 times more difficult to acquire than the latter.
The game also desecrates the point of having "skins" for weapons and armor, in any other game, a skin is meant to be unique, it's meant to be difficult / expensive to get as a trophy of dedication, but no that didn't happen.
It may appeal to oldschool gamers.

Carlos Viola deserves a lot of credit for an excellent score.
After that, I fail to see what any of the fuss is about.
The first thing you notice is the writing.  It's stilted and flat, in what may be an attempt to mimic period dialogue but instead comes off as insincere at best.  Playing off all-too-common tropes of abandoned text scattered everywhere, animals being weird, and an explosive case of amnesia, vast portions of the game just feel forced.  The characters aren't coherent and motivations seem to change between episodes.  This isn't about an Unreliable Narrator or the mysteries that lie behind the adventure; the writing is fraught with such problems it simply challenges your ability to stay immersed at all.
Stuff just happens.  Spookily, I suppose you'd say.  Spooky stuff.
All of this adds up to a storyline that's just been ripped straight from HPL's "Rats in the Walls" and Rob Zombie's "Lords of Salem" between extended bouts of coveting Ben Croshaw's 10 year old Chzo Mythos.
Adventure fans won't find much here, either.  Puzzles are trivial when not adolescent, and inventory choices make sure to slick your gears as soon as possible.  The whole experience was over in under 3 hours, and I'm simply disappointed by it.

The graphics are very unique,  it looks like a child drawing. No, i'm not saying it's bad, it's good and interesting. It's a very interesting style. I have only seen 2 games that has child drawing style: this one, and there was other game but i don't remember its name (pew die pie played that game though). I understand that this is a game made for children, pff, a game for three-year-olds. But, really? Girl first lost her teddy bear, then her socks, then umbrella, and finally she lost her barrette. Even her own kitten was "surprised". But there is something good in this "plot", a moral. Yes, the moral in this game is good. It teaches kids that "sometimes" it's easy to lose their own things and it's hard to find them, but there is a way to find them, you can remember where you seen them last time. Remembering where you last seen them can help find it. Not a bad moral.
This game uses a "The Ren'Py Engine", an engine for Visual Novels (Like: Doki Doki Literature Club, Everlasting Summer ,and others). But you know what? This game has more gameplay than a "Visual Novel". It's a simple Point'N"Click, but still has more gameplay than games where you have to read wall of text spoken by chinese girl with big eyes. And this game can become hard, where at first you found first thing, then you found second thing, and suddenly you can't find the third one, and even fourh one. After looking through entire park, you randomly click on a red spot and... Yay, you found umbrella. Places in this game are clickable, you can interact with it. It's simple, but okay.
Overall, not a bad game. It's good, but it's not a masterpiece. It could be better, and i hope to see more games looking like this.

Background: Huge Final Fantasy Fan, Bought a PS4 just for FF7 Remake. Anyways!
Replayability: Now this is a weird one. You can swap out the class of your character by merely going into the menus, and putting the correct equipment on. You then get to experience that class story. It is actually 100% recommended and I would go as far as to say it is required as you need at least 2 classes to obtain the Advanced Classes. But this is true for most Final Fantasy Games.
Combat Options: Final Fantasy XIV is the 2nd attempt at a FF Themed MMORPG. For those of you with vast FF backgrounds the Combat type is FFXII with more control of your character placement and equipment slots. For those not familiar with FFXII it is an Active Time battle played out in the general vicinity of enemy spawn points, meaning you can run by just physically running away but you can also attract more enemies as well.
Social Options: The game has been around enough to have many guilds on every instance Server. Experience is shared between those who participate, not just the initial aggressor which means you can't 100% kill steal something, which is a problem in other games.
Final Thoughts: I have since retired from this game after 628 hours due to Burnout...I have great respect for those who continue the good fight, but I just can't continue.
This has consumed my life, yet still no regrets.

What a strange and beautiful thing Transistor is. With a world as vivid and complex as Cloudbank, it's hard not to applaud Supergiant Games for yet another visually jaw-dropping game. The character design is spot on with an eerie painterly style that is very reminiscient of Bastion with a more "grown up" look and feel. The flip-flop of 2D to 3D animation flows with uncanny brilliance from scene to scene, making the world around Red sink behind her while still demanding the attention it deserves. With environment art and lighting being a spectacle of Transistor, it's gameplay and battle system can be rather monotonous. Your aresenal of skills along with the semi-frustrating movement of Red make combat rather easy-to-do-difficult-to-master scenarios. Unfortuantely, once you do get the hang of it, the game seems to just fly by, even with a few Bastion-esque "limitations" on (things that raise the difficulty of the game but reward the player with boosted experience). The story is intoxicating with the level of mystery. There's so many questions asked and so few answers directly given that it forces the player to push on, to dig deeper, to really try and piece what's happened together with the meager shreds of information that are scattered about and hinted at. It's a game that takes some dedication to understand, and it's not much of an "action-thriller", but it's extremely rewarding in its own unique way.

Well, Supergiant games has done it again. If you liked Bastion, you'll like this game too. The gameplay is definitely more turnbased than Bastion's reflex-based action, but the system works well.
For those of you who haven't played Bastion, Transistor is an incredibly stylish, cyberpunk(ish) game where a mysterious calamity takes over the city (it's a reoccuring theme).
Great music and art. Once you learn the gameplay it's pretty solid. Thoroughly enjoyed.

This is a game series about saving the world in 30 seconds... sort of. Actually anywhere from 2 to 5 minutes in practice but it still has the "Wario Ware roleplaying game" feel about it.
What's kind of interesting and ambitious is that the nature of the parody is naturally running a little dry, so the game doesn't sell itself strictly on its core gimmick anymore. That was a very smart move on the developer's part, in my opinion. It doesn't strictly feel like a series of action levels emulating an RPG this time around. This game is actually a true RPG as well. You explore, grind on enemies, search for collectables, all that good stuff. Just that the original game's arcadey gameplay is the meat of the story segments and are replayable in much the same way (with the ability to turn off the advantage the RPG-side of the game offers). The story is a bit more substantial and the characters have a more coherent and central role, with the ability to set your own party and no restrictions on equipment. It's not quite as *overtly* silly as the original game, it takes itself a bit more seriously -- but not by a whole lot. A defining silly moment for me is when one of the protagonists goes inside a virtual boy game and inside the game you have to use a controller to clear a path. Trippy.
There aren't other gameplay modes besides the standard this time, but those were kinda weak additions to the original game in the first place. Instead you play through different protagonists across time and each story has a distinctly different tone or feel, ranging from deadly serious to a lighthearted Chrono Trigger-style affair. The best part to me has to be the expanded multiplayer functions  -- you can play any of the protagonists! -- and the ability to make your story maps. Being able to share through the steam workshop is a plus too. The interface is a lot better and it's a much more natural PC port than the original and doesn't suffer the same shortcomings i.e. the lag, bugs and cut features.
It's a great sequel and consider it strongly recommended if you enjoy the original. The story has a lot of continuity and connection to the original, a really surprising degree. I'd recommend trying out the original game to really feel some of that impact, but it's far from required to enjoy the whole thing.

The Last Door is a horror point-and-click set in a victorian setting inspired by the works of Edgar Allan Poe and H.P Lovecraft.
I normally avoid point-and-click games alongside graphic adventures, why? Because this games are usually in extreme cryptic, where you end up clicking everything or reading a guide in order to beat the game.
The Last Door is an exception to that rule, here the puzzles are more intuitive and logical than anything, if you pay attention to the game and think logically about it you will easily solve most of the puzzles of the game. That's not the case for every
of the game however. Yes, it's an episodic game and I consider it a mistake, I mean, the game is linear, episode 2 goes right after episode 1, I think it's pointless to divide the game's events in 4 episodes if what happens in those 4 episodes happens in a linear way, yeah I know the game was originally sold through episodes but it's a collection, you can simply put them together. Another problem I find is through episodes 3 and 4 where the things stop being intuitive and logical and become more cryptic. For example there is a part where you need a red lightbulb, you have the lightbulb BUT in order to get the red stuff to paint it you need to go back at a previous location and the game doesn't tell you, you literally have zero reasons to go back at that area.
They are more present in chapter 4 than everything.
Another thing that bothers me is that the game does build up a creepy atmosphere and tension, BUT there is always one or two jumoscares, the cheapest expression of horror, there are about 1 or 2 in every episode and at the most obvious places you would expect, it brokes the tension and atmosphere that the game built.
I don't have any complains story wise, I think everything flows perfectly through the game, yeah there are small parts where the game feels a little convinient but that would be nitpicking from my part as this scenes are usually insignificant, it's quite the good creepy story with lovecraftian-like elements I only have 2 problems with this story:
Despite saying that one of the main appeals is to bury ourselves into the mysteries of his psyche. Jeremiah Devitt is the most bland, boring guy you can imagine, he's as average as your average Joe. He's a guy who's entire dialogue is based around describing stuff, I don't what he likes, what does he think of himself, heck I barely even know the guy at all, I can't think on a small description about the guy. In other graphic adventures and point-and-click games the main protagonist has at least a bit of personality and charisma, think Guybrush of Monkey Island or think Fran Bow of... Fran bow, you know how the dudes are and they make the journey a bit more pleasant.
The ending is... really confusing. It doesn't offer a conclussion at all and even as a pseudo cliffhanger fails because I am scratching my head rather than wondering what will happen to Devitt (Not like I care, though) or Alexandre (He's a character that barely appears through the game yet he has more personality than the protagonist, sadly soemthing that happens through the whole game)
In fact, I didnt understood what what happened there until I saw the recap at the second part (Yes there is a recap at the first episode of the second part, there is a small recap at the beginning of every episode that tells you what happened at the previous episode, this makes the game even more episodic and fragmented) that explained it.
The SFX is more prominent than the music, the music when it appears is really good, the SFX previously mentionated is also really good and since it's somehting you will be hearing for the most part is a good thing. The graphical aspect is meh, my main complain is that the character's sprites look incredibly awkward, look at a trading card and you will see how strange they look like. As for the actual backgrounds they are average, some look good, some don't.
I would talk about the secret's of the game but they are mostly cryptic and hard to get without a guide. The game also counts with "minisodes" that fill the void left between episodes.
Overall, The Last Door is a nice point-and-click game that isn't cryptic which makes it enjoyable. Sadly it's ending it's garbage, the game's quality lowers itself  through episode 3 and 4, the protagonist is pretty bad and the game counts with cheap jumpscare that breaks the inmersion.

As well, the whole weapon upgrade pickup system is a bit flawed. Let me first explain. When you kill someone, they drop a glowy blue block that, when picked up, upgrades your weapon. The problem is: anyone can pickup the block. This means you could be sniping away at one end of the map, but all the blocks are miles away. In a way, this is good because it supports your teammates fighting on the front lines, but you still arent realy getting rewarded for your efforts. As well, you could be fighting on the front lines, get a kill, but have a teammate or enemy run by and pick the block up before you get there. I'll admit, I've done that before, but I still get a little mad when it happens to me :P
In the end, this game is a must buy for TDM-based shooter fans. I hope the devs will tweak the weapon upgrade system a touch, and I don't think the microtransactions are game-breaking (rather just immoral).

While I only spent enough time in the game to complete the tutorial, I feel like I have a good idea of what to expect from its current state. As others have said, please take the EA warning seriously with this title; it's very rough around the edges.
While the graphics are decent for 2016, I feel that's more a testament to UE4 than anything else. Looks aside, the game has a very long way to go (ie. years, not months) before it can be considered for an official launch that stands up to its promise. That's to be expected of course, coming from a small development team, but it's something to consider when making a purchase.
Further, what aspects
been implemented already, still need a lot of work. The main issue with it's current iteration is the combat system, which is frustrating beyond belief. It's very hard to target the creatures of the tutorial, partly due to the fact they're scripted to leap directly up to your feet and you can't really look down close enough to target them at your feet. Compounding the frustration is the long reload animation process and short ammo clip, which leads to a minute or so worth of frustrating combat in order to kill a creature that would otherwise take about five seconds if those problems weren't there.
The second major hurdle they're facing is the voiceovers, which are frankly far too amateur at least for the male protagonist. While they have stated they will be recording new voiceovers before launch, I feel like they should have kept them out of the EA entirely because they do more harm than good as it stands.
While lacking professional actors can be excused, the quality of the writing suffers just as much, if not more. My feeling is that some jokes are lost in the translation, while others simply aren't funny. Perhaps if the game was developed entirely in Russian, directed at that market to start with, and then had the writing and voicing translated before pushed to a US audience, this wouldn't be an issue.
In short, while there's a wonderful vision from the team, it's nowhere near there and in my honest opinion might never reach it. If you're buying this, do so only to support the team's efforts and do not expect to have a game you'll enjoy playing for at least another year or so.

Oh I really enjoyed Transistor. I finished the regular and NG+ playthroughs of the game across a span of about 3-4 days. One could probably rush through the story in as little as 3 hours, or take time unlocking all the lore, doing the side challenges for extra xp and game knowledge, listening to the catchy music, and stopping to smell all the roses along the way and end up taking easily triple or quadruple that.
The game and combat mechanics are pretty fun, with a number of subroutines that you unlock or add to your Transistor weapon as you level up. You form actual skills with those subroutines, using a combination of active slots, support slots (that you slot subroutines into to improve active slots), and four passive slots (buffs to improve your character as a whole). Each subroutine does a different, but thematically similar, thing depending on whether it's currently in an active, passive, or support slot.
There are thus many different possible and valid skill combinations and loadouts, and I found myself constantly swapping back and forth between them as I went through the game, especially once I started doing the side challenges where constraints force you to experiment and find new and efficient (or slow and steady) ways of killing things. In addition, each subroutine represents a character within the game's lore and to unlock the full lore for a character, if so desired, requires you to use their subroutine in each of the three slot types for at least one battle, each slot type unlocking about 1/3 of their character bio.
Combat itself is a combination of real time and planning mode, and is split up largely into a number of self-contained encounters. Planning mode pauses the map and allows you to preview, queue, and execute in quick succession a number of attacks at once in an interface similar to Xcom or Shadowrun Returns, except that you can preview and rewind options before finally committing. There is no miss chance, or random skill damage, damage is constant but modified by variables depending on if the enemy is stunned or backstabbed, for example.
Carrying out actions in the planning mode enables them all to be done in less than a game time second, so it become a power play of sorts whenever planning mode is up, but each ability used in planning mode has a cost which is subtracted from the remaining amount of action points you have in that round of planning. Once you leave planning mode, however, you cannot use most skills until the cooldown for the next planning round is up, leaving you with a few seconds of vulnerability between planning rounds. However, skills used during real time do not trigger a cooldown, and so in some cases it is very beneficial to fight things in real time (or a combination of the two) instead of always in planning mode.
An interesting mechanic that I did not figure out until I was into NG+, was that while you have a certain number of action points to spend per round, not actually spending them all allows your downtime before you next skill use to be proportionally smaller, which is critical versus a certain enemy in the game. On the flip side, spending "over" what you normally have in planning mode locks your skills for that much longer before you can use them again!
The story in the game was pretty neat, if a little on the short side, with a narration style similar to Bastion, but this time the narrator is also the Transistor and with you from the start. Like Bastion, you are dumped right into the plot to start off, and the story is revealed in pieces as you go along. The narration is touching in places, boring in others, but overall quite well done. That ending though. It came unexpected to me the first time, as I didn't think that was the end of the game yet, but hit harder the second time through for me when I knew what was coming. I didn't want to end the game. I did love the ambience though! A combination of the music and the dystopian steampunk background scenery. I am a sucker for night-time big city skylines, and the art in this game evoked so many wistful memories.
A couple cons of the game: It's very easy to miss certain lore terminals and the game often doesn't let you back up if you went a little too far in one direction. It is often not obvious which way is "onward" and which way is a dead end with a lore piece. Your only options then are to load back from the last save (and you can only save at certain locations, though there is pretty much one before or after nearly every fight) or wait until NG+ to see what you missed. Or YouTube. The narrator is also overly talkative at times, though I guess that's a personality trait. There are also several plot holes in the story to me still, like *why* the Transistor's ownership got passed over to Red, and several other things I feel are little plot holes here and there that are not adequately explained.

Game Name: Transistor
Original Release: 2014
Personal Rating: A
Estimated Playtime:18 Hours
Multiplayer/Coop?: None
Played on: Steam Controller
Transistor is an indie game created from the same makers of Bastion. It is a unique rpg that has an interesting balance between turn-based gameplay and real time gameplay.
Controls: When I played this, I used the Steam Controller. It wasn’t hard to use at all, and it seemed rather natural to use a controller with the game. Joystick seemed prime for the movement option, and the four buttons on the face of the controller worked really well with the four skills that you have to use in-game.
Graphics: This isn’t a Crysis level of graphics. Coming straight out of an indie studio, it seems unique and more like art. Cut-scenes mix in well with the 2.5D gameplay, and it’s easy to figure out what is happening as time goes on.
Music: Much like Bastion, Supergiant Games (the creators) release excellent soundtracks and this is no exception. Between the songs that you unlock and Red’s (the Main Character) humming, you find yourself playing the game for the music instead of the gameplay.
Overall: Transistor has a unique and potent combination of great music, easy controls and compelling gameplay, all within a fun game with an interesting plot. No super strategy is needed as you will eventually figure out the game throughout time. I would recommend it at any price, but it does drop down during the sales.

"Half Minute Hero: The Second Coming" is the sequel to Marvelous's Half Minute Hero, which I strongly suggest playing first. The first game is shorter, lighter, and a good indicator of how you'll feel about the sequel. If you liked the first game, you'll also like the sequel. If you didn't like the first one because it didn't feel enough like a JRPG, you should try this one. If you simply didn't like the first game, you won't like this one either.
I'm going to write this review as though you're familiar with the first game.
Quick summary:
- Much longer than the first game. Supports multiplayer with lobbies and Community Maps. Community Maps are awesome and could add a lot of replayability.
- Very much a sequel to Half Minute Hero. It's a JRPG/Puzzle/Action hybrid that focuses on fun, but allows for challenge.
- Only has RPG-mode, so Evil Lord/Princess/Knight fans are out of luck. RPG-mode fans are in for a huge treat.
- Story is more of a take on epic SNES RPGs (e.g. Final Fantasy VI) than of classic NES RPGs (e.g. Dragon Quest).
- Story mode less arcade-y. All the half-minute quests are in the framework of a traditional overworld RPG, although quests are individually replayable with leaderboards.
- Lots of secret equipment/party members, as well as significant post story content. Maybe a 20-40 hour game, unless you really get into score attack or user levels.
- Lots of extra modes, notably user generated levels and infinite play modes.
- Music, graphics (retro 16 bit), and gameplay elements are all a big upgrade over the original.
From all this, you can probably tell if you'd like the game or not. It's definitely not for everyone. I personally loved it. I'm arbitrarily giving it a score of 9, mostly because it's a niche game and I'd understand people who find it repetitive. I'll go into much more detail now.
- GAMEPLAY -
Like in the original, you take control of different main characters in different eras. Unlike the original, this game plays much more like a traditional JRPG. It is huge world with a lot of text and a lot of cutscenes. You explore an overworld map, fight battles, and progress the story. You equip yourself, you choose your party members, you choose your battle formations, you can switch classes, and you can look for secrets.
How does the overworld map work? You wander around and any leveling you do contributes to your "global level." Grinding this way is slow, but you do get unlimited dash. Grinding isn't necessary to beat the main game at all. As you explore, you run into areas that lock you into a subarea and start a Half Minute Quest. Your starting level is your global level and the quest plays out a lot like a quest from the original game, in which you have thirty seconds to defeat an Evil Lord before they destroy the world. Sometimes you have to trigger certain events, like finding a key or building a bridge, in order to find and defeat the boss. You can pay a money hungry goddess to reset your thirty second timer. When you finish the quest, the barriers and time limit go away and you reset to your global level. And you continue on like you were playing a traditional JRPG.
The basic game mechanics are almost exactly like the first game, except that you can see your enemies. If you're at a much a higher level than the enemy, you won't be forced into a battle screen when you touch them... you'll just automatically win. The quests are still very creative in this game and there are lots of new gimmicks (hope you don't mind solving ice puzzles or dealing with flipped controls in 30 seconds...) Some of the quests feel really epic. It's a lot of fun.
In addition to the five part story mode, there are four other modes to play.
Time Attack: You can replay the quests you've unlocked from story mode. You can freely set your equipment, party, and formation to go for a high score.
Infinite Mode: You fight an infinite number of evil lords. You go through different maps and have to kill ten evil lords that randomly spawn in the stage. After you beat ten, you move to a different stage and repeat until you can't restart the timer.
Map Editor: Make/Share your own quests. This is pretty well done and not too hard to use. You can search for, download, and play other people's quests. Most of the highly ranked quests are really fun.
Battle: Multiplayer mode, you compete with other people to defeat the evil lord first. There are eight different maps in this mode.
- STORY -
The story is a lot richer and more serious this time around, but it still keeps its tongue-in-cheek tone. It is a continuation to the original Half Minute Hero story. There are actually a lot of callbacks to the first game. A surprising amount of familiar faces show up again as villians, heroes, or both. It's a good take on the huge RPGs of the SNES era. I enjoyed the story (especially from the second chapter onwards), but I could understand people thinking it's too slow or too cliche (even though it's cliche on purpose.)
The story mode follows three generations of heroes: Yuusha, Yushia, and Yuja. Yuusha is a play on the amnesiac, emo hero. He's even got one wing. He's captain of the royal forces on a special mission. Although he has a cold demeanor, he's a very caring guy. Yushia is a student of the Goddess school in a world ruled by the Empire. She's a bit naive and has to deal with a crazy escalating situation. Yuja is a brawn over brains kind of guy who's living in a post-apocalyptic type world that's been ruined by the gods. Each story mostly deals with saving the world within 30 seconds, but the overarching threat is different each time and each story has its own themes. Each of the heroes makes a contract with a Time Goddess who will reset time for them... for an increasingly high fee. Both main characters and supporting cast are pretty endearing.
As you can guess, this game addresses a lot of RPG tropes. You get lots of adventure, romance, betrayal, artifact collecting, and plot twists. There are evil empires, dark lords, time streams, and rivals to fight. You take on evil groups like the "Eight Elementals", "The Three Generals", the "Dark Time Goddess", and the "Venus Seven." The creators use a lot of cliches, but they use them knowingly. The story is clearly a take on character driven SNES-rpgs, especially Final Fantasy.
- PRESENTATION -
The graphics follow the original Half Minute Hero's retro look, although this time around, the style is much closer to 16-bit RPGs of the SNES era. If you like that look, you'll love the art. There are a ton of sprites and a ton of maps. Most of the main characters and villians have concept art you can collect in game. The concepts were drawn by different artists and it's fun to compare the concept to the actual sprite.
The music is really great and done by a large group of great composers. There are vocal songs this time too, which add a really epic feel.
- CLOSING -
I'm a huge Half Minute Hero fan and grew up playing SNES RPGs, so I really loved this game. It's not just more of the same, I'd say the developers took even bigger risks this time by trying to make a full length game. It feels like a loving, fast paced take on a great traditional RPG.
Best game in a while.

You sit in the office. Day after day. The days blend into each other.
Every time someone hands you a passport, you have to decide. Do you glanse over the information quickly, or do you carefully inspect everything?
More stamped passports mean more food. Your son is sick. Your mother-in-law died yesterday.
You check the passport, stamp it, shove it back at the man, along with all the other papers.
You call the next person in as soon as the previous one steps out of the booth. The moment you take their passport, a ticket is printed out. The previous man's ID card's image hadn't matched. You hardly ever check the pictures anymore, they're rarely different and who'd be stupid enough to get a fake ID card with the wrong image?
You've gotten too many tickets today. You're too tired and stressed out. You wonder how long it'll take until they fire you. Maybe you'll starve before that happens.
Well. What's done is done. You wonder whether you should save on heating or food. Maybe you should just let your son die.
Glory to Arstotzka.
