The world is not what it seems. There is a threshold between this world and the next. The last door awaits...
It's an amazing feat how many emotions these developers managed to conjure up from as few pixels as possible. Make no mistake, this is a scary game. It'll draw you into its Lovecraftian world of loss, madness and fear over the course of the four episodes, and the foreboding atmosphere it builds up over their course is in a league of its own.
It's difficult to describe how this game manages to be scary to those who have not played it. It's due to the phenomenal story for the most part, but also the masterful sound design. As events take a turn for the worse, you'll hear howling behind walls or singing from someone who isn't there or hear footsteps following you.
Perhaps ironically, this game isn't one that'll force you to go on a pixel hunt for the next item. It's very clear what you can and cannot use, what items to combine, and what interactions you have left. Usually, in a point and click game, I'll resort to using a walkthrough for one part at least, but this wasn't the case with The Last Door. These developers took their time to make it accessible for all types of players. It's clear how much they cared for this project.
Kudos to Carlos Viola for the brilliant soundtrack. Not only does it work perfectly for this game, but I've found it atmospheric enough to listen to while reading horror. It's far more listenable when a horror game goes for a memorable soundtrack, rather than a generic scary one. "Crows over the city" is probably the best theme tune for a horror game I've heard.
By the time I got to the final episode, I was hopelessly hooked on this series, but I wanted to turn it off because that episode is terrifying. There's an achievement called "The Angels Protect This House", that I'd suggest reading before playing the final episode. It made me dread playing it, and I promise you, you'll dread turning your back on them.
I'd suggest this game to anyone remotely interested in Lovecraft, or fear of the unknown.

Even though the first chapter of the first season is available for free online, its atmosphere doesn't remotely scratch the surface of the incredibly vast range of feelings that the series causes the player to experience - admittedly, most of the emotions revolving around the core feeling of horror.
The Last Door is a game that should be left completely unspoiled, and even if I tried to ruin someone's joy of experiencing this dark journey for themselves, there is an immense amount of lore, events, and characters to it, so it would be incredibly difficult to even semi-accurately reflect the brilliance of this series.
The game is not only praised by me for its story and writing - don't get me wrong, I'd still claim it to be one of the best puzzle or horror games I've ever played with other elements being sub-par. It isn't, however, the case with The Last Door. I tried to find flaws with the game and couldn't find anything that everyone could agree with it being a flaw. Let me begin with the things that some people could find undesirable:
-No voice-overs. Sure, some people are lazy and don't want to read much. To those people I can only say - fair enough. However, even if you don't enjoy reading because it might bore you, I very much doubt that The Last Door will make you not want to read the dialogues or notes that you may stumble upon, as they help uncover the story in an incredibly fascinating way. If you're still reading this - perfect. Now on to why I don't think that the lack of voice-overs is an issue. It leaves you, the player, free to assign all the characters your own imaginary voices - perhaps to you one character sounds rough and strong, while to someone else they might sound sensitive and caring, judging by their words. There is also always a chance that voices would damage the game's atmosphere, as without them, the player can listen to The Last Door's music - there is a plethora of tracks, all of them carefully composed to suit the atmosphere of the location the player is in.
-Jumpscares. Some people enjoy them, some don't. I belong to the group of the latter. The amount of them in the game is very low, and I have to admit that they're really well-executed, even though I got scared by none of them. However, they do help shape the atmosphere of the location and after the initial feeling of being caught off-guard has passed, the player is left with being disturbed by what had happened.
Now, with cons out of the way, let me go over the pros!
-The audio. I love music - I'm absolutely fascinated by it, from composing and playing to listening to it. Music can be really beautiful and stimulating; it can cause us to feel different emotions and get us in different moods. It can illustrate the atmosphere of something or some situation better than any words ever could. That is precisely what The Last Door's soundtracks do. Apart from being mostly extremely enjoyable to listen to due to their composition and execution, they set the feeling that locations or events carry with them. The ones that aren't extremely enjoyable? Those would be the few tracks that are really dissonant (i.e. they make you wince when you listen to them, which doesn't make them bad per se, mind you. For example try playing or looking up a tritone, which is a very much dissonant interval) and are not to be enjoyed, but they create this really haunting atmosphere.
-The graphics. It seems that a lot of people are divided here; The Last Door's graphics are really pixelated by design. Sure, it is sometimes difficult to make out what is what, I suppose, even though it never prevented me or made it more difficult for me to progress. Personally, I really enjoy that stylistic choice. Not because I am a fan of pixelated graphics, I usually prefer it when there is a lot of detail. So why do I enjoy this world of pixels? Again, it's because it leaves you, the player, free to interpret what's going on - to shape the looks of the locations and chaaracters for yourself. What you see on the screen is merely a canvas with a few outlines, and your mind is the brush, completing the painting. You can never see the face of any character, and so you're left to imagine whaat they look like for yourself, to shape their looks the way you believe fits best, and I find that amazing.
-The storyline (spoiler-free). *Page left intentially blank*
-The characters (spoiler-free). Every person that appears in the game has their own personality, even ones that barely speak or interact with the player. You are guaranteed to find some characters that you will like, and some that you will hate, most likely the moment you read their first line of dialogue. They also look different in terms of appearance, even though they're heavily pixelated. The player can also learn more about many of them through reading various notes that can be found in the game's world. I'd love to elaborate, but then spoilers would inevitably occur.
-The controls. Well, it's point and click, so a mouse is all you need. You just click on objects, you can combine some of them, and so on. There's no dragging, quick-time events, or anything else. You just click to move your character around, go to different locations, and interact with your surroundings. Really straight-forward.
-The puzzles. At first you might get stuck here and there occasionally, not knowing what to do. You might need to look up guides to just learn where you're supposed to use that one item you have to progress because you're utterly lost. After a while, hopefully sooner than later, you will get used to the puzzles and will have much less difficulty figuring out what to do. It may temporarily damage the immersion, but it might very well be just me who got stuck a few times, not knowing what to do. It is, of course, possible to figure it all out without any guide, but they're there, just in case you might need them.
*TL;DR/Conclusion here*
So, what do I think of The Last Door? In short, it's a game that has left me stunned and longing for more, for some game or any other medium that would make me feel similar emotions to the ones I felt while playing this one. It made me at times scared, or feeling sympathy towards certain characters, while despising others, all while I was well-aware that they are perfectly fictional. However, two emotions that were constantly there while I was playing The Last Door were being disturbed to a various degree, and the utter curiosity to discover what was waiting for me next.
Thank you for reading my review, and I wish you a good day.

The radio stations have extremely good music compared to other games like GTA. In addition, the oriental-style OST added to the immersion factor.
Combat: 9 / 10
The combos prevent button mashing while keeping it interesting. Fighting is very fluid, and shooting is solid. Weapons can be picked up, and the environment around you can be used to defeat your enemies in entertaining and enjoyable ways. Also, as small of a feature as it is, the blood forming on combatants and inanimate objects give the feeling that you're really doing something.
World: 9.75 / 10
This is probably the best world I've seen in an open world game comparable to GTA and others. The city sounds, small alleyways, street vendors, city lights, bystanders, and beautiful weather bring this area together in a living, immersive, atmospheric, awesome world. My only complaint is that there aren't many areas with nature, and instead the world is 95% city.
Overall: 52 points out of 60. A must buy for those who love any of the following: PORK BUNS, open world games, fighting games, crime games, and of course, the amazing PORK BUN. All hail PORK BUN.

"Minimum" is a fitting name. There is minimal innovation here, and the minimum number of active players for it to not be officially dead. There's nothing overwhelmingly bad about Minimum, it's just average. The store page makes comparisions to twitch shooters and MOBAs, neither elements actually exist in the game. Combat is third-person and rather slow, with regenerating health and unlimited ammo. Strategy is pretty barren, as all characters are the same. Some weapons can provide utility in area control or slowing enemies, but they must be crafted in the awkward Blueprints system.
The core game mode is team deathmatch with minor lane-pushing elements. Two titans spawn and meet in the lane, while everyone shoots them or shoots each other. Killing enemies lets you pick up orbs to "customize" your weapons in linear upgrades. "Customize" normally means options, but this is all automatic. These upgrades are decreased when you die, which means you
weaken a fed opponent, but good luck. Armor can be applied and upgraded, which offers some real choices, but those upgrades are never lost in death. An opponent with max weapons and max armor will always be a problem. To make snowballing worse, there is a creep-farming period after both titans die. The team with more damage will destroy creeps quicker, and pressure the weaker team from farming creeps. The next Titan spawn will consistently be stronger for the snowballing team, enabling them to trap the weaker team in the spawn. A titan with creep advantage will win the fight and push naturally, and the only way to stop it is for the weaker team to shoot it down. Base turrets are pitiful against Titans, and there is little to stop opponents from filling your base with unlimited bullets while hugging cover.
The graphics style is interesting, but the game lacks engagement. Unlocking content is a confusing process with 4 different unlocking resources in a
. The progression system is trying to keep players hooked, but it clearly hasn't worked. Despite developer statements of over 120 thousand sales, there are only a few hundred active players. See
for details.

The game doesn't do anything great enough to justify consideration, and I don't see new content other than maps and skins. The potential was taken to the minimum, and playerbase rests at the minimum, how fitting.

Game Name: Transistor
Original Release: 2014
Personal Rating: A
Estimated Playtime:18 Hours
Multiplayer/Coop?: None
Played on: Steam Controller
Transistor is an indie game created from the same makers of Bastion. It is a unique rpg that has an interesting balance between turn-based gameplay and real time gameplay.
Controls: When I played this, I used the Steam Controller. It wasn’t hard to use at all, and it seemed rather natural to use a controller with the game. Joystick seemed prime for the movement option, and the four buttons on the face of the controller worked really well with the four skills that you have to use in-game.
Graphics: This isn’t a Crysis level of graphics. Coming straight out of an indie studio, it seems unique and more like art. Cut-scenes mix in well with the 2.5D gameplay, and it’s easy to figure out what is happening as time goes on.
Music: Much like Bastion, Supergiant Games (the creators) release excellent soundtracks and this is no exception. Between the songs that you unlock and Red’s (the Main Character) humming, you find yourself playing the game for the music instead of the gameplay.
Overall: Transistor has a unique and potent combination of great music, easy controls and compelling gameplay, all within a fun game with an interesting plot. No super strategy is needed as you will eventually figure out the game throughout time. I would recommend it at any price, but it does drop down during the sales.

Before I review this game, I'd like to give information about myself (the reviewer) first.
I've been playing point & click games since 1990 on Commodore64, Amiga, PC and own quite a large collection.
The product review is for the first season game, which I've played from the beginning to the end.
Visual: While most of you may not like the pixel graphics, I did like them in the game. It didn't bother me at all and actually I was quite impressed as to how much detail you can see in the pixel art itself. If you played one of the old Lucas Arts series in the early 90s before and you loved it, you'll love this one too. The effort of detail and coloured contrast they put in, gives it a beautiful realistic look, but yet it preserves the feel of a retro classic point & click game.
Audio: High quality stereo sound, the sound fx are moving from one ear to another as you're moving your character. The music gives also the atmosphere of a "creepy" game, since it's been designed to be a little scary. Melodies / music are somewhat similar to what you would expect in an old-fashioned horror movie. There are no character voices, just pure background music and sound effects.
Game Control: quite good. There is no "push, pull, take, use..." etc. It's simply point & click. Try out a few cominations from your inventory with objects in the game. No keyboard use, just mouse.

Story: captivating. I really liked the story, making me want to finish the game and also play the next season. I won't go into the story on this occasion, as obviously I don't want to spoil anything. Also the reading involved in the game is not too much in comparison to some other p&c games, where you mostly skip dialogs because it's somewhat useless information or boring. Note, there are very little puzzles in the game! Puzzles are more towards the end, but they are easily solved.
If you have a slight interest in this point & click game / adventure, I highly recommend it.

I loved Sleeping Dogs begining to end, with it's great radio soundtrack, interesting story and characters, amazing fighting mechanics which will actually keep you from button mashing, and it's atmospheric and immersive world. A game like this will really make you wish it was first person.
Now, on with the ratings.
Story: 8.25 / 10
You play as undercover cop Wei Shen, working with the Hong Kong Police Department to bring down triad gangs in Hong Kong upon moving back to the city after living in the United States.
Characters: 9 / 10
I felt the characters were unique and amazing in their own way.
Missions: 7.5 / 10
Although the main story missions were somewhat cliched and mostly combat-oriented, I did have fun with them. The activities are quite lacking, but the side missions are very enjoyable.
Soundtrack: 8 / 10
The radio stations have extremely good music compared to other games like GTA. In addition, the oriental-style OST added to the immersion factor.
Combat: 9 / 10
The combos prevent button mashing while keeping it interesting. Fighting is very fluid, and shooting is solid. Weapons can be picked up, and the environment around you can be used to defeat your enemies in entertaining and enjoyable ways. Also, as small of a feature as it is, the blood forming on combatants and inanimate objects give the feeling that you're really doing something.
World: 9.75 / 10
This is probably the best world I've seen in an open world game comparable to GTA and others. The city sounds, small alleyways, street vendors, city lights, bystanders, and beautiful weather bring this area together in a living, immersive, atmospheric, awesome world. My only complaint is that there aren't many areas with nature, and instead the world is 95% city.
Overall: 52 points out of 60. A must buy for those who love any of the following: PORK BUNS, open world games, fighting games, crime games, and of course, the amazing PORK BUN. All hail PORK BUN.

A bad server browser, poor audio and visual effects design, a limited amount of maps and imbalanced melee weapons bring down would could have been a well-off third person shooter.
The server browser button opens up a spreadsheet in a window in the steam overlay and from it you can see the IP, player count, and gamemode of each server but you CANNOT see the ping. I don't know of a solid multiplayer title that does display ping times in the server browser. Even in game I assume the ping amount that is seen in the scoreboard is false. I have 20-28 ping yet am rubberbanding and seeing delays in item pickups, delays in player deaths, and am not seeing all bounce minigun projectiles appear while firing is how I assume the ping number is false.
The audio fades out when you are at low health and even before then, many weapons sound as powerful as water pistols, like the speed shotgun. The audio fade makes it very difficult to hear incoming fire, and does not do a good job of discerning the already blocky(literrally) weapons one another. The visual choices of what should be displayed in the HUD(hint - a healthbar, which isn't) don't really make sense. Your equipment recharge icon is very small so it's difficult to tell when exactly it will be ready again. Instead of a health bar you can see how much health you have by purely guessing from how yellow and bright your body is. Seriously, there is not way of understanding exactly how much health you have at any one time. This game more than many others should show your health amounts, especially when there are weapon upgrades that do more damage the more they are upgraded, and when armor pieces either increase damage done to you or increase maximum health or increase resistances to certain damage types. If it was a game with fixed health amounts and fixed weapon damages then I could understand, I wouldn't need to know the exact amount of hp to see if I am winning a fight or not, or whether or not I can peak one more time for an extra shotgun blast for a kill, knowing I can trade a hit and still win. In this game you just guess. In addition to those poor visual design choices there are the effects. Upgrading your katanas will allow you to have fire burst in a significant area around you, many times making sight impossible past the fire. having very bright and obnoxious weapon effects on characters makes trying to tell the already innacurate hp to brightness system even worse.
A perfect example of bad sound design is the fact that there is a hitmarker placed near your crosshair everytime you land a hit and the option of turning on hit sounds. Even the designer(s) knew it was bad.
But all of this is still bearable, despite the sounds, server browser, visuals, the unlock system being quite a pain to grind through and the maps being very few, the game itself is very fun... until someone uses the katanas.
The katanas, any type really, are the strongest weapon in the game and are very overpowered. They kill faster than any weapon in the game, have a large hit radius(even vertically) and do not require any ammunition or aim, as they will turn you in the direction of your opponent on every attack. The only way to kill a player with a katana is to kill them before they get close to you which is very difficult when you can see around corners with the 3rd person camera, can sprint and can use the alternate fire button to instantly close the distance on an opponent. Coupled with the fact that many weapons have a very substantial time to kill, unless you are in a very open area and the katana-wielder is far away, they will get to you 4/5 times and at that point you will not get away. They are simply ridiculous and most TDM matches come down to how many people are using katanas on each time. Every other weapon in the game requires you to put the enemy in your crosshair while trying to get yourself out of theirs. The katanas don't care and sword fights boil down to 2 players spamming attacks wildly and uncontrollably in an attempt to kill the other player. Due to the fact katanas can close gaps instantly means they are massively overpowered and have no direct counter other than using certain items to evade and run away from the sword.

Endless Sky is a freeform economic space adventure that puts you in the pilot seat of a pathetically weak ship (at first) with the promise of riches in your future. To do so, you must decide whether you will follow the law or operate outside of it. Though the economy is simple and it is very easy to find a lucrative trade route and then supplement it with jobs, the universe itself is more than alive enough to keep you engrossed.
In my time, I have had the exquisite pleasure of desperately fleeing across outer rim worlds from a vastly superior pirate fleet that refused to give up its pursuit, periously weaving my way through a system engrossed in a massive all out battle, and dogfighting a significantly better ship while my lumbering merchant ships aligned for a jump out of a losing fight.
In this time, I've also had to learn how to bum hyperdrive fuel off of other ships when I warp into a new sector only to learn there is no civilization there, abandon a crippled member of my fleet to pirates in order to ensure the survival of my remaining ships, and bribe a successful pirate not to finish my sorry self off.
Though by no means a perfect game, it is an engrossing and absolutely enjoyable experience that I recommend entirely to fans of economic sandboxes or space settings.

I quit playin this not long ago, and now that the irritation has subsided, here's my experience.
tl;dr - Really good mmorpg(8/10), prolly the worst FF(2/10) I've ever played.
The easy stuff first: The visuals are beautiful, it's FF after all. The sound is worth the price of admission alone. Seriously, I've played mmorpgs for a long time, and it doesn't take much longer than a few days for the game music to get muted and my own tunes turned on...for this game it took over a month, the soundtrack is just that good.
The storylines aren't bad. Nothing special, but the way FF uses its cutscenes it gets ya engrossed, so you find yourself actually listening to the voice acting and even paying attention to what they're saying...from time to time.
The crafting system is so damn close to perfect and totally unique, if it weren't for the RNG aspect it would be perfection.
You make 1 character, and they can level all the things. Changing jobs is easy as switching your main weapon, it's great.
Ok, that's about it for the good stuff. Now the bad:
The job system is trash. Nevermind the combat itself feels like a very slow WoW rotation, there's basically no customization in the jobs at all. You cross class skills, once unlocked through leveling, and you have materia sockets in your gear, and that's all the customization ya get. The amount of skills able to be CC'd is laughably small, and if you've every played any other mmorpg with sockets you already know how many options that isn't.
The crafting system actually feels like it was the main job system, cause there's actually options there, but one thing brings it down, and this one thing actually hurts many other aspects of the game: The RNG.
The RNG is just...rage-inducing.
Everything about this game feels too balanced, to the point where the devs chose balance over fun.
Also, loldrg is alive and well.

I should preface this review by saying I have only spent around 250 hours playing this game, and still have a fair amount of content to experience. While 250 hours is quite an investment for most types of games, I feel for games as large as MMOs I am still a relatively new player. There’s tons of sub-content such as Gold Saucer and player housing that I don’t touch on in this review and that probably deserve mentioning, but to touch on every aspect of this game would be to write a novel rather than a review.
Although FFXIV is an MMO, it is still a Final Fantasy title, and to me at least, it lives up to that standard. To date it’s the only MMO where I can recognize and remember the names of NPCs that have never participated in any fights by their appearance only, and care about those characters. I strongly encourage new players to take the time to read the quest dialog for the main quest, as it gets good, especially the quests leading up to Heavensward content. Other side quest lines, such as class/job quests and beast tribe quests, also follow a story arc, and can be quite entertaining, if not a little formulaic.
FFXIV marks a decided shift from FFXI to more solo-friendly content. The majority of the content it offers can be completed solo by any class or job. I personally really appreciate this, as it allows me to do whatever it is that I want to do (for the most part) without worrying about finding a party with the same agenda. Others may argue it undermines the sense of community central to most MMO’s, and I can appreciate that argument. However, players who seek out and engage the FFXIV community will find one that is much less toxic than other popular MMOs today.
Graphically speaking, FFXIV is absolutely gorgeous. There is overall much less real estate than MMOs like WoW, but each zone is beautiful and unique (except Thanalan, deserts are boring). Views of Limsa Lominsa lit up at night under a starry sky from the next zone over are breathtaking. Walking through the deepest part of the Sylphlands, with its orange lanterns and purple hues, is equally enchanting. The game easily runs at a smooth 60 FPS (on my rig at least), and supports high and ultra-wide screen resolutions. Little details like nets and scaffolding on cliff sides to prevent erosion and catch falling rocks show the attention to detail that went into creating this game and its environments.
FFXIV has an insane amount of polish. This is best exemplified I feel by the custom chat log menu, an obscure menu several layers down that allows you to control what kinds of information appear in your chat log. When creating custom chat logs, each type of information that can be displayed is given an example in the menu. For the most part, the examples are for a player named “Cloud Strife”, and include jokes about and references to Final Fantasy VII.
FFXIV brings back the ability to master many different jobs and classes on one character, which is a welcome feature. The crafting/gathering system in FFXIV is also unique and engaging, with a variety of skills that have many different effects on the item being crafted or gathered. Another unique feature is cross-class skills, which allows certain skills unlocked in other jobs or classes to be accessible while playing different jobs or classes. These skills usually improve performance of other classes significantly, and in some situations are nearly mandatory to use.
Final Fantasy XIV is a paid MMO, but offers players willing to devote to a single character a small discount. Other items, such as costumes, mounts, and even in-game weddings are available to purchase through the Mog Station, Square Enix’s FFXIV account management portal. A nice feature here is the ability to link payment for monthly subscriptions and other additional content to your steam account.
Final Fantasy XIV isn’t without its share of problems, however. After reaching cap, expect to grind the same dungeon again and again to grind tokens to get your gear level up in order to participate in raid
content. For those players wanting to jump right into Heavensward content, you’ll need to first complete all the story quests between the end of the main scenario and the beginning of Heavensward, a whopping 100 story quests. PVP is limited to designated zones, and has little purpose. Additionally, nearly all skills are tied to a 2-second global cooldown, slowing down the pace of battle significantly. While I personally didn’t mind this too much, this was the primary complaint from other friends of mine with far more time invested in MMOs. It’s also worth mentioning that until rather recently, gold farming chat spam was a real problem. In main towns, it was fairly common to get several gold selling site PMs a minute. As of this review, Square has somehow managed to COMPLETELY eliminate the problem. I haven’t seen ANY real-money trading spam in my chat logs at all in the past two weeks.
In the end, FFXIV feels like a celebration of Final Fantasy as a franchise. It freely borrows assets such as music, characters, and enemies from previous titles, and uses them to augment a base experience that is unique and fun to play. I highly recommend it to fans of either Final Fantasy or MMOs in general, and expect to play it for many hours to come.

It's a solid game. If you liked the original HMH, you'll like this. Just make sure to turn off skill animations. Trust me >_>
Unfortunately, this port leaves unchanged what I felt was one of the greatest flaws of the PSP version, which is that the time trial mode doesn't limit equipment you can use in any meaningful fashion. This makes the mode extremely boring (having OP equipment makes most stages complete jokes), which is a shame; trying to get better and better times on each stage is what made the first game awesome.
Furthermore, the translation is... questionable at best. Much of the original characters' charm is gone (for instance, there's a character whose entire shtick is that she tries to act dignified, winds up getting angered by something, and then tries to switch back to formal speech as if nothing had happened; in the translation, she never acts dignified, barely sounds like she's getting mad, and then says "Yes, I would." Yes, I would have liked her to be localized better); literally translated names make puns unintelligible ("Yuusha" literally means "hero"... Why leave this untranslated? And there's one character whose name is a shortened version of his name in the previous game, but the names in the translation are completely different!); and "Ojisama" was translated as "Geezer," which makes me cry.
I realize I've been mostly negative, so let me say again: the core gameplay is still solid. If you treat it as a JPRG with a time-limit twist, you'll be in love. But after how superb the localization of the first game was, and how addicting and satisfying it was to solve the puzzles that were the individual level runs in the original, it's a shame to see the ball dropped so... thoroughly.

it's a combination of factors :

-losing all your life makes you lose functions that you may need for future combats
-no manual saves, all autosaves. you made the mistake to finish a battle with too many lost functions ? you might be stuck then (didn't happen to me but I see how that could happen, I got a few frustrating combat battles though)
-turn() is both OP & your worst vulnerability, because when it's on CD you can't use most abilities unless modified in a way
-there's ways to not use turn that kinda break the game

examples :  tractor beam that does a ton of damage, shield himself & another enemy for total invulnerability, cloak forcing you to wait till it's out of cloaking, a huge pushing type of enemy that will fill your screen of so many particles & graphic effects that you lose sight of your character.
-in essence in this game, everyone is OP, you are OP and can oneturn() most enemies in this game, but so can enemies.
changing your build depending on next batch of enemies is effectively the solution...

the interface to install/uninstall functions is also horribly unpractical albeit beautiful.

Surprisingly effective point-and-click horror. I was genuinely surprised how much I got into the atmosphere at times despite (or perhaps because of?) the simplistic graphics. There are many secrets and references to Victorian horror classics, but the game stands on its own as an intriguing mystery. Unlike many point-and-click puzzle games of olden days, the puzzles in The Last Door rarely get frustratingly obscure, allowing you to focus on the story and atmosphere. The melancholy, elegant and suspenseful music truly elevates the game beyond its pixelated trappings. The episodes are short, about an hour each, which I found the perfect length for such a simple game. I was so pleased with season 1 that upon finishing it, I immediately bought season 2.
Creates an ominous atmosphere and is enjoyable to play.

Yes, art, clad in the clothes of old school pixelated point-and-click adventure with mostly logical but sometimes absurd problems to solve and in that way to go on with the plot. First, the atmosphere. It gets you twitching with the sudden images and makes your hand hair stand with its soundscape, and all this is done with very crude and suggested graphics. Then, the legacy. With sometimes subtle nods, sometimes heavy underlining, it borrows and tips its hat off to numerous sources of classic horror literature and film. I'm not spoiling much by saying that friends of Poe, Lovecraft and several pieces of Gothic horror get served first and foremost, but film buffs will have their share too, especially with the 3rd episode. Quite quick to play through, clever enough to get you puzzled in a few places, all thrills and pleasant chills. On the other hand it is a tour de force of "less is more", on the other hand you find plenty inside. I'm already thrilled to start the episode 2 after finishing the minisode extras. Heavily recommended. Don't wait. Buy it already.

This game probably is my favourite Open World game so far. With GTA and others, I usually get bored pretty fast, but not with this one. You are an undercover cop infiltrating the Hong Kong underground. Combat-wise, there is a lot of engaging bare-hand fighting.
The story kept me entertained and coming back for more. There has been put quite some effort in character-development. The protagonist isn't an empty shell, but filled with personality.
The game looks great. The city is very atmospheric, especially when walking through Hong Kong at night. Personally, I really liked the dynamic weather system - the streets look amazing when it's raining.
Fighting, running, driving, shooting - everything in this game controls nicely. Some people complained about the driving but I really can't understand why. It's not a racing game focusing on driving only, so why would anyone expect perfect physics? The cars and motorcycles control fine (and differently depending on the model) and drifting around corners is a lot of fun (use the handbrake). I loved the arrows displayed directly on the street, telling you which turns to take when driving to a waypoint (hate looking at the tiny map in GTA).
Go play this game. This is the definite edition with polished graphics and all the available DLC. I bought it during the Holiday Sale and it was totally worth it. Also, it has a Nimbus-Cloud-style Motorcycle ;)

I still have chills running down my spine writing this review...
Fingerbones is absolutely wonderful. From a horror perspective, there are very few problems I had with it. Despite the somewhat slower controls when you walk over objects you walk at a very slow pace and everything you interact with in The Bunker serves to add more tension that you read as you continue to read and follow the trail of breadcrumbs. Everytime you unlock a new secret you have to go back up to the keyboard, type it in, and then walk back to the previously locked door, which serves to add even more stress and mystery as you return. Oh, and the sound of a child crying and screaming is pretty terrifying, too.
Graphically speaking, Fingerbones has a Minecraft-esque vibe (which might be more visually appealing to people who want a similar manner of storytelling like "the static speaks my name" and want specifically better looking graphics). But the story is interesting as you learn more and more about a father, his unfortunate daughter, and The Bunker. Plus, the game is totally jumpscare-free, and yet the amount of tension and ultimate fear you feel by the end of the game is absolutely overwhelming. In 16 minutes, my palms were as damp as the Amazon Rain Forest.
Fingerbones is a true testament of how good horror is made and paced, and how even a single person can create a great game. But you probably already knew that from Undertale.

This is a somewhat lengthy review, so if you're looking for a simple answer, this game may not be for you, or you may want to look at other reviews. Let's be super clear about what this game is, and what it isn't:
What it is:
1) The most realistic hunting experience to date (IMO).
2) Offers a plethora of options, weapons, locales, and equipment.
3) Beautiful, even by today's standards. It's starting to show it's age, but still has wonderfully beautiful moments.
4) Content is updated weekly, with new equipment, animals, new locations, etc., added regularly as well.
5) Enjoyable, with patience. The game mostly calms me.
6) Offers a fun multiplayer experience, including competitions and cooperative play.
7) A free game, that allows you to hunt some species, and are given a few weapons to help you get along. There are weekly rotations on animals that non-members can hunt.
8) A membership service for a larger experience.
9) The free version is essentially a demo.
What it isn't:
1) A game that allows you to hunt everything, with all the equipment, etc., without spending money.
2) A pay to win game. Winning is only in the eye of the beholder. You're generally only competing with yourself.
3) A game with a low learning curve.
4) Perfect.
I've put over 500 hours into this game, and likely a few more hundred if you include my time spent in the game prior to transferring it to Steam. I feel as though I might have a complete view of this game, flaws and all. This game certainly has it's flaws, some of which stem from it using an older gaming engine, some of which stem from a team switch (probably some legacy code), and some of which stems from a misunderstanding of the payment model. Simply put, when you get this game for free, you're given a limited amount of items and weapons, and can only hunt a limited amount of species. To some, this may seem like a pay to win game, but there is no "end-game," and "winning" is subjective at best.
About being a new player, this game requires an investement of time. First, you have to learn what the game is trying to teach you (there's plenty of tutorials, videos, etc., available to help you understand some of this). The developers sometimes keep rather quiet about certain aspects of the game, such as where animals spawn, etc., but this is purposely done to keep you guessing, and never 100% sure about the mechanics of the game. This keeps the game lively, and allows you to learn from others. Many of my conversations with other players center around the best spots for hunting, and other unknowns, with a large amount of incorrect information. I don't mind this, because as I said, it keeps the game interesting, and even after this many hours, I'm still learning.
Seeing the game advertised as free, then realizing you can't hunt everything in the game can put a lot of people off. I place blame on the way the game is marketed, but if you enjoy hunting game experiences, don't let this put you off. You do NOT need a membership to enjoy the game, although you're going to be limited to a few species, and two species that are rotated weekly. You get free ammo for the weapons you get as a non-member. You can hunt on any reserve, but are limited in the species you can legally hunt. In order to unlock the game fully, you must get yourself a membership. Alternatively, you can purchase licenses as a non-member to hunt specific species. If you purchase a firearm, you will have to purchase ammo for it. As I said, this can be daunting, and put new players off.
Let's talk about memberships. A basic membership allows you to hunt all species, on all reserves, for a period of time. This will also allow you to get free replenishment on ammo for all weapons you own. Some memberships last for up to a year, which means if you pay into this game, you'll eventually be paying to upkeep your membership (I pay about $30 a year my membership). Some memberships come with equipment, which help you get started, and are cheaper than trying to buy the equipment indivudually. Once you have purchased equipment (via membership or otherwise), you always keep it. Some of the equipment is centered on equipment bundles for species, such as ducks, etc. It's up to the user to decide which membership they want.
Let's talk about equipment. As a new member, you're given some basics, which is helpful for most deer species. You're give a rifle and a shotgun, which allows you to hunt anything in rotation or that comes with a non-member. Should you upgrade, the weapons you have allow you to hunt everything except one or two animals species. Everything else in this game is entirely optional. Many of the firearms are redundant (same weapon, different or unique skins). Some weapons are better for certain types of species, such as the .22 (useful for rabbits, geese, etc.), while others such as the .370 are excellent for very large game. There are decoys, dogs, blinds, stands, and all sorts of items that can be optionally used in your hunts. Some of this equipment makes it easier to hunt a particular species, such as a duck caller, and a blind, but they are not essential to getting them. These items cost money. Again, this can be daunting for new players, because there are so many species, and so many items. Certain memberships provide you with everything you need to hunt the vast majority of species with ease. If you were, however, to buy everything in the game, especially if it's not on sale or in a bundle, you're going to drop a huge amount of money (perhaps upwards of a thousand U.S. dollars or more).
Buying items should only be done in the long term, when you realize your issues in hunting specific species. It requires you to invest some time, and to educate yourself so you get the best bang for your buck. It's part of the reason why this game has a high learning curve. In this way it mimics real life to some extent. You wouldn't use a bleat deer caller, for example, to call a moose. Throwing money at the issue won't assist you in becoming a better hunter, but time and patience will. Spend your money wisely, if you choose to spend money.
When I first purchased a membership with this game, it was prior to Steam, but there was only one map, and a limited number of weapons. For me, over the years, I have been able to attain everything simply because it's within my gaming budget. I spend less on this game than what I would spend on buying other games during a month, and it keeps me coming back because of the high diversity, skill, and serenity the game provides. If you're someone going after achievements, you may be frustrated, and I would say this game isn't for you. As I said, this is about the long term. If, however, you have a lot of patience, and are looking for a deep hunting game experience, I highly recommend this game. There is just simply nothing else out there that can do what this game does.

Overall I would steer clear of this game as it will most likely never leave early access in order to justify how little content and nemerous bugs are in the game. Do not buy it even on a 95% off sale.

Everyone who has the time should play Transistor through for the first time in one sitting in my opinion - it really captures such a beautiful world. It has a stunning art style, which paired with possibly the best OST I have ever heard, it makes for a really stunning experience. I can't recommend that you play this game enough

A lot of people are starting to realize that video games are art, and Transistor truly stands out as a prime example.
The universe is mysterious and futuristic, with scattered bits of lore just begging to be discovered. It paves the way for a simple, yet compelling story, allowing you to absorb or ignore as much of the supplementary narrative as you desire.
The voice acting is incredible, even though one of the characters reminds me of W Bush. Your companion gives tips, narrates the story, and makes snarky remarks when you do silly things. The main character has lost her voice, but can hum along to pretty much every background track. It's beautiful, haunting, and emotionally invoking at certain parts of the game.
Did I mention it's gorgeous? Paintings make you stop and say "Ooh" or "Aah." Transistor makes you stop every 5 seconds to "Ooh" and "Aah." Some environments made me sad to leave because they were so pretty. Visual effects are flashy, and can be a crux in heated battle but never to the point where you get lost.
Combat is interesting, using an AP bar and acquired spells of sorts instead of merely hacking everything with a sword. Each skill can be equipped, combined with another skill, or set as a passive ability. With something like 20 skills total, you can play and discover your own unique battle style.
Enemies scale as you level up, and gain abilities that make you change your equipped skills to cope. Even if you find a skill configuration that seems godlike, obsolescence is never too far off. There are also little training rooms and challenges that introduce you to new mechanics and combinations that you may never have considered.
When your HP depletes, you lose a skill and get another HP bar. This skill is lost for a random number of upcoming battles, and can snowball if you were pretty dependent on it. You only die if you lose all of your skills, up to 4. I never found the game difficult enough to lose more than one skill, and in that instance I just played defensively until I got everything back.
There are also limiters that make the battles much harder while offering piddling EXP bonuses of 2-6%. I will definitely explore these more on my second playthrough to up the difficulty.
My only real complaint with the game is the skill UI. It's very unintuitive when you first start, and took me a while to figure out. Those unfamiliar with games may find the equip screen a high hurdle. Then, once you get the hang of it, other things start to niggle you: Why isn't there a dedicated "unequip all" button? When you're juggling 20 skills near the end of the game, any major change to your skillset can take quite a while to click through.
Overall, Transistor really hit the mark as an enjoyable experience. It's not a fast paced Call of Duty action game, but if you appreciate good art, music, or gameplay, you'll find something to love in Transistor.

Half Minute Hero 2 tries to add a lot of things to the gameplay, but not a lot of them work. You get a pilotable walking castle that only ends up slowing down the gameplay instead of being fun, and an explorable overworld that just turns the usual parody of grinding into actual grinding. The original HMH had a single Hero 30 mode that served as the main event and a few side games like the scrolling shooter Princess 30 or the actiony Knight 30, but 2 just has 5 different Hero 30 modes, and while that might appeal to some people, I thought it got old pretty fast and didn't have enough variety to justify spreading itself so thin. I would mention that if you liked HMH1's steam port's alternate art style from the 360 port then you'd be disappointed to not have it here, but that's purely hypothetical, because nobody actually liked that style.
Despite all of these complaints, it's still not a bad game, just not as good as the first. It's still just as funny, and the story is good when it's moving, but so many of the new additions end up being misses instead of hits that if you've already played the first game you might end up bored by the end.

This game probably is my favourite Open World game so far. With GTA and others, I usually get bored pretty fast, but not with this one. You are an undercover cop infiltrating the Hong Kong underground. Combat-wise, there is a lot of engaging bare-hand fighting.
The story kept me entertained and coming back for more. There has been put quite some effort in character-development. The protagonist isn't an empty shell, but filled with personality.
The game looks great. The city is very atmospheric, especially when walking through Hong Kong at night. Personally, I really liked the dynamic weather system - the streets look amazing when it's raining.
Fighting, running, driving, shooting - everything in this game controls nicely. Some people complained about the driving but I really can't understand why. It's not a racing game focusing on driving only, so why would anyone expect perfect physics? The cars and motorcycles control fine (and differently depending on the model) and drifting around corners is a lot of fun (use the handbrake). I loved the arrows displayed directly on the street, telling you which turns to take when driving to a waypoint (hate looking at the tiny map in GTA).
Go play this game. This is the definite edition with polished graphics and all the available DLC. I bought it during the Holiday Sale and it was totally worth it. Also, it has a Nimbus-Cloud-style Motorcycle ;)

text:
So, I'll start it off with some cons. No in-game option for Sound. Might not be too big an issue, but it is. A lot of the HUD and stuff needs some work, but that's not too much - it is alpha afterall. Then, suddenly it falls down into the confusing quests and stuff like that. Confusing may not be the word - it is explained somewhere in the journal, but it is fine nonetheless.
The game has voice acting that sounds like some lame-russian porno, but it is fun with all of the little remarks. Makes me feel like I'm really in the scene. The porn-scene that is. Now, back onto the important stuff. The game feels fine as it is - fun, not complete, but fun. Complete isn't even close to describe what I have seen in it, and potentially promised. It feels like it is where it should be for an Alpha. Now all that we have to wait on is for the devs to run off with our money as is so popular.
No, truthfully I feel the game has full potential to head somewhere. FPS spikes, sometimes it seems my computer may be out-dated, there's server-side lag that makes running around more hilarious. The sound seems out of synch, I got shot by an enemy with a rifle and heard nothing. Nothing. Not all enemies make sounds, some bullets phase through enemies (still registered as a hit, whaaa?!) and then there's the occassional range issues. An enemy bashes you from 20 meters away. Happens, right?!
But, it's an Early Access - not even beta, hell stage 1 alpha is what it feels like. I bought it, I don't suggest to avoid it until it is full-priced (IF THE DEVS WILL WORK ON IT), it seems fun, early-days firefall fun. Levels of creativity and a powerful attribute of soon-to-be depth that could put a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of games to shame. I wish I didn't pay the fifteen dollars. I like free things more than paid things - but at the same time I am glad I did. To have my hand in the goo while its still mushy is always a blessing. So, pros? Guns, aliens, a lot to do, people need help, you help 'em. Development seems unlimited all you need to do is pop on some armor or weapons and get to farming.
There's this level of old-school Sci-Fi in the game. Aliens meet Fifth Element, meet some Star Wars like vibe in the planet's design. There's probably going to be layers upon layers upon layers in the game (eventually) but until then, I'm happy with what I got. 10/10 would play for 3+ hours again in one sitting while busy and needing sleep.

Everyone who has the time should play Transistor through for the first time in one sitting in my opinion - it really captures such a beautiful world. It has a stunning art style, which paired with possibly the best OST I have ever heard, it makes for a really stunning experience. I can't recommend that you play this game enough

A lot of people are starting to realize that video games are art, and Transistor truly stands out as a prime example.
The universe is mysterious and futuristic, with scattered bits of lore just begging to be discovered. It paves the way for a simple, yet compelling story, allowing you to absorb or ignore as much of the supplementary narrative as you desire.
The voice acting is incredible, even though one of the characters reminds me of W Bush. Your companion gives tips, narrates the story, and makes snarky remarks when you do silly things. The main character has lost her voice, but can hum along to pretty much every background track. It's beautiful, haunting, and emotionally invoking at certain parts of the game.
Did I mention it's gorgeous? Paintings make you stop and say "Ooh" or "Aah." Transistor makes you stop every 5 seconds to "Ooh" and "Aah." Some environments made me sad to leave because they were so pretty. Visual effects are flashy, and can be a crux in heated battle but never to the point where you get lost.
Combat is interesting, using an AP bar and acquired spells of sorts instead of merely hacking everything with a sword. Each skill can be equipped, combined with another skill, or set as a passive ability. With something like 20 skills total, you can play and discover your own unique battle style.
Enemies scale as you level up, and gain abilities that make you change your equipped skills to cope. Even if you find a skill configuration that seems godlike, obsolescence is never too far off. There are also little training rooms and challenges that introduce you to new mechanics and combinations that you may never have considered.
When your HP depletes, you lose a skill and get another HP bar. This skill is lost for a random number of upcoming battles, and can snowball if you were pretty dependent on it. You only die if you lose all of your skills, up to 4. I never found the game difficult enough to lose more than one skill, and in that instance I just played defensively until I got everything back.
There are also limiters that make the battles much harder while offering piddling EXP bonuses of 2-6%. I will definitely explore these more on my second playthrough to up the difficulty.
My only real complaint with the game is the skill UI. It's very unintuitive when you first start, and took me a while to figure out. Those unfamiliar with games may find the equip screen a high hurdle. Then, once you get the hang of it, other things start to niggle you: Why isn't there a dedicated "unequip all" button? When you're juggling 20 skills near the end of the game, any major change to your skillset can take quite a while to click through.
Overall, Transistor really hit the mark as an enjoyable experience. It's not a fast paced Call of Duty action game, but if you appreciate good art, music, or gameplay, you'll find something to love in Transistor.

Transistor is quite simply an amazing game.
Supergiant Games really got to the next level with this work, a gift to the eye and the ear, as well as an amazing experience for any player I could possibly think of.
Transistor's soundtrack is on an entirely different level. Not only is it immersive, but incredibly well put-together, and it seems to fit the game in a way you can't fully understand while playing. This is precisely why it matches the story so well; combining with a plot brilliantly constructed, built upon blurry facts hinting themselves out of the mysterious atmosphere of Transistor. The battle system is so original that it takes some time to believe it's really happening (I swear).
Its only flaw would be how little it will last you. If devouring the story the way I did (which tends to be the case, given how captivating this game can get), it does not live past its tenth hour, assuming the player would want to get everything they can out of it. The main storyline can hardly get to the eighth.
In spite of this, it is undeniably worth its price, and would probably be worth twice as much too. If you're hesitating, please do not think twice. This work of art is... well, a work of art. That's faster and just as clear.
Transistor is an incredible game, result of an extremely classy interpretation of what "technique" should look like. Stunning visuals, unforgettable music, and a story you will not regret welcoming into your life. Just go and buy it if you haven't yet done so.
Really.

This game is truly a masterpiece.
The game-play: Man, where do I begin? This game doesn't force you to play in any specific style. Instead, it allows you to decide what you want to do. How do you want to dispatch enemies, with what abilities and upgrades that can mix and match for different effects? How do you want to fight, using the Turn(), fighting in real time, or a mixture of both? How hard do you want your enemies to be? There are few games that allow this much freedom in how the player wants to play, and I think it is completely underrated in this aspect.
The art and soundtrack: The art is simply breathtaking. Each area, a new visual showpiece. The soundtrack goes so well with the game as well. I especially love when Red hums along with the current tune, either by player choice or in Turn(). Again, games that do this well with the music (FTL: Faster Than Light and Undertale as other examples of stunning music) and this much thought into the tunes deserve more credit than they get.
The little-things: I love the interactions between Red and Transistor, the connection they have. Transistor's voice acting and narration over Red's actions is a truly unique and one-of-a-kind experience, as well as a very nice touch to the game and it's story. The details in each new ability are also very interesting.
The story: I haven't beaten the game yet, so I can't completely review this part. However, with as far as I've gotten as of right now, it is very interesting and engaging.
Overall: 10/10. I picked this up and it's soundtrack on a Steam sale. After playing, I felt like a thief. Transistor is definitely worth every cent.

I first played this game in my darkened room, in bed, on my iPad. It was like curling up with a favorite Victorian horror story, and believe me, I know that genre well. I loved the intriguing tale so much that I bought the game again on Steam to play on my laptop or PC. I've played it many times over, and the same with Season Two. The cast resonates in their struggles, and among all the many, many low-res indie games, this one makes great use of the stark old-fashioned style to create a unique electronic peephole into Victorian-era UK. A fantastic original soundtrack by Carlos Viola rounds out the romanticism and tragedy of the story, and clever usage of sound effects polish the atmosphere to perfection.
Gameplay-wise, it is a point-and-click, which is, for me, very underused these days. The emphasis is on puzzle-solving, with challenges ranging from easy to moderate. It is possible and enjoyable to go through it without a guide. This depends on personal opinion and gameplay experience, but I did not find it frustrating or tedious. The puzzles were well-designed and fit with the story very well; some were downright creepy!
The developers of this game were very open and appreciative of the fan community during development. They even published graphical content free on Creative Commons on their blog. I've never seen such engaged developers, and that was a very refreshing thing to see.
In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game enough. I've played it over many times, and I'll play it again in the future. You can see the care that went into telling this story and crafting the gameplay experience. It sticks with you, even now that Season Two has concluded and the story is told. One of my all-time favorites, right up there with the big-budget titles. Don't pass up giving this series a try!

In
, you play as an unnamed cat whose loyalty to their Mistress is unwavering. The story begins with a joyous fun-filled day adventuring with your Mistress in City Park; however, the following morning she is distraught over having lost her teddy-bear. As her faithful companion, you retrace your adventure to retrieve her teddy-bear as any pawesome feline friend would do. The remainder of the game follows the same repetitive structure of finding your forgetful owner’s lost valuables (which also include her socks, an umbrella, and her flower-like barrette).
While the art style itself was not bothersome (in fact, it was refreshing), its execution felt rushed and unrefined. The lackluster artwork could have been more easily forgiven had the voiceovers – which themselves were unpleasant on the ears and awkward at times – been in sync with the text as it appeared on the screen. Despite the disconnect between the voiceovers and story text, the background music was enjoyable and felt appropriate in setting the mood.
Although likely intended for children, one would still hope for a moral or lesson to be clearly drawn – even from such a short game – and it was unclear what the author/developer was trying to convey. Is the lesson simply, “do not lose your stuff” or “if you lose your stuff you can count on your friend to find it for you”? While the kitten is eager to aid their Mistress upon her first loss, they grow increasingly unenthusiastic with each subsequent request (despite continuing to assist her). Is the lesson here then one of unconditional love?

As a point and click game, Kitten adventures in city park merges a short story with hand-drawn pictures that could, with a few exceptions, well be in a children's book for ages 2-4. Apart from a few rough edges it's a lovely title.
Since there are no moving pieces within a scene, the game consists of a series of pictures with hotspots to interact with. The pictures are roughly sketched and generously coloured resulting in beautifully drawn scenes. Irritatingly though, the human faces show elements of manga iconography. Together with the rough and overly excited cat's voice it seems as if this game was influenced by kid's anime, the annoying type, which sadly lessens its coherence in style. An option to have the more gentle Russian synchronisation and English subtitles separate would've been nice, maybe even educative.
The redeeming factor for those small issues is the implementation of an option to rewatch the introductory scene for clues by talking to another cat. That's a charming way of giving hints, albeit in no way necessary, showing how well-suited this title is for toddlers. It's a simple and sweet game, but only really enjoyable for children, unless the art itself is appealing enough.

I hate to be a downer on such a nice and more importantly, unique game in the Steam store- but as far as Kitten Adventures goes, there were too many good opportunities missed for me to give this a thumbs up, even with it being a free game.
Firstly, I absolutely applaud the use of hand drawn images for the game. I love this, and would love to see it more in games. The drawing themselves however, are completely sloppy, and unless this is a child's artwork (which, if it is, please disregard this section!), it is simply dreadful quality to be put into a finished piece.
The gameplay itself runs quite well, my only niggle with this would be that, as it is a game probably better suited to young children, some of the items are extremely difficult to locate. For instance,
Now, my main gripe with this game has to be the dreadful voice acting. It is so irritating, that I thank the creator for adding the option to turn it off via a sound slider. If you're trying to get through the game relatively quickly you will have that rusky american kid accent blasting non stop through the speakers, repeating phrases over and over. Enough to drive anyone mad within a few minutes.

The very last great Call of Duty game.
Hello, I originally began playing the original WW-2 set CoD on PC back when I was a boy on my Uncle's computer. I was fascinated with how fun and "realistic" it was. I was immediately hooked on the games. I played Cod 2 and 3 religiously, and I will never ever forget the day I heard about Modern Warfare. Finally. FINALLY a game of 21st century setting. I was ecstatic. I played through the campaign and had endless hours of multiplayer logged on my Xbox 360. After doing everything I thought possible in that game, my dream came true, and another was released. To some, there's almost no difference between CoD4MW, and MW2. To others, like myself, there's an indescribable gap between the two games, where MW2 is on a whole new and higher level. To me, no other shooter game has had the balance MW2 had. It has set a standard for me that I look to in other FPS games, often times I find no equal, save the original Black Ops game. This balance is what made the game for me. I've never been a person to be "naturally" good at video games. MW2 was one where I excelled. Because I had a fighting chance. I found my niche and I stuck with it. I maxed the game on my Xbox 360, and eventually grew into PC gaming, leaving consoles behind. I only have a few minutes played on this game so far, but I had to actually back out and type this up even after the first few matches. It has been such a trip for me going through the menus and the lobby system. If you're considering buying this game for nostalgia, do it. Do it and don't take any flak that comes to you. Do it, and relive your early teens of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ girlfriends, mountain dew, and yelling at your parents. If you've never played MW2 and are looking to see the hype, I'm afraid it's gone forever. There's a few people around on the servers, but the HYPE, the actual maxed pace heartbeat of a game that took the world by storm is gone forever and ever. Then again, maybe that's the beautiful thing. Maybe that's what has this game frozen in time as one of the all time greatest.
Forever and ever, Modern Warfare 2.

Bottom Line Up Front: Be a hero of the people, a captain of industry or a pirate king. C'mon, it's free!
A free game is always worth a look, and almost always worth a few minutes of play. At time of writing, Endless Sky has held my attention for eight hours.
You start out by taking out a high-interest loan from the bank and buy one of three ships - shuttle, transport, interceptor - and you can guess what each is for. I went for the transport because I was channeling Firefly and felt like pretending to be Malcom Reynolds. Once you start, it's time to get to work - that debt isn't going to pay itself!
After the first hour, the gameplay is what it is. Pick up cargo from Planet A and take it to Planet B - sometimes as a mission, sometimes hoping to buy low and sell high, sometimes on a timer. You can even mix it up and carry people or escort ships. Alternatively, you can go hunting for pirates, or be one yourself and raid other ships.
The controls are what you might expect from a 2D space simulator - sluggish. If you've ever played S.P.A.Z. the controls will be familiar (and equally frustrating in a firefight).
The story will automatically unfold at specfic moments when you land your ship, and if you visit the spaceport at each planet you can potentially pick up story missions for one of the various factions in the galaxy or chance upon a unique mission (though it is almost always a variation of what I mentioned earlier). You can pick up jobs from the job board or, as mentioned above, figure out the price of goods at your destination and buy them cheaper at your location for resale.
Put on some suitable music (there's none in game) and use your imagination as to why you care to build a fleet of ships. After all, it's free!

Transistor is  a sci-fi-themed action slasher with a post apocalyptic feel from the creators of Bastion. The music in the game, though well done, it isn't woven into the experience of the game and it's mechanics as well as it could have been. Graphically the game runs to a more abstract simplistic feel, though it does carry it's own unique beauty.
Combat
The combat can be confusing at first, because it has a hack and slash feel combined with a turn based regenerative time style. This is mostly due to the abilities. You can use four active abilities, but beyond that, the abilities have additional properties that you can integrate into your primary four abilities to augment them. Your choice of what properties you combine determine the new ability that you create. You have 16 different augments to choose from to tweak and synergize  each ability. The game provides a safe area for you to experiment and practice new abilities and traits to find what works for you. While I like this availability to combine traits and create a build that works for you, it has been my experience as I went through the game that in boss battles, you have to go for a more obvious dps build rather than something you have created in order to generate the damage you need to defeat them. I go into more detail about this in my video, which I encourage you to watch if you want further explanation.
The story is a bit confusing, and hard to get into at first. There is a lot of information coming at you at once, and little relate-ability and emotional involvement to your character and their actions. The main character doesn't talk during the adventure, but her weapon/companion does. It's been my experience that the companion talks way too much, and is off-putting.
Overall I have found that there are some faults to the game, such as a confusing ability interface, having to fall back to traditional dps builds to defeat bosses, and an abstract storyline. Even with these shortcomings, the game is still enjoyable. The story is not a detriment to the game, and the ability to customize your characters abilities makes it intriguing to play, along with the play + mode for longer experiences. I can easily recommend this game.

A beat 'em up for adults done right.
Mother Russia Bleeds combines gameplay of classic games of the genre that many of us played in the 90s, while also giving it all a more mature and violent theme.
Thus:
Yes, you do scroll to the right while stopping to beat up a bunch of enemies.
Yes, the enemies aren't threatening, but rely on numbers and gimmicks to make up for it.
Yes, you get a few simple combos to vary things up.
Yes, you get a variation of enviroments along with arena hazards to complicate your fights.
Yes, you can play with a friend at the same computer.
And of course there's bossfights, some playing more like a puzzle, others just figuring out patterns.
While the base gameplay is pretty much the same as the classics that inspired, its mostly the ultra-violent theme that puts the game apart. You're playing a group of hobo streetfighters kidnapped by the government for drug testing, who are now out for violent revenge. The enemies you fight don't have health bars, but become bloodied and slower the more damage they take. Bodies don't blink out of existence but litter the ground. You can beat on downed enemies and it's as brutal as the pixel graphics allow. And you don't get healing items, but heal through dosing up on drugs that you extract from spasming enemy corpses mid-combat. Overally the violent theme isn't self-serving but is used to portray a distopic alternate reality soviet russia where the only justice that can be had is street justice and it works pretty well as far as I'm concerned.
The game does have issues too, story mode isn't particularly long, I've finished it in 4 hours on normal and I'm no fighting game expert. Arena mode is fairly bland and serve more like challenges to beat than anything else. Difficulty can catch inexperienced players off guard and stunlocking is huge if you get caught by surprise in a crowd of enemies, the dodge button is essential in tougher fights. Oh and as of writing this review online coop is not yet implemented, though the devs have stated they intend to add it over time.
All in all, it's a solid game, that's simple fun with enough challenge to satisfy the veteran player too. Though it doesn't bring any particularly new gameplay to the table, if you played a beat 'em up before, this one won't surprise.
On the other hand you get beat a downed opponent to death with a fire extinguisher. Hard to say no to the simple joys in life.

I have 117 hours on the Steam Edition (discontinued), so disregard my .4 hours for this game. I only bought it because it was on sale and I wasn't really liking the idea of playing from the discontinued version, despite it not actually being any kind of issue.
On the plus side, all of my Steam Edition stuff carried over; if you own the Steam Edition and have been thinking about getting this copy as well, do it. Right now for $2.50 + ($.74x4) you can have all 4 of the perm mercs; if you already had them with the Steam Edition, you will get them again. This is great on paper, but be prepared to powergrind for cash/mats to kit them out. ;)
Also, any Achievements you have will transfer between the two titles, so there's that if you're looking to pad your cheev stats a little.
If you've played the older JA games, don't expect this to be anywhere near them. It's quite lacking in a side-by-side comparison.
The character development is somewhat lacking, as you only have a handful of physical stats and weapon skills (each with their own skill point pools to spend from as the merc levels).
The gear is somewhat awkward.
- Head/Body to be equipped with Light or Heavy armor; there is no middleground and you're more or less forced to spec into one or the other.
- Weapon 1&2; you have 2 slots that can each hold any weapon of your choosing, but with the limited merc class:weapon skill setup, you will likely end up going with archetypical stuff (sniper mercs will have sniper/pistol, scouts will have rifle/shotgun, etc).
- 3 Ammo Belt slots; this is where you put your actively-used ammo for the weapon(s) you carry in battle. Generally, 1 box of ammo per weapon + 1 special ammo type for whichever weapon you prefer (AP for your close range, perhaps)
- 3 Hip Belt slots; this is where you put your consumables such as medkits, injection kits, energy drinks, etc.
- 6 Backpack slots; you can carry additional weapons, ammo and consumables here and transfer them to the appropriate slots during a mission. This is also where you will usually place the loot you pick up during missions (unless you equip them in their corresponding slots, of course).
-- None of these categorized slots can be upgraded to expand their capacity, unfortunately.
Further, the weapon/armor crafting becomes somewhat tedious. It isn't /terrible/ but it's very farm-grindy. Do handfuls of missions to get a couple hundred thousand dollars, then spend $30k+ to do the crafting itself (for 1 item), +thousands of dollars more for 'insurance' to keep your components from breaking on failure, and even more $ on the crafting kits needed to actually craft anything to begin with. Failure results in loss of money and components (unless 'insured'), so this results in a potentialy COSTLY experience. Just for a singular item.
You can both farm and purchase nearly every component needed, but eventually at higher levels you'll generally have to buy a small crate of each item, then craft a number of those items together to up-tier it to a better 'quality', then craft a number of /those/ up-tiered components to make even better ones.
Then you take the required components and craft-combine them with "craftable"-flagged weapons/armor to advance said weapon/armor to its next state. When you max out at L50, you'll pretty much end up with a bottlenecked set of gear you can modify, and that will usually only have 1-2 different craftable options (based on components used).
It could be so much better than it is now, but even now it's so much better than the trainwreck garbage it used to be years ago.
Your headquarters is where you will be able to hire mercs and buy/sell gear. There's an on-site 'hospital' and mechanic shop, both of which can be upgraded by gathering the proper resources + $. These upgrades will add passive bonii (different upgrades boost different stats) to mercs' stats, or add storage space for armor/weapons/ammo/consumables.
While this is a neat-o thing to help further enhance the already-limited mercs, it does add quite a bit of grinding to the game.
I won't get into the missions, mainly because it's been so long since I've gone through all of them; however, they were all generally interesting and had a decent amount of replayability. Some more than others, some not at all; many will be forgotten while others will be required to farm along the way for cash/components/resources ('Back to the Roots' to get TREE SAP <--- This will be your endgame grind for a while)
There's also Warzones and PvP, which I didn't personally do any of. A few warzones here and there to see what it was about, but never any PvP.
Overall, I'd say it's worth any JA fan to at least look into. However, I would not suggest getting hyped about it being anything near what JA2 or JA:BiA was (BiA was real-time garbage; but that's a whole different review). It does a much better job than the recently 'revisioned' JA game.. "Flaming Pile Of Wet Fart Garbage" was its title, I think? Anyhow, it's not a nightmare like that failsauce, but it's nowhere near the originals.
