Emily is away was a great, then boring, then a great experience again for me.
**SPOILER ALERT**
The games controls are pretty weird as you can just type whatever you want while the character types the actual message. I found a meta game in trying to type the same letter he was going to type before he typed it.
But that's not the point.
Towards the very end of the game, there are plenty of opportunities that you have to tell emily your true feelings (to me they seemed a little needy, "Do you ever miss me?") and when you select for your character to tell her the true feelings you have, the character begins typing the message you intended. However, he will then erase the message and enter his own small talk, asking how the weather is or if she's seen any good movies lately.  This seems very frustrating to players because we are in a very saturated industry with games where "Choice changes the game!!" and little decisions do change a little piece of the game, but the outcome is always the same in the end, emily leaves, and you never get your chance with her.
So why do I recommend this game? Well the way I felt during the game, was that I was my character's desires.. His mind, i suppose.  I would tell him what to say, and he would type it, sometimes not even the way I worded it.  That's where it gets interesting at the end of the game. I tell my character to tell Emily he misses the way they used to be, and he types it, then erases it because he's scared.  I'm left thinking to myself "You idiot! You're ruining your chance!!" But that is when I realized that the character I believed I was controlling must be thinking the exact same thing.  Sometimes in life your whole being wants to do something, and yet, you just don't do it. Whether it's asking that person out on a date, taking that risk on a dream job, or whatever else.
That is why I like the game, that is why I recommend it to anyone who is looking for an interesting narrative and a new look at the art of video games.
Overall? 7/10.  The game didn't blow my mind, but I really liked the direction it got my mind to take.

Again, it may be charming for younger audiences, but here's basically the voice cast:  Squeeky voices (that only come off as corny) for mice and ants, an 8-year old child for the kitten, a South African woman for the yellow cat, and what sounds like a guy trying to be a little girl for...the young girl.  That's the basic gist of the VA roles...but that's just my perspective.
Aside from gaining an easy 100% for your AGC percentage, I cannot find myself recommending this game to anybody unless they're looking for easy achievements or if they're below the age of 10.  If you're 10 or above, you'll probably want to just play

FILLING:
1/2 teaspoon five-spice powder
1 pound pork tenderloin, trimmed
Cooking spray
1 cup thinly sliced green onions
3 tablespoons hoisin sauce
2 tablespoons rice vinegar
1 tablespoon low-sodium soy sauce
1 1/2 teaspoons honey
1 teaspoon minced peeled fresh ginger
1 teaspoon minced garlic
1/4 teaspoon salt
1. To prepare the filling, rub five-spice powder evenly over pork. Heat a grill pan over medium-high heat. Coat the pan with cooking spray. Add pork to pan; cook 18 minutes or until a thermometer registers 155°, turning pork occasionally. Remove pork from pan, and let stand 15 minutes.
2. Cut pork crosswise into thin slices; cut slices into thin strips. Place pork in a medium bowl. Add onions and next 7 ingredients (through 1/4 teaspoon salt); stir well to combine. Cover and refrigerate.
3. To prepare dough, combine 1 cup warm water, sugar, and yeast in a large bowl; let stand 5 minutes.
4. Lightly spoon flour into dry measuring cups; level with a knife. Add flour, oil, and 1/4 teaspoon salt to yeast mixture; stir until a soft dough forms. Turn dough out onto a lightly floured surface. Knead until smooth and elastic (about 10 minutes). Place dough in a large bowl coated with cooking spray, turning to coat top. Cover and let rise in a warm place (85°), free from drafts, 1 hour or until doubled in size. (Gently press two fingers into dough. If indentation remains, dough has risen enough.)
5. Punch dough down; let rest 5 minutes. Turn dough out onto a clean surface; knead in baking powder. Let dough rest 5 minutes.
6. Divide dough into 10 equal portions, forming each into a ball. Working with one dough ball at a time (cover remaining dough balls to keep from drying), roll ball into a 5-inch circle. Place 1/4 cup filling in center of dough circle. Bring up sides to cover filling and meet on top. Pinch and seal closed with a twist. Repeat procedure with remaining dough balls and filling.
7. Arrange 5 buns seam side down, 1 inch apart, in each tier of a 2-tiered bamboo steamer. Stack tiers; cover with lid.
8. Add water to a large skillet to a depth of 1 inch; bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Place steamer in pan; steam 15 minutes or until puffed and set. Cool 10 minutes before serving.

A beat 'em up for adults done right.
Mother Russia Bleeds combines gameplay of classic games of the genre that many of us played in the 90s, while also giving it all a more mature and violent theme.
Thus:
Yes, you do scroll to the right while stopping to beat up a bunch of enemies.
Yes, the enemies aren't threatening, but rely on numbers and gimmicks to make up for it.
Yes, you get a few simple combos to vary things up.
Yes, you get a variation of enviroments along with arena hazards to complicate your fights.
Yes, you can play with a friend at the same computer.
And of course there's bossfights, some playing more like a puzzle, others just figuring out patterns.
While the base gameplay is pretty much the same as the classics that inspired, its mostly the ultra-violent theme that puts the game apart. You're playing a group of hobo streetfighters kidnapped by the government for drug testing, who are now out for violent revenge. The enemies you fight don't have health bars, but become bloodied and slower the more damage they take. Bodies don't blink out of existence but litter the ground. You can beat on downed enemies and it's as brutal as the pixel graphics allow. And you don't get healing items, but heal through dosing up on drugs that you extract from spasming enemy corpses mid-combat. Overally the violent theme isn't self-serving but is used to portray a distopic alternate reality soviet russia where the only justice that can be had is street justice and it works pretty well as far as I'm concerned.
The game does have issues too, story mode isn't particularly long, I've finished it in 4 hours on normal and I'm no fighting game expert. Arena mode is fairly bland and serve more like challenges to beat than anything else. Difficulty can catch inexperienced players off guard and stunlocking is huge if you get caught by surprise in a crowd of enemies, the dodge button is essential in tougher fights. Oh and as of writing this review online coop is not yet implemented, though the devs have stated they intend to add it over time.
All in all, it's a solid game, that's simple fun with enough challenge to satisfy the veteran player too. Though it doesn't bring any particularly new gameplay to the table, if you played a beat 'em up before, this one won't surprise.
On the other hand you get beat a downed opponent to death with a fire extinguisher. Hard to say no to the simple joys in life.

Fingerbones is a short game, yet it achieves the psychological horror it set out to accomplish. This game won't give you cheap jumpscares, wont place eerie otherwordly creatures in your path or abandon you in the middle of a haunted forest (those seem to be all the rage in most horror games), but it will unsettle you and it will make sure you still feel chills running down your spine even after the game ends.
The theme it deals with isn't scary per se but rather it is a subject that most people prefer not to mention and would rather ignore. To this purpose the developer of the game places several letters around the environment you'll explore, slowly unravelling the disturbing narrative that will surely leave you creeped out.
The controls are very simple and the download time is very short, plus it's free, so if you have some time I would recommend giving this game a go.

This is an okay MMO. Here's a recipe for meat jelly:
Ingredients
3-4 pig trotters (feet), sliced in half
2 ham hocks/pork knuckles, cut into smaller pieces
300 grams fresh pork rind
2 Carrots, peeled
2 Onions, peeled
Garlic (depending on taste, from 3 cloves to 2 heads), peeled
8-10 Whole peppercorns
2 pork ears (around 500 grams), optional
Salt to taste
Instructions
Carefully trim and clean the meat products and place in a large pot with all of the other ingredients (except for the salt). Pour just enough cold water to cover everything.
Bring to a boil and then reduce the heat to low. Slowly simmer for 4-5 hours until all of the meat is tender, making sure to add water to replace the water that evaporates. All of the ingredients must be covered throughout the long cooking process. Add salt after about 2 hours.
When done, remove the undesirable fat from the top and separate the meat and vegetables from the broth. The vegetables will no longer be needed.
Remove all of the bones and gristle from the meat. While the broth cools, portion out the ingredients into bowls/molds. Once the broth is cool (but not solidified, after about 20-30 minutes), strain it through a cloth and pour it over the meat.
Cover the mold/bowls with aluminum foil and let them stand overnight outside or in the fridge.
Serve the kocsonya cold with sweet paprika (optionally with tomato, parsley, and half a boiled egg) and thick slices of bread.

This game is definetly an odd duck. It manages to succeed in what hundreds of similar things before it failed at. You play as  Wei Shen, an undercover cop from san francisco, who has been recently deported to Hong Kong, on an assignment to infiltrate the Sun-on Yee, and hopefully bring an end to the Triad all together. Wei was born in Hong Kong, and left when he was either 10 or 15, (Depending on who's reports and biographies you want to believe.) and thus is familier enough with the people in the Sun-on Yee to already have pre-established relationships with them. This leads to Wei having conflicted loyalties to the police, as well as his friends in the Triad. The story then leads into a web of intrigue, decete, and is one of the netter stories told in it's respective year. The gameplay is familier, using te same punch-counter combat that I'm sure the Arkham Asylum people really wish they's pattented, but it works well, is responsive, and fun, so there's nothing to really complain about. The game aslo does indulge in the goofy over-the-top humor of a Hong-Kong action film, but there's nothing wrong wit it as it doesn't interfere with the tone or mood of the story, and honestly just adds some more charm to an already great game.
I'd give Sleeping Dogs, a 9/10 - a must own.

Transistor is an art-aesthetic game made by the same people behind Bastion, which will give you a good idea of what to expect from the game from a graphical perspective so I won’t waste time on that (except to say that it’s really pretty). As the story goes, you play a rogue vocalist on a quest to find out the meaning behind the mysterious events happening around her. The most important of which involving the accidental death of one of her biggest fans by a sword called the Transistor.
You might think the gameplay is somewhat similar to Bastion and if you were to ignore the Turn() aspect, you would probably be right. However, this is where the game distances itself: at any point during combat, you can stop time and plan your next few moves, in a sequence, to be executed when you press the end turn button. This allows for some significant advantages over certain hardy foes that would normally steamroll you in real-time. Additionally, each of the processes you pick up can be slotted in one of three roes: active (for active-weapon use), upgrade (boosts active weapon), or passive (various passive benefits). This allows for a wide variety of process assignments that really lets you find your own personal combat style. If for some reason, you find the game to be too easy, you can add ‘limiters’ you have earned at any save point to spice things up in exchange for extra experience.
I found the narrator to be a bit sycophantic, almost to the point where I expected him to wear a fedora and use phrases like “m’lady” while rambling about what it is to be “a gentleman” (especially certain parts of the game where he resembled a drunk version of himself with embarrassingly low levels of restraint). Despite all the cringe, the game is pretty fun and a good challenge if you turn on all the limiters and there are some challenge sections that may warrant a replay if you so desire.

Quite a different kind of action RPG. Excellent story, good music and unique art noveau style graphics.
The combat system is mix of realtime and turn based isometric, fairly similar to mix between XCOM and Bastion, but with one controlleable character and no random factors. You plan your attack in turn based mode and enemies attack in real time between player actions. The real fun is in combining different attack upgrades and functions. You can turn the measily basic starting attack into a murderous speed combo with ligering damage and negative effects far outreaching the initial damage.
There's also some achievement collecting once you get through the fairly short story mode.

Transistor is that kind of indie game that focuses more on being art than on gameplay. By using well-timed music and a constant stream of disconnected bits of narrative, it successfully creates a vague sense of nostalgia for the duration of the story.
Surprisingly, between all the artsy bits, there is a very simple, but also very deep fighting system. You get a number of powers, which can be combined in different ways to create actions and those actions are then chained into combos against your enemies. The amount of possible strategies is surprisingly large and it is a pity that Transistor doesn't play on this quality more.

Not great but ok. I can't avoid comparing it to Bastion. You have main story, you have storyteller, you have your own place where you can rest (Bastion in Bastion, Backdoor in Transistor). But the problem is that story is not that great, art is not as detailed as in Bastion, soundtrack is boring and repetitive and whole Backdoor concept is useless.
As for Backdoor I hate it the most. In Bastion you could build your own island to receive new stuff and complete trials to receive parts needed to upgrade your weapons. In Transistor you have Backdoor where you can complete trials to unlock new songs from soundtrack to listen in only in Backdoor. And thats all.

It took a while for Transistor to really hook me (about 2/3 of the way through my first playthrough), but at that point I went from mildly disappointed (I really loved Supergiant's previous game, Bastion), to entirely satisfied.  I think the reason for all this is that the combat system is really quite deep, and it took a lot of experimentation before I really started understanding the potential there.  I'm playing it through a second time now and really enjoying it.
Aside from the mechanics, the game is beautiful and the soundtrack is excellent.  The story is really intriguing and told in a very minimal way.   A lot of it is told through short voice clips, but if you want to learn more about what is happening, you can also get snipets of story through interacting with the environment, from experimenting with the combat system or from reading message boards :)  Even the way the soundtrack is done complements the story.
I didn't play Bastion on new game+ because I felt like I experienced the whole thing and was satisfied at the end.  I think Transistor essentially requires a second playthrough because there's so much subtle detail packed in that you are bound to miss a lot of it the first time through.  Transistor is a really excellent game, but it is especially rewarding if you are willing to put some effort in.

Disclaimer: this is going to sound like a "funny" review. This is not meant to be a "funny" review.
As some of my regular readers might know, I'm quite the avid horror game player. There's a definite "art" to making a game genuinely creepy, and this game excels at that WITHOUT EVEN TRYING. From the unnervingly unnatural "meow" sound you receive each time you accept a menu option, through to the decidedly off-kilter voice-over work, all the way to the dauntingly spooky synth score, I am genuinely befuddled as to whether this product was meant to be some sick parody or a game sincerely aimed at children. It's virtually The Garbage Pail Kids Movie in video game format.
Which isn't to say that it's "bad". It's quite well done in its way, especially for a free game. But...something just isn't quite right. Then again, as a single, childless male in his early forties, it's entirely possible that I'M the weirdo, and perfectly earnest children's entertainments just get unaccountably creepier with each passing year.
Honestly. It's probably my fault, not the game's. I'm quite sure I'm not its intended target audience. I'm going to be generous with my verdict below to reflect this error, and vow to avoid any game with "kittens" or any of its derivatives in the title from this moment forth.
Oh-oh. "Kitty Cat: Jigsaw Puzzles." Wishlist button hit. Don't...press...buy...button...
Verdict: 6/10.
(PS Points to the game for fighting the Patriarchy (TM) by having your cat - gender unknown - undertake a number of tasks for his or her "mistress". I for one felt suitably humbled by the journey's end.)

Fantastic. Mother Russia Bleeds is a damn fine brawler that gets all the genre fundamentals right while adding a few great new innovations and gimmicks. Solid enemies, memorable and varied bosses, a surprising number of stage hazards, and decently large movesets are all present here. The core combat is extremely deep, satisfying, and tight. This is a game that rewards skill and encourages you to play aggressively and creatively.
Brawler experts will really appreciate everything that's going on here. However, lesser players will likely only enjoy this on the easy difficulty and/or by playing co-op. But if anybody tells you this game is "sloppy," "cheap," or "unfair," it's because they don't grasp how the genre works. If you take a minute to learn your moves and figure out how to use them, it's no problem fighting upwards of 30 enemies at a time. Your arsenal of techniques is extremely powerful to compensate for the huge enemy waves. If you're having a hard time, try moving up and down more to evade attacks and use moves with crowd control potential (throws, dash-attacks, jump-kicks, and grounded kicks) to knock enemies down.
At any rate, the game has unlimited continues and rather generous checkpoints so difficulty really shouldn't be an issue for anybody.
Although I'd prefer a more classic (90's arcade) pixel art style, the graphics have a distinct identity, good color usage, and plenty of detail. However, the OST is pretty bad. Sure, it's techno, but it's far too simple and bland for such an awesome game. Really though, the lame OST is my only complaint with this game. Would highly recommend 9/10.

Mother Russia Bleeds
---Spoilerless Review---
Myself being an avid player of beat'em ups throughout the years, i was all too happy to see a new one released recently, seeing that the genre as been very much dead in recent memory. Prior to buying the game i didn't expect much, after all coming from the excellent streets of rage remake, the bar was set very high so i proceeded cautiously when buying it.
Firstly i noticed when looking at the video options i noticed a CRT filter which is a nice touch, it's obviously a nod to the 90's kids when the beat'em up genre was at it's zenith. Their is options for resolutions and gamma control, other than that their isn't anything much else with the graphics options which isn't a problem, especially for a sprite based game.
-Control-
The control system is horribly bad let me explain, on the steam page it says 'full controller support' which inevitably means 'Xbox360 controller only' for most new games, and this game is no exception. You can only use the Xbox360 controllers effectively with this game so forget about using 3rd party or old controllers, i have SNES and Megadrive style controllers but i can't use them for that simple reason which is ridiculous.
The good news is that you can use the keyboard and remap the keys to whatever configuration you want. A good way around this is to get software like 'joytokey' that allows you to use your controllers as a keyboard, so at least you have that if you're desperate to use your old controllers. Why can't modern games have a menu and remap system for whatever device you have connected, so that way you can use practically any controller, most emulators have this feature, beat's me (no pun intended)
-Gameplay-
When you start the game you have an option to play through the story or play in a arena survival mode. When you pick either one you are greeted with the character select screen and you have a choice of four characters. Like most if not all beat'em ups each character has their own strengths and weaknesses, in comparison it's very much like streets of rage, with Sergei being a well-rounded fighter like Axel and Ivan being very strong like max.
The game is surprisingly story heavy for a beat'em up and the visuals are quite excellent, it reminds me of Hotline Miami, Nuclear Throne or Not A Hero, although the game could used an upscale filter like 2XSAL to make it a bit more smoother in my opinion. The tone and atmosphere is very mature and is defiantly NOT suited for children, mainly because it features strong language, blood and gore, male/female nudity, sex and other mature themes.
The combat is solid for the most part, you have punch, kick and grab buttons for your main attacks and also a jump button for an aerial strike or grab. These attacks can be used separately or in quick succession which racks up more points if you successfully do an intricate combination. Their is also a directional element to the grabbing and striking that allows you to pull off specific moves either from pressing up, down or left/right on the directional pad.
Ground attacks are also an option that allow you to commit light and strong strikes to your opponent. Health comes in the form of an injection that you manually use when your health is low though more can be obtained by leeching life essence from convulsing enemies lying on the ground, your injection meter can also used to fuel your berserk mode, this feature allows you to go into a frenzy and pull off fatality's or just enhanced strikes that sends your opponents flying.
The enemy's usually come in their usual variety like sliders, aerial attackers, grabbers and anti-air specialists, these keep you on your heels for every fight and it can be very difficult when you fight many different types at once. The best strategy is not to get swarmed and keep your distance from the crowd of enemies so you can attack from the outside.
If their is anything i don't like about the combat system it's the manual grabbing and a lack of a back-attack or a block button, these features were quite common in the old beat'em ups so i hope they add them in the future.
-Overall-
Overall it's an excellent beat'em up which is high praise believe me, especially coming from the excellent streets of rage remake and final fight gold games. I was quite impressed with this game but i cannot ignore the flaws, nonetheless a very enjoyable beat'em up even if it is very difficult at times.

Being crowdfunded on a relatively small budget gives the game both advantages and disadvantages. A small budget leaves relatively no room for polish, this makes for some of the cheesiest and expected jump scares I have encountered in the horror genre. This has nothing to do with aesthetic, its timing and predictability. (I’ve played Clock Tower which is a good counter example of how a little polish goes a long way in the horror genre). A small budget also makes the game linear, devoid even of any perceived choice in both the narrative and the puzzle solving, all of the puzzles have one solution and most of the time the item will disappear immediately after one use.
The Last Door occasionally suffers from obscure puzzle solutions (like any game of this genre) SPOILERS:

Even having only played for a few hours, I can already tell this game has some serious issues that need to be fixed before I'd consider recommending it to anyone. Yes, it's a fun and unique experience, and I hope these flaws are addressed,  but some of the mechanics, while well-implemented, just aren't good mechanics to have. They sound great on paper, but are terrible when put into practice.
I'm speaking of course, of the weapon power up system. When you get a kill, the victim drops a resource that "levels up" your weapon, granting it extra abilities, damage, fire rate, etc. Okay, not that bad, rewarding the player for getting kills. Except these powerups are lost in full as soon as you die, putting you at a massive disadvantage when you respawn. Not only does it reward the player who got the kill beyond the reward of the kill itself, but it punishes the player who got killed beyond the punishment of having died. All it really serves as is a massive snowball effect. The more kills you get, the easier it is to get more. This also applies to the rest of your team. If you're doing well, you'll quickly max out your weapon level, leaving the rest of the power boost resources on the ground for your team-mates. The game becomes easier as you progress not only because you do more damage, but because the enemy player has lost all of their weapon's progress, meaning they can't out-damage you, and the only chance they have of making a comeback relies on you and/or your team making a mistake. Also, it influences what weapons are viable, as you have to actually move to where the victim died to pick up the resource that powers your weapon, meaning sniping is an inferior playstyle that provides no reward. Why even have a sniper if using it is more punishing than rewarding? Not only do you not get a boost to the weapon by using it as intended, but the resource is left on the ground in the open, where anyone could pick it up, whether they're on your team or not. So in sniping, you risk rewarding the other team more than yourself.
Furthermore, most of the Death Match maps I've seen have all lended themselves almost exclusively to close range combat. Cover is abundant, making mid and long range combat a frustrating game of peek-a-boo, as all of the weapons suited to mid-long range combat have such long kill times, the player can simply duck around a corner before you have a chance to inflict a lethal amount of damage, recover their health, and come back, inevitably rushing you and making the  fight a close range encounter. Also, the melee weapons are all absurdly broken, as they're equally as powerful and even stronger in some cases than the projectile weapons, take less skill to use, and are more rewarding, as close range fights make powering up your weapon even easier. That leads to a majority of the players in a match, outside of the bots that fill the empty slots in the teams, using melee weapons as a primary, making the projectile weapons seem like a mere afterthought. There shouldn't be a clearly better option in a game centered around balance and variety. And in my opinion,  weapon's damage output should scale with their difficulty to use, which I don't think is reflected in the game's aresenal of weapons.
Moving on from that, a lot of the game feels very unpolished. When moving around, I've gotten stuck clipping on obstacles that should have easily been walked or jumped over, gotten stuck in walls, titans, and machine turrets, and even just gotten stuck on oddly shaped geometry due to what seems like bad collision detection.
Also, in pretty much every game mode, be prepared to have your shots completely blocked by team-mates getting between you and your target. I don't think team-killing is possible, but I've gotten killed plenty of times due to a team-mate blocking my shot on an enemy, then dying while reloading after wasting half a clip into the back of their head.
The game's Titan mode is fun and interesting, but isn't very well explained. I had to figure out the objectives, as well as how to achieve them, through trial and error. The tutorial tells you what to do, but it doesn't tell you WHY you should be doing it. And I didn 't even get to watch most of the tutorial, because I opened a menu in the middle of it, which was impossible to close once it had been opened, and obstructed almost the entire screen, including the "hint" text fields that are meant to provide information about the game. In addition to the lack of in-depth explanation, there are fixed spawn zones in Titan mode that can be outright camped by one or two enemy players, making it impossible for you or your team to collect resources to power your titan, destroy the enemy titan, or  defend your own from enemy fire.
There's also no visible health indicator in your in-game HUD (I eventually figured out that the more damage you've taken, the brighter your character glows orange, but the game never told me that I should be watching for that) as well as various UI problems, like the in-game scoreboard rarely shows an accurate readout of the match, instead displaying only your own stats, and the stats of the best player from either team, leaving your team-mates readout with a bunch of zeroes,  spite the actual score indicating otherwise. (This has been my experience with it at least. I tend to open the scoreboard whenever I die to keep tabs on the match, and I've seen an accurate, completely filled scoreboard like twice out of more than two dozen games. )
On top of all of this, every time I close the game, it hard-locks and can't be closed without hitting ALT+Ctrl+Del, opening the task manager, typing the name of the program (Because the blank game window stays on top of every other program you're running, making it impossible to see what you're doing) and hit delete to force close it.
In conclusion, this game is not bad by any stretch, and has a lot of potential to be incredibly good, in fact. It just needs to have a lot of these glaring flaws smoothed out before that can happen. If you're an optimist, and like the idea of what this game COULD be, then by all means, purchase it. If you're just going to casually play for fun, and not care about whether it's fair or balanced, go ahead. But if you're a competitive player that wants a tactical team-based shooter, don't bother. 90% of the players I've seen use swords, as they require the least skill and provide the most reward. The developers may as well just make a swordfight game mode, then maybe the sword kids wouldn't be such a plague in the deathmatch mode.
If these changes are addressed in future updates, I'll gladly change my review to be more supportive of the game, as I like the idea of a shooter/MOBA crossover and would like to see it succeed.

This game helped me through severe depression after my wife left me. I was a mess, binging on coke and strippers to try and forget the pain she brought to me. Next thing I knew I was shooting Heroin in a Vietnamese rice farmer's hut. Don't ask me how I got there and why I decided to stay for 7 months amongst his family of 12, but I thought this was the end of my miserable life. As I lay naked in a pile of my own and what was mostly the vietnamese family's vomit and excrement... there I saw it. The light glistening on the screen. It seemed MW2 had swept the world by its feet and even in the remote jungles of Vietnam it managed to find itself. It was clear to me, this was a sign. God himself intended for me to see it. The little vietnamese child obviously didn't know what he was doing, as the little noob camped in the corner with his ACR with dual attachments of a heat sensor and a silencer, I marvelled at the beauty of this game. At once I got up, and I ran. Did I know which way to run? No. But I didn't let that stop me. Sooner or later I was back in the humble streets of my hometown. I picked up MW2 for PS3 at tescos and went on to play the game for 4 days straight without food or water. My mother and father were a little worries considering they presumed me dead and I hadn't bathed since I was back. But if there's anything I learned it's that In those 4 days I was born again, although I soiled myself several times and passed out once, I knew what it meant in life to experience pure joy and happiness. As a married man with 2 beautiful children now I really hope MW2 is brought on to next gen consoles; it will bring the utmost joy to me, and my children will be able to relive the pure ecstacy I felt. Of course they're not old enough to play yet and not even nearly mentally developed to even comprehend what would be going on as they are still babies. But the bright and vivid images of their father getting that 30th kill streak with his ump-45 silencer will fill their small hearts with pride. As they watch their father roar in triumph as the screen goes white and the battle ceases. There I will stand proud a man. A man with a 5.2 K/D ratio. A true champion. A figure to look up to. A figure to learn from. And you better believe that once they are of legal age I'll teach them and guide them to achieve the successes I have. But alas as my imagination delves deep into a utopian world it hits me that in fact this is not the case. Instead I lay here in bed next to my Russian mail-ordered wife. where only these fantasies numb the cruel pain of life. In a word, FIngerbones can be described as "interesting". Like most psychological horror games, it is mainly suspense through apprehensive assumption and visuals that give implications, with the final moment giving way to a startling realization. That being said, it's not really scary per-se, but gives way to a startling thought process through its storytelling. I myself have never been one for these kinds of horror games; I never really found them scary, and this one is no different. But that's not why I'm recommending Fingerbones. I'm recommending it for the story it tells. The story is very engaging, and while it doesn't really incite fear, it does incite other emotions and raises questions about human philosophy and morality. If you're a fan of psycological horror games, or well-told stories, then you should definitely give this game a try (and for the low price of free, there's really no reason NOT to)!

JA Reloaded got a lot of negative feedback mainly due to a couple of things.One is the name Jagged Alliance because it makes you compare it to JA2. The Gameplay might not be nearly as deep as JA2 but it is good enough on its own to make the game worth playing. The other thing is the connection problem it had on launch. The connection issue has been fixed and while fixing it the devs tried to explain what is going on and not hiding and stay silent which was very nice.
At this point I'm 14 hours in and there is a huge amount of content I have not yet seen so the below is based on the missions I've played so far.
The gameplay cannot compare in complexity with JA2 and it is not something revolutionary which doesn't mean it is not worth the price. There are plenty of missions in variety of locations. Each mission is divided in several sub-missions. The level design is not allowing approaching the target location from multiple directions as in JA2 . In some levels you can use alternative routes and that's about it. The gameplay focuses on utilizing the different character classes and using the environment (cover, explosive tanks) to your advantage. The mercenary classes are not that strict and you can put the points you get wherever you like. For instance it is wise your sniper character to get a few points in a short range weapon like pistol, shotgun or smg since the sniper rifle is not effective at short ranges and if enemies get close you will need a short range weapon. In general you need team which consists of different classes that complement each other. Till now I've encountered one boss battle so there are bosses too. The variety of weapons and armor is quite nice.
There is a light base management part in which you can upgrade your storage and clinic but it only consist of upgrading the building when you have met the requirements. There is also multiplayer although since the player base is not very big you first need to ask in global chat if someone wants PvP so you can setup the match.
There are some things that I find oddly missing from this type of game: no grenades, no hand to hand combat, no melee weapons which means that stealth is useful only for taking better position and setting ambushes, You cannot move the camera so sometimes is hard to click at the place where you want your character to move. These are the things I find the game is lacking.
JA reloaded might be not that complex(something a lot of tactical tuned based fans are looking for) but the action oriented gameplay creates a fun and fast paced experience.

Genre - Turn based squad combat
I was never a massive player of the orignal Jagged Alliance games, but got quite into the online version and enjoy these type of games.
They have now released a one off payment version of the same game with added achievements etc. As the price was quite reasonable I thought I'd give it another go. It kept all my progress, which is handy and I have been able to play a couple of missions. The game plays the same as the online version without pesky micro-transactions. You unlock missions across the map as your mercs progress and can upgrade their weapons/armour/ammo with those you buy or find. You also have a mini-base to upgrade, if that takes your fancy.
It is a fun turn based game and although there are some limitations like no higher ground or explosions. The combat is still enjoyable and now it can't be accused of being P2W. Although I think they would be silly not to offer some mercs as permanent DLC. Luckily I was able to carry two of mine across already.
At a price of £5-£6 I think you should definately get your monies worth for a casual turn based combat game. The developers also appear to be fairly active and hope they will continue to support it. There is also a multiplayer mode if you want to fight other pesky humans,
However, I have been told it is isn't the best JA game, so you will have to ask a real fanboy for that.

Minimum is a game where players in teams of five fight against another team, upgrading weapons, armor and their titan. Each team has one titan, which respawns shortly after death, and it's up to each team to defend their titan, while attacking the other, in the hopes of pushing their titan towards victory. It's a dynamic variation on the 'ARTS/MOBA' formula.
This game style works great, and is a tonne of fun but there are a few issues that need to be brought up.
1. Nobody likes to communicate in this team game where co-operation is nearly always vital to victory.
2. The game gives you the opportunity to get kills (which lets you upgrade your weapons and equipment while simultaneously getting score), or focus on killing or upgrading the titans (which lets you win the game). Being a video game, played by imperfect people, people often focus on getting kills instead of winning the game.
3. It's really quite irritating that a player needs to grind to try out new things, and considering the fact that the balance can often end up wonky, it feels like Minimum asks for too much time.

Yeah, Minimum as in "Minimum thought went into designing this game"
Unbalanced system, broken matchmaking, lackluster weaponry, screwy hit detection, and laggy servers are what you have to look forward to if you install this thing.
I really really wish it were on the Wii U...

This is an update of my original review, after having about a week to get to know the game better.
Going to give this a thumbs up with some reservations.
Pros:
1. Can't beat the price.
2. Captures the feel of the old Escape Velocity series extremely well, with some much needed ease-of-use updates (such as being able to tell from the map what a system will pay for a given commodity, something you had to do by memory or with a notepad back in the day).
Cons:
1. Piracy is not a viable option from what I can tell.  Even if you are able to disable a ship without destroying it (not easy in my experience), you only have maybe 3 seconds before some do-gooder tries to help you by blasting your prize into space dust.  If you do successfully manage to board a ship and attempt to capture it, you will very likely lose crew members in the process and end up paying death benefits.  Death benefits are, from my understanding, calculated as a percentage of the captured ship's value so you'll always make some profit if you sell the ship, but it can be too small to make it worth it.
2. Combat itself needs a little work.  Large combats involving a lot of ships get chaotic and if your target is offscreen it can be next to impossible to track them on the minimap.
3. There is a fair amount of grinding in the early game in the form of "deliver 12 tons of rubber goods to the Vega system" type missions.  That's true to the original series, but it's also not very exciting.  The good news is that if you're smart about it, that part won't last long.  I've seen a lot of people complain that you start the game with a mortgage on your ship, but if you trade intelligently and pick good missions (hint: plan your route efficiently!) you should be able to pay the mortgage off within an hour or so of play.  Once that's done, you should be able to work your way up to afford a decent ship not long after, and that's when things become fun.
In spite of those problems, it can be very addictive and will definitely scratch the nostalgia itch for those of us who remember EV fondly from back in the day.

This game helped me through severe depression after my wife left me. I was a mess, binging on coke and strippers to try and forget the pain she brought to me. Next thing I knew I was shooting Heroin in a Vietnamese rice farmer's hut. Don't ask me how I got there and why I decided to stay for 7 months amongst his family of 12, but I thought this was the end of my miserable life. As I lay naked in a pile of my own and what was mostly the vietnamese family's vomit and excrement... there I saw it. The light glistening on the screen. It seemed MW2 had swept the world by its feet and even in the remote jungles of Vietnam it managed to find itself. It was clear to me, this was a sign. God himself intended for me to see it. The little vietnamese child obviously didn't know what he was doing, as the little noob camped in the corner with his ACR with dual attachments of a heat sensor and a silencer, I marvelled at the beauty of this game. At once I got up, and I ran. Did I know which way to run? No. But I didn't let that stop me. Sooner or later I was back in the humble streets of my hometown. I picked up MW2 for PS3 at tescos and went on to play the game for 4 days straight without food or water. My mother and father were a little worries considering they presumed me dead and I hadn't bathed since I was back. But if there's anything I learned it's that In those 4 days I was born again, although I soiled myself several times and passed out once, I knew what it meant in life to experience pure joy and happiness. As a married man with 2 beautiful children now I really hope MW2 is brought on to next gen consoles; it will bring the utmost joy to me, and my children will be able to relive the pure ecstacy I felt. Of course they're not old enough to play yet and not even nearly mentally developed to even comprehend what would be going on as they are still babies. But the bright and vivid images of their father getting that 30th kill streak with his ump-45 silencer will fill their small hearts with pride. As they watch their father roar in triumph as the screen goes white and the battle ceases. There I will stand proud a man. A man with a 5.2 K/D ratio. A true champion. A figure to look up to. A figure to learn from. And you better believe that once they are of legal age I'll teach them and guide them to achieve the successes I have. But alas as my imagination delves deep into a utopian world it hits me that in fact this is not the case. Instead I lay here in bed next to my Russian mail-ordered wife. where only these fantasies numb the cruel pain of life. Although I am happy to have a wife and children, my profession as MW2 montage specialist has failed to provide for me in recent years; in fact my primary source of income is the allowance my mother gives me weekly. I forgot to mention that my job situation has resulted in me living at my parent's home... But I digress. Thus I cannot even begin to explain the importance of bringing MW2 to next gen consoles. It has become a joke that not a single person will pay for a copy of my ps3 MW2 360 no-scope montages. The dedication and time I put into these videos cannot be overstated. I hope that this petition succeeds. For the sake of my wife Vladimir, and my children Terminal and Highrise I pray this comes true. Nothing will bring me more joy. Nothing.

Steam tells me I now have over 500 hrs in this game so I feel somewhat qualified to give an opinion on it.
Bulletpoints since I know text scares most of you:
- Casual (no active full time commitment required)
- Fun (its engaging and enjoyable)
- RPG (distinct classes with separate mechanics, perhaps not perfectly balanced)
- Semi-afk (can play for a minute and minimize while waiting for quest to complete etc)
- Surprising depth once you spend some time with it (nothing too complicaed but can min-max)
- Needs some time to unlock all game features (can take a month of gameplay to unlock all features when ftp)
- Poor ingame manual and tutorials, you will need to do some research in order to understand how to play the game effectivelly (core gameplay needs little explanation but there are some wtf moments until you get up to speed)
- Decent community (good forum with a lot of experienced and knowledgeable players and information but no global game or server chat)
- Multiple servers to make an account but language is an issue (my International server is almost exclusively people from Chech republic, Poland, Russia etc. with English VERY much a second language)
- COMPLETELY TIME PLAYED DEPENDENT (unless you joined as soon as a new server is opened you will ALWAYS be a noob. Progress in the game is directly dependent on time spent adventuring amd if you join later there is NO way to catch up to the leading players if that is something you will want)
- COMPLETELY PAY TO WIN (an aspect of the above point - progress in the game is completely dependent on your XP and level. If you are f2p your quest energy bar is 100. If you pay money its 300. The game gives some help to f2p players but p2w players can still progress at least 2 times faster at the very least)
- Energy bars to limit actions and activity (if that wasn't clear)
Overall, its a decent game and i'm enjoying it but be aware that it can be a time and money sink if you want to play in a more competitive way and that the top few hundred in the rankings is completely p2w.
Cheers

An eerie and atmospheric point and click adventure with a simultaneously simplified and detailed art style and a Lovecraftian, "elder gods and creeping insanity" story. Each chapter is relatively short and the puzzles aren't too difficult so you'll rarely feel stuck but it shouldn't feel like a walk in the park either. Especially for its price, I would highly recommend it.

The Last Door (Season One) is a retro crowd-funded point and click adventure game with lovecraftian overtones. The protagonist, Jeremiah Devitt receives a letter from an old friend asking for his help and sets off on an adventure fraught with mystery and terror.
Visuals in TLD are minimalistic to the point of being almost incomprehensible and I immediately had flashbacks of playing old Sierra text-parser adventure games. Thankfully, there is a point and click interface. Additionally, the graphical minimalism actually works in favor of the player since, with larger pixels, there is less of a “hunt” to find interactive objects.
Puzzles range from generally easy to extremely easy with maybe one or two particular puzzles requiring the player to stop and think, so it’s best to go into TLD treating it as a story-based PnC game (a la telltale games) than as a serious adventure game.
The game is about 4-5 hours long and, for an average minimum sale price of $2, will give you just enough bang for your buck for a quick game to play over the course of a single evening. I’m looking forward to trying the sequel, once another sale rolls around.

There is definitely some good art here to be sure, but the experience really falls apart in the game portion.  There aren't really any puzzles to speak of.  Anything nearly along the lines of a puzzle like pulling levers or adjusting the hands on a cuckoo clock to the proper time are incredibly simple.  Most of the game is just wandering around hoping of the rooms you've past through 10 times before has something different in it.  A slow story that really never does get anywhere even in the last act is made mind numbingly slower by giving you nothing to do.
There are some nice effects in the pixel art--although that is a mixed bag as the overall crudeness of it makes it sometimes hard to see what might be worth clicking on.  But the light and shadows in the art is very nicely rendered.  The aural landscape is very good, except in the last chapter where they seem to have forgotten it.  If the Edgar Allen Poe/H.P. Lovecraft pastiche had been more interesting or the puzzles more present, or your direction through the game less vague, I would have recommended it.

The Last Door - Season One is a game that's a conglomeration of four chapters; each that were released on Kickstarter throughout 2013. At first, developer The Game Kitchen saw very few backers, but that gradually changed with the creation of each new episode. Finalized and bundled into one season title, The Last Door has seen great success with the gaming community, and it has received many awards since its release in May of 2014.
The player will control Jeremiah Devitt, a man who receives a letter from his old schoolmate and friend, Anthony Beechworth. The arcane contents unsettle Devitt, and so he goes out in search of the whereabouts of his former classmate. What disentangles is a vague, perplexing mystery as Devitt uncovers long forgotten secrets from his youth. Each episode takes place in a different area of Victorian England, ranging from a creepy old manor to an unsettling nunnery, and even crypts. The story is very convoluted and at times dry, it's definitely not something that is going to appeal to a large variety of people. As well, one couldn't necessarily call this a horror game so much as it is a mystery title at best.
The Last Door has been heavily inspired by the works of famous authors such as H.P. Lovecraft, Jorge Luis Borges, and Edgar Allan Poe. Judging by many of the reviews and comments on this game, people seem to believe that it's more so Lovecraftian than anything, but I did not have this perception during my 4 hours with the title. If anything, The Last Door feels overwhelmingly Poe inspired; not only given the large amount of ravens that are dealt with, but the overall writing style. There's nothing here discussing the void, abyss, cosmos, or anything else that would indicate a huge presence of Lovecraft, though the obscurity of the storyline may fall into a Lovecraftian twist category.
In relation to other point and click pixel graphic games, The Last Door doesn't stand out much from the crowd. The art is well done, but it's also become a fairly standard style within the last couple of years. Objects are easy to spot since they're highlighted when you mouse over them, and there's only so many items that you can click on; needless to say, the puzzles are relatively easy to solve, so long as you don't mind a bit of repetitive wandering. There are plenty of notes and diaries to read to delve further into the story, and there are a handful of "minisodes" to explore that last between 1-3 minutes. The soundtrack on the other hand is absolutely incredible, it's extremely dramatic and it easily overwhelms the senses. It's nice to know that as of September 6, 2016, the developer has included the OST with the game for free.
I'm personally a big fan of Victorian Gothic style, and I love the works of Poe and especially Lovecraft. That being said, I didn't find The Last Door to be everything that people have hyped it up to be. The story can come off really dry at times, and it's shrouded in mystery; you get the general gist of what's going on by the end, but nothing is revealed for certain. The gameplay doesn't have very many puzzles so much as simply running around and collecting items to use at a later time. The Last Door is neither bad nor something to praise to the sun and back, it's really just an average Victorian Gothic point and click.

Let me just start by saying that you will never be as scared of pixels in your life as you will be if you play through The Last Door. There were more genuinely chilling moments in this point and click adventure game than in most AAA horror games. It is Lovecraftian which is a very endearing factor to me, but they introduce that factor in such a creative way. I truly believe that if H.P. Lovecraft were in the indie game scene today, what he came up with would not be far off from this amazing work of art by The Game Kitchen.
The cult scenes were some of the most frightening ones in he first season. They tell a story in such a way that you are at the same time perplexed as to what could be at the root of everything, while so drawn to the mystery that you can not put the mouse down. I do mention the mouse, but these games are also available on mobile if that is more up your alley. I thoroughly enjoyed the PC version, but I would urge you to play them however you are most comfortable. I personally started on mobile a while back but got so stuck that I didn't pick it back up until I got the first season on Steam. This is, I'm sure, much more a testament of how I am with mobile gaming rather than how well the mobile version plays.
I was so excited to learn that the second season is up and ready to go, I think it is worth saying that the first season made it into my short list of favorite steam games and with very good reason. It is not always easy to solve the next step of the journey, it sometimes takes tracking through the different rooms and pondering how you could combine your collected objects or use them to interact with the environment. I am honestly blown away by the level of emersion they were able to pull of with the graphics that are used and the point and click system. I am by no means a person who demands high quality graphics and resolution for games, but still the level of depth and story they were able to pull off with the most basic level of quality, is simply breathtaking.
I could rave about the reasons this game is a must play for any gamer for hours, but I really think that I would be wasting time that you could be using to just go and play it now, it is just that good. I seriously appreciated all the time and effort spent in making this game into a genuine addition to the Cthulhu Mythos. It utilizes some of the more eerie aspects of Lovecraftian horror in an unexpected way that made for one incredible experience.

(In future, I may rewrite this review, as currently I am posting it with a view to those considering Minimum while on sale, and so need to write it quickly. My views on the game would remain the same, however.)
To sum up my opinion: Although much of its content remains unimplemented, Minimum currently is a robust game that is quite well made and enjoyable to play. Be aware, however, that you will have to make an account with the game in order to play (or, at least, it was required at some point in the game's life).
I bought this game shortly after it came out of Early Access, as it sounded to me like it kept the elements I enjoy of MOBAs while adding in the aspects of team-based shooters that I enjoy more. And, for the most part, Minimum does so.
-What exactly is this game?
Sort of a cross between the standard MOBA and TF2, in my experience. There are three gamemodes, Titan, Deathmatch, and Horde. Horde can be somewhat confusing and is geared towards co-op (perhaps a bit like Mann vs. Machine in TF2) while Deathmatch is the standard shooters game type. Minimum's main uniqueness comes from Titan mode, a 5v5 format where each team attempts to activate and protect their Titan mech as it battles the enemy Titan and breaks through enemy defensive walls, eventually shattering their base to win the match. Although each Titan has a massive amount of health, players are able to deal noticeable amounts of damage to them if left unhindered, so each team will usually be fighting one another while the Titans are battling themselves. After both Titans have been destroyed, each team begins collecting charges by killing creeps located between the team bases. Whichever team obtains more charges for their Titan has an innate advantage in the next Titan battle, or 'Clash'. Games can last varying lengths of time depending on how many Clashes are required to break the enemy base, but in my experience they are usually on the order of 10-20 minutes, possibly 30 on the outside, similar to a round of Payload or Attack/Defence in TF2.
-What do I do in this game?
Mainly, players run around and shoot Titans, creeps, and each other. There are no set classes, but as is common in shooters, players set loadouts of weapons and gadgets before matches and then may quick-swap while in-game. Also, there is an armor system- each player can craft a head, torso, and leg armor from materials dropped from various sources or found around the maps. These armors usually grant either a situational bonus, such as increased speed at low health, a weak all-around bonus, such as reduced bullet damage, or a strong bonus paired with a potent downside, such as significantly increased health but much lower speed.
The weapons are mainly what you would expect in a shooter- sniper rifles, shotguns, assault rifles, miniguns, and launchers, along with melee weapons in the form of swords. There are some interesting subtypes of these weapons, however- for example, their are shotguns with forward dashes or high-jumps as altfire options. Another of Minimum's important systems is the weapon upgrade mechanic- every killed player, and certain other entities, drops an upgrade part. Picking this up increases the power of the currently equipped weapon, up to five times if I remember correctly. Most or all of these upgrade levels are lost on death.
-That sounds somewhat unbalanced for some players to have powered-up weapons and others not in a shooter. Also, aren't those melee weapons overpowered, like many have said?
Occasionally, yes, but in my experience most times good aim and possibly suprise can take out any player, even if they possess a maxed gun, as they will still have roughly the same health as any other player. Yes, they have an advantage in drawn-out fights or in ambushes, but when they die, they feed that advantage to other players. And in their own respect, katanas are fairly reasonable- it takes several swings to kill another player, and should they escape out of range, you are extremely vulnerable, as the distance-closing dash on the basic katanas has a recharge time. Shotguns especially are highly effective against melee enemies. As is often the case in multiplayer games, if the teams are heavily imbalanced or if every person on one team is using the same weapon, things can become annoying and unfair, but most of the time, Minimum is as balanced as any other team-based game.
-How are the graphics?
Although not intensive, Minimum has some beautiful visuals, in my opinion. As the title might suggest, they are often minimalistic, but they come across much as the best pixel art does, vibrant, elegant and clear simultaneously. The colors are quite nice, the Titans look great, and the weapons and projectiles all match the art style well. Character movement and reload animations are perfect most of the time, and are animated in substantial detail. And, each map feels unique, with its own movement lanes and seperated levels, paths and flanking routes, and eye candy, such as Japanese designs or industrial machines. The only real problem I have is that the player characters are rather empty, being just pure white cube people, until armor is equipped, after which they look somewhat more detailed.
-Final Notes
Minimum has a reasonably long-term item unlock mechanic, where each completed match earns you XP and resources. Each time you level up, you may unlock one new item blueprint, which can be crafted with enough resources. Without playing all that much, I have unlocked enough weapons to enjoy myself, but it takes quite a while to unlock everything. For the most part, you may not purchase resources with real money, so it is mainly fair to all players, although it seems that purchasing a reskin of an item with real money may grant the item, even should you not own the normal version.
At least at release, Minimum required the creation of an account with a back-end manager called Mber, which syncs with Steam and does not require much attention beyond initial setup.
Finally, many of Minimum's future mechanics, such as weapon modification, are not implemented yet, even though the game is out of Early Access, the daily tasks and menu screens could still use some work to function better, and, at least for me, the game occasionally crashes when attempting to exit. However, the devs have shown consistent support of their game and have continued implementation of the content they have promised, and have repaired many of the bugs since the game's release.
Especially at 75% off, I would highly recommend Minimum as an enjoyable, well-made team shooter with much potential.

What do I have to say about this game..
Endless Sky is a completely free, top-down, 2D space game. But there's more to it than that; think Elite Dangerous meets 2D with text-based story telling charm.
Gameplay:
Gameplay typically goes along the lines of this:
Game: "Buy your first ever spacecraft! Pick from a transport, cargo ship, or a fighter!"
Player: "I want the fighter!"
Banks: "Let me just set your mortgage appropriately..."
*Proceeds to suffer paycheck to paycheck*
Yeah.. Never start with the fighter. Bad idea.
Once you get the basics down, a lot of the gameplay boils down to your character trying to earn a living through either pirating, transporting tourists around, and/or shipping cargo around the galaxy, and avoiding pirate raids. Be warned, this game does take a little trial and error before you're able to get the hang of it.
What catches my attention is the surprising amount of story a free game like this has. The random events can range from a funny little fetch quest (Go save my pookie!), to helping scientsts with something, to throwing you the chance to go off on a sudden story quest.
The writing has a charm to it. The dialog is surprisingly well written, every planet, starport, and space station has it's own bio and photo (There are a LOT of planets), and the science is well researched.
OVERALL: 8/10
Upsides:
This game is clearly someones passion project, and the passion shows. From how far I've played, the characters have personality, the writing is vivid, the planets are well thought out, and the story that I've experienced thus far is interesting. I can honestly say this is the first time a completely free game has thoroughly impressed me. This game has well over 15-20+ hours of potential minimum playtime.
Well thoughtout universe and story!
Huge number of ships, upgrades, and planets!
No Microtransactions!
Good autosave system!
Forgot to save and now your flagship is destroyed, along with that cargo that was going to net you 124,000 creds? Don't worry about it, you can pick up back at whatever planet you last took off from!
Downsides:
The initial tutorial quests, which do have some variation (+Brownie Point Get), don't cover as much as they could. They explain the game concepts well, but the only way to learn the controls, how to hyperjump, target, fire, et cetera, is to look in your options menu. This isn't a huge issue, as there aren't many controls for the game and they're fairly simple at that.
The UI could use a little improvement. I'd like to have my flagship's shield and hull stats next to the rest of my fleet, and the enemy's stats nearby, rather than have all three seperated. It makes it difficult to properly manage a ship (let alone a fleet) during combat.
There isn't any way that I've found that will make all of the ships in your fleet jump at once, they go at their own pace and become scattered between planets if you move too fast.
Still not convinced that this game may be a hidden gem? Try it out, it's free, you have nothing to loose!

I bought Transistor because people recommended it for having a good story. The gameplay is a somewhat fun fusion between strategy and action RPG, albeit very repetitive since the enemy types aren't mixed up that much - in the final area you almost exclusively fight a single enemy type in every battle which gets tedious.
However, the story isn't very good. The ending is interesting, but the rest is lacking. Half the plot is buried in logs that you have to unlock by using your abilities in different ways. The logs are very dry and not particularly interesting to read. If they'd been spiced up, like by having them take the form of diary entries, they might allow some character development. Unfortunately, they read like encyclopedia entries.
The other half of the plot is okay, but I couldn't bring myself to care very much about the city, the process, or the Camerata. Unfortunately the story doesn't do much to make you invested in what happens to the city since it's a pretty empty setting and you don't see it before the process starts attacking it. You also don't get to interact with many characters in the city, which doesn't help.
The plot also just doesn't have much meat to it, with few twists and not much happening. That's not so bad since it's a fairly short game, but I would have liked to see a bit more. It has a good sense of atmosphere and the style of the dialogue has a noire feel. As a backdrop to the gameplay the plot is fine, but it doesn't stand well on its own.
As far as characters go, the man in the sword is fairly interesting and you get pretty attached to him through the course of the story. Unfortunately, he's the only interesting character in the game. Red, the protagonist, had potential, but is unfortunately silent. She does occasionally communicate with the man in the sword through writing in terminals, but those moments are few and far between and don't convey an interesting personality. You get hints at an interesting relationship between Red and the man in the sword, but since she's silent it can't develop very much.
Overall, I felt pretty disappointed by the story. But if all you're looking for is fun gameplay then this game might entertain you for a few hours.

Transistor, to me, is one of those frustrating games where it does some things just amazingly well, but the rest of the game just doesn't go very well.
Transistor doesn't really fit into any real genre molds. It plays from an isometric view and is an action game (akin to Bastion in a way), but you have the ability to freeze time using Turn() and plan out a series of moves, after which you will be unable to use most abilities until your Turn() becomes available again. There are access points periodically (read: after every fight, sometimes 2 after every fight) where you can choose your loadout, which is based on what functions you have available. You get to use up to 20 different functions, which can be assigned to either active abilities (abilities you actually use in combat), passive abilities (passively grant you bonuses, some of which must meet certain criteria), and enhancements/upgrades (buff a specific active ability to have extra effects). There are some really great combos that can be achieved, but you have to manage your abilities with your available memory, meaning you can't just dump all of your best available skills into your loadout and leave the smaller ones out to dry. There is a good deal of tactics involved.
Another good point about the game is the enemy design. They gradually scale up throughout the course of the game in terms of what abilities they have. Early on it's easy enough to dispose of them, but when an enemy is able to cloak itself, and another is able to block out most of the screen during a turn, it can be quite frustrating to finish off the opposition before they knock out one of your abilities. Many of them also compliment each other in such a way that you have to be extremely tactical in how you maneuver so that you can eliminate a certain target while getting out of harm's way long enough for your next turn to come around.
Now, for the bad stuff. My personal pet peeve was in how the loadout menus were managed. You would think that you could just bring up the loadout with all of the slots and just mix and match until your memory is full, but no. You are given your list of functions, and you get to assign each one individually. You want to put Breach() as an active ability? Better go find the correct function that is taking up the slot you want it to go in! Oh, you deleted the wrong one? Oops, lets go click on... Oh, you double clicked and accidentally put the wrong ability in that slot. And now you deleted the correct one, only to find out that it has one open enhancement slot when you want Breach() to have 2 enhancement slots. Time to go delete everything and just start from scratch. Yes, it was that tedious.
The voice acting was just incredibly frustrating. I really liked Red (the protagonist), but she had her voice taken away right before the game started, meaning she doesn't talk. She can still hum (she's a professional singer), which is quite good, but that's it. The guy stuck in the Transistor that serves as the narrator has a lot of short quips that don't provide anything, and listening to the final boss talk for about 20 minutes until you reach him is as exciting as drinking battery acid.
As for neutral stuff, the story is about a futuristic city where people can be digitized into this Transistor, and this group of people tries to take control and make their ideal world, and then they goof up and their army just obliterates everything because they accidentally threw away their only ability to control them. It's kind of interesting from a programmer standpoint, but it's not that interesting to me, especially from such a limited perspective (the only outside input you get are short quips from scattered terminals).
The game includes limiters, which make certain aspects of the game harder, such as doubling enemy damage, making enemies spawn double cells when they die, shielding those cells, etc. They make gameplay more interesting, as you can essentially toggle the difficulty settings during the course of the game, with the reward being a small increase in experience.
Overall, I would still recommend Transistor from a pure gameplay perspective. But by far the biggest pro of all..
+Cash shop does not offer ANY in-game advantages, in fact, it hardly offers any aesthetic advantages either.

I could list a couple other ones, but those are pretty MMO-generic.

A lot has changed since I played so I'll change my review to reflect what I experienced in Heavensward and what I assume hasn't changed about the game.
Dungeons: They're incredibly linear and shallow. Boss battles can be mechanically satisfying but the majority of your time is spent grinding mobs with a lot of health. There's really nothing fun or rewarding about them. You'll find yourself spamming queues for them in order to level up after the story stops leveling for you. All of these issues wouldn't matter too much if the combat this game has to offer was fun. There is nothing enjoyable about cooldown dependant combat. Especially if your class has buff micro-management.
Raids and trials: Essentially giant sponges that have a long list of mechanics to memorize. You'll find your party wiping tons of times. Drops are rolled on so good luck getting what you wanted. There is nothing fun about completing the same battle over and over again. Why not add longetivity elsewhere? They're another aspect of the game negatively affected by the limitations of the combat system as well.
Fates and hunts: Look, I know you want to give people a reason to revisit locations but collecting items and grinding mobs is not a good way to do it. Yet another aspect hindered by the combat system.
PVP: It doesn't have much to offer, desperately needs more maps and more of an incentive to do them. You'll have to convert your friends to your grand company as well.
Relic weapons: Probably the most boring, time demanding aspect of the game. Trust me, it's not worth the time and effort.
Crafting: Literally useless for armor and weapons. Really just a tool for running the economy.
Gathering: I'll admit, I like fishing. It's good when you just want to relax and take a break from what should be redundant. But the others, all you do is run around and press one button. Just WTF...
Weekly capped gear: This is my biggest complaint about the game. There's gear that gets released with every update and you have to collect tomes by repeating already completed content in order to get them. By the time you have the set the next one is out so you feel like you wasted all of your time doing something boring and repetitive.
IL: Item level, it's important as it dictates a lot about what you're able to do in this game. Forget skill, it's all about having the best gear in the game. That's why the game pulls in a lot of people with a superiority complex. Instead of getting better at the game through experience with the combat system, you get better by remembering patterns and getting a just as studied group to do raids all day (Or get the somewhat inferior capped gear)...
Queues: Yep, you don't need any friends, play with random people from other servers.... Mostly easy stuff anyways.
Story: Probably the only reason to play, ♥♥♥♥ endgame.
So, do you want to do the same boring content over and over again for months just get better gear or do you want to play a game where every victory is rewarding and every challenge is engaging and satisfying?

All shock, no awe.
I REALLY wanted to like this game, being a fan of Devolver Games, as well as classic beat-em-ups and generally challenging games.  But after playing through the normal campaign of Mother Russia Bleeds, I ended up hating it.
The pixelated visual style is pretty great at nailing the gritty, ugly aesthetic that I think it was going for.  The violence and gore are presented in a way that at first, looks and feels pretty satisfying. However, after a short while, this just devolves into a clumsy, frustrating monotony.
The game seems like its really going out of it's way to try and shock me, rather than be a good game.  It has some moments where you think "oh this is like Streets of Rage 2!" and other parts that are reminiscent of SplatterHouse.  However, ultimately it lacks the finesse of SoR2, which came out nearly 25 years ago!
All the characters play pretty much identically, with the exact same movesets, just animated differently.  There's a satisfying "head crush" execution move you can pull off, however you are discouraged from doing it as you are guaranteed not to get health from it, same goes for the fatality moves (of which disappointingly, there is only 1 animation per character....really?!).  Why have these in the first place if they don't benefit you in gameplay?  You can rely on the groundpound move (which as well was an interesting and satisfying mechanic) in the early stages of the game, but later on it becomes useless as the game eventually just swarms you with enemies.  In addition there are certain sections of the game where you can depend entirely on environmental elements rather than actually fighting.  It's odd design decisions like this that made me dislike this game.
I LOVE difficult games, but the difficulty in this game just feels cheap.  Brutal checkpoints where you end up repeating the same sections over and over again, which isn't inherently bad, however, having to sit through a loading screen every single time is absolutely ridiculous.  The enemies end up just becoming a big mass of bodies that you attack, and it doesn't feel like a proper beat-em-up.  There's no subtlety with the important things like hitstop and hit/hurtboxes etc. On top of this, you can be shot and killed pretty easily (I generally don't like the idea of guns in beatemups) and the final bosses, dont even get me started!  How unnecessarily frustrating?  Make it challenging! Not annoying!
In conclusion, I just can't recommend this game.  I see and appreciate what the devs were trying to do, but it was a really disappointing experience for me and I think it fell shot of what it could have been.
