After coming to the end of the game in six minutes with very little fanfare or fear drawn, I can easily say this is not a horror game or some experiment in art. It's simply a shock game that tries to make you disgusted by throwing as many touchy traits within the main character to make you cold to them as possible, then have him commit so horrible that the player is supposed to feel sickened.
I didn't feel that sickening. I felt irritated, really. It's a very cheap trick to toss in too much shock at once rather than let a story happen naturally. Fingerbones doesn't do this. I implore any gamer to consider Serena, which introduces you to a plot that doesn't intend to smother you with shock but gently pull you into a plot and then slowly allows you to see the true horror to the story instead of smacking you repeatedly with it. Heavy handed and overly dramatic, skip Fingerbones. Please. Spooky's House of Jumpscares has more development than this should you complete the required actions. Both games mentioned are free.
The developer has done better than this. As others have also indicated, The Moon Sliver and The Music Machine are games that are worth being looked at. The Music Machine deals with similar topics you find in Fingerbones and is worthy of an artistic title due to not just how beautiful and creative it looks, but how it bends religious dogma to create a sort of universe that ties into The Moon Sliver but stands alone just as well.
While this is, of course, a short game and one that is free, it's just not worth it. While there's nothing awful with the blocky and Minecraft-esque graphics, it's all about the tone set in the story. There was nothing here but a few sound effects and what I imagined would have been a "you're supposed to be scared here" sign. The mouse sensitivity has to be turned all the way down to the minimum on my end and I have to insist, I have a pretty new computer. This game will cause severe motion sickness.
The only thing I can say about this game that is good is you'll be over this game in about six minutes if you figure things out relatively quickly, but because many of the notes are fairly vague, I highly doubt that will happen.

A lot has changed since I played so I'll change my review to reflect what I experienced in Heavensward and what I assume hasn't changed about the game.
Dungeons: They're incredibly linear and shallow. Boss battles can be mechanically satisfying but the majority of your time is spent grinding mobs with a lot of health. There's really nothing fun or rewarding about them. You'll find yourself spamming queues for them in order to level up after the story stops leveling for you. All of these issues wouldn't matter too much if the combat this game has to offer was fun. There is nothing enjoyable about cooldown dependant combat. Especially if your class has buff micro-management.
Raids and trials: Essentially giant sponges that have a long list of mechanics to memorize. You'll find your party wiping tons of times. Drops are rolled on so good luck getting what you wanted. There is nothing fun about completing the same battle over and over again. Why not add longetivity elsewhere? They're another aspect of the game negatively affected by the limitations of the combat system as well.
Fates and hunts: Look, I know you want to give people a reason to revisit locations but collecting items and grinding mobs is not a good way to do it. Yet another aspect hindered by the combat system.
PVP: It doesn't have much to offer, desperately needs more maps and more of an incentive to do them. You'll have to convert your friends to your grand company as well.
Relic weapons: Probably the most boring, time demanding aspect of the game. Trust me, it's not worth the time and effort.
Crafting: Literally useless for armor and weapons. Really just a tool for running the economy.
Gathering: I'll admit, I like fishing. It's good when you just want to relax and take a break from what should be redundant. But the others, all you do is run around and press one button. Just WTF...
Weekly capped gear: This is my biggest complaint about the game. There's gear that gets released with every update and you have to collect tomes by repeating already completed content in order to get them. By the time you have the set the next one is out so you feel like you wasted all of your time doing something boring and repetitive.
IL: Item level, it's important as it dictates a lot about what you're able to do in this game. Forget skill, it's all about having the best gear in the game. That's why the game pulls in a lot of people with a superiority complex. Instead of getting better at the game through experience with the combat system, you get better by remembering patterns and getting a just as studied group to do raids all day (Or get the somewhat inferior capped gear)...
Queues: Yep, you don't need any friends, play with random people from other servers.... Mostly easy stuff anyways.
Story: Probably the only reason to play, ♥♥♥♥ endgame.
So, do you want to do the same boring content over and over again for months just get better gear or do you want to play a game where every victory is rewarding and every challenge is engaging and satisfying?

I bought Transistor because people recommended it for having a good story. The gameplay is a somewhat fun fusion between strategy and action RPG, albeit very repetitive since the enemy types aren't mixed up that much - in the final area you almost exclusively fight a single enemy type in every battle which gets tedious.
However, the story isn't very good. The ending is interesting, but the rest is lacking. Half the plot is buried in logs that you have to unlock by using your abilities in different ways. The logs are very dry and not particularly interesting to read. If they'd been spiced up, like by having them take the form of diary entries, they might allow some character development. Unfortunately, they read like encyclopedia entries.
The other half of the plot is okay, but I couldn't bring myself to care very much about the city, the process, or the Camerata. Unfortunately the story doesn't do much to make you invested in what happens to the city since it's a pretty empty setting and you don't see it before the process starts attacking it. You also don't get to interact with many characters in the city, which doesn't help.
The plot also just doesn't have much meat to it, with few twists and not much happening. That's not so bad since it's a fairly short game, but I would have liked to see a bit more. It has a good sense of atmosphere and the style of the dialogue has a noire feel. As a backdrop to the gameplay the plot is fine, but it doesn't stand well on its own.
As far as characters go, the man in the sword is fairly interesting and you get pretty attached to him through the course of the story. Unfortunately, he's the only interesting character in the game. Red, the protagonist, had potential, but is unfortunately silent. She does occasionally communicate with the man in the sword through writing in terminals, but those moments are few and far between and don't convey an interesting personality. You get hints at an interesting relationship between Red and the man in the sword, but since she's silent it can't develop very much.

Transistor, to me, is one of those frustrating games where it does some things just amazingly well, but the rest of the game just doesn't go very well.
Transistor doesn't really fit into any real genre molds. It plays from an isometric view and is an action game (akin to Bastion in a way), but you have the ability to freeze time using Turn() and plan out a series of moves, after which you will be unable to use most abilities until your Turn() becomes available again. There are access points periodically (read: after every fight, sometimes 2 after every fight) where you can choose your loadout, which is based on what functions you have available. You get to use up to 20 different functions, which can be assigned to either active abilities (abilities you actually use in combat), passive abilities (passively grant you bonuses, some of which must meet certain criteria), and enhancements/upgrades (buff a specific active ability to have extra effects). There are some really great combos that can be achieved, but you have to manage your abilities with your available memory, meaning you can't just dump all of your best available skills into your loadout and leave the smaller ones out to dry. There is a good deal of tactics involved.
Another good point about the game is the enemy design. They gradually scale up throughout the course of the game in terms of what abilities they have. Early on it's easy enough to dispose of them, but when an enemy is able to cloak itself, and another is able to block out most of the screen during a turn, it can be quite frustrating to finish off the opposition before they knock out one of your abilities. Many of them also compliment each other in such a way that you have to be extremely tactical in how you maneuver so that you can eliminate a certain target while getting out of harm's way long enough for your next turn to come around.
Now, for the bad stuff. My personal pet peeve was in how the loadout menus were managed. You would think that you could just bring up the loadout with all of the slots and just mix and match until your memory is full, but no. You are given your list of functions, and you get to assign each one individually. You want to put Breach() as an active ability? Better go find the correct function that is taking up the slot you want it to go in! Oh, you deleted the wrong one? Oops, lets go click on... Oh, you double clicked and accidentally put the wrong ability in that slot. And now you deleted the correct one, only to find out that it has one open enhancement slot when you want Breach() to have 2 enhancement slots. Time to go delete everything and just start from scratch. Yes, it was that tedious.
The voice acting was just incredibly frustrating. I really liked Red (the protagonist), but she had her voice taken away right before the game started, meaning she doesn't talk. She can still hum (she's a professional singer), which is quite good, but that's it. The guy stuck in the Transistor that serves as the narrator has a lot of short quips that don't provide anything, and listening to the final boss talk for about 20 minutes until you reach him is as exciting as drinking battery acid.
As for neutral stuff, the story is about a futuristic city where people can be digitized into this Transistor, and this group of people tries to take control and make their ideal world, and then they goof up and their army just obliterates everything because they accidentally threw away their only ability to control them. It's kind of interesting from a programmer standpoint, but it's not that interesting to me, especially from such a limited perspective (the only outside input you get are short quips from scattered terminals).
The game includes limiters, which make certain aspects of the game harder, such as doubling enemy damage, making enemies spawn double cells when they die, shielding those cells, etc. They make gameplay more interesting, as you can essentially toggle the difficulty settings during the course of the game, with the reward being a small increase in experience.
Overall, I would still recommend Transistor from a pure gameplay perspective. The tactics required in this game are very fun and even more rewarding; however, everything else just detracts from the wonderful gameplay. It's visually quite impressive, but that should never come into the equation when weighing whether a game is good or bad.
I would give this game a 6/10. It pains me to be forced between a yes/no option, but I will ultimately say that it is worth playing if acquired during a steam sale.

For example, most games of this genre have healing items that are often pieces of food that appear after destroying trash cans and pay phone booths.
You won't get that here, you essentially fight people who are hopped up on a drug called Nekro and you must harvest the drug off their convulsing bodies. Doing so will fill your Nekro guage for you to either use it for healing your character or to wreak havoc. Here's a rundown on what I think are pros and cons of the game:

-Bosses require strategy to defeat them.
-Fatalities.
-Decent roster of characters. Each having their qualities.
-Level design.
-Mature themes (sex, drugs, and brutality).
-Soundtrack.
CONS:

-Rats and nekro parasites.
Grade: C+

Mother Russia Bleeds is a brutal Beat 'em Up inspired by Streets of Rage and Hotline Miami taking place in alternative, dystopian Russia(however the game is pretty much regular Monday in some dark corner of Russia). Bootleg Russian Jacket Siergiej and his 3 friends: Bootleg Russian Sagat Ivan, typical Russian teenager Natasha and regular Russian Boris earn a living by beating up some hobos who will do anything for a bottle of vodka, but one day they get kidnapped and used in some strange experiment involving a drug called Nekro. They get away and travel all around Russia that turned into Hell on Earth, leaving behind a long trail of bodies.
Now that we have the story explained: the game is a typical Beat 'em Up. What makes it different is the drug mechanic and huge amounts of violence. Nekro is stored in a syringe that has 3 charges. You can use one charge to heal yourself or revive your partner in co-op. A charge can be also used to enter a "rage mode" that turns you into a killing machine for a short period of time and allows to perform fatalities. You can gain Necro by harvesting it from killed enemies.
The combat is violent and really satisfying. It feels good to punch someone so hard that blood splatters everywhere or slam a hobo to the ground and turn his head into a gory mess with your bare hands. Combat is pretty simple, but once you get the hang of it you can really kick♥♥♥♥♥ After I catched someone mid air and slammed him on the ground the sound effect was so satisfying that I had a tiny ♥♥♥♥♥♥. If you are a fan of savage, bloody combat, this is for you.
The music is really good as well. It's not funky disco tunes of Hotline Miami, the OST is heavy and grim. It fits the atmosphere of the game perfectly. Some people complained about pixel art, but IMO it's pretty well done and fits the image of 80's Russia descending into madness.
Scrolling through the reviews you probably saw complaints about bugs and unfair difficulty. Don't worry, devs already fixed some serious issues and tweaked the campaign and arena mode to make them less frustrating.
Online co-op is also supposed to arrive in around a month.
In the end, I rate the game a mid air slam dunk/10.

My purchase of The Room was a risky one, as the last puzzle game I played through and enjoyed was Portal 2. I was immediately captivated by the games aesthetic - the art style, the lighting, the sound design. I typically play games with some kind of second monitor content running, like a podcast or some music. I quickly found that The Room is not a game for that. Though these aren't the most difficult puzzles in the world, I found them frequently demanding my utmost attention - meaning that I very quickly turned up my in-game volume and listened to the ambience and sound effects instead of my 2nd monitor media. From then on it was very easy to get adequately immersed, as if I was in the environment interacting with this 'safe'. A level of interest and immersion that very few games have to offer in recent years.
As previously mentioned, the majority of the puzzles aren't going to have you taking notes and trying to deduce the solution after hours of thinking. The puzzles are challenging enough that they'll keep you thinking for a few minutes and at that point if you can't figure it out, the first tier of hints is typically enough for you to reach the solution. There were only 3 or 4 puzzles out of what felt like hundreds that really felt like they were shoe-horned in or thrown in for filler (Sometimes the offered context wasn't enough for you to draw the proper conclusion, luckily the hints are enough to guide you through these 'lacking' puzzles). The vast majority of the puzzles instituted some very critical thinking, and offered instant gratification upon solving - the way the camera pans to the meticulous, beautiful animation of another section of the overall puzzle opening up. The Room offers a feeling of progress and gratification that I feel most modern RPGs fail to accomplish, let alone puzzle games.
TL;DR - Looks great, sounds great, puzzles are challenging and rewarding, 3 hours to complete. I immediately bought The Room 2 and will be buying The Room 3 if it comes out on Steam.

This is a fun little game IF you understand what it is and isn't.  It is essentially a mildly amusing time killer.  If you expect more than that, you're going to be disappointed.
Much of what you would expect from an RPG is missing.  You do not explore new locations; you just watch a timer count down as your "travel".  You do not control combat; it's all automated with only the most basic of animation.
What you do is select 100 minutes' worth of available quests for your hero to automatically complete each day.  You can buy mushrooms (in-game purchase), if you want to do more than the allotted 100 minutes.  Then, you can use the rewards from these quests to buy equipment, bump stats, etc.  You can also challenge people in the arena and do some dungeon delving, but these incorporate the same automatic resolution/minimal animation as the quest stuff.
In short, this is the kind of game you have going while you are watching Netflix, grading student assignments, or maybe working on own school assignment where you want the occasional quick diversion to break up the drudgery.
It's a time-killing mobile phone-esque game that you happen to be able to play on your laptop.  If you use it for that, it's great! If you are expecting a real game, it's not.
Either way, it's free! Just give it a try.

I just finished Season 1, and let me say... fantastic.
The pixel art style really lends itself to the horror dynamic - where there is a lack of precise detail, your mind fills in the blanks, and the game plays with the darker side of your imagination. Some of the scariest horror games I've played have been in pixelated styles. It's also very important to have a solid colour palette for a pixel game - and its very obvious that a lot of effort was put in to make the background colours both work together and be beautifully striking.
The story can be vague but not so vague that you can't follow along with it, and has a loving grounding in Lovecraftian Mythos. The puzzles are -great-. This game does not suffer the 'puzzles that are hard because they make no sense' sickness; they're challenging at times, while still being logical.
The 'horror of sound' is utilised very well in this game, from the sounds of birds scratching about in the ceiling rafters to Devitt's footsteps on the creaky floorboards to the blood-curdling stab of piano keys when a horrible discovery is made.
The atmosphere is truly breathtaking, helped along by an eerie, poignant soundtrack - however I hope the actual implimentation of the music is better in Season 2, as at least for my playthrough, it kept stopping and starting at times.
Most of all, this game is scary. It can be a bit heavy-handed with the jump scares, but they're not used cheaply, if that makes sense. The creators have a good understand of pacing, and of how much tension to allow to build up before tossing a live one at the player.
If you like horror, buy this game. If you like Lovecraft, buy this game. If you like point-and-click, buy this game.
Hell, just buy this game.
Now if you'll excuse me, I'm off to play Season 2.

The Last Door is a beautifully satisfying and mysterious adventure where you, as a player, are dragged along to find what is causing all the recent happenings that surround you.  If you're into Lovecraft-esque horror, check this game out; even if you dislike point and click as a genre.
This game is beautiful.  From the vague yet striking pixel art, to the amazingly composed music, and even the puzzle mechanics itself, The Last Door oozes Lovecraft themes and the unknown, ambiguous feelings that come with it.  I don't want to give away any spoilers, but I will say the story itself follows much of Lovecraft's overarching plot ideals, yet is still filled with twists and turns that only makes you want to dive further into its madness.
Many people have different opinions when it comes to the graphics, but I myself think they are perfect for a game with this theme.  Everything is defined enough to understand what you're looking at, yet still is vague enough to make one feel uncomfortable and out of place.  The only problem are the smaller items, like pieces of paper, that are a tad easier to gloss over than they should be, as they are often rather important.  Nevertheless, it wasn't much of an issue for me.
The music is brilliant.  It sets the mood for every scene and adventure you find yourself in.  It's often calm or nonexistent when solving the puzzles - which only drives the eeriness further - and picks up as things become more tense.  The soundtrack is good enough to hold itself outside the game, and I would recommend listening to it if you're into macabre/dark romanticism classical music.

It's a departure standard intuition; often, you're searching around trying to find out what you even need to do.  I usually found myself knowing a vague goal (e.g. I must figure out why the guy died) but at a complete lack of knowledge of what I would need to know to achieve that goal and how to even get there.  Many times, you'll explore and find some items that end up working together and complete some task that, at first, has no real connection to your "main" goal, but you work on completing that task anyway because, well, the items you have kind of point you to do it.  This is against what, I think, most people look for in a puzzle/point and click game.  It's not "I must unlock the door, and I'm in a key shop, so where's the mold and metal" so much as "I must unlock the door, but all I have is a candle and piece of paper... and the shrine back there was missing a candle..." and in that shrine is a dead cats head that you must place in a grave so the weeping widow beside it is comforted and drops a key to the seemingly, at first, unrelated door.
In a way, then, the puzzles kind of "suck;" however, I have grown to like them and the more I think about it the more I feel it really captures the feeling of Lovecraft characters and especially the character you control in this game.  You, the player, have a vague sense of what you must do yet you often don't know exactly why, but you do anyway - and in that sense, it almost feels like you youself are part of the madness, rather than an observer.  Of course, if you don't appreciate that kind of meta-feeling, and would like wholly intuitive puzzles, then you may dislike these.  There is no shame in looking at walkthroughs.
If the description from myself and other reviewers of the puzzles don't scare you, then I would extremely recommend this game.

Pros:
-Damn fun to play and fly around. I chose to start as a trader, and it's really easy for me to take on 20 missions at once and keep getting missions as I fly around completing them.
-The descriptions and the detail put into it is great.
-The idea of it being open-sourced and available to modify is great. I haven't tried it yet though.
Cons:
-A bit of a confusing interface, and limited controls. When one of my fleet ships was disabled, I couldn't figure out how to repair it for a couple of minutes. I ha to beat off around 7-8 pirate attacks while I was trying to figure it out. A lot of those more hidden mechanics could be more obvious.
-It's very confusing on what is mounted onto your ship, what isn't, and how each module affects the ship stats. I largely have only bought ships and put an extra cargo area on them. I'd reccomend putting a seperate window on the right side that shows the ship slots, and as you change modules, it also displays the changes in stats.
-The game seems (so far) pretty limited to small fights and trading. It would be neat to have more space in between planets, allowing for ambush attacks and whatnot instead of jumping into a sector and immediately knowing whether there are enemies there or not. Things happen incredibly fast, and most of the time I die before I even knew I was taking significant damage.
-After the short tutorial storyline, apart from a couple of things happening in the galaxy, I haven't been able to find the main stroryline again. Some subtle hints as to where it is would be nice.
-Please, give me more control over my fleet's ships. I have had so many times where we're extremely far away from a battle, yet one of my ships insists on firing it's missiles and wasting credits.
Conclusion: I hope that this is not the end of development for this game. It feels complete, yet still missing a lot of potential. If this was paid, I wouldn't reccomend people get it unless it's extremely cheap, but as it's free to play, I would say that there's no harm in trying it out.

I haven't even dipped my toe into the pirating/boarding/capture or even the combat systems in general.  I'm so addicted to making those fat loots and upgrading my ship.  In other words, this game has a ton more to offer than I have already discovered, and I see no sign of bordem in the future.

The art is amazing. It's close to being amongst the most beautiful HOGs out there.
And that's about it.
The story is so disjointed that twice I thought I had skipped a scene.
It's lack of attention makes it almost unplayable. Interactive points don't have prompts, and you need to click an object many times for it to work. I don't know why, but it's very frustrating. If you haven't played many HOGs, playing this will seem like a chore.
For example. You hover over an object you can interact with, you know this because your cursor turns into either a hand or a magnifying glass, and click on it expecting something to happen. Nothing does for the first couple of times. The third time maybe you'll manage it. [You can poke or take objects with the hand, and you can zoom in with the glass and a window of a close-up of the scene pops-up, sometimes it's a puzzle.]
Usually when you click on a puzzle, or an object, games will give you a clue, or hint what you need to do with it. Good HOGs take this chance to also provide you with a tiny snippet of the story or some exposition. Most of the time you get something like "hm this lock is missing a piece", "something was written here but it's so dirty I can't make out what it says","wow someone has removed this piece from the clock", "this statue was holding something", so you know to look for the missing object, or objects, in order to open the lock/solve the puzzle/advance in the game.
Here, you get nothing. Not even a single word. You click on a portair, real example, and see that it has the silhouette of a bat in each corner, each with a different background colour. Now as a veteran of HOGs you know that you'll have to find the approprietly coloured bats and place them there to open a safe or maybe get another object. Here the game tells you nothing. Alludes to nothing. I kept wondering if they were bored or stoned and forgot to write the instructions when they made this. And it's not a budget problem either, because parts of the game have voiceovers, which means that there were enough funds to add that luxury since very few HOGs have anything more than vague ambient background noise.
This happens not only with puzzles, but with other random items you need to pick up. I was playing it with a friend who has played only a couple of similar games, and he could just not get what we were supposed to do, because the game is so badly designed. Sure, if you have played over 20 HOGs you won't have a problem with this or find it difficult, but it makes the game so much less enjoyable.
Coupled with the fact that the theme is random and there isn't any cohesion between setting/puzzles/story/characters/art, the game seems like a chore. There are ghosts, a vanishing fiance, wild dogs, dragons, creepy ghost girls, a sh!t-ton of bats for some reason, freezing potions, cthulhu-like monsters, demonic incantations and I don't know what else, and still the game is boring and with absolutely no cohesion. I truly felt sorry for the artists, because it's visually stunning.
It's not a HOG, it's just random, visually appealing, puzzles thrown in without instructions or an overarching theme. I got apps in my phone that generate tons of random puzzles, I came here to play a HOG with a story. This wasn't it.
There were no instructions for puzles, Seemed that there are some buggy places, as I tried to click on some objects and somewhere there was a need to repeat the same clicks just to to trigger action.

Do you like being knocked down by literally every single attack and then gang banged until someone shoots you dead off screen? If so this game is for you!
Every attack you take knocks you on your♥♥♥♥♥and makes the game unplayable.
I wanted to like it. I really did but with these ridiculous enemies I just couldnt. at least the soundtrack is cool.

Strengths: - Really cool art style, though some might have grown tired of the pixel-flooding in the market in recent years
Soundtrack- Fixions nailed it with this one, a really addictive soundtrack that fits the game vibe well, I enjoy beating dudes faces while listening to them. Doesn't compare to the Hotline Miami soundtrack by any stretch, but its a soundtrack worth buying.
Issues:
Tons of potential, but I simply cannot recommend the game in its current state. The difficulty isn't 'hard' in a traditional sense, so much as it is more frustrating. There are mechanics that need to be fixed in order to make it an enjoyable experience. Far too many times are you jumpkicked, only to stand and be jumpkicked immediately before being able to move, followed by being stunlocked on the ground etc. This just makes the game not fun to play, because you can't play the way you want to without having the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of you. I found myself forced to constantly slide tackle or jumpkick my enemies just to have even a chance of beating the hordes they throw at you. Of course, just to grind your gears even more, there are enemies that are borderline game-breaking, the rats/dogs were one example that comes to mind, they don't even do that much damage, but they are just so frustrating, and leave me asking what was the point of them? The whole thing feels like a giant chore, not an experience I can look back fondly on. The story isn't even that creative, and I was so gutted about that. Having played a lot of other games from the publisher, I expected much better. The dialogue is borderline cringeworthy at times.
The A.I is borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, don't even bother adding bots to your game, because the added difficulty of the hordes is a complete mismatch to the assistance that the bots can provide. I don't think I've ever seen a bot attack an enemy while they are down to finish them. They always get picked off immediately in boss fights, for example, walking into the combine harvester in the third chapter boss fight, or standing still to be shot in the second chapter. They also fail to utilize the weapon drops effectively, but will always pick them up before you manage to.
-Really hoping online co-op becomes a thing, because I want to play this with my friends, who I no longer have the luxury of sitting in the same room around a screen with. For the devs to omit this from the release is one of the games biggest downfalls in my opinion, what on earth were they thinking?
The harvesting mechanic for the drugs needs to be fixed. I know it is about risk/reward, but I've found that the bodies aren't convulsing for nearly long enough for you to be able to harvest them, if you try it mid-fight and get caught out, your enemies are going to beat half of your health bar out of you anyway. But if you try to beat all of the enemies first, you will mostly miss out on the opportunity to harvest, which means you will likely die at a later stage of the level.
There are several glitches I have encountered in the game so far too, such as getting stuck in the syringe animation as you try to heal yourself, or after using berzerk getting stuck in constant slow mo following the special kill. The worst I have seen so far though, is even after clearing a wave the game just won't let me progress to the next screen, I can walk to the edge to try to continue the level, but nothing happens. And when you've just tried your best to slog through a fight only to be screwed over, it makes me not want to play anymore. Music just stopping is another one, the soundtrack might cut out mid fight, whilst all of the other sound effects still work perfectly.
The arena battle system is also one of the least appealing modes I have ever experienced, remember that horrible stage from the story mode? Well lucky you, you get to try to survive even more waves of hell just to unlock some additional drugs for single player, that to be completely honest seem like a lazy attempt to add variety, and should never have been behind an unlock wall anyway. These arena modes are absolute hell, I commend you if you can beat more than the first two to three.
Finally, we move on to the price. For the time it takes to experience everything the game has in its current state i.e less than 10 story missions and a lackluster arena mode, I don't think the game is worth the money. The dealer edition is slightly better value, in that you receive two copies of the game as well as the OST and a documentary, however the fact that you can't play online takes a lot of the benefits of this deal away.

I see a lot of bad reviews for this game from people who don't understand the game. The game is fun, but It's a side game. If you've come here to find a game you can look at for ours with non-stop repetitive action, keep looking, this is not the game for you. But if you wan't to find a game that you don't have to be focused on 100% of the time, and still have fun... This IS the game for you.
Now the more detailed stuff:
This game is definitly NOT pay to win despite what a lot of bad reviews claim. Paying simply speeds up the natural procceses of the RPG factor, but paying or not paying, you will EVENTUALLY hit a cap where you can't do anything more for the day. TO BE CLEAR: If you pay in this game, you can obtain mushrooms which can be used to speed up the "questing" times, refresh shops, and to spin a wheel that gets you different drops depending on what you land on, ranging from;exp, low amounts of gold, random low level weapons,  MORE mushrooms, etc. HOWEVER, mushrooms are not money exclusive items. You can find them randomly with EASE when questing or in dungeons. Just by questing throughout the day, you can find ~30 mushrooms, 10 of which will be used to refill the adventure bar which you NEED for questing. The other 20 mushrooms? you can do everything listed above EXCEPT your not paying $5 every time your too lazy to get something done. And if you, as a F2P player , also don't want to be grinding for mushrooms when you have stuff to do, shops and the adventure bar naturally reset every 24 hours.
To Summarize: Paying is a feature that you as a player have the option to use. After all, this is a F2P game, and the dev's need to make money somehow. But playing this game without spending money is not only cheaper, but will land you with the SAME gear as everyone else.
Hope this helps

There are pros and cons to Cursed and I think a decent amount of people simply won't enjoy it, and that's fair. It was a fun experience for me though, and I'll recommend it in case someone else might enjoy it for the same reasons. Disclaimer that I haven't played any other hidden object games since I was a kid, so I don't really know the standards for the genre.
I enjoyed Cursed in the way I might enjoy a haunted house attraction around Halloween. It isn't about being frightened, seeing an amazing narrative, or even being immersed. It is worth it for those who like horror to experience the spooky atmosphere and enjoy the well-done props and art. Same for Cursed. The story is far from the worst I've seen, plausible but cheesy at times. There are some bugs, I only encountered one that was easily bypassed but some people have had worse ones. The puzzles and hidden objects I assume are standard for this genre and not really special, and the gameplay could be boring if you're uninterested in the scenery and visuals that play out.
But as a fun showcase of skeletons and ghosts and cursed books and demonic critters, it's not a bad time. I got to sit down after work one evening and spend a few hours exploring a nicely visualized game, I got to chuckle at some cool creatures, melodramatic ghosts, and a charmingly nonchalant main character exploring a bizarre estate like it's nothing. The illustrations are nice, the atmosphere is an enjoyable romp through classic horror imagery. Nothing truly frightening (only once did it get me to jump in my seat, curse you tree goblin) but only what I could describe as a pleasant day trip through a haunted house.
So for that I liked playing it and would recommend others to play it too, maybe not for everyone at full price but I'd encourage you to try it on sale if it looks interesting to you. With the right expectations this is a nice couple of hours, an easy 100% achievement game, and some fun horror emoticons, profile backgrounds, and achievements if you're into Steam's profile customization.

Disclosure: This is my first game review here on Steam. I thought I would give it a shot since I would like to help people make decisions on games that they could enjoy.
Transistor is a game that thrives on customizability, story through text and verbal thought, and solid gameplay. The music ties well into how the main characters are feeling in the story. Stopping time just feels so great and the ability to choose the actions to take is such a nice feeling. It is difficult for me to state just how amazed I am by this game because the “Future-Punk” setting, enemy sounds, and character dialogue is relatable and real.
The gameplay reminds me of Diablo 3, except the skills and modifiers to these skills have potentially more combinations. A demon hunter roll is similar to a particular skill while some ranged attacks were a nod towards the elemental arrow. I just really enjoyed the flexibility that Transistor offered to me and its honest attempt in balancing its skillset.
I know many of you may wait for the next sale for this game and if so, this is definitely a game worth 5-10 dollars. Even at 20 dollars, I think it offers an experience that 2 movie tickets could not match equally (And I have yet to finish the game). I rate this game 5 out of 5. I really recommend it.

Transistor is an astoundingly beautiful game with excellent voice acting and music. The combat system is my favorite part of this game, as the combat is actually quite deep and rewarding once you understand the basics. Everything in this game comes together to form a cohesive aesthetic that perfectly suits the mood and tone of the story.

TL;DR "Much better than originally expected, 8/10"
I really dislike the MOBA genre, so when a friend of mine talked me into giving SMITE a try, i was rather apprehensive. I mean, a MOBA is still a MOBA even with the TPS style right? Well, i was proven wrong real fast. The gameplay is engaging and dynamic, the battlegrounds look fantastic, and the TPS element makes for a nice challenge landing your shots.
However, the game is by far not perfect. No game is after all, there is always something that will just rub a player the wrong way. For me, it's mostly the balancing issues. Most characters see the cycle of being completely overpowered on release, nerfed real hard the next patch around, then buffed or nerfed again depending on player feeback. And that happens despite the test server opening like 2 weeks before the patch hits every time, meaning that there should be enough time to gather said feedback and make adjustments.
Some characters are just inherently better than others in their class, often on the account of having a more useful passive, or a real nasty kit. And the bad thing about it? They often don't get adjusted for months.
Then, there's the bugs. It seems that these days, every single patch breaks something, and it takes a minimum of 3 hotfixes to get it working properly again. Now i love my cosmetics and stuff, but dear HiRez, maybe it's time to switch your focus from sweet skins, jump stamps and whatnot to actually fixing your game? Just sayin'.
Talking about cosmetics, we naturally drop into the topic everyone hates talking about: MICROTRANSACTIONS. In SMITE, there are 2 currencies: Favor, which you earn by playing games, clearing weekly quests and as daily login rewards, which lets you unlock new gods, their recolor/mastery skins and basic emotes, and gems, which let you do EVERYTHING favor does faster, and alot more than that. There are very few ways of earning gems ingame, the final 2 login rewards of the week give you a total of 50 gems, and every now and then there are small even quests that let you earn 50 gems upon earning first win of the day in 3 game modes. Too bad that most of the cool stuff, AKA chest rolls, voicepacks for the characters etc, start at 200 gems. On the plus side, gems can at best buy you cosmetics, or help you unlock gods faster, so it's more of a "Pay to look cool", not really "Pay to win". A rarity these days.
Overall, despite my dislike for the MOBA genre, i've sunk almost 1200 hours into SMITE as of this review, and probably am going to play it along more. Final verdict: Much better than originally expected, 8/10

Sleeping Dogs is a 3rd person open world game where you are an undercover cop that wants to bring down a triad. Within this, the main protagonist has a "struggle" between become one of the gang members or a cop. This part is really played up in the entire game but doesn't really make sense because he always wants to bring down the gang. Hell, when is offered to leave near the end, he still wants to bring down the gang. I wish this part of the story was better because the game does a good job of showing that he really is an undercover agent. The game kind of takes me back to kung fu movies because you can slow jump over cars and beat the living hell out of everyone (plus the ip man costume and DLC).
Additionally, this part of the game plays into the gameplay as each time you break the law, you lose some "cop points" and each time you do something evil, you get some "triad points". Stupidly, the cop points go down even if you hit a car or do something else minor which means you can lose an entire star worth of cop points just because you bumped a car. It's VERY annoying.
The mechanics of the game are standard with a heavy emphasis on the fighting. Guns are rare and there isn't a place to buy some. The missions that use guns will provide you with guns. The guns handle averagely but you run through ammo fast. The fighting is Arkham style with throws, grabs, and combos. However, they all do around the same amount of damage so I just stuck to about 2-3 the entire game and was fine. It's a bit hard to master at first but it's passable. The driving is OK again.
The open world aspect of the game is again OK as there are the average races, collectibles, and minor missions to complete which gives you useless money and experience. The world is a decent size but there are major sections separated by highway and it takes forever to get from one city to another.
Overall, the story is all right, the gameplay is all right, and the open world is all right. Not bad but not amazing. So pretty OK/goodish.

Alright, lets set some things straight. Yes, when you quest, you just wait and the quest will finish for you. But that is how the game is, its just an rpg for REALLY crappy computers.
You don't walk around and attack monsters, its not 3D, but it is a pretty cool game.
When you quest you get money, which is silver and gold coins (100 silver = 1 gold), you use the money to buy stuff for your character, such as equipment, potions, and stat points. When you quest, you can also get equipment and various items.
There is a lot to do in the game, such as PvP, which is basically just a bad animation of you shooting arrows or stabbing eachother, but the more that you play in the arena, the higher score that you are able to get and rank up on the leaderboards, you also get rewards from PvP. You also have guilds and friends list and all that cool stuff.
You can also build a fortress, which is like a town in Clash of Clans, or one of those kind of games, but in order to be able to build in that fortress, you need to be a certain level, which I don't really like, but its whatever.
There are pets in the game as well, which is a pretty cool touch on a game that is 2D and more like a flash animation game.
All-in-all, its a pretty cool game, there isn't a lot of action in the game, but it is a pretty cool concept and I personally enjoy the game. If you have a very bad computer, but still wan't an RPG-like experience, then I HEAVILY prefer this game!

So to start this off, I think it's worth mentioning my somewhat lacking MMO experience. When in like 5th grade, I played Runescape (mostly because I didn't know there were more MMOs), a couple years after that I played a lot of Maplestory, then after that I played a lot of League of Legends (if that counts at all), then I bounced between a lot of MMOs looking for that experience everyone else was getting into with stuff like WoW (which I didn't have the money for at the time). I really wanted to find something good, but there was always some...level of jankyness about other MMOs I've tried. They felt weird, the inventory management and stuff was always clunky, the worlds were largely uninteresting, and the games were largely unhelpful in terms of actually finding the content worth finding. They felt unpolished, and I couldn't get into them.
From the very first moments for playing Final Fantasy XIV, I knew I was going to love it. Everything
good. The world was interesting, there was actually a
. The game looks really good and feels like a Final Fantasy game, a series I've loved since I was a kid pretending that I knew how to play Final Fantasy 7 and 8 on my brother's PS1. It has a lot of helpful resources in game to help you learn things, and the community is incredibly helpful, too. I can number my bad experiences with other players on one hand.
Despite being what is described as a "tab-target" MMO, the combat feels good. Every class seems to be worth playing and they all have their merits and feel good. Animations on spells and attacks feel pretty good and it has a nice quick pace to it. If combat isn't quite your speed, crafting is totally worth diving into. It has a lot of cool risk and reward going on with the crafting system, and it's a great way to make gil and great equipment. Usually I think of crafting as an afterthought, but in FFXIV I feel like it's a significant part of the game and the community.
An added bonus is that playing this game on a controller is totally viable and is also my preferred method of playing, I think it feels way better to move with a stick and have my shortcuts all in one place instead of having to stretch my hand across my keyboard. Using a Steam Controller on this game has its merits as well, with easier mouse control and being able to set some neat little shortcuts to help things go a bit smoother.
My few problems with the game are mostly technical issues. The DX11 version of the game has issues that I (as well as others) have experienced and have thus needed to switched to the DX9 version which has decent performance and a slight graphical downgrade. Registering for this through steam and making an account was pretty weird, too.
Also playing a gathering class is boring as hell, even if it's a good way to make money and get those all-important materials for crafting.
I give it a...
The Sub Was Worth It/10
Added: Something seriously worth mentioning is that the expansion rarely goes on sale on Steam. I would highly recommend getting this game from somewhere else because it is frequently on sale or just flat out cheaper. Although if you made an account and did the free trial through steam you will need to purchase the steam version of the game to continue with that character.

I don't normally bother recommending games on here, but hoo boy is this one fun. It's like a wave based tug of war similar to dota, with excellent 3rd person shooting mechanics, and an awesome levelling system.
Each weapon has 5 levels that you upgrade through by getting kills and picking up the dropped item (kind of like kill confirmed). When you die, your weapons are reset to level 1 again. So it's a similar feeling of levelling to a dota game, but with the fast paced nature and balance of a more standard shooter like CoD. Your armour upgrades are persistent for the whole match however.
The aesthetic is wonderful, this is a perfect example of a minimalist design being extremely effective, as opposed to so many games these days that could be considered amateur or lazy. The weapons upgrade visually aswell to indicate their power level, from a basic grey sword, to dual weilding red flaming swords.
You can play just solo for points, but it also rewards team play, focusing titans or strategically sweeping caves during the creep phase. It also takes points for spawn killing to actively discourage that kind of play which I think more games should do (although we were winning a match and they were pushed right back, we had to keep them at spawn to protect our titan and this one guy stayed at spawn for ages shooting and taking damage and popping back behind the sheild, but despite his long time being alive, when I killed him, I still got points deducted. I assume it IS on a cooldown and not based on distance to the spawn, but it could do with tweaking I think)
I got this cheap from humble store on sale, but I would recommend this at regular price too, now I know just how fun it is, and how surprisingly good the production values are (special effects, lack of bugs, etc)

So, when we first started playing, me and my two friends were all on the same team. The mechanics seemed simple enough and we were having a good time but then for some reason I was forced onto the other team away from my friends and that's when the awful mechanics started becoming more apparent.
1: The game is pretty much filled with bots. If there aren't enough players to play, the server will be filled with bots, and to be completely honest, are just kill fodder which will come up at a later mechanic.
2.The whole "MOBA" aspect is kind of forced. You don't really feel like you're accomplishing much by shooting a titan, it does very small damage and kind of feels like you're just powering them up with the creep waves to pit them against each other in a rock-em-sock-em robots match.
3. The weapon upgrading system is broken. It's an interesting idea and I can see why they would put one in to put some semblance of needing "momentum", but there's two issues with what happens that need an explanation. As you get kills against other players, you get weapon power upgrades that go up to level 5 which are lost on death. These power upgrades have differeing effects based on which weapon you're using but the main thing that can be said is that it makes your gun better and do more damage. Now the two issues with this is, one: Bots make it very easy to get these level 5 upgrades and two: certain weapons are VERY powerful at max level. All I needed to do to pretty much steamroll was to get a few kills with a shotgun and then proceed to blaze around the map at insane speeds two shotting everyone.
4. The game doesn't seem finished. I'm not actually even talking about the art assets/models, I get that it's supposed to look minimalistic, but it looks like there's some missing features.
An interesting idea, but really kind of falls apart due to poor design and mechanics choices.

The Last Door Season 1 is a pretty good point and click adventure game with a focus on telling a Lovecraft inspired horror story. It does a pretty good job with that, mostly thanks to a great atmosphere created by the moody visuals and the fantastic soundtrack. The pixel art style works well most of the time.
The game's biggest weak point is definetly the puzzles. The problem is that most of the time you'll be solving a puzzle without any clear narrative reason as to why you are doing that. For example, you read a note about someone's cat, and find its food bowl. You have to open the window and put some food in the bowl, so the cat comes back. Why are you doing this? You don't need a cat, there's no reason. But when the cat comes back, by chance it leads you to another item you need for another puzzle.
You find a darkroom for developing photos, find the chemicals needed, and some undeveloped photos. Why do you need to develop them? The only reason the game gives you is because they exist.
See a door that's locked? Well now you know you need to find a key. Not because you know what's behind the door or that you need to go there, but just because it exists. How do you find the key? By doing something completely unrelated that you had no reason to do in the first place.
Many point and clicks are like this but I guess because this is more of a serious and narrative focused game it felt a lot more out of place. If you're a seasoned point and click adventure game player you'll probably find the puzzles pretty easy, but if you're not the way they often don't make logical sense might be an issue for you.
There are four episodes in total, each takes one or two hours to complete. Definetly recommended for fans of point & click adventures and horror.

Episode 1 was amazing. However I believe the rest of the game was funding by Kickstarter and I can only presume the undoubtedly deserved success inflated the creators ego.
Episode 2 is the polar opposite of Episode 1. We now have the introduction of 'cutscenes' and tedious dream sequences, that force you on to rails and to simply just keep clicking through them. The common annoyances of point-and-click genre, that were so excellently avoided in episode 1, all return in episode 2. For example:
SPOILERS
A music box item, that upon examination doesn't even tell you can't open it or use it. The only way you would discover it's use is by doing the classic, immersion-breaking, technique of attempting to combine all your items in your inventory together.
An NPC stands by a window, blocking your progress. However at no point are you told that you need to access the window or move the NPC to progress. Furthermore, there is no clue given as to which item you use to move the NPC. The only way this puzzle is solved is by systematically using the correct item in every room. This really dragged me out of the intense claustrophobic atmosphere the first episode immersed me in.
A statue requires an item placed in it, a fair point-and-click trope. However upon examination, there is no indication the statue requires something placed in it, or that it is possible to. The only way to solve this puzzle is by systematically trying all your items against the statue
END SPOILERS
The first episode flowed so well, was sensible and really drew me in. Then episode 2 threw me right back out, it's tedious gameplay stopping me from wanting to play on, despite the story starting to hook me.

Alright so first off, I've never played one of these 'Hidden Object Games', as the demographic for such has, as far as I was concerned, been pretty much middle aged women. I do enjoy point and click adventure games but generally the likes of Curse of Monkey Island have a bit more substance to them than hidden object games. I actually initially found this game while looking for all cthulu-related games and apparently this one showed up. There is one tentacled' monster but it most certainly has nothing to do with cthulu mythos. It is, at best, mildly spooky even for the intended audience.
The voice acting is tolerable though corny and the art is certainly nice looking though the manner in which they did some of the 'motion' looked a bit janky. Dissolving between two still images and slightly swaying them side-to-side does not spooky animation make.
The puzzles usually consist of finding item a to use with slot b (they're really big fans of shape-based locks), rinse repeat. There are some amusing moments where the character slays some creepy beast but from a gameplay standpoint it is the exact same as using item a on area b. There are a few legitimate puzzles but they're not particularly fun, though I recall the skull and thread puzzle to be oddly satisfying even if there was little rhyme or reason on how to complete it and you mostly just moved them around.
There is some attempt at horror and I suppose for the genre it could be considered mildly spooky but my own mother wouldn't be the least bit spooked by any of this game so I doubt you'll get much actual 'horror' from it. The story is also terribly predictable and if not for the interesting and beautiful visuals I wouldn't reccommend this game even to the most diehard hidden object game fans.
I think my biggest gripe with the game is how nonchalant the lead character is towards all the goblins and ghoulies and clearly overtly supernatural mumbo jumbo happening around her. Granted it's not actually scary but she seems not to question a single thing in the entire game. Perform a blood ritual? Sure thing! Shoot the scary bat thing that looks like a demon from hell? Just another day in the life of a vaguely victorian betrothed woman! Later in the game the situations got so legitimately ridiculous that when coupled with the character's complete lack of response to pretty much anything I found myself laughing out loud.
So after all was said and done I managed to get about two hours of 'gameplay' into this thing. Someone less adept at problem solving might meander around enjoying the scenery for another half to full hour. Make no mistake, for five dollars canadian this was at least a mildly entertaining use of my time and money but I wouldn't reccommend this game to any but legitimate fans of the genre. If you don't usually play hidden object games, like myself, I doubt there's anything here to give you a wow factor.
At least the plot was about saving the world... and not finding your grandma's missing recipe.

As an avid Escape Velocity Nova fan, and having played through it several times, along with many of it's smaller and larger mods over the years, I can say this is a lovely clone.
This review is mostly intended as a comparison to the Escape Velocity series. If you do not know this series, much of the information here won't be as relevant, but should still give good insight as to what kind of game it is.
For the sake of comparison I will be using a Pro's and Con's list.
*Gameplay has been made significantly smoother compared to the EV games.
*Travel is a breeze now;
-Landing is done automatically.
-Jumping through multiple systems only requires a single command.
-You can initiate a jump from anywhere in the system.
-Simplified controls.
*The dialogue, port info and item descriptions are well written and fit in perfectly.
*A treasure of content in terms of places to visit, ships to encounter and buy, outfits to use and secrets to uncover.
*You can have a LOT of ships in your fleet.
*You can outfit every ship in your fleet seperately.
*Once in space, everything seems to be real-time. Meaning that a fleet jumping to another system can be found back if you follow them there, and your own ships can be several systems away while you are "jumping" ahead of the pack. (You can avoid this by holding the jump button.)
*More advanced, better boarding mechanics with more options and actual finiancial risks, such as "death benefits" you need to pay when a crew member dies.
*Simple but lovely graphics.
*It's obvious, but still worth mentioning: It's absolutely
*Occasional typo.
*Sound effects could be better. The dev has this high up on his priority list, however.
*No music. Great opportunity to put up your own tunes though.
*Currently only the "Free Worlds" main plot is available, meaning story-wise the game is quite limited. I believe the dev is still working on more main plot lines.
*Lack of a Bar or something similar.
Edit: The Space Port acts as the Bar, but without a news function, betting function or hiring function.
-Instead of hiring escorts, you buy or capture ships. (I see this as an improvement as you can customize your own ships.)
-Instead of news you occasionally get a text pop up when entering a port explaining some current events across the galaxy.
*Doesn't seem like taking a loan will ever be worth the costs.
Edit: It's worth the costs when using the money to buy more or bigger freighters, once you've found a good trade route.
Edit 2: It can become quite tricky to balance out your loans' daily interest payment vs the gain in profit from increased cargo space. I stand corrected, this is not a con, it's a well balanced mechanic.
I highly recommend giving this a try, whether or not you've played any of the EV games. There's something here for fans of RPG, Adventure, Exploration, Trade and Sci-Fi setting. If any of that interests you, don't let this one slip away.

It's a pretty game and is certainly intriguing. It has interesting gameplay mechanics - mainly the turn based grid system, the interesting number of skills and it's combinations, modifiers etc. - it has a nice feeling of progression.
That said, it never becomes a good game. Why? I'll tell you: while it has all of that mentioned above, it has no interesting challenges (except, perhaps, for the last Boss), enemies or encounters. It takes place in corridor levels and has no interludes or content besides combat and some challenges (that is, more combat!).
On top of that, the game sabotages itself by locking certain features in order to punish the players for failure. In combat you can only use your skills (except for Jaunt, as a main or as accessory) when your turn bar is filled up. Since you'll often use your turns to avoid punishment, it means that you are disallowed to do anything besides moving while the bar fills up again. And when you get beaten, instead of restarting, you lose one of your four skills, making combat poorer while it remains and for at least two more save points. You probably will just reset it instead of trying new stuff.
The story is pretentious. It can be pieced together and it is really quite simple at the end, but it fails from the get go to instigate the player in it's quest for retribution. You won't look forward to unveil anything, since you'll only get breadcrumbs and too little to work with.
Thus meh/10.

This game is flawed in a myriad of ways, but the most important one is this: it's boring. So incredibly boring. The variety of the weapons and the level design is so low you've pretty much seen it all within an hour of playing.
There's this idiotic system where kills upgrade your weapon, but dying resets it. This means the rich get richer and the poor stay poor. While I enjoy a good hunt on a player who's topping the charts, it should be about skill - not whoever gets the lucky first kill. Once someone gets ahead, the rest of his team picks up the spoils for his kills and get equally beefy. This means the match is pretty much decided by this point. Armor stays between lives, but most of the options are more of a trade-off than a downright improvement like the weapon upgrades.
Do not be fooled by the game's lack of textures and low polygon count; your system will struggle like a moped trying to haul an elephant, and the fact that the elephant appears to be wearing a corset doesn't help very much. Even the main menu isn't smooth. I run a Radeon 7670M for a graphics card, which is not much but enough to run most games at low to medium settings smoothly. It can run Far Cry 3 no problem. But this game... even with
set to minimum (including turning shadows off completely and running at a lower resolution), this game STILL didn't hit the stable 60 FPS mark. 30 FPS may be fine for some games, but this game is very twitchy; not to the extend of, say, Doom, but twitchy enough you're at a disadvantage running at anything below stable 60 FPS.
Even the tutorial text says features are still missing. Besides, there's plenty of bugs. I often got a second aiming reticule drawn on screen and was unable to get rid of it, leaving me to guess as to which one was the one which actually indicated where my bullets will go. If the match starts while you're in the menus it'll force you back to the main menu. Energy cores often disappear when titans hit them. The news on the main menu displays 'Lorem ipsum' text while it loads. When you select 'titan' as the game mode and hit the server browser, it'll take you to a shoddy webpage and show you all game modes anyway. Oh, and there's no server names or ping display, making it very likely you'll pick a server halfway across the world with terrible lag.
The game's own account system which the unnecessary password restrictions (it needs to contain at least 7 characters which one capital letter and one number). The keyboard input lag when entering said password. The unexplained glow on the titans when they first spawn (I'm assuming this means they're invulnerable at that time). Stats on the weapons (damage, firerate, etc.) are nowhere to be found, making your guess as to which weapon to unlock next as good as any. The sheer number of different pick-ups that all look the same, especially in the heat of the moment. Nowhere is it explained that health regenerates (it becomes apparent pretty fast, but I'd sooner associate making someone glow with a power-up, not being low on health). Aim assist and mouse smoothing are on by default. The giant hitboxes on titans, making it impossible to shoot enemies behind them. The jerky animations on the titans. The ledges that look like you don't have to jump over them, but you do. There's no hit indicator on the titan. You get the point. I also find the 3rd person view very cumbersome on a twitchy shooter like this, but that may be personal.
Nope. Don't get this. Save your money. Even if you can stand all the aforementioned problems, the gameplay really isn't that good. There's only so many weapons and they're all slight variations on a simple sniper, shotgun, launcher, or sword. The levels are all very similar. Games are decided way too quickly. It's simply
. The idea with the titans and the creeps is interesting (though nothing new), but the execution is just abysmal. If you're looking for an FPS with a little bit of MOBA mixed in (like I was), Titanfall really does the whole creep thing a lot better, and you can actually pilot the titans in that game. If you want the big titan to protect and move forward, Team Fortress 2's cart mode is vastly superior (not to mention free and runs like a dream on old hardware).
Nothing to see here, move along.

When i first started playing this game, i had a good feeling about it because of the way the story started. I liked the macabre development and the 1800s english setting in low resolution. I thought this was going one of those lower budget games with a great story. I was hooked.
Having just now completed the game, I'm sorry to say that I am disappointed.  This game feels like an originally decent story has been spread over not only multiple episodes but also multiple seasons. What I mean is that the pace of this game has been slowed down to make it fit in episodes and the ending has been postponed. This kind of manipulation to a game concept is unfortunate for two reasons:
First, when i bought the game, I thought i was buying a full game. The title does say "The Last Door - Collector's Edition".  Episodes are fine as they can also be viewed as chapters to a story, but being told at the end of the game that there's a season 2 coming up was unsettling (I wouldn't expect a collector's edition for only part of a story). I felt like a kid being the end of his bedtime story. No way i can sleep.
Second, because the game makers are trying to fit the story in a predetermined marketing plan, the story feels broken. For example, the story slowly unravels through the first three episodes only to crash with an ending on episode 4 that does not make sense at all. I felt frustrated because I had been very patient with the first episodes to try to make sense of the story and then suddenly we jump to a conclusion which cannot be explained by any of what was told prior...   Did I miss something? I'm pretty sure I didn't. It was so slow I had plenty of time to gather everything.
The Last Door had a good concept to build upon and I think it could have been a great game if the focus had been on unraveling the story and keeping the player hooked rather than building around an episode/season system.
There are also problems with the game mechanics. I had to use a walkthrough in order to progress in the game. There were quite a few instances where I didn't know what to do because the required actions didn't make much sense. Also, the story is being told through text at the bottom of the screen, but sometimes you need sound in order to understand what you have to do. I think it would have been a good thing to add text-based cues of what's going on because I personnally didn't hear the crucial sounds until I read about them in the walkthroughs and boosted the volume up.
My final verdict: i do not recommend the game and will not be playing season 2. I've lost interest in the story. Good concept, nice pixel art, though.

This season is more 'horrory' and there are few jump-scares I didn't care for but still I have enjoyed it. Very straightforward, so pretty short because of that but I think it takes just right amount of time to complete.

The Last Door is a pixelated adventure/suspense game. (Not really horror, though there are some jump scares and some blood and icky stuff, but it's highly pixelated, so keep that in mind.) The story starts off relatively benign as you play a character in Victorian-esque times, investigating his old friend's suicide. As time goes on, you start uncovering your own odd, disturbing, mysterious past. The first season has 4 episodes, and the collector's edition includes some mini-games that give you a little more insight into the events of the season, and are worth a quick 15 minutes.
Pros:
+Story. There is tons of it. It's creepy, it's unnerving, and it's wonderful. I really, REALLY hate horror games, but this was glorious. Not too gorey, not a ton of jump scares, but just enough to keep you on your toes.
+Good puzzles. None of them are too challenging (though a few of them are obvious but make you go "Who on earth would ever do that?")
Neutral:
~Art style. It may be pixelated, but it is HIGHLY pixelated, almost to the point of you going "What the heck is that thing?" It leaves a lot to the imagination, which I would rate as a positive, but a lot of people might be turned off by it.
~Length. Each episode is only about an hour long each, so I finished all the episodes in about 4-5 hours including some AFK idling. I really don't mind the length, because you never end up with "Adventure game fatigue" where you're wandering around aimlessly trying to solve a long series of puzzles. This is short and sweet. Still, some people might feel ripped off at full price. I got it as a gift so I loved it despite the length.
Con:
-Season 1 ends on a cliffhanger, so you're committed to buying Season 2 to finish the story (if they even finish it then. I hope they're not planning a really long story that gets so convoluted you'll never get a satisfactory ending.)
10/10. I really like this game and look forward to playing Season 2 when I buy it.

I grew up in a time, when Double Dragon 3 was one of the most popular Beat-em-ups. As a 13 year old boy, I was playing lots of hours, together with my best friend; never did we think about the game being unfair, we tried and tried to succeed and so we did: it was hard work! There always was funny stuff like enemies running out of the screen, never returning, so you couln't move on, one of the characters being trapped etc. etc. etc.! We were annoyed and laughing like hell, when things like that happened. It added to the charme of the game.
Mother Russia Bleeds gives me the feeling of nostalgia, I love it, it's like the grown-up-version of the 2010s of Double Dragon. It has beautiful pixel art, a grotesque story and hordes of enemies. It's not on the easy side, it's somehow frustrating - I think about the german shepherds e.g.... -, but it's like returning to the past for me. And yes, it has lots of unfair moments; but, just try again! Luck is a factor in gaming again! Gameplay as it used to be, when not everything was done just to make the player comfortable. People played games because they loved the story, the graphics or certain elements. And many of them didn't care about the negative aspects, when there were positive ones, they found important.
If you want a crude and really one-of-a-kind because of its setting, graphics and story (and brutality) Beat-Em-Up, especially, if you want to play with a friend, this has to be the ultimate game!
And no, it's not true that in former days the games were perfect and didn't have bugs, when they were released; lots of games were released far from being good to play; and there were no patches! You just had to cope with these partially unplayable games, you had to learn what actions in what situations you had to avoid if you didn't want the game to crash. This to all the players complaining that devs in our days are releasing games that have flaws and telling other ones, it hasn't been like that in the past. That's just nonsense.
It's just not that black and white, this is what I want to say in general.
And of course there ares devs, too, that release pieces of crap, just to earn money, modifiying their "games" a little bit in a future that sometimes never comes.

If you had told me that a point & click game with highly pixelated graphics would prove to be a disturbing and genuinely creepy experience, I would have been skeptical. I never believed that a point and click game could be scary...until now.
The Last Door takes its inspiration straight from the masters of horror: H.P. Lovecraft and Edgar Allan Poe. The story and themes draw on various themes that they wrote about, and it is done in such a way that those who are familiar with their works will appreciate the homage done to them. For those who have not read their work, they will be chilled by this dark and disturbing story...and hopefully get interested and read the source material.
Now, if you are willing to give the pixelated graphics a chance, I think you will be amazed at how they lend themselves to the story and the overrall tone of the game. This game takes place in the Victorian time period, and the graphics call back to an earlier time as well. The disturbing scenes, I believe, are made to be even creepier in pixelated form.
I love the music in this game. It really captures the tone of a dark, gothic, Victorian, horror story. The lighting, music, and overrall atmosphere create an atmosphere of dread in which you know there will not be a happy ending.
The puzzles themselves are not difficult, but very intuitive. The gameplay is a standard point-and-click format. The episodes themselves are not that long. This game could probably be beaten in a few hours. The only negative I could find (this is a tiny nitpick) is that there are certain Easter eggs in the game, and to discover them, you really need a guide. It's not a matter of exploring everywhere, but making sure that the timing is right to unlock said Easter eggs. However, the overrall gaming experience is not hindered by this.
Since this is The Last Door Season 1, the game ended on quite a cliffhanger. It wrapped up enough questions answered but left enough to ponder and anticipate for Season 2. I am really looking forward to continuing the story.

Difficult to decide whether to click 'yes' or 'no' on the recommendation of this game. It's not bad, some of the animation is pretty, and it kept me occupied for nearly 2 hours, so it's not like it's awful. It's also not quite as laughably bad as Dracula:Legacy which is a very similar game.
But...the animation of the mouths is annoying as they flap like fish with no real timing of what they're saying. The story is derivative, and the voice acting of the protagonist is a little limp. The puzzles are not particularly challenging - the main challenge comes from whether you've spotted there's a particular area you haven't reached yet and now you've got the item to reach. There are also very few hints about what object you're meant to combine with what. That wouldn't be a problem if there was a clearer icon e.g. whirling cog, to show that there was somewhere you hadn't yet performed an action. Sometimes there are also areas where you've cleared out all that there is and they still haven't gone.
Like others I also found the moving back arrow sometimes didn't work and that the inventory disappeared at random intervals.
So...on the whole it was interesting enough for me to spend a couple of hours, but I won't really find it memorable, nor do I particularly want to play it again.
