Cue Club 2: Pool and Snooker is the sequel to the original Cue Club game which was released in 2000 by Bulldog Interactive. It’s a game which features many game modes related to pool and snooker. This game improves almost everything from the first game but on the other hand also skips on somethings that were available in the first Cue Club. Now, for me it was one of the best childhood memories. playing those Cue Club virtual tournaments and trying to beat the AI in the game and virtual chatting with the AI. Such nostalgia.

The game looks absolutely beautiful. The graphics are clean and detailed.  It’s a top down snooker/pool game and this type of art-style looks very good for it. The art-style is very similar to the first game but in this one is HD and it’s much more polished and has more eye candy. Some of the effect that were included in the first game seem to be missing, namely the strobing disco light effect. The game is locked at 60 FPS and I did not get any dips in performance throughout my gameplay.
Cue Club 2 features very awesome soundtracks. These soundtracks, I can listen to them all day long. It’s sort of like club music but a bit slower paced. The sound of the cues, balls hitting other balls, even chalking your cue are good. Just listen to the music in the video posted below.
The gameplay is pretty simple and straight forward. The good part is the variety of things you can do. You can play 8 ball pool, 9 ball pool, 6 ball pool, killer pool, full snooker or 10 and 6 balls snookers. You can play against the AI or play 2 players locally taking turns each. The physics of the table cloth can be adjusted and the size of the balls can also be changed. The game’s physics is one of the best pool physics in a pool game I have seen. The AI opponents will say stuff like “nice shot” if you manage a good shot, which can be pretty entertaining. Another thing missing is the virtual chat option. That was one of the prominent features of the game and highly entertaining. As you could get in chats with the AI players and mess around.
There are tons of design choices you can select for almost everything in the game. You can change the table cloth color, the finish of the wood, the pattern on the table cloth. The balls size can be adjusted and plenty of different types of balls can be selected. You can even choose the color of your chalk. Many different types of cues are available as well. Even some match rules can be changed. All of these are unlocked and ready to use, so no more grinding to unlock these cosmetic items.
You can play different modes such as a tournament mode where you and several other virtual AI opponents will enter and there are fixtures just like a real snooker/pool tournament. Other than that there’s also bar mode where you start off in the lowest basement level bar and make your way up to a more expensive penthouse bar. The difficulty will increase as you progress to higher level bars. You can play solo as well. You can also play quick mode where you can just go and play any type of game with AI opponent. Another mode is solo mode. This has a game type called “Slam”. In this you can drag the cue ball with your mouse as if it were attached with a string and play that way. This mode was pretty fun. Other solo game types include speed pool mode where you have to clear the table as fast as you can and that time is recorded so you can come back and try to beat your own time.

I own the original Cue Club, and I once thought it was the best pool game ever made. I dunno whether it still is, perhaps it's tied with it's sequel.
The original Cue Club had plenty of games including Killer Pool and a few other fun options for party play. I'm glad they're all here in Cue Club 2. I also love the fact that you have every aesthetic option available from the beginning, unlike the original in which you had to unlock things mighty slowly.
There were several features now missing in Cue Club 2. Some were quite fun, such as disco lights, strobe, and "dynamic" cue play. Of all of these I miss it's the "dynamic" cue play, as it made the mouse become the friggin' cue. No such feature here. A feature that some might miss from the original is the "chat" feature, but that had too many flaws for me to work it out. I'm glad it's refined so the computer actually feels more human. Pretty cool.
OK, now that I've gotten an old vet's fit out of the way, it's time to put the olive branch where it belongs. Cue Club 2 is well worth your money if you're looking for a pool game. The music makes you feel like you're in a club, which is awesome. The physics are as equivalent to real life as humanly possible, and the visuals can fool you into thinking you're playing the real thing. You actually click the chalk block in order to chalk your cue, in contrast to a command in the original. In my opinion, Cue Club 2 is the very closest you can get to playing a real pool game on a computer.

If you love Final Fantasy games and are unsure about picking it up because its a MMO and it'll take away from the experience. Then allow me to reassure you, Even though its an MMO, FFXIV has done it amazingly well with their Story. Taking part with the MMO basics of Dungeons, Raids and Guilds, as well as putting their own twist on it with Aeons/Primals, If you don't get hooked on the fights, The music will get you to come back to them, Each having an amazing soundtrack as it fires you up to fight onward, Coming from someone who enjoys Final Fantasy games in a whole and has put hours upon hours into them, Going to A Realm Reborn was a great refreshing feeling.
So far my best experience is the Trial fights with all the different Primals they have in store for you, Not only in A Realm Reborn, but in the Heavensward Expansion as well. Each having a great impact and leaving you wanting to go at them again and again.
One other thing to mention is that Final Fantasy 14 allows you to change classes at will, so theres no need to make another character to play a different class, You may begin a new class at anytime by talking to their respected Guilds and taking on their Quests.
Long story short, The games great, Ive had countless hours of fun, Trials kept me wanting to come back and VS tough opponents, Dungeons had great mechanics and a great level curve, The music is amazing to listen to, Although it is Pay to Play, You can start a free trial to see if you would like it or not, But Would recommend.

PROS:
* The storyline and cutscenes are every bit as good as any other Final Fantasy, even though your main character is generically referred to as the "Warrior of Light." The characters surrounding the story have their own arcs, all of which are interesting, especially in the expansion. Tasteful bits of humor, throwbacks to previous games, and a generally well-put-together campaign make for a game that will have you playing well into the night and early morning.
* Beautiful and varied environments, great animations, UI leaves little to be desired, everything visually (and functionally) has that polish you'd expect from Final Fantasy. Also, it might just be my rig--it's decent but not amazing--but I almost always floated around 60fps unless I had my camera on a heavily saturated marketplace.
* Plays amazingly well with a controller for an MMO with a decent amount of moves for every class. Granted, I think this was meant for PS3 first anyway, but still, it optimizes perfectly with a PC/XBox controller.
* Very few "tank and spank" boss fights, though most of them aren't very hard if you just know where to stand. 99% of charged boss attacks have visual callouts on the ground, the other 1% only have the charging bar. Still, there's almost always something interactive to keep every party member on their toes.
* As usual, the venerable Nobuo Uematsu among other composers make some amazing tracks, many of them experimental. There *will* be times where you enter a dungeon group for the first time and thirty seconds in you're like "damn, this song is good." Or you might think "damn, this doesn't seem like it belongs in a Final Fantasy game, but I like it!" OST is awesome, long story short.
* Very flexible visual customization for your character, with many varied and fun glamours and any dye you can think of (for most gear--stuff you get from dungeon drops usually can't be dyed).
* Class system is a bit restrictive, at first. Mechanically, there is almost no difference between those of the same class, but with all the tools every class has available, there's a lot of ways *to* play them. It's like instead of having to choose what you do all the time, it's about adapting to the situation. For example, most classes have some sort of "toggle" ability that switches up their function, such as tanks being able to turn off/on their aggro generation to deal more damage, healers switching from doing slightly less healing to more damage, or black mages alternating between fire/blizzard to drain/regain mana at will.
*** For a more specific and personal example, I played almost exclusively Dark Knight when I FINALLY got it, and prioritized my gear 3 different ways: pure tank, pure DPS, and off-tank (a combination). Since tanks can freely turn off their respective tanky moves, and it's not particularly hard to get a lead on threat (protip: there's a built-in aggro meter), I would usually go with my slightly higher damage setup and gauge how well the healer can keep up versus how much threat I've got. And since turning off Grit (DRK tanky toggle) allows for the use of Blood Weapon (bonus attack speed/cooldown reduction), the damage alone usually still kept my threat up to speed. I would usually save my tanky cooldowns for that switch to compensate and ease the healer into it.
***Update: As of Stormblood, DRK got the shaft real bad.
NEUTRAL:
* The voice acting is good, but completely changed in the first expansion for ALL characters, mostly for the better... mostly. There's some spotty acting in both OG and HW, but what really didn't make sense for me was Tataru's voice in Heavensward. We go from a tiny, cartoony female voice befitting a tiny, cartoony character, to what sounds like a British woman in her mid-thirties. Was very jarring to hear the first time and every time throughout.
* Some dungeons can be looooong, making grinding for a specific item or simply for experience a massive undertaking. The combat is fun enough to make it not feel quite as grindy, but definitely expect a grind.
* Gathering, however, is grindy, but overall profitable since a lot of people who already have money don't wanna do it. It's only really hard to level when multiple people are in the only spot you can reliably skill-up at the level you're at.
* Triple Triad is back, and as much as I love it, I hate the way they implemented card restrictions. Until you've collected a certain number of unique cards, you're limited in how you can construct your deck based on the rating of the cards (i.e. at the start you can only have one 3* and four 2*s, rank up for one 4* and four 3*, then a 5* and 4*s). I guess they were encouraging you to have to look up where you can find unique cards or something, because you have no way of knowing what cards can be dropped from NPCs you beat.

The game was genuinely creepy and I'd dare say disturbing, it achieved actual psychological horror using the medium of video games in a way that no other game does it quite right.  You're apprehensive, you can hear something that sounds like a ghoul or a wraith, otherworldly.  It shocks your senses in the right way, and it never betrays you with a cheap RAHHH jump scare, it keeps you on the edge of your seat wondering if and when something terrible might happen.
Something terrible does happen, but it's based on really good use of video game mechanics, and not on crappy fluff where you get assaulted with Alma from F.E.A.R. or Kayako Saeki from The Grudge.  Instead, this game will freak you out in the right ways.  The only thing I might criticize is that the game's writing is a little too revealing at the beginning.  The game could pull back from a few of the plot reveals so early on (as I was able to easily see what was hiding), but I suppose at the same time, it leaves you with the apprehension of what's to come, so maybe it's not such a bad thing.
In the end the monster is revealed, but if you hadn't spotted it already, you'll wonder why you hadn't.

Well first of all I was motivated to write this review(my first) by a promise of 5 mushrooms (in game currency)... (although it did say rate, so maybe I'm mistaken, think I got the mushroms though so I'll be a good sport and write something) *edit* here I would like to say that 5 in game currency is not much and the review is not positive because of this, it is positive because i really like this game hence the 55h+ game time*
First glance, I like this game, it's nice, it's casual and it helps me relax (except when it frustrates me, but it doesn't do it often so it's ok, trust me). The main components are questing (gold and exp grinding with a touch of gear drops), the dungeons (challenging oponents that make all the grind worth it), and pvp fights (for honor&glory, with honor determining the position in the rankings, I made up the glory part). There is the guild feature which allows you to socialize with different players and has it's own rewards. At this point I haven't accessed the full features of the game(castle and pets) so I can't say much about them.
It's basically every rpg once you passed the main story and have only the grinding part left, except, here you don't have to actually run around the map, find distant areas, kill swarms of monsters, or push a lot of buttons.
To keep the spoilers minimal, the initial progress is a bit slow but it gets fun and exciting afterwards. The quests don't require a lot of attention and I like this type of games since they can be played in the background(usually in the mornings when my brain is still booting). The in-game currency can be purchased but it is also obtainable from questing and other sources so it doesn't make such an great impact. I don't believe this to be an play for free but pay to win type of game since paying will mostly just speed things up but will not give you unbelievable boosts, and I don't feel like I'm missing out on alot for not paying (although maybe you should ask me on that in a few weeks from now when i get to levels where waiting is frustrating). As for that, quests have time durations and you can basically sit back and fiddle your fingers while the time doesn't run out. So if you are impatient types maybe this game is not for you.
Battles are instantanious and while you do not actively participate i found the waiting and anticipation thrilling, especially when you are on your death door and hope the next hit will be a crit for win...
I do not have a lot of negative stuff to say, because the concept of the game is simple enough and at this point it has not let me down, I'm looking forward to the new stuff and features (level unlockable) and hope it will not let me down. Maybe a background story would be nice but then again I'm grinding clicker heroes so what do I know.

Let me start by saying that anyone who is complaining about this game difficulty has NEVER EVER played beat em up games on the old consoles where you only had a few lives and few or no continues, not to mention the arcades where you played at the highest difficulty setting with just 1 or 2 lives. Mother Russia Bleeds gives you infinite lives and checkpoints, so if you die you automatically restart at a checkpoint. It's true that the game may proove itself difficult in some stages, but it also gives you a way to manage your health and damage thanks to the Nekro drug, so if you can combine the Nekro management with the dodge ability and the various attacks then you can survive even the most furious horde of enemies. Technically speaking, the game graphics and presentation are sick and there is literally tons of physical and psycological violence to be seen. The music is awesome and while the sound effects are ok, I would have loved some voice acting. As wrote before, the gameplay is very good and all the levels have enemies who behave differently and an end level boss which you have to beat following some minor strategy.
Now the cons: every character plays the same, it's just a matter of appearence, there are no different special moves to be pulled off or different strategies to be used according to the selected character. The other thing I didn't really like is the final boss, the idea is cool but the fight is a bit boring to go through.
That said, I would recommend this game to every old school beat'em up fan and to people who loved Hotline Miami, Cronenberg movies and of course are not offended by some violence.
Cheers!

I'm going with a positive score because the first playthrough was actually super entertaining. Take my advice and don't play twice. Emily Is Away doesn't distinguish between your choices very well.
I load it up and BOOM, nostalgia bomb right in the god damn face. I wouldn't say I miss the days of AOL Instant Messenger and pimping profiles or whatever, but the game does a really spectacular job of emulating that era. Right down to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pop punk lyrics that "describe me perfectly". This aspect of the game really REALLY impressed me. It's just too real.
I expected some sort of emotional roller coaster in the story department though and was pretty let down. I start by chastising Emily for her taste in music and calling all of her friends♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Something I probably did pretty often as a young angsty teen. She didn't seem to care that much, after all we're just sorta friends at school right?
Maybe not though because as detached as I wanted to be, the game was pretty good at letting me know that Emily and my character (CrapfaceSmokeGod) were supposed to like each other or something. Even though we both seem like unsufferable selfish♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I didn't have any say in whether or not I gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about Emily and every option leads to some soap opera nonsense. Emily freaks out at me like some teenage girl (weird huh?) and makes everything my fault no matter how sycophantic I'm being. Even the neutral options lead in this direction it seems (again kind of a bummer).
So it leaves me to think about what kind of impact this game had on me. It definitely had one but maybe not the one the developer was hoping for. It's a great trip down memory lane. I recounted the girls in high school who I had blown my chances with and felt sort of bad. But then I realized they were all like Emily and felt okay. But at no point did I ever feel sad for any of the characters considering they're all pretty bad people, but hey that's what being a self centered teen is all about.
At the end of the day it's a quick fun game that serves as a vehicle for your own ♥♥♥♥♥♥ memories to come flooding back to you. Just remember that you're a big boy now and probably have better things to worry about than some ego queen from the "good old days". Like not losing your apartment to any combination of fire, pests and the landlord who is bashing down your door as we speak.

The Last Door is a luscious exploration of why you don't mess around with ancient, morally ambiguous powers who think of you like we think of insects. After a visit to an old friend from his schoolboy days ends with an unpleasant surprise, Jeremiah Devitt's days seem to just get worse and worse. Occult dabbling from his youth seems to have come around to bite him and several co-dabblers in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and it's unclear whether the dark secrets they stumbled upon are out to kill them, save them, or are merely playing with them for their own amusement.
This Victorian English-set romp is beautifully rendered in a fairly simple but effective pixel-art style, with a wonderful soundtrack to complement all the weirdness going on. The blockiness of things leaves much more to the player's imagination than clearly illustrating the frequent gore or other horrors would have, which I, for one, quite enjoyed. It also leaves a lot of the characterization of the people you meet to the mind, though even side characters who play roles in Jeremiah's quest are well-written to the point you understand their motivations and, to some extent, their own peculiar histories.
Rarely, if ever, does The Last Door give you a clear look at the game's overall, lurking menace, but when it does, it's a sharp contrast to the more minor threats that frequently crop up. This reinforces a constant sense of dread behind every action, leaving you wondering what might get you into trouble (especially after the second chapter). The puzzles, on the whole, strike a good balance between being complicated and being easy to find what you need; there were only one or two instances where I got stuck, and at least one was just me trying to do something earlier than possible and worrying about my chances to resolve it after proceeding further. Gameplay flows smoothly otherwise, and while there is occasional backtracking, most of the areas are condensed enough that it's not a chore to do so.
Just remember to pay attention to the audio when you have to deal with the fog eventually. Maybe bring headphones. I think the subtitles reflect what you need to listen for as well in that section.
But yeah, play The Last Door. I haven't gotten my hands on the second season yet, but I imagine it's going to be just as good.

I don't usually feel compelled to write reviews for games I purchase on Steam but The Last Door was different in that aspect.  Although used to games from the 90's my first thought on loading the game was that the graphics were terrible (they actually grew on me after a while).  However, I knew that graphics are not what makes a game good and continued playing.  What a good decision that was.  Although short (four episodes) the game is absolutely brilliant.  As a point and click game it is well structured, fantastically written with some of the best music I have ever heard in any type of game, bringing a great atmosphere to the Victorian setting.  Although the puzzles are fairly simple it does manage to provide a good balance between being a game and ensuring that the story flows.  Sometimes, I find that similar point and click games feature overcomplicated or nonsensical puzzles which can frustrate or alternatively you are railroaded through the game too quickly with too much handholding and not enough interaction. The Last Door is also one of the few games I have played recently where I was genuinely intrigued to see what was behind each door or what the many characters in the game had to say and it was also genuinely unsettling at certain times (with a certain Lovecraftian feel).  If you are a fan of old point and click games, horror games or fancy something a little different than your mainstream games, then give this game a go.  Highly recommended.

TL; DR version: not worth 5 euros. Like, one of the worst Point-and-click adventures i've played in last 2 years. For me, it's like 2,5/10. Or, if you find it on sale like me (0,50 € instead of 5 €), then you can add one point, so 3,5/10.
How to start this review? Well, i want to say that i love point and click adventures. Usually short games (under 5 hours), in which you have to use brain a lot, many puzzles, nice story, sometimes a plot twist. Pretty visuals, maybe animations and cutscenes, good atmosphere, soundtrack, etc. Cards and achievements are nice bonus.
But this game. Ehm. To describe this game with one word: disappointment.
Yeah, it is a point-and-click adventure. You can finish it in 2-2,5 hours, witch all achievements, without hints, etc. The problem is, that there are almost no puzzle. You don't need brain for this adventure (like, seriously, 4 puzzles in whole game? And to "kill" final boss, you have to solve 4x4 sudoku. Ehm.).
What's next? Story? Well, there is some, but really unoriginal, bullsh*t story, the only horror part is demon and skeletons, bats, old house. And one jumpscare (but it is maybe my fault, i did not notice that it is "horror" game).
Okay, so almost no puzzles in this game. But it is still adventure, you need your brain to continue in story and finish it. Well, you don't. There is absolutely no logic in this game. Plenty of locations, but almost nothing to do there. Go to that location, pick item 1, go to another location, use item 1 to open a box, there's item 2, which you have to use in another location. And, that's it. The sad part is, that locations are totally random, there's no logic in that how the item 2 appeared in that box.
Oh, there's also awful controls. Inventory? On the bottom of screen. But, it automatically hides after 2 seconds. How to go back to the previous location? Click on the bottom of screen. See? Inventory just popped out. You want to use some item from inventory? Well, maybe you will go back to previous location instead :)
What else can this game offer? Nice visuals, cutscenes, atmospheric sounds and music. And bugs. To be honest, i had only problems with subtitles, not synchronized well. But if you check the discussions part on Steam, you can find that many people had problems with this game, and not small ones, but really big, like unable to take some items = unable to finish the game.
So, yeah, that's it. As i've already said that, you can buy it while on sale, but it is not worth the full price. 5€ for 2hours gameplay, with a chance to find gamebreaking bug (= unable to finish the game), and with no replayability. Just not worth. There are plenty of games like this, which can offer much more. So, keep looking :) And buy this one only if you are totally desperate, that you've already completed all point-and-click adventures on steam :)
PS: i don't know why this game has 80%+  score on steam. But maybe i can understand. If casual gamer (who played only 2-3 point-and-click adventures in his life) finds this game for 0,50 €, he could say it is good. But this isn't a hidden gem, just some average adventure (when you close one eye).

My friend bought this game as a gift to me. At first I didn't know if I'd like it or not. I read the other reviews and decided to download the game.
To start off, the tutorial is simple and effective. I knew the basics of the game from that 5 minute tutorial.
There are 3 different game modes:
The first one is called Deathmatch. It's very similar to the Deathmatch in Halo Master Chief Collection (Halo 2 Part). Team that gets to 50 first wins.
The second one is Titan. Titan is the main gamemode. It's a 5v5 MOBA styled game where you and your team must work together to upgrade eachother and strengthen their Titan. After a while the Titans will spawn in and fight eachother in the middle of the map. The Titan that survives continues to go towards the enemies core, fighting through walls and turrets along the way. Your team wins if the enemy team's core is destroyed.
The last one is Survival. In Survival you must fight against waves of enemies in a small group. I haven't played Survival too much, but it is very similar to Nazi Zombies from the CoD series.
As you play games, you earn different resources. These resources allow you to craft different items, which will allow you to customize your loadouts. Things like Flame turrets are unlockable and equipable after crafting.
Now, this game is not P2W. You cannot buy resources to make you advance faster, and with that, there are no "Premium items" that you can only buy.
The only thing I have seen that require real money purchase are skins for weapons in the game. A lot like Valve's CS:GO game.
My only complaint about this game is the rubber banding/lagging situation.
When I play on the game's servers I get 16 ping maximum. I have a very powerful computer as well.
The game has a problem where you will be shooting or moving on client side, but the server isn't catching up, so you will rubber band back to where the server has you at.
This has caused me to die many times. It's frustrating, but thankfully it isn't too hard to recover in this game.
Now, I believe this is an early access game, constantly being updated, which is really cool to me.
I would rate this game 6/8 if the Devs left it like this and never came back.
I see a TON of potential in this game and I'm very excited to see where it goes from here.

this game is really good. why is this review marked as negative? because despite being really good, this game is horribly imbalanced and definately not finished. first of all, the biggest problem with this game is that despite the fact that the game is literally nothing but untextured cubes, it has FRAMRATE ISSUES. I kid you not, a game where literally the entire world and all it's characters are made from untextured cubes, the game has framrate issues on lowerend pcs. secondly, on top of that, matches come standard with massive amounts of rubberbanding, and just general lag. players have a tendency to intermitently teleport all over the place (which is made worse due to the fact that there is a dash funtcion on several of the games weapons). at it's worst I had a case where I was in spawn, hit the dash button, and sprint buttons at the same time and started flickering back and forth for about half a second until I remateralized at the center of the map (come to think of it that would be a cool game mechanic. too bad it's just a massive glitch!)
now that I've touched on the games massive technical issues, there are several game balance and design issue that I feel I should mention for starters the game has a really stupid progression system. basically because the game has moba elements, it has an in match crafting and resource system that acts very similarly to gold farming and item buying in mobas. it's a really neat mechanic IMO. the problem is that there is ANOTHER resource and crafting system OUTSIDE of matches that you have to use to craft the blueprints that you use in match to craft the items! I can't think of any other moba-esque game the forces you to unlock the ability to purchase in match items OUTSIDE OF MATCHES! and for good reason! it's really stupid! admittedly the default blueprints that they give you are pretty good, and it doesn't take much time to unlock all of the rest of them, but it's still unessecary, unjustified, and annoying for new players as it limits their ability to adapt their build.
there are numerous other potentially game breaking balance issues, such as a sniper rifle that when fully powered up makes it's targets unable to move, which isn't very fun to play against, melee weapons are a bit too strong/easy to use, etc.
TL;DR this game has truely amazing potential, but it's no where near there yet. I desparately want to reccomend this game, but right now it has so many major game breaking issue that I have to reccomend that you avoid it like the plague until they are fixed. I hope that someday I'll be able to take this review down and give this game all the praise that it otherwise deserves.

Setting aside all the controversy about this game, this has to be one of the best Call of Duty games ever created by the developers. The graphics looks great even in 2017 and the gameplay is superb. Highly recommended for all FPS fans.
The campaign is about 6 hours long roughly. It can be shorter or longer depending on your selected difficulty. The story itself is very good and is set 5 years on from Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. It is not a Hollywood Blockbuster but at the same time it is not some random quickly written story that was put together in a few hours. Every mission has different objectives and you can feel the climax building up to the finale of the game. Every level is action filled and there is never a dull moment in the campaign. As you progress you will play in different locations in the world such as: Afghanistan, Brazil, Russia, the Atlantic Ocean and the United States. Even after completing the story there are Intel collectables to find and of course Steam achievements. There are also quite a few Easter Eggs in the campaign levels. The story for this then continues on into Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3
The Multiplayer is what is considered the strongest part of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. Unlike COD4 this time the game uses Steam Cloud, so your rank will all be stored online and will sync every time you close MW2. The highest level you can reach is level 70 with the addition of 10 prestige levels. When you reach Rank 4 you will have the ability to create your own classes where you can choose your main weapon, secondary weapon, perks and equipment. You can also stick attachments to pretty much all of your weapons on here. You can also unlock weapon camos for your main firearms, which some look very cool when placed on. You have the ability to join friends in a session and vice versa (provided there is space) and host your own private matches for this.
Conclusion: I highly recommend buying this game if you are reading this out of personal interest or if the game has gone up for sale. I recommend playing the Campaign before going to Multiplayer to get a feel of the game, but it is of course entirely your decision.

Shakes and Fidget is a free to play animated webbrowser RPG with asynchronous multiplayer and everything RNG.  It is an international web browser and mobile game, so it will be populated with many other players. This game is translated into many languages, so there will be many Non-English reading players.  It worked on Win 10, looked ok, sounded ok, played ok, was understandable.  It is light on resources used, so it will be runnable on any computer.
Has funny quest text and gear descriptions.  The artwork is cartoony and funny. Has varied weapon sounds. Has some animation.  Has a manual and official wiki in english.  Pretty Easy to play.
The level cap is 550, but it will take you long time to reach it, very TIME consuming game.  (At my current hours, i have a 149 scout and 135 warrior)  Quests and other things take an amount of real time to complete or cooldown reset.  More time you put into it, the higher you climb on the leaderboard.
Mushrooms are the store currency, but you can earn some from quests rewards and gambling.   Some gear cost mushrooms, but you might find the same and better later for gold only or quest reward.   You can spend mushrooms to skip waiting on timers or add time to questing endurance and the best mount.   There is hourglasses that you can buy with gold for skipping the travel time on questing.
It has PVP and PVE.  It is RNG combat where better stats and gear will give you some edge, but RNG is a fickle goddess, you still can lose to bad rolls. Difference in Level between you and target is a factor of success. You can make 2? characters per server, picking one of 3 classes ( warrior, mage, scout).  Has an PVP Arena where you have a choice of 3 players to attack for gold, honor and xp.
You can raise your all your stats with gold and use potions to temporary improve a stat.   Gear you can buy or get from quests can now be modded in the blacksmith shop and in the tavern watercloset. At level 75, you can collect Pets that improve your stats and you can fight other players pets. There are many other things that you can do to improve your stats.
It has 31 dungeons you can unlock and raid.    Finishing Frost Blood Temple Dungeon, you unlock The Tower which gives you three companions (Mage, Scout, Warrior) to raid with through 15 harder dungeons that unlock with the Tower.  You have to outfit your three companions with gear to improve their stats.  But ends up having to wait for your level to catch up to the dungeon level.
You can make your own fortress, with some buildings that improve your character and other building for protecting your fort or raiding others forts.  You can raid other players forts for resources and pour your gold in to defending your fort.   It has Guilds and guild wars, where guild members all attack other guilds or defend from other guild's attacks.  Guilds have stuff they can build that increases gold and xp gain for guild members.  But above level 25 guild upgrades require someone that Buys mushrooms.  You can increase your guild level also by completing guild house raids.
The 17 plus servers are located in Europe somewhere (Central Europe time zone).  Devs keep adding more servers, which pulls active players from the established servers.  Leading a guild is easy but hard to get enough active dedicated players to reach the very top of the guild leaderboard.  Make several accounts with 2 characters on same server then make your own guild and put all your own alts in it, then don't bother with recruiting other people to guild.
Try it, maybe you might like it.  You can play this game for free, and it keeps you busy serveral hours a day.

You have to buy a Basic Membership if you plan on enjoying this game. So you have all licenses & ammunition without either expiring. In hindsight, the membership is actually cheaper then your average MMORPG, which charges you at average $15 a month. theHunter only asks for $31 for the entire year. Or if you want extra stuff to work with, $50 for the Trailrunner, and you can keep everything in the package even after it expires.
The animals do not interact with each other realistically like in Deer Hunter Season 2005, but even with that, the game is still extremely enjoyable especially in its Multiplayer. Making new friends in this game is very easy and motivates you to hunt newer species, explore more of the reserves, and try out different ways of hunting.
Also, this is not a run & gun arena shooter game like Call of Duty. So if you have the patience span of a gnats d*ck, you'll hate this game.
So understand specifically that this is not a total free game. But the asking price is not terrible either especially with the content that can be explored. Buying things in the game is optional. Some things you do need but can buy in packs.
Duck hunting you do need the callers or you cannot hunt ducks. Camoflauge plays a big deal in it too. So if you plan on spending money in spots for different hunting, then plan out where you'll spend it without going broke. Manage your cash, is all I can tell you.
So, give theHunter a chance. Or if you're too broke then you will not be able to enjoy this game.

I was really looking forward to this game since I saw it about two years ago at during the sony e3 press conference.
After a few hours with the game, in it's current state, it's hard for me to recommend this game. Two things hurt this game: Hit detection, and number of enemies on screen.
So many times you will miss attacks that should connect because you're not lined up exactly with the enemy, while the enemies can be planes above or below you and still hit you. This compounds with the excessive number of enemies. How is that I run at a group of 6 with an attack and I miss all of them? Someone here said it already that the devs should have known better. There have been previews of the game that mentioned the hit detection as a concern, and it seems nothing was done about it.
As for the amount of on-screen enemies; it's hard to do more of the fancier things like the ground n pound, or sucking up nekro, because you're swarmed by many enemies. At points in the game, I couldn't even see my character.
Alas I stopped playing the game at stage 5 because the game started to lag at the bar section of the night club. All my inputs were delayed, and I couldn't do squat against the mobs. It could be my pc, but the game was running fine until then.
My hope is the devs see the criticisms of the game and patch it or something, because the game could be great. I do not feel it's a bad game, but these to issues ruined my enjoyment of the game.
One last thing; This game will make you hate dogs, especially German Sheppards

The controls are tight and responsive, and the combat is light enough to easily learn while still deep enough to keep you on your toes to the very end. Enemies are varied, not only in appearance but in behavior and preferred manner of attack, forcing you to constantly adapt to changing situations, especially when stage hazards present themselves.

I think this game's contention is that all love ends in despair.  That's a viewpoint I can get 100% behind.
However if I wanted a story of a guy's romance going down the tubes, I have my life.  Thumbs down.
In all seriousness, Emily is Away is truly an emotional ride.  Anyone playing it will certainly be brought back to moments in their young adult life; everyone has been on a similar journey.  I guarantee that at least one line in Emily is Away will hit you in the gut.  It has a real emotional weight to it and that's a shame because that impact never really goes anywhere.  That's the problem with Emily is Away;  its suppositions about our relationships are essentially circular.  While it may highlight a universal part of the human experience, it doesn't draw any conclusions or make any influential observations beyond a sense of futility.  Emily is Away only serves as a reminder to a lesson most young adults have already learned.  It's just a refresher course no one really needs.
I suppose one has nothing to lose by playing it as it's free, but there are no real conclusions to be drawn when it's all said and done.

I can't not recommend this game but I do have a warning for potential buyers.  This game is a lovely little thing if you aren't distracted by the fact that an "8-bit" game has gradiented lighting and full resolution sound files.  The atmosphere is masterfully crafted; suspenseful and engaging.
Now for the warning.  I chose the word "atmosphere" here because I didn't want to use "story".  Clearly this is a story based point and click and that's where my big complaint lies.  There isn't much of a story.  There is cliffhanger after cliffhanger, but by the end of the game there is no real pay off.  Cliffhanging is the clickbaiting of storytelling, and that sucks.  Half of the episodes end on the same scene that the episode opened with.  You learn the arbitary details of what brought about that scene, but the reasoning and the weight of the situation is a constant mystery.  In reality the whole season feels like a single episode, it's not till the end of the season that you're really beginning to know anything, but you still have to buy "season" 2 to get any closure.
The Last Door Season 1 is literally a typical "we looked through the door and what was through the door looked back" story with much left to be desired in Season 2.  The atmosphere and exploration is top notch and worth while, but based on the round about story telling of the first 4 episodes, I'm not optimistic for satisfaction in the next season.

Coming from someone who didn't buy the Pandemic version of the game and someone who is into different strategy games, I really enioy this. I feel that you can get enough hours out of the game that the price as it stands now is justified. The way the game is now, without the promised multiplayer, already can give you tens of hours of playing time which is really all I can ask for out of a game like this.
Although only a few hours in, I find countless reasons why I should get back on the game instead of doing other things. Only having access to one type of disease from the start encourages you to keep playing in order to unlock the others, among other things like obtaining achievements or even just conquering different difficulty levels and testing different strategies gives the game an incredible amount of replay value.
I absolutely dig the simple but sweet design of the game as well. Something about playing on a simple map in HD with good particle effects just is really fun. The menus are very easy to navigate and understand and overall it looks really polished.
Some people claim that this game can be boring in the sense that they claim all you are doing is clicking and waiting, but I disagree. Although this game doesn't require as much attention as some other games that I have played, you clearly make strategic decisions throughout your game in order to go about spreading your disease but at the same time trying to keep a low profile so you are not noticed before spreading the entire globe. You are continuously involved by clicking bubbles that appear on the screen for "DNA points" that you use to go about "leveling up" your disease through different transmission methods, abilities, and symptoms. Lastly, I enjoy reading and reacting to some of the random "news" events which may contribute to my playstyle. For example if bird migration was up, I may consider using my DNA points to make transmission with birds more effective among many other things.
I suppose I can go on all day with this but i'll just finish with saying that I am excited to check out the multiplayer in the future and finally just see how this game turns out when it is officially released.

Highly enjoyable. It reminds me of an old game I used to play with friends. (CURSE YOU, MADAGASCAR!!!) But while the old one was slightly crude and browser-based, this one is much improved, even as an Early Access title.
The objective? Quite simple: infect the world. Every person, every city, every country.
How? Well, that's your choice. Mostly. What you want your virus to DO is entirely up to you, however in terms of spreading the infection, it's basically a race against time to ensure that you spread EVERYWHERE before someone wises up and shuts off from the rest of the world.
I think that's my only real gameplay-wise gripe about the game: what your disease DOES is up to you. How it SPREADS is basically mandatory and should probably be rushed ASAP before harbors and airports close. Beyond that? I'm impressed with the amount of options the game gives in designing your virus initially. The upgrade paths seem limited, however this may be because it's early access, and due to the fact that the game is trying to stay somewhat grounded in reality.
Is it good? Yes! That said, though, it's a bit of a one-trick pony. There's only so many ways you can plague the world before it gets boring. The price-point is going to be a thing of contention unless there's more to the game than this. More modes, more concepts, just more to do would be nice and would go a long way towards justifying more than say ten or fifteen bucks for the game.
For the devs: please don't be afraid to go too outrageous. Super-Villain Mode, Xenomorph Mode, anything that would give this game more to do and more fun would be appreciated. Let's not get too bogged down in reality when we could toe the line or step over it a bit and achieve greatness.

Setting aside all the controversy about this game, this has to be one of the best Call of Duty games ever created by the developers. The graphics looks great even in 2017 and the gameplay is superb. Highly recommended for all FPS fans.
The campaign is about 6 hours long roughly. It can be shorter or longer depending on your selected difficulty. The story itself is very good and is set 5 years on from Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. It is not a Hollywood Blockbuster but at the same time it is not some random quickly written story that was put together in a few hours. Every mission has different objectives and you can feel the climax building up to the finale of the game. Every level is action filled and there is never a dull moment in the campaign. As you progress you will play in different locations in the world such as: Afghanistan, Brazil, Russia, the Atlantic Ocean and the United States. Even after completing the story there are Intel collectables to find and of course Steam achievements. There are also quite a few Easter Eggs in the campaign levels. The story for this then continues on into Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3
The Multiplayer is what is considered the strongest part of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. Unlike COD4 this time the game uses Steam Cloud, so your rank will all be stored online and will sync every time you close MW2. The highest level you can reach is level 70 with the addition of 10 prestige levels. When you reach Rank 4 you will have the ability to create your own classes where you can choose your main weapon, secondary weapon, perks and equipment. You can also stick attachments to pretty much all of your weapons on here. You can also unlock weapon camos for your main firearms, which some look very cool when placed on. You have the ability to join friends in a session and vice versa (provided there is space) and host your own private matches for this.
Conclusion: I highly recommend buying this game if you are reading this out of personal interest or if the game has gone up for sale. I recommend playing the Campaign before going to Multiplayer to get a feel of the game, but it is of course entirely your decision.

One of the tags for this game says “difficult”. Normally it would mean avoiding lightning-fast sawblades, navigating penny-sized platforms that executing pixel-perfect moves. Not here though – all jumps are easy, deadly sparks are rather slow and timing in general is quite relaxed. But make no mistake, this game IS difficult – for a totally different reason. All those jumps and dodges you’ll have to do, you do for two (or more) balls simultaneously. With only one set of controls to do it.
You ever heard of how difficult it is to simultaneously “tap you head and rub your tummy” or “draw circle with one hand and triangle with another”? That’s exactly the skill this game will put to the test. This is multitasking brought to the extreme, this is the ultimate twofer, this is the stone to kill two birds with.
Level design definitely deserves a praise too. With 101 levels, developers really explored the concept of simultaneous control to the fullest, finding time and time again in what particular way it goes against any instinct you had so far.
Add minimalistic, but very clean design, simple, but appropriate soundtrack – and you not only swearing and breaking your keyboard, but doing it in stylish and relaxing environment.
All in all – “Binaries” is puzzle platformer with rather unique twist in it for those who have seen it all. Sure, you have defeated Dr. Fetus or whoever it is the hardest platformer boss out there. This time your enemy is your own brain. Fight!

From the stylistical visuals to the intoxicating soundtrack by Fixions, from the satisfying crunch of smashing a mobster's skull to paste to the blissful crack of fire spewing from the barrel of a bloodstained AK-47, this game is an experience to be savored. Having played through to the end of the game (on Normal), this game is brutally fun.  The difficulty lies more with the fact that every enemy seems to be of the special variant (focused on something other than trying to get close and punch you).  With that in mind, you need to work more on moving around and not getting pinned while at the same time taking them out of the fight with knockdown attacks so you can focus on killing off each one while also developing a strategy for enemy and enemy groups (jumpkicks can counter enemy jumpkicks, slidekicks leave dogs open to a headsmash, ranged enemies can kill their allies while taking a bullet for you, etc).
The Nekro mechanic only becomes viable once you can keep enemies away/down while you harvest it to replenish your supply (which you can either heal yourself, buff your damage, or heal allies).  The game certainly balances out better with at least one extra player but solo isn't impossible, you just need to move more and kite enemies.
I know for sure I have a new couch game for friends I love playing (and raging at).

At the time of writing this I have finished the game once on normal with stages 1, 7 and 8 done solo and 2-6 with 3 AI partners.
Mother Russia Bleeds is a game I have been looking forward to with high expectations since I saw pre-alpha trailer in March of 2015, from what I saw in that trailer it looked like it combined two games I love; Streets of Rage 2 and Hotline Miami. Did the game satify me or did it leave me hollow... yes and no and maybe and... I don't know yet.
The game's pixel art is outstanding, it's the right type of detailed and messy that fits the dirty tone of the game with each character and enemy standing out and the backgrounds for stages being something I would want as my desktop background.
The beating in this beat 'em up is satifying and just as bloody as I wanted it to be but I do have issues:
1. There is no move list, a move list is very important for a game like this since players may not know about certain moves(DODGE THEN KICK TO SLIDE TACKLE THIS WILL MAKE MOST OF THE FIGHTS MUCH EASIER HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ I think I saw a launch move being performed by my character but after spending a good ten minutes figuring out how I did it I still had no clue how to perform it.
2. The game goes for a mix between high amounts of enemies with high amounts of health even though the majority of games in this genre go with one or the other, now this isn't too much of an issue when playing solo on normal but when I tried it with 3 AIs I got floored due to the sheer amount of enemies that just won't die and that's not a good sign for a game with coop.
3. ENEMIES WITH GUNS SHOULDN'T TAKE A PRETTY BIT OF YOUR LIFE AND ALSO KNOCK YOU DOWN WHILE FAR AWAY (Stage 6 is the worst)
4. While some bosses were enjoyable (The final one being my favorite for it testing the player on everything they have learned) others are just either dull or annoying to fight(2, 3, 6, 7) at least for the first time you fight them.
Like Hotline Miami the audio is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic, the crunch, the squish, the gun shots, THE MUSIC. While the game did bug out sometimes with audio(Music not playing after restarting from checkpoint), my only gripe with the music is that there wasn't enough of it.
If you are a veteran of the beat 'em up genre and grew up with stuff like SoR and Final Fight then you will love Mother Russia Bleeds as it will put you on the edge of your seat with it's crunchy combat, beautiful audio and sexy pixel art but if you are new to the genre then it is a solid start even if it's much harder than most games in the genre.

As a boy I would play Beat 'em ups over and over again. Final Fight. Knights of the Round. Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (Arcade and Turtles in Time), X-Men, Simpsons, Captain Commando, etc... They were all essentially the same formula, but it was a beloved formula; Left to right, kick♥♥♥♥♥savagely, pick up the pipe, eat the trash-can chicken off the street, wash, rinse, repeat. Its hyper violence is unrelenting.
This game combines a few things I really love. It is pornographic and exploitative in a way that I think is a reasonable and exciting evolution of the genre. As noted above it has that terrific Beat 'em up feel of yesteryear, along with a horrifying look BEHIND THE IRON CURTAIN. Back in the day when these games were in vogue, in the eighties and very early nineties, Russia was the big bad here in the US. They were going to turn us into a radiated wasteland. All of our movies were full of ruthlessly cruel and efficient Russian villains. They were an ever-present doomsday lurking in the periphery of our lives.
Of course there's also the couch co-op aspect, which I truly appreciate. Most of my time with this has been spent with my girlfriend on the couch just pounding scumbags into a fine paste and shooting up junk into our arms to go into a Berserker rage. I threw a junkie at my girlfriend and she hit him with a bat, killing him. We were darned close to sharing a high-five. Seeing her sitting there beside me, destroying dudes by beating them with a telephone pole until not even their mothers could identify them, I knew I was with the right person for me.
Lastly the music is a fitting wrapping to this package. Dark. Paranoid. Disturbing. Unpleasant. There is no balm in this siren's song, only distress and alarm.
Now, I know that this isn't reviewing great. I will say this; if you are of a certain age and you grew up in the shadow of the titans of the genre then you will adore this game. There is a criminal lack of these games being made these dark days. This is a rare bird, indeed, and we need to foster it. If this game does well despite the reviews it may yet spark a fire of resurgence. Regardless, the game is very worthwhile. It is EXACTLY what it claims to be and nothing more or less. I feel many of those critics reviewing this poorly would also review Final Fight similiarly if it were released in 2016.
If you are open to a straight up Beat 'em up in 2016, boy howdy, do I have a game for you...

This game surprised me. I tend to chew through adventure games and spit most of them out in the process, looking for those rare gems and refusing to waste time with anything less. This one had me hooked right from the start. It hits those necessary notes perfectly and with careful deliberation.
. Lots of games use pixel art to justify a low art budget, but this makes pixel art look pixelated. The resolution is something like 120x120, less than old CGA games. And as a result the art takes on this impressionistic feeling that just works in a compelling way. It's ultra low res, but it's crafted extremely well. The combination works in surprising ways.
. The writing is good, and what isn't written is communicated visually with a similarly deft hand.
. The orchestral soundtrack is absolutely bonkers in how good it is. A three hour long game should not have music this rich.
. Finally, the length of the game is just right. It ends before any adventure game fatigue sets in. To be fair, if I had been waiting for this to come out episode-by-episode, I would have been less than impressed, but taken as a whole and burning through the entire game in a night, it fit.
. It ends on a sequel which is a -1 point deduction, I can give them a pass.
It still contains your typical adventure game inventory stuff, but I never really struggled with where to go or what to do next. The few instances where I did backtrack aimlessly were because I overlooked something clickable. That didn't happen often enough to frustrate me.

I'm going to do my best to dance around certain details of the story here so as not to spoil it for anybody, but I may have to ruin some of the gameplay surprise a little bit in order to address what I did and didn't like about the game.
It's difficult to really explain this without just fully divulging everything about it, which is largely due to it's short play time and small play area, but also because it's essentially so one-note in what it does. It doesn't faff about with superfluous information or character/world building, but instead pretty much aims straight for its intended target and fires, paying little attention to anything else around it. In this particular instance this really didn't bother me. We're pretty much given all we need to know about the situation and the people involved in the tale, both directly and indirectly, and kept on point with the story the developer wants to tell. Directly, you'll be playing as a man wandering around a... room (the nature of the environment is eventually revealed and is best discovered by the player, but at first it appears as a relatively non-descript living area with scattered furniture, boxes and notes). Indirectly, you'll be learning about the people closest to him and the roles being played by both the people and place.
Gameplay consists of reading notes that fill in the details while you sniff around the dwelling and occasionally flick switches or enter codes on a keyboard to gain access to certain things. Unless you immediately walk out the door behind your starting point, it should take you no more than 20 to 30 minutes to finish and has little real incentive to revisit, unless you just want to breathe in the incredibly unsettling atmosphere so masterfully constructed here. With the intentionally low res, pixelly art direction mixed with its effective lighting and chilling audio, it had me on edge for the entire duration of my time with it. That's easily the best thing about the game. The worst thing is, well... I hate to say it, but... pretty much everything else.
The problem I had with it is, after all that work spent crafting a tone and having the player right in the palm of your hand; being able to make their skin crawl and constantly have them looking over their shoulder, it just never actually does anything with it... nothing actually happens. The store page description does state there are no jump scares and it's more about psychological horror rather than something more manifestly horrific, but I was at least expecting some kind of pay-off to everything, for there to be an actual event to speak of, but there's no such thing here. It was a real disappointment, and more than anything, such a waste as well.
I may be mixing up my quotes here, but I think Hitchcock used to describe the tension in his movies and its effect on his audience as being like blowing up a balloon. It keeps building up more and more, bigger and bigger, and with it, the audience's expectation. But you can't keep doing that without end, there has to be a release for that tension, a pop or a bang to finally get it out of your system and kill any sense of expectation, only then can you begin to build it back up again. The problem here is there's no bang, it just... ends. Right at the final moment when you expect a big reveal or something of consequence, be it an event or some information, it merely fades to black and the game closes. There's no sense of closure to proceedings and as a result I was left feeling pretty empty and unsatisfied by the time it ended, having no release for all that built up tension and anxiety it worked so hard to create. To its credit, it at least didn't resort to cheap scares or have any silly plot twist or ineffective monster, but then, it didn't really have anything else, either.
I wish there was a Neutral verdict to click on for these reviews, and I'm so close to wanting to hit No instead, but given that it's free, it's competently constructed, is bold enough to approach some disturbing themes that are rarely ever tackled in other games (a lot of praise has to go to that especially), and the fact that it's the developer's first release (described in his own words as an experiment), I'm inclined to think it deserves a little more leeway than most. Plus, as much of a let down as it was, it still isn't actually bad at all. David Szymanski very much seems like one to watch, though, and I'll definitely be playing his other releases sometime too as they all look promising and other reviews for them seem reassuringly encouraging, but for this, at least, it's a semi successful attempt that holds lots of potential but sadly fails to truly capitalise on it.

A fun, unrefined game oozing with style is how I'd describe Minimum. (7/10)
I bought this game during the winter sale as it was only 3 bucks, so why not? I've been keeping track of this and jumped onto the game. It's got a very stylish artstyle which works well with their approach, and the solid gameplay also helps enforce this. However, the main issues that plagued the launch for many still persist now. The biggest problem that currently holds this game back is the balance. The melee in this game is extremely overpowered, so if you get slightly proficient at it, you'll find it easy to run into people with rifles and just 2 hit them. Since the game has a snowballing system, this makes it even worse to try to climb back when someone's ahead, where they will keep decimating others. Some guns are also much better than others, making it bad for newcomers, as guns are unlocked by playing and then using the reources to acquire new guns. Still, even with the base guns you will likely be able to grab a kill or two when someone is glowing (meaning they are damaged/injured) when they are busy fighting someone else in this chaotic game, but as it is right now, the devs MUST look into the balancing of combat. A combat roll may be useful (possibly only for ranged, as in melee form you get a dash).
Currently, there are 3 modes. The titan mode, which is similar to a MOBA where you try to destroy the enemies core, team deathmatch, where teams work to get to 50 kills, and hoard mode, a coop survival where you fight dinosaurs, and robots a-like with up to 4 other players. Team deathmatch is very easy to jump into and fun, as everyone is running around trying to kll each other, where tactics is thrown out the window, and is best for anyone looking for a quick jump in and play style. Hoard mode takes a bit more time to find players, as most prefer team deathmatch, but is quite a challenge as some of the enemies are very tanky and can kill you really quickly. Working together is key to surviving in this. In titan is where the game advertises it's biggest strength, with a shooter like MOBA where you farm creeps and take down the enemy core. It's fun and requires better timing, as killing yourself can hurt your team. Since you lose upgrades on your gun if you die, the snowball effect comes into full play, and a team in the lead can push further, although since it's much more skill based, the losing side can still make a comeback. All three modes are moderately fun, and the menu screen works well with the game. Although there are still bugs with the scoreboard which sometimes makes players disappear (which happens more in Hoard mode), overall the game itself is decent, with a TON of potential because it blend gunplay with the very popular (albeit saturated) MOBA genre. It's fresh and interesting, and I would love to see what the devs bring in the future. To sum it up in easy to read Pros/Cons:
Pros
- Great blocky style
- Fun, cool looking maps
- Solid gunplay
- Interesting concept of killing/upgrading
- Similar to Unreal Tournament in terms of gameplay
- Simple controls
- Decent community
Cons
- Melee is too strong, better guns are unlocked so their is an imbalance for new users
- On some areas (specifically hoard mode), the minimalist white block style makes it too bland
- Menu bugs out some times
- Server browser is less than optimal
- Grindy
- Exiting a match sometimes doesn't work (there isn't an "exit match" button, or it's not clearly shown)
- Grenades feel clunky when thrown (delay)
Overall I would recommend this game with friends, which is fun and exciting, but it's a bit harder to commit the full price of $10 if you are solo, as there are several issues that plague the game. At the time of this review, however, the price ($3) is definitely worth a try.

Not going to lie, they actually went all out with this. It's a pretty deep story considering this is a simple beat 'em up game. There is some fairly rich dialog during and between the stages that set up a lot of the story and tap in to your emotions so you care more about the journey / characters lives. The bosses usually all have some kind of "Bad guy monolog" so that it fires you up to just want to kill them before the fight begins which I thought was a really nice touch.
Usually in beat 'em up games you have the setup and the ending and nothing in between but they did a good job showing how much they care that the game doesn't become a boring punch fest... which is good because it helps offset the lack of variety in the fighting system... which brings me to my next subject:
It's smooth, it's fluid, it feels right... but it's a bit too basic for my liking. I was expecting at least Streets of Rage 2 complexity with the battle system, like secret moves and unique character attacks but there's none of that here.
It's basically, punch, kick, jump, grab, dash... that's about it. There are no hidden movies like Streets of Rage 2, such as tapping forward twice then attacking or even a special attack button which is rather disappointing; Instead it's replaced with the Nekro drug system.
By using Nekro you can heal about 1/4 of your health bar or you can go in to a berserker rage that lasts about 10 seconds. During this mode your characters speed and damage are bolstered and you can perform a fatality by just grabbing the enemy, this automatically occurs and seems to be fairly random.
You can also just punch enemies to death and hope you randomly punch their head off... This feature only occured for me three times the entire time I played and I was rather disappointed considering I killed over 200 enemies in berserk mode... better to just go for grabs if you want to instantly kill trash mobs.
There is a severe lack of throwing animations as well, the developers just seemed to have gotten lazy with it. Even in Double Dragon II: The Revenge there were three different attack moves based on which direction you were pressing after grabbing the enemy that resulted in a different finishing attack but in MRB it's basically, 3 different throw directions and punching them / head butting them in the face as you grab them. Pressing a direction while attacking doesn't change the animation or the attacks.
All in all, for gameplay mechanics, Streets of Rage 2 is still the godfather of beat 'em up games, this game does nothing exciting other than gore... For a game with a combo counter, there's a severe lack of variety going on. It's basically, punch some guys, kick them away for some crowd control, grab a dude and throw him away from you, resume attacking the guy that just stood up... that's basically how advanced game play goes... It's all just crowd controlling the ridiculous amount of enemies on the screen as you have no time to sit around doing different combinations on enemies.
I found the Nekro system to be incredibly frustrating to use as well while playing alone because you have no time to gather Nekro when 12 enemies are trying to kill you. I basically just used it to heal myself as you have 1 life per area, if you die and you're playing alone, that's it... The A.I. bots won't revive you either, they're about as smart as a brick... they'll just continue to fight until they're exhausted.
This game is meant to be played with 3 to 4 people at the same time and that's a shame because there's no online co-op mode, only local... There's some decent tracks strewn about the game here and there, is it legendary though? Not even in the slightest... Double Dragon III on NES has more memorable songs and that game was complete garbage for a beat 'em up game and it's 20+ years old.
Don't get me wrong, some songs really set the atmosphere, like the train level and the final stage, the rest of it just kind of fades in to the back ground... Nothing you can really remember or humm along to after you're done with the game... It's all just super over produced and sounds like generic electronica / dubstep music with no real catchy beats or hooks.
It's about a 2 to 2.5 hour romp on Easy mode if you sit through all the cut scenes and have minimal deaths. I beat it on easy mode with an A.I. Sergei bot helping me out. 1 Tutorial Level (Opening stage to set up the story - skippable)
8 Main Stages (All vary in length, on average they're anywhere from 6-10 minutes long with a couple levels being upwards of 15-20 minutes long)
Final Boss Battle (Not selectable)
So basically 10 Stages total if you count the tutorial and final boss as seperate entities from the 8 main selectable stages.
It's a passable game, it doesn't do anything interesting other than pushes the envelope with it's gritty, dark and controversal setting. For more sensitive and niave people, this is probabably enough to add a lot of appeal to the game, for me, it's just another game trying too hard for shock value.
Thing is, this isn't anything really new or interesting, if you're a fan of this game then you've probably seen a lot of ♥♥♥♥ed up♥♥♥♥♥♥like underground movies or are in to violent horror movies etc... You'd definitely have to be educated in some of the stuff in this game like the BDSM gay club and whatever otherwise it might scar you or something, it's one of the more memorable moments in the game any way.
I know this review kind of talked more about the negative points about the game but I'm just pointing out the things I thought could of been better. If some of these things were changed, mostly the game play, balance and music, it could of been a really legendary game but instead it's just above average which, by todays standards, is the same thing as being mediocre...
It almost had the magic but it fell kind of short. This is coming from a veteran of beat 'em up games, I mean, I've beat them all, all the good ones and even some of the bad ones. A stylish, smart, and sexy game from start to finish.
The game begins by tantalizing you with a bit of it's story, and drags you in and doesn't let you go, being vague but telling you what you need to know to get you thinking. Every moment of playing Transistor I was wondering where it would take me next, and I was never disappointed by what followed my anticipation. It has a very intereting take on a futuristic politics landscape, and has very well-thought out characters and developement.
The combat is fluid and tactical, while somehow having an elegance about it. It utilizes such simple mechanics, however that does't mean it won't push your understanding of these mechanics to the limit as the difficulty definitely does ramp up as the game proceeds. The game will follow exactly what you want, and it is all up to your skill and cunning to successfully defeat all foes that come your way. The game mixes many genres but with flawless results as you level up and collect new abilities and powers a la an RPG, while you switch into turn-based strategy, and then into a fast-paced action game. The game keeps you on your toes and always tries to throw something new at you, but never going overboard and bringing you a challenge that is impassible.
However the show-stopping point of this game, as similar to other Supergiant success, Bastion, is the art direction. The voice over by Logan Cunningham, and the tunes sung by Ashley Lynn Barrett seal the deal of the package as they drive home the emotion, setting, and character of the game without eveer seeming forced or clunky. The look of Transistor is sleek and futuristic and as you delve deeper into the story the surroundings transition perfectly. Near the conclusion of the game you return to where you had started but the setting has changed drastically,  and the score has been remixed. This point really displayed the kind of talent the creators have, and how powerful an indie developer can be.
Transistor is a marvel to look at, a blast to play, and has a story dripping in charm and intrigue. If you were a fan of Bastion, it will not disappoint you, and I highly reccomend it.

Options include separate sliders for sound effects and music, system or custom cursor, Windowed or Full-screen, Tutorial (OFF by default), and Advanced Mode (also OFF by default.)
At the bottom of the screen is our standard inventory bar, whilst at the top are buttons for Menu, Map, Hint, and Navigation (highlights exits and items you can zoom-in on).  By default these items retract until you bring your cursor to the top or bottom of the screen, but if you'd like them to stay visible, you can "lock" them in place by clicking on the skull in the bottom left corner of the screen.
The graphics are quite nice, although some of the animations of people speaking and moving (especially early on) is laughable.  I really loved the "guardians" (no spoilers!) and the way they were animated... It's just the humans that didn't move naturally.  The music is a nice mood-setter, the voice-overs fairly good, and the sound effects appropriate.
The flow of the game is simplistic.  "Here's an interesting lock, I wonder where the key is... Oh never mind, here it is, right in the next room."  Sure there are things you have to do that will take a bit longer, but very little thinking (or waiting) is involved, and chances are that if you need something, you'll find it within a scene or two.
The achievements are all obtained via playing the game... In other words, you don't have to work for them.  No point to having them there, really.
Something I really appreciated about the game is that there are some items that stayed with you throughout the game.  You know, those useful things that most games take out of your inventory after you use them once?  Another thing I liked was that there was at least one (that I found) instance where -- when something I wanted to do wouldn't work -- the game told me WHY it wasn't going to work.
There's nothing unique or groundbreaking about Cursed, but it was enjoyable nonetheless.  The game took me less than two hours to complete, but at the current $0.49 price point, that's quite a steal.
Recommended for those who are seeking a non-challenging game with some spooky moments, and those who enjoy pretty graphics.

I have put a lot of time into this game since it came out in 2013 and I think a lot of that has to do with the community of the players. I haven't played a ton of MMO's before, but of my limited experience Final Fantasy XIV has the best community yet. People are usually very helpful and, depending on your server of choice, there is almost always a place for you no matter what kind of player you are.
The game itself is almost a love letter to long-time Final Fantasy fans in some ways. There are so many references and homages to other Final Fantasy games that the most hardcore fans can really appreciate it. Personally I learned a lot about some of the games I either hadn't played or not played a lot. New content is constantly in development and each patch regularly brings enough content to keep me busy until the next one. Not only the frequency but the quality of these patches has been pretty astounding. Each patch usually brings along with it a whole new set of references as well.
Graphically the game is quite beautiful. There are plenty of cracks if you look close enough, but the characters and scenery are very well-done. In the pre-Heavensward areas you would be hard-pressed to find details in almost any zone that seem lazy or unintentional. There are many small, hidden spots with their own little stories to tell through short NPC dialog boxes.
The story is easily one of the strongest points of the game. As you level up and journey through Eorzea you can really feel your character being tested and tried to become the Hero of Light. Everywhere NPC's will recognize your strength, whether it be as a seasoned Adventurer who has killed literal gods or as a world-renowned artisan that can craft the finest items in the realm. They really make your accomplishments feel just like that.
The combat is probably the least notable thing the game has, but the large range of classes and the fact that you can master every one on a single character is very welcome. So far the Heavensward expansion has increased the enjoyability of all classes, really expanding them to be much deeper than complex than before. My personal favorite, black mage, has especially seen some much-needed love in making it less of a bore to play.
This is a lot more than I intended to write, but I can't help myself when it comes to FFXIV. I really love everything about it.
