A top contender for one of the best-worst MMO's ever.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
FFXIV had a bit of a rough start when it first launched which prompted Square to create an end-of-the-world Event that ended Version 1.0 ( 1.23 or higher ). This event is always shown as the intro to the game in form of a fantastic CGI video with a rather sad sounding song. However, if you ask me, I dare to say that they planned it from the start as it would give them a great amount of publicity.
Here are some of my top complaints of the game.
* There is no freedom. It's another Hallway-game.
* The storyline is absolutely atrocious, but it does have a few gems.
* It feels like work, without pay. You work, and you gain nothing.
What I mean when I say there's no freedom, is that just like FFXI it isn't an open world game. You walk from zone to zone. This was fine when it was in FFXI because of it's role as one of the first MMO's. This is
okay in an MMO of 2010+. For example, every single town is split up into two separate zones, usually as one top and one lower section. In Limsa Lominsa, this can become utter ridiculous where the lower Limsa crystal can have 20 people standing around, yet because of it's divide you'll never see any people if you are on the upper half because the lower part when watching from upper is a separate instance.
This was done I recon in order to make things run smoothly or whatever, but it's just stupid in all honesty.
This leads us into the other part. Jumping is a lie. You don't actually jump in the game - You just display a Jump animation. Let me explain: There's no true Z-axis in FFXIV that measures if you are moving vertical. If you can walk it, you can jump it. But if you can't walk it, you can never jump it. Combine this with the fact that everything is divided into zones and we find out the true nightmare of a player of the explorer type - A gilded Cage.
Which leads us into the expansion, Heavensward where they introduced flying mounts. They work differently in that they do count the Z-axis, but your jumping still don't. And the most damning fact of it all that everyone I know hate - Aether Currents. A completely, arbitrary thing that Square Enix pulled out of their asses just to spite players. If you want to fly, you better hunt each and everyone down in ONE ZONE in order to fly in just THAT zone. And the hilarious part of this is that usually when you've found all Currents, you're done with that zone so why would you ever go back to it? This makes it so that the only zone worth spending time finding them in is the Churning Mists because at least there, you can fate grind from like 52 to 60
Make no mistakes. FFXIV is work. It's not a journey to gain strength, it's just good ol' labor for everything except by the end of the day, you'll have gained nothing of true worth. You're not stronger, you're not more skillful - You're just screwed over.
Finally, and here's the golden anaconda of it all.
The storyline, is rancid. You really need to try hard to make a story that sucks this much. Just about every single NPC has a special kind of stupidity to them that's out of this world. I have heard D&D players who made joke characters
be better than these numbnuts! And just like how Square usually makes games these days,
People have joked around about MMO's always telling how everyone is special and they are the chosen ones and all that. FFXIV does this the opposite way. It makes you do all the work, but you are never the hero of this tale. Even after you complete a full storyline and have your fame reach the far wides of Eorzea, you're still going to be everyone's errand boy and if some special NPC shows up, they'll push you aside and go "
" or "
" even though you just eliminated an entire army just to get to that point.
It's like Square looked at Mystic Quest and went "
"
= = =
In conclusion, I cannot recommend FFXIV to anyone.
I have spent over 800 hours with the game.
I've had some good moments, and I have screamed from the top of my lungs about the story.
I have met friends, I got a random guy and his girlfriend to get into the game and they love it, but my hate only grew.
If you think you can stand all these things, then I implore you to try the trial out.
But otherwise, I cannot recommend this game to anyone with two braincells.
PS. I am slightly wrong about Jumping, but in grand gist of it I am right. Jumping in FFXIV is largely a pointless ordeal.

Yet another quick game with a quick review. Fingerbones is an indie exploration, psychological horror game from David Szymanski. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Like my previously reviewed game (Port of Call), Fingerbones is completely free of charge. This alone should make anyone interested in playing it.
The graphics are very much Minecraft-clone quality, but, they have a certain, eerie feel to them that really do it for Fingerbones.
The story is pretty dark. There are no jump scares here; only notes left in an abandoned bunker for you to read an reveal the story at your own pace.
The music added to the creepy atmosphere of the game. This is always a major bonus as far as immersion goes.
The Bad
Nothing to see here. Move along please.
The Meh
Some of the puzzles (yes, there are some light pseudo-puzzles you’ll be solving) require a little bit of back and forth. I wished there had been an option to move just a bit faster for this reason.
Verdict: Yea
Fingerbones is a spooky enough game that I’d recommend it for anyone looking for a quick, light scare. It is great for the Halloween season and, if you’ve been looking for something new, Fingerbones is sure to keep you occupied for a few minutes. As always, thanks for reading.

A side-scrolling beat-'em-up that pays tribute to its predecessors (Super Double Dragon, Streets of Rage, Final Fight ect.) and brings uncanny levels of gore to the genre.
MRB takes the player on a trip through the depraved underbelly of a fictional Russia, all the way to the upper echelons of power in a quest for - what else - revenge. It's a story that we've heard before and come to expect out of this genre.
The graphical direction is without a doubt the games strongest asset and the characters stand out beautifully on the detailed backgrounds. It is a moving art gallery of pixelart that fans of retro beat-'em-ups can appreciate... if they have the stomach for it. It's a re-enactment of the elevator scene from Drive but without the kissy-kissy part. Again and again.
The controls are tight and the player will have the basic knowledge of moving and mashing buttons after playing the (pretty clever) tutorial, although several more advanced techniques and special moves exist.
The main issue (disregarding the lack of online multiplayer. Really, what the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ were you thinking?) is that progression is effordless. You see:
Dying will respawn the player at the last checkpoint with full health and fully supplied. Factorio, as advertised, is a game of automation.  You collect resources using machines to build other machines that make allow you to make armor, weapons, and yet more complex and powerful machines.  You start off burning wood, move to electricity from steam and solar, all to power your ever growing factory that will one day get your stranded butt off this hostile world.
For the local lifeforms do not take kindly to the savaging of their wilderness.  Smoke, dirt, and other pollutants are a byproduct of your industrial methods, and they respond, growing more aggressive and powerful with each passing moment.
You must build a ship capable of getting you back home, but the materials needed are huge, and it's just you, your wits, and a batch of technical know-how versus an entire planet!
While still early-access, it does show great promise.  There's always something to build, something to optimize, and many ways of doing things.  Some prefer decentrailizing, with a vast network of bases connected by train.  Others will bring all material to one master location, where processing and construction all take place.  With a great world-generation algorithm, no playthrough is the same, and being mod-friendly, you can always add and make changes to suit your style.
All in all, a great game, expecially for those with logical minds that can visualize workflows.

As Wei Shen you'll be infiltrating the Sun On Yee Triad in an effort to bring it down not only to do your duty as a police officer but also to avenge your sister, who died of an overdose after being introduged to drugs by a triad member.
Sleeping Dogs is a truly good game providing an interesting storyline, realistic open world, a good amount of quests and side activities and a fun melee combat system: the Definitive Edition features several improvements such as better graphics, more side missions and previously released DLC.
-great plot, the story is truly engaging and mantains a good momentum from beginning to end
-a good cast of characters that, while not extremely deep, manage to be as realistic as they are interesting
-Hong Kong is a very interesting setting and one the devs managed to recreate very well both in looks and ambience: it truly feels alive
-good graphics overall, while not extremely detailed they feature many small details both on characters and in the game world
-excellent soundtrack, the ingame radios have a good amount of different genres available and, while not as famous as GTA, they're all very good
-huge amount of things to do between main missions, side quests, favours, lockboxes, cop jobs and even more collectibles
-meleee combat is extremely fun and gets better as you unlock new moves, gunplay happens a bit less often (especially at the beginning) but works well and has a decent cover system
-the extra content from the DLCs adds even more hours to a long base game
-if you already played the base game, the graphical improvements are generally minor
-some extra activities (races, cop jobs) can get repetitve in the long run
-camera can sometimes turn at awkard angles during melee fights or while entering a vehicle
-a few hiccups with the AI, especially pedestrian or civilian drivers
-lacks Cloud saving
-a few bugs here and there (a cutscene zooming out due to my character getting slightly stuck on a rock, some NPCs getting stuck on scenery,a couple flashing textures): very minor things though
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition was a joy to play, and I say so as someone who had played the original game back then and decided to replay it in its improved form: the story is great, Wei Shen is a good lead character and the plethora of missions, activities and stuff to buy/ collect ensures you never have time to get bored. If you somehow missed the game back in 2012 then you owe to yourself to buy this one.Igf you already own the base game, well, I'd be worthwhile to get this one if you havn't experienced the story DLCs since they'll add about 2 hours each.
I got this on sale for around 8$ and got 30ish hours out of it, that's a great bang for your buck: if you also consider the game's quality, they make Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition a game I fully recommend, previous consideration notwithstanding.

Sleeping Dog's is a GTA style action and adventure game set in open-world Hong-Kong, where you take the role of Wei Shen, an undercover cop that infiltrates one of the HK triads Sun On Yee. As game progresses, you gain both Police and Triad XP that provides different perks for each next level. Additionally, you gain face XP that provides additional bonuses and certain collectibles (jade statues) allow you to unlock melee combos in the local martial arts club. The game offers a wide range of various side missions (chase sequences, beat-em up missions, drug busts, dating missions, shooting missions, races) and mini games ♥♥♥♥♥♥(rooster) fights, tournaments, karaoke). In overall, there's a heavy focus on driving and puzzle solving, as well, as hand-to-hand combat. Although, hand-to-hand combat is enjoyable, the driving and puzzle solving starts to get annoying and/or repetitive after a while. It seems, that the game was artificially made longer through driving, lock picking, camera hacking and collectible searching. However, the story is really strong and interesting and you grow attached to the main character and some of the NPCs. The graphics and voice acting are of high level and overall Sleeping Dogs is a fun, action-pumped open-world experience with a nice dose of Hong-Kong action flick influence. But, unfortunately, there are quite a few little faults that pull the game down and, as a result, it offers only a slightly above-the-average experience. Definitely enjoyable, but with more polish it could've been excellent.
PROS:
- Interesting main story missions
- A vast variety of side missions
- A skill tree
- A vast variety of character skins and wide range of vehicle choices
- Great combat mechanics
- Good graphics (although the Definitive Edition is actually not that much of an improvement compared to the Standard Edition)
- Open-world environment that is a simplified and not a very accurate replica of Hong Kong (who cares though?)
- Emma Stone and Lucy Liu as voice actors ;)
CONS:
- Lack of convenient fast-travel options (only taxis that cost money and are not available everywhere and the car valet)
- Dependence on foods and drinks that need constant replenishing for stat boosts
- Annoying driving experience from time to time (narrow streets, intense traffic, AIs suddenly stopping in the middle of the road or changing lanes, camera spins on reverse, exaggerated momentum)
- Sometimes it's hard to find the objective in the street mazes of Hong Kong
- Inaccurate ranged weapons and barely noticeable cross-hairs
MISCELLANEOUS
- Romance is very superficial, it should have had more substance
- Both the Definitive and Standard Edition didn't recognize my Nvidia videocard on Windows 8 and 8.1 and they crashed or freezed on the first loading screen. The forum solutions didn't work. I was able to play Sleeping Dogs only after the upgrade to Windows 10.
My overall rating: 7.5/10
DLCs:
- Nightmare in North Point: imo, the best DLC of them all. A fun combat experience with elements of Chinese folklore. Adds some additional combat mechanics that allows you to fight demons and the blood-craving ghosts.
- The Zodiac Tournament - also a fun story around a fighting tournament in the style of Enter the Dragon
- Year of the Snake - a heavy focus on driving, repetitive side missions. The story is about Wei Shen investigating a terrorist cult. Quite boring.

A great collection of the first seasons' 4 episodes of The Last Door series. Season 2 is already in the making, and even 2 episodes out on their site (Edit: When editing this review, the 2nd season has already been released).
I simply loved the retro pixelated graphics, the mood setting artwork, colors, music and selection sound. You immediately get the whole creepy vibe over you when you play. It plays upon your fears, like fear of dark and open empty spaces. You never feel quite safe anywhere you go as something might happen suddenly.
Despite the game playing upon horror themes, it isn't quite like any horror movie or game out there. It's more about the suspense, and about the thrill of the search and hunt for answers. You can discover many secrets while playing, which makes you play episodes several times to find all the answers you need. The game also includes a few intriguing puzzles that you will need to solve in order to progress.
This collector's edition had some nice extras added, and a few more features I didn't remember from the initial episodes I played on Kongregate. It's a nice purchase and a great addition to any game library. I urge any point-and-click fan, horror/thriller fan, mystery/crime fan etc to try this out. It reminds me of the good old games from LucasArts like Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle. It includes some nice referances to H.P. Lovecraft's works, and it is also considered a tribute to him in several ways. In short, this game is a must-have. Give it a shot, and maybe you will find out what lies behind the last door?

The Last Door is a haunting tale with a touch of Lovecraft mixed in. The developers pay homage to the Sierra-era of adventure games both mechanically and graphically, and the narrative benefits from some above average writing. I never found myself anything less than compelled by the story unfolding across all four episodes, which had its atmosphere augmented by a quite chilling soundtrack of piano driven sonatas. I highly recommend this for any fans of adventure games, horror, or literary works in the vein of Lovecraft, Poe, and Chambers.

As an avid fan of HP Lovecraft, and an old skool gamer, I've been looking for a Lovecraftian game (my favorites are Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of Earth [would kill for a sequel], Amnesia: The Dark Descent, Darkness Within I and II), and I stumbled upon this game. Although I'm not a big fan of pixel graphic games, this one actually filled the gap. I recommend this game to point-and-click adventure lovers. This game could be a lot better, if it had at least the graphics quality of the Black Mirror series. I started with a C=64 as an 8-year old, but c'mon. Update: Ok, I confess, less graphics means more imagination and more immersion. On the other hand, I got this game for Linux. And although the game installer  installed Adobe Air itself with no problems, it did not work (didn't care to mess with it, either). I got a dual-boot system to deal with such problems, so I had to reinstall it on Windows 7 to be able to play it.

What I liked about this game most is its pure logic: I didn't use a guide, except for some secrets, and got stuck only two or three times, and not for long. Most of the time you know where to go or what to do, and if not, some additional exploration will quickly put everything in its place.
What I dislike is that this game, in fact, didn't get me get scared, didn't get me a feeling of pure madness, walking on the edge and struggling for protagonist's life. If you need a really horror game, better refer to "Downfall" or "The Cat Lady," for example.
But if you want to play a really well-thought point-and-click adventure and a piece of art, then this game is definitely worth your attention. There are four episodes which occupy about two hours of playthrough each, if you don't use a guide, and plus about two hours on minisodes and looking for secrets. It's a perfect timing for enjoying the game and not getting bored, and it perfectly fits the current price. And then comes the time for the next season :)

The Last Door is described as a "journey to the brink of madness" and "a love letter to H.P. Lovecraft".  During the introduction the influence was clear and as a big fan of Lovecraft, I was immediately hooked.  Fans of Lovecraftian horror should enjoy this point and click title.  Despite it not being an actual Lovecraft story, the themes are familiar; helplessness, hopelessness, the fragility or sanity and human vulnerability.
As a big fan of point and click games, I have played surprisingly few horror point and click titles.  The Last Door isn't terrifying by any means, but it succeeds in creating a creepy atmosphere through the use of pixel graphics and orchestral music.  While the pixel graphics sometimes make things more confusing (objects becoming difficult to spot), the orchestral music is definitely one of the strongest features of the game.  I would go as far as to say the score is perfect.
The graphics may not be for everyone, but for others it is probably a plus.  The length is spot on, the atmosphere is creepy and the interface is simple and clever.  It may not be a game for everyone, but if anything I have written sounds interesting, then you should at least pick up Season One on sale.

Mother Russia Bleeds has the potential to be a modern classic. It has a terrific soundtrack, an interesting concept, fast and brutal gameplay, and positively drips with style. While in the past i had a number of issues with difficulty, a recent patch has more or less fixed all of those issues. This is a very worthy sucessor to the arcade brawlers of old.
It is tough, and perhaps a bit unfair, but then again fairness was never a big selling point. Make no mistake, this game will challenge you, but with good reflexes, practice, and fast thumbs it is very beatable. Enemies are dangerous, able to take a beating and dish it out just as well, however their numbers are low enough that a skilled player can control them, and the use of dangerous stage hazards adds to this to create a hectic and brutal brawl on every screen.
The Nekro mechanic works quite well with this style of gameplay, forcing the player to create safe windows to gather Nekro for use as healing or a temporary powerup, without the task being too burdensome. In addition, the unlockable drugs allow for varied strategy with one's Nekro.
All things considered, this certainly justifies it's price tag, and i would highly reccomend it to anyone who is looking for a fast paced arcade brawler.
Overall, a solid 8.5/10 all it's missing is online co-op.

This review is subjected to changes since it's an MMO which goes on a continous implementation of patches. As a veteran player I do not recommend this game. It's super bland grindy at the end game.
TL;DR - End Game content (Very important in all MMO): Live letter which boasts and sugar coats about upcoming patch/expansion > patch/expansion gets released > Content worth only 1 week or more of actual fun > Game gets bland and just daily grind heavy even with the new patch > becomes pretty dead for over 2 1/2 month until next patch > cycle repeats..

At the end...it ends up being the same grinding content with the same agenda to kill a monster or do a dungeon (where you kill a monster too), or other similar elements that is sugar coated in different animation/graphics. Example in game - Diadem.
Many Veteran players have left this game and many have unsubscribed who resubscribes when a patch gets released which brings their hope up that the game got better but then unsubscribes disappointed. The majority of the players now that are recommending this game are players who have recently just started the game months ago and don't understand the cycle and brags how good this game is with having no experience on the entire game. Also some loyal fans.
Pros and Cons of this game:
Raid - If you are a hardcore player, you'll be disappointed from the fact that these raids lasts about a week and a half until hardcore players complete it. After completion, the next set of raids do not get released for another 2 1/2 month or even more. In other words their short. This applies to the 24 man raid as well. In heavensward expansion there has been twice where no raid content was released for 6 month each. Making it 12 month total now. They usually release 4 8-man raids every patch and 1 24-man raid every 2 patches. WoW on the otherhand has raids that lasts for months or a year because they release it in Huge contents and content itself is much harder then this game.
Dungeons - This is joke. Lasts about a day or two and then it becomes a simple repitiion and grind. The problem with dungeons is that every new dungeon they release, which is about 2 dungeons each patch, makes the old dungeons obsolete which they seem to take out of blizzard text book. However, a good element of the dungeon is that they do bring a new style of fights usually which is displayed on the boss fights. It's another grind just letting you know.
Crafting & Gathering - In no way, this element within any MMO is the Bread and Butter. It's useless and a game can be entirely enjoyable without it. This is just another form of grinding to make money within the game or make gears so players stay subscribed longer. The unique part though this game has a different style of system for crafting and gathering which makes it like you are actually fighting a monster with crafting skills. It requires some brain and once you get it down you can just make a macro, and sleep over night and let it do everything. That's all there is but let me say this element isn't the one to draw people to the game and people who say it is...haven't played other MMOs before and haven't tried all other content to it's fullest in any MMO.

Player Versus Player Arena - Called Feast(Score Match) and Wolves den(Death Match). First due note that the netcode sucks in this game so get ready to experience some server lag. Also, they haven't resolved to deal with the cheaters that boost points during a season. Every season lasts about 1 patch and some people at the top 100 are involved in cheating to boosting their points higher. The FFXIV team did nothing to deal with them. Instead left them alone which you can see in the forum. The Score match Arena modes are based on Guild Wars 2 style. Needs lots more polishing. There is no pure PVP death match because they made it obsolete with the release of Feast and advertising it. Also, every arena requires one healer, one tank, one range and one melee. Final Fantasy 14 is a truly enjoyable game, and it's something I'd highly recommend to most people; whether they be attracted to good storylines, beautiful graphics, sexy dragon waifus, or raiding. However, there were still a bit of cons that followed along with the many pros. Many other people have gone in depth about game play, so I'd be keeping that part brief.
Pros:
- Dude, you can freaking play as a sexy dragon waifu. Who doesn't want that?
- Raiding in this game is spectacular. It's really fun, and does require a bit of skill. It's not faceroll at all, unless you're doing super old content, where your new gear carries you through mechanics, allowing you to skip phases. Even then, it's still good to tackle old content, as it does have lovely story. Especially the Coils.
- Great story. C'mon. It's Final Fantasy. You expected that.
- People in this game are pretty playful for the most part, and Balmung is great for rp, with friendly enough people hanging around in towns, feel free to start up a convo with them, there's not ... that much that could go wrong??? :D
- You don't have to make a new character to play different jobs, but you do have to level your new job. You just change your weapon, and you become a black mage from a Warrior.
- It's a pretty popular game, and finding a raid group shouldn't be hard in case you want to try it. Reddit would be your best bet, but there are facebook groups as well.
Cons
- If you're not interested in raiding, things can get a bit dry. Even if you do raid, there's not much to do at end game besides that and weeklies/dailies.
- There's no in game parser, but you can download Attack Combat Tracker to help you track your damage. (It's only a bannable offense if you tell the person how much damage they did exactly and harrass them about it.) However, because there isn't one in game, people do tend to get a case of the bads a lot. For example. There are DPS that will do half the damage of a healer or a tank, and have no intentions to improve. They're mainly just drawn to the Square Enix/ Final Fantasy name. Patience with people would be nice to have.
- Quite a few of the people in the game are pretty PC/politically correct, so they'll be offended pretty easily. Might be best to tone down on the language.
- A great deal of people in this game know eachother or know of eachother, even if you're from a different server. You'll notice that the longer you play, the more people you know from all around. Could be a good or bad thing. (:
TL;DR: Game's freaking great, but stale in the late game. The community could be either good or bad in your eyes, but it's by far, the worst one I've ever seen due to the unwillingness of people to improve at their class (even in raid.) STILL RECOMMENDED THOUGH.

I do not recommend this game. For the following reasons I cannot recommend anyone spend their time on this game without significant improvements made to account set up and initial updating.
In life there are certain necessities: obtaining resources, developing skills, overcoming obstacles and entertainment to name a few. What motivates one must satisfy a need with a reasonable investment of time and effort. My sole purpose in this game is to play as an imaginary character in an imaginary world filled with imaginary things. As a purchaser I cannot make money, or update my resume with anything related to this effort which is now becoming something of an unjustifiable obstacle relative to the outcome.
I will now chronicle the genesis of this obstacle in order to play as an imaginary character in an imaginary world filled with imaginary things (a meager need that has yet to be satisfied):
1.) I purchased the game on steam and installed it - no problem.
2.) Upon starting the game I needed to set up a Square Enix account which I attempted to do through the launcher (naturally, as the option is provided right there). In my experience, this was a convoluted, glitchy process that resulted in several attempts and approximately two hours of my time wasted. As setting up an account is usually a straightforward process I did not make a log like a dutiful beta tester. Essentially, my email was at once recognized to the extent I could not repeat the registration process to clarify what might have gone wrong, yet not recognized to the extent I could not recover a password. Eventually I simply made an account directly through the Square Enix website. A painless, wonderful and perfectly pedestrian result that by comparison had me shouting joyfully "It's alive! The Room is a neat little puzzle game that even boneheads like me can solve in under 4 hours.
The game consists of the titular room in which you have to solve a variety of puzzles on some kind of container/machine. The more puzzles you solve, the more the machine unlocks, even transferring you to other rooms, etc.
The game is originally a mobile game, but it doesn't show. The graphics are superb and the controls precise enough. Unlocking the machine is like an addiction. And even if you get stuck, after a while there are more or less helpful hints that should carry you forward. You of course don't have to read the tips if you don't want to. There is no time limit or anything. Only 1 puzzle requires a bit of timing as I recall, but very simply indeed. Most puzzles revolve around finding missing pieces, hitting hidden switches or aligning something in the correct order. Your helpful eyepiece, which shows a different kind of reality, is your trusty partner in this endeavour.
For the price, let alon on a sale, it's definitely worth it. Just beware that "The Room 3" is currently not yet available on Steam, so for anyone wanting to finish the "story" (it's only notes really, but interesting nonetheless), you either have to play on mobile or wait. I'm pretty sure they will port the 3rd installment as well. Would be silly not to.
One word of advice: One puzzle is currently a bit broken. A gem just won't slide the way it should. This is at the very end of the game and can be fixed by changing from Fullscreen to windowed mode (and/or also changing the monitor's refresh rate to 60 for whatever reason). Just google the problem. Too bad they haven't fixed that.

Ever since I was a child I had an interest in horror- or occult-stories, books and movies. I think most of you would agree if I say that’s typical for a young human being that widens its horizon every day but can’t figure out why darkness is so much more uncomfortable yet exciting than daylight. Even now as a grown up I love Lovecraft and Poe, but also modern representatives of this genre, for example Hohlbein, and it still catches me when there is something you try to imagine but you can’t figure out what it looks like. As the famous H.P.Lovecraft said:
So, enough of an introduction, let’s have a look at the game you came to read about here.
The Last Door is a Point-and-Click Adventure that is set in the 1890s in Victorian England, a time when science was already established but ancient beliefs and a secret organisations such as the freemasons were well known among the people. You get in touch with Jeremiah Devitt, a man in the mid-thirties who received a strange letter from his childhood friend Alexander Beechworth. Not knowing how to deal with this, Jeremiah decides to visit Alexander, unraveling the mysteries about his whereabouts and his family. But that may be only the start for a journey that will lead you to places of Jeremiah’s childhood and past that have been forgotten for some reason. It seems like an ancient evil is making its way back into your life..
I can’t write any further without spoiling but you should already feel how this story will suck you in, not releasing you until finished. A man gets snatched from his everyday life right into a victorian nightmare, how much more lovecraftian could it be? This game relies solely on its mysterious plot and manages this with two main attributes: Sound and Style. When I first saw some screenshots of this game before playing the first Episode “The Letter”, I couldn’t imagine how this pixelated art would manage to give me the creeps or offer details I need to make myself comfortable. But this game did not only manage to revive my passion for retro-styled games, it simply worked out what my introductive quote should show - that fear of the unknown is the strongest one. It feels like the devs from
simply built a framework from what a scene
look like and relied on the player’s imagination to make it a truly living and frightening place. Colours are not mixed up, no they are shaded differently to create a certain mood like the warmth of a living hall.
. After listening to “Crows over the City”, which is the main theme of The Last Door, you will likely want to know what the composer’s name is. Don’t thank me for that, thank him for creating this game’s amazing classical music. Every aspect of this game gets pushed by its clever and well written tones and also sound effects, whether its the creeping dark or a simple wave along the old English coast.
Owning a mouse is key for this game since you don’t need any other instruments. You have an inventory at the bottom screen, containing everything you will find and need to interact with other objects. The puzzles are logic-based, really challenging sometimes and it gets tough if you haven’t found the right object yet. This didn’t happen often to me but it might also happen to you so I should mention that. There is no hint system and no button press will highlight any useful items but your cursor will switch from a cross to a lens if you can look, or a hand if you can take or interact with something.
You might have already recognised that I love this game. But besides my own opinion you can’t really go wrong with The Last Door. Its graphics and sound make up for a great journey into a story that even Lovecraft himself would call a masterpiece. If you are not sure about it, enter
and check out the first episode “The Letter” for free. If you liked it, do yourself a favor and enjoy the enhanced textures, sounds and bonus content of the Collector`s Edition on Steam.

Final Fantasy 14 is a truly enjoyable game, and it's something I'd highly recommend to most people; whether they be attracted to good storylines, beautiful graphics, sexy dragon waifus, or raiding. However, there were still a bit of cons that followed along with the many pros. Many other people have gone in depth about game play, so I'd be keeping that part brief.
Pros:
- Dude, you can freaking play as a sexy dragon waifu. Who doesn't want that?
- Raiding in this game is spectacular. It's really fun, and does require a bit of skill. It's not faceroll at all, unless you're doing super old content, where your new gear carries you through mechanics, allowing you to skip phases. Even then, it's still good to tackle old content, as it does have lovely story. Especially the Coils.
- Great story. C'mon. It's Final Fantasy. You expected that.
- People in this game are pretty playful for the most part, and Balmung is great for rp, with friendly enough people hanging around in towns, feel free to start up a convo with them, there's not ... that much that could go wrong??? :D
- You don't have to make a new character to play different jobs, but you do have to level your new job. You just change your weapon, and you become a black mage from a Warrior.
- It's a pretty popular game, and finding a raid group shouldn't be hard in case you want to try it. Reddit would be your best bet, but there are facebook groups as well.
Cons
- If you're not interested in raiding, things can get a bit dry. Even if you do raid, there's not much to do at end game besides that and weeklies/dailies.
- There's no in game parser, but you can download Attack Combat Tracker to help you track your damage. (It's only a bannable offense if you tell the person how much damage they did exactly and harrass them about it.) However, because there isn't one in game, people do tend to get a case of the bads a lot. For example. There are DPS that will do half the damage of a healer or a tank, and have no intentions to improve. They're mainly just drawn to the Square Enix/ Final Fantasy name. Patience with people would be nice to have.
- Quite a few of the people in the game are pretty PC/politically correct, so they'll be offended pretty easily. Might be best to tone down on the language.
- A great deal of people in this game know eachother or know of eachother, even if you're from a different server. You'll notice that the longer you play, the more people you know from all around. Could be a good or bad thing. (:
TL;DR: Game's freaking great, but stale in the late game. The community could be either good or bad in your eyes, but it's by far, the worst one I've ever seen due to the unwillingness of people to improve at their class (even in raid.) STILL RECOMMENDED THOUGH.

I do not recommend this game. For the following reasons I cannot recommend anyone spend their time on this game without significant improvements made to account set up and initial updating.
In life there are certain necessities: obtaining resources, developing skills, overcoming obstacles and entertainment to name a few. What motivates one must satisfy a need with a reasonable investment of time and effort. My sole purpose in this game is to play as an imaginary character in an imaginary world filled with imaginary things. As a purchaser I cannot make money, or update my resume with anything related to this effort which is now becoming something of an unjustifiable obstacle relative to the outcome.
I will now chronicle the genesis of this obstacle in order to play as an imaginary character in an imaginary world filled with imaginary things (a meager need that has yet to be satisfied):
1.) I purchased the game on steam and installed it - no problem.
2.) Upon starting the game I needed to set up a Square Enix account which I attempted to do through the launcher (naturally, as the option is provided right there). In my experience, this was a convoluted, glitchy process that resulted in several attempts and approximately two hours of my time wasted. As setting up an account is usually a straightforward process I did not make a log like a dutiful beta tester. Essentially, my email was at once recognized to the extent I could not repeat the registration process to clarify what might have gone wrong, yet not recognized to the extent I could not recover a password. Eventually I simply made an account directly through the Square Enix website. A painless, wonderful and perfectly pedestrian result that by comparison had me shouting joyfully "It's alive! It's alive" with Handel's "Messiah" ringing in my head.
3.)  After the account was set up I could then update the game. Whereas the registration was likely to have different results for different people depending on wind currents caused by butterfly wings and their relationship to which particle collider test had run on a that day with reference to the alignment of various celestial bodies, the size of the update is massive - and is taking a long time.
With reference to needs and motivation I have run a gauntlet with no satisfaction in sight for another 1386 minutes, and at this point am making two major recommendations:
1.) If the option to create an account via the launcher is intended, it needs to be as simple as creating an account on the website. My experience has shown a discrepancy in ease of use between the two.
2.) The initial update is as massive as the investment of time required for the game to be ready to play; a possible way to mitigate this is to sell a more recent version. If this has no effect on overall download time, find ways to make it more effiecient.
At this point I will complete the updating process, but cannot recommend this game unless these two recommendations are given serious consideration. Butterfly wings and all.

is the first game that David Szymanski made in the horror genre, and he confesses in the game's brief description that he has learned much since completing this project. Still,
is a narrative and atmospheric success for a game which wouldn't take any longer than 20 minutes to complete, plus it is free for you to experience.
We open our eyes to an old bunker, and start our exploration. We are quick to discover some scattered notes around left by a man, a father who supposedly lived here. We know one thing: whoever left these notes to us as bread crumbs all around the house, is one obsessed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ over the concept of "societal norms". What happened to him? That is one major spoiler, so if you'd like to find out, you have to spare 20 minutes and discover yourself.
The atmosphere of the game, in my opinion, serves as a foreshadowing for David Szymanski's future games. The usage of beaming lights, flickering screen and creepy background noises are used conventionally to establish a successful setting. Graphics are very basic, yet they do not fail to deliver the kind of uneasiness that you expect from a proper horror game.
Game mechanics consist of a basic exploration, and 3-4 very easy password puzzles. Is there anything extraordinary about the story? Well, aside being particularly disturbing, the story isn't incredibly interesting. The imaginative or enlightening factor is the concept David Syzmanski decided to build the game over: the true nature of mankind. When given total freedom, away from societal norms and binding rules, human isn't even slightly glorious or benevolent than an ape, a wild animal. This game is a symbolic ode to the theory of men being evil - or primal - at their core. I bet Thomas Hobbes would be proud.
I personally prefer games with more elaborate social theories, but if you have 20 minutes to spare, capable of ignoring some disturbing implications and enjoy atmospheric horror genre, there is no logical reason for not checking this game out. It is free, and it is really good in that context.

SUMMARY
Don't expect any leveling, loot, or any other kind of irrelevant features, expect alot of satisfying punches and violence with diverse moveset and weaponry, in the vein of old school beat 'em ups brought to modern day with respect what actually makes a good beat 'em up and without adding anything unnecessary. If you like Streets of Rage you will love this game.
LONG VERSION
At long last we get a proper beat 'em up in the vein of Streets of Rage, D&D Shadow over Mystara, Double Dragon, Final Fight. Forget your Castle Crashers and Rampage Knights, those are beat' em ups as much as modern roguelites are roguelikes. (I am not saying those are bad, they look similar on the outside but they play quite differently). So yeah, they bear a certain resemblance and have some elements in common, but in the end they are very different games.
So MRB is a proper (I will elaborate what I mean with "proper" here) beat 'em up, in the sense that it doesn't have any rpg or roguelike elements or any other modern "lets put this feature here since its trendy" -features. It is a pure beat 'em up. Other important things for a beat 'em up that MRB has, are the diverse moveset that you must learn to use to your advantage. You can't just spam the attack button (like in some other modern games that people call beat 'em ups), that will get you surely killed in no time. You must use punch, punch+kick combos, dodge, slide kick, jumping kick, charged attack, running punch, grabs&throws and punching baddies on the ground (well I guess you don't exactly have to use all of your repertoire to succeed, but you get my point).
This game is not easy (on normal difficulty, there are also easy and hard) by modern standards. To be successful in this game, in addition to use your moveset diversely, you have to learn crowd control. This means that you can't let the baddies corner you, and be mindful of your surroundings for exemple enemies with guns. You grow to know when to do the combos and charged attacks to do most damage, and when to use attacks that knock down enemies to get a little room to breathe. Also the grab+throwing game comes in here as an important part, and it is always rewarding to throw a baddie into 4 other baddies to make a pile of 'em, then load your home-run attack with baseball bat and when they stand up you let them have it. Ahh. Lovely.
From the trailers I feared that the syringe mechanism would be a gimmicky thing that would be annoyingly interrupting the gameplay flow. It is not. It is great addition to the beat 'em up mechanics, and bring the lore of the game into the gameplay in a cool way. And it is more "beliavable" (/cool) than whole fried chickens found in the dumpsters and crates in warehouses.
There are many objects that you can pick up and hit enemies with. It is extremely satisfying to pick up a baseball bat or a crowbar and release a charged blow to the enemy's face. Speaking of which, the whole game feels very satisfying to play. Punches feel that they have impact, and it is very rewarding to do those execution moves or bash up a enemy's skull with a brick while he is on the ground. I really like the graphics and pixel art, animations, music and the whole setting and mood of the game.
I like how the game has no lives or continues, but just a time for each level. If you die, you restart from the checkpoint, but the time keeps running. This way you can't "cheat" with spamming credits, so the game won't escalate too quickly a point where you die in 5 seconds, since it requires you to be certain "skill level" when passing a stage. It cleverly teaches you to experiment and use your moveset to get past a certain point. You must to remember to use all your moves yourself though, the game won't hold your hand. For example, at one point I completerly forgot about the dodge move, which was pretty necessary against a boss with a gun. There I learned to dodge vertically and after that the boss was pretty easy.
So, there you have it. MRB is everything it promises, SoR inspired beat 'em up with influences from Hotline Miami. I am so thankful for LeCartel for making a proper beat 'em up, a thing which hasn't happened since SoR remake came out in 2011.

I have been playing this for a few hours and I can honestly say this was exactly what I had hoped it would be. When I first started I was a bit worried because of how chaotic the fights were and how my character seemed to be lost in a sea of thugs. Soon, however, everything seemed to click. Also that all of the different types of enemies have various attack patterns to watch out for so the game challenges you to stay on your toes.
It feels a lot like all of the old school beat-em-ups that I still play to this day and the Hotline Miami style spin on the violence makes for a much more brutal and gritty experience. I have seen a few people complaining about things such as dialogue length but that can be skipped by simply pressing a button. The checkpoints are also very forgiving and even though the game can be difficult, I never found myself upset where it placed me after a death.
I can say that the hyper-violence, bizarre sexual themes, and vengeful (as well as drug-fueled) story will not appeal to everyone, but those willing to take the plunge into this insane world should have a fun and bloody time.

A unique experience interacting with beautifully designed and rendered puzzle boxes. As little doors flip open, crystals shimmer, and strange lights appear through each step of the puzzle, the experience is strangely rewarding. There's barely any story here, but the game doesn't suffer for it. Puzzles are not very difficult, but a system with well-balanced hints makes sure you don't get stuck endlessly. A really enjoyable two hours or so of gameplay.

I bought this little gem on sale and it was worth every penny. Though I finished the game in only 3.5 hours, I found it completely absorbing and had a great time solving the puzzles. The visuals are stunning and the music is pleasant. The optic device in the game makes the puzzle solving even more complex and interesting. If you like puzzle games that require attention to detail and a lot of brain work, I can highly recommend "The Room".

The Room is a puzzle game divided in 5 chapters. Rather than searching a large area (e.g. a room or even an entire building) for clues, you find yourself examining oddly-shaped boxes, vaults and other kinds of objects that contain secrets. For people who like exploration in puzzle games, this could be a con.
The puzzles are not too difficult and some of them are just trial and error, but you may overlook small details. You also have a special lens that allows you to see things that are not visible to the naked eye. This makes the game a little bit more challenging. However, you're still likely to beat this game in a few hours (probably 2-6 hours).
You play the game using your mouse to rotate the camera, zoom in and out and interact with certain objects. Although the controls are very simple, they can also be quite frustrating. Sometimes you may find yourself accidentally pulling a lever or rotating another object when you were simply trying to rotate the camera. I am aware that this game was originally developed for mobile platforms, which explains the simple controls, but in my honest opinion it would have been better if they altered the controls for the PC version. For example, instead of holding down the mouse button and dragging the mouse to rotate the camera, they could've used the arrow keys for camera rotation (or simply excluded the action of holding down the mouse button). That way, players are less likely to accidentally interact with things.
Both the visuals and the music in the game are beautiful. The graphics are incredibly detailed, which makes you look for the tiniest details in every box you try to open. The background music is mysterious like the game itself.
Something that surprised me was the lack of jump scares in the game. Since the tag 'horror' was included, I was expecting the game to have some visual and aural jump scares, but I didn't find The Room scary in the slightest.
The Room is without a doubt a fun puzzle game with stunning graphics. If you are looking for a casual puzzle game, you should give it a try, but if you like challenges and tons of exploration, this might not be your cup of tea.

Despite it is far away from excellence, The Room is not a complete mess either: it's just a middling game.
First, it could be more challenging. Indeed, the puzzles are really easy to solve: you won't need to think a lot to figure them out, and the game provides a lot of advices, even when disabling them in the options. I was never stranded while playing, and never had to struggle in order to get the logic of the puzzles. Too bad, I like being challenged, especially in this kind of game. 2h30 to complete the 5 episodes (counting several breaks, so more or less 1h30-2h), it's too short in my opinion. Secondly, the story could be more complex and better written. It was neither enthrolling nor intriguing, though the studio tried to create a supposedly strange and mysterious atmosphere. I've never felt immersed in this poor story. If it was only for the story, I would've thought this game was created for 10-years-old children maximum. Which is not a problem in fact, but they should tell it.
Nevertheless, the beautiful graphics and the atmosphere (visuals+musics) compensate for the poor narration and the easy puzzles, rising the game to an average level. The different boxes and platforms are really well made and beautiful. Besides, despite their lack of difficulty, several puzzles surprised me because they are ingeniously made.

I wanted to recommend this game. I really did. But while the game has some intriguing ideas, it doesn't really execute on any of them. The game only has four chapters, and then ends with an abrupt tonal shift like it's suddenly a horror game or something. There's little to no payoff for the game itself, or satisfaction in playing it.
A bigger problem is that there are only two kinds of puzzles. Extremely obvious and easy ones, and ones that you are unlikely to get or understand because it expects you to notice tiny, insignificant details to discover things. Often, puzzles don't flow, meaning you will finish one, not get anything, and be left looking around trying to find something without any clue as to what it actually wants you to solve next. This is likely because, when they fall into each other, one after the other, they become obvious and easy. The issue with this game is that there is not challenge outside of being lost; there are no logic or thought based puzzles to make you think. It's essentially a game of eye spy in 3D.
And that's a shame, because the game is visually interesting. I do wonder, however, why it gives letters with some semblance of a story if it goes nowhere, explains nothing, and results in more questions of why I spent two hours playing through it.
So If $5 is worth 2 hours of your time, you'll probably like this. If not, I'd skip this one. It's not bad, but it doesn't leave you with anything other than a feeling of 'yeah that sure was a thing I played.'

The Last Door is an interesting subject. It is one of the strangest, yet most conventional horror adventure games I have ever met.
Graphics are secondary in a story-driven genre, but in this case it is worth mentioning that the very old-school pixel presentation adds a strange layer to the already eerie atmosphere. Something, that may or may not work with a modern (3D) engine.
And this game is all about atmosphere. It is a unique, but working mix of Lovecraftian suspense over the unknown, blended together with Amnesia-like fear of the dark (and a few mandatory jump scares). It is especially strong in the first chapter, where there is no dialogue at all.
A horror is all about story and presentation, and Last Door for the most part knows its trade. The introduction of dialogues in the 2nd chapter hurt quality somewhat: a good chunk of them are clumsy exposition dumps that slowly turn the game into a weak Cthulhu rip-off. But they quickly steer away from this pit and soar into new heights in chapters 3 and 4.
Sadly it’s still one of those types where you don’t get a single answer regarding the mystery, although there is a promise of a second season.

This Lovecraftian point-and-clicker features an intriguing story and the richest atmosphere you'll ever encounter in a game with pixels the size of cinder blocks!  The text can occasionally be awkward, betraying the game's non-English origin, and this irritated me at first -- but I soon became so overwhelmed by the moldy, miasmatic charm of the game's eldritch narrative that I ceased to notice.  Highly recommended!  I am looking forward to season 2 with bated breath!
The Last Door has easily been one of the scariest and most fun games I've ever played! Perfectly done horror, amazing audio and visual storytelling and an incredible atmosphere!
Highly atmospheric, very story-driven and decent puzzles! A very good games!

The Last Door is a stylish low-res horror game divided up into several small episodes. These episodes come together to form the first ‘season’ (the game you see here).
From the opening moments of the very first episode you are plunged into a stylish and engaging Lovecraftian tale. I won’t spoil these moments, as they are part of what gives The Last Door its power and potency. The game draws on multiple horror staples (Poe, Lovecraft, even a touch of Chambers's 'The King in Yellow'), but whilst the game plays on these themes it builds its own universe to play in. There are no tentacled horrors patrolling corridors, the game carves out a new and creepy world, and hints at the things that may lie beyond. As a result, the story felt less like it was ticking off Lovecraftian references and a little less predictable.
Whilst a few of the horror moments fell short by being expected, they hit more often than they miss and there are plenty of them. The game plays more on creeping, foreboding horror than outright frights, although there are a fair share of those too. The music adds brilliantly to both the tension and the feeling of grandeur, the pixel art adds power to your mind’s eye, whilst the sound design brings each scene to life and the writing style keeps you engaged.
Each episode is interesting and engaging, moving the story forward and introducing new characters and twists. There’s a surprising amount of depth to be uncovered here. The puzzles are relatively straightforward, but the storyline gains more depth with each episode you play through. There are several side-episodes available in the ‘extras’ menu too, offering a few extra plot points and a little more intrigue to each episode.
I eagerly await season two, and thoroughly recommend season one to those who enjoy adventure games and horror stories.
Oh, and play it with headphones on if you can, it’s an experience worth immersing yourself in, and the sounds and music do that spectacularly.

If my time in this game doesn't say it alone, this game is really good. There's a lot you can do in the game. Raiding, Interesting story (ish. until you hit 2.0 the story is hit and miss), and a huge world to explore, and that's just the beginning of it. There's an initial five races in the game, plus a sixth dragon race if you own Heavensward, with plenty of customization options making it extremely difficult to find a character designed the same as you. You can also use real world currency to change race and such if you decide you don't like it. There's an entire shop where you can get vanity items for real world currency and we won't go into details about how much money I have put into this game. This game is actually 0% pay to win, which I absolutely love. The beginning of the game is slightly unforgiving for newcomers to the game, but it gets better as you go on. The game for me was rather slow until I hit around level 20 which is where it speeds up in my opinion. There's also in game gambling at the Gold Saucer, which you can spend SO much time at. Triple Triad is super addicting when you're trying to collect all the cards. I do recommend having a friend to start with, though, as not having that friend to play with can actually make the game less fun at some parts. I should probably also mention the class system. There's  9 battle classes to choose from, differing between Tank, Healer, and DPS. These classes go into jobs when you hit level 30, all of these classes except for Arcanist goes into 1 class. Arcanist goes into Summoner and Scholar. There's also crafting classes that you can get lost in, as well as three extra jobs in Heavensward. Level 50 raiding is kind of on the deader side since Heavensward released, but I'm sure if you get people to do it, it won't be as bad. At level 50 you can get your job armour, which is actually some of the better armor at level 50. Your job weapon for level 50 can also be upgraded through a quest line making it comparable to level 54 gear (I think. I never maxed mine cus I'm lazy). Subscriptions are $12.99 for an entry level account which allows 8 characters and no duplicates on a single world, or $14.99 for a standard sub which allows 40 characters and more than one in a single world. All in all, if you're looking for an MMO to try, give this a shot. The trial version actually isn't bad and shows you most of the leveling of the game. It doesn't show you, however, the raiding and such as far as I know. Definitely give this a shot if you're an MMO fanatic or just want to try something new. The playerbase is one of the most helpful towards newcomers I've seen probably ever. I'd try to avoid Cactuar though, as it's gotten slightly more toxic than I would like.

But that alone would not have made me love this game so much, that I's play through it again for the 100 % achievement. I genuinely love the story, and the soundtrack, which is creatively told. If you like a good strategy game, turn-based gameplay and action and if the idea of having a mix of those elements into one. This is the game.
It's gameplay and art style make it a unique and novel experience and is a lot of fun too!
To start the soundtrack is superb, and the fact that it is significant and relevant due to the circumstance of the main character is double cool.
The gameplay as mentioned is novel and doesn't fail to dissapoint, its both entertaining and strategic. I can honestly say that if ever I was  finding it hard or failing I never felt like it was the game's fault. It works in which you can fight in real-time but have the ability to stop time and queue movements and skills in order to defeat your enemies with this it mixes in a sort of unique turn-based system. Once you initiated this power, you must wait a very short period where you are most vulnerable till it fills up and you can do it again.
The skills you accuire are very different from one another and you can even combine them so to speak to garner different effects when you use them. It's very well thought out and works well.
The story, well, it is also a thing. I'm not sure how I feel about the story since it was definetly unique but it really wasn't memorable and I just didn't understand the ending either, it makes you feel like there was no point to anything, it really was the weakest part of the game in my opinion. The voice acting was great and hearing the transistor talk about the things as traverse the areas was cool but I really didn't understand in the end what was going on other than someone else want's your talking sword and it's helping you take back the voice which was stolen from you I think. There were aspects of the story that I can remember that seemed well thought out however.
The graphics, oh man do I ever love the art style. There really isn't a question of if they are good or not. It's an appealling style and the colour palette chosen looks so dam good. It doesn't compare to anything else.
In all if not for the forgettable story this game is entertaining and brings forth something different.

The overall experience of the game was adequate; I played it long enough to beat it and enjoy it thoroughly, but I can't fight the feeling that if the developers spent as much time tweaking the game's combat system (abilities, movement, etc.) as they did creating the exhilerating world with the artwork and the music and the emotion poured into each character, they would truly have a masterpiece in their hands. Thirdly, as pointed out, it is not made clear to buyers that all chapters but the last one are always free, and the last one is a "pay what you want" campaign, as this is how the game developers have decided to fund their game. Steam obscures this fact; therefore you may be a bit disappointed to find this out after you've paid full price.

The developers of the theHunter have done something very different and I think that is why there are so many negative reviews. So instead of purchasing a whole game and just blazing through a story line to have it sit at the bottom of a pile of new games after a month or so, the dev's have made an online store / outfitters, (which is exactly what it is. welcome to cabela's.) where you can purchase just the gear that you want. there are no weapon unlocks; no clothing upgrades; no higher-powered uber ammunition that is going to kill 3 deer with 1 bullet. Instead, you open "Store" and buy what you want for gear, wether its a treestand, a bow, some duck decoys or a dog.
This was a very smart move by the dev's and I can appriciate the new approach. I would however like to see a better use for gm's (game money) so it may be used on a broader range of items. currently it is used to buy licenses and replenish consumables. The em's (electronic money, purchased with your dollars online) are for your weapons, clothing, and other equipment and pets.
I think it's this new style of purchasing stucture that players have a hard time with as many reviews just say "Let me buy the whole game". When in fact you can, just in small pieces at a time that would cost you a fortune.
Personally I think this is a 5 star game. I found no bugs. I do however wish there was a way to increase the detail distance beyond what seems to be about 250 yards or so, but its not game breaking and allows the game to run smoothly.
My advise:
Download it. Give it a shot. Spend some time in a few different areas. Focus on big game. Do "Missions" for whitetail and mule deer to get your gm's up. Find out which +2 species are open for hunting on facebook (Check to see your weapon can kill them legally) and do those missions too, the gm's earned will pay for a 1 day, 7 day or 28 day license on an animal of your choosing. (purchaseable in the store).

If think you can alt-tab out of this game to do something else (if only for a moment) with the intention to quickly return to the game, think again. There's just one thing to say, this game is addicting!
If you're like me and liked Terraria, Minecraft, Rust, and every other game where crafting stuff is part of the core of the game, Factorio will take it to the top and the game will push you to make the most efficient Factory there is!
The principle concept of Factorio is straight forward! Mine ressources like Coal, Iron, Copper etc. to craft stuff which will help you mine more efficient! You need a lot of ressources for Research, but here is the point: Why do it all yourself? Build belts, automatic miners, robot arms which will move your crafted stuff around the map, research robots, use trains and see your little 'Factory' produce stuff on it's own! It's really nice to see your little factories create so many things out of the few Ressources there are available on the map itself!
But don't think you're alone! There is also a huge part devoted to defend your Factory from little pests and Aliens (ALIUMS!) - If you can't manage to keep up, it'll be really hard to survive!
Graphics might discourage some from buying, but as I said in the beginning: don't mind them, if you liked the games I mentioned! Factorio is really deep and there are Higher Resolution Texture already announced for later patches of this game.
Speaking of patches, there is a lot of content still coming and the Devs are really trying to make this game perfect in every way possible - it already is, as there are almost no bugs (or at least it is highly unlikely you will encounter any!) and the Devs are trying to optimize it to run even smoother for bigger Factories!
Also the Community is really huge, I recommend taking a visit to the Wiki if you start out and maybe check out the /r/Factorio subreddit on reddit. You'll find a lot of information about the game, and you will notice there is a huge modding Community available! (Although I recommend playing without mods for your first time, the game already offers enough 'content' for you to get the full experience).
Is it worth it? Maybe even more! I promise, if you're into managing games, crafting games, and always trying to be the most efficient, then this game will make the prize you paid seem like nothing. It's really easy to get 20 hours into the game and just have your basic production running, that's already 1€ for every hour - WORTH!

It will take your life away.

text: Fingerbones is a great example of a developer using low-level assets to create a powerful sense of atmosphere and tension. However, I don't feel as though the story is up to the standard of the developers later games. The narrative of the came is centered the caricature of a (secular?) man who fantasized about being the last man on earth who could be free to do whatever he wants, and his sick interactions with his daughter. Written from the perspective of someone who obviously disagrees with the type of person the father is, he's winds up being nothing more than a one  dimensional monster. Which is a shame because if his fall was more nuanced and we could find ourselves sympathizing with him, then it would make the end result all the more disturbing. Overall it's a good little horror gem, and definitely worth the price.

A short, simple exploration game that does psychological horror right.  While we see many tales of heroism in the face of disaster, Fingerbones reminds us that tragedy brings out the worst in men as well. This game has excelled at the unity of form and content.
If you know, and admire, the content of the Lovecraftian literature, you also know that there is no explicit form to the wonders and horrors he tells about. Mostly shallow representations, shadows, eerie sounds, feelings and visions... that will creep you out and fire up your imagination.
This game pays a 100% respect to this, while telling its own, deep story. The pixel graphics may seem odd and outdated at first, but they grant exactly the form that is needed for this type of eerie Lovecraftian imagery. So let this not be your con on buying it. And while the graphics may be "basic" the sound is outstanding. Like in a radio play it gives you just the amount of vivid details that you need to be sucked up into this dark, victorian story. Finally, the music is excellent and very moving.
Thus, if you like reading Lovecraftian stories on a lonely, dark evening - try this interactive one. You will not regret it!
(or will you...?)
Don't be discouraged by the ve-ry simple pixel graphs. The story and atmosphere more than make up for it!

A fantastic old-school style point-and-click horror adventure game. The sound design and soundtrack are brilliant, the plot is amazing (hearkening back to the best of Lovecraft and Poe), and there are some incredibly unnerving, genuinely scary moments; the unnerving atmosphere is absolutely top-notch.  You *technically* could play it for free on their website, but a game this amazing deserves your support and is worth every penny of the $10.

This classic-style adventure game is brilliant.
The story has many layers of complexity and unfolds as a detective story/mystery with increasing intrigue and HP Lovecraft-hinted surrealism over 4 episodes. The world & story drew me in, I absolutely HAD to know what is going on and what happens next; each episode I played through in one sitting!
The darkness in the scenes and the classical piano-and-string music set the tone of a gothic Victorian world perfectly; the illusion is never broken for the player.
The 8-bit pixel graphics serve the game well: the lack of extreme detail on everything keeps things a bit vague and thus a bit mysterious.
The inventory item use puzzles are extremely logical, and so are the times you must re-visit a room to advance the story or get an item.
Each episode has a few well-placed jump-scares accompanied by a crescendo in music, and they are tied in to the story and not just for a thrill. If you think a pixelated game can't scare you, you're wrong!

Shakes and Fidget is the ultimate waiting game. You click a bit here, click a bit there, wait, rinse and repeat. It's basically the same cycle of clicks every time. You could call it grinding, if you want to, but I think there's way too much waiting and too mindless to be called grinding. Heck, even games where you can skip scenes/sweep to gain xp, gold, or items are less mindless than literally just letting this game run in the background while you do other stuff. In the 13 hours or so I've "played" this game, less than an hour was actually spent with the screen in front of me. It's *that much* of a waiting game. There aren't even any achievements.
It has it's good points as well, I'll have to admit. Art is cute and the text can be quite humorous. But there's no actual plot, there aren't any actual things that you *need* to do to progress, and there's just... waiting. The graphics and aesthetic doesn't make the lack of actual content disappear.
I'll keep it installed simply because I'm that kind of person, and by that, I mean the kind of person that doesn't mind waiting. But I know most people would even loathe to call this a game, satire or not, so I guess Shakes and Fidget is not a game I can recommend.

One of the most frustrating games I've ever played.
Every inch of progress you claw from this game feels like a boring slog. Every time you enter a new area and begin a fight you know you’re in for an uphill battle. We’re not griping about the game’s overall, difficulty; the Souls series of games have proven developers can be unforgiving while still making a game that’s fun. Mother Russia Bleeds has a problem beyond difficulty.
Slow character movement makes progression tedious and it also ensures every encounter with an enemy with ranged attacks exasperating. The fact that every singular enemy can stun-lock you is bad on its own, but it’s made worse when a crowd of enemies corner you, as you’re guaranteed to lose most of your health bar.
Every enemy seems to be made out of titanium and requires dozens of hits to permanently put down. Each of the four playable characters has varying stats, but it just doesn’t gel when the one giant character that hits the hardest still takes multiple punches to put down even the weakest of enemies.
So, while you’re sitting on top of one enemy attempting to turn them into paste, an entire gang of enemies is trying to do the same to you. Any moment you start enjoying a fight in this game is usually the point at which a new band of foes arrive to destroy any warm feeling for the game you had.
We thought the co-op would make this better. By adding in more good guys we figured that the issues we had with the game could be overcome. Unfortunately we were wrong. The difficulty scaling to counterbalance more players works too well and you’re likely to become mentally defeated before too long.
The local-only co-op is a “choose your own poison” affair when you’re deciding to use AI or more real people.
The AI violently swings between impressively competent and something worse than brain dead. While the AI is great at simply brawling, as soon as anything special happens (such as any and all boss fights or objective items) you can count on your AI buddy to die immediately.
Real people are a better fit thanks to improved competence, but there’s no real progression to be had for your group and nothing that makes it more fun than single player. Castle Crashers, another group beat ’em up did this much better. There was loot to steal from your friends, the ability to battle each other to win the heart of a princess and online play.
It seems that the developers have kept the frustrating nature of the genre – forgetting that no arcade owners will be profiting every time we hit continue, and Mother Russia Bleeds suffers immensely because of it.

Some games you play to build empires. Others you play to shoot things in the head. This one... you play to exterminate humanity. Fun!
Plague Inc: Evolved is a game where you make horrible diseases, spread em around the world, and try to kill everyone before those pesky humans make a cure for your plague. There is strategy involved, but there is some luck too which can be rather frustrating (F***ing Greenland). The game is fun, but also relatively easy to master. Once you figure out how things work, the challenge is mostly gone. Good thing this game has plenty of opportunities for messing around.
The variety comes in the form of each different type of plague having different strengths or weaknesses, like viruses mutating alot which can lead to your disease being detected earlier than you would like. Most of the plagues are real, but the imaginary ones allow for some comic situations to arise. The Neurax Worm allows you to mind control people, leading humans to either kill themselves or worship the worm as a god. And, of course, the Necroa Virus, which allows you to unleash the zombie apocalypse rather than fighting it.
The game can get a bit repetitive in time, but there is alot of crazy fun to be found as well. So, if you want to play a game where murdering everyone is the objective, then this is one that can possibly satisfy. :)

Sleeping Dogs is more or less a title in the vein of Grand Theft Auto freeworld genre with a few alternative choices. There are tons of cars to hijack, random civilians to beat the crap out of for no reason, and an infinite and ceaseless police force to hopelessly oppose you should you decide to rampage. Or you can be a cop for a bit and beat on gangsters if that's your slice of cake.
The biggest definer for Sleeping Dogs is the focus on Kung Fu and action movie tropes, like jumping to a moving car from another car, or shooting out tires which flips a vehicle like some sort of speed racer spring gaget. In between which, you'll be kicking the living daylights out of anyone silly enough to attack you 1 on 20.
Sleeping Dogs does pay for these features though. That's why they're more alternative choices rather than straight upgrades. While the Kung Fu aspect is tons of fun, the system lacks depth for the amount of time you're forced to use it. Almost every mission and minigame features Shen beating on thugs that do more standing and yelling in Chinese than actual attacking, and it quickly boils down to a routine before you get halfway through the story (without any freerome durdling). This is particularly because most of the upgrades to the Kung Fu system don't do all that much to change how you fight.
Even more problematic is the fact that the game seems to not want you to have a gun. Shen can't holster anything besides a pistol, and holding a assault rifle in public is apparently an issue in Hong Kong... who knew? If you manage to get ahold of said pistol, any death, mission start, or mission end will take it out of your inventory and you have to go try to find another one in near gunless gangster territory. You also have something like 3 clips worth of ammo max.
There are plenty of missions with arms, most of which splice in a car chase or two which is fantastic (seriously the car chases are good), but the fact that the design seems to really make it hard to go on a shooting rampage is really bizzare, considering that's more or less the allure of the freeworld crime games.
Sleeping Dogs is definitly a game that's enjoyable, but it doesnt' really have the stick to keep you there for as long as other titles. If you like the freeworld crime vein of games, or even think Sleeping Dogs looks fun from the trailer, I'd recommend it simply because it does so much good. It doesn't mess up anything a player of these types of games tends to love without at least putting something new in it's place. Just know that there's a tradeoff in this games design, rather than an upgrade.
