The Treasures of Montezuma 4 is really fast-paced, you're constantly playing against the clock.  It's not relaxing, your brain will constantly be on a heightened state of alert!!  It's a good feeling!
The mechanics are designed excellently, which is what makes it shine so well.  Once you're fully powered up by progressing through the game you'll have access to totem bonus's which are activated by creating chains of two or more  matches.  Each of the totem's has a different bonus effect.  You also make bonus effects by matching 4+ at the same time.  So there is a lot of opportunity for effecting the game.  There can be some wonderful moments of scoring when you start chaining bonus's and totems together, it's possible to clear the whole board and get some massive scores, and it feels satisfying!
I've clocked 25 hours currently and am still finishing the game and chasing achievements.  There are multiple game modes which you score gold, silver and bronze in.  As with all match-3 games there is an element of luck involved but you can battle against this with your skills, reactions and an eagle eye!
The music is pretty cool too!
I'd highly recommend Treasures of Montezuma 4, if you want a fast-paced match-3 game there is no better.

Fun, stylish, varied and engrossing, with that just-one-more-go feeling.  Games of Monetzuma 4 are fast paced and filled explosive action, with fast fluid gameplay despite a fair amount of repetition.  The variety of level challenges ensures that you rarely get bored and the learning curve is just right until you reach a good mastery of each game mechanic, required to complete the game.  That and some patience and stamina.
Production is excellent and it doesnt feel like you are playing what is essentially a tablet game or an indie title.  All mechanics and elements work sublimely together giving an explosion of sound and colour that makes playing the game such joy.
Match three nirvana!
Casual Match 3 with story elements.
The game is based around an imaginary Inca temple and setting.
You take on the role of an up and coming archeologist Anna, who is a direct descendent of Emperor Montezuma.  Your aim is to uncover an ancient secret and reunite Montezuma with is beloved wife.  To do this you must complete the challenges to unlock the knowledge of the distance past.
There are three game modes: the campaign, puzzle challenges and the quest.  Together they form a varied and challenging amount of levels, with many different objective types and mechanics to make each game different and interesting the previous ones.
The campaign comprising of 6 chapters of 14 levels.  These levels have singluar objectives and are easy to straightforward to complete if only against the clock.
The puzzle mode consists of 8 different challenge types with mechanics that work in parallel to match 3, like revealing hidden treasures beneath the tokens/board or smashing the ice covering some tokens by repeating using match 3.  Each challenge has 8 short quick-fire levels which when completed release an valuable collectors item that form a collection where all items must be obtained.
Finally the quest mode has multiple objective levels.  Each completion of the puzzle mode sees the player move towards one of four temples each of which main contain two parts to Montezuma's fabled face-mask.  Find both items and complete the quest.  You do not have to complete all objectives to progess unless you want to achievement perhaps the hardest achievement.
Gameplay consist of your basic Match 3 mechaincs.  At its core you must match three or more tokens (tiles) to collect points. Multiple sequential matches of the same coloured tokens provide chains which trigger totems.  These provide much needed bonuses which can obliterate the tokens in play and award copious amounts of points to your score.  Using these basic methods you can clear a level or its objectives in quick-time, circumventing the need to spend the limited time you have to complete a level.
Completing a level gives you experience points and a certain amount of coins. The more games of match 3 you complete the higher your level.  The higher your level the larger the temple.  You must get to max level to complete the game.  There are 100 levels in total.   Coins allow you to buy up to 14 unlocks which make completing level easier.  These include: greater effects on matching 3 or a certain color, providing additional time, changing token colours, arming tokens with dynamite, etc.  Each unlock can be upgraded four times to make using it highly effective.
Once you have all the unlocks you will still need to collect coins to unlock 12 temple collectibles which are just furniture, for another achievement
No enemies here except the clock.  All levels must be completed with the time-limit given, which can be extended through unlocks and matching chains.
An excellent variation of challenging levels and game modes provides plenty to do and never gets boring even after 50+ hours.
No A.I required as there are no enemies.
Simple mouse point, click and drag.
Bright. Colourful. Excellent.  All graphic elements fit perfectly into the setting and the Inca theme.  One of the high-points of the game.
Sound is very atmospheric, with most tunes a variation on a theme.  There are different tunes for different puzzles.  If you're not a fan of pan-pipes you can always mute the musical score and whack on an M-player.
The only voice acting can be found in the cutscene at the start of the game and the six end-of-chapter cutscenes in the story mode.  All are brief but top notch.
The game provides a pretty good learning curve.  It may not be difficult to match three titles but to do so and complete the various objectives within the time-limit gets really taxing the further you progress with each game mode.  Provides an engrossing and ultimately a frustrating challenge, if only at the very end to clear those last free achievements.
No problems to speak of.  Once you understand which tokens (tiles) to manipulate and when to get the bonuses you should enjoy playing the game.
An almost perfect selection of achievements from those easy to get ones when learning the game to those few taxing ones at the very end.  Achievements consist of those required to complete each game mode, using certain mechanics and acquiring all collectibles.  An almost perfect set of balanced achievement is spoiled only at the very end, by needing to spend five or so hours grinding for the coins needs to complete the temple upgrades and find any the elusive puzzle collection items.  But they are not far off being perfect.
None but there are other versions of this game available.
In total I completed the game modes in 40 or so hours.  All achievements took another 10 additional hours to complete.
How long have you got?  You can of course replay any of the game modes as the puzzle mode collection can be continued until you tire of it and the quest mode can be reset multiple times.  So in theory you can play and replay infinitely or until you find something new.
Will appeal to casual players, fans of match 3 (tiles) or those who want kill a few minutes in between their main sources of video-game leisure.

Now that I passed 100 hours, figured this was worth an update. This game is absolutely amazing and one of the best early access experiences I have had.
TL;DR :::  Definitely worth the buy if you like development and base building games.
I'll start with the game it self. Your goal is to get a rocket launched off this alien world you're stuck on. You do that by constructing massive assembly lines to build more and more complex sturctures. The user interfaces are easy to understand and make it simple to be as top level or in to the weeds as you want (there is a circuiting ability that can be used to automate EVERYTHING).
The enemy of the game are aliens that evolve throughout the course of play. They are affected by not only time passing, but how much pollution your factories are spitting out as well. The evolution style of enemy is awesome and makes you have to adapt your security measures throughout a run through. There is also peaceful mode if you just want to build without attack worries.
The developers and community are the true shining star of this game. The devs have constant communication with the players on a weekly basis, they have a clear development path for the game, and the community has an incredibly robust modding community if you want to add your own flavor.

I've bought this game in february 2015 as a Furnace Attendant membership (which is equal to the Steam version) before its release on Steam.
Factorio is a base-building game. You build a huge factory to build things to build even more things and have to extend your base and production to resolve bottlenecks.
You have several buildings which mine ore, smelt them and assemble products in several production steps.
(ore -> metal -> base products -> intermediate products -> final product)
If you like planning ahead, doing micromanagement, optimizing stuff, resolving bottlenecks and polluting the environment - this is a game for you.
Building a factory requires some planning. You'll need to plan at least roughly your factory layout or you will end up with a huge spaghetti-like mess.
Belts which transport stuff will be all over the place. Eventually you don't have enough space to extend your base.
Preventing this situation and resoving gordian knots is the permanent struggle of the game.
This permanent optimization is what makes the game fun.
Generating energy for your base and the assembling things cause smog.
Smog makes the native insectoid aliens angry and causes mutation which makes them stronger.
So you'll need some kind of defence. You can protect yourself with personal armor, several guns or even with a tank. But you can also build a defensive perimeter around your base with turrets and walls.
Against big hordes of biters sometimes it feels like tower defence games. A good stategy in the past for fighting enemy bases was tower crawling (set up some turrets, build new turrets in front of it, repeat it until the turrets are in the middle of their base).
This felt repetitive but the developers improved this aspect in the past.
For some types of high-tech gear and research you need alien artifacts which are currently only dropped by alien spawners. So you'll have to fight them to get the artifacts and to prevent beeing overun by the enemy.
The graphic of the game is pure 2D. There are some really nice graphical details like trees dying over the time from pollution or fishes swimming in the lakes.
In my opinion in a great game like Factorio graphics are secondary because in this type of game the gameplay matters a way more.
When playing the game there are no real performance issues. Unless you use e.g. 20.000 logistic robots or play with over 100 player on a single server (Yes, some crazy youtubers did this XD).
This game is still in early access. It already contains a lot of content and runs quite stable. The developers improves the game continously.
There is also a huge amount of modpacks available. The developers added native mod support in the past. Lately I play mostly with mods enabled because they add even more content and features.
Pros:
+ great gameplay
+ good training for your brain
+ story mode and freeplay mode
+ lot of mods
+ continous development
+ good controls
+ runs on older computers
+ available for Windows Mac OS and Linux
+ translated into a lot of languages
+ costs only 20 €
Cons:
- fighting biters is repetitive
- no weather (only day-night-cycle)
- story is a bit too short at the moment
- can't stop playing this great game it's a addiction ;)

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is a vast improvement over Final Fantasy XI. One thing this game improves most on is the grindy feeling that the first online game had....No more running around killing monsters on an endless basis till you level....The game supplies many opportunities to level, including plenty of quests, and events you can do in open areas with other players to earn large amounts of xp quickly.
Not only that, one thing that Final Fantasy XIV does differently than most MMORPGs, is that it allows you to change your class/job on the fly. Only have a Level 20 character, but tired of being a mage? No problem, switch right over to a Gladiator and wield a sword. No starting over required.
One final bit to point out on this game, is the nostalgia...Final Fantasy XIV brings together all the different worlds of Final Fantasy....Gunblades from FF8, Materia from FF7, Magitek Armor from FF6, The Judges from FF12, etc. There is plenty of Final Fantasy nostalgia in this game...
Definitely worth every penny...Do not be afraid to buy.

I feel that Modern Warfare 2 as one of the best multiplayer experiences. Despite being peer to peer, removing modding, restricting the player count to 12-18 players, the game had what competition didn't, and that's insane amount of content.
I would go as far as to say that the game had 4 times as much content than any game of that time: Medal of Honor 2010, Bad Company 2, and even the older CODs like COD4 and World at War.
This game an insane amount of replayability to the game. The are 70 levels in the game, and there is a certain unlock at pretty much every level. At the same time it's well placed. It takes 2,500,000 XP to reach the max level. In terms of kills, it would require to do 25,000 kills before reaching it. That takes a while, believe me. It's actually the biggest XP ceiling in the whole franchise.
Back in 2009, it was the bomb. It was the first call of duty to require steam, and everyone on steam was playing this game.
It had its problems - mostly overpowered weapons, generally grenade launchers. That said, unlike COD games of today, it did have great maps and proper spawns. The spawns were basically static predefined areas. Spawn kills were a possibility, but were no happening very often. The maps were generally pretty big in size too, especially for a COD game.
Map design, spawns, weapon balance, content - all that makes up a good multiplayer game. The game wasn't perfect, but it was close. These days, a lot of multiplayer games followed the same suite, but let's not take it for granted. Some respect is ought to be given.

Honesty, it was amongst my first coop experiences, along with left 4 dead, so i have a lot of fond memories with it, so i might be a bit biased. If you still don't know, the team that was working on this game, Infinity Ward, had a big argument with the publisher and about 46 IW employees left the company. The writer for the game - Jesse Stern, was also replaced with somebody else. So honestly, MW3 isn't even a real COD game anymore.

Transistor is a beautiful, lovingly-crafted experience, following the vein of Bastion: a visually and auditorially stunning game that delivers an emotionally impactful story in a short amount of time. The art direction and soundtrack are both superb; it's one of the prettiest games I've ever played, and has one of my favorite OSTs of all time.
Cloudbank feels like a real city, despite being wholly void of interactable NPCs; it truly feels like you're strolling through the remains of a city that merely hours ago was full of life, with nobody around but the automated Process and the voice of your companion. The storytelling is excellent, the voice acting is incredible, and the characters — especially the villains — feel like actual people with motivations of their own. The story is as much about the Camerata as it is about Red, and it's damn compelling.
On top of all of this, the gameplay is excellent. The combat is incredibly customizable and fluid, with hundreds upon hundreds of viable combinations of abilities. It feels almost like a combination of Bastion and Dragon Age: Origins; you could play it just like you would Bastion, or you can pause time and plan out your moves each turn for maximum efficiency. It's engaging, and acts as a perfect segue between plot points.
Transistor is masterfully crafted, and I'd recommend it for just about everyone.

Overall Score: 6/10
This game was for sure overrated by many reviewers on this page. The puzzles were very simple, it only took 2.5 hours to beat, and the story, while not the focus, did not have a satisfying conclusion (maybe in the Room 2 it does, I don't know). The graphics and visuals were great, and that honestly the best part of this game. Coming from someone who isn't an avid puzzle enthusiast, I had no issue beating this game and never found myself stumped for more than 2-3 mins (which happened only once), I generally felt like the game was too afraid to let you try to solve any of it on your own, and any independent ideas that I came up with on my own were immediatley confirmed by the pop-up text which regularly appeared at the bottom, and the game sometimes panned you over to certain parts of the puzzle, instead of allowing you to actively find the next step (but it did this only a few times). I rarely had to actually guess what the next step was in the puzzle. There were puzzle types that were recycled atleast a few times (gears, lining up images, keys) and towards the end it felt repetitive at points.
But despite this criticism, I enjoyed how laid back and casual it was. I never got stuck, which may be bad if you enjoy challenges, but it also meant less frustration when playing through. Even though $5 was pretty cheap, I still feel like it lacked content, the whole game was 2.5 hours in total. Top marks for visual quality, sound design, and atmosphere, though. The complexity made it feel like you were unraveling steampunk contraptions, however sometimes when I got the impression that the contraptions didn't make logical sense, sometimes I felt like the creators didn't bother to try to think of how these contraptions would actually fit all of these mechanisms within its volume, instead opting to create a magical box which anything could spring out of, despite its size limitations. This is just nitpicking and I may have failed to convey just what I mean by this to anyone who hasn't witnessed the game.
I'm recommending this, despite this harsh review just because I enjoyed myself throughout the play through.

The Room is hands down one of THE best puzzle point and click games I have ever had the pleasure of owning.   I'm ashamed not to have discovered it before now.   This is not your average point and click affair roaming around lots of locations gathering inventory items. Oh no !
It's just you, in a room looking at a table on which is perched a strange, ornate, largish wooden box that it jam packed with secrets.   From one single first clue you are left to thoroughly examine every aspect of the strange box looking for clues as to how to get inside it.  Its feet, its sides, panels, placards all have secret clues, and hidden functionality.  What is this thing?
As you progress you discover hidden drawers and compartments, clockwork mechanisms for which you need to find cogs, and keys and winding handles.   You soon begin to understand that this is no ordinary box and is much much more than a Japanese puzzle box.
The graphics are utterly utterly, let me say it one more time, utterly exquisite.  The experience is breathtaking from the start sucking you deeper and deeper into the secrets of the box, examining every inch of it for clues which will help you unlock the next part of it, peeling back its layers like an onion, puzzle by puzzle.  What's more, you don't just point and click, you are required to move things yourself, such as turning keys, dragging drawers, winding handles, sliding . .  well slidy bits of the box !  This makes the game so much more engaging.
I have never played a game like it, and am currently eagerly downloading The Room Two for more !
Make no mistake, this is an outstanding piece of software that will engage you, enthrall you and keep you interested from the first second to the last and will leave you yearning for more.
The objects are rendered beautifully and the motion of the various pieces and components just staggers you over and over.   Boxes within boxes, waiting to be deciphered and unlocked through numerous tests and mechanical puzzles none of which are overly difficult but equally not giveaways either.
Each time you think you are nearing the end the boxes surprise you and open up new parts, sliding, rotating, presenting new mechanisms and puzzles.
This is the kind of game that deserves pride of place in a viewing cabinet to own for all time and no wonder it has won so many awards.  Just a truly truly pleasurable experience from start to finish.
Please please Fireproof,  keep making more of these!

Here's my main problem with this game:  The platforming feels too hard.
When I bought this game, I was looking forward to dying dozens of times on cleverly designed pitfalls, traps, and genre-subverting jackassery.  This stuff is all there, and it is by far the highlight of the game.
However, to make a game like that work, these traps need to be the main antagonist.  The game needs to feel like it would be easy breezy were these traps not there.
This is not the case in Eryi's Action.  The true enemy in this game lies in the controls, which feel floaty and imprecise.  Even when the player knows exactly where the deathtraps are, and exactly how to circumvent death, it is still very difficult to actually pull off the necessary stunt.
For example, at a certain point, there is a thorny bush that appears to be in the background, but should you walk past it, it will impale you as though it was in the forground.  The solution is to jump over this obsticle.  Unfortunately, there are only about 2 pixels of room on the other side of this bush.  Overshooting the bush means you fall into a chasm, and undershooting the bush means thorny death.  With the floaty contols, landing in the exact necessary spot is much harder than it should be.
Shortly after this trap, there is another.  There are three platforms, A,B, and C.  If you land on platform B, it crumbles and you fall to your death, so a jump from A to C is necessary.  It's possible, but BARELY.  it requires a running start and pixel perfect precision. That type of jump has no place being in any platformer - it sucked in crappy games for the Sega Genisis, and it sucks here.
Overall, I am frustrated with this game, but for the wrong reasons.  I love the evil a-hole developer bits, but hate the nuts and bolts platforming.

Gunmetal Arcadia Zero is a 2D platformer in the vein of 8 bit NES Castlevania games. The graphics, while nothing special, suit the retro aesthetic Minor Key were aiming for. The gameplay reminds me of Castlevania III, while being less punishing. From its 8 bit era graphics to its simple 2D platforming to its 'only one weapon and one sub weapon' combat, Gunmetal Arcadia Zero would've fit right in with 8 bit NES offerings.
Gunmetal Arcadia Zero is also very accessible. The button layout, supporting XInput controllers, is simple: jump, attack, sub weapon, bomb, Start, and a D-pad or thumb stick. The hardware requirements are pretty modest. Windows, Mac, and Linux (Ubuntu/Mint) are all supported. All-in-all, $6 ain't a bad price for a game of Gunmetal Arcadia Zero's ilk.
Played on Linux Mint 17.3 64 bit, with Nvidia GT 720 graphics and a Logitech F310 controller set to XInput.

Tomb Raider became a worldwide sensation among gamers, back in 1996. And Lara Croft became an icon for both men and women for many reasons. Mainly either because of the games or the character herself.
After 1996 when the first game was released for the PC, the Playstation and the SEGA Saturn and a year after Tomb Raider II was released for the PC and the Playstation, we were presented in 1998 with Tomb Raider III: Adventures of Lara Croft, which brought back pretty much the same formula from the last two games, but with a new story, new artifacts to find, new locations to explore, new vehicles, a new arsenal of weapons and a new mechanic that was exclusive to this game.
For starters, the gameplay. The controls didn't change much since the last two games. And there's a bit of a mix of opinions concerning the controls. All you pretty much use is the keyboard to control Lara and navigate the menus in the game. And while old school Tomb Raider fans will feel completely comfortable with these controls, new players may feel a little uncomfortable at first, as you don't really use the mouse to control anything, as there were no camera controls, back then. But I believe that these controls are easy to get used to and it's not really something that will make players quit the adventure.
The game's graphics suffered a few improvements. Nothing really major, but if you have played Tomb Raider and Tomb Raider II, you may notice a slight difference.
Now as for the story, it starts with the intro showing us a meteorite crashing onto the earth's surface, then jumping into a few years later, showing a research being conducted by a company called RX Tech at what is Antarctica, nowadays. Now we never really learn much about RX Tech except that they're looking for this meteorite or what's left of it. One of their scientists, Dr. Willard, finds a grave in Antarctica which turned out to be the final resting place of a sailor who was part of an expedition crew.
As for Lara, we find her later in India, looking for an artifact only known as the Infada Stone. Which unknowingly for her, is connected to the meteorite. After she finds it, she meets Willard and tells her the story about the crew who had lost a sailor in Antarctica and that the Infada Stone is connected to the meteorite. He also tells her that there are 3 other artifacts and requests her for assistance in finding them.
Now this is where the new mechanic that is exclusive to the game gets into the picture. After India, the game gives you the opportunity to choose where to go next, as there are 3 other areas to explore. London, the South Pacific Islands and Area 51, in the Nevada desert. And you can do these in any order you like.
Now let's talk about the vehicles. This is probably the only Tomb Raider game so far to provide the player with the widest variety of vehicles to drive. Although it's still not much, there are more vehicles here than in other games. Though truth be told, the snowmobile in Tomb Raider II was sort of iconic. From quad bikes to minecarts to a kayak and even an underwater propulsion unit. FYI: some of these vehicles are a little difficult to control. I mean, most of them control just fine, but the kayak for example can be a little tricky to control.
As for the weapons, this is also probably the largest arsenal in the series, so far.
Aside from the good old pistols, shotgun and uzis, Lara also gets a desert eagle, an MP5 and a rocket launcher. The grenade launcher and the harpoon gun also make a comeback from Tomb Raider II. And all the weapons in the game are pretty fun to use. I recommend conserving some ammo towards the end (mainly for the Desert Eagle), as it's all gonna be needed.
Now I haven't talked about any down sides to Tomb Raider III, though that doesn't mean there aren't any. The game is not perfect, of course. Even games nowadays have their own down sides and glitches. On my end, I didn't see any sort of major glitches. Maybe only one texture failing, but that was just once. There are a few bugs you can exploit for shortcuts and other stuff. Some people also disliked this game a little as it didn't focus on exploring ancient tombs as much as the other games. If you ask me, I liked the game, despite that. And for those of you who don't like short adventures, you will love the length of this one. My playthrough must've taken me like at least a total of 8 or 10 hours to complete. Took me more according to Steam cuz I was using a walkthrough for the secrets. Which I recommend looking for, as it will give you access to a bonus level, after you finish the game!
I know this is a pretty old game, but since I worked on this... "review" of it, I might aswell give it a personal score. I give Tomb Raider III: Adventures of Lara Croft an 8/10. It's an awesome game!
I see that more and more people are getting into Tomb Raider cuz of the 2013 reboot and now Rise of the Tomb Raider, which I haven't played but I'd love to. But I feel like I should try to get those people to play the old school Tomb Raider titles. I feel like they should learn about where this franchise began. So far I loved all the Tomb Raider games I played. From Tomb Raider to Tomb Raider (2013). And especially loved Angel of Darkness, despite how broken the game was. It was broken, but it had potential. But now is not the time to talk about it.
If you are able to, buy the classic Tomb Raider games. Give them a shot. And try to have fun with them!

Tomb raider 3 end the triology,  however after TR1 and 2 , the game really feel ... stretched. The core game is the same, but it's bigger, more advanced with more mechanic, more however doesn't make it better.
An exemple is the plot, the storyline in TR1 was simple but efficient, TR2 was less elegant but you still could follow it. In TR3 it's all over the place with an abrupt ending that doesn't really make sence. In my own opinion, the team behind the game put it together in the last minute probably after some disagreement.
The game is built around those large levels but they don't seem to work well together, they're not horrible, but the difficult spikes, the bugs, the cheap deads make them very annoying at times. Making those levels bigger probably sounded like a good idea at the time, but they add to the difficulty as often I had no idea where to go or what to do next as the game is very stingy with hints . Trying and failing (often dying) was my only option. For parts of the game a walkthrough is necessary unless you feel like using weeks on end exploring the vast levels for small keys or crystals hidden in dark corners to open secret doors.
To make things worse , some parts of the game are positively dull, the London levels are the worse in that respect. They're dark, confusing and depressing with few positive moments, as a player you fell you have to plough through those levels and get them over with.
TR3 has its good moments, the core gameplay is there, solving the mysteries or finding your path in the sometimes confusing levels feels rewarding. But smaller and bigger problems in the gameplay cheapen those moments. The controll which never was very good hasn't changed much since TR1 and 2 making things harder for the player as they feel as uneven as ever in an environment that is bigger and more difficult than previous games. This results in cheap deads very often and the liberal use of saves and loads to progress.
The great atmosphere in the game is hit and miss, some level felt almost like the original tomb raiders, others felt just dark and cramped and I couldn't wait to finish them. To it's benifit they're varied, you even get to visit a couple of temples , but they still don't give the feel of awe the original gave you. TR3 isn't as pretty as TR2 either, and while it has its moment, it's easily the ugliest of the three.
In Conclusion, TR3 isn't a bad game , it's good in its core, but a miriad of problems and bugs makes it a lesser game than it could have been. Play only if you want to experience the Tomb Raider serie (as I do) , you'll have some good moments if you can oversee all its faults. I can't however objectively recommand this game to most gamers.

I never thought a game I picked up for less than a cup of coffee would be up there with my favorite Match 3 games of all time, but it is.  With gameplay that is easy to learn but hard to master, I found myself addicted to The Treasures of Montezuma 4 in no time.
Gameplay consists of your standard Match 3 fair, swap the position of the tokens to match 3 of the same color to remove them from the board and score points.  The twist comes in with totems and power-ups that you purchase with coins earned by completing levels.  Chaining color matches will power up your totems and release their abilities onto the board. Determining which power-ups are most beneficial for each game board is where the real strategy comes in. Running out of time? Start chaining those oranges.  Find yourself stuck with few good matches?  Chain up a couple reds and let those fireballs fly.  Snap decisions and twitch reactions are required, especially when playing on Expert, but finally FINALLY earning Gold on that one level that's been giving you fits is so incredibly satisfying you'll want to keep playing until you can't possibly play anymore.
And there are plenty of game modes to play through.  Aside from Story mode which consists of 98 increasingly difficult boards, there's Puzzle where you can play through sets of specific games (Catch the Frog, Spring, Archaelogy, etc.) to earn collectibles, and Quest where certain objectives must be met on each board as you search for the missing pieces of a medallion.  The variety of games gives you lots of options depending on what you're in the mood mood for, whether it's the marathon session or just a quick fix.
Good or bad, luck is a bit of a factor in the gameplay.  If you're stuck with a bad board layout, it's often better to restart the level and hope for better token placement than waste time trying to work with the wrong totems.  Sometimes you just don't have enough of the right color to pull off the chains you need; however keeping a level head and planning your moves and power-ups wisely can help you overcome some of the bad luck.  Then there are the boards where everything lines up so perfectly that you snag Gold within seconds of starting despite trying dozens of times to beat the timer.  Sure, that's luck for you, but I choose to believe that I'm just that awesome!
Unfortunately, the rate in which you purchase your power-ups can be a bit slow.  The game plays best when you have all the tools at your disposal to deal with any given situation.  Later levels tend to be more enjoyable because you have most of your power-ups which makes things a lot easier to deal with.  On the other hand, purchasing abilities one at a time helps teach what each does without confusing you too much, so there is some merit to it.  But the game is most fun when you're fully empowered and chaining like a madman as power-ups, explosions and multipliers rack up your points.
As one of the best impulse buys I've made on Steam, The Treasures of Montezuma 4 does not disappoint. If you are looking for more relaxing and casual fair, however, this may not be the game for you. But if you're in the market for a fast-paced and rewarding Match 3 title that will have you playing to the wee hours of the morning, you cannot go wrong with this gem! Even at full price, it's a steal. Steam achievements and trading cards are just icing on this already delicious cake.  Move over Bejeweled, there's a new king in town!

Bottom Line: Highly recommended for all Match 3 lovers and is a worthy addition to any gamer's library.

is a fantasy RPG idle game. Welcome to the caricatural world of heroes and buffoons where your search for glory will have you fight monstrous bats, evil bunnies and moronic bandits while undertaking the most ridiculous of quests.
: The game is a Steam port of the decade-old browser game that still runs today. Everything about this game, from character creation to weapon and armor design, parodies the tropes of fantasy RPGs, while each quests are randomly composed of the most stereotypical stories that mock the genre. In no way does the game take itself seriously, and every line of dialog reeks of satire. As an idle game, it is perfect to run in the background while working on something else or playing another game, you just take a peek every once in a while to see if you're ready to undertake another quest, fight another player, or explore another level of a dungeon. If you bother to involve yourself in the community, guild battles and competition can be fun to participate in. Should you play long enough, further content will unlock, such as fortress building and raising your companion animal. On top of that, microtransactions are completely optional, as it is possible to get plenty of mushrooms (secondary currency) during bonus weekends or from guild boosts.
: As an idle game, there is absolutely no gameplay whatsoever. You simply you pick a quest, and wait for the timer to end to see if your stats allowed you to win battle against whatever opponent you were facing. All quests and fights are resolved the same way: your character strikes (random result, based on your stats), the opponent strikes back, auto-repeat until someone reaches 0 hit points. Clicking and waiting is pretty much all you do. Fight a player? Wait for the timer to tell you you can fight another one. Select a quest? Wait for the timer to tell you it's finished. Expand your fortress? Wait for the timer to tell you you can expand it again. Unless you're easily amused, you'll soon stop reading the humoristic text, at which point you might start finding the game boring.

I am a big fan of horror and scary games, but, as with the world of horror films, a majority of the genre seems to be cheesey or poorly written. This is not the case with The Last Door, which, despite the Atari-level graphics, has a beautiful atmosphere and fairly effective story behind it.
I am not very knowledgable about the Lovecraft lore or universe, but did not find that stopped me from enjoying the story of this game. The Last Door has actually made me want to research that area and check out some of Lovecraft's stories. While it's not the best writing I've ever seen in a game, it's very well done for being told through text and certainly kept me on the edge of my seat. What is expertly done is the pacing of the game, I enjoy how it is split into the different chapters, and the atmosphere.
I have played some other similarly designed and toned games, such as Home, but The Last Door is the first to really interest me in the style. There were several moments that did make me start, and some of the occurances made me uneasy, but not enough to scare me into taking a break. The scares aren't over the top, but they are definitely effective, and typically made me more excited about moving forward. This was especially true for the first chapter, which I think is my favorite.
I highly recommend this to anyone looking to satisfy a craving for a good story, a good scare and a bit of nostalgia. I hope it's not the last we see from this team!

The Last Door is an episodic, horror point and click set in 1800s England. You might think due to it's low-res graphics you couldn't possibly be scared by playing this game. But that's exactly what makes it so creepy. I never new pixelated blood could unerve me so much. You play as Jeremiah Devitt, and he's just recieved a strange and urgent letter from an old school mate of his named Anthony. Upon entering his house, you notice that it is oddly deserted. No servants, no wife, no Anthony. The only evidence that people once lived there are scattered notes you find in different areas of the house. Each detailing the bizzare behaviors that Anthony has been exhibiting. Concerened for his friend, Devitt searches the house for clues. That's when he slowly starts to discover the disturbing story of Anthony, and his own past that all leads back to a ritual he and his friends performed at their old bording school.
You learn something new and gain more information of the story within each episode. The atmosphere is gloomy, the music is dramatic, and the story is something straight out of Edgar Allan Poe's notebook. Despite being short (you can easily finish the entire first season in one sitting) it is well worth the play. If you're a fan of good story telling and creepy pixelated crows, The Last Door is a must to satisfy that blood on the wall hunger.

Pros:

Cons:
-Unbalanced when its expierenced vs newer players
-Not many maps, but its a game still in beta
-They need to make base camping more punishable or some sort of turrent protecting spawn area
-Game was planned to be Free to Play
-Half of the armors need to be reworked due to the fact they are often useless compared to others.
Overall:
-Game is entertaining and quite enjoyable
-Consider reworking armor
-Looking forward to it when it comes out of beta
-A game worth trying and great with friends
-Game may be blocky but graphics look great
-Wish more people would check out some guides for the game
Other thoughts:
The game is perfectly balanced until more experienced players fight newer players. This is when it becomes unbalanced. The more experienced players tend to work together rather than running solo. This ends up making the the newer players having a difficult time being able to compete. In the end, the newer players get pushed back into spawn until they all move out together which often end up killing the geared experienced players. Several times me and my friends almost beat the enemy team in the first titan clash where we would usually break the first wall and do some damage on the second. We all knew what to do and how to start off while the other team didn't. You can solo pretty well, but if your team isnt working together, you will often loss.
As for the swords being overpowered, it is both true and false. Swords do great amount of damage but their reach is somewhat short. To counter this, just carry a loadout with taser shotgun or cryo sniper, this is a perfect counter to all melee users. One or two shots will stop them in their place, keep your distance and finish them off with another weapon, the slow effect last about 4 seconds  which is enough to finish them off. You could also just stay near a friendly turrent which can be used as a decoy to distract the enemy and finish them off.

Please note: I don't recommend this game because it still feels too fresh from Early Access to be worth buying. To be sure, the dev crew does deserve support, but I think another content and balance update or two is necessary before buying is really worth it.

Imagine Quake Live in third person. Now add in systems common to traditional Dota-like games. You farm creeps to power up your team's titan, which you then assist in beating the crap out of the enemy's titan. From there you escort your titan as it destroys the enemy's defensive walls (akin to towers in a MOBA) as it marches to the core (or ancient in other games), which then achieves victory for your team. Rather interesting and original, combining these two concepts.
But here's where the game hits a snag. They have another unique mechanic: fragging players results in them dropping a pick up that in turn increases your weapon by adding damage and extra effects (such as AOE, multiple rounds per shot, a movement slow, etc.) Furthermore, dying resets your weapons back to zero (there is a caveat here: your PRIMARY WEAPON ONLY will retain its level, up to 3, with each titan spawn; so after the first titan, your primary stays level 1, the second it'll always be level 2, and from the third till match end, it'll always be level 3). I know what you're thinking, and unfortunately, you're correct. If you're very good at fragging, the power balance is almost guaranteed to stay in your favor. Because level five weapons make fragging enemy players, farming creeps, and defending your titan much easier than level three weapons, you really only can maintain your momentum in the match unless you simply suicide into the enemy team without defending yourself.
There is also a part on armor crafting. With armor, you collect materials during the match from slain players and creeps, or as pickups around the map. The armor you craft gives you an innate damage resistance, as well as neat abilities or added defenses (things such as extra health, a double jump, increased damage with certain weapons, etc.). Armor, luckily enough, is permanent for the match duration once crafted.
Creep farming is also somewhat...weird. You see, towards the end of the creep farming time, a golden creep will spawn. This creep drops a golden titan crystal that counts as 10 regular creep crystals and basically gives your titan some extra "oomph!" This golden creep is currently unmarked on your screen, meaning a player that knows its spawn location, will camp it, always netting the golden crystal for his team. This crystal usually does two things: make all the regular creeps you farmed mean nothing by evening the scores, or giving the team that secures it an unbeatable titan crystal margin.
Besides that, the menu suffers from this weird frame drop issue, the UI doesn't explain weapons and armors fully enough (armors aren't even noted as having passive resistance - I learned this from the devs themselves on their stream!), and winning...earns you the exact same amount of crafting materials (the stuff you need to unlock weapon blueprints and armors, as well as craft weapon so you can actually use them in-game) as you do for losing. Your performance and whether you win or not currently mean absolutely nothing as of the last time I played. Which only leaves me asking "why even play this game?" after a match.
Lastly, the matchmaking system is terrible. Long wait times, frequently being matched against more skilled players with a larger weapon variety than you, and most disappointingly, an apparently rapidly deteriorating player base (Search the game on SteamCharts. I was appalled by the data returned, and even a sizable margin of error wouldn't make a big improvement.).
To be honest, Minimum has loads of potential and is very distinct in both gameplay and visuals. But these more glaring issues (Did I mention the 2-3 hit kill, AOE, large hitbox, frame-locking katanas with a built-in dash ability? No? Petty gripe then.) really make this game suffer. But potential is just that: potential. It looks promising, but is not an actual promise. It still feels very much alpha. The good news is that the devs are constantly working and dealing with the community on their weekly streams. Time will tell if this becomes the great game it has the potential to be. For now, it's worth watching, but not buying into just yet. I personally hope for the best.

This game is kind of fun, but it's also honestly pretty stupid and sloppy. Want to know how to beat every boss in the game, including the final boss, without even moving? Grab the boomerang subweapon, don't use the subweapon during levels (which you won't need to do anyway) and then just spam the boomerang. You can literally just stand in front the final boss' face and do this and win.
The game also has a somewhat complicated, for the genre, in-game economy that doesn't make any sense either. Your biggest income will be gems you find, and the best way to earn money from those is to sell them to a specific type of gem merchant since other merchants will pay less. This is also true in reverse, where different merchants will sell different items more cheaply than others. The problem with this is that not every level has each type of merchant and you'd need to be psychic to know if you should sell your gems at a loss and buy this new weapon now, or if the next level is going to offer a gem merchant and...you get the point. You have to be psychic to be able to predict how to properly use this economy in a game that's entirely linear and doesn't allow you to go back to the previous level or some kind of hub map to visit the gem or weapons merchant. There's a final merchant right before the final boss, and you'd expect that dude to sell some sick weapons, right? Especially considering he's hidden behind a locked door and you need the anti-lava upgrade to even reach him, right? Nope, he sells inventory upgrades. Because that makes sense.
Oh, and speaking of weapons, this game doesn't have stats. So what's the DPS difference between "Unmade Shard" and "Razor Quill"? You have to spend the money to find out! See above for why spending money to find out if a weapon is any good is a problem. Also on the subject of weapons, I bought a dagger that boasted quick attack speed since that's how I prefer to play, only to find out that the dagger is so short that you can no longer perform the Zelda II-style downward stab because the dagger is actually shorter than your legs. Is that a joke?
And, yes, I do understand that the developer's excuse for the shoddy economy and progression tied to it is the fact that the game loops and can be replayed in NG+ over and over, but that's a weak excuse. Especially considering the fact that I didn't see anything interesting enough in a few minutes of NG+ to feel like I wanted to repeat the whole process and stand in the exact same place tossing boomerangs at the boss all over again.
You know what? I actually intended to write a positive review since I think the game controls well enough, the soundtrack is excellent and the graphics are odd but pleasant enough, but writing this has made me realize that I think I sort of hated the 2 hours it took to beat the game. It is so clearly just tossed together quickly for the promotional benefit of being a Humble Original and for a few quick bucks while they finish the real game, Gunmetal Arcadia. I certainly hope that game has more thought put into it.

If you like the old 8 bit systems, platform jumping, with some rpg-like progression thrown in, this is 100% your game.
Buy better swords to up the damage output.
Buy items like fancy boots to jump higher.
Get some misc. item to make in-air jump control better.
Buy other items like bombs (think Super Mario 2 on NES, or Doki-Doki-Panic in Asia) and ammo for special item.
Keys are also found at stores and sometimes as items to open locked doors.
Beating the 'boss' monsters will get you to the next chapter, and give you a little bit more max health.
Autosaving whenever you beat an end-boss.  No more replaying the whole game if the power goes out.
Hidden secrets abound... look around.
There's an inventory with all your things, you can switch weapons, or equip/de-equip armor or special items.
The graphics and music are authentically 8-bit and most-certainly there is a 'CRT-simulator' mode available.
So if you enjoyed other games like Shovel Knight, Axiom Verge, or Cave Story, this is more of the same, pick it up!
While I do say this is 'more of the same' It's definitely it's own game.  It hails much from Faxanadu, or maybe Legacy of The Wizard (not 100% sure on that), and a bit from Zelda II with the side-scrolling bits.
There's no experience points, there's no level-building, but there IS plenty of progression, and it's not quite 'nes hard' to the point where you'd rage.  Yes, YOU can beat this if I can get pretty far in it!  I have not yet had the chance to finish this game, but will attempt such quite soon.  It reminds me of being a kid and getting a new NES game cartridge.
Yes, it's good.  Please have a GOOD quality controller with a good D-pad or you might rage a bit.
At this price, I'd say it's a steal.  An absolute must have for 2d NES fans.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn takes place in the continent of Eorzea, on the planet Hydaelyn who shares it's name with the Mother Cystal, who will guide you throughout your adventures as the Warrior of Light. The game starts you off as an adventurer with an unknown background and are sent to talk to the Adventurer's Guild in hopes of something to do. You will start off in one of the three main City-states; Ul'dah-the desert city that houses some of the richest and poorest people in Eorzea, Limsa Lominsa-the port city that houses expirates and peopl who love the sea, and Gridania-the forest city filled with people who love the enviornment and the spirits which inhabit our world. Which city you start in will be determine by your class, that you can change later on in the game, meaning that you can level all 13 classes to level 60 (the current max level) all on the same character. These classes are mostly iconic to the Final Fantasy franchise, with new and familiar ways to play them.
In terms of an MMORPG (Massively Multiplayer Online Role Playing Game) FFXIV hits it out of the park. I am an very experienced MMORPG player having played games such as SWTOR, TERA, Guildwars 2 and Wildstar to name af ew of the more popular ones and coming from 7 years of World of Warcraft. FFXIV, while not completely unlike World of Warcraft, is vastly different. I will mainly be using World of Warcraft as a comparison as it is the game i have the most experience with playing as well as it being the most popular MMORPG atm. Like stated earlier in FFXIV you can play mulitple classes if not all the classes, if you really want to which is different thatn World of Warcraft. In WoW you progress with one character until it becomes stale and you must do everything all over again. In FFXIV, your progression is made with the character rather than the class you are representing, meaning that if I get tired of playing a Summoner and I switch to a Dragoon, I will have lost no progress in the mainstory, any of my achievments or titles or anything else along those lines. The only thing i have to do is level my Dragoon up to whatever level I so desire. If I realize Dragoon isn't for me, I can simply switch back to my Summoner (same level as it was before I switched) completely free or try out a new class all together and keep my progress for both Summoner and Dragoon so I can return later.
While I could spend all day talking about this game and all the features it has, it's time for some Pro's and Con's, since unfortunelty this game isn't for everyone.
Pro's
-Hands down the best story that I have every seen in an MMORPG, it will not only keep you captivated but it also puts you as the center of attention, which is different than how other games such as World of Warcraft do it.
-Class system is amazing for someone who wants to try multiple different classes without wanting to re-roll their characters or make alts, it is actually encouraged you try and play all the classes and see what one works for you.
-While not the most graphic amazing game, it will certainly blow a lot of games out of the water. FFXIV just looks stunning if you take a second to enjoy all the great features this game has like dynamic weather, awesome backdrops and  a pretty good character creation page.
-Crafting in this game is hands down the best I have ever seen in an MMORPG. Some people level one battle class up to max level and then focus the remainder of their time playing crafting and gathering classes. Whiel some games make these activities a side thing, FFXIV makes them classes all on their own and completely viable to spend all your time and money just working with these classes.
-You absolutely cannot talk about a Final Fantasy game without talking about the music that goes with it. The music in this game is fantastic in every regard. If you are a music nut you will die for some of the sound tracks in this game.
-Finally, this game gets tons of content periodically in patches. The time between patches is roughly 2-3 months at a time (which sounds like heaven if you come from WoW) and each patch is pack full with fresh new content and things to do (and not selfie cams and twitter...)
Con's
-Although the story in this game is amazing it is a very story motivated game and as such may not interest some people. There is no way around the Main Story Quests (MSQ) in thsi game, you have to do them to unlock the content. Although you can technically rush through all the dialogue and skip all the cinematics, you will be missing a huge part of what makes this game great.
-While the end game raids are all fun, they are not what a raider from WoW would expect. Each major content patch (X.0 X.2, X.4) they will introduce 4 new bosses in the existing raid. At the start of every expansion (well we only have Heavensward and A Realm Reborn to go off of atm) they introduce a new raid with 4 bosses, and like I said every major content patch adds 4 new bosses to that raid, which if you come from wow can be a bit bland. Although I think these fights are great I can also see how some people would not like this.
-Lack of class customization. This game does not have class specilization like WoW or SWTOR do. If I am playing a Dragoon and I see a Dragoon right next to me at the same level, we are going to have the exact same abilities. This feature is kind of made up from the fact that you can be all classes but it doesn't really. That beign said its not terrible not picking talents and whatnot, its just a cool feature that isn't there for reasons that make sense (no cookie-cutter builds or best paths)
-The grind. While no where near as bad as a Korean MMORPG this game has a really really long leveling grind. I basically split the leveling process into 3 major steps. The 1-50 leveling which is made up of the A Realm Reborn story and learning your class and whatnot. This step was made easier when Heavensward launched as they made MSQ give double xp. Not terrible but kinda lengthy. Next is the 2.1-2.55 leveling experience which is by far the worst part of this game. Once you hit level 50 and complete the main story you then enter something similar to a post story. This post story will set up the stage for the Heavensward expansion but is completely manditory and very very VERY slow. If you haven't bought Heavensward at this point you will get 0 exp and if you have bought Heavensward you will probably get one level, maybe. The 2.X series probably takes around 20 hours all together to complete and during said time you will feel like you aren't getting anything (exp wise) but will get little gear upgrades. The final step is the Heavensward part 50-60, I know this is technically a review for A Realm Reborn, but I will talk about it anyways. This step is probably the most enjoyable as you will be introduced with a new story and a new enviornment along with some new chracters. The Heavensward story is fantastic, but you have to slog through the post story to get there.
Those are the major things about this game, obviously there are tons more things I could say but to keep this from being a novel, I will leave the review here. Overall this game is a great buy and any MMORPG player should at least try it out. Some important things to note are that there is a free trial if anyone wants to try it before they buy, you will get 14 days to play the game with a level cap of 20. Also another important note is that if you buy this product on Steam you will be forced to buy every expansion after on Steam, which some people dislike since it regularly goes on sale other places and rarely goes on sale through Steam. On the bright side, you can use your Steam wallet to pay for the monthly fee so it has its ups and downs. Finally, the Square Enix website can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes but don't let that discourage you, this is a great game and I hope to see you all in Eorzea! <3 Sarris Wolf, Behemoth

One of the best MMORPGS since The days of vanilla WoW and Everquest II. One of the things that sets this game apart from current mmo's is the idea that your character is a person just like you. What I mean by that is that your character is not defined as a Mage or warrior, but rather someone who has learned how to be a Mage or warrior; in FFXIV, you can have one character that masters all classes and all professions.
Professions (crafting classes) are very unique in that each crafting profession gets skills to help them in the world, for example, the fisherman profession around level 10 gets a sneak skill so they can traverse the world without being attacked. The fighting classes are separated into decouples of war, and decouples of magic; each with gear specified uniquely for it. The fighting classes include gladiator, pugalist, marauder, lancer, archer and rogue. The magic classes include the thaumaturge, the conjurer, and the arcanist.
What is so incredibly awesome about FFXIV is how all of these classes can be combined with another to create a more powerful and unique class. For example, you can create a paladin by getting your character to level 30 with a gladiator, and getting to level 15 with the conjurer, to create a slight mix of the two.
This game will forever be in my heart as the most immersive MMORPG and the mmo that has truly been worth a monthly payment. If I talked about everything in FFXIV, I'd be here all day typing, but in short, if you are questioning the value of this game, give the trial a try and you will quickly find out if you are a fan. Specs wise, the game runs beautifully, and for a game made quite a while ago, it graphically has withstood the test of time. I would recommend this game to any gamer who is searching for a great community, a great immersive experience, and a great breathe of fresh mmo air.

Transistor is a beautiful, lovingly-crafted experience, following the vein of Bastion: a visually and auditorially stunning game that delivers an emotionally impactful story in a short amount of time. The art direction and soundtrack are both superb; it's one of the prettiest games I've ever played, and has one of my favorite OSTs of all time.
Cloudbank feels like a real city, despite being wholly void of interactable NPCs; it truly feels like you're strolling through the remains of a city that merely hours ago was full of life, with nobody around but the automated Process and the voice of your companion. The storytelling is excellent, the voice acting is incredible, and the characters — especially the villains — feel like actual people with motivations of their own. The story is as much about the Camerata as it is about Red, and it's damn compelling.
On top of all of this, the gameplay is excellent. The combat is incredibly customizable and fluid, with hundreds upon hundreds of viable combinations of abilities. It feels almost like a combination of Bastion and Dragon Age: Origins; you could play it just like you would Bastion, or you can pause time and plan out your moves each turn for maximum efficiency. It's engaging, and acts as a perfect segue between plot points.
Transistor is masterfully crafted, and I'd recommend it for just about everyone.

To start, The Room is a mobile game, just to get that out there, and we all know how mobile games with a PC release turn out on the PC, however, The Room is different. Fireproof remakes the game from the ground up to make sure it plays well on the PC, looks nice, and isn't another clunky mobile port.
To get to the actual gameplay, The Room is a neat little puzzle game with an interesting kind of mystery behind the story. This game requires you to be very observant and pick up on small details and remember every little thing about the room you're stuck in. Of course, if you have them enabled, hints can help you out, but I personally prefer to figure things out on my own. I used hints once or twice when I was really stuck and had no clue what to do, but with the hints, there is no need to use any form of outside walkthrough as long as you're patient and work at your own pace and don't try to rush through the game. The hints will get gradually more and more obvious as to what you need to do. Personally, for me, the game wasn't extremely hard, but it wasn't a walk in the park or anything. If you don't use the hints, there's no hand-holding, it's all up to you to figure things out, besides the tutorial, obviously. The game took me about 2 hours to complete, so it's not a very long game, but it is a very fun and satisfying game to play when you figure out the puzzles. The Room Two took about the same amount of time for me, but the puzzles felt like they had more to do, it's just that I kinda had the hang of the tricks this game pulls and I figured things out quicker. According to my friend who plays them on mobile, The Room Three is much longer, but take that with a grain of salt.
At the time of writing this review, I've just beat The Room Two, which I just recently learned got a Steam release about a month ago. I figured I'd go back and write reviews for both games and try and spread the word. If you find that you enjoy the games, I highly suggest you go back and write reviews and spread the word to your friends, other wise The Room Three will not get a Steam release. It's all about player feedback for Fireproof.

So after replaying all of the games in the series I have to say this is my favourite. It's not perfect, and it is very unforgiving in places but for me there are so many things to enjoy in this game. I should probably mention any bias I have here. Tomb raider 1 and 2 were my first games on the PS1, so this was the first game I really followed the build up and development of. I remember buying magazines the and seeing all the new screenshots, and playing the Area 51 demo where you randomly jump off the tower over the fence instead of finding the articfact.
So for the review bit. The game improves visually on the first two, significantly in the PC version, it might sound strange to say but I find the game to be beautiful in it's own way. The vibrance of parts of the India, Pacific Islands and the first Nevada level is refeshing and the sunset tone of the last two Nevada levels are visually very pleasing. Lara herself looks good, the last of the classic raiders where she looks somewhat normal in game and didn't have two massive ballons slapped on her chest. Her ponytail flickering bothered me when the camera came in too close behind her but that's a minor issue.
The background audio for each of the levels enhances the feeling of being in those places, with sounds of the jungle, tribal drums, snakes and crickets etc., it should be noted the sound quality isn't amazing (noticably worse quality than TR4 or TR5). Lara's voice is how I will always expect it to be, mature sounding, non-whiny, unlike TR4, TR5 and the reboot. Remixes of the classic Tomb Raider music appear in the levels. The India remix is probably some of my favourite music ever from a video game and the military style remix is well done and used suitably.
Gameplay wise it is the same block-based system of old, and if you don't like that then it's not the game for you. I will say that it is a system that takes time to get used to but once you do it's not all that bad. New moves such as crawling and monkeyswing might seem minor but they add to the realism of Lara's movemove through levels much like her being able to climb ladders introduced in TR2. One of my issues with the newer games is that Lara never feels very weighted, she magically flies further forward if the jump is longer and her place in the environement always feels a little unreal. In the older games there is no assist for jumps, you just die if it is wrong, that might sound harsh but it is the challenge of platforming that makes up a large part of the games enjoyment. Combat is as always not a strong point of the earlier games, it is something you get used to though, and there is still something about the the sound of drawing those pistols and her just holing them that brings enjoyment. One big plus for me with this game was the level design. You often pass by earlier/later stages of a level which adds to the environements somewhat. I never really felt as though I was backtracking although you do pass through certaina areas numerous times. The non-linear approach to some of the levels is also refreshing, and there are still parts of the game I haven't seen. You can also play the middle three levels in any order adding to your choice. Collectables, in the form of secrets, are present. Some of these are very challenging to find, but this really added to the game for me, and generally they are built into the levels well.
Story wise the game is a little thin. There is something there but it's really just as an excuse to send Lara off to these locations. Her interactions with various characters are fun though and allow for Lara's wit and some personality to come through. Settings wise, I found nearly all of the 5 sections enjoyable. London was the exception (mainly the two middle levels) but they all have their own looks. There are ruins, I'm not sure there is an actual Tomb, but it fits in with her thirst for adventure.
Overall this is a game I get a lot of enjoyment from. I have played through it 3 times in the last year, the last time just for enjoyment (once you have played through once and don't die at every turn the game is a lot more fun to play) taking in a lot more of the visuals/audio mention in this review. Most definitely my favourite of the series.

WONDERFUL! One of the best games I've played in a while. The story is not complex, but the implications are very nice. I think the art is very in line with the game's theme and I really think the general feeling of working in the conditions presented by the game are close to reality. You memory skills will be tested. And it really provides for a fantastic way to spend you time. Some will surely not call it fun, but again this might just be what makes it a pearl in its right.
Without it, it wouldn't make much sense, but it's only important in its presentation. You could still get by with a wonderful game if we were talking about assembling computer chips in a factory. Your brain will be tested. Make the right moral decision, but the poor official decision and your boss will not like it.
Oh, this is the best part of it. Get something right and you get rewarded. Get something wrong and you get penalized (though not at first, though). I'm sure it would work better in a tactile screen but the mouse doesn't distract you that much either.
Pretty simple, but far out. Adds to the complexity of finding out who's a male or female, for example, and that's a very nice touch.
You might get a bit tired of it, but it's in line with not only the theme but the imagination of what that country would be. I can't remember anything but the theme, though, so either there was no more music or it wasn't memorable enough.
I did replay it to get to the alternative endings (those I could figure out might make a different), then tried some of the other extra possibilities and then left it at that, the memory of it being all that matters now.
8/10 would punch my monitor again.

One of the more fair and tame platform-hell games out there, at least of the ones that I've seen.  Despite the name, the challenge actually comes from using your brain to circumvent most of the traps, instead of intense platform gaming skill.  There's more memorization and crafty dodging than there is frame-perfect timing and exact jumps, though there is still a need for intermediate platforming acuity.
Part of the draw for me was the creativity in the logic-less land of kawaii death.  Many surprise hits actually just made me laugh on the inside thinking "are you serious?  THAT just happened?"  Instead of just surprise spikes slapped onto every other pixel of land, sometimes enemies popped out that block you just hit, sometimes the entire level shifted to send you into an abyss, sometimes you had to outrun things that you didn't initially even know was a threat!  But then, bit by bit, you ignore that block, jump just a little later, and speed just that much faster past these points, making real progress without it feeling like too much of an unfair slog.
Pretty tight controls, a sufficiently cutesy art style, and fun level design combine for an entertaining gauntlet of hundreds of lost lives.  As with any side-scrolling platformer, a controller would be highly recommended.

If you haven't, imagine what I Wanna Be The Guy would be like if it were a puzzle-platformer instead of a precision-platformer.  Hidden traps lurk around even corner, just when you least expect it, and the traps must be manipulated in the right order or in the right position to progress.  The game is much less difficult than it seems, because after the initial "gotcha!" of an unknown trap it becomes simple to bait out and avoid, and the real challenge is often the puzzle of finding out how to grab the goalpost at the end of the level (it's harder than it sounds!).  Levels are fairly short once trap locations are memorized, and despite the frequent deaths and frustration the game can be completed in just a few hours.  The colorful cartoony art style helps the medicine go down smoother, too.

I would take any complaints about balance issues with a grain of salt.  Yes, if you're caught out of position by a sword-wielding opponent, you're dead.  Launchers are excellent on small maps where players tend to bunch up and are vulnerable to splash damage.
On the other hand, if you pay attention to enemy positions and fight at range, swords are useless.  If you stay out of big melees and work the angles, launchers can be countered.  If there's any area where there are balance issues, I'd say it's in the armors.  A big portion of the armor selections are next-to-useless.  Which would you rather have: a helmet that gives a 5% damage bonus for shotguns and rifles, or a helmet that gives a 5% damage bonus for you AND all your nearby teammates for ALL WEAPONS?  Could use some tweaking.
Strategy and teamwork are very important in this game.  Combining weapon loadouts that synergize, and choosing the right armor can make the difference between a useful loadout and one that can't get anything done.  I really appreciate how leveling up and unlocking new weapons and armor opens up new styles of play, while the starting weapons and armor never stop being useful.  Sticking together with your team is critical, as it's almost impossible to win a two-on-one fight (if your opponents know what they're doing anyway).
The map design is great.  Mobility and positioning are a key element of strategy, particularly on Titan maps, which have opportunities for sword ganking, sniping, and everything inbetween.
Personally, I've been waiting for a game to attempt this kind of art style for a long time.  It's very reminiscent of Mirror's Edge, so if you like the visual style of that game, you'll enjoy the look and feel of Minimum.
That said, it really shows that the game is still in development.  There aren't a lot of servers, the automatching often puts you on servers with no players, I've exprienced some audio/visual bugs, and I'm pretty sure the "Pickup Hell" weapon, that claims to make creeps drop more items, doesn't actually do what it says.  On one of the Titan maps, I fell into a crack and was stuck until an opponent killed me (The Event).  I would like to see more maps, of course, and I feel that the Horde mode would be more fun if the difficulty level didn't ramp up quite so fast (I haven't seen anyone make it past the third wave without heavily exploiting the enemy AI and level design).
Overall, a really fun third-person shooter that, I hope, will continue to improve.  It's $10 US, so buy it if you're sick of CoD.  What do you have to lose?

Think about it, the original release of FFXIV probably cost SE over 100 million to develop and launch.   Everyone hated it, so they remade the entire game (an MMO) from the ground up in 2 years.    2 years.    That is not enough time to make a substantial and engaging MMO, and it is very apparent while playing.
- Boring uninspired "quests" that cannot be skipped or ignored, that inolve you running and talking to sometimes 3 or more npc's just to return to the original quest giver and speak to them again to complete.  I'm talking main story quests too.
- Lazy combat system.   Literally a dumbed down version of WoW's combat system, but with even less penalty for death.
- Invisible walls.  Who even remotely thinks a world with invisible walls is fun to explore?  Walkways you cant jump down? Check.  Ladders you cant climb? Check.  Doors that don't open? Everywhere.
- Bad social aspect.   Want to buy this game with a friend and roll new toons to take to level cap together?  HAH.   You will be forced to do the main quest and class quests, and you will do them solo.   Dungeon groups will be made matchmaking style.
- Travel is a joke.  Who cares about the gameworld?  You're just going to teleport back and forth between static quest givers instantly.  No encouragement to explore, everything is mapped for you with all points of interested labeled upon entering a zone.
- Boring classes.   They butchered what could have been a great job system.  No cool utility spells.  Odd class progression; I have to have one class at level 30 and another at 15 before I can become a......... warrior?  Short of the castrated holy trinity combat system used in groups, and the odd crafting request deep in end game, classes can provide each other nothing.
One positive I will give this game is the robust character creation tool, (lucky it's so good as you are forced to pay a larger monthly fee if you wish to roll an alt.)  Characters look incredible, you can customize right down to different colored eyes and you can pan the camera really well in game to stare at all your pixels.
If you are an MMO vet pining for an experience like FFXI, Pre Wrath WoW, Pre Luclin EQ, DAoC, Asheron's Call, Star Wars Galaxies etc. stay far away from this shameless cash grab.
If you arent, go play Project 1999 and be enlightened as to what an MMO could be.  WAS.
Think about how much It must have cost to originally launch this game. Over 100 million easy.  Do you think they spent that amount on a game twice?  No, I think they spent a fraction of the amount of time and money on the actual reboot and instead put the bulk of the cash towards marketing, and perhaps toward making all these positive reviews I keep seeing appear.  Don't be fooled.

I really enjoyed the first Treasures of Montezuma game on iOS, but this isn't as good. ToM is a match 3 series where the main twist is that you can activate various powers by matching the same color twice. In the first game (which isn't on PC), your exciting and straightforward goal was to match up a quota of specially marked tiles before time ran out. But this fourth game switches between several different gimmicky goals, none of which is very satisfying. There's still a brutal time limit... but only for getting a gold rank on the level, because there's no way to fail a level, and you get to progress regardless of how long you take. Doing poorly doesn't give you as much money to unlock better power ups, but you'll always get to move on to the next level so who cares. (Basically the game does the equivalent of dumping a poor student in the "remedial" math class that's so full of delinquents and idiots that no one learns anything, but they all 'graduate' anyway). And even if you decide to take the game seriously and try to get gold on every level, you'll be slowed down by the distracting animations of the powers activating, and the matched blocks' exploded fragments raining down ON TOP OF THE BOARD THAT YOU'RE TRYING TO SEE WHILE THE CLOCK COUNTS DOWN EVERY PRECIOUS SECOND.
One of the other reviews mentioned that (SPOILERS!) a time traveling Cortez shows up, so I was hoping for wacky characters like the cannibal ogre in the first Puzzle Quest but so far it's been just "MATCH COLORED TOKENS TO MAGICALLY EXCAVATE THE TEMPLE!"
tl;dr - Go play the first Montezuma game if you've got an iPad, or I guess go play Bejeweled if you want a PC equivalent.
